The first limb is answered squarely and bluntly — "No, I can't confirm that," with a counter-claim and a reason (population growth). The NCEA limb is not touched at all. There is also a quiet reframe from 'kids going to school' (attendance) to 'kids in the school system' (enrolment). Half the question was engaged head-on, half was passed over.
question: Can he confirm that despite spending $5 billion more a year on education, there are fewer kids going to school and more leaving without NCEA than six years ago?
statement: No, I can’t confirm that there are fewer kids in the school system. In fact, there are more kids in the school system than there were when we became the Government; it’s called population growth.

explanation: Asked to confirm longer waits for surgery, cancer treatment, GPs and EDs. Opens with a jibe about the questioner's script, then substitutes his own proposition — 'our health system has performed remarkably well' — and never confirms or denies any of the four waiting-time claims. Answers a different question than the one asked.
question: Can he confirm that despite spending half a billion dollars rearranging district health boards, Kiwis are waiting longer for surgery, longer for cancer treatment, longer to see a GP, and longer in overcrowded emergency departments?
statement: He gave up on education relatively quickly—clearly it wasn’t part of the script. What I can confirm is that our health system has performed remarkably well, despite having to support New Zealand through a global pandemic.

explanation: Asked to confirm 57,000 more on jobseeker and 35,000 more children in benefit-dependent homes. Neither figure is confirmed or denied; he confirms a different, favourable statistic (more people exiting benefits into work) instead. The 'I can confirm' construction mirrors the question's form without engaging its content.
question: Can he confirm that despite spending $2 billion more on social development than six years ago, there are 57,000 more Kiwis on the jobseeker benefit, and there are 35,000 more children growing up in benefit-dependent homes?
statement: I note he’s given up on health now already, as well, after a single question. But I can confirm that we have more New Zealanders exiting a benefit and going into work under this Government because of the investments that we’ve been making in that system to ensure that we are supporting Kiwis back into work.

explanation: Asked to confirm under 2 percent of the 100,000 KiwiBuild houses were built. '2 percent more than was built under the last National Government' implicitly accepts the 2 percent figure, so the core is touched — but it is never stated as a confirmation, and the bulk of the answer moves to State houses, consents and National's RMA position. Partial engagement.
question: Can he confirm that the Government has built less than 2 percent of the 100,000 KiwiBuild houses it promised six years ago?
statement: I note that’s still 2 percent more than was built under the last National Government, because on this side of the House we believe that when you’re in a housing crisis, you should build more houses. We’re building more State houses than any Government since the 1950s. We’ve had record building consents, and I note, for example, that one of the things we’re doing that’s helping to build more houses faster is the fast-track consenting. I note the National Party’s pledge to repeal the repeal of the Resource Management Act and cut the funding for the people who would have to design the alternative replacement.

explanation: Asked to confirm $155m spent and not a metre of track delivered. Calling it 'an intergenerational project' tacitly concedes nothing is built yet, which is a glancing engagement, but neither the spend nor the zero-delivery claim is addressed, and he moves to National's unstarted roading projects.
question: Can he confirm that despite spending $155 million on Auckland Light Rail over the last six years, the Government still hasn’t delivered a single metre of track?
statement: Auckland Light Rail is an intergenerational project. Unlike the members opposite, we’re not going to give up on that. I noticed, for example, some of the roading projects that National promised in the nine years they were in Government never started in the entire nine years they were in Government.

explanation: A narrow yes/no follow-up: is KiwiBuild also an intergenerational project? The reply refuses the frame without answering it — 'I'm not going to make any apology for...' is neither a yes, a no, nor a stated refusal to answer. A tightly-drawn question left entirely untouched.
question: But, based on that, is KiwiBuild also an intergenerational project?
statement: As I’ve indicated, I’m not going to make any apology for the fact that our Government has been focused on building our way out of a housing crisis.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his police Minister that New Zealanders feel safer. Opens with a jibe at the questioner, then lists police numbers and resourcing; 'there is more work to be done' gestures near the topic but he never says whether he agrees with the Minister, and none of the three cited statistics is engaged.
question: Does he agree with his police Minister that New Zealanders feel safer than six years ago, despite a 107 percent increase in serious assaults, 70 percent increase in gang members, and two ram raids happening every single day in New Zealand?
statement: The most surprising thing about that question was that Nicola Willis’ lips didn’t move while he was asking it. I am very proud of the fact that we have 1,800 more police on the beat under our Government, and that our police are better resourced than they ever have been before. There is more work to be done in the law and order space—there’s no question about that—but, unlike the National Party, who talk a tough game on law and order and then fail to deliver when they are in Government, we are backing our police to do the job that’s ahead of them.

explanation: Asked whether he regrets the listed outcomes. 'So many of the claims in his statement... simply do not add up' is a real, if indirect, answer — it disputes the premise, implying no regret. But the regret question itself is never answered and most of the reply pivots to National's tax policy and online gambling. Partial.
question: Does he regret that despite the Government spending $60 billion more than six years ago, he’s left the country with a shrinking economy, more crime, worse health, worse education, more job seekers, higher rents, higher prices, higher interest rates, and a record number of Kiwis saying this country is going in the wrong direction?
statement: The member just needs to cheer up. So many of the claims in his statement—much like the claims made in their alternative tax policy released yesterday—simply do not add up. I would note that National’s vision for the future of New Zealand is that we will sell $5 billion a year worth of houses to foreign investors and we will have four times as many New Zealanders gambling online in order to make their numbers add up. Perhaps those New Zealanders taking up online gambling will be those who get shut out of the housing market and just give up hope.

explanation: 'Does he stand by all of his Government's statements and policies?' — answered 'Yes' in the first word, directly and completely. The long list that follows is elaboration; its length and self-serving content bear on Specificity and Focus, not on whether the question was answered.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and policies?
statement: Yes, particularly the fact that there are 77,000 fewer children living in poverty than when we became the Government; that we have taken record numbers of New Zealanders off benefits and got them into work. We have delivered a hundred million free and healthy school lunches. We have 3,800 more teachers in our classrooms, and, in fact, there are 2,250 more classrooms under this Government. We’ve provided 1.4 million packs of period products in schools. We’ve reduced the strain on the families of 400,000 students by not asking them for school donations. We have delivered 26 weeks of paid parental leave. Kiwis are enjoying healthier homes and cheaper power bills because of the 110,000 low-income families that have benefited from warmer Kiwi homes. We’ve delivered free doctors visits for the under-14s. We’ve delivered more than 13,000 additional public homes—one in seven of the public homes that we have at the moment. We have 1,800 more police on the beat. We have delivered lower emissions three years in a row under our Government, where we have record levels of renewable electricity generation, and the lowest level of coal imports since 2013. I could go on.

explanation: Asked whether he is proud of the housing record, plus a rhetorical rider about what failure would look like. He answers the core squarely — 'I am very proud of the work that we have been doing' — and gives his reasons. The rider is not addressed, but it was the softer, rhetorical half of the question.
question: Is he proud of his Government’s record on housing, when the average house price is up $220,000, or 33 percent, while average weekly rents are up $175 a week, or 44 percent, both significantly outstripping people’s wage growth since 2017, and, if that’s success on housing, what would his Government failing have looked like?
statement: Given the shortage of houses that the Government’s inherited, and the work that we have done to build record numbers of new public homes, and the record numbers of building consents that we are seeing, we are starting to turn around the situation that we inherited in housing. That was never going to be an overnight answer, but I am very proud of the work that we have been doing to ensure that we build our way out of the housing crisis.

explanation: Asked whether he understands that rising prices despite added supply mean the policies failed. 'What I do understand is...' redirects to what would happen under a change of Government. The supply-price logic and the failure claim are both left untouched; the answer is about the Opposition, not the question.
question: Does the Prime Minister understand that if his Government inherited a shortage and increased supply, the price would go down, but the fact that the price went up means that his Government’s housing policies have failed at great cost to New Zealanders?
statement: What I do understand is that all of the problems that the member asked questions about will get worse under a change of Government that proposes to cut funding for public services, that proposes to put more people out of work, and that proposes a range of economic policies that will take the country backwards.

explanation: A two-part question: was Ardern right, or were the gestures ineffectual given a 3 percent net emissions rise? He contests the emissions premise ('in the last three years, our emissions have gone down'), which engages the effectiveness half, then pivots to what ACT and National would cut. The Ardern question is never answered.
question: Was Jacinda Ardern right when she said, “Climate change is my generation’s nuclear-free moment” and declared a climate emergency, or, given the Ministry for the Environment’s latest Greenhouse Gas Inventory reports net emissions increased 3 percent under his Government, were those gestures just a warning to New Zealanders they’d be subject to six years of ineffectual gesture politics by Labour?
statement: I note that the member neglected to mention that, in the last three years, our emissions have gone down because of the work of this Government. I note that almost every one of the initiatives that the Government has in place that have helped to achieve that reduction in emissions are on the chopping block either by the ACT Party or by the National Party.

explanation: Asked whether he is proud of his education Ministers given falling attendance. He does not answer the pride question, but he takes on the substance directly: attributes the first figure to COVID isolation rules and concedes the doubling of persistent absence is 'completely unacceptable'. That is squarely engaging what was asked rather than dodging it, so it scores well above the pivots elsewhere in this set.
question: Is he proud of the performance of his Government’s education Ministers, when the education budget has increased by 38 percent in five years, but the portion of children regularly attending school has fallen from 70 percent down to 60 percent, the portion of kids who are chronically absent has doubled from 4 percent to 8 percent; is he proud to have a lower portion of kids going to school, despite spending an extra 5 billion bucks a year on education?
statement: Well, of course it’s not schools that determine which kids actually regularly attend; that, of course, is what parents determine. But in terms of the regular non-attendance, I note that the first figure the member quoted has been most significantly influenced by the mandatory seven-day isolation period for COVID-19. In terms of the doubling of the number of students who are persistently absent, that is completely unacceptable and we do need to do more to get those kids who have been disengaged from the education system for far too long back into some form of education, training, or employment.

explanation: Asked whether the 30% prison-reduction goal still stands and whether it has affected public safety. Davis engages both halves — he disputes the premise, states he is 'progressing no specific policies to further reduce the total prison population', and addresses public safety directly — but never plainly says whether the target itself is still held. Partial engagement with the core, so mid-range.
question: Does the Government still have a goal of reducing the prison population by 30 percent, irrespective of the level of crime in our communities; if so, has that goal impacted on public safety?
statement: When we became Government, there was a prison population crisis—a moral and fiscal failure, according to Bill English—which was predicted to see the population balloon to more than 13,000 people by now, far more than the network could accommodate by some 2,000 extra places needed. That’s why we set a long-term 15-year target reflecting the situation at the time. When we set the target, it was not, as the member’s question implies, a policy to do so instantaneously or without regards for any other factors, including public safety. The Government will continue to protect public safety and support the justice system to hold offenders to account, and I am progressing no specific policies to further reduce the total prison population. We inherited a prison system that was bursting at the seams, and we faced things like quadruple bunking and converting old boarding schools into prison facilities. The member asks about public safety, but I don’t think having to put prisoners in old boarding schools would have been safe for anyone.

explanation: Two-part question: do you stand by the statement, and if so why. The first part is answered directly and immediately ('I stand by my full statement'). The 'why' is never reached — the answer pivots to a jab at the National spokesperson. Half the question squarely addressed, half dodged.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “It is my view that New Zealanders feel safer”; if so, why?
statement: I stand by my full statement at the time it was given. It is important, though, to consider all statements in full and the context in which they were given. For instance, I’m advised that, in speaking with Today FM last year, the National Party spokesperson for police was reported saying, “When I was in police, I was a police dog.” [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what further steps she has taken to improve community safety. No step is named at all; the entire answer is a joke about investigating Nicola Willis' tax plan and charging Peeni Henare. The question is not engaged.
question: What further steps has she taken to improve community safety?
statement: I’ve previously spoken of the importance of police’s operational independence, and I respect this important principle. However, if I did have the power to direct police, I would be tempted to ask police to immediately begin an investigation into the wilful damage caused to Nicola Willis’ tax plan, which has been found absolutely full of holes. Further, I would consider asking police to lay charges against the Hon Peeni Henare for the illegal possession of firearms—specifically “Gun No. 1”—

explanation: A narrow two-part factual question, and both numbers are given: 52,404 more on jobseeker support than September 2017, and 34,872 for more than a year. The surrounding framing and favourable comparisons are spin, but spin does not lower forthrightness — the figures asked for were delivered.
question: How many more people, if any, are on the jobseeker benefit as recorded in the June 2023 quarter compared to the September 2017 quarter, and how many more people, if any, spent more than a year on the jobseeker benefit as recorded in the June 2023 quarter compared to the September 2017 quarter?
statement: It is hard for some to reconcile our near-record unemployment rates, our record labour force participation and employment rates, and the record number of Kiwis in work with benefit numbers because it is complex. Despite the strength of the labour market, we do have 52,404 more New Zealanders receiving jobseeker support than in September 2017, with 34,872 for more than a year. But as at July, around 37,000 of our job seekers are actually earning an income while on benefit, 16 percent more than in 2017, and in March 2011—three years after the beginning of the global financial crisis—12.3 percent of our working-age population were receiving a main benefit. In March 2023, three years after the beginning of the global pandemic, that number is 11.1 percent. We have come through COVID strong, but we certainly know that there is more to do.

explanation: Asked to explain WHY jobseeker numbers rose despite labour shortages. The answer offers only 'it is complex' as explanation, then pivots to 100,000 moving off benefit and pride in training investment. It acknowledges the tension but never supplies a reason, so the core of the question is avoided.
question: Can she explain why, despite two years of businesses crying out for staff all over the country, there are now over 57,000 more people on the jobseeker benefit and there are 35,000 more people who’ve spent longer than a year, so are now long-term welfare recipients under her watch?
statement: As I said, it is hard to reconcile our near-record low unemployment and more Kiwis in employment with the benefit numbers sometimes because it is complex. But I do want to just mention that more than 100,000 Kiwis moved off benefit and into employment last year. That was 25.7 percent higher than the 79,737 in 2017. I’m very proud of the investment we have put into upskilling and training, and supporting New Zealanders into employment. We need to continue that work, and we certainly are the people to do that.

explanation: Asked to explain why a record 211,000 children are in benefit-dependent homes. No explanation of the number is attempted; the answer asserts those children are better off and then warns about what National might cut. It answers a different question than the one asked.
question: Can she explain why, after two years of businesses in every part of New Zealand being desperate for staff, there is a record 211,000 children being raised in benefit-dependent homes under her Government?
statement: I want to say that the children that are living in homes that are receiving a benefit are better off under us because of the investment that we’ve made, and I’m really proud of that. We continue to support their parents, including those sole parents who are on benefit, with things like the Training Incentive Allowance, which has been reinstated under us. It was axed under the former National Government, and I would be fearful if I was a New Zealander about what could potentially be cut in the welfare system if they had the opportunity to take the reins.

explanation: Asked whether she takes any responsibility for rising welfare dependency. The answer inverts the frame — 'what I take responsibility for are...' followed by a list of programme numbers. An implicit refusal is buried in there, but she never says whether she accepts responsibility for what was actually put to her; she answers her own reframed question instead.
question: Does the Minister take any responsibility for consigning more New Zealanders to a life of welfare dependency—and their children—and wasting a golden opportunity to support New Zealanders into work?
statement: What I take responsibility for are the over 5,000 young people that have successfully gone through Mana in Mahi; over 50,000 New Zealanders who have participated in the Apprenticeship Boost programme; nearly 30,000, I believe, with Flexi-wage; and the nearly 5,000 who have taken up the training incentive allowance. That’s what we take responsibility for.

explanation: Asked what changes are being made to early childhood education. The answer names the change immediately: extending 20 hours' free ECE to two-year-olds. The cost-of-living framing around it is padding, not evasion.
question: What changes is the Government making to early childhood education?
statement: We are easing cost of living pressures for parents by extending 20 hours’ free early childhood education (ECE) to twoyear-olds. Childcare is one of the biggest costs New Zealand families face, so this change will make a big difference. We know that people are feeling the pressure right now, and we are determined to do all we can to support New Zealand families through these tough times as we plan for the future.

explanation: Asked how many families will benefit. A figure is given directly — around 40,000 two-year-olds, plus 79 percent of children attending ECE. The unit shifts from families to children, but the question is squarely engaged and quantified.
question: How many families will benefit?
statement: The changes brought about by the Government at the Budget this year mean around 40,000 two-year-olds will benefit from breaking down the cost barrier to early childhood education. It means that 79 percent of all children attending ECE will now get help with childcare, compared to 60 percent when we became Government. Extending 20 hours’ free to two-year-olds follows Labour’s legacy of introducing 20 hours’ free childcare to three- to five-year-olds in 2007, and it will continue to significantly reduce financial pressures on families at critical early years.

explanation: Asked how much families will save each fortnight. The answer gives $130 per week — the quantity asked for, in a different time unit. The core of the question is met; only the unit is off.
question: How much will families save each fortnight?
statement: Under our policy, families with two-year-olds are expected to save $130 per week, which is much more than what other parties are offering in this space. It builds on the progress that we have made over the last six years, supporting hardworking families through increases to the childcare subsidy, free healthy school lunches, and free period products in schools, and boosting Working for Families and Best Start.

explanation: Asked what other ECE changes are being made. The answer lists them: funding changes to boost teacher pay, address the funding model, support the home-based sector, and close the pay parity gap. Direct and on-point.
question: What other changes is the Government making to the early childhood education sector?
statement: Today, I am proud that we have confirmed a raft of early learning funding changes to boost teacher pay, to address systemic issues in the ECE funding model, and to support the home-based sector. I know from personal experience that those who work in the ECE sector must be recognised for the work they do with our littlest tamariki. We have delivered on our promise to make things fairer for ECE teachers by closing the pay parity gap this term of Parliament. On this side of the House, we value teachers and the vital role they have in educating our young people to be the best that they can be.

explanation: Asked what recent reports he has seen on greenhouse gas emissions. The answer names the source and the figures immediately — Stats NZ, 18.43 million tonnes for the December 2022 quarter against 20.5 million at the end of 2017. Direct and complete.
question: What recent reports, if any, has he seen on New Zealand’s greenhouse gas emissions?
statement: Stats NZ has recently confirmed that greenhouse gas emissions fell to 18.43 million tonnes in the December 2022 quarter, following a downwards trend. This compares to 20.5 million tonnes at the end of 2017, when we came into Government. This proves that this is a Government committed to delivering effective climate action.

explanation: Asked whether the Government is delivering on its promises given polling showing 55-37 wrong-direction and an 18% vote loss, and whether Kiwis or Hipkins is wrong. Hipkins opens by attacking the questioner's own poll standing, offers a general 'proud of the track record' line, and closes attacking ACT's funding cuts. The 'is it Kiwis or you who is wrong' core is never touched and the polling numbers are never engaged. A sprawling multi-part question given a partial gesture at limb one only.
question: Is his Government really doing a good job on delivering on its promises, and, if so, then why does he think New Zealanders tell the Labour Party’s own pollsters this country’s going in the wrong direction, by a whopping margin of 55 to 37 and the governing Labour Party is being abandoned by 18 percent of voters since the last election; is it Kiwis that are overwhelmingly wrong or Chris Hipkins?
statement: Of course, one of the things that comes through in the polling is that he is one of the least popular politicians in this Parliament, and I do happen to believe New Zealanders when they make that remark. But I am very proud of the track record of this Government leading New Zealanders through a very tough set of circumstances. There is more work to do, but I notice in every one of the questions that the member has asked, he has failed to mention that he intends to cut funding for all of the support put in place to deal with the very issues he is questioning about.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen regarding foreign buyers in the housing market. Woods names the report subject directly — proposals to remove the foreign-buyer ban above $2 million — and describes what it says. It is a patsy question and the answer is campaign material, but that is Focus/Specificity; on the one question asked, it lands squarely.
question: What reports has she seen regarding foreign buyers in the housing market?
statement: I have seen some concerning reports regarding the proposed removal of the foreign-buyer ban for houses over $2 million, enabling more speculation in the housing market. We know that increased speculation will increase house prices, and that’s why we introduced legislation within our first hundred days in office to ban foreign buyers of existing houses in New Zealand. This Government believes that New Zealanders should not be outbid by wealthy foreign buyers.

explanation: Asked what proportion of foreign buyers bought houses over $2 million before the 2018 ban. Woods supplies numbers (4,120 homes/year, '$2 million homes were only 5 percent of the market') and then pivots to National's tax plan. The figure given is the share of the whole market rather than the share of foreign buyers, so it slightly misses the denominator asked for, but it reaches for the same statistic instead of dodging.
question: What proportion of foreign buyers bought houses for over $2 million prior to the 2018 ban?
statement: Before this Government’s foreign-buyer ban in 2018, an average of 4,120 homes were sold every year to foreign buyers. Homes over $2 million were only 5 percent of the market. In contrast, reports I have seen assume that nearly half of those homes would be sold for over $2 million in order to pay for some proposed tax cuts. I can advise that on this side of the House, we are not banking on an influx of overseas-based speculators in the housing market to fund tax cuts for millionaires. Once again, the evidence shows that National’s tax take does not add up.

explanation: Asked whether Government actions contributed to recession and an ongoing cost of living crisis. Robertson disputes the recession premise (with a data caveat) and then answers the cost of living limb head-on: the Government's actions 'contributed to softening the impact.' That is a clear no to the question as put. Heavy padding with achievements and an election-risk line follows, but the answer is given before the padding starts.
question: Have the Government’s actions contributed to the New Zealand economy being in recession with an ongoing cost of living crisis?
statement: Most economic commentators would reject the member’s assertion that the country is currently in recession, although we will not get the updated data for the second quarter of 2023 until next month. With regard to the longer-term pressure on the cost of living that the country has been facing, I think the Government’s actions have contributed to softening the impact, particularly on low and middle income households. While this has been a challenging time for many households, we have also managed to maintain historically low levels of unemployment and record-high levels of labour force participation during this period. More recently, we’ve also seen wages keeping track with inflation, which put more households in a stronger position to manage the current economic headwinds. Every country in the world has had to fight hard to protect their people from rising inflation. Our targeted measures—such as free and half-price public transport, the removal of prescription co-payments, and making 20 hours’ free early childhood education available for two-year-olds—do make an important difference to household budgets, and I note they would be at risk under a change of Government.

explanation: Asked whether he thinks he has been a good steward of taxpayers' money. He explicitly declines to give his own view — 'it doesn't matter what I think' — and substitutes what Fitch and Moody's think. The substance conveys an affirmative, and he does not run away from the topic, but the question asked for his own assessment and he deliberately withheld it. Partial.
question: Does he think he has been a good steward of taxpayers’ money when Government spending is up 80 percent but hospitals are in crisis, educational achievement is in decline, and many New Zealanders feel worse off?
statement: It doesn’t matter what I think about it; it matters what people like Fitch Ratings and Moody’s Analytics think about it—and they think that the Government has been responsible.

explanation: Asked whether his position is that rating agencies matter more than New Zealanders' financial security, or whether he is unaware how bad it is. He answers 'No' outright, explains why he cited the agencies (he was asked what he thought), and addresses the second limb by stating households have been doing it tough. Both limbs engaged. The 'spring is coming, cheer up' quip is tone, not evasion.
question: Is it his position that it matters more what Fitch Ratings think than it does whether New Zealanders feel financially secure, or is he that blissfully unaware of how bad the cost of living crisis is?
statement: No. The member asked me what I thought, and I told her what those two independent rating agencies think. What I also think is that a lot of New Zealand households have been doing it tough over the last little while—and that’s exactly why we’ve stepped in to support them by lifting main benefits, by lifting the family tax credit, by lifting childcare assistance, by seeing the minimum wage go up. This has been a tough time, but as indicated in today’s ANZ New Zealand Business Outlook, confidence is rising, spring is coming—the member should cheer up.

explanation: Asked why Labour Governments always wreck the economy — a loaded 'when did you stop beating your wife' question. He rejects the premise directly with a counter-narrative about Labour's record, which is the only substantive way to engage such a question, then pivots to attacking National's foreign-buyer policy via CoreLogic. Premise rejection counts as engagement; the pivot away in the back half pulls it down.
question: Why is it that whenever a Labour Government is given long enough in office, they wreck the economy, mess up the books, and leave the country going backwards?
statement: The history of New Zealand is, in fact, that when Labour is in Government, we come in, clean up the mess of the National Party, grow jobs, build houses, and support New Zealanders through tough times. We also, when we’re in Government, make sure that what we’re promising, we can pay for—and that what we promise adds up. The member might like to reflect on CoreLogic head of research Nick Goodall’s comments about what would happen with the foreign buyer policy that the member is promoting, which says that, actually, it would “affect the broader market” and it would mean that there would be a reduction in the “overall supply of housing for locals”, and this would “flow through to higher prices for all properties.” It’s the member’s policy that will make things worse for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he will join the questioner as founding members of a Johnsonville amateur dramatic society. Jocular, but a genuine yes/no with an attributable reply, so it is not a point of order or procedural motion. He answers: interested in working together on dramatic skills, but he wants to be paid so he will not join an amateur society — a qualified no, given plainly, plus a joke about a cartoon.
question: Will he—once the dust is cleared and the election campaign is over—join me as the founding members of the “Johnsonville Amateur Dramatic Society”, with a successful local performance of the 1998 young adult novel Holes?
statement: Well, I would be interested in working with the member on both of us—[Looks through papers] you’ll just have to give me a minute—honing our dramatic skills. I would like to be paid for mine; I don’t want to be in an amateur dramatic society. [Holds up printout of cartoon] But I do think we could certainly re-enact this moment from Sharon Murdoch in the Dominion Post yesterday.

explanation: Asked whether this is really the lasting impression he wishes to give — cartoons and name-calling to cover a mess. He says 'No' and immediately follows with a quip about facing an eighth National finance spokesperson. The one-word answer is complete on the yes/no put to him; the quip afterwards is Civility/Focus territory and should not move this.
question: Is this really the lasting impression that this Minister of Finance wishes to give—that in the end, he had to resort to putting up cartoons and calling people names because he had left the economy in such a mess?
statement: No. I look forward to being back here facing my eighth National Party finance spokesperson, delivering from here more of the professional, dramatic performances.

explanation: Asked how the Community Connect package is benefiting New Zealanders. Parker answers exactly that — free fares for 5-12s, half price for 13-24s from 1 July, plus flow-on congestion benefits. Direct and complete on the question put; the closing swipe at cancelling the programme is an addition, not a substitution.
question: How is the Community Connect package benefiting New Zealanders?
statement: The Community Connect package is helping ease cost of living pressures on families by providing free fares on buses, trains, and ferries for children aged five to 12 and half-price discounts for all passengers aged 13 to 24 from 1 July. This has meant cheaper public transport fares for many hundreds of thousands of Kiwis, and it’s not just public transport users benefiting from this great initiative. Access to public transport means less congestion on our roads for all road users. Cancelling the programme would increase bus fares and the cost of living, add to traffic congestion, and increase road building costs.

explanation: Asked how much a family with two primary-school-aged children would save under Community Connect. Parker gives the number for exactly that family composition: $30 per week. The question was narrow and factual and the answer hits it precisely.
question: How much would a family with two primary school - aged children save under Community Connect?
statement: Making public transport free for children makes it easier to get kids to school and helps with family budgets. Free fares for under-13s can save $30 per week for a family with two primary school - aged children. These are real savings and actual back-pocket boosts to New Zealand families that are at risk if that setting was ever to change.

explanation: Asked whether he can understand why victims are angry and cynical about a minister announcing tougher penalties 88 days from an election. He directly grants that victims have a right to feel angry — that is the core of the first half, squarely engaged — but never touches the cynicism-about-election-timing part, moving instead to disputing the 122 percent figure. Half the question reached, half sidestepped.
question: Can he understand why victims like Mrs Patel, who I spoke to just last week, might be angry that someone who’s overseen a 122 percent increase in serious assaults causing injury, over five years, decides to introduce tougher penalties only 88 days from an election but still can’t get the most basic details right; who is cynical about crime and politics now?
statement: I would say that the victims of those crimes have a right to feel angry about them. They have a right to feel aggrieved about them. And the Government is absolutely committed to addressing those issues. I would also point out that the increase in violent crimes that the member has referred to includes an increase in the reporting of family violence, something that the members on this side of the House have encouraged, and in fact we have introduced new offences in that area, which have also contributed to that increase in the overall reporting of violent crime.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: has he read the released Treasury advice on school lunches. He says he is 'aware of the Treasury report' — engagement with the subject, but 'aware of' hedges around the actual question of whether he read it, and he moves immediately to countervailing reports. Partial answer with the core hedged rather than dodged outright.
question: Has he read the recently released Treasury advice about the school lunch programme, saying “have found no impact on attendance, and ākonga Māori, who make up around 48 percent of students receiving the programme, have not benefited on most metrics, such as school functioning (e.g., paying attention in class), health, and mental wellbeing (with mental wellbeing worse off for those in the programme).”?
statement: I’m aware of the Treasury report. I’m also aware of countless reports from school teachers and principals who disagree with it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a specific prior answer. 'Yes.' One word, direct, complete — nothing about the question left unaddressed.
question: Does he stand by his answer to my question on 9 May: “Well, I’ll give the member one policy initiative: there are 220,000 children who go to school every day and receive a free and healthy lunch because of the policies introduced by this Government.”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked why he used the school lunch programme as an example of measurable improvement when Treasury found none. He gives a reason directly — the programme is 100 percent better than five years ago because it did not exist then. Flippant and arguably a bad argument, but that is Rigor, not this. He reached the 'why' and answered it; he simply did not separately confirm recall of the earlier question.
question: Does he recall that that answer was to the question “can he give a measurable example of any Government service that is 34 percent better today than it was five years ago?”; and, if he can remember that, why did he use an example that Treasury shows has not resulted in measurable improvements and, in some cases, made the outcomes worse?
statement: Because that programme is 100 percent better than it was five years ago, when it didn’t even exist.

explanation: A sprawling multi-part question: does he stand by the belt-tightening statement, does he think households accept 30 percent more spending for no measurable gain, and is it acceptable to give snide answers. He opens by attacking the questioner, never says whether he stands by the statement, but does engage the substantive middle by contesting where the money went (nurses, police, superannuation). Partial coverage of a diffuse question rather than a narrow dodge.
question: Does he stand by his statement “It’s not right for households to be tightening their belts if the Government isn’t also being seen to be doing the same” and can he think seriously that the average household is sitting there saying, “Yes, I’m spending 30 percent more money but getting no measurable improvement in outcomes” and that it’s OK to make churlish and snide answers like the one he just gave?
statement: Well, if I wanted lessons in “churlish and snide”, I’d only need to look at the member for an example on that. But the member’s use of the figures that he does fails to account for where that money has gone, which includes pay increases for our nurses, our doctors, our teachers; more police on the beat; an increase in the population; more older people requiring more healthcare—the list could go on—more people eligible for New Zealand superannuation. I know the member wants to cut all of those things.

explanation: Asked for one example of an improved outcome from 34 percent more spending. He supplies several — healthcare access, learning support, infrastructure. Whether those are measurable or true is Veracity and Specificity; on the only question here, examples were asked for and examples were given.
question: Can the Prime Minister just give us one example of an improved outcome—a result for New Zealanders—that has come from his Government spending 34 percent more money, adjusted for inflation, in the time it’s been in office?
statement: Thousands of people are getting better access to healthcare under this Government. There are kids going to school, now, who are getting access to learning support, who didn’t get access to learning support under the previous Government. The Government has significantly increased our investment in infrastructure so that we can do things like repair potholes, which were run down under the last Government.

explanation: Asked how the Government is partnering with businesses on low-emissions technology uptake. She names the Low Emission Transport Fund and its 19 business partnerships, and explains the mechanism. Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: How is the Government partnering with businesses to support the uptake of low emissions technology?
statement: Through the Low Emission Transport Fund, the Government is partnering with 19 businesses to support the uptake and roll-out of innovative low-emissions marine and off-road technology. While the Government is making significant progress in supporting the transition of the light vehicle fleet, emissions in the marine and off-road sector are harder to abate. Our partnerships with businesses will help to de-risk these projects, speed up the uptake, and provide opportunities to demonstrate new low-emissions technology.

explanation: Asked how the Government is partnering with marine businesses to decarbonise fleets. After a brief framing statistic she names CentrePort shore-based power and Next Generation Boats — the specific partnerships the question sought. Squarely answered.
question: How is the Government partnering with the marine businesses to decarbonise their fleets?
statement: Each year, our maritime and off-road sectors together use an estimate 1.6 billion litres of petrol and diesel, which equates to around 13 percent of New Zealand’s total energy-related greenhouse gas emissions. To accelerate the decarbonisation of the marine sector, we’re partnering with the likes of CentrePort to roll out shore-based power to Wellington ferries, and Next Generation Boats Ltd to deploy electric boats—including for tourism—as part of our plan to support the marine sector to decarbonise.

explanation: Asked how the Government supports uptake of low-emissions off-road technology. She names the TDX electric wheel loaders and Brian Perry Civil excavator partnerships. The question is answered head-on.
question: How is the Government supporting the uptake of low-emissions off-road technology?
statement: Technology to support the transition for our off-road and heavy vehicles sector is rapidly evolving, and the Government is partnering with businesses to help de-risk the roll-out of these vehicles here in New Zealand. We’ve partnered with TDX Ltd to support the demonstration of the three electric wheel loaders, including one pre-production Volvo 20-tonne electric wheel loader, and we’re working with Brian Perry Civil Ltd to roll out an electric excavator and wheel loader to support the creation of a zero emissions construction crew.

explanation: Asked how else the Government is partnering with businesses to decarbonise transport. She answers with the NZ Steel electric arc furnace while flagging it goes 'beyond transport' — a real further partnership, so the 'how else' is engaged, but she substitutes an industrial example for the transport scope the question set.
question: How else is the Government partnering with businesses to decarbonise transport?
statement: Recently, the Prime Minister announced a broad range of measures that go beyond transport—to partner with New Zealand Steel to install an electric arc furnace which will remove 800,000 tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions each year; that’s the equivalent of taking 300,000 cars off the road. This is New Zealand’s biggest ever emissions reduction project and the first of our large emitter partnerships through the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund.

explanation: The standard 'does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions' — answered 'Yes' immediately, then padded with unrelated trade-mission material. The padding is irrelevant here; the question got a direct and complete answer.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in particular my decision to lead a trade mission to China in June this year, which helped to deliver on a number of priorities that will grow our exports, create jobs, and increase incomes. The economic relationship between New Zealand and China is worth around $40 billion annually to New Zealanders. Among the agreements that we were able to renew included agreements in tourism cooperation, forestry cooperation, and agricultural cooperation. We saw the launch of new direct airline routes to New Zealand, adding thousands more seats every month. We were able to take the opportunity to promote New Zealand as a travel destination to a very significant Chinese consumer base. And, of course, I was able to welcome international students from China back to New Zealand, who make up 35 percent of all international students who come to New Zealand. This Government’s record on trade speaks for itself. As a result of our commitment to trade, the share of our exports covered by trade agreements will increase by nearly 50 percent—another example of how this Government is backing our Kiwi exporters.

explanation: Asked why the finance Minister said a wealth tax was something he would have liked to happen on the day the PM ruled it out. The reply — 'I didn't try; I did' — corrects the questioner's word 'tried' and stops there. It never addresses why the finance Minister said what he said. A narrow question answered by contesting an incidental word in its framing.
question: Why did his finance Minister say that a wealth tax is “something I would have liked to happen” on the same day that the Prime Minister tried to rule it out from overseas?
statement: Well, I didn’t try; I did.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Shaw's 2017 claim that rising/falling emissions is the one measure of success. He answers the agree/disagree squarely ("I always agree with the Green Party co-leader") and then argues from the emissions trend, which is the subject of the claim. Docked slightly because the specific 'one measure' framing is never explicitly endorsed or qualified — but the question was engaged, not dodged.
question: Does he agree with Green Party co-leader James Shaw, who said in 2017 that the one measure of whether a country was succeeding or failing in its fight against climate change was whether its greenhouse gas emissions were rising or falling?
statement: I always agree with the Green Party co-leader. When I became the Minister of Climate Change in 2017, I had one goal: to bring down greenhouse gas emissions in New Zealand, and, as the Prime Minister said in this House on Tuesday, climate pollution fell in 2020, 2021, 2022, with the December 2022 quarter delivering the lowest figure in at least nine years. This is important. We do have so much more work that we need to do, but we are bending the pollution curve downwards. New Zealanders need to know that amidst all the bad news on climate change, there is hope, we are winning, and our hard work is paying off, and we need to continue that momentum through the next Parliament.

explanation: Asked why emissions are falling. He gives a causal answer — a long list of Government actions he credits for the fall. It is self-congratulatory and the causal reasoning is unexamined, but that is Rigor, not Forthrightness: a 'why' question was asked and reasons were supplied.
question: So why are emissions falling?
statement: Emissions are falling because the Green Party, with our Labour Party colleagues, in Government have taken more action on climate change than the previous three decades of Governments combined. We have passed the zero carbon Act and become one of the first countries to put the 1.5 degrees Celsius global warming threshold into primary legislation. We’ve released the Emissions Reduction Plan, the Government’s first ever plan for reducing emissions in every part of the country. We’ve established the Climate Emergency Response Fund, with money paid for by polluters. We’ve established the Climate Change Commission and agreed to our first three emissions budgets. We declared a climate change emergency and committed the Public Service to be carbon-neutral from 2025. We committed $1.3 billion to support the countries that are most vulnerable to the effects of climate change. We launched the New Zealand Green Investment Fund. We invested billions of dollars into buses and trains, walking and cycling. We introduced the Clean Car Discount, which means that, in the month of June, one in two new cars sold in this country was an electric vehicle (EV). We’ve invested in EV charging infrastructure in this country and brought in vehicle emissions standards for the first time in New Zealand history. We’ve helped businesses to switch to clean energy, with the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund. We’ve made Green Star 6 the minimum build standard for all new State homes. We’ve started the Building for Climate Change programme to cut emissions in building and construction. We’ve—

explanation: Asked whether he has seen reports on the best uses of ETS revenue. Answers 'Yes, as it happens; I have' and then enumerates the reports. Direct and complete.
question: Has he seen any reports about the best ways to use revenue raised from polluters through the emissions trading scheme (ETS)?
statement: Yes, as it happens; I have. I’ve seen reports that ETS revenue could be used to fund solar panels on homes and community centres and marae to reduce both emissions and power bills. There are also reports the ETS revenue could fund clean transport options, making it safer for kids to walk and bike to school instead of making their parents sit in traffic, and also for paying bus drivers decent wages. I have seen reports the ETS revenue is helping investment in major industrial polluters to switch to clean energy. I’ve also seen reports the ETS revenue could be used to pay for tax cuts for property speculators, but those reports just don’t make any sense.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees patsy questions are a waste of time. Answers 'Well, yes, in general I do' before adding a jab at the Opposition. The yes/no core is answered plainly first.
question: Does he agree with Green Party co-leader James Shaw that “We think patsy questions are a waste of time.”?
statement: Well, yes, in general I do, but I think it’s less of a waste of time than asking the police Minister the same question 14 times over.

explanation: Asked how much has been spent on light rail contractors and consultants over six years. Answers with the figure — sixty-six million dollars. A narrow factual question given a narrow factual answer.
question: How much money has been spent in the past six years on contractors and consultants for light rail in Auckland?
statement: Sixty-six million dollars, less than half a percent of the likely project cost. I note for the benefit of the member that none of the revenue raised by the Auckland regional fuel tax has funded this.

explanation: Two-part question: is it true no track has been delivered, and will the consultant clampdown extend to light rail. He implicitly concedes the first by explaining that planning precedes building, then pivots entirely to RMA reform and the Opposition's record. The second half — will the clampdown apply — is never reached.
question: Is it true that after $66 million has been spent on contractors and consultants for light rail in Auckland, not one metre of track has been delivered, and will Grant Robertson’s supposed clampdown on consultants and contractors extend to the failed light rail ghost train in Auckland?
statement: It is true that as with the City Rail Link, the planning and design of those projects proceeds before the building starts. The member doesn’t seem to find that easy to accept. I would also say that if the member was really worried about compliance costs for projects, he would’ve backed this Government’s reform of the Resource Management Act, because, through the Infrastructure Commission, we proved that in New Zealand, consenting costs—not the design and engineering costs, but consenting costs—for mid-size infrastructure in New Zealand averaged 5.5 percent of project cost compared with an average of between 0.5 percent and 5 percent in Europe. We fixed that problem through the resource management reforms and through the fast track, which the prior Government didn’t do in nine years, and they now say they’re going to repeal and go back to the Resource Management Act.

explanation: Asked how devastated he is that no track has been laid despite the 2021 Mount Roskill promise. He refers back to his earlier answer about the $66m being a small share of project cost, which addresses neither the promise nor his position on it. Borderline eligibility — the question is rhetorical in intent — but it was directed at a minister who responded, so it is scored rather than omitted.
question: How devastated is he that on the last day of this Parliament, not one single metre of light rail track has been delivered, despite Labour promising it would be built to Mount Roskill in 2021?
statement: I refer to my original answer—that the $66 million so far spent is less than half a percent of the likely project cost.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees light rail is an 'intergenerational project' and, if so, in which generation it will start or be completed. The quip 'during that member's lifetime' is a loose but genuine answer to the timing half; the agree/disagree half is left unanswered. Partial engagement.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister, who told question time earlier today that light rail in Auckland is an “intergenerational project”, and, if so, in which generation will it start or be completed?
statement: I think it will be built during that member’s lifetime.

explanation: Asked which of two things will be completed first — light rail to Mount Roskill or 100,000 KiwiBuild houses. He answers with a defence of the Government's housing record and expresses surprise the question was asked. Neither item is given a completion order or date; the comparison at the core of the question is untouched.
question: Which will be completed first: Auckland Light Rail to Mount Roskill by 2021 or 100,000 KiwiBuild houses in 10 years?
statement: As has previously been said, the record of this Government on housing—which has been enabled through, among other things, investment in roading—is unparalleled for many, many decades in this country. It’s a record that we’re proud of, and I’m surprised the member asked that question.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and policies. Answers 'Yes' and then elaborates on which policies in particular. The yes/no is delivered first and completely; the elaboration does not displace it.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and policies?
statement: Yes, particularly the policies announced this week to break the cycle of offending, back the police to fight crime, and increase the accountability of offenders. These changes include a new aggravating factor to crack down on adults who commission or reward young people to commit crime, an aggravating factor to better hold to account people who post their crimes online, changes to the Family Court that will allow the Family Court to require young offenders to participate in community service programmes, the building of two new youth justice facilities for up to 30 high-needs youth, and changes to improve family group conferences—among other changes. This Government is very much focused on the three pillars of prevention, protection, and responsibility.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the quoted statement, and is there any policy to make using a child to commit a crime a new offence in itself. The second and substantive half is answered squarely — no new offence, an aggravating factor on the existing one, with the pass-through mechanism explained. The 'do you stand by it' half is only implicitly affirmed.
question: Does he, then, stand by his statement that “Using a child to commit a crime is cowardly, exploitative, and destroys lives, so the consequences must be serious”; and, if so, does the Government have any policy to make using a child to commit a crime a new offence in itself?
statement: As I indicated yesterday, what we’re doing is adding an aggravating factor to an existing offence that already exists. That, effectively, allows for the pass-through of that offence to the person who commissioned the crime. For example, if an adult used a young person to commit an aggravated burglary, which has a maximum sentence of 14 years, the adult who commissioned that could be liable to that sentence themselves.

explanation: Asked what he says to a named assault victim given the premise that the PM confuses a crime with an aggravating factor. He does address her directly — saying he would never use such an incident for political purposes — so the literal 'what do you say to her' is answered, but the embedded substance is redirected to the questioner's motives rather than engaged. Partial.
question: What does he say to someone like Bhavana Patel of Jyotis Dairy in the Mt Roskill electorate, who was bashed with a hammer while trying to make an honest living, when the Prime Minister of the country doesn’t even know the difference between a crime in the Crimes Act and an aggravating factor in the Sentencing Act? What does he say to her?
statement: I say to her that I’d never use a tragic incident like that, which is utterly unacceptable, for political purposes.

explanation: Asked whether it is normal for Ministers to publicly back tax changes the PM has ruled out. Hipkins answers the substance — he restates that he ruled it out and says Ministers putting up Budget bids that don't proceed is normal and happens in every Government. That is a direct 'yes, it's normal' with a reason; slight deduction because the 'or is that just how things work in his Cabinet' framing is sidestepped.
question: We don’t know about that yet. Is it normal for the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Revenue to publicly back major tax changes that the Prime Minister has tried to rule out; or is that just how things work in his Cabinet today?
statement: I did rule it out, and I would note that a number of Ministers put up bids during the Budget process which they support, which ultimately don’t proceed through the Budget process. That’s not unique to this Government; that happens in every Government.

explanation: Asked to confirm all tax work at Treasury and IRD has stopped. The reply — no further work will be done ahead of the election — is effectively that confirmation, delivered plainly. Marked slightly below full because it converts 'has stopped' into a forward-looking commitment rather than confirming the present state.
question: Can he confirm that all work on new taxes at Treasury and IRD has now stopped?
statement: No further work will be done on those things ahead of the election, clearly.

explanation: Asked which of two tax policies the Finance and Revenue Ministers support. 'The one Cabinet agree' picks one of the offered options and answers it. Terse and unhelpful in detail, but detail is Specificity, not Forthrightness; the question was engaged, not dodged.
question: Which tax policy does his Minister of Finance and his Minister of Revenue support: the one he’s trying to run on or the one that the Greens are?
statement: The one Cabinet agree.

explanation: Asked why three Labour Ministers give three different answers on tax. 'I reject that' denies the premise, which is a complete and direct response to a loaded 'why' — there is no 'why' to give once the premise is refused. Not a pivot to talking points and not an attack on the questioner, so it scores well above a dodge, but below a full answer since nothing is offered beyond the denial.
question: Why is it that if you ask three Labour Ministers on what the tax policy is, you get three different answers?
statement: I reject that.

explanation: Asked why officials spent nine months working on new taxes after he said he wouldn't introduce any. The answer addresses only the timing of his ruling-out decision and restates that he stands by it; the core of the question — why the work happened at all — is never reached. It gestures at the question without answering it.
question: Why did he tell New Zealanders he wouldn’t introduce any new taxes and then have public officials spend nine months working on them?
statement: As I’ve indicated before, my decision to rule those out happened before the Budget, and I stand by that decision.

explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can take his new tax commitments seriously given the old ones. 'I utterly reject that' refuses the premise, which is engagement rather than evasion, but unlike the earlier rejection it addresses a question whose premise (that a prior commitment was broken) had just been left unanswered, and it supplies nothing at all. Partial credit for a direct denial that never reaches the 'how'.
question: Yes. Thank you, Mr Speaker. This is a very good question. How can New Zealanders take his new commitments on tax seriously when he didn’t uphold his old ones?
statement: I utterly reject that.

explanation: Asked what announcement was made about the cataract postcode lottery. Verrall states the announcement squarely — a nationally consistent surgical threshold delivering an estimated 3,500 more cataract surgeries. Direct and complete.
question: What announcement has the Government made about removing the postcode lottery for cataract surgery?
statement: It has been a priority for this Government to eliminate the inconsistency patients experience when they need surgical treatment because of where they live—the so-called “postcode lottery”. That’s why I was proud to announce that an estimated 3,500 more cataract surgeries will be delivered as a result of a new nationally consistent threshold for surgery. A nationally consistent threshold will remove the postcode lottery that has denied some New Zealanders access to this life-changing procedure.

explanation: Asked why a nationally consistent threshold is being implemented. The answer gives the reason directly: DHB thresholds varied from 46 to 61 points, so eligibility depended on location, and that is unfair. The question's core is met head-on.
question: Why is the Government implementing a nationally consistent threshold?
statement: For decades, the former district health boards used a point system that held widely differing thresholds for access to cataract surgery, varying from 46 to 61 points. A score of 46 points represents mildly reduced vision; a score of 61 represents poor vision, that a person could no longer legally drive. In Auckland and Waitematā, for example, you could become eligible for a cataract operation with a score of 46, but in Canterbury and Southern, you needed a score of 61. That variation represented the worst of what’s become widely known as “postcode lottery” in healthcare, and it isn’t fair.

explanation: Asked what the nationally consistent threshold will be. Answered with the number — a maximum score of 46. Exactly the thing asked for, nothing dodged.
question: Given that, what will the nationally consistent threshold for cataract surgery now be?
statement: In a first under the new health system, there will a nationally consistent score of a maximum of 46 in order to access surgery, opening up eligibility for approximately 3,500 more surgeries. A score of 46 means patients with mildly reduced vision—such as a result of cataracts—will have much earlier access to surgery, improving their quality of life considerably.

explanation: Asked how the change will be implemented. The answer names the funding ($180 million), the delivery agent (Te Whatu Ora working with referring specialists to identify eligible patients) and the mechanisms (outsourcing, model-of-care and theatre-efficiency changes). Squarely responsive; a shade off full for not addressing timing of implementation.
question: How will this be implemented?
statement: In the Budget, we allocated $180 million to reduce wait-lists and standardise access to healthcare, including cataract surgery. Te Whatu Ora’s hospital and specialist team will work with referring specialists to identify who will be eligible under the new score and ensure they have timely access to the procedure. Actions being taking by Te Whatu Ora include initiatives such as outsourcing to other providers and ophthalmologists, as well as improving the productivity through innovative models of care and improving theatre efficiency.

explanation: A two-part question: does he stand by the statement, and is it consistent with months of work on new tax proposals. Robertson explicitly answers both — he stands by the statement, and 'the answer to the second part of the question is yes' — and concedes Ministers received advice on tax changes Cabinet did not proceed with. The 'in its full and proper context' hedge and the long recitation qualify the first part slightly, but both halves are reached.
question: Does he stand by his statement in June this year that “the extent of the Government’s work on tax was outlined after the 2020 election. That has been the work programme for tax”, and is that consistent with the months spent working on proposals for new taxes, including a minimum tax, wealth tax, and a capital gains tax intended to be part of Budget 2023?
statement: I stand by my statement of 21 June 2023 in its full and proper context. This includes my answer to the member’s primary question, which was, “…the Budget process for 2023 began around August of last year, and, as at all Budgets, it considered whether specific tax changes were appropriate”, and then the full statement in the supplementary question, “…the extent of the Government’s work on tax was outlined after the 2020 election. That has been the work programme for tax. In respect of the Budget, we had the announcement on the trustee tax rate. In respect of this Government, those are the actions on tax that we are taking.” The Government’s tax policy work programme was last published on 20 July 2021, and included decisions that the Government had taken at that time, including, for instance, the removal of mortgage interest deductibility. As such, the answer to the second part of the question is yes. As indicated above, Ministers did receive advice on tax changes during the course of the Budget process, including ones that Cabinet did not agree to proceed with.

explanation: Asked at what point after the 2020 election he disclosed the commissioned work on new taxes. No point in time is ever given; the answer pivots to the 2009-2010 tax work programme and Budget 2010 measures under a previous government, then to a general claim that the Budget process tests ideas. The specific 'at what point' is avoided entirely.
question: At what point after the 2020 election did he front up to New Zealanders that he had commissioned extensive work to design massive new taxes documented in these reports, including proposals for a minimum tax, wealth tax, capital gains tax, inheritance tax, gift tax, corrective taxes—all paid for by taxpayers?
statement: As noted in my primary answer, at this Budget, as indeed at many Budgets in the past, work was done on potential alternative tax policies. For example, the Government’s tax policy work programme 2009-2010 did not include the following measures that were included in Budget 2010: the increasing of the rate of GST from 12.5 percent to 15 percent, a cut in the company tax rate, ending landlords and businesses’ ability to claim depreciation on buildings with an estimated useful life of 50 years or more, a cut in the top tax rate for most portfolio investment entities from 30 percent to 28 percent, and changes to the thin capitalisation tax rules. The Budget process is the process in which ideas are tested and explored.

explanation: Asked for the date the PM informed him. He gives one — "in the lead-up to the final Budget paper... which I believe was on 11 April". Slightly hedged and the date anchors the Cabinet paper rather than the conversation itself, but the question is squarely engaged with an actual date.
question: On what date did the Prime Minister inform him that he would rule out the introduction of a wealth tax?
statement: In the lead-up to the final Budget paper going to Cabinet, which I believe was on 11 April.

explanation: Two-part question. Part one answered outright ("yes"). Part two — was the commissioning consistent with the no-new-taxes pledge — is engaged on the merits: he argues the proposals would not have come into force until after the election, which meets the core of the charge, though he never states a plain yes/no on consistency.
question: Is he aware of a statement by Labour Party finance spokesperson on 9 September 2020 that Labour will not implement any new taxes next term, and, if so, does the Minister think the finance Minister has acted consistent with that in commissioning extensive work for months, designing new taxes?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, the member may or may not be aware that, has she not worked her way through those documents, the proposals being made would not have come into force in terms of new taxes until after the election. In the event, as we all now know, it didn’t happen.

explanation: The "why" is met only with "that was part of the evolving work programme", which restates rather than explains. The second part (was it Hipkins' arrival?) gets a partial concession — the new PM "gave me and others pause to reflect" — so the question is touched but its core is largely left unreached.
question: Why, on 16 February, did he direct his officials to focus on proposals for a wealth tax, rather than the minimum tax he had previously prioritised, and was it because he felt newly enabled by the election of Prime Minister Hipkins?
statement: That was part of the evolving work programme. In answer to the second part of the question, the arrival of Prime Minister Hipkins gave me and others in this caucus pause to reflect on a number of different issues. The member is aware of the reprioritisation programme that has taken place.

explanation: A detailed two-part question about reconciling the official advice and whether a future wealth tax is possible, answered with a one-line quip quoting the questioner's leader. Nothing in the question is engaged.
question: When the Minister says the Prime Minister informed him a wealth tax wasn’t a goer anymore, can he clarify the statement in the official advice he received which states, “The decision has been taken that now is not the right time for these changes.”, and can he confirm that there may indeed be a future time where he will consider it the right time to impose hefty new wealth taxes on New Zealanders?
statement: In the words of that member’s leader, “we’ve got years of this”.

explanation: "Is that a bid for the leadership?" gets "No" — a complete answer to a yes/no question. The jibe that follows is a civility matter, not a dodge; the question itself was answered.
question: Is that a bid for the Labour Party leadership?
statement: No, but it is for you!

explanation: The direct question — is he concerned? — is answered plainly ("No, I am not concerned about that") before he pivots to what does concern him. The "why should New Zealanders trust him" tail is left unaddressed, but the substantive question asked was engaged head-on.
question: Is the Minister concerned that the Prime Minister keeps killing his pet projects—first the jobs tax, then his wealth tax fantasy—and if the Prime Minister doesn’t trust this finance Minister, then why should New Zealanders?
statement: No, I am not concerned about that. What I am concerned about is the prospect of a Government coming in and deciding that now is the time to cut taxes when we need to invest more in health, when we need to invest more in education, when we need to invest more in housing. I’m worried about a Government that thinks there should be a top tax rate of 28c, which will mean billions of dollars of cuts right across public services. That’s what really concerns me.

explanation: Asked what steps the Government is taking; she lists specific steps (new aggravating factors for posting offending online and for commissioning young offenders). Skews to youth offending over gang offending, so coverage is slightly incomplete, but the question is directly answered.
question: What steps is the Government taking to crack down on youth offending and gang offending?
statement: Yesterday, the Government announced steps to crack down on recent increases in criminal offending, to break the cycle of crime, and to make sure offenders are held to account. We will introduce a new aggravating factor for posting offending behaviour online—to apply to adults and young people—and provide the courts with an additional consideration when sentencing. It will send a strong signal that this behaviour is unacceptable. We’ll also introduce an aggravating factor for commissioning or rewarding children and young people who offend. As the Prime Minister said yesterday, these actions are cowardly, they are exploitative and harmful to the children involved, so the consequences must be serious.

explanation: "Does she believe... if so, why?" — answered "Yes" followed by reasons across youth offending, organised crime and victim support. Both halves of the question are met.
question: Does she believe her Government has the right policies in justice; if so, why?
statement: Yes. As I just addressed in the previous statement to the House, we’ve been working on a range of measures to address a recent spike in youth offending. In addition, we are tackling organised crime through measures, including the new Criminal Activity Intervention Legislation Act, which was recently used in the events in Ōpōtiki to search vehicles, seize weapons, and make arrests of gang members. Further, we have prioritised victims. Since 2017, this Government has doubled funding for victim support and tripled support for the Victims Assistance Scheme. We are improving legal protections—for example, for victims of sexual and serious violence, through new legislation to give sexual assault victims more control in court processes, particularly around name suppression. Our focus is a justice system where victims feel safe, heard, and empowered.

explanation: "Will she concede...?" answered with an unambiguous "No", plus grounds for refusing to concede. A blunt refusal to accept the proposition is a complete answer, not a dodge.
question: Will she concede now that her Government’s priority to reduce the prison population by 30 percent, regardless of what’s happening on the ground, has been misguided and has contributed to the explosion in crime that the Prime Minister referred to yesterday?
statement: No. Public safety has always been a top priority for our Government. Where people commit serious crimes, they will do that time. I note that violent criminals are still being imprisoned; that hasn’t changed. The reduced prison population hasn’t led to crime sprees or an overwhelming majority of reduction for people in jail for non-violent crimes, and the stats back it up. We have safely reduced the prison population by 21 percent and we’re doing this by helping non-violent eligible prisoners with the bail process.

explanation: "Was she consulted?" — "Yes, that was a Cabinet decision." One line, direct and complete.
question: Was she consulted on the Prime Minister’s announcement yesterday that the Government will prioritise creating a new offence for those who use young people to commit a crime, punishable with prison for up to 10 years?
statement: Yes, that was a Cabinet decision.

explanation: She rejects the premise and answers the underlying question by arguing the enthusiasm is not new — police numbers, CAIL, an ongoing programme. That engages the core charge, though the specific point about the timing three months before an election is never confronted.
question: Why would the public have confidence in the Government’s new enthusiasm for cracking down on crime is genuine, when it has emerged just three months before an election?
statement: I refute the proposition in that question. This Government has been focused on law and order and making sure that New Zealanders are kept safe. We’ve increased police numbers.
