question: What advice has he received on the impacts of the measures in the GPS, given the answer to that supplementary question?
statement: As I’ve advised to the Minister, there is a range of advice that I have received, but I have not received specific advice in regards to the emissions reduction impacts in that draft GPS. That will be part of the emissions reduction 2 process, of which I will welcome the Minister’s input into that process, and we start consultation in May.

explanation: Asked whether he thinks he should have asked for advice on the specific impacts. He opens with a jab at the questioner and then restates his earlier answer about ERP 2. An implicit "no, it wasn't needed yet" can be read out of it, but the normative question he was asked is never taken up.
question: Thank you. Does the Minister of Climate Change think he should have asked for advice on what the specific impacts of cuts through the GPS on transport would be, and their potential of not meeting emissions budget 1?
statement: I appreciate that the former Minister may not have been particularly listening to my answer to the question, but, as I have stated—and I will state again for the purposes of repetition—that aspect of that process will form part of the ERP 2 process. While I have received advice, I haven’t received specific advice that the Minister had asked in her primary question.

explanation: Asked how much the Government will spend financing debt this year. Answered directly with the figure ($8.8 billion) plus forward forecasts. Direct and complete.
question: How much will the Government spend this year on financing its debt?
statement: In the current financial year, Treasury is forecasting that the cost of financing Government debt—which is almost entirely interest payments—will be $8.8 billion, and according to forecasts in the half-year update, which assume the previous Government policies are continued, this is expected to rise to $9.7 billion in the next financial year, and $10.4 billion in the year after that.

explanation: Asked how finance costs have changed over time. Answered with the then-and-now comparison and the growth rate. Squarely on the question.
question: How have the Government’s finance costs changed over time?
statement: Finance costs are expected to be $8.8 billion this year. By comparison, finance costs in 2017-18 were $3.5 billion, so they have more than doubled, or grown more than 150 percent, since that time. In fact, yes—

explanation: Asked how finance costs compare with other areas of spending. Answered with explicit comparisons to schools and to the Defence Force/Police/Corrections/Customs. Direct.
question: How do finance costs compare with other areas of Government spending?
statement: At $8.8 billion, finance costs are forecast to be higher this year than spending on primary and secondary schools combined, or, putting it another way, finance costs are forecast to be higher this year than Government spending on the Defence Force, the Police, Corrections, and Customs combined. In fact, they are around $1 billion higher than that—$1 billion higher than spending on the Defence Force, the Police, Corrections, and Customs combined.

explanation: Asked what finance costs are per New Zealander. Answered with $1,666. The added swipe at the previous Government is a Focus/Civility matter and does not displace the answer.
question: How much are the Government’s finance costs per New Zealander?
statement: Finance costs of $8.8 billion this year equate to $1,666 for every person in New Zealand. Government debt in New Zealand is too high, thanks to the financial mismanagement of the previous Government.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his statements and actions. "Yes, I stand by all my statements and actions" — complete. The follow-on elaboration is volunteered, not a substitute for an answer.
question: Kia orana, Mr Speaker. Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I stand by all my statements and actions, particularly when I said that investments in the draft Government policy statement (GPS) 2024 will ensure key connections are provided so that Kiwis can get to where they need to go quickly and safely. These investments will also reduce congestion on our roads, provide low-emission transport options in our main cities, and create a more productive and resilient transport network, driving economic growth and unlocking land for thousands of new houses.

explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can have confidence he won't introduce other taxes, fees or levies. He points to the GPS document setting out funding, which gestures at an assurance without ever giving one about further taxes or levies. Partial engagement at best.
question: When he said yesterday, “but the reality is—the reality is—that we need to ensure that we set out the funding parameters to be able to deliver the infrastructure New Zealanders need”, how can New Zealanders have any confidence that he won’t be introducing other taxes, fees, or levies to cover the fiscal holes that his transport plan clearly has?
statement: Because the reality is—the reality is—that the GPS outlines exactly how we’re going to fund—I think it’s on page 27, for the member’s benefit, or 29; I can’t quite remember right now—the projects and the outcomes in our draft GPS document.

explanation: Asked who is correct, himself or NZTA. He picks one — "Simeon Brown is correct" — and gives his reason. He sidesteps the $24.4 billion figure, but the question's core was which of the two is right, and that is answered outright.
question: It’s great support. Who is correct, National MP Simeon Brown, who said, “National’s fully-costed transport plan will deliver 13 new Roads of National Significance and four major public transport projects – and does not require increases to petrol tax.”, or the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA), who estimate that there is a fiscal hole in his transport plan of up to $24.4 billion, or 110 percent more than he had originally estimated?
statement: Well, Simeon Brown is correct, because this GPS is not increasing fuel excise duty and road-user charges in the three years of this Government’s term.

explanation: Asked what advice he requested or received on litigation risk. He invokes privilege — a direct, on-point refusal rather than a pivot, which scores high — but he never says whether any advice was in fact sought or received, which could be stated without disclosing content. Direct refusal, incomplete on the factual half.
question: What advice has he requested or received on any potential litigation risk from the proposed settings, including judicial review risk in Waitangi Tribunal claims?
statement: Well, legal advice that Ministers receive is, as the member knows, privileged.

explanation: Asked to justify ministerial decision-making over independent hearing panels. He offers no justification at all, only that the bill isn't before the House yet and the member should wait. The core — the rationale — is left entirely untouched.
question: How does he justify the proposal to have ministerial decision-making over complex environmental matters rather than having final decisions sitting with independent hearing panels who are able to robustly consider all the evidence?
statement: The bill hasn’t been presented to Parliament yet. As the member will well know, it’s part of the Government’s 100-day plan of action, and I think we’re up to day 97, so the member does not have long to wait.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: will the new law override protections in the Conservation, Wildlife, Reserves and EEZ Acts. He describes the referral mechanism and says panels will set conditions 'in accordance with' those statutes, which gestures at 'no' without ever saying so. Partial engagement, core left implicit.
question: Will the proposed new legislation override the environmental protections contained in many of New Zealand’s key pieces of environmental legislation, including the Conservation Act, the Wildlife Act, the Reserves Act, and the exclusive economic zone Act?
statement: The fast-tracked consenting regime will allow Ministers to refer projects to panels to make conditions upon which those projects will take place, in accordance with the variety of statutes that the member has mentioned.

explanation: Asked whether the listed projects will include previously declined ones such as Te Kūhā and Trans-Tasman Resources. 'Well, maybe — wait until you see the bill' engages the question head-on and candidly declines to commit, but unlike a flat refusal it leaves the substance open. Squarely addressed, not answered.
question: Will the approximately 100 projects included in the listed pathway include projects for which consents have previously been declined or referred for reconsideration due to environmental risk, including the Te Kūhā coal mine and the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining project?
statement: Well, maybe. The member will just have to wait until he sees the bill.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made about rehabilitation access. He states the Sunday announcement and what it does. Directly and completely answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about access to rehabilitation programmes?
statement: On Sunday, I announced that the coalition Government has taken the first steps to ensure prisoners on remand can access the rehabilitation and reintegration support they need to turn their lives around. As part of the 100-day plan, we’re taking steps to make it explicit in the Corrections Act 2004 that prisoners who are on remand and convicted of a crime will be provided with the rehabilitation that helps address the causes of their offending.

explanation: Asked how many more people are on remand than 10 years ago. He gives 146 percent growth and the 45 percent share of the prison population — the magnitude asked for, expressed as a rate rather than a head count. Squarely answered.
question: How many more people are there on remand now than there were 10 years ago?
statement: The number of people on remand has increased by 146 percent over the last 10 years, and remand now represents almost 45 percent of the entire prison population. This announcement will ensure that these people are receiving access to vital rehabilitation.

explanation: Asked who benefits and how many. He names remand-convicted prisoners and gives a figure of nearly 1,400 at any one time. Both halves answered directly.
question: Who will benefit from these changes and how many prisoners are likely to benefit?
statement: Remand-convicted prisoners will benefit from the provision of offence-based rehabilitation, including rehabilitation related to violent and sexual offending. The advice that I’ve received indicates that at any one time, nearly 1,400 prisoners may benefit from this rehabilitation. The biggest benefit, though, will be for the public in that more violent offenders will be receiving rehabilitation while inside, with an aim to improve public safety.

explanation: Asked what other changes will strengthen rehab access. He identifies the Amendment Paper and the specific support it extends to remand-accused prisoners. Direct and complete.
question: What other changes will the Government make to strengthen rehab access?
statement: As part of the Amendment Paper which I’ve sent to the Justice Committee for consideration alongside the Corrections Amendment Bill, the proposed amendment sets out a clear expectation that remand-accused prisoners will be provided with reintegration and other non - offence-focused support while in prison. This includes alcohol and drug treatment, as well as educational or behavioural skills programmes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the statement and, if so, how he reconciles it with the interim evaluation. He says yes and reconciles it explicitly by quoting the evaluation's own limitation. Both halves engaged.
question: Does he stand by his statement that the previous Government had committed to the school lunches spending programme “without commissioning any robust empirical study to evaluate its effectiveness”; if so, how does he reconcile this with the New Zealand Healthy School Lunches pilot/Ka Ora, Ka Ako interim evaluation on the Ministry of Education website?
statement: Yes, I certainly stand by that statement, and I can very easily reconcile it with this interim evaluation, which itself says a larger group of schools is needed to assess whether there has been any improvement in attendance patterns over the longer term. So I think, when a study itself says that it couldn’t reach the conclusion asked, that is almost by definition not robust.

explanation: Asked whether he acknowledges the other Ka Ora, Ka Ako reports showing increased attendance. He answers in substance — five studies, none finding a robust attendance effect — which is a clear 'no' to the acknowledgement sought. Padded with a swipe at the questioner, but the core is met (rudeness does not lower this score).
question: Does he, then, acknowledge the other reports—the many other reports—that have been done on the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme have increased the numbers of schools, have had the voices of 10,694 secondary learners brought into the research, and the final report—or the most recent report—which shows that, thus, in specific schools and kura, we found the programme contributed to increased attendance?
statement: There have been five studies in total commissioned by the Ministry of Education. None of them has done a robust, statistically significant comparison that has been able to find that the programme has increased attendance at school—those are the basic facts. I know that the former Minister probably thinks that she commissioned reports that are good enough for the taxpayer, but this Government is in favour of actually doing robust analysis when we go out and spend their money. But, unfortunately, I read again from the Treasury: “However, the evaluations have found no impact on attendance, and ākonga Māori, who make up around 48% of students receiving the programme, have not benefited on most metrics, such as school functioning … health, and mental wellbeing”. Unfortunately, the former Minister went out and spent nearly 350 million bucks, and she can’t say whether it worked.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the 25 percent wastage claim and whether he is aware the ministry reported wastage halving from 12 to 6 percent. He neither affirms nor withdraws the claim and never touches the 12/6 figures, substituting an anecdote about an unrelated donation scheme. The question's core is avoided.
question: Does he stand by his statement on Checkpoint: “The Treasury got on to that and also pointed out that they were wasting around 25 percent of the food that they had.”; and is he aware that it was never 25 percent, and that the Ministry of Education told the Education and Workforce Committee that food wastage had halved from 12 percent in the beginning to 6 percent?
statement: Unfortunately, there’s a wide range of ways that the food is being wasted. For example, an email received just today from a high school says, “We have a volunteer group in town who picks up all unopened lunch packs to distribute amongst the elderly and needy in town. The quality of lunches has dropped off to such an extent that the elderly people no longer want them. A lot of food is being wasted—money as well.” Unfortunately, in many places, 25 percent wastage would be an improvement.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by 'cuts of 30 to 50 percent' and what he says to the Prime Minister's contrary campaign statement. He says he absolutely stands by it and addresses the message to Luxon directly. Both parts answered.
question: Does he stand by his statement, also on Checkpoint, that “Cuts of 30 to 50 percent are in the ballpark.”; and, if so, what does he say to Christopher Luxon, who said in the election campaign, “We are supporters of the programme and it will continue to improve each and every year under our National Government”?
statement: I absolutely stand by my statement and what I’d say to Christopher Luxon—and the Prime Minister, for that matter—is that we are going to keep improving it: first of all, by wasting less money, and, second of all, by making sure that it’s going to the students most in need in a way that we can demonstrate a difference.

explanation: Asked what industry's lack of interest in Block Offer 2020 means for the Government's plans to reinstate offshore exploration. Jones never says what it means for the plans — he pivots to a general commitment to rebuilding investor confidence and a quip about waiting 12 years. It grazes the underlying issue (investor confidence in policy durability) without answering the question put.
question: What does the lack of interest from industry in Block Offer 2020 mean for the new Government’s plans for reinstating offshore petroleum exploration?
statement: Our Government is committed to rebuilding investor confidence in New Zealand as an attractive and secure destination. They have raised the question: what about if the Government changes? To wit my response has been: wait 12 years.

explanation: Two-part question: does she stand by the no-front-line-cuts promise, and if so why was FENZ told it is 'not necessarily immune'. She answers part one flatly ('yes, I do') and engages part two directly — the email is a FENZ staffer's, not hers, and she quotes its protective wording. The closing swipe at the Opposition is Civility/Focus, not evasion; the core of both parts was met.
question: Does she stand by her answer, “I make that promise”, said in response to the question, “Will you promise no cuts to any front-line services”; if so, why has Fire and Emergency New Zealand been told their front-line services are “not necessarily immune” from Public Service cuts?
statement: Well, yes, I do. With respect to the second part of the question about Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ), the member is referring to an email written by somebody at FENZ, an extract of which I’ve seen for the first time today. I am not responsible for that email, although I can’t see why the member is so offended by an email that says “front-line services are to be protected” and “unless clearly obvious that efficiencies can be gained without affecting services”. Perhaps if members opposite had had a thought about efficiency over the past six years, we wouldn’t have 80 percent increases in spending without better public services delivered.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the 6.5 percent savings target for Police given advice it would undermine recruiting 500 officers. She never confirms or abandons the target and never touches the advice — she recites the generic savings process (agencies propose, Ministers evaluate). Talking points where a narrow yes/no plus a response to specific advice was asked for.
question: Does she stand by the Government’s commitment to 6.5 percent savings in Police, when they have advised their Minister that the cuts they would need to make would undermine their ability to recruit an additional 500 front-line police officers?
statement: As I have said on a number of occasions, our Government will ensure that front-line services are protected in the Budget 2024 savings exercise. We have asked agencies to put forward their proposals for delivering more efficiency; for eliminating back-room waste; for ensuring that they’re not spending too much on consultants and contractors, low-value programmes, and ineffective programmes. Agencies have been asked to put forward proposals. We will then, as Ministers, evaluate those proposals before making any decisions.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that Police savings would be reinvested in the Police budget. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, and it is the complete answer to the question asked.
question: So, in that case, can she guarantee that the 6.5 percent savings she has asked for from Police will be reinvested in the Police budget?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked why her line-by-line spending analysis cost public servants their jobs yet missed the Prime Minister's accommodation allowance. The allowance is never mentioned at all; the response is a defence of public sector cuts aimed at the questioner's own government. The specific object of the question is entirely avoided.
question: Why did she conduct her line-by-line analysis of wasteful spending in a way that puts public servants out of work but didn’t manage to uncover that the Prime Minister was claiming an accommodation allowance for a mortgage-free home he owns while being able to stay at Premier House?
statement: Well, it may be the view of that member that every single extra public servant her Government employed was the best use of a Government dollar. But, on this side of the House, we know that the needs in our schools, the needs in our hospitals, and the need to fight law and order are such that we must ensure that every dollar of taxpayer money goes to its best use in our front-line services, and we make no apologies for driving more value from the enormous amount of Government spending that goes on.

explanation: Asked how she justifies a sixth review of school lunches when the PM's allowance went unnoticed. She does justify the lunch review — funding cliff, cost-effectiveness, waste — which is half the question, but the comparison to the allowance, which is what makes the question bite, is not addressed. Partial engagement with the core.
question: How can she justify the Government’s prioritisation of a sixth investigation into the benefits of giving poor kids lunch, when the Prime Minister’s claiming of an accommodation allowance for a mortgage-free home went unnoticed?
statement: Well, as the member should know, the outgoing Government left an enormous fiscal cliff for the school lunch programme. What that meant was there wasn’t funding provided for that programme into the future. Now, our good, responsible Government has decided that we will safeguard funding so that programme can continue. And in doing so, in line with our values, we will ensure that we’re delivering it in a cost-effective, high-value manner, because unlike that member, we don’t think it’s a good use of taxpayers’ funds to have uneaten lunches stacked a tower high. That’s wasteful, and we’re going to make sure the programme’s more efficient.

explanation: Asked whether integrated projects including busways, bus lanes, stops and footpaths will be deliverable under the draft GPS. Answer: 'Yes.' Direct and complete; brevity is not evasion.
question: Will it be possible for the New Zealand Transport Agency and councils to deliver integrated transport projects that include other improvements, such as busways, bus lanes, public transport stops, and footpaths as part of larger road or highway projects, under his draft Government Policy Statement on transport?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he had received advice on the impact of the page-25 exclusion on cost-effectiveness and delivery of integrated projects. He neither confirms nor denies receiving advice and says nothing about impact — instead he describes how the two activity classes work, which answers a different question than the one asked.
question: Has he received any advice on whether the statement on page 25 of the Government policy statement (GPS) regarding State highway improvements—and I quote—“The Government expects that funding in this activity class will not be used to make multimodal improvements, i.e., cycleways and busways”—what impact that statement will have on the cost-effectiveness and delivery of integrated transport projects?
statement: Well, there is also another activity class called public transport improvements and if the New Zealand Transport Agency or a council would like to make an investment which includes improvements to the roads, they would apply for funding under the State highway improvements. If they also want to make investments around public transport improvements, they’d apply for funding under the public transport investment activity class.

explanation: Asked, yes or no, whether he expects NZTA to futureproof for public transport and walking/cycling on new priority highways. He restates that his expectation is that agencies 'give effect to the GPS' — a formula that avoids saying whether futureproofing is expected. The specific expectation asked about is never confirmed or denied.
question: Is it his expectation that the New Zealand Transport Agency will futureproof for public transport and safe walking and cycling access when building the new priority urban highways that his Government has promised?
statement: It’s my expectation that the New Zealand Transport Agency and road controlling authorities will give effect to the Government policy statement on transport, and that outlines the activity classes, what they will be used to fund, and our expectations around what the priority projects are.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware that no previous GPS excluded multimodal funding from State highway projects. He never says whether he is aware, but he does contest the premise's force by pointing to the previous Government's draft GPS using the maintenance budget for cycleways. Some engagement with what the question was driving at; the question as put goes unanswered.
question: Is he aware that no previous Government policy statement, including under the last National Government, ever treated transport funding and delivery in this way—there was no comparable statement in previous GPSs that excluded multimodal funding from State highway projects?
statement: Well, this is a very new Government and a very focused Government, and we’re focused on outcomes. So when we say that the State highway improvement activity class should be about focusing on building roads, we don’t expect that that money will be spent on then building a cycleway. The last Government, in their last draft GPS, wanted to use the road maintenance budget to build cycleways. Well, that’s not what this Government’s priorities are. It’s to fix potholes. So we have a very focused draft GPS and I just say to the member: submissions are open until 2 April; I encourage her to make a submission.

explanation: Asked whether the reliable-travel-times expectation applies to public transport users or only to motor vehicles. Despite a detour through the last Government's record, he reaches the point: 'regardless of what mode they choose to take' — that is an answer, and it answers the alternative posed.
question: Does his expectation for the transport agency and road controlling authorities, set out on page 25 and 26 of the GPS, to prioritise reliable travel times and investment decisions, apply to users of public transport or does it only apply to motor vehicles?
statement: Well, our expectation is that the New Zealand Transport Agency and road controlling authorities would focus on reducing travel times, reliable travel times, so that people can get where they need to go quickly and safely. Under the last Government, there was no consideration for people’s time. We want to make sure the transport system is working to reduce travel times so that people get where they need to go quickly and safely, regardless of what mode they choose to take.

explanation: Asked how the Government can deliver reliable public transport given the fare scrappings and the $1.5b GPS reduction. Brown engages the fare half squarely — farebox recovery fell from 40% to 13%, so users must contribute — which is a real answer to why fares are changing. But the $1.5b figure and the council subsidy point are never touched, and the second half of the answer leaves the question entirely for Auckland Light Rail and the City Rail Link. Half the question reached, half replaced with attack.
question: How can the Government deliver reliable, effective, and efficient public transport as a priority for Kiwi households when it intends to scrap free and half-price fares for under-25s, and when its draft GPS takes over $1.5 billion from public transport, which also cuts the ability of local councils to provide additional transport fare subsidies?
statement: Well, if the member read the draft GPS document, it outlines the fact that under the last Government, farebox recovery fell from 40 percent of running public transport services to 13 percent, and so the reality is that we need to ensure that people who use public transport are helping support it. But I’d also point out to the members opposite, they had six years in Government, they spent $228 million on “Auckland Light Fail” and failed to deliver it. We started the City Rail Link and we’re going to complete it. We have a proud track record on public transport.

explanation: A narrow, quantitative question: the total value of South Island RoNS against the value of all 15. 'There's a range of estimates around the projects' concedes the number without supplying it, then the answer switches to naming projects — which is responsive to the second clause about signalling to mainlanders, but not to the value comparison asked for. Naming projects where a dollar comparison was requested is the classic gesture-without-reaching. Low because the question was highly specific and its core was avoided.
question: What is the total value of the proposed roads of national significance in the South Island compared with the overall value of all 15 roads of national significance, and what does that level of investment say to mainlanders about the importance this Government places on South Island projects?
statement: Well, there’s a range of estimates around the projects. But what I’d point out is there are a number of key projects in the South Island that we’ll be prioritising: the Woodend Bypass—advocated by the member Matt Doocey—the Ashburton bridge, the Hope Bypass, and better road maintenance. That last Government cancelled, cancelled, cancelled, cancelled. We’re going to deliver.

explanation: Two things were asked: what advice he has received on scrapping the coastal shipping funding, and the resilience impact. Neither is given. He does state plainly 'We're not continuing the coastal fund', which confirms the underlying fact and earns some credit as a direct declaration, but the land/sea joke stands in for the advice question and the Kaikoura resilience point goes unaddressed.
question: What advice has he received regarding plans to scrap up to $20 million of funding for coastal shipping, and what impact would this have on New Zealand’s resilience against major events such as the Kaikōura earthquake?
statement: Well, as my colleague the Hon Chris Bishop says, it is the National Land Transport Fund. Last time I saw, our ships run on water, and cars and trucks run on the land. This is about the land, not the sea. We’re not continuing the coastal fund under the last Government. [Interruption]

explanation: A yes/no standing-by question answered 'Yes' in the first word. The 'within the context in which they were delivered' qualifier is a hedge that slightly narrows the commitment, and the double-crossing quip is padding, but the question was engaged and answered immediately. Not a dodge.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s policies and statements?
statement: Yes, within the context in which they were delivered, and, unlike some, we won’t be double-crossing that bridge when we come to it.

explanation: Asked how it is appropriate to appoint a Minister who called the programme wasteful. Peters gives two responsive answers: that Opposition statements are not something the Government answers for here, and that the characterisation was evidence-based per a July Treasury report — which directly rebuts the question's 'without any evidence' premise. The appropriateness of the appointment itself is only reached obliquely via 'that's why Mr Seymour's having to handle this problem'. Scored on engagement alone; the partisanship and the disputable Treasury characterisation belong to Focus and Veracity, not here.
question: How is it appropriate for this Government to put a Minister in charge of the Ka Ora, Ka Ako free school lunch programme who described it as “wasteful”, “unaffordable”, and a “marketing stunt” while in Opposition, without any evidence?
statement: Well, the reality is that what was said in Opposition is not accountable in this Parliament for the Government. But it’s understandable when you see the Treasury commissioned a report when they were in Government—they made a report in July of last year, talking about how the whole thing was a massive failure, and, worse than that, massive losses were occasioned by wasted food or food being sent home. It was meant to be food in schools, not food in homes. This was careless spending which was never budgeted to go forward into the year we’re talking about, and that’s why Mr Seymour’s having to handle this problem.

explanation: A numeric question — how many schools and tamariki affected. 'At the moment, the Minister is doing work on that, going through school after school' is a genuine response: it says the count is not yet established and work is under way, which engages rather than evades. But that is one sentence, and the remainder pivots to food waste and to who does or does not know about poverty. Partial engagement, core figure never approached.
question: How many schools and tamariki would be impacted by a 30 percent to 50 percent cut to the free school lunches?
statement: At the moment, the Minister is doing work on that, going through school after school. But the reality is that there are some very, very disturbing reports about the amount of waste. There is surely no one who believes in this programme, which was supported across this Parliament, who thinks that that sort of waste should remain unaccountable. I know some people in this country, because they know nothing about poverty, think that sort of waste is good. But out there in the real Māori world and Polynesian world, they want the food delivered to schools to be used by those children, and not by everybody else who’s not entitled to it.

explanation: Asked which schools or kura have been consulted. No school is named, and the answer does not even confirm or deny that consultation occurred — 'the Government has put its programme out there, it's gone public on it' substitutes publicity for consultation, then closes on what the previous Government failed to do with a Treasury evaluation. A specific, checkable question replaced with process language and a counter-attack.
question: Which schools or kura have been consulted regarding potential cuts to the free lunches programme?
statement: Well, the reality is that the Government has put its programme out there, it’s gone public on it, and it’s working its way through it. But it is a result of a July 2023 evaluation that came from Treasury to that Government about which they did precisely nothing.

explanation: Two direct asks: does he believe hunger impacts learning, and will he commit to preserving the programme. The response is an anecdote about community-made school lunches in decades past and who used to prepare them. Neither the belief question nor the commitment question is answered, denied, or acknowledged. Among the clearest non-answers in the set.
question: Does he believe that hunger impacts a child’s ability to learn, and, if so, will he commit to preserving the school lunch programme, given that poverty is not a choice for tamariki?
statement: The reality is that if some people have a memory, they’ll realise that for decades and decades and decades, free lunches have been available at school, made by the local community, and I’m not being chauvinist here but usually made by the senior girls, because they could be trusted. Many of us remember it.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on petroleum exploration; he names the permit granted to Greymouth Gas Turangi Ltd and the forthcoming bill to overturn the exploration ban. The question is answered directly and in full. That it is a friendly patsy question from a Government member does not reduce Forthrightness — the question asked was the question answered.
question: What announcements has he made regarding petroleum exploration?
statement: Today, I’ve announced one petroleum exploration permit has been granted to Greymouth Gas Turangi Ltd. I have also announced that I’ll be introducing a bill later this year that will overturn the previous regime’s ban on new permits for petroleum exploration beyond the onshore Taranaki region. Important steps in the journey of New Zealand’s resilience.

explanation: 'Why do we need oil and gas?' is answered with reasons: sovereign risk from the ban, modelling showing gas supply may not meet demand, and gas being needed to keep the electricity system running. The jiggling-to-keep-warm line is rhetorical decoration on an answer that has already engaged the question. Whether the reasons are sound is Rigor; whether the modelling claim is true is Veracity.
question: Why do we need oil and gas?
statement: The former ban, soon to disappear, created inordinate sovereign risk for investment in New Zealand. Advice and modelling show that the supply of gas is uncertain and may not match future demand. We need gas to keep the lights on in the electricity system, and, as the responsible Minister, on a cold and chilly night, I don’t want to see the men and women of New Zealand reduced to jiggling to keep warm.

explanation: An open 'what else are you working on' question, answered with two concrete items: introducing the bill to overturn the permit cessation, and travelling to meet overseas and domestic investors. A sprawling question covered squarely, with the loaded adjectives ('crippling and ghastly') affecting Civility and Focus rather than whether the question was engaged.
question: What else is he working on?
statement: I will be introducing, as I said, a bill to overturn the crippling and ghastly announcement that led to a cessation of new permits for petroleum exploration. As an act of penance, I am going to visit investors overseas, talk to New Zealand current investors, and convince them that was a minor negative blip in the recent trajectory of New Zealand history.

explanation: Asked what transport announcements he had made; names the draft GPS on land transport and the $500m pothole prevention fund. The jab at the last Government is padding, but the announcement asked for is squarely delivered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about transport investment in New Zealand?
statement: Well, earlier this week, the Prime Minister and I released the draft Government policy statement (GPS) on land transport, announcing that we’re establishing a $500 million pothole prevention fund to tackle the record number of potholes on our roads. There were over 62,000 potholes needing repair on the State highway network last year—a new record made by that last Government—causing damage to vehicles and travel disruptions for Kiwis around the country. We will address it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a quoted statement; answers "Yes" outright, then adds his own qualification. Direct and complete — the added caveat does not dodge the yes/no.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “There is a problem with late payments and long payment terms by large market players”?
statement: Yes. However, I went on to say that the Business Payment Practices Act is not an effective solution, and that’s why we’ve proposed a number of initiatives to try and speed up payment times.

explanation: Asked what in the voluntary code would actually stop a large business withholding payment; answers by restating the code's purpose and its coverage (top 180 businesses) without naming any mechanism. Gestures at the question without reaching its core.
question: What, if anything, in his voluntary code would stop a large business taking advantage of a small or medium business or a sole trader by withholding or delaying payments?
statement: That is the purpose of the code, which is to make sure that there are good measures in place to make sure the large companies in New Zealand—and the proposed code is going to cover the top 180 businesses—do adhere to good policy around payments.

explanation: Asked why a sole trader should have to wait three months for payment; answers "they shouldn't." Terse and offers nothing further, but it engages the question head-on rather than pivoting — brevity is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: Why should a hard-working sole trader have to wait three months or more for payment to come through from a large company after completing the work?
statement: Well, they shouldn’t.

explanation: Asked a narrow yes/no — would he be open to considering a 30-day interest-liability alternative to the Act; never says open or not, and instead redirects to Fair Trading Act rights and the Commerce Commission. A specific question answered as if a different one had been asked.
question: Sorry, sir. Would the Minister be open to considering an alternative to the Business Payment Practices Act 2023 that would make late payers liable for a fair interest rate if they haven’t made their payment within 30 days?
statement: One of the initiatives that I’ve proposed is to make sure that people are aware of their rights under the Fair Trading Act. That is, obviously, administered by the Commerce Commission, and I think that’s the best place where that issue should be dealt with.

explanation: Asked why he is imposing additional costs on small business; responds entirely by turning the question back on the questioner's own party ($3.2 billion of compliance costs). Pure counter-attack, with no attempt at the question.
question: Thank you. Why is he imposing additional costs on every small business in New Zealand?
statement: Well, I could ask the member why did the last Government impose $3.2 billion of additional compliance costs on small business—

explanation: Asked what progress has been made on law and order; states progress on the hundred-day plan and cites the Legal Services Amendment Bill's third reading as a concrete instance. Answers the question as put.
question: What progress has the Government made in relation to restoring law and order?
statement: The coalition Government is making excellent progress in fulfilling its hundred-day plan commitments in justice that are the first steps in our plan to rebuild confidence in the justice system and to restore law and order. Just this morning, the Legal Services Amendment Bill passed its third reading; it will stop taxpayer funding for section 27 cultural reports that proliferated out of control under the former regime, consuming more than $7 million out of the legal aid budget. When this Government says it will do something, it does.

explanation: Asked what other 100-day commitments are being delivered; enumerates several — scrapping the prison reduction target, gang legislation, gang membership as an aggravating factor, firearms search powers, youth offender tools. Directly and fully responsive.
question: What other commitments within the 100-day plan to restore law and order is the Government delivering on?
statement: Well, we’ve abolished the previous Government’s prison reduction target that bore no relationship to the level of crime in our community. Tomorrow, we’ll introduce legislation to give police extra powers to deal with gangs. We’re making gang membership an aggravating factor in sentencing, we’re giving police greater powers to search for firearms, and, as you heard from my colleague Minister Chhour yesterday, we’re giving the justice system extra tools to deal with the repeat serious youth offenders.

explanation: Asked why restoring law and order matters; gives a reason (New Zealanders deserve to feel safe) and supporting crime figures. Whether the statistics are accurate is a Veracity question; the "why" asked for is answered.
question: Why is restoring law and order so important?
statement: Well, indeed, that’s a good question. New Zealanders deserve to feel safe in their homes and in their communities. Gang membership has increased by 51 percent in the previous six years, violent crime up by 33 percent, ram raids went up by 290 percent, and victims of retail crime by 110 percent. These are not statistics that anyone in this House should be proud of, and that is why we need to act.

explanation: Asked what feedback he had received on the announcements; supplies a specific piece of feedback, quoting a commentator (revealed as Stuart Nash). Selective and pointed, but it is an answer to what was asked.
question: What feedback, if any, has the Minister received on recent policy announcements relating to restoring law and order?
statement: Well, I do note one commentator, who said, in response to the Government plans to address harm caused by gangs, “If police have probable cause and know someone’s a gang member they should be able to go after them with the full force of the law knowing that Parliament, politicians and the community has their back.” That commentator was one Stuart Nash.

explanation: Asked what the Government will do after the 100-day plan; names reinstating three-strikes and limiting excessive sentencing discounts. Direct forward-looking answer to the question posed.
question: What will the Government do after the 100-day plan commitments are delivered?
statement: Well, throughout the next three years, this Government will be relentlessly focused on restoring law and order. After the hundred-day plan commitments are delivered, we will progress work including the reinstatement of the three-strikes legislation and limiting excessive sentencing discounts. New Zealanders want to see real consequences for crime.

explanation: Asked what recent economic reports she has seen; identifies the ANZ business outlook and consumer confidence reports and summarises what they show. Names the reports asked for and characterises them.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the New Zealand economy?
statement: Last week, ANZ released its business outlook report and its consumer confidence report, both of which come out monthly. These show that consumer confidence continues to rise, albeit off a very low base, and business confidence is on a strong upward trend, despite levelling out in February.

explanation: Asked how confidence compares to previous years; the answer gives exactly that comparison (record lows in 2022/23, now rising off those lows). Partisan framing and the absence of current figures are Focus/Specificity concerns, not evasion — the comparison asked for is delivered.
question: How does consumer and business confidence compare to previous years?
statement: In 2022 and 2023, consumer confidence fell to the lowest level ever reported in this survey—lower than the global financial crisis and lower than during the COVID lockdowns—and, strike me down, business confidence was also the lowest it has ever been, in 2022 and 2023. Again, it was lower than in the global financial crisis and lower than during the COVID lockdowns. So it is very heartening indeed that consumer and business confidence is rising off the all-time lows recorded under the previous Government.

explanation: Asked what the results say about people's own expectations; the answer states the survey's finding on expectations directly (net expectation of being better off in a year, wariness on big purchases). Squarely on the question.
question: What do the results say about people’s own expectations?
statement: The consumer confidence survey shows that, in net terms, people expect that they and their family will be better off financially in a year’s time. At present, people are wary about purchasing major household items, but this measure is on an upward trend and is considerably better than it was last year.

explanation: Asked what the results say about business expectations; the answer reports the forward-looking indicators from the Business Outlook survey. Direct and complete for the question asked.
question: What do the results say about business expectations?
statement: The Business Outlook survey saw lifts in most forward-looking indicators, such as businesses’ own activity, investment intentions, employment intentions, and profit expectations. Together with the consumer results, this reinforces that New Zealanders are more optimistic about their future under this coalition Government.

explanation: Asked for his most immediate portfolio priority; he names one — stopping implementation of new SNAs under the 100-day plan — and says what stage it is at. A single, unambiguous answer to the question.
question: What is his most immediate priority in the portfolio?
statement: My highest priority is delivering on the Government’s 100-day plan to begin stopping the implementation of new significant natural areas, known as SNAs. SNAs are an unjustified and unhelpful intrusion into private property rights and are getting in the way of productive farming. ACT’s coalition agreement with National commits to stop the implementation of new SNAs and to review their operation. I have been working with officials, and I intend to take a plan to Cabinet on the most effective way to do that.

explanation: Asked for examples of the challenge SNAs pose; he supplies examples (landowner reports of prohibited development, the sheltered matagouri gully). Whether the examples are verifiable is Veracity; as a response it engages the question.
question: What examples has he seen recently that highlights the challenge farmers and other landowners face from SNAs on their property?
statement: Landowners have told me that if you’re unlucky enough to have an SNA identified on your property, you are likely to be prohibited from undertaking any new activity or development in that area. I have also seen that these restrictions will be applied to areas that are not very significant. For example, a sheltered gully with some trees—a bit of matagouri which offers a great sheltered area to graze a few sheep after shearing or in a storm.

explanation: Asked for the effect of the restrictions; he states effects — disincentive to voluntary conservation, and reversion to gorse, broom and wilding pines without active management. Directly responsive.
question: What is the effect of those restrictions?
statement: Apart from being at a disincentive to voluntarily conserve areas of indigenous biodiversity, farmers know well what happens when the ability to actively manage land is restricted. If SNAs are applied to areas with low biodiversity value, then without the landowner managing pest and weed - control, it will just go to gorse, broom, and wilding pines.

explanation: Asked what he will do in the long term; most of the answer describes the existing voluntary position (QEII covenants) rather than future action, and the forward-looking part is an approach ('work collaboratively', 'incentivise') rather than anything he will do. It reaches the question only partly.
question: What will he do in the long term to restore property rights and protect indigenous biodiversity?
statement: It is good. Landowners are already voluntarily protecting areas of native biodiversity—over 180,000 hectares are already protected through QEII National Trust. Put together, that would be our fifth-largest national park, all voluntarily. Many more have committed to enhance biodiversity on their land without formalising it. The way to protect biodiversity on private land is to work collaboratively with landowners, including farmers, foresters, and iwi, to incentivise the sustainable use of land, and to show them that their work to protect the biodiversity is valued and then they will want to do more.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether the new approach will put more people on the streets. The literal 'Yes' is followed by material answering a different question — that the approach is part of a wider response to end emergency housing use — so the affirmative does not attach to what was asked. The street-homelessness core is left untouched.
question: Will the Government’s new approach to emergency housing grants result in more New Zealanders living on the streets?
statement: Yes, the Government’s new approach is part of a wider response to end large-scale use of emergency housing and to get New Zealanders, tamariki, and whānau into homes faster.

explanation: A narrow factual question — has he received advice or evidence on this specific point? He confirms only that advice arrives 'on a regular basis' and then restates the policy intention, never saying whether any such advice or evidence exists. A precise question dodged.
question: Has he received advice or evidence showing that New Zealanders who will no longer be able to access emergency housing special needs grants under this Government’s new approach will all find housing and not end up living on the streets?
statement: We receive advice on housing matters on a regular basis, and the advice that we’ve received is that we will continue to focus on ending the large-scale use of emergency housing and getting whānau and tamariki into homes faster.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Bennett's statement and, if so, why he is reducing access. He neither agrees nor disagrees and gives no reason; the 'genuine needs' formulation only glances at the premise. Both limbs of the question go unanswered.
question: Does he agree with the previous Minister for social development and Minister for Social Housing who introduced the emergency housing special needs grant, Paula Bennett, who stated, “This is the first time any Government has committed ongoing dedicated funding for emergency housing, because we recognise that not everyone has access to a safe and stable home.”; if yes, why is he looking to reduce access to that support, and pushing more New Zealanders back to sleeping in cars?
statement: We recognise that there are many people with genuine needs that need emergency housing, and we will continue to support those people with genuine needs to have emergency housing accommodation.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether reducing numbers on the books is the strategy. The response pivots to 'bold and radical solutions' and the previous Government's record; the mention of prioritising 12-week-plus families is adjacent, not an answer. The strategy question is never engaged.
question: Is it now this Government’s strategy to make it harder to access emergency housing grants so as to reduce the number of New Zealanders in emergency housing on their books at the expense of more New Zealanders sleeping rough outside our businesses, in our carparks, and in our parks?
statement: We need bold and radical solutions to end the housing crisis that has been exacerbated under the previous Government. We need to get the country back on track, and particularly with housing, and we will do that through a wide series of responses and steps, one of which is prioritising the tamariki and whānau who have been sleeping in emergency accommodation for 12 consecutive weeks or more.

explanation: Two limbs: does he agree with the quoted statement, and is the street preferable to a motel. He says 'I agree', but immediately recasts what he is agreeing with into a general call for radical solutions rather than the quoted claim about fewer children in motels, and ignores the second limb entirely. A partial engagement at best.
question: Does he agree with the Minister for Social Development and Employment that “I am not saying that it is going perfect; what I am saying is that we will have fewer children in motels, and that is what we are out to achieve.”, and, if so, is living on the streets more perfect than living in a motel?
statement: I agree with my learned colleague the Minister for Social Development and Employment, the member for Taupō, in that we do need absolute radical and bold solutions for our housing crisis, and it is tough for those folks, and no one in this House wants to see whānau, tamariki, and mokopuna living in emergency housing for an extended period of time, but that is what we have seen over the last six years.

explanation: Asked what implications excluding a Treaty clause has for Māori rights in resource consents, especially unsettled hapū/iwi. Peters does give a directional answer — the implication will be positive, because decisions will run on merit — so the question is engaged rather than ignored, but he never touches the resource-consent or unsettled-iwi core of it and slides into a broader argument about elitism. Partial engagement.
question: What implications will the exclusion of a Treaty clause from fast-tracking legislation have on Māori fundamental rights and interests in resource consents, especially for hapū and iwi who have not settled yet?
statement: The fact is that that exclusion will have a very positive outcome for Māori because now things will be based on merit and not just elitism and racism, which ordinary Māori never asked for in the first place.

explanation: Asked two specific things: what qualifies a project as having significant regional/national benefits, and how benefits are weighted against environmental costs. The answer offers only a process assurance ('jealously guarded', 'a serious process of examination') and then pivots to getting the country's mojo back and elitists blocking projects. Neither criterion nor weighting is ever reached.
question: What qualifies a project as having significant regional or national benefits, and how are these economic benefits weighted against environmental costs?
statement: All aspects for consideration will be very jealously guarded in terms of the research on them—they’ll go through a serious process of examination—but we are a country that needs to get our mojo back and real fast, and not have certain elitists stopping every project that we should be developing. We’ve got the resources, we’ve got the people; we just need—and now have got—the leadership.

explanation: A narrow factual question — how much money is set aside to mitigate failed fast-tracked projects. The answer says only that 'certain expenditure is always warranted' and pivots to a comparison with three waters. No amount, no mechanism; a specific question squarely avoided.
question: How much money will be set aside to mitigate risks of failed fast-tracked projects, such as we saw with Tamarind Taranaki oil projects, which cost the Government hundreds of millions of dollars in bailout?
statement: Certain expenditure is always warranted, but none of it will amount to the $1.2 billion that vanished on three waters.

explanation: Asked how many additional social houses the Priority One category creates. Bishop states plainly that more social housing is not created directly by the policy change — that is the answer (none), given explicitly before the surrounding context and the swipe at the previous Government. Padding and blame don't count against forthrightness; the question was answered.
question: How many additional social houses will be created as a result of the Priority One category for emergency housing announced yesterday?
statement: The Government’s creation of the priority one category will prioritise getting families with children out of emergency housing, under stable social housing, sooner. Therefore, more social housing is not created directly as a result of this policy change. We’ve committed, through our manifesto, to increase the number of social housing places in line with the previous Government’s funding track. The member will note that the previous Government left a fiscal cliff of funding for social housing, so any future funding is subject to Budget decisions. The priority one category is only the beginning of the steps we will be taking to end the large-scale use of emergency housing motels and returning them to rarely and briefly needed—as a last resort. Addressing the issue of emergency housing is complex and, as I said yesterday, will require a sustained and coordinated effort over multiple years to achieve our aim. But the key thing is we’re not going to sit by like the last Government did and ignore it. We are taking action.

explanation: Asked why the announcement was made without committing to more social housing funding. Bishop answers with reasons, enumerated: you don't need to do both at once, and not everyone leaving emergency housing goes into social housing. Whether those reasons are good ones is Rigor; the 'why' was directly engaged.
question: Why, then, did the Government make an emergency housing announcement without committing to funding more additional social housing?
statement: Well, for a couple of reasons. One is that you don’t need to do both things at the same time. The second point is that not everyone who goes from emergency housing goes into social housing. Actually, the housing system is extremely complex. The relationships between emergency housing and social housing and transitional are actually not linear. We see private landlords and the wider housing system as a part of the solution, and work is under way across every part of the housing continuum: from homeownership, through the rental market, through the private landlord market, and through the social housing generally.

explanation: Asked where people are supposed to go if they can't stay in emergency housing and no new places are funded. Bishop rejects the premise and points to 6,000 places already funded through Budgets 2022–23, which implicitly answers 'where', but the destination question for the people concerned is never addressed head-on and future funding is deferred to the Budget. Partial.
question: If they can’t stay in emergency housing and the Government won’t commit to funding more social housing, transitional housing, or rental places, where are they supposed to go?
statement: Well, the member’s question is based upon a false assumption. There is more social housing coming. The Budget 2023 increased social housing places by 3,000. That goes on top of Budget 2022. So between 18 months ago and two years, up until June 2025, there are 6,000 new social housing places, delivered both by Kāinga Ora and by the community housing sector. So there are more social housing places. Decisions around future social housing funding is a matter for the Budget—the member will have to wait.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that social houses will not be sold off. The recorded response is laughter — no engagement with the question at all, not even a refusal. A blunt 'no, I won't guarantee that' would have scored high; this gives nothing.
question: Will he guarantee to the House that his Government will not sell off social houses like what happened the last time National were in Government?
statement: Ha, ha—ha, ha!

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that homelessness will not increase as a result of the announcement. The answer never says yes or no, and instead argues that the inherited funding track would have sold 10,000 State houses and blames the questioner's party. The core — will he guarantee it — is entirely bypassed.
question: If the Minister is unwilling to provide that guarantee, will he at least guarantee to the House that levels of homelessness will not increase as a result of the announcement made yesterday?
statement: The fastest way to increase homelessness would have been for the Government to continue with the funding track we inherited, which would have seen 10,000 State houses sold off by Kāinga Ora because of that member’s party’s woeful mismanagement of one of the biggest companies in New Zealand. Under the funding track we inherited, in writing Kāinga Ora was planning to sell 10,000 State houses. We’re not prepared to sit around and tolerate that. That’s why we’re reviewing Kāinga Ora.

explanation: Asked directly whether he will resign if homelessness rises. The answer talks about planning to be a better Minister than his predecessor and attacks her record. A yes/no question with no yes or no anywhere in the response.
question: If homelessness goes up under his watch, will he resign?
statement: I plan on being a better Minister responsible for homelessness than the last one, the Hon Marama Davidson, who saw homelessness skyrocket to record levels and couldn’t even spend the money that Megan Woods allocated to her.

explanation: Asked what recent transport investment announcements he has made. The answer names the announcement — the draft Government Policy Statement on Land Transport released with the Prime Minister — and its content. A patsy question, but it is squarely answered; the closing campaign line doesn't detract.
question: What recent announcements has he made about transport investment in New Zealand?
statement: Earlier this week, the Prime Minister and I released the draft Government Policy Statement on Land Transport, announcing that we are focused on investing in new roads of national significance, better public transport, and a well-maintained roading network, enabling Kiwis to get where they want to go quickly and safely. Kiwis around the country voted for our focused transport plan, and now we are delivering.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked why economic Ministers rather than an expert panel should decide which projects proceed. Bishop answers the why directly: because the regime's purpose is to fast track economic development projects. The reasoning is close to circular, but circularity is a Rigor failure, not evasion — the question was met.
question: Why should economic Ministers decide what is worthy of proceeding, rather than an expert panel, as suggested in the new fast-tracking legislation?
statement: Because the whole purpose of the fast-track consenting regime that we are introducing is to fast track economic development projects.

explanation: Asked whether specific homelessness outcomes (a named 2017 case) would recur because of the MSD changes. The response never engages the causal question — it restates support for 'genuine need' and the aspiration to end large-scale emergency housing, plus a Hamilton/Waikato statistic. Talking-point pivot; the yes/no/likelihood at the core is untouched.
question: Will we see homelessness situations like that of West Auckland tetraplegic woman Tracey Penney, who was living in her van in January 2017—it was widely reported on—arise again because of the changes to the treatment of homeless Ministry of Social Development clients?
statement: Can I please reiterate that we will support those with genuine need to have emergency housing, but our aspiration is to end the large-scale use of emergency housing, particularly in places like Hamilton and Waikato, where there are over 500 kids living in emergency housing right now.

explanation: Asked what announcements he had made about the fast-track regime. He states directly what was announced, with whom, and that the legislation has its first reading this afternoon. The subsequent 'red and green tape' rhetoric is padding, but the question was answered before it. (Scored on engagement only — that this is a friendly question with a promotional answer is not a Forthrightness deduction.)
question: What announcements has he made regarding the establishment of a new fast-track consenting one-stop shop regime?
statement: Earlier today, alongside the Prime Minister and the Minister for Regional Development and the Minister of Transport, I announced the coalition Government’s new one-stop shop fast-track approvals regime, and, this afternoon, the House will consider that legislation in its first reading. New Zealand has been stuck in the slow lane for far too long when it comes to getting the major projects we need to get our country growing again. We are determined to cut through the thicket of red and green tape holding New Zealand back by fast tracking consents for projects of regional and national significance whilst protecting Treaty settlements and the environment.

explanation: Asked how projects will be fast tracked. He gives the two mechanisms — ministerial joint referral on application, or listing in Schedule 2A — which is squarely responsive. Trails off mid-elaboration, but the core of the question was reached and answered before the cut.
question: How will projects be fast tracked under the new regime?
statement: Very good question. There are two ways projects can be fast tracked: they can either be referred by the joint decision of the Ministers of infrastructure, regional development, and transport upon an application, or by being listed in Schedule 2A of the bill. Projects in Schedule 2A will be automatically referred into the fast-track process—

explanation: 'Does she stand by all her statements and actions?' — 'Yes.' One word, complete, no dodge. Matches the worked example exactly.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked what actions she has taken in light of the Newshub/TVNZ job losses. She names actual actions — the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill before select committee, work with officials on modernising the media system — so the question is engaged, but framed around commitment and intention rather than what was done in response to these losses. Partial: it reaches the question without fully closing on it. Note the vagueness itself is a Specificity matter and was not double-counted here.
question: What actions, if any, has she taken to support the media sector in light of job losses at Newshub and Television New Zealand?
statement: The Government is committed to working with the sector on ways to ensure sustainability. As I have previously stated, the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill is currently before select committee, and I’m awaiting the committee’s report. I’m working with officials to modernise the media system in New Zealand to level the playing field for our local broadcasters. I want to encourage more private and international investment in our local content.

explanation: A two-part question: is singling out reporters appropriate, and has she raised it with Seymour. Neither part is answered — she affirms editorial independence in the abstract (adjacent, not responsive) and then turns on the questioner as 'ironic'. The 'has she spoken with' half is a narrow factual question left entirely unaddressed, which weighs heavily.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does the Minister believe singling out reporters for doing their job is appropriate, and, if so, has she spoken with David Seymour, who is one of the senior Ministers, about respecting the independence of the fourth estate?
statement: I believe and honour all editorial independence of our media because they perform an important duty in our democracy, and that should be protected. In terms of the comment, I think, as I said previously, it is ironic to watch this member ask this question, given his previous interview on Q + A.

explanation: Asked what impression she is giving the public. The response opens by attacking the previous Government, corrects a factual detail about where a photo was taken, and accounts for her own whereabouts — none of which addresses the impression created. Lower confidence: the question text is truncated mid-sentence, though its core is legible.
question: —to have a look at. What was the impression that she’s giving out to the public—
statement: That is the substance of the previous Government. That member does not even know that that photo was taken at the New Zealand Open, and I was there as the Minister responsible for funding the Major Events Fund. However, at the time when the announcement was made this morning, I was in my office doing work, but yesterday I did not actually see the announcement alert that came to my office because I was doing an interview with one of the media companies.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that increased eligibility scrutiny won't increase homelessness. He pledges the Government is working day and night to move families out of emergency housing into their own homes — a commitment to effort, not the guarantee sought, and not a refusal to give one either. A plain 'no, I can't guarantee that' would have scored high; this neither gives nor declines the guarantee.
question: Can he guarantee that the increased scrutiny on emergency housing eligibility he announced yesterday won’t lead to more people becoming homeless?
statement: E oati ana au ki tēnei Whare rangatira nei e ngana ana te kāwanatanga Haumi me au nei, ao, pō, pō, ao, kia puta ngā tāngata me ngā whānau me ngā tamariki e noho ana ki roto i ngā whare ohotata ki ō rātou kāinga ake. E mihi ana.

explanation: Asked the purpose of directing someone below the poverty line toward unaffordable private rentals. The response supplies no purpose at all — 'bold and radical solutions' and the commitment to ending large-scale emergency housing. A narrow, pointed question met with unrelated policy framing.
question: What is the purpose of asking someone living below the poverty line, who can’t afford a private rental, to look for unaffordable housing while waiting for secure, affordable public housing?
statement: As mentioned earlier today, we need bold and radical solutions for our housing crisis, and we are absolutely committed to ending the large-scale use of emergency housing and to help whānau and tamariki, in particular, get into homes faster.

explanation: Asked why he proceeds given he cannot guarantee the outcome. The rationale is at best implied by restating the objective, then deflected onto the previous Government. The 'why proceed despite the risk' premise is not confronted; the risk is acknowledged only as 'tough decisions ... for officials'.
question: If he can’t guarantee that his policies won’t leave more people in the street and without safe shelter, why is he going ahead with them?
statement: As mentioned earlier, we’re absolutely focused on ending the large-scale use of emergency housing, and there will be some engaging and tough decisions and considerations for officials to make. However, we intend to end large-scale emergency housing, which has been absolutely exacerbated by the previous Government.

explanation: 'Does he stand by his Government's policies and actions?' — 'Yes.' Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s policies and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether the yet-to-be-listed Schedule 2A/2B projects would go to select committee with public submissions. Bishop opens with a flat "No, that's not the intention" and then describes the Amendment Paper route instead. The core yes/no is answered squarely; only the sub-clause about public submission is handled loosely ("plenty of opportunities to engage"), which costs it the last tenth.
question: Will the projects yet to be included in Schedule 2A and 2B of the proposed bill be referred to select committee for scrutiny, including the ability for the public to submit?
statement: No, that’s not the intention. Instead, what we’re doing is running a process that is independent of the Government. Recommendations will come to Ministers; the projects will then be inserted into the bill by an Amendment Paper—or it used to be called a Supplementary Order Paper. There will be plenty of opportunities for the public to engage on that, and I look forward to that.

explanation: Asked how the public will be able to engage in the process just described. He does name a mechanism — submitting to the expert panel — so this is not a pure pivot. But the mechanism he names is for people who want projects inserted, i.e. proponents, which is a narrower group than the "public" asked about; the question's core (how does the wider public get a say) is only glanced at. Partial engagement.
question: How will the public be able to engage in the process he just referred to?
statement: Well, it’s a public democratic process. People who are keen on having the projects inserted into the bill will be able to submit them to the expert panel that we’re setting up to consider those projects.

explanation: Asked why the Environment Minister is excluded from decision-making when three other Ministers are not. A reason is actually supplied — environmental considerations are to be handled by the expert panel rather than by that Minister — so the question is engaged. The back half then drifts into the COVID-19 fast-track comparison and thanking the former Minister, which is padding around an answer already given rather than a substitute for one.
question: Why is the Minister for the Environment not involved in the decision-making process when the Ministers of infrastructure, regional development, and transport are?
statement: Because, as I say, this is a one-stop shop fast-track consenting regime specifically designed to accelerate infrastructure, housing, transport, aquaculture, mining, the extractive industries—all of the things that New Zealand needs more of rather than less of. The relevant environmental considerations are best handled by the expert panel. They’re the experts for it. They’re going to be asked to apply the relevant environmental permits and conditions to it, and then those decisions will come back through the process for Ministers to either approve or decline. It’s not actually wildly dissimilar to the COVID-19 fast-track legislation set up by the previous Government. We’ve actually modelled the new law on the old regime introduced by the last Labour Government. We thought it was such a good idea we’ve taken it the next step further, elevated it up a bit, and gone for national and regionally significant projects. I thank the former Minister and the former Minister for the Environment for the idea.

explanation: Asked how the Government is progressing its law-and-order commitments. Goldsmith answers with three specific pieces of progress across three days. Directly and completely responsive to what was asked.
question: How is the Government progressing its commitments in relation to restoring law and order?
statement: On Tuesday, we introduced and have now passed legislation to stop taxpayer funding of section 27 cultural reports that proliferated under the former regime, consuming more than $7 million out of the legal aid budget. Yesterday, we introduced legislation to give police greater powers to search for firearms so that they can keep them out of the hands of serious gang offenders and help keep our communities safe. Today, we will be introducing legislation to give police greater powers to deal with gangs, who, for too long, have been allowed to behave as if they’re above the law.

explanation: Asked what today's legislation will do. He enumerates the four things the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does. Nothing in the question is left unreached.
question: What is the legislation that the Government is introducing today going to do?
statement: The Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill does four things: we’re prohibiting the display of gang insignia in all public places; we’re giving the police the ability to require gang members to disperse from gatherings that disrupt the public; we’re creating new non-consorting orders to stop specified gang members from associating; and, finally, we’re amending the Sentencing Act to make gang membership, on its own, an aggravating factor at sentencing.
