explanation: Asked why the Government is acting now. He gives a because-clause: gang membership rose ~50% over six years, so a firmer response is required now. Whether that reasoning holds up is a Rigor question; as an answer to "why now", it lands.
question: Why is the Government doing this now?
statement: Because the gangs have been recruiting faster than the police over the past six years, from 6,000-odd in 2018, to 9,000 at present—a 50 percent increase. They’ve been emboldened to take over public places and to continue to be associated with crime. That is why a firmer response is required now.

explanation: Asked a narrow countable question — how many law-and-order actions in the 100-day plan have been completed. No number is ever given. He lists examples and closes with "rounds out the 100-day plan", which implies completion and so is not a total dodge, but the specific quantity asked for is avoided. A narrow factual question left unanswered scores low.
question: How many actions relating to restoring law and order in the 100-day plan has the Government completed?
statement: Well, the Government is committed to a number of immediate actions in the 100-day plan, from stopping taxpayer funding for section 27 reports, to abolishing the previous Government’s prisoner reduction target, to taking the first steps to ensure prisoners on remand can access rehabilitation programmes, and many other things that my colleagues—Ministers Mitchell, McKee, and Chhour—have progressed. The first reading of the Gangs Legislation Amendment Bill and Courts (Remote Participation) Amendment Bill today rounds out the 100-day plan.

explanation: Asked whether he considers it acceptable to disagree with officials' advice. "Well, yes, I do, from time to time" — a direct yes, with the rest as elaboration. Complete.
question: Does the Minister consider it acceptable to disagree with advice from his officials?
statement: Well, yes, I do, from time to time. We don’t necessarily agree with every piece of advice that we get from officials here in Wellington, and we treat all advice with respect, but, fundamentally, when a Government is elected to deliver on a policy to keep our country safe, we will deliver on that policy.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his statements and policies. "Yes." One word, and it fully answers the question put.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and policies?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a specific quoted statement about wanting a thorough and transparent process. "Yes." Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by his statement with regard to the fast-track bill, “I want a thorough and transparent process.”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how legislating under urgency, an hour before debate, with two schedules withheld, meets his own "thorough and transparent" standard. He does argue the point rather than change the subject — prior announcement, published framework, consultation with iwi and NGOs, and a stated reason for urgency (to reach select committee sooner). But the two sharpest elements of the question — the withheld schedules and the one-hour notice — are left untouched, so the core is only half engaged.
question: How does introducing legislation with such extraordinary ministerial powers, under urgency, less than an hour before it is due to be debated in the House, with two critical schedules withheld from public scrutiny, meet the standard of “thorough and transparent”?
statement: Well, how do I count the ways? Firstly, the Government announced that we were doing this back in late January, early February. I made that a public announcement, and we published the framework and the design of the scheme. That went out to all and sundry—iwi; post-governance settlement entities; environmental NGOs, who’ve been voluminous in their criticism of it, but we’ll take that as read. The public has had many chances to engage on this. Officials have been working away designing the bill. The bill has been introduced, albeit, yes, under urgency, to meet the 100-day commitment to get it into the House, and the reason why it’s under urgency is to send it to a committee as soon as possible so the public can have their say on this extremely important piece of legislation. There are a number of other examples that I could point to.

explanation: Asked how he justifies limiting consultation given the kinds of projects that could be scheduled. A justification is offered — precedent from Labour's COVID-19 fast-track regime, plus a claim that this process is more transparent. It is a tu quoque and its validity is a Rigor matter, not a Forthrightness one; as engagement it counts. Marked down because the specific content of the question (coalmines, deep-sea mining, court-rejected projects, freshwater and biodiversity protections) is never addressed.
question: How can he justify limiting public consultation when projects that will be on the Schedule could include coalmines, deep-sea mines, and projects that have already been turned down by the courts on environmental grounds, whilst overriding protections for fresh water and indigenous biodiversity?
statement: I justify it in the same way that the previous Government introduced the COVID-19 fast-track regime, which included 17 or maybe 19 projects listed in the Schedule that were automatically referred to an expert panel. That member was a member of the Government that supported that regime in the last Parliament. It’s very similar. Actually, we’ve been even more transparent in the sense that we are running an independent process for projects to be referred to the Government to insert in the bill. In the last Parliament, the COVID-19 fast-track regime, a bill was presented, there were 17 projects listed in the Schedule, and those projects got referred to a fast-track consenting expert panel.

explanation: Asked to confirm that approval decisions now sit with Ministers rather than independent experts. Answers "Yes" outright and owns the design choice. Direct and complete; the follow-on rhetoric doesn't dilute the answer.
question: Can he confirm that one of the key differences from previous fast-track legislation is that the ultimate decision to approve or decline projects will now sit with Ministers rather than with independent experts?
statement: Yes. That’s a key design choice of the regime. We’re proud of it. We’re determined to cut through the red tape holding this country back and to get on with building things this country needs.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware that rushing the bill under urgency creates a risk of consents later being scrutinised or lost without compensation. He engages both limbs squarely: contests the premise that it is being rushed (first reading, select committee, submissions, prior consultation) and responds directly to the compensation point. Rejecting a question's premise head-on is engagement, not evasion — but he never states whether he accepts the residual risk exists, so it stops short of complete.
question: Is he aware that rushing legislation with such extraordinary executive powers through Parliament, under urgency, with little public scrutiny, creates a risk that any of the projects that are approved as a result of this bill could find themselves subject to future scrutiny, which could include the loss of the consent, possibly without compensation?
statement: Well, a couple of points to make there. Firstly, the bill is not being rushed through Parliament. The bill is being read a first time this afternoon, and if it meets with the House’s approval, it will be sent to a select committee for consideration. It will go to the Environment Committee. I’ve got full confidence in the chair of the Environment Committee and, actually, the Environment Committee, to do a good job. There will be a full public submission process. Prior to the bill being introduced into the Parliament, there has been extensive consultation on the design parameters of the bill. There’s been extensive engagement with iwi and Māori groups; I’ve been meeting with them regularly over the last few weeks alongside Minister Potaka. The simple reality is that this will be one of the most well consulted on bills and regimes in recent history. To the member’s second point, in throwing around language around cancellation of consents without compensation, I would just say to the member he needs to be very careful in relation to comments like that. I think all members in Parliament have an obligation to bear in mind sovereign risk to New Zealand and the way in which projects happen.

explanation: Asked if he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. "Absolutely" is a complete answer to the question asked; everything after it is unrequested elaboration, which is a Specificity/Focus matter, not a dodge.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Absolutely, and including yesterday’s announcement that this Government will finally hold Kāinga Ora (KO) tenants who are threatening, abusive, and violent towards their neighbours to account for their actions. Our Government believes in rights and responsibilities, so if you contribute to a culture of intimidation and abuse, it’s time to change your behaviour, and if you don’t, you may not keep your taxpayer-funded State house. There are just far too many families on the wait-list who would respect that property and respect their neighbours to just privilege those current KO tenants who wage a war of abuse in the community. It’s not right, and I agree with the member when he said that after six years in Government, he didn’t do enough to crack down on unruly tenants. Well, the good news is enough is enough. This Government was elected to change, and we’re going to do exactly that.

explanation: Asked whether the Deputy PM is correct about a $5.6 billion shortfall and a gap in pre-election costings. Refuses to engage with the figure at all and pivots to attacking the questioner's record. Note this is not a refusal-that-answers — he never says whether the claim is correct, nor that he won't say.
question: Is the Deputy Prime Minister correct that the Government has a $5.6 billion Budget shortfall and that there is “a huge gap” in its pre-election costings?
statement: Well, I can tell you I’m not going to take any lectures from that member about economic management. That was a Government that was characterised by spending more, taxing more, borrowing more, and we heard from the new finance spokesperson they want to continue to do more of it.

explanation: A narrow factual question — which of two specific revenue figures ($155m vs $716m) is right. The answer never touches either number, substituting a general commitment to tax relief. A precise question avoided precisely at its core.
question: Is the IRD correct that his Government’s proposed tax on offshore online casino operators will raise $155 million over four years, or are the “rock-solid” costings that he and Nicola Willis produced correct, suggesting the change will bring $716 million of revenue over the same period—a difference of over $500 million?
statement: What I can reassure the member about is that this is a Government that’s going to give tax relief to working New Zealanders, low and middle income workers who actually deserve a tax break after 14 years of not getting one, particularly from that previous Government. That’s what we’re going to deliver for them.

explanation: Asked which of two figures on benefit-adjustment savings is correct. Answers a different question entirely — a list of things the Government won't do — using the word "numbers" as a pivot. The $1.3 billion discrepancy is never addressed.
question: Which numbers are correct: his rock-solid estimate of the savings that his cuts to benefit adjustments will make, or the latest official advice that they’ll save $1.3 billion less than he promised before the election?
statement: Well, I can tell the member the numbers that we’re not going to be doing. We’re not going to increase Government spending by 84 percent. We’re not going to hire 16,000 more public servants. We’re not going to increase Government debt from $5 billion to $100 billion and actually have nothing to show for it. We’re a Government that’s going to fix this economy, we’re going to grow the economy, give people tax relief, and ensure there’s a culture of fiscal discipline.

explanation: Asked which costing of the landlord tax change is correct given an $800 million discrepancy. Response moves to rental supply and rent levels under the previous Government; neither figure is confirmed, denied, or acknowledged.
question: Well, which numbers are correct: his rock-solid pre-election estimate of the cost of tax cuts for landlords or the latest official advice that they will cost $800 million more than he promised before the election?
statement: I think what’s great is we care about renters, a group that the Labour Party used to care about a lot. Actually, we’re increasing the supply of rental properties, we’re lowering costs that have just been passed through to renters—because under that Government, average rents went up $170 a week. That’s not going to happen under our Government. We want downward pressure on rents, not upward pressure.

explanation: Asked why he claimed on 11 March not to have seen advice his finance Minister had already confirmed. The "given up" phrasing is picked up as a rhetorical hook to talk about renters; the question of what he knew and when is never engaged.
question: Why did he claim on 11 March that he hadn’t seen the advice that his Government’s tax cuts for landlords had blown out by $800 million, given his finance Minister had already publicly confirmed that that was the case, or has he just given up on trying to keep track of all of his Government’s Budget blowouts?
statement: I’ll tell you who I haven’t given up on, and it’s the renters of New Zealand. Under that Government, average rents went up $170 a week. Well, I’m sorry, we’re here to fix things. We’re here to get the country turned around. We’re going to get things done, and we’re going to make sure that there’s more rental property available. We don’t just load up landlords with costs that pass on to renters that lead to higher rents. We want lower rents, downward pressure on rents.

explanation: A yes/no question: will tenants get $800 million of rent reductions? He stays on the topic of rents and implies downward pressure rather than reductions of that scale, which gestures at an answer, but never says yes or no and never engages the quantum asked about. Partial contact with the question, not an answer.
question: Will tenants get $800 million worth of rent reductions as a result of this policy?
statement: What we will be doing is increasing the supply of rental property and putting downward pressure on rent, as he has received in formal advice before in Government. That’s why his policies didn’t work. They ended up increasing average rents—that’s not acceptable. We’re on the side of renters in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his own quoted claim to be "rock solid in our numbers" given three named discrepancies. Responds by attacking the questioner's economic record; the quoted statement and the three figures go entirely unaddressed.
question: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, “I can tell you in the National Party we understand the economy and we are rock solid in our numbers.”, given his tax promises were $800 million out on interest deductibility, more than $500 million out on gambling, and $1.3 billion out on benefit indexation?
statement: Well, look, I can tell you it is ironic that you are trying to lecture me on economics after six years of being in Government, of actually causing huge damage to our books, having had economic mismanagement and vandalism on a scale we’ve never seen before, an 84 percent increase in Government spending. You drove up domestic inflation, you drove up interest rates, the last three quarters of the last year’s economic growth went down, and you’ve got rising unemployment. So I don’t take lectures from you on anything to do with economics, thank you very much.

explanation: Asked by how much Government debt has increased. She engages the question directly and supplies the comparison figures (5% of GDP in 2008, 19% in 2019) but is cut off by interruption before delivering the current number the question turns on. Engagement is genuine and on-point; the answer as recorded is incomplete rather than deflected.
question: By how much has Government debt increased in recent years?
statement: In 2008, net core Crown debt—a measure which includes Government financial assets as well as financial liabilities—was 5 percent of GDP. Despite the global financial crisis (GFC), both the Key-English Government and the following Labour Government, at least initially, had a goal of keeping net debt to 20 percent of GDP or below. In 2019, it was 19 percent. What is it now? Net core Crown debt, according to the latest forecasts—[Interruption] Members opposite laugh, but I think most New Zealanders would be interested in this grave number. They don’t think it’s very laughable—

explanation: Asked what caused debt to rise so quickly. Names causes directly — COVID-19, non-COVID spending growth, a structural operating deficit — and quantifies the increase. Squarely answers the question asked; whether the attribution is fair or true is a Veracity/Rigor matter.
question: What has caused debt to increase so quickly?
statement: Well, COVID-19 was a big reason that net core Crown debt increased so quickly, but Government spending outside of COVID has also increased significantly, with Treasury advising me that the previous Government left us with a structural operating deficit of around 2 percent of GDP. The result is that net core Crown debt increased from around $59 billion in 2017 to $183 billion this year, an increase of more than $100 billion in six short years.

explanation: Asked whether she had seen other explanations for the debt increase. She says "yes, I have seen reports" and quotes one directly. The question is squarely engaged; the trailing attack on light rail and the cycle bridge is beside the point of Forthrightness, and the patsy nature of the question does not lower the score.
question: Has she seen any other explanations for the recent increase in debt?
statement: Well, yes, I have seen reports that the reason debt increased so much was that the previous Government was making so many high-quality infrastructure investments. In particular, one not exactly impartial observer recently said that increasing debt “has enabled us to invest more in transport, into health and education capital, more into the things we need to underpin the kind of society and economy we want”. I have searched for evidence of such high-quality investment, but amongst the wreckage of light rail, the Auckland harbour cycle bridge—

explanation: Asked whether the Government should borrow for productive investments. Opens with "Absolutely" and states the condition (high-quality investments with lasting benefit). Direct and complete; the added caveat about shocks extends the answer rather than dodging it.
question: Should the Government borrow for productive investments?
statement: Absolutely. That is one of the reasons the Government should borrow: to fund high-quality investments that provide benefits to New Zealanders over time, including those that increase the productive capacity of the economy. But I would add one important note of caution: economic shocks push up debt quite considerably. We’ve seen this recently with the global financial crisis and with COVID. After a shock, Governments have to either bring debt down again as a percentage of GDP, which necessarily requires constraint, or let debt settle at a higher level. New Zealand has seen public debt ratchet up like this since 2008. I would invite members to engage in a little thought experiment, where we went through the GFC and COVID with a starting point for net debt of 50 percent of GDP rather than 5 percent; so Governments should always be thinking about the next shock that’s around the corner, not just maxing out the credit card today.

explanation: Asked whether she has seen commentators arguing for higher debt. Answers "Well, yes" and names the source. Directly answered; the swipe at the questioner's colleague is a Civility/Focus matter, not a dodge.
question: Has she seen any commentators arguing for higher debt?
statement: Well, yes. I have seen a report saying that a future Government would consider taking on more debt, despite New Zealand’s debt being the highest for 30 years, despite us having little to show for it, and despite interest costs rising to $8.8 billion this year. I’m disappointed to hear that coming from a member of this House, Barbara Edmonds.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his quoted statement about State houses as a safety net. Answers "Absolutely" twice, unambiguously. The congratulations and the long Kāinga Ora anecdote are padding around an answer that was already given, so the core was reached.
question: Does he stand by his statement, and I quote, “I think everyone agrees that the State must always provide a safety net for New Zealanders who have fallen on hard times … and State houses will … play a very important part of that safety net”?
statement: Absolutely. But, before I begin, can I just congratulate the member on her ascendancy to the leadership of the Green Party, or co-leadership of the Green Party. Absolutely, including those State tenants who have been abused and victimised by their neighbours. Take Cheyne Smith, who’s been a Kāinga Ora (KO) tenant since 2015 and described the actions of some of his neighbouring KO tenants. He said, “I’ve been beaten, the house has been robbed, egged, bottled. Visitors were assaulted, vehicles got stolen. It was a nightmare.” The previous Government and their friends in the Green Party promoted a policy that facilitated a culture of intimidation and abuse, and I’m very proud that our Government is going to deliver change.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that no children would be made homeless. He never gives or refuses a guarantee; he shifts to what the Government does not want to see and then to parental responsibility. It touches the subject matter but never reaches the yes/no that was asked for — an implied refusal is not a stated one.
question: Can he guarantee that no children in this country will be made homeless as a result of his Government’s policies?
statement: Well, we don’t want to actually see KO tenants being evicted from KO housing, but, actually, the parents are adults and they have a choice to make about whether they want to meet their obligations and their responsibilities. That is the first port of call.

explanation: Asked whether he would resign if children are made homeless. The response never mentions resignation at all, pivoting entirely to wait-list numbers and abused neighbours. A narrow yes/no question completely avoided.
question: Will he resign if any children are made homeless as a result of his Government’s policies?
statement: There are children that are growing up in motels today, that are living on floors of family or friends, or in community housing provider housing, who actually want a shot, and their families want a shot, at being able to get into the State house. The problem today is that there are 24,000 people on a State house wait-list, which went up four or five times under the previous Government. There are neighbours in those KO communities who are getting abused, and I’m sorry, but we’re standing up for those folk and saying to them, “There are rights and responsibilities in this country”.

explanation: Asked whether the plan is that evicted tenants become homeless or end up in prison. He restates what "the plan here is" — engaging the framing enough to reject it implicitly — but never addresses either of the two outcomes put to him. Partial engagement, core avoided.
question: Is the plan here that those evicted from public housing are made homeless or eventually end up in prison?
statement: The plan here is to give people a shot of getting a State house—who deserve a shot at getting a State house and are going to appreciate it and value it, and actually make sure that they can actually get their shot at the Kiwi Dream. That’s what this is about. What this plan is about is making sure that neighbours of KO tenants, who are getting abused and threatened every single day—that stops. It stops.

explanation: Asked whether he cares about the evidence on homelessness, poverty and inequality. The answer is a single sentence about growing the economy and lifting wages — a straight pivot to talking points that answers a different question.
question: Does he care at all about the evidence that his Government’s policies will increase homelessness, poverty, and inequality, or is he intent on running this Government on vibes?
statement: We are wanting to grow this economy so we can drive more prosperity in this economy and lift wages and incomes for everybody.

explanation: Standard "does she stand by all her statements and actions" opener. Answered "Yes" with the routine "in the context in which they were given" qualifier — a direct answer with a light hedge, not an evasion.
question: Kia orana kātoatoa, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given. I particularly stand by my commitment to give tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the upcoming Budget in May.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by two specific statements. Answer: "Yes." One word, complete, nothing left unaddressed.
question: Does she stand by both her statements that she knows a front-line service “when I see it” and that there would be no cuts to front-line public services?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A two-part question: are Customs staff, police, firefighters, school lunches and Whaikaha carers front-line services, and why is the Government cutting them? She confirms police and school lunches, omits Customs, firefighters and Whaikaha entirely, and never engages the "why cut them" half — instead disputing the premise about lunches. Partly answered, with the sharper half sidestepped.
question: Does she see front-line services when she looks at Customs staff, police officers, firefighters, free school lunches, and carers funded through Whaikaha, and, if so, why is her Government cutting the support for these front-line services?
statement: Well, what a gift of a question! This is a Government that sees police as front line and is increasing the number of police. This is a Government that wants to continue the school lunch programme that the other Government didn’t leave any budgeted funding for, so we’re prioritising it in our upcoming Budget.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her commitment to tax cuts without borrowing. "That's right" is a direct, complete confirmation.
question: Does she stand by her statement that she is committed to delivering tax cuts without borrowing a cent?
statement: That’s right.

explanation: Asked whether Willis agrees with the PM's no-new-taxes commitment and, if so, how that squares with three named tax increases. The reply never says yes or no, and never touches the app tax, petrol tax or vehicle levy; it does gesture at the reconciliation by noting coalition negotiations amended campaign proposals, then pivots to a talking point about tax relief. Partial engagement with the second half only.
question: Does she agree with the Prime Minister when he committed to no new taxes or increasing existing taxes; if so, how does she reconcile that with breaking her promise to axe the app tax, increasing petrol taxes by 22c a litre, and introducing an additional $50 tax on every New Zealanders’ vehicle?
statement: I’ll give the member a little instruction on coalition Government, because the Government’s tax and fiscal plans reflect coalition negotiations which resulted in a number of amendments to the proposals that National and other parties campaigned on. And I’d just reassure the member that we will be delivering tax relief to the hard-working Kiwis who missed out on her Government’s watch and who haven’t had a tax reduction since 2010.

explanation: Asked why three promised-against taxes are being introduced, why wheelchair servicing is cut, and why school lunch funding is uncommitted. The reply squarely denies the premise on the spending items and commits to funding school lunches and disability services — that is an answer, if a flat one — but the tax half of the question is never reached before it turns to back-office waste.
question: Why is she introducing at least three new taxes she promised not to, cutting funding for wheelchair servicing, refusing to commit to funding school lunches as set out in her fiscal plan, and is she worried she will run out of election commitments to break?
statement: Look, the member can list a bunch of assertions that are completely incorrect but it doesn’t reflect well on her. Because we are committed to funding the school lunch programme, we are committed to funding disability services, we are committed to sustaining good front-line services—our Budget will reflect that. And here’s the thing: when you’re actually careful about eliminating waste in the back office, when you actually drive down the amount wasted on consultants and contractors and ridiculous processes and low-value programmes, that frees up more cash for front-line services that New Zealanders rely on. Our Government’s doing it; their Government should have—sorry about that.

explanation: Asked what actions were taken to set expectations for Kāinga Ora. The reply names the action directly: an interim letter of expectation sent yesterday, instructing the board to end the Sustaining Tenancies Framework and use specified Residential Tenancies Act tools. Directly and completely on point.
question: What actions has he taken setting out his expectations for Kāinga Ora-Homes and Communities?
statement: Oh, well, yesterday, the Minister of Finance and I, as shareholding Minister, sent an interim letter of expectation to the board of Kāinga Ora - Homes and Communities (KO), instructing them to end their Sustaining Tenancies Framework, the policy of the last Government that enabled intimidation, abuse, and destruction in communities up and down this country. We have directed Kāinga Ora to make better use of tools in the Residential Tenancies Act 1986, including formal warning notices, relocations, and, in severe and persistent cases, terminating tenancies. KO records hundreds of serious incidents every month, including alleged illegal activity, harassment, intimidation, threatening behaviour, and verbal abuse. Despite this, only three people were evicted last year for bad behaviour. There is no incentive for tenants to improve their behaviour or to stop damaging their taxpayer-funded house unless they know there are consequences. We’re bringing them back.

explanation: Asked what prompted the change. The reply states the prompts plainly — the harms the previous policy enabled and a National–ACT coalition commitment — then illustrates with cases. The illustrations are long but the question is answered before them.
question: What prompted the Government to make this change?
statement: Well, we’ve all seen the stories of the kind of misery that the last Government’s policy enabled, which is why we have directed Kāinga Ora to stop it. This also fulfils a coalition commitment between the National and ACT parties. To name just one example, we saw the elderly Whangārei couple subject to death threats from the patched Black Power Kāinga Ora tenants next door. They allegedly threatened to slit the 82-year-old man’s throat and watch him bleed out. To give you another example, we heard the heartbreaking story from a Te Awamutu homeowner who said a campaign of abuse from his Mongrel Mob Kāinga Ora neighbours cost him his marriage and left him with post-traumatic stress disorder. He told the New Zealand Herald of a night where a meth-crazed man linked to a Kāinga Ora property next door smashed up his house at 3 a.m. and tried to break in. These sorts of activities and behaviours need to stop, and under this Government, they will.

explanation: Asked what the letter said about rent arrears. The reply states exactly that: the expectation that Kāinga Ora stop letting tenants accrue arrears and be proactive in preventing them. Direct and complete.
question: What did this interim letter of expectations say about rent arrears?
statement: Well, the Government has laid out its expectation that Kāinga Ora stops letting tenants go into massive rent arrears, as we’ve seen happen over the last few years. To give you the exact numbers, in 2017, tenants’ rent debt was $1 million; six years later, it has ballooned to $21 million. At the moment, there are more than 450 Kāinga Ora tenants who each owe more than $10,000. That is a staggering amount of debt to let a State house tenant get into. It’s not fair on taxpayers. It’s not fair on the tenants themselves. We have instructed Kāinga Ora to be much more proactive about preventing this from happening in the first place.

explanation: Asked what else the letter said. The reply enumerates the remaining contents — faster placement into vacant homes, community engagement on developments — and notes an updated letter to follow. Squarely responsive.
question: What else did the letter of expectation say?
statement: We’ve made it clear that we expect Kāinga Ora to move families into vacant homes much more quickly than they are currently doing. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of homes vacant at any given time, and when the wait-list is over 25,000 people, that is not OK. We are also concerned about the loss of social licence for social housing in communities, often because communities feel that social housing developments happen without engagement from Kāinga Ora. We have therefore instructed them to do more to genuinely engage with local communities about their development plans and activities, above and beyond their existing legal requirements. We’ve sent this interim letter to make sure that they are focused on the right things right now, and we intend as a Government to issue an updated letter of expectation later this year in response to the independent review led by Sir Bill English, which is reporting to Ministers very soon.

explanation: Asked whether Mitchell stands by all statements and actions. Answered "Yes." One word, complete.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether Mitchell stands by a specific quoted statement on the police pay offer. Answered "Yes." Complete.
question: Does he stand by his statement regarding the police pay offer: “No, we are not offering less than what Labour offered. That’s not true at all.”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether Mitchell agrees with the Police Association president's quoted criticism, and if not, why not. The reply neither agrees nor disagrees and gives no reason; it offers mutual respect and a statement that good-faith negotiations continue. The core of the question is left untouched.
question: Does he agree with the president of the New Zealand Police Association, Chris Cahill, “It’s like a slap in the face. It’s like saying how dare you turn us down, we’re going to give you an even lower offer. They just misread the room. They’ve misread it badly.”; if not, why not?
statement: I respect the role of the president of the Police Association and he respects our role. The police and the Police Association are engaged in good-faith negotiations, and they carry on.

explanation: Asked whether the pay offer's terms are due to funding going to landlord tax cuts. Answered "No." A bare denial, but it is a complete answer to a yes/no question.
question: Is the real reason the police pay offer is not backdated and contains three significant clawbacks due to funding now going to tax cuts for landlords?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked which of two formulations is correct — a two-year commitment to 500 police, or a "goal we are heading towards". The reply restates the coalition agreement's commitment and asserts the PM's wording is consistent with it, so it does engage and effectively picks the commitment; but it declines to confront the tension the question was built around, so it is not a complete answer.
question: Which is correct: the coalition agreement that promises 500 new police in two years, or Christopher Luxon’s statement that it’s “a clear goal that we are heading towards”?
statement: Well, we’ve been very clear that the coalition agreement says that we will deliver 500 additional police officers in two years, and the Prime Minister is absolutely right in restating that.

explanation: Asked whether Luxon stands by the Government's policies and actions. Answered "Absolutely", with a caveat about context. That is a yes, lightly qualified.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s policies and actions?
statement: Absolutely—in the context that they were made.

explanation: Asked for a dollar figure Operation Emerald kept from gangs last year; answer gives the figure directly ($128 million) plus the harm-index number. Squarely answered.
question: How much money did Operation Emerald prevent going into the hands of gangs last year?
statement: Police destroyed over 35,000 cannabis plants and prevented $128 million going into the pockets of gangs through Operation Emerald. Based on the drug harm index, the estimated social harm prevented by Operation Emerald last year was $127 million.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with two named criticisms of Operation Emerald. He never says 'no', but condemning the comments as showing 'a lack of respect or understanding' makes his position on them unmistakable. Engaged, though the yes/no is left implicit and he drifts into praising police.
question: Does the Minister agree with the characterisations of Operation Emerald as “ineffective” and “police playing tin soldiers in the sky”?
statement: Comments like that show a lack of respect or understanding for the outstanding job our police officers do, in often difficult situations and circumstances, keeping our community safe and slowing down and disrupting the flow of harmful drugs into our communities.

explanation: Asked what his message to large-scale cannabis cultivators is; he states the message explicitly ('My message is quite simply this...'). Complete and on point.
question: What is the Minister’s message to criminals taking part in large-scale cultivation of cannabis?
statement: My message is quite simply this: if you choose to cultivate a drug that remains illegal and if you use it to fund your criminal lifestyle and perpetuate misery in our communities, you can expect police to hold you to account and to seize illegal firearms, drugs, and ill-gotten gains. I’m proud of the police and the work that they do in targeting organised crime, and I back Operation Emerald 100 percent.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on medicines access; he names the announcement (Pharmac assessing funding in parallel with Medsafe approval). Directly answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about improving New Zealanders’ access to medicines?
statement: Thank you to the member for his question. Pharmac is changing its processes so that it can assess a funding application at the same time Medsafe is assessing an application for regulatory approval of the same product. This means that medicines will be able to be considered sooner for funding in New Zealand. Access to medicines is a crucial part of many Kiwis’ lives, and this Government is speeding up the process so that more people have access to the medicines they need, quicker and sooner.

explanation: Asked how parallel assessment improves access; he explains the mechanism and the effect (up to nine months off the approval process). The question's core is reached.
question: How will the parallel assessment process that the Minister has outlined improve access to medicines?
statement: Well, currently, Pharmac waits until Medsafe has completed its assessment before it begins a funding assessment, unless the treatment is in relation to cancer. Doing both the regulatory assessment to see if it’s safe at Medsafe and the funding assessment to see if it is a good use of taxpayer funds at Pharmac at the same time is common sense. It’s a change that costs nothing but it will help Kiwis in need by shaving up to nine months off the approval process. It will also bring us into line with countries such as Australia and Canada, which do it and have been doing it exactly the way that we now will.

explanation: Asked whether he has seen reports of risks to medicines access; answers 'Yes' and identifies the report (Budget documents showing declining Pharmac funding). Direct and complete.
question: Has he seen any reports of any risks to access to medicines for New Zealanders?
statement: Yes. In fact, I have been looking at Budget documents that show that Pharmac’s funding over the next three years was left by the previous Government as reducing by several hundred million dollars each year for the next four years. In total, to maintain the level of pharmaceutical funding that New Zealanders are used to, the Government would have to find nearly $2 billion of extra funding over four years, and that is something that this Government is now working very hard to do in challenging economic conditions.

explanation: Asked what steps he is taking for further access; he lists three concrete commitments (30-day Medsafe recognition pathway, medicines strategy, Pharmac decision-model update). Answers what was asked.
question: What steps is he taking to ensure even more access to medicines for New Zealanders?
statement: The coalition Government is based in part on an ACT-National coalition agreement which contains a commitment to updating the rules for Medsafe to speed up the processing of new medicines for regulatory approval to within 30 days if two recognised overseas regulators have already approved it. It is to design and publish a medicines strategy and to update Pharmac’s decision-making model to ensure that it appropriately accounts for patient voice.

explanation: Asked whether she has seen recent reports on the economy; answers 'Yes' and identifies the IMF review with its findings. Complete.
question: Has she seen any recent reports on the New Zealand economy?
statement: Yes. The IMF has recently been in New Zealand to conduct its annual review of the economy. It released a concluding statement today that describes its preliminary findings. Consistent with other forecasters, the IMF expects growth to remain slow in 2024, before picking up in 2025. It’s the lagged impact: the legacy of the last Government of monetary policy tightening, suppressing domestic demand. As a result of this slowing in demand, the IMF expects inflation to come back into the Reserve Bank’s 1 percent to 3 percent target range in the third quarter of 2024.

explanation: Asked what OTHER reports she has seen; she explicitly redirects to the same IMF report ('he's allowed to ask me any question he likes about the IMF report') and gives further IMF content. She answers a different question than the one asked, though the question itself was vague.
question: What other reports has the Minister seen?
statement: Well, thank you to the member. He’s allowed to ask me any question he likes about the IMF report, because I have a lot of comments to make about it. One of the things the IMF report comments on is New Zealand’s fiscal position, saying that the Government is running a structural fiscal deficit with a spending-to-GDP ratio higher this year following Budget 2023’s sizeable operating and capital allowances. The IMF also says that, in recent years, debt has increased more rapidly in New Zealand than in many other advanced economies, and that New Zealand’s debt will continue its upward trajectory if there is no decisive consolidation. Members will recall that I have consistently been saying the same thing about New Zealand’s deficit and debt in this House.

explanation: Asked what policy prescriptions the IMF made; she lists them (fiscal consolidation, tight Budget 2024 stance, housing supply/zoning, productivity reform). Squarely answered.
question: What are the IMF’s policy prescriptions that she’s seen?
statement: The IMF says that the Government’s fiscal strategy should signal a strong commitment to consolidation, and it says that Budget 2024 should adopt a tight fiscal stance to help reduce inflation. More broadly, the IMF’s statement says that policies to boost housing supply are urgently needed and that changes in zoning can be effective. I’m sure my colleague the Minister of Housing clearly agrees wholeheartedly. The IMF also goes on to say that reforms are needed to revive New Zealand’s slow productivity growth.

explanation: Asked how the Government will address productivity; she names the growth strategy and its five pillars. It engages the question directly — the pillars are broad, but breadth-vs-detail is Specificity, not Forthrightness.
question: How is the Government planning on addressing New Zealand’s productivity challenges?
statement: Last Friday, I set out the Government’s growth strategy in a speech to the Auckland Business Chamber. The strategy has five pillars: building infrastructure for growth and resilience; lifting educational achievement and skills; strengthening trade and investment; promoting innovation, science, and technology; and improving regulation. The Government cannot do this alone; it requires businesses to pitch in as well, and feedback is that business welcomes the chance to work with a Government intent on removing obstacles rather than tying them up in regulation and red tape.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions; opens with 'Yes, I do'. The question is fully answered in the first clause; the subsequent Kāinga Ora material and jab at the questioner are additions, not a substitute for an answer.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, I do, and in particular I stand by this Government’s action to restore responsibilities by Kāinga Ora tenants to respect their home and their neighbours if they want to remain in their State house. The status quo is not fair on neighbours faced with disruptive or abusive behaviour and nor is it fair on taxpayers, who foot the bill for that house, to fail to uphold the standards expected of that rent. And I have to say, I agree with that member when he said that he didn’t do enough on unruly tenants in six years, and that’s quite obvious, because there are 335 serious complaints every month over the last three months and, in particular, there are three evicted tenants in the last year. So I make no apologies for being tough on making sure we make sure Kāinga Ora tenants are meeting their obligations.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the quoted statement, and will experts/communities/iwi also be able to submit to the panel. The reply neither confirms nor disowns the statement and never says who may submit — it retreats to a generic description of "a very good process". Both halves of the core are left untouched.
question: Does he stand by his Minister Responsible for RMA Reform’s statement about the fast-track approvals bill that “people who are keen on having the projects inserted into the bill will be able to submit them to the expert panel”, and, if so, will experts, local communities, and iwi Māori groups concerned by these proposed projects also be able to submit to the panel?
statement: Well, we’ve got a very good process that involves Ministers, expert panels, and decisions by Cabinet.

explanation: Asked what advice he had received on constitutional appropriateness. He asserts the practice is "completely appropriate" — his own view, not the advice — then pivots to the obstruction-economy talking point. Answers a different question than the one asked; the "what advice" core is never reached.
question: What advice, if any, has he received on the constitutional appropriateness of adding a list of projects into the legislation after the select committee stage, and the ways in which this could undermine public input, scrutiny, and transparency?
statement: Completely appropriate, but what I’d say to you: the purpose of fast-track consenting is it’s taking too long to get anything done in this country. We have built an obstruction economy. We are here to get things done. That’s why we’re taking fast track, introduced by David Parker, beefed it up, put it on steroids, and are actually going to get some outcomes for some people.

explanation: The first half (does he stand by the Te Tiriti statement) is answered squarely and explicitly: "yes". The second half — can he guarantee no mining consents affecting Treaty settlements — is openly left unanswered. Half the question engaged directly, half dropped, with the more demanding half the one dropped.
question: Does he stand by his statement that he will “ensure the fast-track consenting legislation upholds Te Tiriti”, and, if so, can he guarantee that his Government will not fast track any mining consents that may impact Treaty settlements?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

explanation: "Absolutely rubbish" is an unambiguous no to the agree/disagree part, and he then offers a reason (consenting delays, climate goals), so the "if not, why not" limb gets a response. The reason restates the fast-track case rather than rebutting the pork-barrelling allegation, so the engagement is real but glances off the core. Its rudeness is not counted against it.
question: Does he agree with former chief press secretary for the National Party Janet Wilson that “the fast-track consenting bill is not an act of political alliance so much as pork barrelling at its finest, providing a new golden age for National and New Zealand First’s backers”, and, if not, why not?
statement: Absolutely rubbish. I mean, the bottom line here is that we have an obstruction economy. We’ve actually taken an awful long time to consent something, and it’s costing a huge amount of money. We want to actually deliver on our climate goals, something that I think the Green Party would want to identify and align with us around, but you can’t take eight years to consent a wind farm and two years to build it. Why don’t we just take one year to consent and build renewable energy and then two years to build it, and get the benefit in three years, not 10 years?

explanation: Asked what steps the Government has taken on health outcomes; he names the five health targets as the step taken. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What steps has the Government taken to deliver better health outcomes for all New Zealanders?
statement: The Government recently announced that we are putting health targets at the forefront of our health policy. We are introducing five key targets that clearly spell out faster cancer treatment, improved immunisation for children, shorter stays in emergency departments, and shorter wait times for both first specialist assessments and planned care. We are an outcomes-driven Government, and these health targets show that.

explanation: Asked why targets were moved to the forefront; he gives the reason — targets direct attention and resources, set the agenda, and create accountability. Directly and completely responsive to the question as put.
question: Why was it so important to shift health targets to the forefront of the Government’s health policy?
statement: This Government believes that health targets help direct attention and resources and sets a clear agenda for where our health system should be heading. That is why it is important to have targets at the forefront of decision making. Targets are also accountability and transparency at all levels of our health system, which is vitally important for ensuring the delivery of timely access to quality healthcare for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked how robustness will be ensured; he names the mechanisms (data validation, clinical engagement, independent review) and pre-empts the gaming risk. Directly answers what was asked.
question: How will the Government ensure that the health targets are robust and will deliver better outcomes?
statement: I am aware of the potential for gaming targets and will keep a close eye on this. There will be mechanisms to ensure that our health targets will remain robust. These include quality assurance processes to validate data, clinical engagement with discussions on emerging concerns, and the use of independent agencies such as the Health Quality and Safety Commission to support reviews, as needed.

explanation: Asked why immunisation was chosen as a target; he answers with the reason — the fall from 93% to 83% and the gap to comparable countries. On point.
question: Why has the Government chosen immunisation for children as a key target?
statement: In 2015, when targets were still at the forefront of Government policy, the immunisation rates for children stood at just over 93 percent. Today, that number is worrisome, at 83 percent. This is well behind countries like the UK, Australia, and Canada. We should be doing much better for our children, and this target is one step to enable that.

explanation: A "do you stand by" question quoting him including "it would be unwise to bother". He affirms a restated, narrower version of the statement and adds that statutory obligations still apply, but never confirms or disowns the quoted clause itself. Substantial engagement with a quiet reframing of what he is standing by.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “For now, the Government has agreed to suspend the obligation to impose SNAs under the NPS Indigenous Biodiversity, and we’re sending a clear message that it would be unwise to bother”?
statement: I stand by my statement that the Government has agreed to suspend the obligations for councils to impose significant natural areas (SNAs) under the national policy statement (NPS), Indigenous Biodiversity. I also stand by my statement last week that there has been no change to statutory or regulatory obligations on councils. Those obligations continue to apply until they are amended. Cabinet has agreed to amend the NPS for Indigenous Biodiversity through a legislative vehicle, and suspend the NPS requirements for councils to adopt new SNAs into their plans.

explanation: Asked what the collaborative group got wrong. He engages by rejecting the premise — the group reached no consensus, so there was no landed decision to accept or reject — and explicitly marks it as his answer. It addresses the question, though it never says what, if anything, was wrong with the framework itself.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What, if anything, does he consider the biodiversity collaborative group got wrong when they developed the framework of rules for councils to follow, when working with farmers and iwi Māori landowners to identify significant natural areas?
statement: The biodiversity collaborative stakeholder group did not actually reach a consensus in the end. There was a minority statement, by a number of groups, so there was no consensus on an outcome. The decision was not taking into account what the biodiversity stakeholder group—actually, they didn’t land on a decision. So that’s the answer.

explanation: A narrow factual question; he says plainly that he does not have the figure and will come back to it. That is a direct, complete response to what was asked rather than a dodge — no pivot, no talking points. It is scored as an answer, not penalised for lacking the number.
question: What, according to his own ministry’s reporting, is the proportion of native species in Aotearoa that are threatened or at risk of extinction?
statement: I do not have those numbers on hand at the moment. I can come back to it.

explanation: Asked what recent results he has seen from Operation Emerald; he reports the results — warrants, arrests, seizures, plants destroyed. Exactly the question asked.
question: What recent results has he seen from Operation Emerald?
statement: Today, Police announced outstanding results, including in the member’s electorate. In a recent five-day operation, Bay of Plenty police have delivered a massive blow in stopping a major source of funding for organised crime groups. The execution of 39 search warrants saw 29 firearms seized and 25 arrests made. Additionally, police seized more than 80 grams of methamphetamine, over $7,000 in cash, two stolen vehicles, and a stolen motorbike. During the operation, 11,372 cannabis plants were destroyed. Operation Emerald targets the back pockets of gangs and organised crime by targeting the large-scale commercial cultivation of cannabis, and I’m proud of the work that police have done around the country to keep their communities safe.

explanation: Asked who made the decision to change the disability entitlement criteria and whether Cabinet was consulted. Neither half is touched: the answer redirects to the size of the total budget and asserts that a tightening happened, but never names a decision-maker and never mentions Cabinet. A narrow two-part factual question left entirely unanswered.
question: Who made the decision to change the criteria for access to disability support entitlements, and was the Cabinet consulted on that decision?
statement: What I’d say on that is that there has been no change to the disability services support budget from the budget that was set in your last Government. What there has been is a tightening up of the criteria of the modifications and equipment budget to make sure that disabled people are getting the direct support that they need.

explanation: Same two-part question, and this time the first half is answered squarely and without hedging — 'the ministry made the decision'. The Cabinet-consultation half is still ignored. Partial answer to a narrow question, so around the midpoint; the brevity and lack of elaboration are Specificity concerns, not Forthrightness ones.
question: Who made the decision to change the criteria for access to disability support entitlements, and was the Cabinet consulted?
statement: The ministry made the decision to tighten up the criteria for modifications and equipment, which is a piece of the total disability services budget.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister sought additional funding before criteria were reduced. The response talks about the total budget being unchanged and about Budget considerations, but never says yes or no to the request-for-funding question. A yes/no question converted into a talking point about budget continuity.
question: Did the Minister for Disability Issues seek additional funding to meet the shortfall in disability support funding before reducing the entitlement criteria?
statement: Well, what I want to be clear with that member about is that this Government is maintaining the total budget that the member’s Government signed off in May last year. The total budget for disability services has remained unchanged. That is an area of pressure, and that is something that we’re considering for our Budget with respect to how we can better support front-line services.

explanation: The narrow yes/no question is put a third time, stripped to its core: did the Minister ask for more funding? The answer retreats to 'we're in the middle of a Budget process' and general commitments to front-line services. The core is squarely avoided, and it is avoided after the questioner had already isolated it, which makes the dodge unambiguous.
question: Did the Minister for Disability Issues ask for more funding to meet the shortfall?
statement: And as I’ve explained to that member, we’re in the middle of a Budget process where we are working through the needs of the Budget for May. That is part of that process. We are cognisant of the need for better front-line services support in a number of areas, and we’re working hard to deliver that.

explanation: Asked for an estimated shortfall figure. The reply defers it to the Budget process rather than giving or refusing the number. It is short and signals that no figure is coming, which is marginally more engaged than a talking-point pivot, but it is not the plain refusal ('I won't tell you') that would score high — it answers a different question, about when such matters are discussed.
question: What’s the estimated funding shortfall for disability support entitlements in the current financial year?
statement: Again, that is a discussion for the Budget process, which is up and running right now.

explanation: Asked for the annual cost of reinstating interest deductibility. The answer offers no figure at all, praises the policy, and pivots to attacking the Labour Party's record on rents. Attacking the questioner instead of answering a narrow costing question is the clearest form of evasion in this set.
question: What’s the estimated annual cost of reinstating interest deductibility for landlords once that policy is fully implemented?
statement: Well, what I’m very proud about that policy is making sure that it delivers for the renters of New Zealand. The Labour Party used to care about renters in New Zealand, but they lifted rents up $170 per week—

explanation: Asked why Cabinet could agree tax changes pre-Budget but not disability funding. The answer disputes the premise's characterisation ('I disagree completely with that last part'), which is a form of engagement, but then restates the inherited-budget line and never addresses the comparison the question turns on. Some engagement, core unanswered.
question: Why can Cabinet agree on tax cuts for landlords prior to the Budget, as announced on 10 March and as indicated in the statement that he’s just made, but not on boosting disability support funding and instead cutting entitlements for the families who receive them?
statement: I disagree completely with that last part of that statement. What I’m saying to the member very clearly is that this Government is working to the budget that that member and his Government put in place last year. That is the total budget that we’re working for. We have a new Budget coming at the end of May, and we are considering a range of needs and a range of front-line services.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken on cancer services; the answer names actions — progress in diagnostics and management, and a faster cancer treatment target with a stated threshold. It addresses the question asked without deflection. A soft, friendly question, but that bears on nothing here: the question was engaged.
question: What actions has the Government taken to deliver better cancer services?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. In our first few months, we have made progress in both the cancer diagnostic and cancer management spaces. These announcements have been backed up by the introduction of an ambitious faster cancer treatment target. That target aims for 90 percent of patients to receive cancer management within 31 days of a decision to treat. This will help ensure the delivery of timely access to quality healthcare for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what steps were taken to improve access to diagnostic cancer services; the answer gives one — the mobile breast screening unit in Counties Manukau — and ties it to the screening age extension. Squarely responsive to what was asked.
question: What steps has the Minister taken to improve access to diagnostic cancer services?
statement: Just last week, the Prime Minister and I were at the launch of a new mobile breast screening unit in Counties Manukau. This is a great example of taking health services directly into communities and is expected to reach up to 6,000 women a year. These mobile units will have an important role to play in our recently announced age extension for breast cancer screening, which was announced as part of our 100-day plan.

explanation: Asked why improving diagnostic access matters. The first sentence answers it outright — 'it will save lives' — and the rest supports that answer rather than wandering from it. Direct and complete.
question: Why is it so important to improve access to diagnostic cancer services?
statement: Improving access to diagnostic services will save lives. That is why it is so important to us. The extension of breast cancer screening means that around 120,000 additional women will be eligible for screening every two years. We know that catching more cancers early means better treatment outcomes. I’m informed an additional 22 lives could be saved every year on the current uptake and 65 with full uptake.

explanation: Asked what other steps were taken on diagnostic technology across New Zealand; the answer identifies the PET/CT scan funding decision and what it changes for South Island patients. The opening thanks to the member is a pleasantry, not a pivot — the question is then answered directly.
question: What other steps has the Minister taken to improve access to diagnostic technology across New Zealand?
statement: I thank the member for his question—I’m sure that, as a representative for the South Island, this answer will be of particular interest to him. The Government recently announced that Health New Zealand has approved funding for an updated set of criteria that will allow for about 1,000 more publicly funded PET/CT scans per year in the South Island. For example, this will remove geographic variation that previously meant people in the South Island would have to travel to the North Island to access publicly funded PET/CT scans.

explanation: Asked what actions he has taken to establish a fuel security plan. He names the coalition commitment and a planned study into NZ fuel requirements including Marsden Point — that is a substantive answer to 'what actions', though the actions are prospective rather than taken. The jab about the closure is Focus/Civility, not a dodge.
question: What actions, if any, has he taken to establish a fuel security plan?
statement: Apologies, Mr Speaker, there’s a frog in my throat. The coalition agreement between New Zealand First and the National Party commits to the establishment of a fuel security plan to safeguard transport, logistics, and emergency services from any domestic or international disruption. The Government is moving quickly to establish such a plan, with a study into NZ fuel requirements planned to begin this later, including an investigation into the reestablishment of the Marsden Point refinery, shamefully closed down.

explanation: Asked which fuels are critical for fuel security in coming decades. He names gas and Indonesian coal. The Enid Blyton and 'people under a rock' rhetoric is irrelevant to this attribute; the fuels were actually named.
question: What fuels does the Minister see are critical for our fuel security in the coming decades?
statement: We share a desire that Kiwis should be free of reliance on fossil fuels in the near future. That stuff, however, belongs in an Enid Blyton storybook. New Zealand will continue to need gas to keep our economy functioning. Sadly, from time to time, Indonesian coal will be relied upon to keep the lights on. This is a stark reminder to the people who sit under a rock, not appreciating the genuine complexity of energy resilience.

explanation: Asked what recent causes of fuel insecurity he is aware of. He identifies one squarely — the closure of the Marsden Point refinery — and elaborates on its consequences. Heavy partisan framing, but the question is engaged and answered.
question: What recent causes of fuel insecurity in New Zealand is the Minister aware of?
statement: I am aware that, despite the willingness of the executive and directors of the Marsden Point refinery to seek an accommodation with the last Government, the last Government watched the demise and death of the Marsden Point oil refinery—an awful blow to Northland, and a wicked act undermining the resilience of New Zealand. But not only has it put fuel security at risk, it has endangered cardon dioxide supplies for beer and food. It was also, we should remember, the majority producer of jet fuel. In fact, all shipping fuel and more than half of our diesel came a lot more confidently and reliably to New Zealand as a consequence of that refinery. And the people who closed it down thought that they were doing the right thing via climate change—they have worsened the resilience of our nation.

explanation: Asked what actions he is taking to review opportunities at Marsden Point. Answers directly: investigating reestablishment of the refinery. Truncated mid-sentence, but the core was already delivered.
question: As a result of that closure, what actions is the Minister taking to review the opportunities that there are around Marsden Point?
statement: As I have said, we are investigating the reestablishment of Marsden Point refinery. Sadly, we are left to gather the—

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. Says yes, with the routine 'in the context in which they were given' qualifier, then volunteers one she particularly stands by. Direct.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given. I particularly stand by my statement from yesterday’s question time asking whether New Zealanders can see $123 billion worth of value generated for the $123 billion worth of Government debt racked up since 2017.

explanation: Two limbs: does she stand by the no-cuts commitment, and how does she reconcile it with the Police Association's claims. The first is answered outright ('Yes'); the second is pushed away as 'an operational matter for the police', which touches the reconciliation only glancingly. Half the question is engaged, half is sidestepped.
question: Does she stand by her commitment to not cut front-line public services; if so, how does she reconcile that with the Police Association’s comments today that the indefinite freeze on hiring non-sworn officers is already causing backlogs and delays, and that this policy would take police officers off the street?
statement: Yes. That is an operational matter for the police.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the quoted statement that health funding must rise at least at the rate of inflation. She never says yes or no to the quote; she pivots to National's fiscal plan matching Labour's cost-pressure quantum and says that amount was good. It is adjacent to the question and implies endorsement, but the core proposition is never confirmed.
question: Does she agree with Nicola Willis that “obviously we will need to increase health funding at a minimum at the rate of inflation.”?
statement: In a rare breaking out of bilateral consensus across the House, National, in its fiscal plan, had the same quantum of cost pressure funding for health as the Labour Party, and I agree that that was a good amount.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to increase Whaikaha funding. 'Yes.' One word, complete.
question: Will she commit to increasing funding for Whaikaha to maintain crucial front-line services?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked which she considers the greater Budget priority — respite care or the tax-cut cost blowout. She rejects the assertion behind the question and never addresses the choice. Premise-rejection is a response, but the question asked was left entirely unanswered.
question: What does she see as a greater priority for her Budget allowance: respite care for Debbie, the parent of two adults who have disabilities in my electorate of Mana, who has been a caregiver for 36 years and a sole caregiver for 30 years, or meeting the $800 million blowout in the cost of tax cuts for landlords?
statement: I reject the assertion at the back of that question.

explanation: Asked why the Government's coffers are open to landlords but not disabled communities. She rejects the premise — a legitimate move against a loaded 'why' — and adds that the disability ministry is running on Labour's own appropriation, which is at least a substantive counter on funding. Still, no reason is given for the contrast that was put to her.
question: Why are Government’s coffers an open pit for landlords but not for disabled communities?
statement: Well, I reject that entirely, and I would note and caution the member that the ministry for disability services is operating on the appropriation that the previous Labour Government gave it.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken to support the primary sector. Lists the adverse-event declaration, the regional visit, the tax and MSD support it unlocks, and prior Rural Support Trust funding. Direct and complete.
question: What actions has the Government taken to support the Primary sector?
statement: Last Thursday, I declared drought conditions for the top of the South, as a medium-scale adverse event, to give farmers certainty. Conditions on the ground across Marlborough, Tasman, and Nelson districts are extremely dry and likely to get worse in the coming months. On Monday, I visited the region to meet with farmers and growers, and was told that day-to-day conditions on the ground are extremely tough and they are particularly concerned about access to stock or feed and water. This declaration unlocks further support for farmers and growers, including tax and Ministry of Social Development support, and is on top of the $20,000 that the Minister for Rural Communities, the Hon Mark Patterson, and I made available to the Top Of The South Rural Support Trust last month.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his statements and actions. 'Yes.' Complete.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether there will be a hiring freeze on non-sworn staff. Mitchell neither confirms nor denies it, deflecting to the commissioner's deployment decisions. It is a short, non-evasive-sounding deflection that at least states why he won't engage, but the yes/no fact asked for is never given — closer to a dodge than a refusal, since he doesn't say 'I won't answer', he reassigns the question.
question: Will there be a freeze on hiring non-sworn police staff, including those who answer 111 calls and prepare police files for court, as reported today by the New Zealand Herald?
statement: That’s an operational matter for the commissioner in terms of where he deploys his personnel.

explanation: Asked whether HE agrees with the released police advice, and if not why not. That is squarely a question about the Minister's own view, not an operational one, so 'again, that is an operational matter' answers a different question than the one asked. Neither the agreement nor the 'why not' is touched.
question: Does he agree with police advice released under the Official Information Act regarding police employees that these corporate functions will be an important and necessary enabler to support the Government’s priority of recruiting an additional 500 new front-line police over the next two years; if not, why not?
statement: Well, again, that is an operational matter and a matter for the Commissioner of Police.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that 111 wait times will not increase. The answer swaps in a different guarantee ('what I can guarantee is... a Government serious about reducing violent crime') and moves to violent crime statistics and the previous six years. The word 'guarantee' is retained while the subject of it is replaced — a textbook pivot to talking points.
question: Will he guarantee that waiting times for 111 calls will not increase under his watch?
statement: Well, what I can guarantee the public of New Zealand is that they have got a Government that is serious about reducing violent crime. And, in the last six years, we have seen a massive increase in violent retail crime and violent crime relating to gangs, and you have a Government and a Minister that are actually committed to getting on top of that.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that uniformed officers won't be pulled into support work. Same substitution: 'what I will guarantee is this Government is going to support our police with legislation...', then gangs and retail crime under Labour. The specific undertaking sought is never addressed.
question: Yes, we have a further question. Will he guarantee that uniformed officers will not be pulled off the front line into support-staff work as a result of this freeze on police employees?
statement: Well, again, what I will guarantee is this Government is going to support our police with legislation that will allow them to go out and police gangs properly so they don’t take over rural provincial towns like they did under the previous Government, and they get on top of the violent retail crime, which grew at over 500 percent under the previous six years of the Labour Government.

explanation: 'Does he stand by his statements and policies?' — 'Yes, in the context they were given.' A direct yes; the qualifier is a mild hedge on scope but the question is answered in one word plus a caveat.
question: Does he stand by his statements and policies?
statement: Yes, in the context they were given.

explanation: Asked to name one action that directly reduced the cost of living. He names two concrete things (removing the Auckland regional fuel tax, refocusing the Reserve Bank on inflation) before trailing into generalities. Whether those actions in fact reduced costs is a Veracity matter; as a response, it supplies the named action that was requested.
question: Can the Prime Minister name one action his Government has undertaken since coming to office that has directly reduced the cost of living for New Zealanders?
statement: We have removed the Auckland regional fuel tax. We have actually ensured that the Reserve Bank of New Zealand is focused on reducing inflation. There are many things that we are doing to actually grow this economy, reduce the cost of living, and lower inflation.

explanation: Asked whether fuel is now cheaper in Auckland than before he took office. 'Well, it will be from 1 July' concedes the actual answer — not yet — squarely and immediately. He then pivots to fruit and vegetable prices and general inflation talking points, which pads but does not undo the direct concession.
question: Is the Prime Minister telling us that petrol or fuel is now cheaper in Auckland than it was prior to him coming to office?
statement: Well, it will be from 1 July. But what I’d say to that member is what has been exciting to see and good to see is that fresh fruit and vegetables are down 9.3 percent. That’s a step in the right direction. We are determined to lower the level of inflation, to lower the cost of living, so we can get interest rates down, so we can get this country growing again, and, importantly, so we can keep people in employment. It’s that simple.

explanation: A binary question about who benefits most from the tax cuts. 'You'll have to wait till the Budget' is a legitimate direct refusal, and he then asserts the relief goes to low and middle income workers — which leans toward one of the two offered options without ever answering 'the most'.
