explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made in her portfolio. She names them: her priorities on the Holidays Act, contracting arrangements, health and safety reform, and public service performance metrics. The surrounding argument is padding, but the question is squarely answered.
question: What recent announcements has she made in her portfolio?
statement: I recently announced my priorities, which are intended to restore business confidence and certainty. That is the way businesses are able to create more and better jobs, which is better for Kiwi workers. My priorities are related to the Holidays Act, contractors’ arrangements, health and safety law and reform, and performance metrics for public services. Over the last six years, employers would be forgiven for feeling like they have been pitted against workers, but I believe that the frustrations both employers and workers are facing are connected. Labour market regulations are becoming increasingly complex, making it harder for employers and workers to reach the solutions that work for both of them. Flexible labour markets are the best environment for businesses to grow. When businesses thrive, the economy thrives.

explanation: Asked what she plans to do to improve certainty in contracting relationships. She answers: implement the ACT-National coalition commitment on freedom to contract, and she has sought official advice on upholding contracting parties' intent. Engages the question directly, though the plan is at the advice-seeking stage.
question: What is she planning to do to improve certainty in contracting relationships?
statement: An important change I intend on making comes from the ACT-National coalition agreement. It includes the commitment to better protect choice and freedom to contract for workers and businesses. I’ve asked my officials for advice on how to achieve certainty for contracting parties, so that their intent, when entering into a contract for services, is upheld. Many New Zealand businesses use contractors in situations where engaging an employee to do the work would be inappropriate, or not as effective. I understand that 90 percent of contractors report that they are satisfied, or very satisfied, with their jobs, and that they would prefer to continue being self-employed, rather than to have a paid job working for someone else.

explanation: Asked whether she plans changes to the Holidays Act. She confirms it directly — improvements to the Act are a top priority — and states her first action. Answered.
question: Is the Minister planning to make changes to the Holidays Act?
statement: I want to confirm that delivering improvements to the Holidays Act to simplify and clarify the law is one of my top priorities. I understand that change has been a long time coming. The previous Government’s Holidays Act Taskforce began work in 2018, but were not able to deliver on changes by the end of their term in Government. I’ve heard from many a small business who spends a lot of time trying to comply with the Holidays Act rather than getting on with their core business. The first action that I’m going to take is to make sure that any changes to the Act are workable, that they are a material improvement on the status quo. One of the reasons why it has taken so long to deliver change is that the previous Government’s proposals were so complex that it was very difficult to get draft legislation. If the draft legislation is hard, then it is going to be very difficult to implement—

explanation: Asked what health and safety reforms she is planning. She answers the shape of it: reassess whether the system is fit for purpose, simplify and clarify the law, starting with public consultation before reform. Specific reforms are not named, but that is a detail question, not a dodge — the question was engaged.
question: What reforms to health and safety is she planning?
statement: The Health and Safety at Work Act is now almost 10 years old. I think it is an appropriate time that we take a step back and assess whether the health and safety system is fit for purpose. Businesses want to keep people safe and healthy at work, and workers want to keep themselves and their colleagues safe and healthy at work. But one of the things I hear consistently is that businesses and workers alike either struggle to understand the reason for some of the costly health and safety regulations, or they are struggling to know what to do in order to comply. So we want to simplify and clarify the law for both workers and businesses. Before we embark on that reform, I want to hear from workers, I want to hear from businesses, and I want to hear from people who know how to keep workers safe at work. So we will be starting public consultation.

explanation: Asked what she has recently announced to support low- and middle-income families. She answers immediately with the FamilyBoost ECE rebate, its rate, cap and payment schedule. Direct and complete.
question: What announcements has she made recently about supporting low- and middle-income families?
statement: Yesterday, we announced that from 1 July, low to middle income parents with early childhood education costs will be able to claim back up to 25 percent of their early childhood education (ECE) fees to a maximum of $75 a week. Families who qualify for the maximum reimbursement will receive $975 in their bank accounts from October and another $975 every three months thereafter. This new FamilyBoost initiative will provide real relief for families struggling with the cost of living.

explanation: Asked how many families and children will benefit from FamilyBoost. She gives the numbers asked for: 21,000 families at the maximum rate and more than 140,000 children in total. Direct.
question: How many families and children will benefit from FamilyBoost?
statement: Many families are struggling with high housing, childcare, and daily living costs. An estimated 21,000 low to middle income families will qualify for the maximum reimbursement of $975 every three months, and, in total, FamilyBoost will help support more than 140,000 children and their families. I am very proud that this Government is able to provide extra assistance to support so many hard-working New Zealand families.

explanation: Asked how families access the support. She answers the mechanism: invoices submitted through Inland Revenue's myIR system, quarterly, refunded as a lump sum. Answered.
question: How can Kiwi families access this support?
statement: To ensure the repayment goes swiftly and accurately to eligible parents and their caregivers, early childhood invoices are submitted directly through Inland Revenue’s online system, myIR, which I am advised can be used from a phone. Parents and caregivers will be able to submit ECE invoices every three months, with FamilyBoost refunded as a lump sum. Inland Revenue is currently talking to the early childhood sector about the best way to make this as simple as possible. Overnight, I am advised that early childhood services are already considering measures to make this as easy as possible for the parents they serve, including talking to their IT providers about issuing three-monthly invoices and assisting parents to upload these to the IRD.

explanation: Asked what the other benefits of FamilyBoost are. She names them: childcare is a major household cost, and lowering it reduces a barrier to workforce participation, especially for second earners. Responsive to what was asked.
question: What are the other benefits of FamilyBoost?
statement: Well, childcare is one of the biggest costs for families, and members of this House who have had young children will know that full well. According to the OECD, childcare costs in New Zealand are among the highest in the world—at 37 percent of household income. Being able to afford early childhood education fees can be a barrier to entering the workforce, particularly for a second earner in a household. FamilyBoost will make it easier and more worthwhile for families with young children to work, by directly assisting them to pay those ECE fees.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her commitment not to cut frontline services. She says 'Yes' outright, then qualifies what the commitment covers. The qualification hedges the edges, but the core question is answered plainly and the caveat is a genuine part of the answer, not a substitute for it.
question: Does she stand by her commitment not to cut frontline services?
statement: Yes. I stand by the full text of that commitment, which I spoke to at the Finance and Expenditure Committee, and where I went on to say, “In committing to front-line service, we are not committing to doing things the way they have always been done necessarily because, actually, we think there’s a strong case for improving the delivery of front-line services.” In some cases, it may be that the services that New Zealanders are receiving, whether it’s from their hospital or their school, aren’t actually delivering the results they want. So we are not going to ban ourselves from looking at other ways we could do things better, differently, so that we can ensure the resources we are deploying have a bigger impact for the people we are seeking to serve.

explanation: Two-part question: is the additional IRD invoice-processing staffing a back-office function, and if so how fast will parents be paid. She answers the first part squarely ('I would consider it a back-office function') but never reaches the second — 'as quickly as possible' and 'we're consulting' gives no timeframe for a question that asked precisely for one. Half the question engaged, the harder half avoided.
question: Does she consider the additional staff at the IRD processing over 7 million invoices a year for her early childhood education tax credit a back-office function; if so, how fast can parents expect their childcare rebate to be paid into their bank account?
statement: I would consider it a back-office function, and I think it’s important that all back-office functions are as efficient as possible. We are currently in consultation with the early childhood sector to work out how we make the delivery of this policy as efficient as possible. It’s our expectation that this rebate be delivered as quickly as possible, and that’s why we’re consulting.

explanation: Asked whether she will reverse the decision to remove diabetes-monitor funding eligibility. She never says yes or no — she redirects the member to put the question to another Minister. A portfolio deflection is not an answer to the question asked; unlike "no, I won't", it leaves the substance untouched, and the question was narrow and factual.
question: Will she reverse her Government’s decision to remove eligibility for funding for diabetes monitors that allow carers to sleep through the night without having to worry about sudden death from a slump in glucose levels?
statement: If the member wishes to ask questions about the disability services portfolio, she should put them on notice to that Minister.

explanation: Asked whether she is confident no restructuring changes will hit front-line services. She answers about a related but different thing — the expectation conveyed to chief executives — which implies the position without ever stating her own confidence. Engages the core obliquely; hedges around it rather than dodging entirely.
question: Is she confident that none of the changes proposed in the recent restructuring documents released by the Ministry of Health, Ministry for Primary Industries, Ministry for Ethnic Communities, Ministry for Pacific Peoples, Customs, and other ministries will impact front-line services?
statement: That is the expectation we have conveyed to chief executives.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with John Key's reported criticism. She disputes the premise (that Key said that) and lectures the questioner about honour in the House, which is a partial engagement with the framing, but she never states whether she agrees that funding tax cuts via Public Service cuts is too hard. The core is avoided and the reply turns on the questioner.
question: Does she agree with John Key that her commitment to fully fund her tax changes through Public Service cuts is too hard and risks plunging the country into discontent, as reported by the New Zealand Herald?
statement: John Key would be very unhappy to hear the member opposite mischaracterise his comments in that way. And I would put to her that we should have honour in this House with comments that we make and how we represent others.

explanation: Asked a narrow yes/no: is she committed to meeting the $2.8 billion Treasury estimate. The reply is a general commitment to "more funding for front-line services" — a talking point that never touches the $2.8 billion figure or gives a yes or no. Squarely a pivot.
question: Is she committed to meeting the $2.8 billion Treasury estimates is required to maintain the level of existing services for the impact for forecasted inflation and wage growth?
statement: We have previously made clear our commitment to ensure that there is more funding available for front-line services.

explanation: Asked what steps the Government is taking on the infrastructure deficit. He enumerates five specific steps. The question is engaged directly and completely (the answer's detail and self-promotion are not this attribute's concern).
question: What steps is the Government taking to address New Zealand’s infrastructure deficit?
statement: This morning, I laid out the steps the Government is taking to close New Zealand’s infrastructure deficit. Estimates vary on the size, but let’s call it $100 billion or more—that’s 80 Transmission Gully motorways. We have outlined a plan to fix this deficit: firstly, doing a better job of maintaining our existing assets; secondly, a credible pipeline of infrastructure projects—as part of that, developing a national infrastructure plan over 30 years—thirdly, reducing the barriers that are holding back infrastructure delivery, such as the Resource Management Act; fourthly, improving value for money; and, fifthly, new ways of funding and financing infrastructure.

explanation: Asked what the 30-year national infrastructure plan will involve. He states who is developing it, by when, and what it will include. Direct and complete on the thing asked.
question: What will the 30-year national infrastructure plan involve?
statement: I’ve asked the Infrastructure Commission to develop a 30-year national infrastructure plan by the end of next year. This will include a national view of infrastructure projects that are planned and are being planned, an assessment of infrastructure priorities, and an analysis of long-term infrastructure needs. The purpose of the plan is to demonstrate a pipeline of major projects that make New Zealand a place worth doing business. We need the talent and the capital in this country, and part of that is to demonstrate the scale of the opportunities in the coming decade. The 30-year plan will help get our infrastructure system humming again.

explanation: Asked what he said about the proposed national infrastructure agency. He states the agency will be established by 2025, its purpose, and why he commissioned prior work instead of rushing. Addresses the question squarely.
question: What did the Minister say about the Government’s proposal to establish a national infrastructure agency?
statement: We’ll be establishing a new national infrastructure agency by 2025 to connect offshore capital with New Zealand domestic infrastructure opportunities, amongst other jobs. The public sector infrastructure landscape is a crowded one and there are overlapping roles and functions, so rather than rushing into establishing a new agency, I’ve commissioned a piece of work to fully understand what the Crown wants and needs from a high-performing infrastructure system and who’s doing what in the system and what needs to change. Treasury’s leading this work alongside the Infrastructure Commission, and I’ll have more to say on that very soon.

explanation: Asked how the Government intends to improve and increase use of infrastructure funding and financing tools. He answers on the mechanism — openness to private capital, cost-benefit tests, and instructing officials to modernise the funding/financing frameworks. It reaches the question, though the closing rhetoric drifts; the generality of the measures is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: How does the Government intend to improve and increase the use of infrastructure funding and financing tools?
statement: The coalition Government’s very open to opportunities for the private sector to invest its capital to deliver high-quality infrastructure for New Zealand. These projects leveraging private finance obviously need to stack up based on cost-benefit analysis and the public good. To pave the way for more projects that leverage private finance, I’m asking officials to modernise the Crown’s infrastructure governance, procurement, funding and financing, and asset management policies and frameworks. Solving New Zealand’s infrastructure challenges will be hard, but with a good plan and a clear target, we can do it—and this Government will deliver.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the aged-care sector. She names the report, its author, its date and its content. Directly and completely answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen regarding the aged-care sector?
statement: On 7 March, the Aged Care Commissioner released her first report, titled Amplifying the voices of older people across Aotearoa New Zealand. The report has drawn on engagement with thousands of people from our important older communities alongside their families, whānau, carers, and service providers. The report is consistent with and aligns to what I’ve been hearing from the older New Zealanders and advice I have received around opportunities to better support aged-care services going forward.

explanation: Asked whether she is aware of ongoing work to improve aged-care services. She confirms a funding and service-model review is under way and describes its emphases. Direct answer to what was asked.
question: Is the Minister aware of any ongoing work to address opportunities to improve aged-care services?
statement: A review into aged-care funding and service models is under way, and I expect it will create a pathway to deliver better care for older people. The review will emphasise some key points, among these a stronger focus on supporting New Zealanders to receive the support they need at home. Additionally, we must ensure more efficient transitions through aged-care services, as well as greater capacity to support those with complex needs. I’ve asked for advice on immediate vulnerabilities and what is needed to sustain capacity while this work is being completed.

explanation: Asked what other initiatives are under way to support older New Zealanders. After a short preamble about priorities, she lists concrete initiatives (SuperGold upgrades, rates rebate scheme, subsidiary dwellings) plus stakeholder engagement. The question is answered; the promotional framing does not count against Forthrightness.
question: What other initiatives are under way to better support the lives of older New Zealanders?
statement: This Government knows that supporting seniors across all aspects of their lives is critical for safeguarding their health and wellbeing. That’s why improving the lives of seniors is stated as a priority for the Government in our coalition agreements. The Office for Seniors, in collaboration with other departments, has been progressing work on coalition priorities, including upgrading the benefits of the SuperGold and Veteran SuperGold Card, building on the local government rates rebate scheme, and making it easier to build subsidiary dwellings that can be used to support multigenerational living. I have been meeting with key stakeholders across the sector, who have been open about the opportunities to better support seniors across New Zealand. Finally, we have a dedicated, capable, and committed workforce and NGO sector, who I applaud for their ongoing efforts to respond to the needs of our older people.

explanation: A two-part question: does she stand by her statement, and if so why are insulin pumps and monitors excluded from Whaikaha funding. She answers both — "Yes, I do stand by my statement", then explains such devices sit under Vote Health/Pharmac and that continuity continues for existing recipients. Both limbs engaged; whether that account is accurate is Veracity, not this.
question: Does she stand by her statement in the House, “no disabled person will lose access to funding for essential services”; if so, why are insulin pumps and diabetes monitors being excluded from Whaikaha’s disability support funding?
statement: Yes, I do stand by my statement. Diabetes is a serious health condition affecting many New Zealanders, and I’m advised that avenues such as Health New Zealand and Pharmac support New Zealanders to gain access to funding for insulin pumps and monitors. The expectation is that health devices to address health conditions are dealt with under Vote Health. If, however, these have previously been funded with disability funding, I am clear that continuity of service continues for those individuals while these funding services are clarified.

explanation: Asked what she says to carers fearing that defunding monitors will cause 'dead in bed' deaths. She engages the funding-of-monitors half — she has sought clarification and says access must be maintained for those who had them before 18 March — but never speaks to the carers or their safety concern, and closes on previous-Government budget talking points. Partial engagement, core of the question skirted.
question: What does she say to carers who are concerned that defunding these critical devices will lead to an increase in “dead in bed” syndrome?
statement: So I have sought clarification from Whaikaha whether these monitors are funded through third-party providers under the previous rules with disability funding. I am clear—absolutely clear—that we must ensure that access is available if there have been people that have received them through disability services prior to 18 March. But I will be asking Whaikaha to work with those individual families to see whether they have been accessing health support where it is appropriate. This highlights the issues that we are working with, with Whaikaha. They are working to a budget that was put in place by a previous Government that was insufficient in terms of being able to meet needs. It has also had to put in place guidelines, and so it is important that we review the systems, processes, financial management, and the policy settings so that funding is coming from the appropriate source.

explanation: A yes/no question with an 'if not, why not': is speech therapy for this young man support that should be funded by Whaikaha? The answer gives neither yes, no, nor a reason — it retreats to a general statement that Whaikaha has been asked to work with families on essential services. The specific case asked about is never adjudicated.
question: Does the Minister consider speech therapy for a 17-year-old non-verbal, severely intellectually disabled young man effective support that should be funded through Whaikaha’s disability support funding; if not, why not?
statement: Again, we have asked Whaikaha to ensure that they are working with families where there are essential services needed for the disabled person to be able to function, they will be working with them to ensure those services and equipment are provided.

explanation: Asked (a) does she agree with Seymour that the cuts went too far, and (b) will she reinstate funding flexibility. She squarely rejects the premise — 'there has been no cut in funding' — which is genuine engagement with (a) and implicitly a no. But (b) is left untouched, and the rest is previous-Government framing. Half the question answered.
question: Does she agree with David Seymour that her Government has gone too far in its cuts, and that “we do have a responsibility in our society to help people who genuinely have no other source of help and have no other way of changing their situation”, and, if so, will she reinstate flexibility of funding while she works with the impacted communities on a longer-term solution?
statement: It needs to be very, very clear that there has been no cut in funding. There has been additional funding given to get Whaikaha through to the end of the year. Whaikaha has been working to a budget that was put in place by the previous Government, which was insufficient for the policy settings they were working to. We have further indicated that there will be additional funding put in place. There is no cut in funding.

explanation: Asked what she says to a constituent told she could not use her funding for psychology despite meeting the guidelines. She answers it directly: she doesn't know the individual case, but if it meets the guidelines it should be funded. That is a responsive answer to what was asked — its correctness or helpfulness is a separate attribute.
question: What does the Minister say to the woman who emailed to say—and I quote—“Today I found out from Enliven Disability support services and my psychologist that Government has said I cannot use my funding to pay for psychology sessions, despite it meeting the four purchasing guidelines outlined by Whaikaha. For me, it was the pathway to rehabilitation, successful social interactions and managing crippling anxiety, and I was hoping to return to work in the not too distant future. Now that has been taken away from me.”?
statement: I’m not aware of the individual case, but the member has answered the question herself, if she said that it met the guidelines of the funding. Therefore, if it meets the guidelines of the funding, it should be funded.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made on period products in schools. She states the announcement — increased funding for free period products across intermediate, kura and secondary schools. Directly answered; the surrounding credit-claiming doesn't displace the answer.
question: What recent announcements has she made on period products in schools?
statement: I’m thrilled to announce this Government has increased funding to ensure free period products are available for all young women in intermediate, kura, and secondary schools. It’s through careful spending that this Government has redirected funding to where it matters most: learners and schools. We’re committed to ensuring that all young women have equal opportunities in education to go on to live the life they want.

explanation: Asked what data and evidence supported the decision. She names a University of Otago study estimating up to 95,000 young women missing school for lack of access. The evidence asked for is supplied up front, with talking points appended after.
question: What data and evidence supported this decision?
statement: A study by the University of Otago estimated that up to 95,000 young women could be missing school because of a lack of access to period products. This Government is committed to reducing barriers for learners. I want to be clear about the link between attendance and achievement: regular school attendance is essential for lifting student achievement. This announcement is just one of our plans to reduce barriers to attendance and lift achievement in schools.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has received from the public. She gives it — Dignity New Zealand, the Children and Young People's Commission, a member of the public — with quotes. Complete and on point.
question: What feedback has she received from the public?
statement: I’ve already received lots of positive feedback. Dignity New Zealand wrote to me, expressing their relief and appreciation upon hearing our announcement. The Children and Young People’s Commission wrote, “I’m pleased to see the Government making this investment to reduce barriers to school attendance and normalising this aspect of mokopuna health.” One member of the public reached out to write that this increase in funding has created one less concern for young women in their school. We will continue to empower our young women to fully participate in their education without the burden of period poverty.

explanation: Asked who benefits from the announcement. She answers: 200,000 young women in schools, and explicitly closes with 'yes, it is targeted at young women who have periods'. The beneficiary group asked for is named.
question: Who is going to benefit from this announcement?
statement: This initiative will continue to support 200,000 young women in our schools. A lack of access to period products can be stressful, disruptive, and can impact students’ confidence and wellbeing. This is an issue of dignity. Young women should never have to miss out on their education or face the embarrassment because of something as simple as access to period products. This support will help families get their children to school feeling confident and supported so they’re ready to learn and do their best. And, yes, it is targeted at young women who have periods.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statements and actions. 'Yes, and in the context they were given.' A complete answer with a minor qualifier attached — no dodge.
question: Does he stand by his statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and in the context they were given.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees the private market has failed and the state should have a stronger role in owning rental housing, and if so what steps he'll take. He says 'I do agree' but redirects the agreement to a failure of the previous Government rather than of the private market, and the 'steps' are a three-way supply list. The state-role core is glanced at via social/State housing but never actually addressed.
question: Does he agree with A People’s Review of Kāinga Ora—In Defence of Public Housing report, released today, that “The private housing market has failed to provide everyone with a decent, stable and affordable home. The state should have a stronger role in the ownership and provision of rental housing.”, and, if so, what steps will the Government take to increase the supply of publicly owned rental housing?
statement: Well, I do agree: housing has been an abject failure in this country after six years of the previous administration. What we have to do is increase supply of private houses, increase the supply of rental properties available, and increase the supply of social and State housing available as well. We’ve got plans to deal with all three.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of the report's cost-saving finding and whether it makes public housing consistent with the Government's social investment commitment. He answers neither — he repeats verbatim the supply list from his prior answer, expressly flagged as 'as I said earlier'. The social investment link is never touched.
question: Is he aware of the finding of the report that building good quality public housing at scale and pace can save Government spending in the long term through reduced need for landlord subsidies and through savings in health budgets, and, if so, does this suggest that increasing the supply of public housing is consistent with this Government’s stated commitment to social investment?
statement: As I said earlier, we want to increase the supply of houses available in the private market, we want to increase the supply of houses available in the rental market and increase the supply of houses available in the social housing part of the market, too.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about the private rental market's affordability given 350,000 people on the accommodation supplement. He never says whether he is concerned and never engages the accommodation supplement figure; he restates the 'and, and, and' supply formula for a third time. A narrow question left unanswered by repetition.
question: Is he concerned, then, at the ability of the private rental market to provide New Zealanders with affordable housing when almost 350,000 people have to access the accommodation supplement because private rents are too high?
statement: Again, I don’t know how to explain this any differently to the member but it’s an “and, and, and”. We need to make sure that we have private housing made available to people who want to purchase homes, we need to make sure that we increase the rental supply of rental properties for people who need to rent them, and we need to increase the supply of social housing stock as well. It’s an “and, and” so that all three aspects of the housing market are actually accelerated.

explanation: Asked for a commitment that Kāinga Ora changes be directed at scaling the build programme rather than winding projects down. He neither commits nor plainly refuses — 'we will await the findings' declines to pre-commit, which touches the ask, but the rest pivots to 'better performance', leaving the actual either/or unanswered.
question: Will he commit to ensuring that any changes to Kāinga Ora, following the review, are directed at creating a more efficient and effective build programme to deliver public housing at scale rather than any wind down of existing projects?
statement: We will await the findings of the review but what we are clear about is that we want better performance from Kāinga Ora.

explanation: A 'why are you prioritising X over Y' question. The answer never engages the tax-cut premise or gives any reason for the prioritisation; it restates a general commitment to building houses and attacks the previous administration. Talking points in place of an answer.
question: Why is he prioritising tax cuts for landlords instead of building more public housing?
statement: We are committed to making sure that we build more houses in general in this country. That has been an absolute disaster under the previous administration. This Government takes getting houses built seriously. We do that through the private market, the rental market, and the social housing market.

explanation: A yes/no question answered 'Yes', with a light qualifier ('in the context they were made'). Direct and complete; the qualifier is hedging at the margin, not avoidance of the core.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context they were made and undertaken.

explanation: Two-part question: does she stand by the quoted projection, and how does she reconcile it with a 14 percent staff reduction. She offers a different current figure without saying whether she stands by the projection, and answers the reconciliation only by citing cost-of-living savings before ruling staffing 'operational and Budget sensitive'. Partial engagement, core of both parts left short.
question: Does she stand by her statement that—and I quote—“More than a quarter of our population in 10 years’ time will be from ethnic communities.”, and, if so, how does she reconcile that with the proposal to reduce the number of permanent staff at the Ministry for Ethnic Communities by 14 percent?
statement: There are currently about 22 percent of New Zealanders who actually belong to ethnic communities. However, you know, at a time when New Zealand is facing a cost of living crisis, agencies have been asked to identify where they can make savings or make changes in order to deliver savings. Decisions related to staffing numbers at the ministry are operational and Budget sensitive.

explanation: She engages the question squarely at first by disputing the 14 percent premise — challenging a premise is a response, not a dodge — but then routes staffing to the ministry as 'operational' and is cut off before reaching the oily-rag justification. Partly answered on the record as given.
question: Does she stand by her statement that the Ministry for Ethnic Communities has a budget analogous to—and I quote—“the smell of an oily rag”, and, if so, how does she justify that with the ministry staff reducing by 14 percent?
statement: I’m not so sure if the member is actually correct in suggesting that there is actually a 14 percent cut, because anything that is related to staffing numbers is actually for the ministry to answer as it is operational. In terms of the ministry operating on the smell of an oily rag, the member should know, as the former Minister—

explanation: Asked to justify the cuts. She answers the load-bearing part directly: there are no cuts currently, it is consultation, decisions come in the Budget. That denies the question's premise cleanly rather than evading it, though the oily-rag justification itself goes unaddressed.
question: How can she justify, given that she made a statement that said the ministry is operating under the smell of an oily rag, the cuts to the ministry?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. There are no cuts currently. Everything in relation to staffing numbers that the ministry are currently consulting is just that—consulting—and the decisions will be made as part of the Budget process.

explanation: A narrow commit/don't-commit question about the ECDF. She neither commits nor says plainly that she will not, deferring to Budget sensitivity and the ministry, then filling with praise for the fund. A blunt 'no, I won't commit' would have scored high; this circles the question instead.
question: Will she commit to no cuts to the Ethnic Communities Development Fund—ECDF?
statement: As I said, the decisions on the actual funding or staffing numbers, it is actually Budget sensitive and the decisions are for the ministry to answer. Having said that, the ministry does an amazing job. As the member who actually asked the question—who was a former Minister—will well know, it is a very small ministry who works very hard to support the work of the ethnic communities, and the Ethnic Communities Development Fund does amazing work to provide for the ethnic communities.

explanation: Disclaiming responsibility for Seymour's comments sidesteps the 'do you agree' part, but the follow-on — the ministry does an amazing job, supported 100 percent — implies disagreement and effectively rules out the abolition conditional. Responsive by implication rather than directly.
question: Does she agree with her coalition partner the Hon David Seymour when he stated—and I quote—“I very seldom find someone that can point to anything concrete that they’ve done.”, when talking about the Ministry for Ethnic Communities; if so, are these cuts a step towards abolishing the Ministry for Ethnic Communities?
statement: I don’t have responsibility for Mr Seymour’s comments. However, I feel that the Ministry for Ethnic Communities does an amazing job, and I support them 100 percent.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken; the answer is a sequence of actions taken (UAE exploratory discussions, two ministerial trips, launch of consultations, decision timeline). Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: What actions has the Government taken to support trade with the Middle East?
statement: Since taking office a few months ago, we’ve worked quickly with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) to progress exploratory discussions on a possible comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA). In January, I travelled to the UAE to meet with ministerial counterparts, and again the following month to attend the 13th World Trade Organization ministerial conference. While there, and following constructive meetings with the UAE trade Minister, New Zealand announced the start of public consultations on a possible CEPA with the UAE. Exploratory discussions between our two teams are progressing well, and a decision on launching negotiations will be taken later this year.

explanation: Gives reasons for consulting — interest in public views and the Gulf gap in FTA coverage — so the 'why' is reached, though it drifts into who can submit and how, which is beside the question. Answered, with padding.
question: Why has the Government asked for the public’s view on an agreement with the UAE?
statement: Well, we’re interested in what the public think—73 percent of New Zealand’s trade will be covered by trade agreements once the EU-NZ free-trade agreement (FTA) enters into force on 1 May. However, an important gap in our FTA coverage is the Gulf region. The launch of public consultations represents a significant next step in New Zealand’s ongoing consideration of a deal with the UAE, complemented with three rounds of exploratory discussions held to date. We’re keen to hear from civil society and businesses currently exporting to the UAE market, or with an interest in doing so—Māori exporters and all New Zealanders. Submissions are open until 31 March, and information on how to submit is available on the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade website.

explanation: Asked how an agreement would be important to New Zealand; the answer states the importance directly — top-20 export market, over $1 billion in exports, regional hub, competitive pressure from Australia. Squarely on point.
question: How would an agreement with the UAE be important to New Zealand?
statement: The UAE is a top-20 export market for New Zealand and our largest market in the Middle East, with exports totalling over $1 billion last year. The UAE is also an important hub for New Zealand companies operating in the region and vital to New Zealand’s connectivity to the Middle East and beyond. Other countries are progressing trade negotiations with the UAE—including Australia, who are expected to conclude a deal by the end of this year—so the Government is committed to ensuring New Zealand exporters remain competitive in that market.

explanation: 'Yes, I do' answers the confidence question completely at the outset. The attached attack on the previous Government is a Focus/Civility matter and does not reduce the fact that the question was engaged head-on.
question: Does he have confidence in the Minister for Disability Issues?
statement: Yes, I do, and the Minister has a very important job to do, fixing a system that is, frankly, not fit for purpose which she inherited from that member’s previous Government, and I am confident she’s going to do exactly that.

explanation: Asked for the date his office was informed. He never gives a date, but he answers the substance of it — he was not informed, he found out from the media. That engages the question rather than dodging it; docked only because the literal 'what date' is left open.
question: On what date did either Penny Simmonds or her office inform his office that Whaikaha had changed entitlements to disability support services and respite care?
statement: I found out when it was released in the media.

explanation: Asked who removed Simmonds' delegated decision-making. He denies the premise outright ('that is not what's happened') and states what was actually decided. Denying the premise is a direct engagement — if no such decision was made, there is no 'who'. Slightly short of full because the follow-on is a prepared line rather than a resolution.
question: Who made the decision to remove Penny Simmonds’ ability to make decisions around disability support funding or criteria without Cabinet sign-off?
statement: That is not what’s happened. All that we have said is that we expect major changes to front-line services across a range of portfolios that impact New Zealanders to be brought to Cabinet for a good discussion.

explanation: Asked whether Willis was incorrect, and if so who decided. He says 'that is correct', which answers the operative half and moots the conditional 'if so'. The added Cabinet expectation is restatement rather than evasion. (The tension with his previous answer is a consistency problem, not a forthrightness one.)
question: Well, was Nicola Willis incorrect when she said, “We’ve also directed, as a Cabinet, that any further decisions that the ministry makes about changing its criteria, its funding, needs to be properly consulted, properly sequenced. It needs to go [before] Cabinet before it’s enacted.”; if so, who made that decision?
statement: That is correct, but we expect all Cabinet Ministers to bring forward issues in their portfolios when they’re making significant changes to the front line for discussion in Cabinet.

explanation: A narrow 'why didn't she' question. He confirms that she did not bring it to Cabinet and that she apologised, but never supplies a reason — the causal core of the question is left untouched while the surrounding facts are conceded. Partial engagement.
question: So why didn’t Penny Simmonds do that before changing those criteria?
statement: As we have said, she didn’t bring it to Cabinet, and as a result there was no Cabinet discussion. That is something the Minister has apologised for, and she will do going forward.

explanation: Asked why the public should have confidence in the Minister. He disputes the premise and then does offer an implicit answer — she admitted it, learnt from it, and it will not recur — but most of the reply is a restatement of Cabinet process rather than a case for confidence. Half-answered.
question: Why should the New Zealand public have confidence in the Minister for Disability Issues when he has, effectively, removed decision-making delegations from her?
statement: I disagree completely. All we’re saying is that all Ministers, on their portfolios, need to bring forward to Cabinet conversations around any changes to front-line services that are major and significant and that will impact New Zealanders. That didn’t happen in this case. The Minister has admitted that up front, has learnt from that experience, and we’re moving forward.

explanation: A yes/no commitment question. 'That is a mischaracterisation of the situation' rejects the framing without saying what the situation is and without ever addressing whether he will restore eligibility. A bare premise-rejection with nothing behind it leaves the question untouched.
question: Will he commit to restoring full eligibility for carers in disability communities now that the responsibility for that has been taken off the Minister for Disability Issues?
statement: Oh look, that is a mischaracterisation of the situation.

explanation: Asked whether he believes the 50 percent figure signals over-claiming. The answer pivots entirely to funding increases and the review — the belief question is never approached, let alone answered. Classic talking-point substitution.
question: Does he believe the Minister for Disability Issues’ claim that “since 2018, the number of people accessing disability supports has increased by around 50 percent compared to population growth of 8.5 percent” is a sign that too many people are claiming disability support?
statement: What I’d say is what we have is a Minister who is actually ensuring there’s more money going in this year, over and above the Budget that the previous Government left us, and, importantly, is making sure there is more money going into Budget 2024. There is a review of disability services to make sure that, actually, money being spent has actually been going to disabled people to get the support and the resource they need. That’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked what Budget announcements she has made. Names the Budget Policy Statement 2024, its statutory basis and contents, and volunteers the operating-allowance point. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has she made on the Budget?
statement: Earlier today, I released the Budget Policy Statement 2024. The Public Finance Act requires such a statement to be presented to the House each year. It contains the goals and objectives that will guide the Government’s decisions in the forthcoming Budget and it sets out the Government’s short-term fiscal intentions and long-term fiscal objectives. And, yes, I can confirm that the operating allowance will be less than that left to us in the half-year update.

explanation: Asked what will be in the Budget. She declines plainly — wait until 30 May — which per the rubric is a forthright refusal, not a dodge, and then begins to give broad parameters before being cut off. Marked below a full refusal only because the reply is truncated mid-answer.
question: What will be in this year’s Budget?
statement: Members will have to wait until Budget day—30 May—and I’m so glad that they’re anticipating so eagerly to see the details of this year’s Budget. But in terms of the broad parameters—

explanation: Asked what else will be in the Budget. Gives three contents directly: tax relief, reprioritised front-line spending, and coalition-agreement commitments. The jab at opponents is a Civility/Focus matter and does not displace the answer.
question: What else will be in this year’s Budget?
statement: Tax relief is just one part of Budget 2024. The Budget will also have a strong focus on public services. Spending on front-line services will be reprioritised, despite some people practically fainting at the thought that the Government could do things differently and more effectively, and the Budget will deliver on Government policy commitments, including many of those in the coalition agreements.

explanation: Asked for fiscal intentions and objectives. States them squarely — return to surplus, debt down, spending reduced as a share of the economy, over several Budgets. The partisan aside about the last five years sits alongside the answer rather than replacing it.
question: What are the Government’s fiscal intentions and objectives?
statement: As set out in the Budget Policy Statement, the Government’s fiscal strategy is to return to surplus, get debt going down rather than going up, as it has been over the last five years—and as some members opposite want to continue to see it do—and it will reduce Government spending as a proportion of the overall economy. The legacy we inherited of elevated, lazy spending will take several Budgets to fix, but the first steps will be taken in Budget 2024.

explanation: A 'does he stand by' question answered with an unqualified 'Yes', then elaborated. Complete engagement; the elaboration is volunteered detail, which is Specificity and does not affect this score.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s policies and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially today’s Budget Policy Statement (BPS), which is setting out the coalition Government’s Budget priorities, and they are to deliver meaningful tax relief to low and middle income working New Zealanders, to identify enduring savings, to improve public services, to keep tight control of Government spending while funding high-priority initiatives and urgent cost pressures, and to develop a long-term, sustainable pipeline of infrastructure investments. The BPS charts, I think, a moderate, responsible course correction for New Zealand which will support New Zealanders struggling with a cost of living crisis.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the 2% minimum wage decision. He opens with "Yes" — the question is answered outright — then pivots to growth/tax-relief talking points. The pivot doesn't undo the direct answer; the core was engaged.
question: Does he stand by the Government’s decision to only increase the minimum wage by 2 percent when inflation is at 4.7 percent, which is a cut to the minimum wage in real terms?
statement: Yes. What I support, though, is actually growing our economy and making sure that we do everything we can to end the wasteful spending so we can protect front-line services, doing everything we can to give tax relief to low and middle income working families, and to make sure that we have growth in our economy. That’s what we’re focused on.

explanation: Asked for his response to the claim that the real-terms cut will increase child poverty, given 64% of families in poverty are in work. "I disagree" is a direct response to the proposition, but he then addresses only economic growth and never engages the poverty claim or the in-work statistic. Half-answered: the yes/no limb is met, the substance of the question is stepped around.
question: What is his response to the fact that this effective cut to the minimum wage will increase child poverty rates, given that 64 percent of families in poverty are in work?
statement: I disagree. The real opportunity for New Zealand is to grow our economy. Our economy, for four of the last five quarters, has been shrinking and been in recession. We need to grow our economy. That’s how we get to lift wages for all and get people out of a cost of living crisis.

explanation: Asked how workers are meant to keep up with food and rent costs given a real-terms wage cut. He redirects to the previous government's spending and the inflation chain. An implied answer is buried in there (bring inflation down, so costs stop rising), but the question about workers' position now is never reached; most of the answer is directed at who is to blame.
question: How are workers meant to keep up with rising food and rent costs when the Government is cutting their wages in real terms?
statement: Well, what they need is a Government that’s going to have responsible financial management, rather than an 84 percent increase in Government spending, which drove up domestic inflation, which drove up interest rates, which put the economy into shrinking, into recession, and creates a rising risk of unemployment. We need to deal with the underlying cause, which is inflation; get spending under control; bring inflation down; get interest rates down; get the economy growing; and keep people in employment.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to annual minimum wage increases that keep pace with costs, and if not, why not. He answers a different question — what the Government is committing to instead (FamilyBoost, tax relief) — and never says yes or no, never gives the "why not", and closes with an attack on the questioner's party. A narrow, explicitly two-limbed question wholly dodged.
question: Kia ora. Will he commit to delivering annual increases to the minimum wage that keep up with rising costs to ensure workers have a livable income to support their w’ānau; if not, why not?
statement: What we are committing to is FamilyBoost, which is a programme to give 100,000 low and middle income working families some relief so that they can put that towards their early childhood education centre costs, and we’re also committing to tax relief for low and middle income workers—a group, frankly, that the Labour Party and Te Pāti Māori used to care deeply about.

explanation: "Does she stand by all her statements and actions?" — "Yes, in the context in which they were given." A one-word answer with a qualifier attached. Directly and completely responsive; the qualifier narrows the claim but doesn't evade the question.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given.

explanation: Asked what evidence or data underpinned her statement about carers spending on pedicures, massages and overseas travel. She names the source directly: a February paper from Whaikaha reporting provider accounts of such spending. Whether that evidence is adequate is a Veracity/Rigor matter; as an answer, it lands squarely on what was asked.
question: When she told this House last week that carers have been able to spend on “such things for themselves as pedicures, as massages, as overseas travel”, what evidence or data does she have to base that statement on?
statement: I had a paper that was given to me by Whaikaha in February which noted, from providers, that the fund had been used for such expenses. I didn’t make any insinuation that those would be inappropriate; that was just stating what the fund had been used for at that time.

explanation: Two limbs: does she agree with her office's account to Newshub, and does she make policy decisions on hearsay. She answers the second squarely ("No, I don't make policy decisions based on hearsay") and implicitly rejects the first by re-stating the documentary source. The office-account limb isn't addressed head-on, which costs a little.
question: Does she agree with her office, who told Newshub that they didn’t have any numbers but that the Minister had heard it anecdotally, and, if so, does this Minister make policy decisions based on hearsay?
statement: No, I don’t make policy decisions based on hearsay. I had a paper from Whaikaha which indicated that providers had stated the fund was being used for such purposes.

explanation: A three-limbed question: does she accept her statements weren't evidence-based, that disability communities have lost trust in her, and that the PM has said Cabinet will decide on her behalf. She answers only the first limb ("No") with the same Whaikaha-paper line, and leaves the lost-trust and Cabinet-oversight limbs untouched. The core proposition is engaged; roughly half the question is not.
question: Does she accept, based on what her office has told Newshub, that her statements and actions haven’t been based on evidence and they have led to disability communities writing in droves, saying that they have lost their trust in her, and to the Prime Minister saying that Cabinet will be making major decisions on her behalf?
statement: No, I have not been making decisions on hearsay. I had a paper from Whaikaha that outlined, from providers, what the spending had been spent on. Thank you.

explanation: Asked what the point is of her remaining as Minister, and whether she will resign. She answers the resignation limb explicitly ("I won't resign") and gives her reason for staying — the inherited budget and the coming review. That the reason is a deflection onto the previous government doesn't change that both limbs were reached.
question: Sure. What is the point of her remaining as the Minister for Disability Issues, given that she has lost the confidence of the very communities that she represents in Government and has made statements about carers that her office has confirmed were based on anecdote, and, if so, will she resign?
statement: First of all, I will confirm that my decisions weren’t based on hearsay; they were based on a paper that was given to me by Whaikaha. Secondly, I won’t resign, because I have inherited a situation where Whaikaha have a budget set by the previous Government that was insufficient for the settings that were in place, and so additional funding has had to be given to ensure they can get through the end of this year. A review will be undertaken to put in place the systems, the processes, the settings that should have been put in place by that Government when they set the ministry up.

explanation: A patsy question asking what announcements have been made on travel assistance for health treatment; he states the $18 million NTA boost, what it changes and why it was needed. Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about assisting New Zealanders who need to travel to receive health treatment?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Yesterday, the coalition Government announced an $18 million boost for New Zealanders that have to travel for health treatment. These changes are long overdue for the national travel assistance (NTA) scheme, with its last increase to mileage and accommodation rates back in 2009. During this time, the scheme has been plagued by bureaucratic claiming processes and local variations that have seen families who couldn’t afford the upfront costs of treatment having to delay their treatment or choose less-effective options. This needed addressing, and this boost will help to remove those barriers.

explanation: Asked why boosting the scheme was a priority. He gives reasons — the cost of living pressure and the scheme's role for cancer, dialysis and complex-care travel. Squarely responsive to the "why".
question: Why was it a priority to boost funding for this scheme?
statement: New Zealanders have endured a prolonged cost of living crisis, making it more difficult for those who need to travel for health treatment. We know that the NTA provides critical financial assistance for those who need to travel for treatments relating to cancer, renal dialysis, diagnostics, and other complex care that can’t be provided locally. It is important that we support this group of New Zealanders with increased assistance during their time of need.

explanation: Asked what changes to the scheme New Zealanders will see. Reti names the changes directly — mileage and accommodation rates, prepayment/claiming options, eligibility targeting, promotion — and the number who benefit. The question is engaged squarely and completely.
question: What changes to the scheme will New Zealanders see?
statement: Those who claim the NTA will see significant changes. This boost allows for increased mileage and accommodation rates, easier prepayment and claiming options, changes to eligibility in order to better target those in need, and better promotion and awareness of the scheme. We expect that around 4,500 extra New Zealanders will benefit from this boost.

explanation: Asked how the announcement eases cost-of-living pressure for people travelling for treatment. Reti answers on point: the rate rises from 28c to 34c/km and $100 to $140 a night, plus prepayment and online claiming replacing paper forms. Directly responsive to the mechanism asked about.
question: How will this announcement ease the cost of living challenges for those who need to travel for treatment?
statement: This boost will see the mileage rates rise from 28c to 34c a kilometre, and the nightly accommodation rate change from $100 to $140 a night. More flexible payment options, including prepayment and the ability to do more online, will also be piloted and phased in. While some districts offer prepayment options, most whānau currently need to fill out paper-based forms to seek reimbursement. For many, this has been a challenge. We will support them with this boost.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. Willis says "Yes" and then reaffirms a specific statement. The "in the context in which they were given" rider is a mild hedge but the yes/no core is answered outright.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given. I particularly stand by my statement earlier today that in Budget 2024, this Government’s spending will be targeted, effective, and within our means.

explanation: Two-part question: did she confirm Cabinet approved additional Whaikaha funding, and how much was pre-committed. She answers "Yes" to the first and explicitly refuses the second as Budget-sensitive. A stated refusal is a direct response, not a dodge; only the withheld figure keeps this off a top score.
question: Did she confirm to reporters yesterday that Cabinet had approved additional funding for Whaikaha until the end of the financial year; if so, how much money was pre-committed against Budget 2024 for that purpose?
statement: Yes, and that figure is Budget-sensitive, so I won’t be releasing it.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the "vast orders of magnitude" statement and why the funding did not reverse the eligibility changes. She restates a general funding commitment without confirming the quoted statement, then redirects the substance to the Minister for Disability Issues. The redirection is explicit rather than evasive padding, but the core of the question is left unanswered.
question: Does she stand by her statement that Whaikaha will “get vast orders of magnitude more in additional funding for front-line services”; if so, why was the additional funding allocated not enough to reverse the significant eligibility changes that her Government made without any warning or consultation?
statement: I have repeatedly confirmed in this House and elsewhere that in our Budget, more funding to provide front-line support to people with disabilities will be a priority, and that member is now asking me to comment on issues that are a matter for the Minister for Disability Issues and that are matters that that member should put on notice.

explanation: Asked whether the promised funding will be sufficient to reinstate respite care and why carers must wait until 1 July. Neither part is answered — she repeats that funding will increase and refers detailed questions elsewhere. The referral is stated plainly, which is better than a pure pivot, but the sufficiency and timing questions are both sidestepped.
question: Will the “vast orders of magnitude more” funding she has promised be sufficient to reinstate funding for respite care; if so, why is she making carers wait until 1 July when she has already committed to more funding?
statement: I have made myself clear already, and so I’ll make it even simpler: we will be increasing funding for disability services in our Budget because we view it as a priority front-line service, and if the member has detailed questions about ministerial decisions relating to that service, she should put those questions to the Minister responsible.

explanation: Asked why she won't finalise the funding commitment now. She disputes the questioner's paraphrase — legitimate engagement with the premise — then pivots to FamilyBoost, cost-of-living framing and criticism of the previous Government. The "why not now" is never reached.
question: Why won’t she finalise her commitment to provide “vast orders of magnitude more in additional funding” now and end the significant distress her Government’s changes have caused, or are Budget pre-commitments only prioritised for residential property investors?
statement: Well, there’s a couple of problems with that statement from the member, which actually are similar to her last supplementary question yesterday, where she also paraphrased things quite inaccurately. Actually, what I had said in relation to vast orders of magnitude was that the additional funding going in would be vast orders of magnitude more than the savings that were being asked for, and then the second part of her question made another false assertion. Just this week, the Government announced significant new money—hundreds of millions of dollars—to ensure that low and middle income families with young children get more money in their bank accounts with our FamilyBoost childcare policy. That’s a priority for us. This is a Government that understands working people have done it tough for too long with the prolonged cost of living crisis that the previous Government presided over. Our Budget will make sure that they get relief in their bank accounts and back pockets, that we target additional spending carefully to the services they rely on, and that we won’t waste it like the people opposite did.

explanation: Asked what recent reports he has seen on the Brynderwyn Hills. Brown responds with substantive Brynderwyns news — the road reopening tonight until 2 April and paused resilience work. He does not identify reports as such and adds tourism promotion, but the subject matter asked about is addressed.
question: What recent reports has he seen on the Brynderwyn Hills?
statement: Well, good news for Northland: State Highway 1 across the Brynderwyns will open tonight until 2 April, for the Easter weekend, with work currently under way to ensure the resilience of this critical route being paused to allow holidaymakers to travel north. As Kiwis prepare their travel plans for Easter, the coalition Government is encouraging New Zealanders to support, visit, and explore Northland, as the region is open for business.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. "Yes, in the context they were given" — one line, direct, complete. Brevity is not evasion.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context they were given.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his climate-delivery answer and, if so, how he will deliver having axed the just transitions unit and MPI emissions roles. He affirms the 2050 commitment and offers one delivery mechanism (doubling renewable electricity) but never engages the axed units the question was built around.
question: Does he stand by his answer to me at question time yesterday that “what we are interested in is actually delivering on our climate … goals”, and, if so, how does he intend to do that when his Government has axed the just transitions unit and emissions reductions jobs at the Ministry for Primary Industries?
statement: We are deeply committed on delivering our net carbon zero 2050 goals, and one of the ways we’re going to do that is doubling the amount of renewable electricity in this country.

explanation: Asked how many climate change jobs he is comfortable axing. The response pivots entirely to wanting more jobs, growing the economy and fast-track consenting. A number was asked for and the topic is changed; the question is not engaged at all.
question: How many climate change jobs is the Prime Minister comfortable with his Government axing?
statement: I want to make sure that there are more jobs for people in the New Zealand economy, and what we’re doing is wanting to grow our economy. One of the ways we do that is by introducing fast-track consenting.

explanation: Asked whether the Government has paused Climate Change Commission appointment processes. "That's something that I'm not aware of" does not resolve the factual question, but it is a direct, plain response to what was asked rather than a pivot — a stated non-knowledge, not a dodge.
question: Has his Government paused the appointment processes for the independent Climate Change Commission?
statement: That’s something that I’m not aware of.

explanation: Asked how the seabed-mining consent benefits Taranaki. Jones does not engage the substance at all; he says the application is before a judicial panel and invokes comity. It is a stated reason for not answering rather than a bare pivot to talking points, so it is not a zero — but he never says plainly that he will not answer, and the question asked is left untouched.
question: How does it contribute to the Taranaki region to allow an Australian mining company to suck 50 million tonnes of seabed each year for 35 years in a way that harms local fisheries and, in the mining company’s own words, “totally destroys the seabed”?
statement: Obviously, the matters pertaining to the application and the activity the member refers to are currently before a panel chaired by a retired High Court judge. The value of the principle of comity between Parliament and judicial processes should not be underestimated.

explanation: A narrow factual yes/no: did he raise the objectors' concerns in the 23 January Straterra meeting? He says the meeting involved him listening to the minerals sector and then pivots to a defence of that sector. Yes or no is never given; at most it can be inferred. A specific factual question squarely avoided.
question: Did he raise the concerns of environmental groups and experts, local iwi, and the fishing industry—who have fought against this seabed mining for 10 years—in his four-hour meeting with mining lobbyists Straterra on 23 January?
statement: Well, obviously, that meeting involved me listening to that minerals sector. The minerals extractive sector has a rich, legitimate, and profoundly important place to play as we derive responses to climate change, rather than hysteria and alarmism.

explanation: Asked whether he thinks it appropriate to override the Supreme Court, the EPA and environmental law via fast-track. He answers a different question — the bill's procedural status and an invitation to make submissions — and never gives a view on appropriateness.
question: Further to your point about the importance of not interfering in judicial processes, does he think that it is appropriate to override the Supreme Court, the Environmental Protection Authority, and all of New Zealand’s environmental protection laws to fast track destructive seabed mining?
statement: Well, obviously, in the event that the member’s referring to the fast-track legislation, it’s in the House, it’s before the select committee, and I encourage all New Zealanders, either private or public, to bring their concerns—

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his statements and actions. "Yes and yes." One line, both limbs, complete.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, yes and yes.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Dr Prickett's quoted claim and, if not, why not. He says no, he does not accept it, and gives the reason (the household economic survey is being retained and is the more robust instrument). Both limbs answered directly.
question: Does he agree with Dr Kate Prickett of Victoria University of Wellington that “In short, the cancellation of the Living in Aotearoa Survey means the government will escape being held to account for how our most vulnerable children are doing.”; if not, why not?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, no, I do not accept that observation. The household economic survey is being retained, whereas it would otherwise have come to an end in 2024. That’s a more robust, better-quality survey to provide the information that the Government needs on which to base policy decisions in relation to child poverty reduction and other Government aims, and also to monitor the effectiveness of those policies going forward.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned the cut will limit tracking of child poverty. He disputes the premise ("there is no cut") but then answers the question as asked — no, he does not believe there is any negative implication — and cites the chief statistician. Contesting the premise while still giving the answer is not a dodge.
question: Is he concerned that this cut will limit the Government’s ability to track and reduce child poverty?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, there is no cut, and as I’ve said, I do not believe, on behalf of the Government, that there would be any negative implication in terms of our ability to measure child poverty. Indeed, the chief statistician, who has statutory independence for these operational decisions regarding methodology of collecting data, has assured various Government Ministers that he does not see that there would be such an outcome either.

explanation: Asked what steps he has put in place to ensure Stats NZ meets its Child Poverty Reduction Act data obligations. He repeats the previous answer's assurance from the chief statistician. That does bear on the question and implies the answer is "reliance on the chief statistician's independence", but no step taken by him is identified. Partial engagement with a "what have you done" question.
question: What steps, if any, has he put in place to ensure Stats NZ can comply with its obligations under the Child Poverty Reduction Act to collect data on persistent child poverty?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, I reiterate my comment in response to the previous supplementary question that the Government has been assured by the chief statistician, exercising that person’s statutory independence, that they will be able to monitor that data, in particular to meet the statutory objectives—the 10 requirements under the child poverty Act—to be able to measure that progress.

explanation: Asked how quality decision-making remains possible once this measure is removed. He rejects the premise that it is the sole measure and then answers the "how": the household economic survey, administrative data, census analysis, other agencies. The core of the question is reached, though the closing digression about digitising services drifts.
question: How, given that the coalition agreement commits to decisions being made using data and evidence, will quality decision-making with and for some of our most vulnerable New Zealanders still be possible when the very measure of their needs has been quietly taken away?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, I reject the characterisation of that one particular, relatively new survey as being a sole measure or the sole measure. Indeed, there are a number of measures. I’ve referred already to the household economic survey. Additionally, there’s the use available of administrative data, which—as per the last census—conduct and analysis enables us to fill in gaps, so to speak. There are a lot of Government agencies that contribute to the ability to gain a full picture, and, in addition, I note that work is being undertaken by other Government Ministers for which, on behalf of the Minister, I’m not responsible, but I know it will be very helpful—for example, digitising Government services will be very helpful in this regard.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made about the Budget operating allowance. She states the announcement directly — under $3.5 billion in Budget 2024 — and contextualises it. Squarely answered.
question: What recent announcements has she made about the Budget operating allowance?
statement: In the Budget Policy Statement (BPS) yesterday, I announced that the operating allowance in Budget 2024 would be less than $3.5 billion. The operating allowance is the amount of money allocated in the Budget to fund new spending and revenue initiatives. To put this amount in perspective, the operating allowance, on average, across the past four Budgets was around $4.5 billion. In Budget 2022, the allowance was around $6 billion, and in Budget 2023, it was $4.8 billion. So the Budget we will release on 30 May will be significantly tighter than those in the immediate past, and it will also contain personal income tax relief for hard-working New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked when she will announce operating allowances for future Budgets. Answered directly: in the Fiscal Strategy Report, a Budget document. The long historical excursion and the jab at Labour follow the answer rather than substituting for it.
question: When will she announce the operating allowances for future Budgets?
statement: As I said in the Budget Policy Statement, the operating allowances for Budgets 2025 to 2027 will be set out in the Fiscal Strategy Report, which is one of the Budget documents. Operating allowances for future years are planning assumptions that improve the accuracy of fiscal forecasts. They are often amended and revised over time. To give the House one historical example, the operating allowance for the most recent Budget in 2023 was announced as being $2.6 billion in Budget 2020, but as the years went by, it was raised to $2.7 billion, then to $4 billion, then to $4.5 billion, and then to $4.8 billion—some $2.2 billion more than indicated three years earlier. That is why I take any comments about future allowances with a large grain of salt when those comments come from the Labour Party.

explanation: Asked what reaction she has had to the Budget Policy Statement. She reports the reactions — many positive comments and one specific criticism, which she then rebuts. The rebuttal is argumentative but the question (what reaction) is engaged and answered.
question: What reaction has she had to the Budget Policy Statement?
statement: Well, I’ve seen many positive comments on the Budget Policy Statement.
