explanation: Asked why the Act needs reform. The answer gives reasons directly: 40 years old, outdated rules, costs, delays, complexity, plus third-party endorsement of that view. Squarely responsive.
question: Why is the Conservation Act in need of reform?
statement: It’s nearly as old as me. It’s 40 years old. Its outdated rules have created unnecessary costs and massive delays. More than 1,600 businesses already operate on conservation land, contributing an estimated $5.3 billion to our economy each year. Area planning, as well as the current decision-making process, is just too slow; it’s too complex and too difficult to navigate. This is not just the Government saying the system needs updating; people like New Zealand Ski have said the current framework has struggled to keep pace, while the Tourism Industry Association has welcomed reforms that better align tourism, conservation, and regional growth—

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Duffy's statement that the Government got it wrong. 'Kaore. No.' is an explicit answer, followed by his reasoning. Direct and complete.
question: Faiȧkse‘ea , Mr Speaker. Does he agree with Consumer NZ chief executive Jon Duffy’s reported statement that the Government has “got it wrong” regarding proposed changes to retirement village capital repayment laws?
statement: Kāore. No. The proposed changes strike an appropriate balance between improved consumer protections for residents and ensuring continued growth, innovation, and consumer choice within the retirement sector. The Government has agreed to practical reforms that reflect the feedback of residents and operators, and we look forward to the introduction of the bill in due course and feedback through the select committee process that will follow.

explanation: Asked how a 12-month repayment window is acceptable. He engages with the justification - balance between consumer protection and sector viability, and why three months would not work - but never defends the 12-month figure itself. Partial engagement with the core.
question: How is it acceptable to give retirement village operators 12 months to repay when it is the residents’ own money and, for many of them, time is not on their side?
statement: We consider that we have struck the right balance between consumer protections and the need to have a viable, financially responsible retirement village sector. Any suggestions that the mandatory repayment time frame be moved to a three-month period go completely against financial responsibility, and it fails to take into account the incentives and the types of business practices that we need to ensure that aged care remains viable and, indeed, respects the sanctity of contract that many residents entered into when they entered into these villages.

explanation: Asked why the reforms exclude current residents. He gives the underlying reason - opposition to full retrospectivity, credit lines and capital adequacy - which addresses the 'why' obliquely rather than stating it as the answer. Partially reaches the question.
question: Why is he excluding current residents by applying the proposed reforms only to new residents?
statement: We are absolutely supportive of some changes to typical consumer protections—for example, more objective decision-making around dispute resolution and some better clarity around chattels—but we’re not supportive of full retrospectivity with mandatory payments at three months. We are interested in a balanced system that takes into account the importance of credit lines and capital adequacy, and I’d encourage all of the responsible members of the Opposition to do so too.

explanation: Asked why some provisions are mandated for current residents but repayment is not. After calling the question confused, he draws exactly the distinction asked about: typical protections like ceasing fees versus a retrospective shortened repayment deadline he says would threaten sector viability. It answers, if incompletely.
question: Why is he mandating some provisions to current residents’ licences, such as stopping weekly fees immediately when they vacate, yet refusing to mandate repayment to those same residents?
statement: My sense is that question is a little bit confused. As I mentioned in the previous answer to the previous question, there are some consumer protections that are typical. For example, if you move out of a place, you should stop having to pay fees. But if the view is that it is typical that there should be retrospective application of a shortened mandatory time frame that will severely compromise the financial viability and responsibility of the entire sector, we’re not up for that on the side of the House. What we are up for is the right balance around consumer protections and ensuring that the retirement village sector continues to be successful and a place where 53,000 residents continue to enjoy the māramatanga of their lives.

explanation: Asked what evidence he has of listening to residents rather than operators. After a jab about his diary, he offers evidence: visits to many villages and residents telling him directly they are comfortable with the arrangements. Evidence was supplied, so the question was engaged; whether it is good evidence is not this attribute.
question: What evidence can he give this House that he has listened to the residents—56,000 of them, not 53,000—rather than simply the retirement operators who have been lobbying him?
statement: I’m not aware that the member has insights into my diary, but what I am aware of is that I visited many villages right throughout this country, and there are many residents that are very, very comfortable and expressed to me that they are comfortable with the arrangements that they contracted after independent legal advice and informed decision-making, that they respect the sanctity of that contract, but, more importantly, that their retirement villages absolutely look after them and will continue to show that manaaki into the future.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all the statements and actions of his Government. 'Yes.' One word, complete and unambiguous.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts that tightening eligibility away from school leavers risks undermining early intervention. He responds with his personal fondness for the Mayors' Taskforce and his own involvement in Clutha — never engages accept/not-accept or the risk claim. The transcript is cut by an interruption, but nothing in what he said reaches the question.
question: Does he accept that tightening eligibility criteria for these programmes away from school leavers risks undermining early intervention efforts that have historically kept long-term benefit numbers low in rural districts?
statement: Look, I’m a big fan of the Mayors’ Taskforce for Jobs, and I’ve had involvement myself in the Clutha region with the Jobbortunities programme—[ Interruption ]

explanation: Asked what steps, if any, he is taking on rural-appropriate funding models. He engages the question directly: no official advice, but he made inquiries after the written questions, and the allocation change is an operational decision for MSD — i.e. the steps are 'inquiries' and beyond that it isn't his call. That squarely answers 'what steps, if any', even if the answer amounts to very little. Not docked for thinness (that is Specificity).
question: If the member is a strong advocate for the Mayors’ Taskforce for Jobs, what steps, if any, is he taking to ensure that funding models for youth employment programmes reflect the realities of rural labour markets?
statement: As I’ve said in my primary answer, I haven’t had any official advice because it’s not something that’s been raised directly with me by the mayors. Subsequent to your written questions, I have made some inquiries. I am aware that there have been some adjustments in how the funding is allocated and the emphasis on jobseekers as opposed to just school leavers, and so that’s an operational decision for MSD. But—

explanation: Asked why the Government is cutting the programme. He contests the premise head-on — there is no cut, there is a reorientation, and it is an MSD operational decision. Rejecting the premise is engagement, not a dodge, and it addresses the mayor's characterisation implicitly. Held below high because the 'why' behind the reorientation is never given once the premise is corrected.
question: Why is the Government cutting the Mayors’ Taskforce for Jobs programme, given the Mayor of Kaikōura, Craig Mackle, said in response to these cuts: “we’ve gone from being the fence at the top of the cliff, to the ambulance at the bottom.”?
statement: Again, I’m not sure that—there has not been a cut; there has been a reorientation of where the funding is allocated, and that is an operational decision for MSD.

explanation: A yes/no standing-by question answered 'Yes.' Complete.
question: Does his Government stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Rātana and Te Ao Māori News statements on building trust with Māori. 'Yes' — direct and complete, with an added gloss on how trust gets built.
question: Does the Prime Minister stand by his own words at Rātana in January 2024 that he was committed to “building relationships and building trust with Māori”, and, again, in December 2025 to Te Ao Māori News, when he said that rebuilding trust would be a “focus” of his Government?
statement: Yes, and the way trust is built is by delivering improved outcomes for Māori.

explanation: Two-part question. He answers the 'why' — generic Treaty principle clauses are a problem, the aim is certainty about roles and obligations. He never touches the second half: whether he considers constitutional changes affecting Māori consistent with building trust. Half the question engaged, half left untouched.
question: Why then did his Cabinet decide to weaken Treaty obligations across 23 pieces of legislation, and does he consider making constitutional changes affecting Māori to be consistent with building trust?
statement: We think there’s a problem with generic Treaty principle clauses. We want to create certainty and make sure that everyone is very clear about their specific roles and obligations to each other.

explanation: Asked (a) did he read the Ministry of Justice advice and (b) if so, why did Cabinet proceed anyway. He answers (b) with a reason, but 'did you read it' — a narrow factual yes/no — is passed over entirely. The reason given also restates his previous answer verbatim rather than responding to the specific findings quoted.
question: Did the Prime Minister read his own Ministry of Justice officials’ advice that found the proposed Treaty clause changes had “no apparent benefits, failed to meet the quality assurance standard due to an absence of consultation with iwi and hapū, and carried significant risk to the Māori-Crown relationship”, and, if so, why did Cabinet proceed anyway?
statement: Because we think there’s a problem with generic Treaty principle clauses, because when they’re open-ended, they create uncertainty and legal risk for everybody.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: does he believe iwi Māori ceded sovereignty? He says the matter has been discussed before and that article 1 'deals with that issue very well' — pointing at a document instead of stating his own belief. A tight question whose core is squarely avoided; a plain 'yes' or 'no', however unwelcome, would have scored high.
question: Does the Prime Minister believe iwi Māori ceded sovereignty?
statement: Again, we’ve talked about this before. In terms of the Treaty of Waitangi, article 1 deals with that issue very well.

explanation: Standing-by question answered 'Yes', followed by supporting examples. Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, particularly many practical policies that have had a lot of benefit for Māori. For example, the Government has reformed the Residential Tenancies Act and taxation around residential property, which has seen lower rents. We’ve also seen a higher portion of homes being sold to first-home buyers. With Māori housing statistics being below the New Zealand average, this is something that disproportionately benefits Māori. In education, we have seen a dramatic increase of standards thanks to our Minister of Education introducing the science of learning, which has seen the number of young students at or above the standard for reading and writing nearly double in only two years. Then there are charter schools, which are being embraced by iwi Māori up and down the motu.

explanation: Asked what aid and assistance has been given. He states MFAT is aware, is engaged with the American authorities and will present the New Zealand Government's view — that is what has been done — and then plainly refuses to say more in the House. An explicit refusal to elaborate is forthright; the question is engaged rather than sidestepped, though the 'what, if any' is answered only in outline.
question: What aid and assistance, if any, has been given to Everlee Wihongi, who has been detained by the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for over a month without any charges?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade (MFAT) are very aware of Miss Wihongi’s situation. They are engaged with the American authorities and will continue to work with them to ascertain all of the facts and present the New Zealand Government’s view. I don’t think it would be helpful for me to say in the House any more than that.

explanation: Two-part: his response to Peters' alleged false accusations, and will he require a correction. He does respond to the first by disputing the premise — the member is not in a position to know the accusations are false — which counts as engagement. The 'will the Prime Minister require him to correct the record' is never answered either way; it is deflected into a suggestion to talk to the Minister. The jab about grandstanding is a Civility matter and does not move this score.
question: What is his response to Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters when he made false accusations about Everlee Wihongi, blaming her for being detained, and will the Prime Minister require him to correct the record?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, I don’t believe the member is in a position to know that the accusations are false. If he does, the right thing to do would be to talk with the Minister of Foreign Affairs, because it sounds as though he may have information that would be helpful to Miss Wihongi, rather than grandstanding in the House about it.

explanation: Asked a direct will-you: will he strongly condemn Everlee's treatment. He recites MFAT's process, redirects the complaints to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and says politicising it is unhelpful. That last clause is an implicit no, which is why this is not near zero, but he never states whether he will condemn it — a plain 'no, I won't' would have been fully forthright.
question: Will he strongly condemn Everlee’s treatment by ICE when her whānau have stated that she has been shackled for hours, waiting in hot weather, being deprived of food, sleeping on the ground, and not being able to shower?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, as I’ve said earlier, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade are in contact with the American authorities. They seek to establish the facts, and they will present New Zealand’s position in line with our values as a country. Those complaints are best presented to the Minister of Foreign Affairs so that MFAT can use them in order to best serve her as a New Zealand citizen. I don’t believe that it is useful to try and politicise the issue, which is obviously very sensitive for her.

explanation: Asked what penalties the Government can impose on the US. The answer rejects the premise ("we don't generally think of ourselves as penalising other countries"), which is a partial engagement, but then never says what NZ can or would do and pivots to generalities about representing NZ's position and a swipe at the previous Foreign Minister. The specific question — what penalties — is left unreached.
question: What penalties can the Government impose on the United States if they continue to abuse New Zealand citizens and other immigrants in ICE detention centres?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, we don’t generally think of ourselves as penalising other countries. None the less, where we believe there has been a breach of our understandings between countries, we ensure that we are doing the best to represent New Zealand’s position on the world stage, behind closed doors and openly, and I think our Minister of Foreign Affairs has had a good couple of years of doing that, after we were nearly invisible on the world stage under his predecessor.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to do everything in his power for detained NZ citizens. The answer says plainly that this is exactly what the Government is doing through MFAT — an affirmative response to the commitment sought. The jab at the questioner is a civility matter, not a dodge; small deduction because "released as soon as possible" is not separately engaged.
question: Will he commit to doing everything in his power to ensure that Everlee Wihongi and all New Zealand citizens detained by ICE are treated humanely and released as soon as possible?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, that is exactly what the New Zealand Government is doing through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. This is the answer I gave to my first question, and my advice to the member, if he wants it, would be to try to vary his questions in relation to the answers he has received. He might find out more.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on the fiscal position. She names a specific report — today's announcement of the $2.1b operating allowance — and discusses it. Directly responsive to a broad question; the surrounding contrast with previous Governments is extra, not evasion.
question: What reports has she seen on New Zealand’s fiscal position?
statement: Today, the Prime Minister announced that the new net operating package in Budget 2026 will be $2.1 billion, which is less than the $2.4 billion allowance set last December. The operating allowance is the amount of net new operating funding, on average, per annum that the Government intends to spend on policy initiatives in the Budget. Previous Governments have announced an allowance, then used it as a springboard to ramp up Budget spending even higher. This Government, on the other hand, considers the operating allowance to be a ceiling, not a floor, and has committed to keeping new Budget spending below it. We did so in Budget 2024, in Budget 2025, and we will do so again in Budget 2026.

explanation: Asked how the Government is delivering a tighter operating package. The answer explains the mechanism: a net envelope where savings and revenue initiatives offset new spending, with reprioritisation across Government. The core "how" is engaged; the closing attack on the alternative doesn't displace the answer.
question: How is the Government delivering a tighter operating package?
statement: Operating packages are a net concept. Spending increases are offset by savings and revenue initiatives within a single envelope, so Budget 2026 will continue to invest in front-line public services, such as health, education, and law and order, but it will also identify savings across Government and reprioritise those savings to higher-value areas. That approach has been a feature of previous Budgets and will again be a feature of Budget 2026. There is an alternative. The alternative would be to fund essential new spending through higher taxes or more borrowing. That would weaken the economy, increase Government debt, and leave New Zealand more exposed to international shocks.

explanation: Asked how the international environment has shaped the fiscal position. The answer addresses it squarely — volatility, supply chain and energy shocks, the IMF's April warning, and how that bears on the domestic books. Question engaged head-on.
question: How has the international environment shaped the Government’s fiscal position?
statement: The international environment has undoubtedly become more volatile. Ongoing political tensions, supply chain disruptions, and energy shocks have increased uncertainty and dampened global growth, but that reality strengthens, not weakens, the case for fiscal discipline. In April, the International Monetary Fund warned Governments not to take their eye off the ball at this time and to continue to pursue credible medium-term fiscal consolidation to rebuild essential fiscal buffers. That fiscal consolidation is sorely needed, because, here at home, the Government’s books have been in deficit since 2020 and debt has grown as a share of GDP, from below 20 percent to above 40 percent.

explanation: Asked what the Government's fiscal strategy is. The answer states it directly and enumerates the three targets (core Crown expenses toward 30% of GDP, OBEGALx surplus by 2028-29, net debt on a downward path toward 40%). Direct and complete.
question: What is the Government’s fiscal strategy?
statement: The Government’s strategy is to achieve fiscal consolidation over the medium term through ongoing spending restraint. In particular, the Government’s specific targets are to reduce core Crown expenses towards 30 percent of GDP; they are to return the headline operating measure, OBEGALx—the operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC revenue and expenses—to surplus by the 2028-2029 fiscal year; and they are to put net core Crown debt as a percentage of GDP on a downward path towards 40 percent. Having an operating package of only $2.1 billion is a significant contribution to each of these targets, and the Budget will show exactly what progress is being made in meeting them.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answer opens "Yes, exactly, I do" — a complete answer to a yes/no question. The subsequent talking points and attack on the Opposition are additional material, and detail/focus/civility do not move forthrightness.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, exactly, I do—and particularly the Government’s announcement today that we will be keeping to a new operating allowance of $2.1 billion. The Government making careful use of taxpayers’ money and gradually driving down the proportion of the economy that’s consumed by Government leaves New Zealanders in a stronger position to weather the storms of trade wars and actual wars that have affected us in the last two years. The alternative is a Government that has a long history of blowing out the credit card, leaving New Zealanders with very few options except for high inflation and high interest rates—and now they’re not even doing that; they’re just producing lame TikTok videos.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Peters' characterisation. The answer is an unambiguous denial — the Government is not attempting to write a Budget out of the Super Fund, and superannuation policy is not changing. That squarely answers the agree/disagree question, whatever its accuracy.
question: Does he agree with Winston Peters that his own Government is attempting to “write a Budget out of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund because of their failed economic policies”?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, the Government is not attempting to write a Budget out of the Superannuation Fund because the Government Budget is not changing superannuation policy, as is agreed between our parties. This is the difference: three parties work together—

explanation: Asked why the third-ranked Minister said the Government would raid the Super Fund. He does engage — "I can only guess he was alluding to future policy positions" — which is a real, if thin, attempt at the "why". But he then turns the question back on Labour, and no account of what his colleague actually meant is given. Partial.
question: Why did the third-ranked Minister in his own Government tell the New Zealand public just this morning that the Government was going to be raiding the New Zealand Superannuation Fund in order to prop up its Budget?
statement: I can only guess that he was alluding to future policy positions that parties might take. It’s a good question for the Labour Party: show us the money. How are they going to pay for the pay equity and the superannuation and the fees-free, and all those cheques that they’re writing out that their body can’t cash?

explanation: Asked whether the Government will draw down on the Super Fund in this year's Budget. Answer: "No." One word, but it is the complete answer to the question asked.
question: Will the Government be drawing down on the Superannuation Fund in this year’s Budget?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that no Super Fund money will be used for anything other than its legislated purpose. "I can absolutely confirm that the Government will follow the law" gives the guarantee sought, in slightly reframed terms. The Ihumātao attack that follows is off-topic but the core commitment was already stated.
question: Will the Government guarantee that it will not be using, in this year’s Budget, any funds from the New Zealand Superannuation Fund for anything other than their legislated purpose?
statement: I can absolutely confirm that the Government will follow the law, and the reason for that is very important. You see, we had a Government that didn’t follow the law; they took $30 million to buy out Ihumātao and created a steaming pile of that member knows just what that this Government is still trying to fix after they misappropriated funds and didn’t follow the law.

explanation: Asked what Peters was referring to. He restates the same guess as before — future positions parties might take — which touches the question, but adds nothing and immediately turns to Labour's fiscal management. The questioner's actual query about his colleague's meaning is left largely unanswered.
question: What was Winston Peters referring to when he said that the Government was going to be attempting to write its Budget out of the New Zealand Superannuation Fund?
statement: I think we’re having either a communication or a memory problem here. As I said earlier, I can only guess that he is referring to positions that parties might take in the future, and one of the parties I like him referring to is the many positions that the Labour Party takes on its fiscal management.

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should believe the Minister of Foreign Affairs is fit to be a Minister, given his and Willis's remarks. Seymour disputes the premise (he wasn't referring to that Minister), which engages the question's basis, but he never reaches the fitness question and spends the rest jabbing at the questioner's memory. Partial engagement via premise rejection.
question: If he thinks the Minister of Foreign Affairs has a memory problem, and Nicola Willis thinks the Minister of Foreign Affairs is very confused, why should New Zealanders believe that he’s a fit person to be a Minister?
statement: As I wasn’t referring to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, you see the member asking the question may have, himself, forgotten that I’ve answered his question only seconds earlier.

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should think differently about the Government's economic record. Seymour supplies actual reasons — mortgage rates lower than under the previous Government, inflation down from 7.3 to 5.3 percent, unemployment down slightly — and states there are many reasons to trust the Government's management. That is the question engaged; the closing insult and any dispute about the figures' accuracy are other attributes.
question: If his own Minister of Foreign Affairs thinks that his Government are pursuing failed economic policies that have seen the economy shrink, unemployment increase, interest rates going back up, inflation going back up, and more New Zealanders losing their jobs, why should New Zealanders think any differently?
statement: Oh, Mr Speaker, they’re spicy today. First of all, mortgage rates going back up: now, that’s an interesting concept isn’t it because they can only go back up to the place they were when he was in Government, so what he’s conceding is that they have come down dramatically for Kiwis under this Government, as has inflation which peaked at 7.3 percent. We’ve got it down to 5.3 percent, and even unemployment has just gone down slightly in the last quarter. So there are many, many reasons why people might trust in the economic management of this Government; three parties united behind a careful, fiscally responsible Budget that gives New Zealanders a much better future than they would if Mr Marmite Sandwich, with his TikTok memes was in charge of the company credit card again.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all the statements and actions of his Government. Answer opens with a flat "Yes" before moving to an example. Direct and complete; the padding afterwards doesn't dilute the answer.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and I’d particularly like to highlight the Hon Andrew Hoggard’s recent announcement that the Government will be endorsing a marketplace for environmental good deeds mainly done on farms. If you plant trees or save wetlands, there’ll actually be a marketplace where you can be funded by those good people in the community and in business who would like to pay for those kinds of things to happen somewhere in the country, because they care about the environment. It’s a very good example of a practical approach from practical people, ensuring that all of us can be better environmental custodians. I highlight this because the Green Party aren’t always focused—

explanation: Asked whether he accepts the forecast deficit is smaller because of dividends from Government-majority-owned power companies. He concedes the general principle that SOE ownership "sometimes, but not always" delivers dividends that improve the fiscal position, but never confirms or denies it for the forecast deficit, then pivots to a lecture on electricity price controls. Hedges around the core.
question: Does he accept that the Government’s forecasted deficit is now smaller because of the large profits paid out in dividends, made by Government - majority owned power companies?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, it is certainly true that the ownership of State-owned enterprises—sometimes, but not always—delivers dividends that improve the Government’s financial position. However, I have seen suggestions that would ensure that that almost never happens. I have seen suggestions that energy companies should somehow limit the price of the energy that they sell to the rate of inflation. Now, let’s just think about how that works for a moment: the price they sell it at is set in a uniform auction at the price of the highest bidder in the electricity market every half an hour. In order for them to limit the price they sell energy, every single participant in the electricity market in New Zealand would need to collude and breach the Commerce Act to achieve that. Now, the reason I say this is that I happen to be Parliament’s only electrical engineer and I know a little bit about it. On the other hand, there are people that listen to their focus groups and decide—

explanation: Asked whether he understands the difference between wholesale and retail power markets. Answer: "Yes, I do," followed by a distinction between energy, lines and retail costs. Direct answer plus demonstration.
question: Does the acting Prime Minister understand the difference between wholesale and retail power markets?
statement: Thank you for that invitation. Yes, I do. You see, the thing is there are actually three costs. There’s your energy cost, there’s your lines cost, and there is your retail cost. The thing about retail is that you are beholden to the price of the energy that you buy. If the suggestion is that somehow retailers should charge nothing or perhaps even pay people to take electricity by selling it for less than they can buy it on the wholesale market, well, that’s a very interesting bit of bumper-sticker politics, but I don’t think it’s going to work. What I’d say to the member is that electricity markets are very delicate things, not best designed by a focus group.

explanation: Asked whether it is fair that shareholders collect near-record dividends while 200,000 people cannot heat their homes. He explicitly refuses the terms — "the question is not whether it's fair but what can be done about it" — and answers the substituted question about investment instead. He is open about the swap, but a fairness question was replaced rather than answered.
question: Is it fair that shareholders, including the Government, are collecting near record dividends from power companies while 200,000 New Zealanders cannot afford to heat their homes?
statement: On behalf of the Prime Minister, the question is not whether it’s fair but what can be done about it, and what is being done about it to improve everyone’s situation is a record level of investment in generation, the highest since the 1970s and 1980s under Think Big, but it’s being done without a cent of taxpayer money. Now, the one thing that could really bugger that up is if someone came in and put price controls on the electricity market and made sure that nobody wanted to invest, just like member helped do with the oil and gas market.

explanation: Asked whether Government-owned gentailers have the power to reduce prices immediately, or not. After complaining it was already answered, he engages the mechanism: not by cutting the wholesale price without illegal collusion, though they could take a smaller margin and send retail arms broke. An answer is recoverable — effectively "not in any workable way" — but he never states the yes/no plainly.
question: Do Government-owned or Government - majority owned gentailers have the power to reduce their prices immediately or not?
statement: It is a bit of a theme—I give answers and then they ask questions that I’ve already answered. In order for one participant in an energy market to reduce the price, they would have to collude with every other market participant to bring the energy price down. Now, that is, first of all, illegal, and, second of all, it would be a total, I guess, destruction of the electricity market as New Zealand generators have known it for the last 30 years. I guess they could start selling it for a smaller margin or less than the wholesale energy price, and all the retail arms could go broke and any other retailer could go broke, and we’d have no other competition, but this is a perfect example—

explanation: Asked whether he has seen evidence and analysis that the 2012 partial privatisation contributed to higher power prices. He neither confirms seeing it nor addresses its findings; he argues the questioner's line is self-contradictory and attacks her policy process. Some contact with the substance, but the question asked is left unanswered.
question: Has he seen the evidence and analysis that the partial privatisation of our power companies in 2012, just by overwhelming public opposition, has contributed to far higher power prices than would have otherwise been the case?
statement: That evidence brings up a certain contradiction in the member’s line of questioning. You see, she started out claiming that the reason power prices are high is that the Government is such a rapacious claimer of dividends boosting its bottom line that Government ownership pushes up power prices. Now she’s saying that fact that half of them are not owned by the Government also pushes up power prices, and this is the problem, Chlöe Swarbrick, when you run all your policy based on focus groups, sound bites, slogans, and bumper stickers.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. Answer: "In context, yes," with an example. A direct affirmative; the qualifier is minor.
question: Fạiȧkse‘ea, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: In context, yes. I particularly stand by my statements that under the Budgets I deliver, operating allowances will be a ceiling, not a floor.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question — how many times Treasury has revised down growth forecasts since she became Minister. She says plainly she would have to check, which is a direct response rather than a pivot, but then fills the rest with talking points about PREFU optimism instead of the count. The number, which was the whole of the question, is never given.
question: How many times has Treasury revised down its growth forecasts since she became the Minister of Finance?
statement: I would have to check, as has been traversed in this House. In particular, the Treasury has acknowledged that the assumptions it made in the pre-election fiscal update were wildly too optimistic and led to significant changes in its forecast outlook, which has changed the projections under this Government.

explanation: Asked whether she intends to use Super Fund money outside its current purpose while she is Minister of Finance. She answers "no", but narrows the scope from "while she is Minister" to this term's Budgets. Squarely answered with a scope hedge.
question: Does she intend to use funding from the New Zealand Superannuation Fund for anything outside its current purpose while she is Minister of Finance?
statement: Well, I hope to be the Minister of Finance for many Governments yet to come. In the term of this Government, for the Budgets for which I am responsible, the answer to that question is no.

explanation: Asked whether she can rule out selling all or part of Kiwibank while she is Minister of Finance. She says the Government will not do that in this term — an answer, but again narrowed to the term rather than the tenure she was asked about, so the rule-out is not given in the form requested.
question: Can she rule out selling all or part of Kiwibank while she is the Minister of Finance?
statement: Again, I am responsible, as the Minister of Finance in this Government, for the policies in this term, and we will not be doing that in this term.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Peters' characterisation of her spending/Budget decisions. She never says agree or disagree — she turns on the questioner, accusing her of mischaracterising the Minister and of misquoting. The yes/no at the core is untouched; the reply is about the questioner's habits, not the proposition.
question: Does she agree with the Rt Hon Winston Peters’ characterisation of her spending and Budget decisions that they are “all coming home to roost now, and here we are, five months, six months ago before an election, and all the birds are coming home”?
statement: I think that the member, as is often her habit, is mischaracterising the Minister of Foreign Affairs and trade. This is a habit she has; she often likes to take my quotations out of—

explanation: Asked to choose between Seymour's 'three parties united' and Peters' 'failed economic policies'. She opens by dismissing the quotes as out of context, but then does implicitly side with the unity framing ('I agree that it is a significant achievement that the three parties... have pulled together an excellent Budget'). The unity half is engaged; the 'failed economic policies' half is never addressed. Partial.
question: Does she agree with David Seymour that all three coalition parties are united on economic policies, or the Rt Hon Winston Peters, who has said that her Government has pursued “failed economic policies”?
statement: Again, I think the member takes quotations out of context, and I agree that it is a significant achievement that the three parties of this Government—the National Party, the ACT Party, and the New Zealand First Party—in a time of global turmoil, with finances under strain and with a fuel crisis, have pulled together an excellent Budget that we agree to, which is delivering our commitments within a smaller operating allowance than we forecast, allowing us to return the books to a better balance sooner.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on national direction under the RMA. He names a specific announcement — changes to the National Environmental Standards for Marine Aquaculture — and describes what they do. Squarely on the question.
question: What announcements has he made on national direction under the Resource Management Act 1991?
statement: It was great to announce last week that the Government has made changes to the National Environmental Standards for Marine Aquaculture, which will remove unnecessary complexity and cost for aquaculture operators. These changes support marine farmers to refine their operations within existing footprints, trial new approaches, and adopt better practices, and they provide councils with a clearer national direction about how certain activities should be assessed. These updates are another step in making the resource management system more workable and proportionate while protecting our marine environment.

explanation: Asked why the changes are needed and why they are important. Both halves are engaged: needed because prior consenting was costly, complex and disproportionate; important because of the sector's growth potential, jobs, exports and the revenue target. Slight drift into the commencement date at the end, but the question is reached.
question: Why are these changes needed, and why are they so important?
statement: Previous consenting processes for aquaculture were costly, complex, and disproportionate, especially for minor changes. It is worth noting, as the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries has noted on so many occasions, that the potential for growth in aquaculture is huge. It already employs more than 3,000 people, it generates over $650 million in exports annually, and we do have a Government target of $3 billion in annual revenue that was set out in the aquaculture development plan led by Minister Jones last year. These national environmental standards come into effect on 4 June and apply to new activities, and we’re making decisions on marine aquaculture consents.

explanation: Asked what other changes to national direction he has progressed. He enumerates them — infrastructure barriers, granny flats/housing, primary sector rules, renewable consenting, EV chargers. Directly responsive.
question: What other changes to national direction has he progressed?
statement: National direction does the heavy lifting in our planning system in terms of what is allowed and where it is allowed, but it has been neglected by previous Governments. This Government has made the largest suite of changes to national direction in New Zealand history. We’ve removed barriers to infrastructure, we’ve made it easier to build granny flats and support housing, we’ve removed unworkable rules for the primary sector, and we’re streamlining consenting for renewable energy. Just last week, new rules for consenting electric vehicle chargers came into force, setting clear national rules to make it easier and quicker to get chargers in the ground—and there is more to come.

explanation: Asked how these changes relate to replacing the RMA. He answers the relation explicitly: unclog the current system now, and the changes are part of the transition and will carry through into the new regime. Complete on the question asked.
question: How do these changes relate to the Government’s work to replace the Resource Management Act 1991?
statement: Well, some may wonder why the Government’s making changes under the existing Resource Management Act (RMA), and there are a couple of reasons. The first is to unclog the system that exists right now and provide quick wins for people out there trying to do things in the real economy. The second point is that this is part of the transition to the wholesale replacement of the RMA with a new regime—a much more liberal planning regime—under the Planning and Natural Environment Bills. Many of the changes—in fact, almost all of the changes we’ve made over the last two years—will carry through into the new system. Whether it’s aquaculture, electric vehicles, farming, mining, quarrying, infrastructure, renewable energy, granny flats, or housing, those changes will carry through into the new, much more permissive, and much more sensible system.

explanation: Asked what recent announcement was made about school property redevelopment. She states it — $56.6 million for projects at six schools — and places it in the wider funding package. Direct.
question: What recent announcement has the Government made about school property redevelopment projects?
statement: Last week, the Government announced $56.6 million in redevelopment funding, delivering projects at six schools across New Zealand. This is part of the Government’s funding increase of $880 million into school property maintenance through Budgets 2024 and 2025 to start to clear the backlog of projects that have been languishing in the pipeline for years. It’s a significant investment into school maintenance, and we understand the importance of maintaining the assets that you have. This investment will give confidence to schools that we are prioritising maintenance that’s been deferred for years, giving families confidence that their children will be learning in warm, safe, dry classrooms.

explanation: Asked which schools benefit. She names all six and the classroom count. Exactly the thing asked for, completely.
question: Which schools are benefiting from this investment?
statement: The investment will deliver 52 new and replacement classrooms at Kerikeri High School, Pinehill School, Hutt Intermediate, Natone Park School, Ashburton Intermediate School, and Māruawai College. This investment will replace ageing infrastructure and address long-standing condition issues at these schools, and construction is expected to begin within the next six months.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to improve delivery of school property projects. She answers with the mechanisms — off-site manufactured builds, repeatable designs, and the new School Property Agency. On point.
question: What is the Government doing to improve delivery of school property projects?
statement: Our approach to school property is clear: deliver more classrooms more efficiently. Through the use of off-site manufactured builds and repeatable classroom designs, we’ve delivered 583 classrooms in 2024—31 percent more than 2023—delivering classrooms to many schools have been waiting for some time. We’re also establishing the New Zealand School Property Agency to further improve infrastructure delivery and to drive even better value for money, and we’re funding and delivering the classrooms that our teachers and students deserve.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has received on the announcement. She supplies feedback — quoted reactions from the Māruawai College and Kerikeri High School principals. Sourced from media rather than received directly, but the question is engaged head-on.
question: What feedback has she received on this announcement?
statement: The Māruawai College principal said to the Otago Daily Times , “Minister Stanford rang me, she’s been taking a big interest in the development. I think this is a sign they’ve committed to modernising our school and once they’ve done this one, I think they’re committed to knocking down the rest. We’re absolutely thrilled. It’s a relief in so many ways.” The principal of Kerikeri High School told The Northern Advocate that the upgrade was long overdue and marked a significant step forward for the school.

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree it's working, and if so have prices come down. The first part is answered plainly ('I always agree... we are starting to see encouraging signs'). The second is dodged — asked whether competition has brought prices down, he lists the factors that influence grocery prices and never says whether they fell. Half the question reached.
question: Does he agree with Cameron Brewer’s statement about the Government’s supermarket policy, “it’s working”; if so, has increased competition brought prices down?
statement: I always agree with the perpetually youthful Cameron Brewer, particularly that we are starting to see encouraging signs that reforms are improving grocery competition and are working. I’d like to thank Nicola Willis for the great work she is doing. This Government has moved quickly to reduce barriers to entry into the grocery sector, including creating an express lane for new supermarkets and strengthening penalties for misleading or deceptive pricing. Grocery prices are influenced by a range of factors, including global commodity prices, transport costs, energy prices, weather events, and wider inflation pressures. This Government is increasing competitive pressure across a range of sectors.

explanation: Asked whether he will equip the Commerce Commission to improve competition law. The first sentence answers it affirmatively — the Government is 'beefing up the Commerce Commission... with the Commerce Commission reforms' — before pivoting to attacking the previous government. Vague and undetailed, but vagueness is Specificity; the will-he question is engaged rather than avoided.
question: Will the Minister equip the Commerce Commission to improve competition law in response to a new report that describes that sector as one with little to no competition?
statement: This Government is beefing up the Commerce Commission, as we will see with the Commerce Commission reforms. The member may point to that report, but everything she points to is everything that we are attacking, as far as financial services, as far as the energy sector, as far as the telecommunications sector. We are doing a lot, lot more than that Government did, which sat on its hands for six years and food inflation increased by over 12 percent in the year to March 2023.

explanation: Asked a yes/no question: is he scrapping the Government's predatory-pricing law change? The answer never says yes, no, or anything about that law change — it recites a list of sectors the Government is 'focused on'. A narrow closed question completely dodged.
question: Is he scrapping his own Government’s big competition law change on pricing to ban predatory pricing?
statement: We are focused on competition. We are focused on improving the competition settings across the supermarket sector, across the financial services sector, across the insurance sector, across the telecommunications and energy sector. We are the Government that is, for the first time in a long time, focused on competition, because we know that, with better competition settings, consumers benefit.

explanation: Asked whether predatory pricing is fine and consumers should accept it. The response ignores the question entirely and attacks the questioner's record over six years. No part of the question is engaged.
question: Is predatory pricing fine, and should consumers just accept it?
statement: If this member was so interested in all these issues, they would not have sat on their hands for six years.

explanation: Asked whether he has funded and equipped the Commerce Commission to investigate supermarket buyer power and own-brand labelling in the Wattie's closure. He does engage the capability half — the Commission is 'being beefed up' and will inherit the Grocery Commissioner's powers — but never confirms funding, never addresses the specific investigation, and never mentions Wattie's. Partial engagement with the core.
question: Has he funded and equipped the Commerce Commission to investigate the role that supermarket buyer power and own-brand labelling played in the closure of Wattie’s operations and the loss of local food production?
statement: As I said before, with our Commerce Commission reforms, the Commerce Commission is being beefed up—is being beefed up—and any powers from the Grocery Commissioner, who is there till 2028, will be transferred over to the Commerce Commission, with a square focus on all the things that she has talked about today. We are focused solely on improving competition settings, and across a range of sectors. Again, I commend the good work that the Hon Nicola Willis has done in the grocery space and will continue to do.

explanation: Asked whether he will advocate for consumers. Opens with 'Of course we will continue to advocate for those who are paying too high prices' — a direct yes to the question as put — before pivoting into a comparison of food-price inflation. The pivot is padding, but the question was answered first. Truthfulness of the inflation figures and the swipe at the previous government are Veracity/Focus, not this.
question: Will he advocate for New Zealand consumers, who are paying record prices for basic food while local manufacturers get priced out of existence?
statement: Of course we will continue to advocate for those who are paying too high prices. That’s why this Government is singularly focused. That is why this Government is not like the other one, which saw, in the year to March 2023, food prices—there we go, Ms Williams—food prices increased by over 12 percent in the year to March 2023. In the year to March 2026, food prices increased by 3.4 percent. It’s a much better improvement than that Government, when they sat on their hands.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on critical minerals. He answers in form and substance — reports on rising value, Conservation Act access, and a named meeting on the American critical minerals strategy. Direct, even though the answer trails off mid-sentence.
question: What reports, if any, has he seen on critical minerals?
statement: I have seen reports that the country now realises that it is far wealthier than it initially thought it was. Critical minerals have now risen in value, and with the change to the Conservation Act it will be possible for investors and prospectors and explorers to gain easier access because of the development potential pertaining to critical minerals hidden in the Department of Conservation estate. I have just finished a meeting with Assistant Secretary Michael DeSombre explaining how the American critical minerals strategy—

explanation: Asked why we need critical minerals. After an opening jab at other members, he gives the actual reason: they are in computers, phones and other essentials, and New Zealand should contribute to supply lines. The insult does not reduce Forthrightness — the question is reached and answered.
question: Why do we need critical minerals?
statement: Sadly, there are some parts of the country, and members from Taranaki, who do not understand the vital importance of vanadium and other such ingredients. From time to time, the matua must excuse the words that come from Luddites. Virtually every modern accoutrement has critical minerals involved, whether it is computers, whether it is phones, whether it is other ordinary essentials. New Zealand must contribute to supply lines and make its contribution as an OECD nation. With characteristic humility, the Minister for Resources will lead that effort.

explanation: Asked HOW critical minerals development can support the economy. Most of the answer rebuts 'troublemakers' and lists mineral types; the only economic content is that a '$1.4 billion sector' should be enabled to grow via fast-track legislation. It gestures at the question — asserting there IS opportunity — without explaining the mechanism asked for.
question: How can the development of critical minerals support our economy?
statement: There are various troublemakers—people spreading misinformation that the critical minerals sector does not represent economic opportunity. Nothing could be further from the truth. There will always be guardrails and various critters; they will be addressed in an appropriate way, whether it’s a gold mine, the development of antimony, or various properties associated with the ironsands or the mineral sands. It’s important that the $1.4 billion sector be enabled to grow, whether it’s through the fast-track legislation—and I accept—

explanation: Asked why we should develop critical minerals in New Zealand. The reply is a joke about hearing aids aimed at another member. Hearing aids are technically named as a use, but the sentence exists to land the insult, not to answer; the question's core is untouched.
question: Why should we develop critical minerals in New Zealand?
statement: It could very well be that critical minerals are needed for hearing aids, and I rather fear that hearing aids are needed for the member from Western Māori sitting to my right.

explanation: Asked what mental health support he has recently announced for businesses. He names it: the Business Mental Health Toolkit, launched today, free and confidential, aimed at small and medium businesses. Directly and completely on the question. (A friendly patsy question, but that is a corpus-level concern, not a Forthrightness deduction.)
question: What mental health support has the Minister recently announced to support businesses to improve productivity in the workplace?
statement: The Government’s mental health plan is delivering faster access to support, more front-line workers, and a better crisis response. Today, I launched the new Business Mental Health Toolkit, which will support businesses to improve productivity in the workplace through better mental health. The tool kit is free and provides confidential mental health support, delivered in a way that works best for both employers and employees. That’s why we’ve worked with businesses to develop the free tool kit, aimed at medium- and small-sized businesses to help reduce barriers to faster mental health support.

explanation: Asked what evidence links workplace mental health to productivity. He supplies evidence: research showing 6–10 percent productivity gains and a $5-per-$1 return on employee assistance programmes. Whether those figures are correct is Veracity; the question was squarely addressed.
question: What evidence shows that by improving mental health in the workplace, productivity can increase?
statement: Poor mental health in the workplace can lead to decreased productivity and high absenteeism rates. Research shows that by improving mental health in the workplace, productivity can increase by around 6 percent to 10 percent. There is strong economic evidence for investing in better mental health in the workplace, with returns of around $5 for every $1 invested into initiatives such as employee assistance programmes. That’s why today I have launched a business mental health tool kit that delivers free and confidential mental health support in a way that works best for the workplace.

explanation: Asked what real-time support the toolkit provides. He lists it: the Groov app, 1737 call/text with a trained counsellor 24/7, and in-person Access & Choice bookings. Direct and complete.
question: What real-time support does the business mental health tool kit provide?
statement: For some workplaces, costs can be a barrier to accessing workplace support. The tool kit connects people to free, real-time, confidential support in a way that works for both employers and employees. People can download the Groov app for practical advice, call or text 1737 for free support with a trained counsellor 24/7, or book a time to see someone in person at Access & Choice mental health services.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen on the launch. He quotes Business Central, the Wellington Chamber of Commerce and a LinkedIn comment. The feedback is selectively positive, but selectivity is not evasion — the question asked what he had seen and he answered it.
question: What feedback has he seen on the launch of the business mental health tool kit?
statement: Business Central and the Wellington Chamber of Commerce welcome the release of the business mental health tool kit, saying, “Often we find SMEs do not have easy access to timely mental health services or at an affordable cost. We are pleased that the Government has released this new tool, which will make these services more accessible.”, while Carly on LinkedIn said, “Cheers to more support for hard-working employees so that they can keep showing up as their best selves.” The business mental health tool kit is just another way the Government is supporting New Zealanders to get faster access to mental health support.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the statement and why. Answers "Yes" outright and gives a reason (NEET numbers track unemployment/economic uncertainty). The tail drifts into government-focus talking points, but both limbs of the question are reached.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “Obviously, when unemployment goes up, NEET numbers go up”; if so, why?
statement: Yes. Young Kiwis who are not in employment, education, or training (NEET) are often more affected during periods of higher unemployment and economic uncertainty. That is why this Government is focused on rebuilding the economy, creating opportunities through education and training, and strengthening pathways from school into further education and work. Our focus is on ensuring that more young New Zealanders are equipped with the skills and the support they need to succeed.

explanation: Two-part: awareness of the ~100,000 figure, and why nothing has been done. The "done nothing" limb is squarely contested with named measures (Youth Guarantee places, Apprenticeship Boost, VET redesign); the awareness limb and the figure itself are never acknowledged. Substantially engaged, one limb left unaddressed.
question: Is she aware that nearly 100,000 young people are not engaged in education, employment, or training, and why has she done nothing about it?
statement: We have done a great deal about engaging young NEETs, and sadly, there have been a number of young people who have left school with low or no qualifications. That member might want to look at the NCEA issues that caused that. This Government has put in place extra Youth Guarantee places, an extra 175 places this year, to a total of 8,400 young people who participated in Youth Guarantee schemes over 2025; Apprenticeship Boost, which subsidises employers—over $25 million was spent on Apprenticeship Boost through Vote Social Development. And, of course, the redesign of the vocational education and training system was to ensure that we restored regional leadership decision-making into the regions and led to better industry connections.

explanation: Asked whether 175 places touch the sides against 100,000 NEET. The response opens on the previous Government's inaction in compulsory education and never turns toward the comparison asked about — a pivot to blame, not an answer.
question: Are an additional 175 Youth Guarantee places going to even touch the sides when there are an additional 100,000 young people not engaged in education, training, or employment since last year?
statement: Well, as I said before, the inaction of the previous Government in the compulsory education system—

explanation: A direct yes/no about accepting responsibility for the apprentice drop. The response begins with the previous Government's budgeting and never engages the question of her own responsibility.
question: Does she accept that by cutting the Apprenticeship Boost, she is responsible for the number of apprentices dropping by the thousands?
statement: Well, of course the previous Government didn’t budget—

explanation: Asked whether the NEET figure shows she is failing. Answers "No" explicitly and then gives her competing account. The account is talking-point heavy, but the question was posed as yes/no and was answered as one.
question: Does nearly 100,000 young people not engaged in education, employment, or training show that she is failing to help young people into work-based learning, polytechnic training, or university?
statement: No, it shows that we are having to deal with an economy that was left in a mess so that we are having to grow the economy, keep inflation and interest rates down, reduce wasteful spending, and show discipline around Government spending to ensure that industries and businesses have the confidence to be able to employ young people.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to fund enrolment demand. "Wait to see at Budget time" declines to commit and says so plainly rather than pivoting or attacking — a stated refusal to answer now, which is engagement, but it leaves the yes/no genuinely undelivered rather than resolved.
question: Will she commit to helping universities and polytechnics so they can provide for increased enrolment demand, or will she continue to make them bear the financial brunt of her inaction?
statement: Well, the member will have to wait to see at Budget time.

explanation: Two-part: does he stand by the statement, and what has he done. Answers "In the context it was made, yes", then enumerates the actions taken (consent exemption, 10-day processing, voltage range, peak rebates, review). Both limbs directly met.
question: Does he stand by the Hon Simon Watts’ statement that “Rooftop solar will play a crucial role in supporting energy security”; if so, what, if anything, has he done to make the installation of solar affordable for New Zealand households?
statement: In the context it was made, yes. Rooftop solar will play a significant role to ensure New Zealand has secure, affordable energy, and that is why this Government is making it easier for Kiwis to get it on their roofs. We’ve scrapped the building consent requirements for most home installations, saving households around a thousand dollars and weeks of red tape. Where consent is still needed, councils now have to process it in 10 working days, not 20. We’ve widened the network voltage range so families can export more power back to the grid and install larger systems. We’re better rewarding consumers who are providing solar to the grid to help meet peak demands. Networks are now required to offer a rebate for electricity injected back into the grid at peak times. And we’re launching a review into the installation of solar to make installation in New Zealand the simplest in the developed world—practical, common-sense changes that help put Kiwis back in charge of their power bills.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with specific MBIE advice that the changes deliver only small reductions. Never says agree or disagree about the advice; instead argues the savings are significant. That contests the premise, which is partial engagement, but the question about the advice is left unanswered.
question: Does he agree with Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) advice in September 2025 that the Government’s regulatory changes to solar policy will only deliver small reductions to power bills?
statement: MBIE provides a lot of advice from time to time to the Minister for Energy, and what we’re focused on is making practical changes—$1,000 off installation is quite a significant amount considering installations could be between $10,000 and $20,000. That’s a significant cut in the cost for people putting solar on their roofs. We’re increasing voltage range so that people can export more back to the grid. It all makes a difference. I welcome the member’s support.

explanation: Asked whether he is satisfied small reductions are sufficient. Pivots to Lake Onslow, the renewable boom and wholesale prices; "satisfied" and "sufficient" are never addressed, and the answer closes on a partisan jibe rather than the question.
question: Is he satisfied that small reductions in power bills are sufficient given the current cost of living pressures on households?
statement: Our focus is on affordable and reliable energy for New Zealanders, and that’s why we’ve made a number of decisions as a Government. We’ve stopped work on the Lake Onslow boondoggle, which was having a chilling effect on our renewable generation. We now have the biggest renewable boom under way. We’re seeing lower power prices in the wholesale market and Australian Securities Exchange futures. Of course, these changes around solar make it easier for people to put solar on their roofs to further lower their power bills. It’s all making a difference. I welcome the member’s support.

explanation: A narrow quantitative question — how many additional households in 12 months. "Many" is responsive in form and not a pivot, but the quantity asked for is the core of the question and it is not reached. Marked down for the unreached core, not for brevity.
question: How many additional households does he expect to install rooftop solar, as a direct result of the Government’s solar regulatory review, over the next 12 months?
statement: Many.

explanation: Asked whether he has received modelling advice. Never says yes or no; "I just know" and "I'm sure" imply he is going on impression rather than modelling, so the answer is inferable but never given. Skirts the core without wholly abandoning it.
question: Has he received modelling advice to tell him that “many” will?
statement: Look, I just know that we’re seeing a significant increase in rooftop solar, year on year. I think, last year, we had one of the biggest increases in rooftop solar, and if we can remove some more red tape, I’m sure many more will.

explanation: Asked about Budget initiatives. "We don't talk about the Budget" is an explicit, reasoned refusal to answer rather than a pivot or an attack — forthright as a refusal, though it still withholds the yes/no.
question: Are there specific initiatives to enable more people to access solar in the upcoming Budget?
statement: We don’t talk about the Budget. I think it’s two weeks away. That’s about 14 sleeps or something or thereabouts.

explanation: Asked a binary: is there more coming on solar, or is this it? "We should always keep watching" is a quip on the questioner's phrasing — it leans toward "not it" but makes no claim about solar policy at all, so the core of the question is glanced off rather than engaged.
question: When Simon Watts said we should “watch this space” on solar, should we still be watching, or is this it?
statement: We should always keep watching.

explanation: Two-part question: has the number of declines increased, and how many last quarter? The second part is answered squarely with a figure (~900). The first part — the trend since she became Minister — is never addressed; the granted-applications figures and economy line are padding, which does not move the score either way.
question: Has the number of declined advances to pay for power bills increased since she became a Minister; if so, how many people had their application for an advance for electricity costs declined in the last quarter?
statement: We acknowledge that winter months bring higher power bills for Kiwis. Around 900 applications for advances for energy costs have been declined in the last quarter. At the same time, more than 6,700 applications have been granted, totalling nearly $4 million in payments. The Ministry of Social Development (MSD) regularly help people with a range of urgent needs and work with them closely to ensure that they are getting the assistance they are entitled to. We encourage people to talk to Work and Income and discuss their situation and the support that they may be eligible for. Our Government is focused on building the economy to ease the costs that New Zealanders face.

explanation: Asked whether she is aware of the near-record declines and whether she will ensure it doesn't recur this winter. She neither confirms awareness nor gives any commitment or refusal — she explains that policy is unchanged and decisions are made at the front line. Topically adjacent, but neither limb is answered.
question: Is she aware that Work and Income declined an almost record number of advances or power bills last quarter between June and September, and will she ensure this does not happen again this winter?
statement: Well, there haven’t been any policy changes around advance payments, and MSD make decisions at the front line to assess an individual’s situation and their needs. Particularly with advanced payments, there is a caution because, obviously, when payments are made in advance, that means there are less in the following weeks for a beneficiary to look after their costs with.

explanation: Asked why declines rose despite rising need. She disputes the premise ("conflating a number of issues") and restates that policy hasn't changed — contesting a premise is a legitimate form of engagement, but she never offers any account of why the declines rose, and the winter energy payment reference is a pivot.
question: Why are more people declined for assistance for power bills despite rising power bills and rising energy hardship demonstrating a clear need?
statement: Well, the member is conflating a number of issues. I’ve just stated that there have been no policy changes around advanced payments for energy. We do know that, over winter, it is more challenging for people to pay their costs. That’s why we have assistance like the winter energy payment.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether she will direct Work and Income to use its discretion. She neither agrees nor refuses; she redirects to advice that individuals should approach MSD. A blunt "no" would have scored high — this instead avoids the decision point entirely.
question: Will she direct Work and Income to use their discretion to ensure that nobody living in poverty goes without power this winter?
statement: As I said, I would encourage anyone who is facing costs that they’re unable to deal with to approach MSD and see if they are eligible for additional assistance and support.

explanation: Asked directly whether she is confident everyone in energy hardship is getting what they need. She expressly declines to address a different matter (energy price drivers) and then cites the winter energy payment's reach, never stating whether she is confident.
question: Is she confident that everyone in energy hardship is getting the assistance they need from Work and Income?
statement: Well, there’s a number of things that contribute to energy price and therefore the subsequent energy hardship, which I’m not going to address here. What I would say is that the winter energy payment is the main mechanism by which taxpayers provide assistance to those with energy costs, and over a million New Zealanders receive that support.

explanation: Asked how the winter energy payment can be fit for purpose given a 28 percent price rise and high decline rates. The reply dismisses the question as already traversed and turns to attacking the questioner ("look in the mirror"), with no engagement with fitness for purpose.
question: How is the winter energy payment fit for purpose when, since it was introduced, electricity prices have surged 28 percent while the winter energy payment hasn’t increased a cent and a very high number of people got declined last winter for power bill assistance?
statement: It’s been traversed in this House on multiple occasions. If you look at the contributing factors to energy costs, that member might want to look in the mirror.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on paediatric palliative care. He names the Budget 2026 announcement of a nationally consistent specialist service with teams in both islands — the question is answered directly and completely.
question: What recent announcements has he made about improving specialist paediatric palliative care support for children and families across New Zealand?
statement: Today, the Government has announced that through Budget 2026 we will establish a nationally consistent specialist paediatric palliative care service, helping ensure seriously ill children and their families can access compassionate specialist support closer to home. For families facing the unimaginable reality of caring for a child with a life-limiting illness, knowing the right care and support will be there can make an enormous difference. This initiative establishes dedicated specialist teams in both the North and South Islands, helping more children receive care in the comfort of their homes and communities, surrounded by the people they love most. Through Budget 2026, we’re investing in the services that matter most to families, building a health system that delivers dignity, compassion, and support during life’s hardest moments.

explanation: Asked why this has been a priority. He gives reasons: the burden on families caring for a seriously ill child, no parent should be alone, more time at home. Whether the reasoning persuades is a Rigor matter; the "why" is squarely addressed.
question: Why has improving special specialist paediatric palliative care been a priority for the Government?
statement: Ensuring children have access to nationally consistent specialist paediatric palliative care services is critically important to not only the Government but also to the many families who, unfortunately, face these circumstances. That is why, today, we’ve prioritised this initiative, because no parent should ever feel alone while caring for a seriously ill child. Families going through these circumstances are carrying an immense emotional burden, often while navigating complex medical needs and long hospital stays. This investment is about wrapping greater support around those families and reducing the emotional, physical, and financial strain they face. It means more children can spend precious time at home creating memories with their families rather than away from loved ones in hospital. This is exactly the kind of compassionate healthcare New Zealanders expect and deserve.

explanation: Asked what the new service will provide. He enumerates the staffing, the training of local providers, national coordination and a registrar training position — a direct, complete response to what was asked.
question: What will the new specialist paediatric palliative care service provide?
statement: The new service will include specialist paediatric palliative care physicians, clinical nurse specialists, nurse practitioners, social workers, and clinical psychologists working together to support children and their families. Importantly, these teams will also support and train local healthcare providers across New Zealand, helping ensure families receive consistent, high-quality care regardless of where they live. The investment also provides funding for national service coordination and one registrar training position each year to help secure the workforce needed for the future, so that this service can continue to grow over time.

explanation: Asked how the investment reflects broader Budget 2026 priorities. He answers the link explicitly — responsible fiscal management is what makes front-line investment like this possible. Heavy in framing, but the connection asked about is stated.
question: How does this investment reflect the Government’s broader priorities in Budget 2026?
