question: Does she stand by her statement, “Good legislation involves everybody, and bad legislation is usually when somebody goes off and does something by themselves … I’m never going to be arrogant enough to think that I have the answers to everything”; if so, why?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. In answer to the question, yes. That means that, for example, we need to avoid the type of rushed lawmaking that led to a three-day select committee and a 10-day—total—process for the last reform of the Arms Act by the previous Government. I also stand by another statement I made in the article that the member references: “I’ve got to make sure it’s not my personal views that go forward but rather collected views.” As part of my four-phase firearms reform work programme, New Zealanders will have four opportunities to submit their views to the select committee. Furthermore, stakeholders from both sides of the debate have had the chance to participate in focused consultation on both clubs and ranges reforms and the review of the firearms registry. This Government cares about the voices of New Zealanders, and we are doing the due diligence that should have been done back in 2019.

explanation: Asked why she attempted to remove Police's consultation comment from the Cabinet paper. She partly reaches it — 'I wondered why they were there in the first place, seeing as it was my paper' is an actual reason — but the bulk of the answer is about being told she couldn't remove them, the Police Association not being on her list, and praise for Police's fulsome responses. The core 'why did you try' is grazed, not squarely met.
question: Why did she attempt to remove Police’s comment “The stakeholder consultation is heavily weighted towards firearm licence holders and should include broader perspectives, including from groups like the Police Association.” from the Cabinet paper on firearms reforms?
statement: As I have actually publicly said, learning about the Cabinet process and how we go about utilising the papers, I was informed that I could not remove some of the comments, and I wondered why they were there in the first place, seeing as it was my paper. I’m very pleased with the advice that I got that I should keep it there and actually respond to those comments. I’d also point out that the Police Association were never on the original list of those that should have been spoken to that was given to me, and the list that the Labour Government used beforehand. I’m quite happy with the very fulsome response I’m getting from New Zealand Police and the fact that they are being so fulsome with their responses. They represent their entire workforce; not just their union.

explanation: Two-part question: does she agree with Cahill's quote, and is she concerned criminals will get A-category firearms without a registry. Part one is answered directly and unambiguously ('I do not agree with Mr Cahill') with a stated reason. Part two — the concern about firearms reaching criminals, plus the 'if not, why not' — is never touched. Half the question squarely answered, half dropped.
question: Does she agree with Police Association president, Chris Cahill, that “Without a registry, you buy as many firearms as you like. There’s no controls, whether you still have them or you pass them on to someone else.”, and is she concerned that without a firearms registry, A-category firearms like Alfa Carbine rifles will get into the hands of criminals who directly threaten front-line police officers’ safety; if not, why not?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, I do not agree with Mr Cahill, because legislation actually has restrictions around the legal transfer of firearms—part of the reason why we need to have people involved in the consultation that actually understand the legislation.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the Police advice that the reform should report back to at least two Ministers, and if not why not. The answer never says agree or disagree, never mentions the two-Ministers point, and pivots to her mandate to lead the reform and an attack on the previous Government. A narrow yes/no dodged completely.
question: Does she agree with Police advice—not Police Association advice; Police advice—on the Government’s firearms reform programme that “This should report back to at least two Ministers, as National Party supports the registry.”; if not, why not?
statement: I have been given the opportunity, on behalf of the Government, to lead this reform in the firearms space. What is really important is that we as a Government, as a whole, agree with the process as we move through the transparent process of four firearms reform phases. I’m really happy with the opportunity that I have been given to make New Zealand a safer place, because that side failed to do that post-2019.

explanation: Asked how she justifies attempting to remove Police's ability to comment given the Government's pro-police-powers rhetoric. She claims to have answered already, then restates gratitude for Police advice and satisfaction with the process. No justification is offered and the tension in the question is never engaged; it is a restatement, not an answer.
question: How does she justify attempting to remove the power of Police to comment in a Cabinet paper when she is part of a Government that has spoken so strongly about increasing the powers of police?
statement: I think I answered that where I had already said that I am very grateful for New Zealand Police giving me their thoughtful and fulsome advice, and I also like the opportunity that I have to be able to rebut or even comment back. I’m happy with the process. I’m happy with New Zealand Police being involved.

explanation: Asked what recent announcement the Government made about gene technology. Answered directly and completely: overturning the 30-year effective ban, new legislation, a dedicated regulator on the Australian model. The added rationale and briefing offer are surplus, not evasion.
question: What recent announcement has the Government made about gene technology?
statement: Last week, the Prime Minister and I announced that we are overturning the nearly 30-year effective ban on gene technology, for the benefit of New Zealand. We will establish new legislation and a dedicated regulator based on the Australian regime. The science has matured, other countries have embraced gene technology, and it has potential to treat cancers, increase agricultural production, lower emissions, adapt to a changing climate, and, ultimately, grow the economy. Gene tech is already being used safely in 29 other countries, including many of our trading partners such as Australia, China, Japan, the US, Canada, and many European countries. New Zealand needs to keep up, and we will be able to do so with this new regime. I’d also point out that I’ve had some good conversations with colleagues across the House on this move and I’m happy to provide briefings for MPs who are interested, and if they just get in touch with my office, we’ll arrange that for them.

explanation: Asked how gene technology can support higher productivity and growth. Answers the mechanism squarely — crop productivity work at Plant and Food, year-round fruit production, faster breeding, better returns for growers and cheaper produce — and notes the current constraint keeping it in the lab. Engages the question asked.
question: How can gene technology support higher productivity and growth?
statement: We’re committed to building a productive and growing economy, and I’m confident that gene technologies will contribute to that goal. In the primary sector, New Zealand scientists, including those at Plant and Food—where we launched the policy—have used gene technology to increase the productivity of crops, but only in laboratories. For example, researchers are looking at how to make fruit like apples and blueberries produce year-round, meaning faster breeding and, potentially, no off-season. Ultimately, this means better returns for growers and cheaper produce for consumers. However, under existing rules, virtually none of this research ever leaves the lab in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked how gene technology will support better health outcomes and lower emissions. Both halves are addressed: CAR T-cell cancer therapy for the health limb, agricultural emissions for the climate limb. The emissions half slides partway into a competitiveness argument rather than the mechanism, so it is a little short of complete.
question: How will gene technology support better health outcomes and lower greenhouse gas emissions?
statement: This policy will allow many more New Zealanders to access highly effective cancer treatments, including CAR T-cell therapy developed at Wellington’s Malaghan Institute, and this treatment has already successfully treated patients with cancer for the handful of those who were able to participate in its trial. This change in the gene technology regime means more New Zealanders will be able to access this advanced treatment and others like it. Gene technologies can also help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. New Zealand is an agricultural nation, which is why around half of our emissions come from agriculture. Our world-class farmers are at risk of being left behind their competitors if they don’t access advanced gene technologies just as our competitors are.

explanation: Asked how the new regime will adequately manage risk. Answered on point: a risk-based regime with stricter rules for higher-risk technologies, a regulator focused on human health and the environment, MPI enforcement, technical and Māori advisory groups, public consultation and select committee. Directly responsive.
question: How will this new regime adequately manage risk?
statement: Gene technologies have moved significantly since the current legislation passed nearly 30 years ago, and I want to assure New Zealanders and this House that risk management will be at the forefront of the new regime. The regulator will focus on risks to human health and to the environment. The regime will be risk-based, which means technologies with greater unknowns or higher risks will be subject to the most stringent rules. The regime includes public consultation, and the Ministry for Primary Industries will be responsible for enforcement. A technical advisory group will support the regulator, and a Māori advisory group will consider implications for Māori. I expect this new legislation will be in the House by the end of this year. It will have a full select committee process, and I encourage members of this House and the public to engage. I intend the new regulator to be in place by the end of 2025. I’m very confident that this regime will get New Zealand up to speed with the rest of the world.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made in her workplace relations and safety portfolio. She enumerates them — income threshold for unjustified dismissal grievances, removal of remedies where the employee contributed, partial-strike wage deductions, hours-based annual leave accrual, the 2025 minimum wage. A complete, direct answer.
question: What recent announcements has she made in her workplace relations and safety portfolio?
statement: This coalition Government has been working hard in the lead-up to Christmas and I’m pleased to share it has been a busy month for my workplace relations and safety portfolio. Over the past month, I’ve announced a high income threshold for unjustified dismissal personal grievances, the removal of remedies for personal grievances in cases where the employee contributed to the grievance, the reintroduction of wage deductions for partial strikes, I’ve asked my officials to develop an hours-based accrual system for annual leave, and today I announced the new minimum wage rate for 2025 in order to give businesses certainty leading into the new year. Together, these changes will help rebalance the employment relations landscape. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked how the announced changes will affect employers. She works through the effects on employers: relief from vexatious personal grievances and their costs and reputational harm, welcome for partial-strike deductions in customer-facing industries, and support for the simpler holidays approach. Stays on the question throughout.
question: How will your announced changes affect employers?
statement: I’ve met a lot of employers up and down the country, and I know that these changes will be welcomed by many. Dealing with vexatious personal grievances can be extremely stressful for employers, who can find themselves facing large and unanticipated costs. An employer’s own wellbeing and reputation can be harmed throughout the grievance process, yet for employers there is no recourse. Reintroducing wage deductions for partial strikes will be particularly welcomed by employers with workers in customer-serving industries, where it is often the public that suffer as a consequence of partial strikes. And employers have welcomed the decision I’ve made to scrap the previous Government’s approach to fixing the Holidays Act and pursue a much simpler and more workable path of an hours-based accrual to annual leave.

explanation: Asked how the changes will affect workers. She does assert worker-side effects — improved workplace culture and morale from the personal grievance changes — so the question is engaged, but most of the answer is framing about hard-working Kiwis and the reply is cut off before the illustration lands. It reaches the question only partly.
question: So how will your announced changes affect workers?
statement: These changes recognise and reward the hard-working, aspirational Kiwis out there who are doing their best to make a good living for themselves and the people they care about. The changes to personal grievances will improve workplace culture and morale. Many workers will be able to recall a time they’ve had to work with a difficult—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered with an unambiguous 'Yes' before moving to the quarterly action plan. The follow-on material is padding, but the question itself was answered outright.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our work to complete our latest quarterly action plan. In the last three months, we’ve completed 42 actions designed to lift New Zealand’s economic performance, restore law and order, and improve the public services that all of us rely upon. This quarter, that included a massive package of changes to the Resource Management Act designed to unlock growth and investment by slashing red tape for farmers and the primary sector, unlocking regionally and nationally significant projects through fast track—it’s still not too late for the other side to support it—and introducing fresh changes designed to unleash investment, housing, energy infrastructure, and farmers. This Government is working hard to make sure that we deliver for New Zealanders, and I want to say thank you to all my hard-working Ministers and the officials, who have been up all day and night making sure we unleash fast track on New Zealand. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked which of two named people is correct about the quarterly action plan, and why Kiwis should not think the plans are 'crap'. The response praises the Deputy Prime Minister and notes he completed his two quarter-four actions — a glancing touch on the plan, but it never says who is correct nor addresses the contradiction, which was the core of the question.
question: So who is correct, then: the Prime Minister, who says that his whole Government is relentlessly focused on his quarterly action plan, or his Deputy Prime Minister, who says—and I quote—“I don’t have this sort of dashboard crap that I see other people perform on and a 50-point plan, or a 100-point plan, or a quarter-year plan”, and if Winston Peters thinks that his plans are crap, why should Kiwis think otherwise?
statement: Well, I just want to say what a fantastic Deputy Prime Minister we have, because not only did he complete his two actions in the quarter four action plan—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked why director fees rose 39–104% while the minimum wage rose below inflation. The response takes only 'the last issue' — the minimum wage — and offers the 1.5 percent figure as a 'balance'; the director-fee half, which carried the force of the question, is not reached at all.
question: Why has his Government agreed to increase the fees paid to directors of Government companies by between 39 percent and 104 percent while increasing the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation?
statement: Well, if I take the last issue first, we have found a balance with a 1.5 percent increase to the minimum wage—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked why minimum wage workers take a real-terms cut while directors get a 100 percent rise. Both halves are engaged: the minimum wage side (1.5 percent plus tax relief, FamilyBoost, Working for Families) and the director side (below market rates, to attract good people for high-quality governance). It is a reason for the disparity, not a deflection; the jab at the questioner is a separate attribute and does not lower the score.
question: Why is it that under his Government, minimum wage workers have to tighten their belts with a real-terms pay cut while company directors get a 100 percent pay rise?
statement: As I said, we’ve talked about minimum wage workers. There’s a 1.5 percent increase, along with income tax relief, along with FamilyBoost, along with Working for Families credits. With respect to professional directors that we’re asking to run some of our largest entities, they are not paid market rates, they won’t still be, but it’s actually acknowledging that we want to attract good people to make sure we have high-quality governance. I’m sure the member would understand that, given the variety of messes that he left behind in the last Government. Good governance matters to deliver—to deliver—and get outcomes. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why minimum wage earners face a real-terms pay cut while Transpower directors get a 56 percent rise. The response contests the premise — wages rising faster than prices for four quarters — which is a form of engagement with the first half, but then slides into comparison with the previous administration and rate cuts, and the Transpower directors are never mentioned.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Why are minimum wage earners having their pay cut in real terms, despite the cost of living crisis, while their power bills keep going up and the directors of Transpower, who are increasing the charges all New Zealand consumers face, get a pay increase of over 56 percent?
statement: Well, I’d just point to that member and say that this is a Government that has, for four quarters in a row, seen wages rise faster than prices—total wages, right? So, if you think about that, under the previous administration, there were 13 quarters in a row where prices were greater than inflation. So real wages are increasing under this Government in our first 12 months. That’s fantastic. You’re in a situation where you see three rate cuts versus 12 rate rises—

explanation: Asked why he agreed to a 90 percent pay increase for KiwiRail directors given the Interislander. The reply openly declines to discuss specifics of KiwiRail board decisions — a plain refusal, which is not a dodge — and then gives the general reason for the increases (improving governance, attracting good people, short of full market rates). It addresses the 'why' at the class level while explicitly withholding the KiwiRail particulars.
question: If KiwiRail did such a lousy job of managing the Interislander, why has he agreed to giving its directors a 90 percent pay increase while minimum wage workers go backwards?
statement: Well, again, I won’t get into the specifics of decisions of the board of KiwiRail around CEO pay, but what I will say is that we are determined to improve the quality of governance of our Government entities across New Zealand. It’s really important. So all we’re doing is we’re not going to full market rates; we’re just finding a pathway to make sure that we can actually attract good people to come on and do those very important roles.

explanation: Asked to adjudicate between two colleagues on whether the ferries have been 'delivered'. He endorses the Willis option in concrete terms (two rail-compatible ferries, 2029) but then leaves the door open to the new Rail Minister improving on it, so he signals a side without ever squarely saying who is correct.
question: Who’s correct: Nicola Willis, who claims she has “delivered” new interisland ferries, despite not knowing who will build them, how much they’ll cost, or who’s going to pay for them; or Winston Peters, who said, “There are far more viable propositions that are yet to be considered.”?
statement: Well, I am very proud of the value-for-money option that Nicola Willis has delivered, because it is a safe, reliable, resilient service that will be in operation in 2029: two rail-compatible ferries. But we have a new Minister for Rail and, given we’ve got time to make the ultimate procurement decision, if he can improve on that: good luck.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made on Government finances. The response names them directly — the Budget Policy Statement and Treasury's half-year update — and characterises their content. Directly and completely answered.
question: What recent announcements has she made on Government finances?
statement: Earlier today, I released the Budget Policy Statement. At the same time, Treasury released its half-year update, which contains the latest set of forecasts. They tell a positive story about growth returning to the New Zealand economy, and they also highlight some challenges for the Government’s books. Forecast provisions have made it more difficult to address the situation we inherited, a rapid increase in debt over the past five years, and an extended period of Budget deficits, but we are firmly committed to turning that around, and the books show we are headed in the right direction.

explanation: Asked what the Budget Policy Statement says about Budget 2025. The response enumerates the four priorities it sets. Squarely on the question.
question: What does the Budget Policy Statement say about Budget 2025?
statement: The Budget Policy Statement sets four priorities for Budget 2025: (1) lifting economic growth through measures to address New Zealand’s long-term productivity challenges; (2) implementing a social investment approach to drive better results from the Government’s investment in social services and thereby improve life outcomes for people with high needs; (3) keeping tight control of Government spending while funding a limited number of high-priority Government policy commitments and cost pressures that cannot be met from reprioritisation; and (4) developing a sustainable pipeline of long-term infrastructure investment.

explanation: Asked why improving productivity is so important. The response gives the reason — growth must come from productivity rather than working more — and quantifies the fiscal payoff. The list of reform areas is padding, but the 'why' is reached.
question: Why is improving productivity so important?
statement: The Government’s focus is not just on the fiscals; we are also focused resolutely on growth, and that must come from productivity improvements, not just from working more. The Government has a busy programme but is collectively aimed at improving productivity, from resource management reforms to overseas investment, to gene technology, to fast-track consenting, to labour market regulation, to education, to infrastructure, and so on, and that has a loop back to the fiscals. Additional growth of even a quarter of a percent of nominal GDP each year would boost tax revenue by $2 billion a year by the end of the forecast period. That’s a win-win.

explanation: Asked what alternative advice she has received on fiscal strategy. She describes it: a letter from 15 economists urging more spending, and advice that the surplus is moot and more debt could be taken on. The partisan framing of who gave the advice is a Focus/Civility matter; the question itself is answered.
question: What alternative advice has she received about fiscal strategy?
statement: I receive a lot of advice about fiscal strategy, much of it unsolicited. For example, I recently received a letter from 15 economists telling me to increase current and future Government spending. I noticed that several people who signed this letter telling me to spend more were advisers to the previous Minister of Finance, and two are currently on the Labour Party policy council. I wasn’t surprised. I’ve also heard advice from a person saying that the Budget surplus is a moot point and that a future Government that they could be finance Minister in would consider taking on more debt. This actually did surprise me, because it came from Barbara Edmonds.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' outright; the announcement that follows is volunteered detail, not a substitute for the answer.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially today’s announcement that we are taking further actions to keep Kiwis safe in emergency departments (EDs) this summer. If you visit, or work in, an ED, you deserve to feel safe. And over the holiday period, EDs can be particularly busy and stressful places. That’s why we’re building on last year’s successful programme and ensuring more support is available to keep Kiwis safe: 20 hospitals will receive additional funding for security, and further funding will be available if there is a major incident or event that requires a greater security presence. Our Government’s working hard at improving public services that all Kiwis can rely on, whether that’s in the community or in an emergency department.

explanation: Asked a binary question — will benefit sanctions put more or less kai on the table for hungry tamariki. The response praises the traffic light system and restates its obligations, never engaging with the effect on food for children either way.
question: Will his Government’s benefit sanctions help to put more kai on the table or less kai on the table this Christmas for the thousands of hungry tamariki in Aotearoa?
statement: Well, I’m very proud of the traffic light system that our great Minister from the Ministry of Social Development has implemented, because what it means is a pretty simple requirement: show up and talk to your case manager, get a resume, and show up to your job interviews.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with CPAG that his decision will push 20,000 more children into poverty. He never says whether he agrees, and never touches the landlord decision; he offers a competing figure (17,000 out of poverty under Budget '24) plus a comparison to Labour. Offering rival numbers on the same topic is a partial engagement — it implicitly disputes the projection — but the question asked was squarely dodged.
question: Does he agree with the Child Poverty Action Group that his decision to put the wellbeing of landlords over the wellbeing of tamariki will put 20,000 more children into poverty by the time his term is up?
statement: What I’m proud about is under Budget ‘24, with all the cost of living measures that this Government delivered for low and middle income New Zealanders, 17,000 children are going to be taken out of poverty—compared to the last year of the Labour Government, where 23,000 more children were put in poverty.

explanation: Asked what he says to a specific child. He does say something addressed to the situation — acknowledging it is 'a pretty tough time' across New Zealand — which is a thin but real response to 'what do you say'. He then pivots to economic-management talking points rather than staying with the question. Partial.
question: What does he say to Logan, a 7-year-old tamaiti who wrote to Santa asking for a burger to share with his mum for Christmas?
statement: I acknowledge that across New Zealand, it’s a pretty tough time. That’s what happens when you don’t run an economy well. If you care about low and middle income New Zealanders, you run the books well. You don’t spend more, tax more, borrow more, and deliver less.

explanation: 'Does she stand by all her statements and actions?' — 'In context, yes.' A direct yes with a light qualifier, then a volunteered specific. Complete answer; the hedge is small enough to cost little.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: In context, yes. I particularly stand by my statement to the effect that now more than ever is a time for disciplined Government spending and a focus on driving economic growth.

explanation: A narrow factual question — was 1994 the last time debt was this high? Neither confirmed nor denied. The response pivots entirely to the previous Government's $100 billion. A specific factual question left untouched is the worst case for this attribute.
question: Isn’t it the case that the last time net core Crown debt was this high, which will peak at 46.5 percent of GDP, was in 1994?
statement: It is also the case that in the past five years, the last Labour Government added more than $100 billion to New Zealand’s debt. And we, as a Government, are now saddled with the task of bending that debt curve back—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked to confirm a specific figure (3.5 percentage points above Budget forecast). She concedes the direction — forecast revisions 'will have an effect on debt' — but never confirms or denies the number, then moves to fiscal discipline and a jab at the questioner. Engages the topic, avoids the core.
question: Isn’t it the case that net core Crown debt will now be 3.5 percentage points higher than what was forecast in her Budget?
statement: As I have set out today in the Budget Policy Statement, it is the case that forecast revisions to New Zealand’s GDP trajectory will have an effect on debt. That is why it is so important that the Government maintain a disciplined fiscal position with lower operating allowances than have been the case in recent years when the last Government blew spending out as a proportion of GDP, leaving our economy in a very challenged state. If that member wants to join those on this side of the House in the pursuit of fiscal discipline, I can only welcome it.

explanation: Asked to confirm $58.7 billion more debt peaking at $235 billion. She explains at length why forecasts were revised and affirms 'this does have an effect on debt', which addresses the mechanism but not the figures put to her. The length is not itself a fault (that is Specificity's business) — the fault is that the specific claim is never confirmed or denied.
question: Isn’t it the case that there will be $58.7 billion more debt, peaking at $235 billion, than what was forecast in her Budget only six months ago?
statement: As I have laid out today in the Budget Policy Statement and as Treasury has laid out in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, downward revisions to the fiscal forecasts have had an effect in two ways. One, the current recession is estimated to have started earlier and to be more protracted than had previously been forecast. And, two, there has been a downward revision to productivity forecasts. This does have an effect on debt. Now, this Government believes there is a place for debt, for borrowing for long-term infrastructure assets. We also believe it is very important to get debt down to a trajectory under 40 percent of GDP. Again, I note that if the member wishes to join us in that pursuit, that would be novel for her and her party—

explanation: 'Will she take responsibility...?' gets a legible answer: no for the cause, yes for the fix. Marked down from high because she reframes the object of responsibility — from the downgraded growth forecast to 'the mistakes of the last Government' — so the yes/no lands on an adjacent question. Still substantially engaged, not a pivot to talking points.
question: Will she take responsibility for the growth forecast being revised downwards since her Budget and predicted to be $20 billion smaller in 2028?
statement: I won’t take responsibility for the mistakes of the last Government, but I will take responsibility for fixing it.

explanation: 'Does she plan on shifting any other goalposts?' — 'I reject the characterisations of the member's question.' Blunt and candid, and it implicitly denies the premise, so it is not pure evasion. But it stops short of answering whether she plans further redefinitions. Unlike 'No, I won't release that advice', a premise rejection leaves the actual question open.
question: Does she plan on shifting any other goalposts to help reach her targets, like she has done with the definition of “OBEGAL” and with child poverty targets?
statement: I reject the characterisations of the member’s question.

explanation: 'Does he support all the statements and actions of his Government?' — 'Yes.' One word, complete, no qualification.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether reducing wealth inequality is his Government's job. He answers about incomes, growth and cost of living — related territory, but he never says whether inequality is the Government's job. Standard pivot to talking points.
question: Does the Prime Minister think that it is the job of his Government to decrease wealth inequality?
statement: Our Government’s working incredibly hard to raise incomes, to provide economic growth, and to lower the cost of living.

explanation: Asked to name one policy; he names several (tax adjustment, Working for Families, FamilyBoost). The question was engaged head-on. Whether those policies actually reduce inequality is a Veracity/Rigor question and must not pull this score down.
question: Can the Prime Minister name one—just one—Government policy that will decrease inequality in this country?
statement: We have adjusted tax for low and middle income working New Zealanders. We have increased the Working for Families credits. We have also provided FamilyBoost for people dealing with expensive childcare. We have provided inflation, interest rate, rent stability, and also tax relief for low and middle income working New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made about councils getting back to basics. He names the announcement made yesterday and its content: removing the four well-beings, benchmarking council performance. Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: What recent announcements has he made about getting councils back to basics?
statement: Yesterday, the Prime Minister and I announced reforms to get councils back to basics to reduce pressure on rates, deliver core services, and modernise outdated rules to drive efficiency and cost savings. These measures include removing the four “well-beings” from the Local Government Act, benchmarking council performance to hold them accountable. Ratepayers deserve councils that focus on the basics, like fixing pipes, filling potholes, and delivering reliable services, rather than expensive nice-to-haves.

explanation: Asked WHY the well-beings are being removed. He gives a reason: evidence that rates rose ~2 percent more per year under them, plus the signalling rationale. Whether that evidence claim is true is Veracity, not this; as a response to 'why', it lands squarely.
question: Why is the Government removing the four “well-beings” from the Local Government Act?
statement: The evidence shows that when the four “well-beings” were in legislation, rates increased approximately 2 percent more per year. Removing them sends a clear signal that councils must prioritise roads, rubbish, and reliable infrastructure. Ratepayers simply cannot afford excessive spending on nice-to-have projects or duplication of roles with central government. By focusing on core responsibilities, councils will reduce unnecessary financial burdens on their communities.

explanation: Asked HOW benchmarking improves accountability. He supplies the mechanism: DIA publishes an annual performance report on named metrics, giving ratepayers information to judge their council. That is the causal chain the question requested.
question: How will benchmarking improve council accountability?
statement: Benchmarking is a crucial tool for improving transparency and accountability. The Department of Internal Affairs will publish an annual report on councils’ performance, including key metrics such as rates, council debt, capital expenditure, balanced budgets, and road conditions. By providing ratepayers with clear information, these reports will empower communities to assess how well their councils are managing resources and delivering services in their local communities.

explanation: Asked WHEN the first benchmarking report will be released. Answer: middle of 2025, ahead of the October local elections. A date was requested and a date was given.
question: When will the first benchmarking report on local councils be released?
statement: Good news: the first benchmarking report on local councils will be released in the middle of 2025, ahead of the 2025 local elections. This report will give hard-working ratepayers and residents across the country clear information about their council’s financial performance prior to going to the polls in October 2025.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all the statements and actions of his Government. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, and it completely resolves the question — the same shape as the worked example scoring 1.0.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked to confirm that no environmental protection remains for covenants, outstanding landscapes or water conservation orders under the Fast-track Bill. He rejects the characterisation — a partial engagement, since it implicitly denies the premise — but never says what protection does or does not remain, then moves to renewables, houses and roads. The specific core is left untouched.
question: Can the Prime Minister confirm that no level of environmental protection will remain for public conservation covenants, outstanding natural landscapes, or water conservation orders under the Fast-track Approvals Bill?
statement: Well, that’s not an accurate—I reject the characterisation of that question. But what I’d say to you is that I am incredibly proud of the fast-track legislation, and I really hope it’s not too late for the Green Party to get on board, because we really do want to have a 30 percent increase in renewable energy projects across this country, we do really want to build 55,000 more houses, and we want to build up 180 kilometres of new roads.

explanation: Asked what he would say to a public concerned that fast-track applicants failed to disclose required compliance and enforcement history. He declines to discuss individual projects and points to the expert panel, which is a thin but genuine response to a concerned public, then pivots to build times and costs. The disclosure failure itself is never addressed.
question: What would he say to the public concerned that some of the 149 project applications that his Cabinet approved under the fast-track process were required to disclose their track record of prior compliance and enforcement actions against them, and didn’t?
statement: Again, I’m not getting into the details of individual projects; there’s an expert panel process that will manage that. But what I would say to that member is that the New Zealand public are actually sick of how long it takes to get things built in this country. There is no justification to take 19 months to build a three- to four-bedroom home that’s 50 percent more expensive than the same home in Australia.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet considered the significance test and, if so, the rationale for including non-responsive applications. He asserts the projects ARE of national and regional significance, which grazes the question, but does not say whether Cabinet considered it or give any rationale. Neither limb is answered.
question: Did Cabinet consider whether the 149 applications contributed to regionally and nationally significant infrastructure, and, if so, what was the rationale for including projects that didn’t even bother answering how they supported regional or nationally significant infrastructure?
statement: Again, we have a process where projects will go through an expert panel. But what I’d say is these are projects of national and regional significance, and we make no apologies for making sure that we prioritise economic growth after three years of being in a recession, thanks to a Labour-Greens Government.

explanation: Asked whether he will commit to reconsidering projects if the Auditor-General finds the conflicts process was mishandled. 'A hypothetical question — I'm not answering it' is transparent and contains no talking-point pivot, which keeps it well clear of the floor. But it is a declared refusal to answer rather than an answer: unlike 'No, I won't release that advice', it does not resolve whether the commitment is given. Mid-range.
question: Will he commit to reconsidering projects included in the Fast-track Approvals Bill if the Auditor-General inquiry into Cabinet’s handling of conflicts of interest finds the process was not managed appropriately?
statement: A hypothetical question—I’m not answering it.

explanation: Asked where localism fits when councils receive no acknowledgement of their opposition and their plans lose weight. He offers one channel — councils can contribute through the expert panels — which partly addresses where local input sits, then turns to building faster and economic growth. The unanswered-councils grievance and the loss of plan weight go unaddressed.
question: Where does localism fit, when his Government won’t give local councils the decency of a response in even acknowledging their opposition to the fast-track projects in their city, district, or region, when even their democratic plans will soon have no weight in protecting their communities and their environment?
statement: There is a way, through the expert panels, for them to make a contribution. But, again, this is a Government that is making no apologies for getting things built quicker, prioritising economic growth, and making sure we get things done. That is what this country needs and I can tell you people are excited about fast track coming to a town near them shortly.

explanation: Two limbs: does he stand by the 'rail-enabled is a no-brainer' statement, and will he guarantee rail-enabled ferries. The second is answered squarely and honestly — nothing ruled in or out, no pledge before the work is done, i.e. no guarantee. The first is never addressed; he neither affirms nor disowns the earlier statement. The opening grumble about question order and the closing jab at Labour are Civility and Focus matters and did not move this score.
question: Does he stand by his statement regarding any new Cook Strait ferries that “Rail-enabled ferries is part of our considerations, yes, and that is a no-brainer”; if so, will he guarantee that the new ferries will be rail-enabled?
statement: Can I say to that member: I’d have thought this is far more important to be question No. 12 today, but we get on with the answer. Nothing has been ruled in or out. We are looking at all the options—the costs and benefits, and the pluses and minuses—and we’ll make decisions based on the best interests of our country. We are not going to make silly pledges before the work is done, and we can guarantee the member that we are not going to be asleep at the wheel like his colleagues were for the last three years.

explanation: Asked (a) whether the Government was advised the Picton wharf work had to start this year and (b) what wharf/linkspan upgrades mean for the Aratere. Neither is answered: he asserts the port needs rebuilding "regardless" and that plans will be looked at. The advice question is never confirmed or denied and the Aratere impact is not touched.
question: Was the Government advised that work on a new Picton wharf needed to begin this year, and, if so, what impact will any wharf and linkspan upgrades in Picton have on the ongoing operation of the rail-enabled Aratere ferry?
statement: Well, it’s not a secret to anyone apart from that side of the House that the port of Picton needs to be rebuilt in the next few years regardless, and we’re going to be looking at those plans as we find out from the experts what it might entail.

explanation: Asked whether the Government was advised the rail-enabled Aratere would need retiring in 2025. He engages: yes, that retirement was a scenario put by the ministerial advisory group, but Cabinet has taken no decision. The advice question is substantively addressed even though the concession is oblique and he shifts to the decision status.
question: Was the Government advised that the rail-enabled Aratere would need to be retired in 2025?
statement: Reality is that that was a scenario painted by the now disbanded ministerial advisory group, and the reality is that the decisions have not been taken by the Cabinet on that matter.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee the Aratere runs until 2029. He answers a different question — what he *can* guarantee (meetings with KiwiRail and MUNZ, consultation, future transparency). The requested guarantee is neither given nor explicitly refused; a plain "no, I can't guarantee that" would have scored high, but he never reaches the point.
question: Can he then guarantee that the Interislander’s sole rail-enabled ferry, the Aratere, will be scheduled to continue operations until 2029?
statement: What I can guarantee is that, having had a meeting early this morning with KiwiRail and MUNZ—that’s the Maritime Union—at midday, and we’re going to consult with everybody, and we’re going to find out exactly what’s going on and what went wrong. And then we’ll come to this House and declare transparently—

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question: was the Government advised the cheapest new ferries were $282 million each. He does not engage the advice or the figure at all, pivoting to the $4 billion iReX cost and blaming the questioner's side, then a vague promise to come in cheaper. A specific question squarely dodged via attack.
question: Was the Government advised that the cheapest and most basic option for new Cook Strait ferries came in at $282 million each, which for two ferries would add up to more than the rail-enabled ferries contracted under iReX?
statement: What’s amazing about that question is this: that we were talking about two ferries and we ended up with $4 billion on the account and no one over there is being responsible. We’ll make one promise over here: we’ll come in far, far, far less than that.

explanation: Asked why Willis missed the advisory group's end-of-July decision deadline. He does address it by rejecting the premise — advisory groups don't set deadlines for this Government, Cabinet does — which is a real, if partial, response to the "why". He then slides into sympathy for her "nightmare" without saying why the decision was not made by that date.
question: Why did Nicola Willis miss the deadline for making a decision on ferries at the end of July this year, as recommended by her ministerial advisory group?
statement: Actually, ministerial advisory groups don’t set deadlines for this Government. We’re not run by the bureaucracy; we run the thing from Cabinet. And the Minister that you’re talking about, the finance Minister, had a nightmare on her hands and I’m deeply sympathetic with her predicament.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made in the workplace relations and safety portfolio. She lists them: dismissal income threshold, personal grievance remedies, partial-strike wage deductions, hours-based leave accrual, the 2025 minimum wage. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has she made in her workplace relations and safety portfolio?
statement: This coalition Government has been working hard in the lead-up to Christmas and I’m pleased to share it has been a busy month for my workplace relations and safety portfolio. Over the past month, I’ve announced a high income threshold for unjustified dismissal personal grievances, the removal of remedies for personal grievances in cases where the employee contributed to the grievance, the reintroduction of wage deductions for partial strikes, I’ve asked my officials to develop an hours-based accrual system for annual leave, and today I announced the new minimum wage rate for 2025 in order to give businesses certainty leading into the new year. Together, these changes will help rebalance the employment relations landscape. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked how the announced changes will affect employers. She answers on employers throughout — grievance stress and costs, reputational harm, partial-strike deductions welcomed in customer-facing industries, the Holidays Act change. It is one-sided advocacy, but that is a different attribute; the question asked is engaged.
question: How will your announced changes affect employers?
statement: I’ve met a lot of employers up and down the country, and I know that these changes will be welcomed by many. Dealing with vexatious personal grievances can be extremely stressful for employers, who can find themselves facing large and unanticipated costs. An employer’s own wellbeing and reputation can be harmed throughout the grievance process, yet for employers there is no recourse. Reintroducing wage deductions for partial strikes will be particularly welcomed by employers with workers in customer-serving industries, where it is often the public that suffer as a consequence of partial strikes. And employers have welcomed the decision I’ve made to scrap the previous Government’s approach to fixing the Holidays Act and pursue a much simpler and more workable path of an hours-based accrual to annual leave.

explanation: Asked how the changes will affect workers. She stays on the asked subject — workers — claiming recognition/reward and improved culture and morale, but reaches only theme-level assertion before being cut off. It gestures at the effect on workers without landing on any, so partial engagement.
question: So how will your announced changes affect workers?
statement: These changes recognise and reward the hard-working, aspirational Kiwis out there who are doing their best to make a good living for themselves and the people they care about. The changes to personal grievances will improve workplace culture and morale. Many workers will be able to recall a time they’ve had to work with a difficult—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. He says "Yes" and then elaborates. One word was enough; the question is answered completely.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our work to complete our latest quarterly action plan. In the last three months, we’ve completed 42 actions designed to lift New Zealand’s economic performance, restore law and order, and improve the public services that all of us rely upon. This quarter, that included a massive package of changes to the Resource Management Act designed to unlock growth and investment by slashing red tape for farmers and the primary sector, unlocking regionally and nationally significant projects through fast track—it’s still not too late for the other side to support it—and introducing fresh changes designed to unleash investment, housing, energy infrastructure, and farmers. This Government is working hard to make sure that we deliver for New Zealanders, and I want to say thank you to all my hard-working Ministers and the officials, who have been up all day and night making sure we unleash fast track on New Zealand. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked which of two contradictory positions is correct — the PM's focus on the quarterly action plan or the Deputy PM's dismissal of such plans — and why Kiwis should back plans Peters calls "crap". He praises the Deputy PM and notes he completed his two actions, which glances at the tension but never picks a side or engages the contradiction.
question: So who is correct, then: the Prime Minister, who says that his whole Government is relentlessly focused on his quarterly action plan, or his Deputy Prime Minister, who says—and I quote—“I don’t have this sort of dashboard crap that I see other people perform on and a 50-point plan, or a 100-point plan, or a quarter-year plan”, and if Winston Peters thinks that his plans are crap, why should Kiwis think otherwise?
statement: Well, I just want to say what a fantastic Deputy Prime Minister we have, because not only did he complete his two actions in the quarter four action plan—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked why director fees rose 39–104% while the minimum wage rose below inflation. He takes only the second half — "a balance with a 1.5 percent increase" — before being cut off, and never touches the director fees or the comparison that was the point of the question. Partial engagement with one limb only.
question: Why has his Government agreed to increase the fees paid to directors of Government companies by between 39 percent and 104 percent while increasing the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation?
statement: Well, if I take the last issue first, we have found a balance with a 1.5 percent increase to the minimum wage—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked why minimum wage workers take a real-terms cut while directors get a large rise. He addresses both limbs: the 1.5% plus tax relief, FamilyBoost and Working for Families on one side, and directors being below market rates and needed for governance quality on the other. He supplies a reason for the contrast rather than dodging; the jab at the questioner is a civility matter, not a dodge.
question: Why is it that under his Government, minimum wage workers have to tighten their belts with a real-terms pay cut while company directors get a 100 percent pay rise?
statement: As I said, we’ve talked about minimum wage workers. There’s a 1.5 percent increase, along with income tax relief, along with FamilyBoost, along with Working for Families credits. With respect to professional directors that we’re asking to run some of our largest entities, they are not paid market rates, they won’t still be, but it’s actually acknowledging that we want to attract good people to make sure we have high-quality governance. I’m sure the member would understand that, given the variety of messes that he left behind in the last Government. Good governance matters to deliver—to deliver—and get outcomes. [Interruption]

explanation: Two-part question: why real wages are falling for minimum wage earners, and why Transpower directors got a 56% rise. Luxon engages the first part only by contesting its premise (four quarters of real wage growth), which is a form of answering, but the Transpower director pay — the sharp end of the question — is never touched, and he drifts to rate cuts. Partial engagement with the core avoided.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Why are minimum wage earners having their pay cut in real terms, despite the cost of living crisis, while their power bills keep going up and the directors of Transpower, who are increasing the charges all New Zealand consumers face, get a pay increase of over 56 percent?
statement: Well, I’d just point to that member and say that this is a Government that has, for four quarters in a row, seen wages rise faster than prices—total wages, right? So, if you think about that, under the previous administration, there were 13 quarters in a row where prices were greater than inflation. So real wages are increasing under this Government in our first 12 months. That’s fantastic. You’re in a situation where you see three rate cuts versus 12 rate rises—

explanation: Asked why he agreed to a 90% director pay rise. He explicitly declines the specifics ('I won't get into the specifics of decisions of the board of KiwiRail'), which is itself a forthright refusal, and then offers a general rationale — attracting good people to governance roles, below full market rates. That gestures at 'why' without addressing this decision or the contrast drawn. Half answered.
question: If KiwiRail did such a lousy job of managing the Interislander, why has he agreed to giving its directors a 90 percent pay increase while minimum wage workers go backwards?
statement: Well, again, I won’t get into the specifics of decisions of the board of KiwiRail around CEO pay, but what I will say is that we are determined to improve the quality of governance of our Government entities across New Zealand. It’s really important. So all we’re doing is we’re not going to full market rates; we’re just finding a pathway to make sure that we can actually attract good people to come on and do those very important roles.

explanation: Asked to adjudicate between Willis and Peters. He does not name either as correct, but he squarely endorses the option Willis delivered while leaving the door open to the new Rail Minister improving on it — effectively picking a side and acknowledging the tension. It reaches the question without landing on it cleanly.
question: Who’s correct: Nicola Willis, who claims she has “delivered” new interisland ferries, despite not knowing who will build them, how much they’ll cost, or who’s going to pay for them; or Winston Peters, who said, “There are far more viable propositions that are yet to be considered.”?
statement: Well, I am very proud of the value-for-money option that Nicola Willis has delivered, because it is a safe, reliable, resilient service that will be in operation in 2029: two rail-compatible ferries. But we have a new Minister for Rail and, given we’ve got time to make the ultimate procurement decision, if he can improve on that: good luck.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she made on Government finances; she names the Budget Policy Statement and Treasury's half-year update. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has she made on Government finances?
statement: Earlier today, I released the Budget Policy Statement. At the same time, Treasury released its half-year update, which contains the latest set of forecasts. They tell a positive story about growth returning to the New Zealand economy, and they also highlight some challenges for the Government’s books. Forecast provisions have made it more difficult to address the situation we inherited, a rapid increase in debt over the past five years, and an extended period of Budget deficits, but we are firmly committed to turning that around, and the books show we are headed in the right direction.

explanation: Asked what the Budget Policy Statement says about Budget 2025; she enumerates its four stated priorities. Exactly the question that was asked, fully answered.
question: What does the Budget Policy Statement say about Budget 2025?
statement: The Budget Policy Statement sets four priorities for Budget 2025: (1) lifting economic growth through measures to address New Zealand’s long-term productivity challenges; (2) implementing a social investment approach to drive better results from the Government’s investment in social services and thereby improve life outcomes for people with high needs; (3) keeping tight control of Government spending while funding a limited number of high-priority Government policy commitments and cost pressures that cannot be met from reprioritisation; and (4) developing a sustainable pipeline of long-term infrastructure investment.

explanation: Asked why improving productivity matters; she answers it — growth must come from productivity rather than working more, and quantifies the fiscal loop back ($2b a year in extra tax revenue). Squarely on the question.
question: Why is improving productivity so important?
statement: The Government’s focus is not just on the fiscals; we are also focused resolutely on growth, and that must come from productivity improvements, not just from working more. The Government has a busy programme but is collectively aimed at improving productivity, from resource management reforms to overseas investment, to gene technology, to fast-track consenting, to labour market regulation, to education, to infrastructure, and so on, and that has a loop back to the fiscals. Additional growth of even a quarter of a percent of nominal GDP each year would boost tax revenue by $2 billion a year by the end of the forecast period. That’s a win-win.

explanation: Asked what alternative fiscal-strategy advice she has received; she names the letter from 15 economists urging more spending and Edmonds' comments on debt. The partisan framing is a Focus/Civility matter, not a dodge — the question is answered.
question: What alternative advice has she received about fiscal strategy?
statement: I receive a lot of advice about fiscal strategy, much of it unsolicited. For example, I recently received a letter from 15 economists telling me to increase current and future Government spending. I noticed that several people who signed this letter telling me to spend more were advisers to the previous Minister of Finance, and two are currently on the Labour Party policy council. I wasn’t surprised. I’ve also heard advice from a person saying that the Budget surplus is a moot point and that a future Government that they could be finance Minister in would consider taking on more debt. This actually did surprise me, because it came from Barbara Edmonds.

explanation: A 'does he stand by' question answered 'Yes' at the outset. The ED security material that follows is unsolicited padding, but the question itself was answered directly and completely.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially today’s announcement that we are taking further actions to keep Kiwis safe in emergency departments (EDs) this summer. If you visit, or work in, an ED, you deserve to feel safe. And over the holiday period, EDs can be particularly busy and stressful places. That’s why we’re building on last year’s successful programme and ensuring more support is available to keep Kiwis safe: 20 hospitals will receive additional funding for security, and further funding will be available if there is a major incident or event that requires a greater security presence. Our Government’s working hard at improving public services that all Kiwis can rely on, whether that’s in the community or in an emergency department.

explanation: A binary question — will sanctions mean more kai or less kai on the table. He describes the traffic light system and its obligations and never says which way it cuts for the children asked about. Pivots to talking points.
question: Will his Government’s benefit sanctions help to put more kai on the table or less kai on the table this Christmas for the thousands of hungry tamariki in Aotearoa?
statement: Well, I’m very proud of the traffic light system that our great Minister from the Ministry of Social Development has implemented, because what it means is a pretty simple requirement: show up and talk to your case manager, get a resume, and show up to your job interviews.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Child Poverty Action Group's 20,000 figure. He neither agrees nor disagrees and never engages the landlord decision or the projection; he substitutes a different statistic (17,000 lifted out under Budget '24) and a comparison to Labour. It implicitly contests the claim, so not a total dodge, but the actual question goes unanswered.
question: Does he agree with the Child Poverty Action Group that his decision to put the wellbeing of landlords over the wellbeing of tamariki will put 20,000 more children into poverty by the time his term is up?
statement: What I’m proud about is under Budget ‘24, with all the cost of living measures that this Government delivered for low and middle income New Zealanders, 17,000 children are going to be taken out of poverty—compared to the last year of the Labour Government, where 23,000 more children were put in poverty.

explanation: Asked what he says to a specific child. He opens with an acknowledgement that times are tough — a minimal engagement — then turns immediately to blaming the previous government's economic management. Nothing is said to Logan; the question's core is sidestepped.
question: What does he say to Logan, a 7-year-old tamaiti who wrote to Santa asking for a burger to share with his mum for Christmas?
statement: I acknowledge that across New Zealand, it’s a pretty tough time. That’s what happens when you don’t run an economy well. If you care about low and middle income New Zealanders, you run the books well. You don’t spend more, tax more, borrow more, and deliver less.

explanation: 'Does she stand by all her statements and actions?' answered 'In context, yes.' The qualifier is a mild hedge, but this is a direct, complete response to the question asked.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: In context, yes. I particularly stand by my statement to the effect that now more than ever is a time for disciplined Government spending and a focus on driving economic growth.

explanation: Asked whether debt was last this high in 1994. Willis never touches the 1994 comparison at all — she pivots immediately to Labour adding $100 billion and to her own task of bending the curve. A narrow factual proposition put to her, entirely replaced with a counter-attack.
question: Isn’t it the case that the last time net core Crown debt was this high, which will peak at 46.5 percent of GDP, was in 1994?
statement: It is also the case that in the past five years, the last Labour Government added more than $100 billion to New Zealand’s debt. And we, as a Government, are now saddled with the task of bending that debt curve back—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether debt will be 3.5 percentage points higher than her Budget forecast. She concedes the direction — forecast revisions 'will have an effect on debt' — but never confirms or denies the specific figure, then spends the rest of the answer on fiscal discipline and the last Government. Grazes the core without reaching it.
question: Isn’t it the case that net core Crown debt will now be 3.5 percentage points higher than what was forecast in her Budget?
statement: As I have set out today in the Budget Policy Statement, it is the case that forecast revisions to New Zealand’s GDP trajectory will have an effect on debt. That is why it is so important that the Government maintain a disciplined fiscal position with lower operating allowances than have been the case in recent years when the last Government blew spending out as a proportion of GDP, leaving our economy in a very challenged state. If that member wants to join those on this side of the House in the pursuit of fiscal discipline, I can only welcome it.

explanation: Asked to confirm $58.7 billion more debt, peaking at $235 billion, versus her Budget six months ago. She explains the mechanism (earlier/deeper recession, productivity revisions) and accepts debt is affected, but never engages either number, then pivots to borrowing philosophy and a jab at the questioner. Partial engagement with a precise question.
question: Isn’t it the case that there will be $58.7 billion more debt, peaking at $235 billion, than what was forecast in her Budget only six months ago?
statement: As I have laid out today in the Budget Policy Statement and as Treasury has laid out in the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, downward revisions to the fiscal forecasts have had an effect in two ways. One, the current recession is estimated to have started earlier and to be more protracted than had previously been forecast. And, two, there has been a downward revision to productivity forecasts. This does have an effect on debt. Now, this Government believes there is a place for debt, for borrowing for long-term infrastructure assets. We also believe it is very important to get debt down to a trajectory under 40 percent of GDP. Again, I note that if the member wishes to join us in that pursuit, that would be novel for her and her party—

explanation: Asked whether she will take responsibility for the downgraded growth forecast. She gives a plain no — 'I won't take responsibility for the mistakes of the last Government, but I will take responsibility for fixing it.' A refusal that answers, so it scores well; docked because she quietly reframes what she is declining responsibility for rather than addressing the forecast revision itself.
question: Will she take responsibility for the growth forecast being revised downwards since her Budget and predicted to be $20 billion smaller in 2028?
statement: I won’t take responsibility for the mistakes of the last Government, but I will take responsibility for fixing it.

explanation: Asked whether she plans to shift any other goalposts. She rejects the question's characterisation, which disputes the premise but never says whether further definitional changes are planned. Brief and direct in manner, but the yes/no at the centre is left untouched.
question: Does she plan on shifting any other goalposts to help reach her targets, like she has done with the definition of “OBEGAL” and with child poverty targets?
statement: I reject the characterisations of the member’s question.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, complete, unambiguous.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he thinks it is his Government's job to decrease wealth inequality. He answers about raising incomes, growth and cost of living — adjacent talking points that never address whether reducing inequality is a responsibility he accepts. The question was a yes/no about the Government's job and no yes/no is given.
question: Does the Prime Minister think that it is the job of his Government to decrease wealth inequality?
statement: Our Government’s working incredibly hard to raise incomes, to provide economic growth, and to lower the cost of living.

explanation: Asked to name one policy that will decrease inequality. He names several — tax adjustments for low and middle income earners, Working for Families increases, FamilyBoost. That is squarely what was requested. Whether those policies actually reduce inequality is a Veracity question and does not move this score.
question: Can the Prime Minister name one—just one—Government policy that will decrease inequality in this country?
statement: We have adjusted tax for low and middle income working New Zealanders. We have increased the Working for Families credits. We have also provided FamilyBoost for people dealing with expensive childcare. We have provided inflation, interest rate, rent stability, and also tax relief for low and middle income working New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he believes the tax system is fair given the IRD finding on the wealthiest 311 households. Citing Treasury on progressivity functions as an implied 'yes, it is fair', so the question is partly engaged, but he never states his own belief and does not touch the IRD figure the question was built on.
question: Does the Prime Minister believe that we have a fair tax system when the IRD told us all last year that the wealthiest 311 households in this country pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander, and his Government has chosen to re-entrench those settings?
statement: It’s well established by Treasury that, you’ve heard them say, we have a progressive tax system.

explanation: Asked whether he heard Treasury say a capital gains tax would make the economy more productive. He answers a different question — asserting a CGT would be a wrecking ball — without ever saying whether he heard or acknowledges that Treasury advice. Substitutes his position on the policy for the factual question asked.
question: Did the Prime Minister also hear Treasury say that we would have a more productive economy if we were to implement a capital gains tax?
statement: I can tell you that would not be the case. That would be a wrecking ball through our economy, because we have been in recession for three years—

explanation: Asked how tough the choices have been to knowingly enable inequality. He rejects the characterisation, which is a legitimate response to a loaded premise, then moves entirely to talking points and blaming the previous Government. Premise-rejection plus pivot, with nothing said about the choices themselves.
question: How tough have the choices been for this Government to knowingly make decisions to enable the rich to get richer and the poor to get poorer in real terms?
statement: I absolutely reject the characterisation of that question. This is a Government that has been working incredibly hard to make sure that we rebuild an economy that helps low and middle income New Zealanders get ahead. That is the failing of the last Labour-Greens Government.

explanation: Asked what recent statements the Government has made on ED safety this summer. He names the statement (Wellington hospital this morning) and its content — extra security in 20 hospitals plus surge capacity. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent statements has the Government made on keeping emergency departments safe this summer?
statement: At Wellington hospital this morning I reconfirmed the Government’s commitment to keeping staff and patients safe in emergency departments (EDs) this summer. We know that EDs can be particularly busy and stressful places during the holiday period. That is why our Government is again taking extra safety steps to ease this by building on last year’s successful programme and our additional commitment in Budget 2024. Over the summer, Health New Zealand will increase security in 20 mostly provincial hospitals across the country and have further surge capacity available if additional security is needed. We want to ensure that our ED staff stay safe this summer.

explanation: Asked why the security uplift was a priority. He gives a reason: violence/aggression against staff and patients won't be tolerated and people deserve to feel safe. A 'why' question met with a stated rationale.
question: Why was it a priority for the Government to provide this uplift in emergency department security?
statement: Violence or aggression against patients, visitors, and health workers won’t be tolerated. Both staff and patients alike deserve to feel safe when they’re working or visiting hospitals in their time of need. This initiative reinforces that. That is why we announced both fixed funding positions as well as a flexible funding package which allows Health New Zealand to surge security support across emergency departments when needed. This is particularly helpful during summer for the many events being held in regional and rural areas.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has received. He reports feedback from staff and patients during regional and rural hospital visits saying the initiative matters. He then drifts into restating the initiative's contents, but the feedback question itself was engaged.
question: What feedback has the Minister received on the importance of this initiative?
statement: Since becoming the Minister of Health, I have travelled across the country, visiting both regional and rural hospitals to hear feedback from the front line. During these visits, both staff and patients have commented to me how important this initiative has been in ensuring that people feel safe when visiting or working in ED. That is why this initiative will provide 44 additional full-time security personnel across our eight high-priority EDs, a flexible funding package to surge security support when needed and further provisioning for 12 security trainers.

explanation: Asked what other initiatives the Government has undertaken on EDs. Opens with a detour into wait-time results, but does reach the question — new acute-flow operational standards, discharge and transit lounges. Answered after a preamble.
question: What other initiatives has the Government undertaken to improve our emergency departments?
statement: Last week, we provided an update on our five key health targets. After years of deterioration, ED wait times remained relatively the same as they were the year before, whilst seeing roughly 18,000 more people presenting to our EDs. This is a particularly impressive achievement given our hospitals were tackling some of the highest rates of respiratory illness in almost a decade. However, there is still more work to be done to continue driving improvements in our ED wait times. That’s why we have introduced initiatives like new acute-flow operational standards and invested in discharge and transit lounges. We are absolutely committed to improving health outcomes for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Two arms: does he stand by the refusal, and can he guarantee care and data will be safe. The first arm gets a flat 'Yes'. The second is hedged — 'it remains my expectation' rather than the guarantee that was asked for. Half direct, half hedged around the core.
question: Does he stand by his refusal to be interviewed on cuts to information technology in hospitals on the ground that it is an operational matter; if so, can he guarantee that hospital care and data will be safe?
statement: Yes. Health New Zealand is undergoing a reset process as a result of the troubled health reforms of previous years. Cost blowouts have meant that Health New Zealand needs to refocus on its core functions, which include providing the healthcare that New Zealanders need whilst living within its means. The health commissioner is leading this process with staff, with the aim of gathering feedback on proposals. It’s important to note that no final decisions have been made. I’ve been reassured by the commissioner that the reset is being undertaken in a careful and considered way, and it remains my expectation that hospitals and data will continue to be safe.

explanation: Two arms: does he stand by the statement, and what does he say to clinicians tied up in admin. He answers the first arm explicitly and says nothing at all to the second, which carried the substance of the question.
question: Does he stand by his statement in the House that redundancies for vital support staff at Health New Zealand are an operational matter as well, and, if so, what does he say to clinicians who are being tied up in admin rather than providing care?
statement: In response to the answer to the first arm of her question, yes, I stand by that statement.

explanation: Two arms: does he stand by the refusal, and what does he say to community members losing after-hours services. He confirms the first arm and restates the 'operational matter' formula, never addressing what he says to those community members.
