question: Does he stand by his refusal to comment on the loss of face-to-face after-hours services in Porirua because it is an operational matter, and, if so, what does he say to community members who want to know if they’ll get the care they need?
statement: In response to the first arm of that question, yes, it is well known that where technical or detailed operational matters are concerned, it is an operational matter for Health New Zealand.

explanation: Asked why he is evading questions on operational realities and on the $1.4 billion in cuts. He rejects the premise — a legitimate partial response to a loaded question — but then pivots to attacking the questioner's former government and never engages the substance of either limb.
question: Why is he evading questions on the operational realities of how New Zealanders are cared for in our health system and the consequences that stem from his direction to cut $1.4 billion in health spending?
statement: I reject the assertions in that question and would point to the fact that we are trying to turn around the reset from the botched two years of health reforms that member was a part of.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his commitment to lower surgical wait times. 'Yes, I do stand by that commitment' — direct and complete on the real question; the 'operational too' clause was a rhetorical jibe.
question: Does he stand by his commitment to lower wait times for surgeries, or are operations now operational too?
statement: Yes, I do stand by that commitment to lower the wait times for surgeries.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about councils getting back to basics. He states the announcement made yesterday and its contents — removing the four well-beings, benchmarking council performance. Direct.
question: What recent announcements has he made about getting councils back to basics?
statement: Yesterday, the Prime Minister and I announced reforms to get councils back to basics to reduce pressure on rates, deliver core services, and modernise outdated rules to drive efficiency and cost savings. These measures include removing the four “well-beings” from the Local Government Act, benchmarking council performance to hold them accountable. Ratepayers deserve councils that focus on the basics, like fixing pipes, filling potholes, and delivering reliable services, rather than expensive nice-to-haves.

explanation: Asked why the Government is removing the four well-beings. He gives the stated reason — rates rose about 2 percent more per year while they were in legislation, and their removal signals a focus on core services. Whether the evidence holds is Veracity, not this.
question: Why is the Government removing the four “well-beings” from the Local Government Act?
statement: The evidence shows that when the four “well-beings” were in legislation, rates increased approximately 2 percent more per year. Removing them sends a clear signal that councils must prioritise roads, rubbish, and reliable infrastructure. Ratepayers simply cannot afford excessive spending on nice-to-have projects or duplication of roles with central government. By focusing on core responsibilities, councils will reduce unnecessary financial burdens on their communities.

explanation: Asked how benchmarking will improve council accountability. He describes the mechanism — an annual DIA report on named metrics giving ratepayers information to assess their council. The 'how' is answered.
question: How will benchmarking improve council accountability?
statement: Benchmarking is a crucial tool for improving transparency and accountability. The Department of Internal Affairs will publish an annual report on councils’ performance, including key metrics such as rates, council debt, capital expenditure, balanced budgets, and road conditions. By providing ratepayers with clear information, these reports will empower communities to assess how well their councils are managing resources and delivering services in their local communities.

explanation: Asked whether he believes the tax system is FAIR, given a specific IRD finding about the 311 wealthiest households. He asserts the system is 'progressive' — which gestures at an implicit 'yes' — but never says fair or unfair and never touches the cited figure at all. It brushes past the core rather than reaching it. (Note: the answer's brevity and its truth are not what lowered this; the substitution of 'progressive' for the fairness question is.)
question: Does the Prime Minister believe that we have a fair tax system when the IRD told us all last year that the wealthiest 311 households in this country pay an effective tax rate less than half of that of the average New Zealander, and his Government has chosen to re-entrench those settings?
statement: It’s well established by Treasury that, you’ve heard them say, we have a progressive tax system.

explanation: The question was narrowly factual and answerable yes/no: did he hear Treasury say a CGT would make the economy more productive? He never says whether he heard it — he disputes the underlying proposition instead. That is answering a different question than the one asked. A narrow question squarely avoided, hence a low score even though he engaged the CGT topic energetically.
question: Did the Prime Minister also hear Treasury say that we would have a more productive economy if we were to implement a capital gains tax?
statement: I can tell you that would not be the case. That would be a wrecking ball through our economy, because we have been in recession for three years—

explanation: A loaded question ('how tough have the choices been to knowingly enable the rich to get richer'). Rejecting the embedded premise is a legitimate direct response — like a blunt refusal, it engages rather than dodges — and he does state his own account of what the Government is doing. But he never addresses the question as posed and closes by pivoting to the previous Government. Half-engaged.
question: How tough have the choices been for this Government to knowingly make decisions to enable the rich to get richer and the poor to get poorer in real terms?
statement: I absolutely reject the characterisation of that question. This is a Government that has been working incredibly hard to make sure that we rebuild an economy that helps low and middle income New Zealanders get ahead. That is the failing of the last Labour-Greens Government.

explanation: Asked what recent statements the Government has made on ED safety this summer; he names the statement (Wellington hospital this morning) and its content. Directly and completely on the question asked. That it is a friendly question with a prepared answer is irrelevant to this attribute.
question: What recent statements has the Government made on keeping emergency departments safe this summer?
statement: At Wellington hospital this morning I reconfirmed the Government’s commitment to keeping staff and patients safe in emergency departments (EDs) this summer. We know that EDs can be particularly busy and stressful places during the holiday period. That is why our Government is again taking extra safety steps to ease this by building on last year’s successful programme and our additional commitment in Budget 2024. Over the summer, Health New Zealand will increase security in 20 mostly provincial hospitals across the country and have further surge capacity available if additional security is needed. We want to ensure that our ED staff stay safe this summer.

explanation: Asked WHY the security uplift was a priority; he gives reasons — violence against staff and patients won't be tolerated, people deserve to feel safe. That is the question, answered. The drift into funding mechanics at the end doesn't subtract; it neither replaces nor obscures the reason given.
question: Why was it a priority for the Government to provide this uplift in emergency department security?
statement: Violence or aggression against patients, visitors, and health workers won’t be tolerated. Both staff and patients alike deserve to feel safe when they’re working or visiting hospitals in their time of need. This initiative reinforces that. That is why we announced both fixed funding positions as well as a flexible funding package which allows Health New Zealand to surge security support across emergency departments when needed. This is particularly helpful during summer for the many events being held in regional and rural areas.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has received; he says staff and patients on regional and rural hospital visits commented on the initiative's importance. That answers it, though the second half swerves into restating the initiative's numbers rather than the feedback. The answer's thinness on content is a Specificity matter, not a dodge — it addressed what was asked.
question: What feedback has the Minister received on the importance of this initiative?
statement: Since becoming the Minister of Health, I have travelled across the country, visiting both regional and rural hospitals to hear feedback from the front line. During these visits, both staff and patients have commented to me how important this initiative has been in ensuring that people feel safe when visiting or working in ED. That is why this initiative will provide 44 additional full-time security personnel across our eight high-priority EDs, a flexible funding package to surge security support when needed and further provisioning for 12 security trainers.

explanation: Asked what other ED initiatives the Government has undertaken; after a preamble on wait times he names acute-flow operational standards and investment in discharge and transit lounges. The question is reached and answered, just not immediately.
question: What other initiatives has the Government undertaken to improve our emergency departments?
statement: Last week, we provided an update on our five key health targets. After years of deterioration, ED wait times remained relatively the same as they were the year before, whilst seeing roughly 18,000 more people presenting to our EDs. This is a particularly impressive achievement given our hospitals were tackling some of the highest rates of respiratory illness in almost a decade. However, there is still more work to be done to continue driving improvements in our ED wait times. That’s why we have introduced initiatives like new acute-flow operational standards and invested in discharge and transit lounges. We are absolutely committed to improving health outcomes for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Two arms. First — does he stand by the refusal — answered directly with 'Yes.' Second — can he GUARANTEE care and data will be safe — he offers only that it 'remains my expectation'. That is hedging around the core of the second arm rather than answering it, so a strong but incomplete engagement.
question: Does he stand by his refusal to be interviewed on cuts to information technology in hospitals on the ground that it is an operational matter; if so, can he guarantee that hospital care and data will be safe?
statement: Yes. Health New Zealand is undergoing a reset process as a result of the troubled health reforms of previous years. Cost blowouts have meant that Health New Zealand needs to refocus on its core functions, which include providing the healthcare that New Zealanders need whilst living within its means. The health commissioner is leading this process with staff, with the aim of gathering feedback on proposals. It’s important to note that no final decisions have been made. I’ve been reassured by the commissioner that the reset is being undertaken in a careful and considered way, and it remains my expectation that hospitals and data will continue to be safe.

explanation: First arm ('do you stand by the statement') answered squarely: 'yes, I stand by that statement.' The second arm — what does he say to clinicians tied up in admin — is not addressed at all, and he explicitly answers only the first. Half the question engaged, half left untouched. The extreme brevity is not the issue; the unanswered arm is.
question: Does he stand by his statement in the House that redundancies for vital support staff at Health New Zealand are an operational matter as well, and, if so, what does he say to clinicians who are being tied up in admin rather than providing care?
statement: In response to the answer to the first arm of her question, yes, I stand by that statement.

explanation: Confirms the first arm ('yes, it is... an operational matter') but restates the general principle rather than engaging, and the second arm — what he says to Porirua community members wanting to know if they'll get care — is entirely skipped. A narrower, more pointed second arm dodged than in the preceding pair.
question: Does he stand by his refusal to comment on the loss of face-to-face after-hours services in Porirua because it is an operational matter, and, if so, what does he say to community members who want to know if they’ll get the care they need?
statement: In response to the first arm of that question, yes, it is well known that where technical or detailed operational matters are concerned, it is an operational matter for Health New Zealand.

explanation: Asked WHY he is evading these questions. Rejecting the assertion is a permissible form of direct response, but he offers no answer to the 'why' and immediately turns to the questioner's own record in the previous Government. Predominantly a pivot to attacking the questioner, with a token denial attached.
question: Why is he evading questions on the operational realities of how New Zealanders are cared for in our health system and the consequences that stem from his direction to cut $1.4 billion in health spending?
statement: I reject the assertions in that question and would point to the fact that we are trying to turn around the reset from the botched two years of health reforms that member was a part of.

explanation: 'Yes, I do stand by that commitment to lower the wait times for surgeries' — the substantive arm answered directly and completely. The 'or are operations now operational too' tag was a rhetorical jab, not a second question requiring an answer. Short does not mean evasive; this is a complete response.
question: Does he stand by his commitment to lower wait times for surgeries, or are operations now operational too?
statement: Yes, I do stand by that commitment to lower the wait times for surgeries.

explanation: Asked when the first benchmarking report would be released; gives a date (middle of 2025) plus the framing of why. Direct and complete.
question: When will the first benchmarking report on local councils be released?
statement: Good news: the first benchmarking report on local councils will be released in the middle of 2025, ahead of the 2025 local elections. This report will give hard-working ratepayers and residents across the country clear information about their council’s financial performance prior to going to the polls in October 2025.

explanation: 'Does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions?' answered 'Yes.' One word, but it fully answers a yes/no question.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked to confirm no environmental protection remains for covenants/landscapes/water orders. He rejects the premise ('I reject the characterisation'), which is a partial engagement, then pivots entirely to renewables, houses and roads. The specific protections asked about are never addressed.
question: Can the Prime Minister confirm that no level of environmental protection will remain for public conservation covenants, outstanding natural landscapes, or water conservation orders under the Fast-track Approvals Bill?
statement: Well, that’s not an accurate—I reject the characterisation of that question. But what I’d say to you is that I am incredibly proud of the fast-track legislation, and I really hope it’s not too late for the Green Party to get on board, because we really do want to have a 30 percent increase in renewable energy projects across this country, we do really want to build 55,000 more houses, and we want to build up 180 kilometres of new roads.

explanation: Asked what he would say to a public concerned that applicants failed to disclose compliance history. Declines to discuss individual projects and points to the expert panel — a small direct element — then pivots to build times and costs. The disclosure failure itself is never engaged.
question: What would he say to the public concerned that some of the 149 project applications that his Cabinet approved under the fast-track process were required to disclose their track record of prior compliance and enforcement actions against them, and didn’t?
statement: Again, I’m not getting into the details of individual projects; there’s an expert panel process that will manage that. But what I would say to that member is that the New Zealand public are actually sick of how long it takes to get things built in this country. There is no justification to take 19 months to build a three- to four-bedroom home that’s 50 percent more expensive than the same home in Australia.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet considered regional/national significance and the rationale for including non-responsive applications. Never says whether Cabinet considered it; asserts the projects are significant, defers to the panel, then attacks the previous government. The 'did Cabinet consider' core is untouched.
question: Did Cabinet consider whether the 149 applications contributed to regionally and nationally significant infrastructure, and, if so, what was the rationale for including projects that didn’t even bother answering how they supported regional or nationally significant infrastructure?
statement: Again, we have a process where projects will go through an expert panel. But what I’d say is these are projects of national and regional significance, and we make no apologies for making sure that we prioritise economic growth after three years of being in a recession, thanks to a Labour-Greens Government.

explanation: 'A hypothetical question—I'm not answering it.' A declared, undisguised non-answer, which puts it well above a talking-point pivot. But unlike 'No, I won't release that advice', refusing to engage the question is not the same as answering it: no commitment is given or withheld on the record. Scored mid-low; see the flagged ambiguity in the rubric's refusal exemption.
question: Will he commit to reconsidering projects included in the Fast-track Approvals Bill if the Auditor-General inquiry into Cabinet’s handling of conflicts of interest finds the process was not managed appropriately?
statement: A hypothetical question—I’m not answering it.

explanation: Asked where localism fits when councils get no response. 'There is a way, through the expert panels, for them to make a contribution' does answer where local input sits, so this is a genuine partial answer, but the unanswered-councils grievance at the core is skipped in favour of growth talking points.
question: Where does localism fit, when his Government won’t give local councils the decency of a response in even acknowledging their opposition to the fast-track projects in their city, district, or region, when even their democratic plans will soon have no weight in protecting their communities and their environment?
statement: There is a way, through the expert panels, for them to make a contribution. But, again, this is a Government that is making no apologies for getting things built quicker, prioritising economic growth, and making sure we get things done. That is what this country needs and I can tell you people are excited about fast track coming to a town near them shortly.

explanation: Two limbs: does he stand by the 'no-brainer' statement, and will he guarantee rail-enabled ferries. The guarantee limb is answered squarely and negatively — 'nothing has been ruled in or out', 'not going to make silly pledges'. The 'do you stand by it' limb is left implicit. The jab about question order is a Civility matter and did not move the score.
question: Does he stand by his statement regarding any new Cook Strait ferries that “Rail-enabled ferries is part of our considerations, yes, and that is a no-brainer”; if so, will he guarantee that the new ferries will be rail-enabled?
statement: Can I say to that member: I’d have thought this is far more important to be question No. 12 today, but we get on with the answer. Nothing has been ruled in or out. We are looking at all the options—the costs and benefits, and the pluses and minuses—and we’ll make decisions based on the best interests of our country. We are not going to make silly pledges before the work is done, and we can guarantee the member that we are not going to be asleep at the wheel like his colleagues were for the last three years.

explanation: Asked (a) was the Government advised wharf work must start this year and (b) what impact upgrades have on the Aratere. Answers neither: says Picton needs rebuilding 'regardless' and that plans will be looked at. Gestures at the topic without reaching either limb.
question: Was the Government advised that work on a new Picton wharf needed to begin this year, and, if so, what impact will any wharf and linkspan upgrades in Picton have on the ongoing operation of the rail-enabled Aratere ferry?
statement: Well, it’s not a secret to anyone apart from that side of the House that the port of Picton needs to be rebuilt in the next few years regardless, and we’re going to be looking at those plans as we find out from the experts what it might entail.

explanation: Asked whether the Government was advised the Aratere would need retiring in 2025. Effectively confirms it — that scenario came from the ministerial advisory group — and adds that Cabinet has not decided. Addresses the question squarely; the dismissive framing ('now disbanded') is Civility, not Forthrightness, and did not move the score.
question: Was the Government advised that the rail-enabled Aratere would need to be retired in 2025?
statement: Reality is that that was a scenario painted by the now disbanded ministerial advisory group, and the reality is that the decisions have not been taken by the Cabinet on that matter.

explanation: Asked to guarantee the Aratere runs until 2029. The 'What I can guarantee is...' construction substitutes a different guarantee — meetings and consultation — for the one requested. A narrow yes/no dodged, so scored low.
question: Can he then guarantee that the Interislander’s sole rail-enabled ferry, the Aratere, will be scheduled to continue operations until 2029?
statement: What I can guarantee is that, having had a meeting early this morning with KiwiRail and MUNZ—that’s the Maritime Union—at midday, and we’re going to consult with everybody, and we’re going to find out exactly what’s going on and what went wrong. And then we’ll come to this House and declare transparently—

explanation: Asked whether the Government was advised that the cheapest basic ferry option was $282m each, exceeding the iReX rail-enabled cost. Peters never says what advice was received; he pivots to the $4 billion figure, blames the questioner's side for irresponsibility, and offers a forward promise. The narrow factual core — were you so advised — is untouched.
question: Was the Government advised that the cheapest and most basic option for new Cook Strait ferries came in at $282 million each, which for two ferries would add up to more than the rail-enabled ferries contracted under iReX?
statement: What’s amazing about that question is this: that we were talking about two ferries and we ended up with $4 billion on the account and no one over there is being responsible. We’ll make one promise over here: we’ll come in far, far, far less than that.

explanation: Asked why Willis missed the end-of-July decision deadline recommended by her advisory group. Peters engages the premise rather than the question: he denies advisory groups set deadlines for the Government, which implicitly answers 'there was no deadline to miss.' But the actual 'why' is never given, and he closes on sympathy for the Minister's predicament. Partial engagement, core unreached.
question: Why did Nicola Willis miss the deadline for making a decision on ferries at the end of July this year, as recommended by her ministerial advisory group?
statement: Actually, ministerial advisory groups don’t set deadlines for this Government. We’re not run by the bureaucracy; we run the thing from Cabinet. And the Minister that you’re talking about, the finance Minister, had a nightmare on her hands and I’m deeply sympathetic with her predicament.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, direct, complete — nothing else was required.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the claim that the landlord tax cut would lower rents, and if so why have rents risen ~10 percent. Luxon contests the rent trajectory by asserting rents have 'stabilised' relative to the previous Government, which glances at the second part, but he neither affirms nor abandons the claim and never addresses the 10 percent figure. Mostly a pivot to comparison.
question: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
statement: Well, I’m very proud of the fact that we actually have seen rents stabilise in this country after having gone up $180 a week under his Government.

explanation: Asked why he believes a 10 percent annual rise indicates stabilisation. He declines to engage at all, calling the topic a waste of time and redirecting to the questioner's record. Unlike a plain refusal ('I won't answer that'), this substitutes an attack for the explanation asked for, and the reasoning behind 'stabilised' is never offered.
question: Why does he believe that rents going up 10 percent in a year is a sign that they’ve stabilised?
statement: I’d just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should believe the economy is improving given that 70 percent of workers had real-terms pay cuts. He does answer the 'why should they believe' half squarely, with a long list of indicators offered as grounds. The specific counter-evidence — real wages going backwards — is never engaged. Half the question met head-on, half sidestepped.
question: Why should everyday New Zealanders believe that the economy’s improving when 70 percent—seven out of 10—of working people received pay rises last year that were less than the rate of inflation, meaning that their pay in real terms is going backwards?
statement: Well, look, we do have an economic recovery under way. That’s evidenced by the GDP growth being 1.1 percent in the last quarter. It’s evidenced with inflation being low at 3.1 percent. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Treasury expect that interest rates will remain low, as will inflation. We’ve got consumer confidence the highest it’s been since 2021. We’ve got business confidence the highest since 2014. We’ve got farmer confidence the highest since 2016. Manufacturing growth, record exports, great growth in tourism, trade surplus for the first time in five years, building consents up 20 percent, construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year, job ads up 10 percent in the last year. There’s still a lot more for us to do, and life is hard, but it underscores some of the conversation we’ve had here in this House today, which is if you don’t run an economy well, if you don’t manage it prudently and responsibly, you end up taxing more, borrowing more, spending more—

explanation: Asked why construction activity was $5 billion lower and 751 firms liquidated if the industry has turned around. He gives an actual causal answer — interest rates, driven by prior spending and inflation — which addresses the 'why', then cites consents and jobs as evidence of the turnaround. The liquidation figure is left alone and he finishes with a counter-question, but the question's core was engaged.
question: If the building and construction industry has turned around, why was there $5 billion less activity in construction last year compared to 2023, and 751 construction firms going into liquidation?
statement: Well, as I’ve explained to the member before, construction is very contingent upon something called interest rates, because you actually need to borrow money to get developments done and built. How you end up with high interest rates is because of wasteful Government spending leading to high inflation, which leads to high interest rates. That really hurts a construction industry, and building and construction. What I’m saying to the member is it’s good to see that we’ve got building consents up 20 percent in the last six months, we’ve got construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year. That’s good progress; there’s more for us to do. We want more New Zealanders feeling the recovery. But if the member feels very strongly about it, why doesn’t he support our fast track?

explanation: Asked whether he thinks the 2,000 people a week leaving feel the economy has turned around. He answers with migration statistics disputing the premise's framing rather than the question about those people's perception; whether they feel the economy has turned around is never addressed. Data-rich, but a different question answered.
question: Does he think that the 2,000 New Zealanders a week who have been giving up and leaving the country under his leadership feel that the economy’s turned around?
statement: Well, I’m pleased to report that, actually, New Zealanders returning back to New Zealand was up 12 percent on the previous year. For the last four months, I’m very pleased to say that New Zealanders leaving is less than in any month in the period that he was Prime Minister. [ Interruption ]

explanation: Asked a narrow, checkable question: has he identified one family receiving the full $250 a fortnight. No family, no number, no yes or no — instead a charge of flippancy and talking points about the questioner's spending record. A specific factual question squarely avoided.
question: Has the Prime Minister identified one single New Zealand family that’s received the full $250 a fortnight that he promised them before the election?
statement: I think it’s quite interesting the member is so flippant about the efforts of this Government to help low and middle income working New Zealanders. It wasn’t deeply ideological to lift tax thresholds to help lots of people with lower tax. But what we know is that member spent too much, borrowed too much, for way too long, caused huge amounts of suffering, and he wants to get a go at doing it all again. Not going to happen.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on economic policy. She names one — the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Covid-19 Lessons Learned, released that day — and identifies economic policy as one of its four focus areas. Directly responsive; the closing editorial about those who minimise errors is extra, not evasion.
question: What recent reports has she seen on economic policy?
statement: The final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Covid-19 Lessons Learned was released today. One of the four key areas it focuses on is economic policy. The royal commission observes that the COVID-19 pandemic was a substantial shock to the economy and the costliest event in terms of fiscal support in New Zealand in the past 40 years. We must learn lessons from the way this event was responded to, because these lessons must inform the Government’s response to the next natural disaster, global downturn, pandemic, or other economic shock. Denial is not an option. Mistakes were made in the economic response, and these mistakes were costly. Those who choose to minimise these errors are not well placed to learn from them.

explanation: Asked what the royal commission said about government spending and fiscal stimulus during the pandemic. She reports its findings point by point: the timely/temporary/targeted advice, the shovel-ready projects failing those tests, the $60 billion fund's 821 programmes, and the conclusion that stimulus ran too long. Squarely and completely on the question asked.
question: What did the royal commission say about Government spending and fiscal stimulus during the pandemic?
statement: Well, it says that Treasury and Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment advice from the outset was that fiscal stimulus measures to address the consequences of the pandemic should be timely, temporary, and targeted. However, the royal commission found that many examples of Government spending, including the so-called shovel-ready infrastructure projects, did not meet these tests. The $60 billion COVID-19 Response and Recovery fund spanned 821 programmes, around half of which were not related to the pandemic, such as conservation programmes, additional public housing places, and school lunches. Many initiatives in the COVID fund extended well beyond the time of the pandemic, and some were baked in, including permanent increases to welfare benefits. As a result, the big increase in Government spending was highly stimulatory and went on for too long.

explanation: Asked what the royal commission said about the consequences of the stimulus. Willis reports exactly that — the house-price surge finding, the limited-review finding, and a direct quote from the report. The question's core is reached squarely.
question: What did the royal commission say about the consequences of that stimulus?
statement: Well, it says that highly stimulatory fiscal policy, together with low interest rates, led to a surge in house prices in 2021 and 2022. House prices, I acknowledge, also rose in other countries but the commission points out that the increase was far more dramatic in New Zealand. This was avoidable. The commission says that fiscal policy set in 2020 received limited review and adjustment. It says, and I quote, “We are not aware of any sizeable component of the fiscal stimulus programme that was reviewed or cancelled to lessen the stimulus once the undesirability of further stimulus became clear.”

explanation: Asked what the commission said about Government debt. After a short lead-in on why debt rose, she gives the commission's conclusion and quotes it verbatim. The framing sentences delay but do not displace the answer.
question: What did the royal commission say about Government debt?
statement: Fiscal stimulus comes from increasing Government spending. In the circumstances, increased Government spending had to be borrowed for. As a result, New Zealand’s Government debt rose from 18.6 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 38.7 percent in the 2022/2023 fiscal year, obviously a very significant increase. The royal commission makes it clear that the large amount of debt accumulated during the pandemic means New Zealand is now in a weaker position to deal with the next large shock that comes along. The report concludes—and, again, I quote—“there is a pressing need to reduce public debt to provide a buffer for future pandemics or other economic shocks.” This Government agrees with that conclusion.

explanation: Asked what recent reports on tourism she has seen. Upston names the Tourism Satellite Account and gives its headline figure. A friendly question, but it is answered on its own terms; the closing plug does not displace the answer.
question: What recent reports has she seen on tourism in New Zealand?
statement: Data released last week shows New Zealand’s tourism sector continues to grow, driving billions of dollars into our economy. The Tourism Satellite Account shows total tourism expenditure in New Zealand is at $46.6 billion for the year ending March 2025. A new travel option that enables eligible Chinese and Pacific visitors to cross the ditch to New Zealand visa-free is also bringing in a considerable boost to tourism with over $210 million being injected into the economy as a result of our Government’s visa changes. These results highlight exactly why tourism is a key part of our Government’s plan to fix the basics and build the future.

explanation: Asked how the visa changes boosted the economy. The response gives the visit counts, the average spend and the resulting $210 million injection — the causal chain the question asked for.
question: How have the Government’s recent visa changes provided a boost to our economy?
statement: In December, we announced that 13,000 Chinese and Pacific travellers had already visited, with 24,000 total requests approved. That number has now almost tripled to 36,800 visits. With average visitor spend at $5,800 for Chinese visitors, that’s an estimated economic injection of $210 million for Kiwi businesses from those who have visited, with Chinese visitors making up 36,200 visits through the new pathway. This visitor spending is going directly into local businesses; it includes shops, eateries, accommodation, and transport, and this is spending that may not have come into New Zealand without these changes. More international visitors mean more customers for our businesses and more jobs being created across the country.

explanation: Asked about employment progress in tourism and hospitality. Answered with the employment total, the percentage change and the net increase — directly on point.
question: What progress has she seen on employment in the tourism and hospitality industries?
statement: The latest Tourism Satellite Account data shows that now one in nine people are employed in the tourism and hospitality industries. Total tourism employment increased 2.8 percent to over 325,000 people. This means almost 9,000 more people are employed in the industry. This data shows the importance of our Government’s commitment to growing tourism and its contribution to employment growth across New Zealand. More visitors mean more spending on our accommodation, cafés, bars, restaurants, and local businesses, which, of course, gives a significant boost to the economy and supports more local jobs.

explanation: Asked what commentary she has seen on these reports. Three named commentators are quoted. That is precisely what was requested.
question: What commentary has she seen on these reports?
statement: Tourism Industry Aotearoa Chief Executive Rebecca Ingram has said, “This summer, we have seen changes to our visa settings for China, which has made a real difference, and we have also seen quite considerable activity to stimulate demand.” Napier City Business Inc. General Manager Pip Thompson said, “When visitors are here, staying overnight, and spending, it supports accommodation, hospitality, and the wider CBD.” Greymouth iSite manager Kelly Ashworth describes tourism at present as “Fantastic—great to see. There’s not accommodation available in Greymouth, Hokitika, or Punakaiki … It’s great not just for the tourism industry but for supermarkets, cafés, boutiques, local businesses that we’re lucky to have. They’ve all benefitted—it’s what keeps everyone employed.” Tourism is critical to our economy, and our investments will help to deliver lasting benefits for communities and businesses from one end of New Zealand to the other.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. "Yes" — one word, and complete. Brevity is not evasion.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he shares the incoming US ambassador's priority of expanding the defence partnership. He asserts an independent foreign policy and working with like-minded countries, never saying whether he shares that priority. A yes/no question answered with positioning.
question: Does he share the incoming US ambassador to New Zealand’s priority of “expanding our defence partnership”?
statement: Well, what we believe in is we have our own independent foreign policy. We work with like-minded countries on making sure we keep the Indo-Pacific region safe and secure.

explanation: Asked whether he is comfortable expanding defence partnerships with the US given the stated conduct. He rejects the question's characterisation and assumptions. That is a direct, unhedged move rather than a filibuster, but it disposes of the premise without ever saying whether he is comfortable, so the core is left unaddressed.
question: Is he comfortable expanding defence partnerships with a country that has launched an illegal war with Iran, further destabilised the entire Middle East, and upended global fuel supply?
statement: I reject the characterisation and the assumptions that are inherent in that question.

explanation: Asked to rule out providing resources or intelligence to the US-Israeli war with Iran. He says the issue has been canvassed and that intelligence sharing complies with NZ law — which neither rules it out nor declines to. A narrow yes/no left unanswered.
question: Will the Prime Minister rule out providing any resources or intelligence to support the US-Israeli war with Iran?
statement: We’ve canvassed these issues before. As I’ve said, any intelligence that is collected and shared is done in accordance with New Zealand law.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a specific quoted statement and, if so, why his Government shares Australia's position. "I don't understand the question" engages neither limb, including the simple stand-by-it half that needed only a yes or no.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “Our position is the same as the Australian position.”, and, if so, why does his Government share Australia’s support for the US attacks on Iran?
statement: I don’t understand the question.

explanation: The same two-limb question re-put. Rejecting the characterisation is a clear stance on the second limb's premise, but the first limb — does he stand by his own quoted statement — is a plain factual question that goes unanswered.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “Our position is the same as the Australian position.”; and if so, why does his Government share Australia’s support for the US attacks on Iran?
statement: I reject the characterisation of that question completely.

explanation: Asked WHY the Government cannot articulate a clear position on the US-Israeli war with Iran. Luxon declines to add anything, pointing to earlier statements. It is a plain, non-evasive refusal to go further rather than a filibuster or an attack, but a 'why' question gets no reason at all — the core is left untouched. Partial credit for the honest brush-off.
question: Why is his Government unable to articulate a clear position on the illegal US-Israeli war with Iran?
statement: We canvassed that last week. We’ve had statements in the House on that. I’ve got nothing further to add to what’s already been said and discussed.

explanation: Asked whether the 24/7 online GP service is on track to reach one million patients a year, and if not why not. Brown engages the question squarely by rejecting its premise: there is no such target, and the 1 million figure came from primary-care access survey findings. Contesting the premise with a stated basis is an answer. Marked down slightly for the promotional padding that follows, not for its vagueness or truth.
question: Is the Government’s 24/7 online GP service on track to reach one million patients a year; if not, why not?
statement: The member opposite appears to be confused. There is not and has never been a target for X number of patients being seen through this service. Since the Online GP Care service was introduced, tens of thousands of New Zealanders have received care they otherwise could not have accessed—making a real difference to patients’ lives. The figure of 1 million, which the member is referring to, was not a projected usage target; it relates to survey findings for access to primary care, not to any target for the Online GP Care service. The Government introduced services like this to work alongside our wider primary care plan, to ensure that patients can get the care they need when and where they need it. Uptake of this service will only continue to grow, and I encourage the member to support it.

explanation: Asked WHEN the service will reach 1 million users a year. Brown restates that 1 million was never a usage target, which implies the answer 'there is no such date' — engagement via premise-rejection — but he never states that plainly, and closes on 'usage will continue to grow'. Reaches the question without landing on it.
question: When will the service reach 1 million users a year, as promised in the fact sheet distributed in the launch?
statement: As I said in the answer to my primary question, the figure of 1 million, which the member is referring to, was not a projected usage target; it relates to survey findings about access to primary care—not to any target for the online GP care service. Ultimately, usage will continue to grow, and we encourage the member to promote it.

explanation: Asked to adjudicate between the Prime Minister's optimism and departmental data showing 5 percent uptake. Brown nominally picks a side ('the Prime Minister, of course, is always right') but treats it as a joke and then pivots to growth talking points and an attack on Labour's policy, never engaging the 5 percent figure the question turned on. A gesture at an answer, then a dodge.
question: Who is correct: the Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon, who said he could see this “taking off quite well”; or his own data, which says that the service is only reaching 5 percent of the patients he promised?
statement: The Prime Minister, of course, is always right, and, ultimately, the tens of thousands of New Zealanders are using this service, and it will continue to grow, as people become more aware of the service. But I do note that the policy of the members opposite, in the Labour Party, was to scrap—

explanation: Asked for a threshold: how few users before the Government discontinues the service. The answer never engages the idea of discontinuation at all, pivoting immediately to a list of primary-care plan components. A narrow, pointed question completely avoided.
question: How few people would have to use the service for the Government to discontinue it?
statement: Well, this service is making access available to New Zealanders who otherwise wouldn’t have access. We’re having to promote access, and it is one part of our plan to increase access for primary care; expanding access to urgent after-hours care, Online GP Care; investing more in record capitation for general practitioners; our Primary Care Tactical Action Plan; growing our primary care workforce, with more doctors, more nurses, more nurse practitioners. We have a clear plan to increase access to primary care: it is multifaceted, and it is delivering for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what the latest trade statistics show about exporter resilience. McClay answers directly with the December quarter figures ($29.2b exports, up $2.2b; $61.2b two-way trade) and ties them to resilience. Directly and completely engaged.
question: What do the latest international trade statistics show about the resilience of New Zealand exporters?
statement: New Zealand’s exporters are winning, despite challenging international conditions. Stats released last week show a robust performance across global markets, reflecting the skill, innovation, and resilience of Kiwi exporters, who continue to compete amongst the best in the world. Exports rose to $29.2 billion for the December quarter compared to a year earlier, up $2.2 billion. Two-way trade also increased strongly, reaching $61.2 billion for that quarter. These results show the importance of opening markets and strong trading relationships, and they show that New Zealand exporters are well placed to navigate ongoing trade disruption and global economic uncertainty.

explanation: Asked which key export sectors are leading the growth. Named directly — meat 21.4 percent, dairy 10 percent, tourism 9.4 percent, transportation 7.5 percent, logs 3.7 percent. Exactly the question asked.
question: Which key export sectors are leading this growth?
statement: Export growth has been broad across our key export sectors, but, again, our farmers and growers are punching well above their weight. In the December quarter, meat exports increased by a significant 21.4 percent; dairy exports were up 10 percent, tourism—thank you to the Minister for Tourism and Hospitality for her work—grew by 9.4 percent; transportation exports grew by 7.5 percent; and for our foresters, log exports were up by 3.7 percent. New Zealand exporters are performing well across both goods and services, and across multiple markets, despite these ongoing global economic uncertainties. These results show our exporters continue to compete successfully in a highly competitive international environment.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to keep exporters resilient and competitive. Answered with the FTA strategy — reducing border barriers, market access, named agreements and markets. Squarely on the question; the self-congratulation does not move the score.
question: What is the Government doing to ensure New Zealand exporters remain resilient and competitive as global economic conditions continue to evolve?
statement: This Government is focused on using our free-trade agreements (FTAs) to back exporters by reducing barriers at the border, improving market access, and giving New Zealand businesses greater certainty in tough global conditions. Statistics show exports have grown most in markets where New Zealand has free-trade agreements: the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, in China, in Australia, the UK, and the European Union—growth across each of these markets demonstrates the value of our FTAs in helping Kiwi exporters remain competitive and succeed internationally. As global conditions evolve, the Government remains committed to strengthening and growing our expanding network of FTAs.

explanation: Asked what export performance means for jobs and incomes. Answered directly: trade supports one in four jobs, exporting firms pay more, $114b exported over the year, underpinning regional growth and wages. Engaged the question as put.
question: What does this export performance mean for jobs and incomes for New Zealanders?
statement: Trade supports one in four Kiwi jobs, and companies who export employ more women and they generally pay their workers more. So strong export performance is important for jobs and drives higher incomes across New Zealand. Over the past year, New Zealand exported more than $114 billion of goods and services, and delivered a small trade surplus. Resilience in our export sector helps underpin regional economic growth, it creates jobs, and it pays Kiwis better wages.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statement on economic growth, and if so why. Willis says 'yes' and gives a because-clause. The reason is circular, but that is a Rigor failure, not evasion — the yes/no core is answered outright and immediately.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “Economic growth means more jobs, higher wages and better opportunities for all New Zealanders”; if so, why?
statement: Well, yes, because economic growth means more jobs, higher wages, and better opportunities for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether wages are keeping up, against a report that 70 percent of workers got below-inflation rises. Willis concedes obliquely that some workers received no rise — partial engagement — but never addresses the 70 percent figure or answers yes or no, then moves to Investment Boost. Circles the question without reaching its core.
question: Are wages keeping up, when Radio New Zealand reported that 70 percent of workers received a pay rise that failed to keep up with inflation last year?
statement: Well, it’s always the case that family circumstances vary. While some workers will have received pay rises or moved to jobs with higher pay, others will not have received pay rises in the previous year. What our Government is focused on is increasing opportunities in this economy, which will allow more job creation to occur, allow businesses to pay their workers more, and ensure that every New Zealander has more choices about the opportunities they face. I’d point out to the member that one key way we are doing that is with the Investment Boost tax policy, which Treasury forecast will increase wage growth significantly over the forecast period.

explanation: Asked whether she expects wages to keep up with inflation this year. Willis answers in substance that no definitive forecast can be given in current global conditions, and adds what the Government wants to see. Declining to forecast, with a stated reason, is a real response to the question rather than a pivot — but it stops short of her own expectation, which is what was asked.
question: Does she expect that wages will keep up with inflation this year given that food prices are up 4.6 percent and economists are now predicting inflation will increase further?
statement: Well, as I outlined in extensive detail yesterday, there are currently a number of issues occurring globally which mean that it is challenging for anyone to give a definitive forecast about what will happen with New Zealand’s annual inflation rate or our rate of economic growth. It is always the case, however—I can confirm for the member—that we want to see people’s wages rising faster than inflation.

explanation: Asked how she can credibly claim "better opportunities" given wages, prices and a mere oversight group. Willis rejects the premise and then does give her grounds for the claim — named fast-track projects employing workers — so the core "how can you say that" is engaged. But the specific pressure points (wages going backwards, the oversight group) are left untouched and she closes on the questioner's party. Partial engagement, not a clean dodge.
question: How can she credibly say that there are “better opportunities”, when wages are going backwards, New Zealanders are now facing higher prices, and the best her Government can do is to set up an oversight group?
statement: I absolutely reject the assertion at the back end of this question, but what I would also highlight is that when I think about those people who are working on the new housing development in Nelson, fast tracked through the fast-track Act; when I think of the construction workers working on the Auckland port extension, made possible by the fast-track Act; when I think of the workers across the country doing work right now that would not be possible without the fast-track Act, then I think it’s pretty clear that this Government stands on the side of opportunity. I would put to that member that members who opposed that fast-track legislation and the jobs it is supporting right now may be speaking out of both sides of their mouths.

explanation: "What reports have you received on fuel security?" — he never characterises any report, but he delivers the substance a reports question conventionally seeks: current stock levels (25 days diesel, 27 days petrol, more in transit) and the Middle East pressure. He then drifts to Marsden Point history. Addresses the topic squarely without ever naming what he received.
question: What reports has he received on fuel security?
statement: Obviously, the war in the Middle East is creating considerable pressure on our fuel importers. We do have, however, a reasonable supply of fuel, with 25 days’ worth of diesel, 27 days’ worth of petrol, and similar amounts safely on its way here. However, in 2022, when the Marsden Point refinery was closed down, with the approval of the then Labour Government—

explanation: Asked what risks the Middle East crisis creates. He does identify a risk — total import dependence leaving NZ "beholden" — but reaches it via blame for the Marsden Point closure and the answer breaks off there. The risk named is structural rather than crisis-specific, so the question is half met. (The partisan framing is a Focus matter, not counted here.)
question: What risks to fuel security does New Zealand face due to the Middle East crisis?
statement: As I’ve said, when the previous Government approved of the Marsden Point closure, sadly we are now reduced to importing all of our fuel and beholden—

explanation: "Why does NZ have a fuel security plan?" is answered directly in the first clause: because New Zealand First put it in the coalition agreement. He then adds why such a plan matters. The self-praise and the swipe at the Greens are Civility/Focus concerns and do not reduce the fact that the question was answered.
question: Why does New Zealand have a fuel security plan?
statement: A far-sighted nationalist party, New Zealand First, put it in the coalition agreement. However, it’s important that our wee nation does develop and implement a fuel security plan, and I’ll be the first to acknowledge that all sides of the House have an interest in fuel security—with the exception of the Greens, who do not believe in fossil fuels.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing about 20,000 construction job losses. Most of the reply is attribution of the downturn to the previous Government; he eventually gestures at "steps to fix the economy and make building easier" and cites improved conditions. The job losses themselves are never engaged. It reaches toward the question without landing on it.
question: What, if anything, is the Government doing about the 20,000 job losses in construction on its watch?
statement: Well, we know that the construction sector has had a hard time over the last several years—since the previous Government’s COVID-19 response, in fact—including through high general inflation peaking at 7.3 percent, high interest rates, and high construction inflation, as well, at a 50 percent increase. But over the last two years, through the actions of the Government, we’ve taken steps to fix the economy and make building easier. Inflation is now under control. Interest rates have dropped, therefore building costs have stabilised and confidence is returning.

explanation: The core is narrow and factual: did the frustrated builders tell him how long recovery will take, given the cancelled hospital builds? He describes the frustration's cause and lists what the Government is doing, but never says what builders told him about a timeframe and never touches the cancelled builds. A specific question left unanswered.
question: When he said in a press release that he’d listened to frustrated builders, did they tell him how long it will take them for the industry to recover from his Government’s management of its construction pipeline when it cancelled and scaled back hospital builds from Whangārei to Dunedin while claiming to be focused on infrastructure builds?
statement: The frustration that’s been expressed by the construction sector reflects the fact that their sector was beset by an even steeper boom-bust cycle, as exacerbated by the last Government’s actions, than they had realised. Therefore, the consequence has been that we have had to work all the harder to make construction easier, faster, and more affordable, as well as getting Government procurement actions, yes, across health, but also education, defence, and social housing at the right settings so we can see the increase—which we have, by the way, with a 15 percent increase in building consents, for example, compared with the same time last year.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to support defence personnel into housing; the answer names the measure — removing the KiwiSaver first-home withdrawal barrier for personnel required to live on base or deployed — and confirms it is being done. Direct and complete.
question: What is the Government doing to support defence personnel into quality housing?
statement: Recently, the Government announced changes to remove barriers that prevent our defence personnel from using their own KiwiSaver funds to purchase their own home. Since 2010, Kiwis have been able to withdraw from their KiwiSaver accounts to assist with the purchase of a first home, so long as they live in the homes that they buy. However, when applied to defence personnel—who are required to live on base, out of their hometown, or overseas on deployment—this is clearly an unfair barrier. I’m happy to say that this Government is removing that barrier.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen; answered in the opening line — "extremely positive from our defence community." The remainder is justification and a compliment to the questioner, but the question itself was met head-on.
question: What feedback has he seen from defence personnel in relation to the KiwiSaver changes?
statement: The feedback has been extremely positive from our defence community. New Zealand Defence Force personnel already sacrifice a lot to serve, often spending large periods of time away from their home towns and away from friends and family in the service of our nation. It’s only right that we make this seemingly small but actually quite meaningful change that will make it easier for them to purchase their own first home, and I do add that the member asking the question provided some of the genesis of the idea that would help our defence personnel, with her initiative around rural farm and home purchases, too.

explanation: "What else is the Government doing?" — answered with the defence estate programme: $138m on regeneration, $16m on housing, 77 new homes across four bases. Squarely responsive to what was asked.
question: What else is the Government doing to ensure defence personnel have access to quality housing?
statement: This Government is putting significant investment into our defence estate so that our sailors, soldiers, and aviators can stay in accommodation that is fit for purpose. The Government spent around $138 million on estate regeneration last year, with some $16 million being spent on housing alone. Currently, Defence is planning and constructing a further 77 new homes in Waiōuru, Linton, Ōhakea, and Burnham, with additional homes planned in the coming years.

explanation: "Why is new investment important?" — answered with reasons: the WWII-era estate is no longer fit for purpose, and a modern estate aids recruitment and retention. The question's core is reached directly.
question: Why is new investment in the defence estate important?
statement: Much of the defence estate was built during the Second World War and it is currently now no longer fit for purpose—and that’s the polite version. Investing in the defence estate, therefore, is investing in our people. Ensuring that we have an estate that is modern and functional will help us to recruit and retain talent, ensuring that the Defence Force can continue protecting New Zealand’s interests.

explanation: A stand-by-your-statements question answered "Yes." One word, but it is a complete and unambiguous response to what was asked. Brevity is not evasion.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga ?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A binary question — increased or decreased fossil fuel dependence — met with an energy strategy that "de-risks our reliance in a dry year" and a note on wholesale prices. Neither direction is ever stated. The core of a narrow question is left entirely unaddressed, which is the worse kind of dodge.
question: Has his Government increased or decreased our country’s dependence on fossil fuels?
statement: What we’ve done is actually made sure we’ve got an energy strategy that de-risks our reliance in a dry year and actually, as a result, we’ve taken the risk premium down. It’s been encouraging seeing recent announcements that maybe electricity wholesale prices have come down by about $20.

explanation: Asked a binary: does the LNG terminal decision increase or decrease dependence on/exposure to fossil fuels. He never says increase or decrease; he pivots to the previous government's record and to cost/jobs benefits. The dry-year 'risk premium' line grazes the 'risky' half of the question, so it is not a total non-answer, but the core binary is left untouched.
question: Does his decision to pour $1 billion - plus of taxpayer money into a new liquefied natural gas (LNG) import terminal instead of, say, distributed renewable energy generation increase or decrease our exposure to and dependence on risky and volatile fossil fuels?
statement: Well, the failed policy of the previous Labour-Greens Government meant that we were making the rather unique transition from domestic gas to internationally imported coal. That’s not good for emissions, but we are also in a place where the risk around the dry year has been costing New Zealand about $5 billion a year since 2017. Building this facility takes that risk premium down, and, as I’ve said before, this will save Kiwis about $265 million a year, or about $50 a household, and will actually protect 2,000 jobs from higher energy prices.

explanation: Asked whether removing the Clean Car Discount increased or decreased dependence on fossil fuels. He offers a generality about the energy mix and then talks about an unrelated fast-tracked wind farm. The Clean Car Discount is never mentioned and the increase/decrease question is never reached.
question: Did his decision to completely remove the Clean Car Discount—which has seen electric vehicle sales plummet from 27 percent in 2023, to 8 percent in 2025—increase or decrease our country’s dependence on risky fossil fuels?
statement: Well, there’s actually a lot that goes into our energy mix across our energy policy and our actions that we’ve got. I’d want to say to the member that it’s been very exciting to see that there has even been a draft approval through fast track for renewable wind in the South Island. That could actually power up a thousand homes and move them into renewable energy, and that’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked whether cancelling $640m of farm decarbonisation support increased or decreased fossil fuel dependence. He answers only that the previous policy was 'total failure' and raised power bills — a different question entirely. No engagement with the cancellation's effect on dependence.
question: Did his Government’s decision to cancel $640 million of support to decarbonise and electrify our farmers and growers increase or decrease our dependence on risky fossil fuels?
statement: Again, as I’ve said to the member, the previous policy had led to total failure. It had led to high electricity prices that actually raised up power bills and put jobs at risk. That’s not something that this Government is doing.

explanation: Asked what it would take for him to back down on the LNG terminal. He opens by attacking the questioner's credibility, then reports an emissions statistic. A refusal ('nothing would') would have scored high, but he never states one — the question is simply never reached. Marked slightly above floor because a refusal is faintly implied by the defence of the policy.
question: What will it take if not new evidence seemingly every single day—like the unfolding war in Iran—that increasing our country’s dependence on risky fossil fuels hurts regular people for the Prime Minister to end up backing down on expensive and, ultimately, resilience-undermining plans, like his billion-dollar, taxpayer-funded LNG terminal?
statement: Sorry, but the member, when she was part of a Labour-Greens Government, caused a huge amount of failure in our electricity market. Prices went up to $800 per megawatt hour. That caused mills to shut down and low and middle income working New Zealanders to lose their jobs. I’m sorry, but the member has no credibility in energy. The good news is—I know the member cares deeply about emissions, and, as I said to the member last week—the October quarter was the lowest level of emissions generated by this country since 2010. That’s good news.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' — one word, direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-part: does he stand by the claim that the landlord tax cut would lower rents, and if so why have rents risen ~10%. He answers neither directly, but does contest the premise by asserting rents have stabilised relative to the prior government — that is engagement with the subject matter rather than a pivot to talking points, so it partially addresses the second part.
question: Does he stand by his claim that giving landlords a $2.9 billion tax cut would lower rents; if so, why have rents gone up almost 10 percent in the past year?
statement: Well, I’m very proud of the fact that we actually have seen rents stabilise in this country after having gone up $180 a week under his Government.

explanation: Asked why he regards a 10% annual rise as stabilisation. He dismisses the topic as 'a waste of time' and attacks the questioner's record. Declining to engage is stated, but as a dismissal of the questioner rather than a plain refusal to answer, and the 'why' is never touched.
question: Why does he believe that rents going up 10 percent in a year is a sign that they’ve stabilised?
statement: I’d just say to that member: asking me about housing policy, which was an abject failure of his Government, is a waste of time.

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should believe the economy is improving, given below-inflation pay rises for 70% of workers. He answers the central interrogative squarely, giving an extended list of reasons for believing recovery is under way, and concedes 'life is hard'. He does not engage the real-wages premise, which is what holds this below a full score; the length and truth of the indicators are not factors here.
question: Why should everyday New Zealanders believe that the economy’s improving when 70 percent—seven out of 10—of working people received pay rises last year that were less than the rate of inflation, meaning that their pay in real terms is going backwards?
statement: Well, look, we do have an economic recovery under way. That’s evidenced by the GDP growth being 1.1 percent in the last quarter. It’s evidenced with inflation being low at 3.1 percent. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Treasury expect that interest rates will remain low, as will inflation. We’ve got consumer confidence the highest it’s been since 2021. We’ve got business confidence the highest since 2014. We’ve got farmer confidence the highest since 2016. Manufacturing growth, record exports, great growth in tourism, trade surplus for the first time in five years, building consents up 20 percent, construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year, job ads up 10 percent in the last year. There’s still a lot more for us to do, and life is hard, but it underscores some of the conversation we’ve had here in this House today, which is if you don’t run an economy well, if you don’t manage it prudently and responsibly, you end up taxing more, borrowing more, spending more—

explanation: Asked why construction activity fell $5bn and 751 firms failed. He gives a direct causal answer — interest rates, driven by prior spending and inflation — which addresses the 'why' asked, though he does not accept or engage the specific figures before turning to favourable statistics and a counter-question.
question: If the building and construction industry has turned around, why was there $5 billion less activity in construction last year compared to 2023, and 751 construction firms going into liquidation?
statement: Well, as I’ve explained to the member before, construction is very contingent upon something called interest rates, because you actually need to borrow money to get developments done and built. How you end up with high interest rates is because of wasteful Government spending leading to high inflation, which leads to high interest rates. That really hurts a construction industry, and building and construction. What I’m saying to the member is it’s good to see that we’ve got building consents up 20 percent in the last six months, we’ve got construction jobs up 43 percent in the last year. That’s good progress; there’s more for us to do. We want more New Zealanders feeling the recovery. But if the member feels very strongly about it, why doesn’t he support our fast track?

explanation: Asked whether he thinks the 2,000 people leaving weekly feel the economy has turned around. He answers about migration numbers instead — arrivals up, departures lower than under the questioner. Related subject matter, but he substitutes his own question about the statistics for the one asked about those people's perception.
question: Does he think that the 2,000 New Zealanders a week who have been giving up and leaving the country under his leadership feel that the economy’s turned around?
statement: Well, I’m pleased to report that, actually, New Zealanders returning back to New Zealand was up 12 percent on the previous year. For the last four months, I’m very pleased to say that New Zealanders leaving is less than in any month in the period that he was Prime Minister. [ Interruption ]

explanation: A narrow, checkable question: has he identified one family receiving the full $250 a fortnight. He attacks the questioner as flippant and recites the previous government's record; no family is named and no yes or no is given. A specific factual question dodged completely.
question: Has the Prime Minister identified one single New Zealand family that’s received the full $250 a fortnight that he promised them before the election?
statement: I think it’s quite interesting the member is so flippant about the efforts of this Government to help low and middle income working New Zealanders. It wasn’t deeply ideological to lift tax thresholds to help lots of people with lower tax. But what we know is that member spent too much, borrowed too much, for way too long, caused huge amounts of suffering, and he wants to get a go at doing it all again. Not going to happen.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on economic policy. She names the report (Royal Commission into Covid-19 Lessons Learned, released today), confirms economic policy is one of its four focus areas, and summarises its finding. The closing jab at those who 'minimise these errors' is a Civility/Focus matter, not a dodge — the question was squarely engaged.
question: What recent reports has she seen on economic policy?
statement: The final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Covid-19 Lessons Learned was released today. One of the four key areas it focuses on is economic policy. The royal commission observes that the COVID-19 pandemic was a substantial shock to the economy and the costliest event in terms of fiscal support in New Zealand in the past 40 years. We must learn lessons from the way this event was responded to, because these lessons must inform the Government’s response to the next natural disaster, global downturn, pandemic, or other economic shock. Denial is not an option. Mistakes were made in the economic response, and these mistakes were costly. Those who choose to minimise these errors are not well placed to learn from them.

explanation: Asked what the commission said about spending and fiscal stimulus. The answer reports exactly that: the timely/temporary/targeted test, that many programmes failed it, the $60b fund's 821 programmes, and the conclusion that stimulus ran too long. Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: What did the royal commission say about Government spending and fiscal stimulus during the pandemic?
statement: Well, it says that Treasury and Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment advice from the outset was that fiscal stimulus measures to address the consequences of the pandemic should be timely, temporary, and targeted. However, the royal commission found that many examples of Government spending, including the so-called shovel-ready infrastructure projects, did not meet these tests. The $60 billion COVID-19 Response and Recovery fund spanned 821 programmes, around half of which were not related to the pandemic, such as conservation programmes, additional public housing places, and school lunches. Many initiatives in the COVID fund extended well beyond the time of the pandemic, and some were baked in, including permanent increases to welfare benefits. As a result, the big increase in Government spending was highly stimulatory and went on for too long.

explanation: Asked what the commission said about the consequences of the stimulus. The answer gives the consequences the commission identified — house-price surge in 2021-22, worse than comparators, no review or cancellation of stimulus — including a direct quote. Fully responsive.
question: What did the royal commission say about the consequences of that stimulus?
statement: Well, it says that highly stimulatory fiscal policy, together with low interest rates, led to a surge in house prices in 2021 and 2022. House prices, I acknowledge, also rose in other countries but the commission points out that the increase was far more dramatic in New Zealand. This was avoidable. The commission says that fiscal policy set in 2020 received limited review and adjustment. It says, and I quote, “We are not aware of any sizeable component of the fiscal stimulus programme that was reviewed or cancelled to lessen the stimulus once the undesirability of further stimulus became clear.”

explanation: Asked what the commission said about Government debt. After one sentence of set-up, the answer gives the debt figures (18.6% to 38.7% of GDP) and quotes the commission's conclusion on the need to reduce public debt. The brief preamble does not stop it reaching the point.
question: What did the royal commission say about Government debt?
statement: Fiscal stimulus comes from increasing Government spending. In the circumstances, increased Government spending had to be borrowed for. As a result, New Zealand’s Government debt rose from 18.6 percent of GDP before the pandemic to 38.7 percent in the 2022/2023 fiscal year, obviously a very significant increase. The royal commission makes it clear that the large amount of debt accumulated during the pandemic means New Zealand is now in a weaker position to deal with the next large shock that comes along. The report concludes—and, again, I quote—“there is a pressing need to reduce public debt to provide a buffer for future pandemics or other economic shocks.” This Government agrees with that conclusion.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on tourism. She identifies the Tourism Satellite Account release and its headline figure ($46.6b for the year ending March 2025), plus visa-related data. The 'fix the basics' line is a talking point appended to an answer, not a substitute for one.
question: What recent reports has she seen on tourism in New Zealand?
statement: Data released last week shows New Zealand’s tourism sector continues to grow, driving billions of dollars into our economy.
