statement: Again, I don’t know how to be any clearer: we’ve had the Ministry of Health come out and say they did not adequately brief the Minister. Within a very quick and short period of time, the Minister responded by saying he wanted the functions of the Suicide Prevention Office to remain, and they will remain.

explanation: The same yes/no question put again, answered 'No.' One word, unambiguous, complete.
question: Was the Minister of Health or any other Minister in his Government briefed on the ministry’s proposals before they were made public?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked why officials described the director role going unfilled, roles being cut and the work absorbed elsewhere. The answer offers only a reassurance that the functions will remain — a repeat of the earlier line that addresses neither the officials' statements nor the 'why'.
question: Why did Ministry of Health officials just yesterday say that the role of the director of the Suicide Prevention Office will not be filled, other roles in the Suicide Prevention Office will be cut, and the work of the office would be integrated into other ministry work, which to most people sounds like the office is being wound up?
statement: Well, I can reassure you, the Minister has been very clear to say that the functions of the Suicide Prevention Office will remain.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that Ministry job cuts, including to the tobacco regulation team, will not increase youth smoking. No guarantee is given or refused; the response substitutes smokefree targets and past progress. Same subject area, but the request put to him is never engaged.
question: Will he guarantee that his Government’s proposal to cut jobs from the Ministry of Health, including from the tobacco regulation team, will not lead to an increase in youth smoking?
statement: We are determined as a Government to deliver on the smoke-free 2025 targets. As that member well knows, we’ve had good progress in the last 12 months, and we’re going to march towards a 5 percent daily smoker target under smoke-free 2025.

explanation: Asked what process was established for Ministers/Cabinet to review and approve the savings proposals. She lays out the process: Ministers tasked in late December, chief executives develop options, refinement via Budget bilaterals, Cabinet approves the full package. That is the process asked for, engaged squarely. Slightly short of complete on the 'review and approve' step for individual proposals rather than the package.
question: What process, if any, has she established for portfolio Ministers and Cabinet to review and approve the cost-saving proposals currently being consulted on by agencies through the Initial Baseline Exercise?
statement: Ministers were asked in late December to work with their agencies to develop credible savings options for Budget 2024. Chief executives were expected to exercise good judgment in putting forward savings proposals, and Ministers have worked with agencies to refine them. The savings exercise is an ongoing and iterative process, including through Budget bilaterals between myself and various Ministers. Cabinet will be asked to approve the full Budget package.

explanation: A yes/no question about her expectation of Ministers. Answered 'Yes.' One word, but it is the complete answer to what was asked.
question: Is it her expectation that Ministers will understand the full implications of their agencies’ final cost savings plans prior to Cabinet considering the Budget package, as set out in question time yesterday?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked (a) is she concerned cuts won't be finalised before Cabinet, and (b) how can colleagues reject proposals if the Budget is already settled. Neither is reached: she reframes into 'two things happening here', notes agencies routinely restructure, attributes some changes to the previous Government, and says agencies are consulting operationally. The concern is never stated and the timing conflict is never addressed.
question: Is she concerned, then, that agency cuts won’t be finalised prior to Cabinet considering Budget 2024, and how does she expect her colleagues to consider and reject those proposals if the Budget has already been finalised?
statement: Well, there’s two things happening here. The first is that agencies, as a matter of course, routinely, and have for many years made decisions to restructure their entities in order to focus on their core priorities and to drive efficiency. Some of the changes that are under way and change processes that are happening across the public service now are actually the result of reforms by the previous Government. For example, in the case of Health New Zealand, it was always an expectation that there would then be reductions in the number of roles at the Ministry of Health. The second thing that is happening here is that in some cases, agencies have made decisions at an operational level to begin change processes and to consult on those change processes.

explanation: Asked how the Minister of Health can understand the impact of cuts before Cabinet agrees the Budget when final decisions come in June. Response is 'I think I just answered that in my previous answer' — but the previous answer did not reach that point, so the deferral does not deliver an answer. It is brief and non-rhetorical rather than a talking-point pivot, which keeps it above the floor.
question: How can the Minister of Health meet her expectations to understand the impact of the Ministry of Health’s cuts prior to Cabinet agreeing the Budget when final decisions are not expected to come until June?
statement: Well, I think I just answered that in my previous answer.

explanation: Asked how she can claim colleagues are able to reject named proposals when those are finalised after Cabinet agrees the Budget. She gives a direct reason — entities have put forward proposals that Ministers have rejected, and will continue to. That engages the 'how can you say' core, though it sidesteps the specific timing objection and the named agencies.
question: How can she say that her colleagues are able to reject proposals to freeze hiring at Oranga Tamariki and Police, or cut jobs from the tobacco regulation team at Health or the Suicide Prevention Office, when these are being finalised after Cabinet agrees her Budget?
statement: Because many entities have put forward proposals that Ministers have rejected. That is happening, that has happened, and I suspect it will continue to happen.

explanation: Asked to confirm or deny that she will pursue cost cutting to fund tax cuts without knowing the impact. She does not engage at all, pivoting mid-sentence to the previous Government's spending record. A complete dodge into attack.
question: Is it not the case that she will pursue significant cost cutting to pay for her tax cuts package without knowing the full impact on the public, while leaving her colleagues to front the consequences of her decisions?
statement: I want to tell you about the impact it had on the public when that Government chose to increase spending—

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made in his portfolio. He names today's announcement on freshwater farm plans and what it signals. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements, if any, has he made in his portfolio?
statement: Today, the Minister of Agriculture and I announced our intention to improve freshwater farm plans to make them more cost-effective and pragmatic for farmers. I see freshwater farm plans as a key tool to support farmers to enhance the freshwater environment in the future, but the current system is too costly, too complex, and too inflexible. This announcement signals the Government’s intention to make farm plans fit for purpose and align to the particular circumstances of each farm and catchment.

explanation: Asked what changes to freshwater farm plans he is considering. He names them: reviewing certification and auditing requirements, and reducing duplication where farmers already hold equivalent plans. Squarely on the question.
question: What changes to freshwater farm plans is he considering?
statement: The sector has told us that the current system is rigid, with time and money needed to complete a farm plan not lining up with the level of risk for many farmers. Among other things, we will take a look at the certification and auditing requirements of the system, with a view to ensuring that future settings are justifiable on the basis of cost and environmental benefit. We will also make sure that we are doing as much as we can to reduce duplication in farm planning. Many farmers are already doing comprehensive farm plans that, in many cases, could easily be recognised as equivalent.

explanation: Asked what value an improved farm plan system will provide farmers. He states the value: plans targeted to each farm and catchment, potentially standing in place of local rules and consents. Answers the question asked.
question: What value will an improved farm plan system provide farmers?
statement: In addition to supporting and to protect and enhance the environment, we intend to develop a flexible but robust system where farm plans can be specifically targeted to the unique needs of each farm and catchment. Ideally, these plans can stand in the place of local rules and consents for a range of common farming activities.

explanation: Asked what he intends to do for farmers in regions where the system is already being implemented. He acknowledges those regions and the certainty problem, then offers only 'we may look into whether the current requirements could be paused'. He reaches the question but hedges at its core — no statement of what he will do.
question: What does he intend to do for farmers in areas where a freshwater farm plan system is already being implemented?
statement: The system roll-out began under the previous Government in parts of some regions, including the Waikato and Southland, where farmers have to put these plans or have them developed by early next year. We want to give as much certainty as possible to farmers as we work through these changes, especially those that may already be putting their plans together. As part of that, we may look into whether the current requirements to complete freshwater farm plans could be paused.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all the Government's policies and actions. Replies 'Āna, āna' — yes, yes — and affirms support for the Government's direction. An affirmative answer to a yes/no question; the added praise is padding, not evasion.
question: Does he stand by all the Government’s policies and actions?
statement: Āna, āna. Kei te tino tautoko i te anga whakamua o tō tātou Kāwanatanga, me ngā mihi matakoakoa ki tō tātou Pirīmia i āna kōrero tongarerewa i te Mane e hangā mai nei he whāinga mō tātou katoa.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements the Government made about shorter wait times for elective treatment. He names the announcement — the PM's health targets, including 95 percent of people waiting under four months for elective treatment. The closing rhetoric does not displace the answer.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made about shorter wait times for elective treatment?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Earlier this week, the Prime Minister launched ambitious health targets as part of the Government’s target suite. This will help improve the lives of all New Zealanders. One of these targets was shorter wait times for elective treatment. This target aims to see 95 percent of people wait less than four months for their elective treatments. This won’t be easy, but the Government is committed to improving the lives of all New Zealanders through better, more efficient public services. We look to deliver the public services that New Zealanders deserve.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that a 6.5% Customs cut won't cause airport queues, trade delays and more drug importation. The answer never says yes or no and never mentions Customs, borders or drugs — it pivots to 'walk and chew gum', wasteful spending, tax relief and growth, plus a jab at the questioner's party. A narrow, checkable ask ('will you guarantee X') left entirely untouched.
question: Will he guarantee that his Government’s proposal to cut 6.5 percent from the budget of Customs will not lead to longer lines at airports, delays for our importers and exporters, and more illicit drugs entering New Zealand?
statement: Well, what I can say to that member is that we finally have a Government that can walk and chew gum at the same time. We can end the wasteful spending, we can prioritise front-line services, we can deliver tax relief for low- and middle-income workers—folk that that member’s party used to care about—and we can make sure we can grow this economy.

explanation: The same guarantee asked again, split into three specific consequences. The answer is a three-item slogan (rebuild the economy, restore law and order, better public services) that engages none of them. 'What I can reassure that member is' substitutes a different reassurance for the one requested; the core is squarely avoided.
question: Will he guarantee that his proposal to cut 6.5 percent from the Customs budget won’t lead to longer times at airports, won’t lead to delays for our importers and exporters, and won’t lead to more illicit drugs entering New Zealand?
statement: What I can reassure that member is that this’ll be a Government that will rebuild our economy, restore law and order, and deliver better public services in health and education.

explanation: Asked what recent tax announcements she has made. The answer names the announcement directly — the Budget Policy Statement released two weeks ago — and states its content (personal income tax relief in the Budget). Directly and completely on the question asked; the added history about thresholds since 2010 is elaboration, not evasion.
question: What recent announcements has she made about tax?
statement: The answer to this question is that two weeks ago I released the Government’s Budget Policy Statement. This confirmed that there will be personal income tax relief in the Budget, and it noted that New Zealanders have not seen any changes to personal income rates and thresholds since 2010, apart from Labour’s introduction of a higher top tax rate. Now, for 14 years, people have been taxed more and more as their incomes have risen, much of that due to inflation. This Government will start to address that in Budget 2024.

explanation: Asked for the consequences of not adjusting tax brackets. The answer engages the question on its own terms, offering the median worker's earnings and tax share in 2011 versus today as the illustration of the consequence. Marked down because the record cuts off after the 2023 income figure without stating the corresponding tax share, so the consequence is set up but never landed. The opening swipe at opponents is a Civility matter and did not move the score.
question: What have been the consequences of not adjusting tax brackets?
statement: I can give the House an example, because I’m acutely aware that there are members of this House who adamantly oppose tax reduction for working people. In 2011, the median full-time wage and salary worker earned $48,000 and paid 15.5 percent of their income in tax. Today, the median full-time wage and salary worker earns $73,400.

explanation: Asked why the Government is concerned about fiscal drag. The answer opens with a remark about 'sensitivity' in the House, then begins 'The fiscal drag—' and the transcript ends. It turns toward the question rather than away from it, but nothing responsive was delivered on the record. Scored mid-low as an engagement that is unevidenced rather than a pivot; the truncation, not a dodge, is what caps it.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Why is the Government concerned about fiscal drag?
statement: Well, I note there’s a lot of sensitivity about the answers to these questions. The fiscal drag—

explanation: A yes/no question — will tax relief be inflationary? — answered 'No' in the first word, then supported (funded by reduced consumption and other revenue, inside a lower operating allowance, no extra borrowing). Direct and complete.
question: Will personal income tax relief in Budget 2024 be inflationary?
statement: No. Tax relief will be funded by reducing Government consumption and increasing revenue elsewhere, all sitting within the Budget 2024 operating allowance. Furthermore, that allowance will be lower than the allowance set by the previous Government. This means that tax relief is affordable, we will not be borrowing extra to pay for it, and tax relief will not add to inflationary pressures.

explanation: The standard 'does he stand by all statements and actions' opener, answered 'Yes' outright. The subsequent list of climate targets and policies is volunteered material and does not displace the answer — the question was reached in the first word.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our announcement of nine priority targets, including reducing New Zealand’s net greenhouse gas emissions to align with our 2050 net zero climate goal. Of course, we’re going to achieve that by fast-track consenting so we can get more renewable energy, like windfarms, built, we’re going to remove the GE ban to empower our world-class agriscientists to actually manage methane emissions down, and, of course, we’re going to restore integrity to the emissions trading scheme.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by having called the Commission's draft methane advice 'speculation'. 'I don't think I expressed it in those terms' contests the premise, which is a legitimate way of engaging rather than a pivot, but it leaves the actual question — does he stand by the position — unanswered. He neither affirms nor withdraws the view, only the wording. Half credit: the question is addressed at its edge, not at its core.
question: Does the Prime Minister stand by his answer to me at question time yesterday that the Climate Change Commission’s draft advice on biogenic methane is “speculation”?
statement: I don’t think I expressed it in those terms.

explanation: Asked what he understands the Commission's role to be; the answer states it: providing important advice to the Government on the state of climate change in New Zealand. Thin, but thinness is Specificity — the question asked for his understanding of the role and he gave it directly.
question: What does he understand the role of the Climate Change Commission to be?
statement: Well, it provides important advice to the Government about the state of climate change in New Zealand.

explanation: A compound question: does he agree with the Commission's statement that there has been no notable change in the physical science on methane, plus a rhetorical gravity jab. He explicitly declines the second part, then substantively contradicts the first — the science 'has changed over the last five years... the last 10 years'. That is a disagreement in effect, though never framed as an answer to the quoted claim, and the Commission's specific statement is never confronted. Partial engagement with the core.
question: Does he then agree with the Climate Change Commission, who said on Monday, and I quote, “there has not be an important or notable change in the understanding of the physical science on methane and how it warms the atmosphere”; or is he to extend his logic also to reopen the science on, say, gravity?
statement: I don’t know how to answer the last part of that question, but what I would just say is that we are determined to make sure that we update the science base on methane. It has changed over the last five years. It’s changed over the last 10 years. It will change in the next five years and in the next 10 years. It’s important that we get a common base of understanding of science knowledge so we can set the right targets.

explanation: Asked what he considers wrong with the Commission's methane science. 'Nothing particularly' answers it directly and, given the earlier pressing, unhelpfully for his own position — then explains the two reviews as answering different questions. A blunt, complete response to exactly what was asked.
question: What does the Prime Minister consider is wrong with the Climate Change Commission’s science on methane?
statement: Nothing particularly. We have two reviews going on, answering slightly different questions to make sure that we get a common understanding of the science base.

explanation: Asked why an elective target matters. He gives the reason directly — wait times have deteriorated from 97% to 62% within four months — which is squarely the 'why'. Answered.
question: Why is an elective target important?
statement: This target was chosen because the treatment times that we used to expect and achieve just six years ago have reduced. Wait times for elective treatments have turned into a highly stressful experience, with patients having no certainty as to when they will receive access to the care that they need. As of September 2023, only 62 percent of patients waited less than four months for their elective treatments, down significantly from around 97 percent in late 2017. This is not good enough, and we want to deliver better care.

explanation: Asked whether the target is too ambitious. He engages the premise head-on: it is deliberately not meant to be easy, and he says why a stretch target is the point. That is an answer (effectively 'no, and intentionally so'), not a dodge, though he never quite concedes or rejects the feasibility framing.
question: Is this target too ambitious given the current state of the health system?
statement: This target is not meant to be easy to achieve. We’re not here to do what is easy; we’re here to do what is needed. Despite the very hard work of our front-line health workforce over the past six years, our wait times have continued to grow. That’s why we are taking a different approach by putting targets back at the forefront of our decision making. These targets will direct attention and resources and set a clear agenda for where our health system should be heading.

explanation: Asked how progress will be tracked. He names the mechanism — quarterly reporting by health agencies, first result for July–September 2024. Direct answer after a one-sentence preamble.
question: How will the Government track progress against this target?
statement: We last achieved 95 percent between early 2015 and the end of 2017, so we know it’s possible. The health agencies will report results each quarter, with the first quarterly result expected to be for the July to September 2024 period. This reporting will be robust to ensure we can target resources appropriately.

explanation: A standard 'does he stand by all his statements and actions' question. He says 'Yes, I do stand beside my statements and actions'. The acknowledgement and the list of priorities are surplus, but the question itself is answered.
question: Does he stand by all his statements and actions?
statement: First, can I just take a moment to acknowledge how triggering the conversations have been around suicide for many people in New Zealand who have been affected by suicide in their families and their communities. Yes, I do stand beside my statements and actions, specifically that mental health and suicide prevention is a priority for this Government. My priorities for mental health, addictions, and suicide are to increase access to timely mental health, addiction, and suicide prevention support; number two, to grow the mental health and addiction and suicide prevention workforce; and, three, strengthen focus on prevention and early intervention.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement that the Suicide Prevention Office would not be cut. Answer opens with 'Yes' and then addresses the substance (5.5 to 6.5 FTE, office remaining open). Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by his statement this week insisting that the Suicide Prevention Office would not be a victim of the Government’s cost cutting?
statement: Yes. Look, can I take the opportunity to clear something up. I saw the change document for the first time, with the officials taking me through it, on Monday. They have taken me through it and showed, with the change proposal, the proposal is actually to go from 5.5 fulltime-equivalents (FTE) in the Suicide Prevention Office, which it currently is, to 6.5 in the change proposal, which is only a proposal but it will increase capacity and capability in that office that will remain open. It has been misleading: the Public Service Association put out a press release that it was to close; I was never informed of that, and it was not to close.

explanation: Asked why his officials repeated the same advice to media. He never explains the officials' conduct — he restates what he was shown on Monday and what he was not told. He touches the surrounding dispute and concedes he wasn't sufficiently briefed, so it is not a pure pivot, but the actual 'why did they' is left unanswered.
question: Why did his health officials double down on their advice to the media yesterday, saying that the number of roles to be disestablished and the number of roles to be integrated were, essentially, exactly the same as what they advised last week?
statement: Well, in response to that question, I can only go by the assurance I got when I was given the change proposal for the first time on Monday. They took me through it and showed me where it has gone from 5.5 FTE to 6.5 FTE. I want to be very clear—and the officials have acknowledged I wasn’t sufficiently briefed—I was not told it was to close. I’ve always been very clear. There’s been a lot of discussion in the sector that is critical of the Suicide Prevention Office. One major commentator has called for it to close. I do not want it to close.

explanation: Asked for the practical difference between retaining only the functions and closure. He answers a different question — his own view of the office's leadership and his intent not to delete it — and never addresses the distinction or the unfilled roles put to him.
question: What is the practical difference between retaining only the functions of the office and closure, given that the Prime Minister has just confirmed in the House today that there are current roles that will no longer be filled?
statement: I’ve been very clear—and I was even interviewed by Jack Tame on Q+A—that I’ve been disappointed by the Suicide Prevention Office; I think it’s lacked real leadership. The sector has been disappointed. But I’ve never been of the view to delete it; I’ve always been of the view to, actually, how we can give it clear expectations, manage it, targets, and goals. As part of the review of the Suicide Action Plan that I’m due to take in the next couple of months, I will be doing that with the Suicide Prevention Office.

explanation: Asked why he asked officials to publicly apologise. He rejects the premise outright: he did not ask them to. A one-line denial of the premise is a complete engagement with the question, not an evasion.
question: Why did he ask his officials to publicly apologise?
statement: I did not ask the officials to publicly apologise.

explanation: Asked why officials are apologising when they are implementing 6.5 percent savings. He supplies a reason of a kind — the savings programme requires quality services to be maintained — which speaks to the cuts half of the question but never to why an apology was made. Partial.
question: Why are officials publicly apologising when they’re actually just following Government directions to find 6.5 percent funding cuts across health?
statement: Well, that’s very simple, because the fiscal sustainability programme clearly states to find savings while still delivering quality public services, and delivering a Suicide Prevention Office is a quality public service.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the Prime Minister's benefit-duration statement. 'Yes, in its full context', followed by the source she is relying on. Direct and complete.
question: Does she agree with the Prime Minister’s recent statement that the average adult now is on the benefit for 13 years on average, and the under-25s are on the benefit for an average of 24 years?
statement: Yes, in its full context. The Prime Minister was referring to independent evidence produced by Taylor Fry in 2022, which reported that someone on the jobseeker benefit is expected to spend 13 years on benefit throughout their lifetime. The same evidence shows someone on a youth benefit is expected to spend 24 years on benefits throughout their lifetime.

explanation: Asked whether she is aware the report says only 0.5 percent are expected to spend 24 years on a benefit. She never engages the 0.5 percent figure or says whether she is aware — she pivots to a talking point about any such duration being unacceptable. Clear dodge of a narrow factual question.
question: Is she aware that the Taylor Fry report she just quoted actually says that only 0.5 percent of people on the benefit are expected to spend 24 years on a benefit throughout their lifetime?
statement: Anyone that spends up to 24 years of their future lifetime on welfare is a major issue for this Government, and that’s why we are focused on fixing it.

explanation: Asked why the claim continues to be repeated. She answers directly — 'Because that's what the Taylor Fry report has said' — and restates the basis. Whether that characterisation is accurate is a Veracity matter; the question was engaged. The later pivot to social investment does not undo the answer already given.
question: Why, then, has the Prime Minister and the Minister continued to say that under-25s are on the benefit for an average of 24 years?
statement: Because that’s what the Taylor Fry report has said. For someone who goes on to youth payment or youth parent payment, unfortunately, the future lifetime expected that they will spend on welfare is up to 24 years. That is a disaster from anyone’s book and why we are focused, with a social investment approach, on where the group have the highest risk of poorer life outcomes and interrupting it. We are not interested in allowing young people in this country, whether it’s a small number or a large number, spending that amount of time stuck.

explanation: Asked (a) whether she was aware the modelling includes seven additional risk factors and (b) why she set no target to reduce those factors. She describes the Taylor Fry modelling in general terms and then pivots to 'every one of those people counts'. The awareness question is brushed past and the 'why no target on risk factors' core is never reached.
question: Is she aware that for that tiny 0.5 percent proportion of people, the modelling has taken into account seven additional risk factors, including acute unplanned care from a public hospital, interaction with Oranga Tamariki, and exclusion from school, and, if so, why didn’t she create a target to reduce those risk factors, as opposed to just getting 50,000 people off the benefit?
statement: The Taylor Fry modelling is based on really careful analysis of the IDI data, which is why it is so rich. It looks at people’s past outcomes with the intention of trying to disrupt that from happening in the future. Whether it’s one person, whether it’s 100, or whether it’s 100,000, every one of those people counts, to me, and I am unwilling to sit by and let them get stuck.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: is she confident in the accuracy of the '24 years on a benefit' claim? She re-explains the context in which the claim was made and asserts the report justifies prioritising the group, but never says whether she stands by the figure's accuracy. Pivot to talking points on a squarely-put factual question.
question: Is she confident in the accuracy of her and the Prime Minister’s comments that the average young person is spending 24 years on a benefit?
statement: As I said in my primary answer, the context in which that was given was a discussion about long-term welfare dependency—the horrendous change that we have seen under the last six years with a significant increase in young people going on to welfare and staying on it—and the Taylor Fry report was one piece of the evidence that shows why we must prioritise this group.

explanation: Asked for a specific commitment (to state that only 0.5 percent are predicted to spend 24 years on a benefit). She substitutes a different commitment — 'we will do our best to get them off welfare' — and never accepts or declines the one asked for. A plain 'no, I won't' would have scored high; this avoids answering either way.
question: Will she commit, going forward, to be clear that only 0.5 percent of people are predicted to spend 24 years on the benefit, as per the Taylor Fry report?
statement: What I will commit to this House is that for every single person, we will do our best to get them off welfare and into work, because that’s what improves their life outcomes. Whether it’s one year or 24 years, it’s not good enough.

explanation: Asked what target the Government has set. He gives it: a reduction of 20,000 in the number of victims of assault, robbery or sexual assault. Direct and complete.
question: What target has the Government set for a reduction in violent crime?
statement: The Prime Minister announced on Monday that the Government has set a target to see a reduction in the number of people who are the victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault by 20,000. By setting a focused and ambitious target to reduce the number of victims of crime, we can focus attention, resources, and accountability towards achieving better results.

explanation: Asked why the Government wants the reduction. He gives reasons — safety in homes and communities, 185,000 victims, not regarded as acceptable. The jab at the previous Government is surplus but the question's core is answered head-on (the swipe is a Focus/Civility matter, not this one).
question: Why does this Government want to see a reduction in violent crime?
statement: It’s important that all New Zealanders feel safe in their homes and in their communities. It’s estimated that around 185,000 Kiwis or 4.4 percent of the population are victims of an assault, robbery, or sexual assault, and we don’t regard that as normal or acceptable. The previous Government targeted reducing the prison population while violent crime increased. We have changed the target to reduce the number of victims of crime.

explanation: Asked what steps have already been taken. He lists steps taken: gang legislation package, expanded police search powers, rehabilitation access, defunding cultural reports. Squarely responsive.
question: What steps have already been taken to help reach the target to see a reduction in violent crime?
statement: Well, the Government’s already taken a number of steps, including the introduction of a significant legislative package aimed at tackling gangs; we’re boosting the powers of police to search gang members and other high-risk offenders, in addition to providing more access to rehabilitation for people on demand; and we’ve stopped funding for cultural reports.

explanation: Asked what steps come next. He names forthcoming steps: restoring three strikes, tools for repeat youth offenders including military-style academies, limiting sentencing discounts. Directly on the question asked.
question: What steps are next to help reach the target to see a reduction in victims of violent crime?
statement: We’re restoring the three-strikes legislation that the previous Government repealed, showing that we will not tolerate repeat violent offending in our communities. We’ll give judges additional tools to deal with serious repeat youth offenders, including military-style academies. We’ll also limit excessive sentencing discounts so penalties actually fit the crime. There are, of course, many factors that have contributed to an increase in violent crime in our communities, but one of the immediate tools available to us is to restore real consequences for crime.

explanation: A two-part question — when she received the briefing, and what she did. She gives the date (23 February 2024) and describes her response (noted the changes, commissioned a review, added funding). The blame-shifting to the previous Government is padding, but both halves are engaged.
question: When did she receive the briefing titled “Changes to Equipment and Modification Services and flexible funding to manage Whaikaha expenditure” and what actions did she take upon receiving the briefing?
statement: I received the briefing on 23 February 2024. I noted that Whaikaha was making changes which were needed to reduce its forecast deficit as recommended, and, as I have said multiple times, these issues are inherited from the previous Labour Government, and I am taking urgent steps to address the situation with a review. We have also put extra funding in to support Whaikaha through to the end of this financial year, and we have signalled that Whaikaha will get more money in the next Budget.

explanation: Asked to reconcile the 22/23 February briefing with earlier answers implying she first knew on 14 March. She offers the reconciliation directly: 22 February was initiatives under consideration, 14 March was confirmation of implementation. The trailing material about the communications plan drifts, but the core is addressed (whether the reconciliation holds up is Veracity/Rigor, not this).
question: How does she rationalise that with answers she gave in the House that suggest the first time she knew about the changes to reduce flexibility of disability support services was when she signed out a briefing on 14 March?
statement: I certainly received the briefing on 22 February that these were initiatives that Whaikaha was considering, and then they confirmed on 14 March that they would be implementing those changes. They also informed me in that briefing that before implementing these changes, Whaikaha had a comprehensive communications and engagement plan outlining the changes being implemented. They also said they had tailored messages for each audience focused on ensuring people needing disability support the most continued to receive support.

explanation: Asked why she only formally advised the finance Minister on 20 March, after the changes were announced. She answers in the form of a reason but points at what was discussed at a 22nd meeting, which does not reach the delay being asked about. It engages the timing question without landing on it — partial.
question: Why did she only formally advise the finance Minister of eligibility changes that resulted from Whaikaha’s funding shortfall on 20 March, two days after the announcement was made and implemented, as she has confirmed in written parliamentary questions No. 3593 and 3599?
statement: Because we were discussing Budget issues at that meeting on the 22nd.

explanation: Asked why it took until 25 March to go to Cabinet. She explains her understanding at the time — Whaikaha had initiatives underway, was working with Treasury, and forecast a deficit within the threshold she could manage — which is a responsive account of why she did not escalate sooner, though it never explicitly addresses the 25 March date itself.
question: Why, given she was first aware of the proposed changes on 22 or 23 February, did it take her till 25 March to first go to Cabinet, considering over 26,000 carers have been impacted by these changes?
statement: Because in that paper on 22 February, Whaikaha had outlined two initiatives that they were taking to reduce its projected deficit. They also outlined that they were working with Treasury to see if their bid for cost pressures could be considered early. Also, in late February and late January, Whaikaha had informed me that their updated forecast showed that they would be within 2 percent of the threshold, which is manageable by me as a Minister, and they were working to reduce it to a zero deficit.

explanation: A direct yes/no on whether the stated timeline is correct. She answers 'No, I'm not saying that' and then gives her own version of the sequence. Unambiguous answer to the question put.
question: Is the Minister therefore saying that this time line is correct: that she first became aware of Whaikaha’s funding issues on 15 December 2023, was briefed on proposed changes on 22 February, signed out changes on 14 March, the changes were then announced and implemented with immediate effect on 18 March, but that she didn’t act till 25 March?
statement: No. No, I’m not saying that. I am saying that throughout this process, Whaikaha were updating me on their financial situation. In January, they updated me that they had reduced the deficit and they were working to bring it down to zero. In February, they put forward initiatives that would further reduce the deficit. In March, they weren’t able to fulfil that reduction, and therefore it was discussed at a budget meeting.

explanation: Asked how she can claim not to be borrowing for the tax package given her FEC admission that it is all funded from one pool. She engages the question head-on — 'Because I am not borrowing for our tax package' — and starts on the 'because what we are doing is—' explanation before being cut off by interruption. The core assertion is answered directly, but the 'how can you reconcile it' part is never reached, so it lands as a restatement rather than a resolution.
question: How can she possibly say that she is not borrowing to pay for her tax package when she confirmed to FEC today that, ultimately, it is all funded from the same place?
statement: Because I am not borrowing for our tax package. Because what we are doing is—[Interruption] They either want the answer or they don’t, I guess.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with a list of five specific fiscal promises, plus a rhetorical barb about which she intends to break. She answers the substantive half squarely — 'I agree that we will keep our commitments' — but does not engage promise-by-promise, and the bulk of the reply pivots to the previous government's record. Half engaged, half talking points.
question: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, who promised to achieve a surplus in 2026-27, reduce Government debt by $3.4 billion compared with the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, not borrow for tax cuts, not cut front-line services, and introduce no new taxes, and are there any promises she doesn’t intend to break?
statement: Not only do I agree that we will keep our commitments, what I also agree is that it is a very good thing that this Government was elected, because if it wasn’t, we would be continuing as a country down a path of deepening structural deficit, of escalating debt, of wasteful spending, and of high inflation, and I am so glad that the adults are back in charge.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made. He names them: the Wairarapa woolshed meeting with McClay and Butterick, and 20+ more nationwide. Directly responsive to a broad question.
question: What recent announcements has he made?
statement: In line with recent announcements, on Monday, myself alongside Minister McClay and local Wairarapa MP Mike Butterick embarked upon our first of our nationwide woolshed meetings, in the Wairarapa. We met with a significant turnout. Not only will we be outlining Government plans and priorities, we will also be seeking feedback. This Government is actually committed to listening to our farmers, primary sector, and rural communities. Over the next few months, we will be undertaking over 20 of these meetings, from Northland through to Southland. Of special interest to me is seeking input in relation to reviving New Zealand’s strong wool sector.

explanation: Asked what engagements he has had with the sector. He names the engagement — convening commercial and farming leadership — and what came of it. Squarely on the question.
question: What engagements has he had with the sector?
statement: Recently, I convened a meeting of key industry leadership. These individuals came from both the commercial sector and, crucially, within farming leadership. This is a group that has, for far too long, had their views poorly canvassed. From this meeting, I have tasked this group with establishing a pathway to a united and recognised industry voice. They are also tasked with exploring alternative pathways to market, capable of delivering much higher returns back behind the farm gate.

explanation: Asked what other actions he is taking. He answers with an action: leading a wool manufacturing delegation to the IWTO conference in Adelaide. Direct and complete for the question as posed.
question: What other actions is he taking?
statement: Next week, I’m taking New Zealand wool to the world. I will be leading a delegation of New Zealand wool manufacturing businesses to the International Wool Textile Organisation (IWTO) Conference in Adelaide. We aim to capitalise on the significant increased trend back towards natural and sustainable fibres. These end uses span from traditional carpets and upholstery to exciting new innovations like 3D-printed acoustics and pigments from wools, broken down into their component parts. Only by increasing demand in high-value end uses will we lift returns to our farmers.

explanation: Asked what benefit this will bring. He states the benefit — first-time NZ wool feature at IWTO, showcasing to an international audience, contributing to the export-doubling goal. Answers the question asked.
question: What benefit will this bring?
statement: This is the first time, actually, that New Zealand wool has been specifically featured at the IWTO—it is quite a big deal. This represents a significant opportunity to showcase the attributes of New Zealand wool and the innovation of New Zealand’s wool manufacturing capability to a large international audience. I am determined that the New Zealand wool sector will make a significant contribution to deliver on the coalition Government’s agreement of doubling our exports in the next decade.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: does she agree with the quoted Our Land 2024 finding that an extractive approach to land puts the economy, food resilience and ecosystems at risk — and if not, why not. She agrees with a softened substitute ('we need to care for our land') and pivots to 'a balanced approach', never affirming or denying the actual proposition about extraction. Gestures at the question without reaching its core.
question: Does she agree with advice from officials in the Our Land 2024 report that “An extractive approach to land reduces nature’s ability to sustain itself and provide for us, putting our economy and livelihoods, food system resilience, natural ecosystems, and quality of life at risk”; if not, why not?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker, and I thank the member for her question. I agree that we need to care of our land and our natural ecosystems. This Government absolutely believes that taking a balanced approach is necessary to best support our economy and livelihoods, food system resilience, natural ecosystems, and quality of life.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned that fast-track will let extractive industries bypass the RMA, Wildlife Act, Conservation Act and EEZ Act. She declines plainly and gives the reason: the bill is before select committee so comment would be inappropriate. A clear, complete refusal — not a dodge. Marked below a substantive answer only because the ground for declining is asserted rather than the question engaged.
question: Is she concerned that extractive industries will soon be able to bypass the environmental protections in New Zealand law, including the Resource Management Act, the Wildlife Act, the Conservation Act, and the exclusive economic zone Act through the Government’s proposed fast-track process?
statement: The fast-track consenting bill is before the select committee at this time and so it would be inappropriate for me to make any comment on that.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question: what advice, if any, was she invited to give Cabinet on the environmental risks of fast-tracking. The reply says the member is interested in the report and that future decisions will be informed by its data — it never touches whether she was invited, or what she said. A specific question completely sidestepped, with no acknowledgement that it was.
question: What advice, if any, was she invited to provide to Cabinet on the environmental risks of allowing extractive industries to fast track projects which are likely to harm natural ecosystems?
statement: I know that the member is very interested in the report and the data that is in the report and, absolutely, policies and decisions that we will be making in the future will be informed by the data and the information that is in this report.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned that an Environment Minister outside Cabinet and no environment committee means environmental impacts get insufficient weight. Answer opens 'No, I'm not' and then explains why. Direct and complete.
question: Is she concerned that having a Minister for the Environment outside Cabinet, and no environmental Cabinet committee, means that considerations about the environmental impact of laws and policies are not being given proper weight in the Government’s decision making?
statement: No, I’m not. As a Government, we are absolutely committed to protecting the resources, and this simply shows that we have a range of Ministers that are interested in environmental factors. We will be taking an evidence-based approach to our decision making. So we welcome this report and the data that’s within it that will inform our decisions going forward.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned at being left out of decision-making on the Fast-track Approvals Bill. Answer: 'Not at all. I've been very involved in the process.' Squarely answered; whether the claim is accurate is a Veracity matter, not this one.
question: Is she concerned that she has been left out of the decision-making process in the Government’s Fast-track Approvals Bill, despite other Ministers being given the power to override legislation that is her ministerial responsibility?
statement: Not at all. I’ve been very involved in the process, and we are consulting widely and, as we work together as a Cabinet, I’ve said that there is a wide range of Ministers who have important interest in the environment, and I’m pleased to be one adding to those voices.

explanation: Asked what MSD advice informed the 50,000-by-2030 jobseeker target. She confirms advice exists, declines to go through it citing time, and names one strand of it (the rise in jobseeker recipients and reversing that trend). That is a sliver of the answer plus a partial refusal to give the rest — it touches the question without answering what was asked.
question: What advice has she received from the Ministry of Social Development that informed the Government target of reducing jobseeker benefits by 50,000 by 2030?
statement: I’ve received lots of advice from the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) to inform the ambitious target of ensuring more New Zealanders reap the rewards and opportunities a job provides. It’s not possible to go through all the advice in the time to answer an oral question, including advice about the substantial increase in jobseeker benefit recipients over recent years and how the target means reversing this trend.

explanation: Asked what she recently announced on curriculum and assessment. She names the announcement (changes to the NCEA Change Programme) and states the concrete decision — a two-year delay pending the curriculum. Some framing about priorities, but the core of the question is reached and answered.
question: What recent announcements has she made on curriculum and assessment?
statement: Last week, I announced significant changes to the NCEA Change Programme that has been under way since 2020. It is a priority for this Government to ensure that we have a world-leading curriculum. This document should be the foundation of a high-performing education system supporting teachers to excel and learners to reach their potential. The current approach puts the cart before the horse, designing assessments before having a curriculum in place, and it is not best practice to design assessment before knowing what is to be assessed. Curriculum is the priority so that we can then deliver well-designed assessment standards that we can have confidence in. And to achieve better public services, I will be delaying the NCEA Change Programme by two years while we complete the curriculum.

explanation: Asked what feedback she received. She characterises the feedback as overwhelming support and cites two named sources with quotes. Directly responsive to exactly what was asked.
question: What feedback has she received on this announcement?
statement: The support for this announcement from principals, parents, unions, and teachers alike has been overwhelming. The Post Primary Teachers’ Association president Chris Abercrombie was quoted in the New Zealand Herald this week saying, “It’s important that we get a really good curriculum base … good assessment folds out of good curriculum.”, while Dr Nina Hood, founder of The Education Hub, agreed that the curriculum refresh needs to be finalised before redeveloping NCEA to ensure that it was “a robust and fit for purpose qualification.”

explanation: Asked how the announcement will lift student achievement. She gives a stated mechanism — a knowledge-rich curriculum as a central resource guiding assessment design, plus nationwide consistency. The causal account is thin, but thinness is Specificity; the question was engaged rather than dodged.
question: How will this announcement lift student achievement?
statement: Parents want to know that their children have every opportunity to succeed, and success starts with strong foundations. In addition to teaching the basics brilliantly in our primary and intermediate schools, this Government has a laser focus on delivering a knowledge-rich curriculum to all students, right up to year 13. This decision will lift student achievement by delivering a knowledge-rich world-leading curriculum which acts as a central resource for teachers and a crucial tool to guide assessment and qualification design. The decision will ensure consistency across the country so that every child, no matter where they live or attend school, will have access to the same knowledge at each year level.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen. She names the Education Review Office report into the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum and summarises its findings. Directly answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the curriculum?
statement: I’ve seen the recent Education Review Office report into the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum. This report highlights issues within the New Zealand histories curriculum but that are also issues experienced across all curriculum areas—high level, vague, and lacking in specificity is not what the sector wants. The report shows that teachers want a more explicit curriculum with more off the shelf material and resources. Teachers are the most valuable resource that we have, and I will be working at pace to deliver what they need to experience success in the classroom, lift student achievement, and get this Government on track to meet our ambitious targets and deliver better public services.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen about the economy. She names the Reserve Bank monetary policy committee's OCR decision and reports its content. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent reports has she seen about the economy?
statement: Yesterday, I saw that the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee agreed to leave the official cash rate at 5.5 percent. The committee noted that consumer price inflation is currently above the 1 to 3 percent target range and that a restrictive monetary policy stance remains necessary at this time to bring inflation back within the band.

explanation: Asked when inflation returns to the 1-3 percent band. After a preamble about the cost of living crisis she states the answer: the committee is confident of a return within this calendar year. The timing question is actually reached.
question: When will inflation be back within the 1 to 3 percent target?
statement: New Zealand has had a cost of living crisis in recent years, with inflation being over 7 percent for most of 2022. Inflation has been falling since then, and the monetary policy committee is confident that inflation will return to within the 1 to 3 percent band in this calendar year. It is also consistent with the economic outlook Treasury published alongside the Budget Policy Statement two weeks ago.

explanation: Asked whether fiscal policy can have an inflationary impact. Opens with 'Yes' and then gives the conditions under which it does. A direct, complete answer.
question: Can fiscal policy have an inflationary impact?
statement: Yes. Strong growth in Government spending can have an inflationary impact when the economy is operating above capacity and interest rates are restrictive. Recent history gives us a very salient example of exactly that. The issue of the interaction between fiscal policy and monetary was discussed at the recent monetary policy committee meeting. On the basis of the forecasts in the half-year update and the commitments outlined by the Government in the recent Budget Policy Statement, the committee noted that Government spending is expected to decline as a share of the economy.

explanation: Asked whether the battle against inflation has been won. Answers 'No, I would not say that' and explains why not. Direct and unambiguous.
question: Has the battle against inflation been won?
statement: No, I would not say that. While the Reserve Bank is making progress in the battle against inflation, it still currently remains outside the target band, and further work is required to keep future inflation near the 2 percent mid-point. In the Budget Policy Statement, the Government signalled a policy of ongoing fiscal consolidation to bring revenue and expenses back into balance and also to support monetary policy to bring inflation within target and maintain it there. We want to see inflation continuing to come down so that interest rates can eventually follow them, giving New Zealanders cost of living relief and allowing the economy to start growing again.

explanation: A two-part question. Part one — did she tell FEC the Government would borrow more — is answered flatly: 'No, I did not say that', with her account of what she did say. Part two — how much the Government intends to borrow — gets no figure, only a pointer to page 45 of the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update, which engages the question without answering it. The attack on the questioner's paraphrasing and interrupting is a Civility matter and did not lower the score; scored down only for the unanswered second half.
question: Can she confirm that she told the Finance and Expenditure Committee this morning that the Government would be borrowing more in the future, and how much is the Government intending to borrow?
statement: No, I did not say that. I checked the transcripts, and, as has become a habit from this member, she’s paraphrased me in a way that is inaccurate. When we read the transcript, we find that the reason that she may not have heard my actual words is that she was interrupting continuously. In fact, what the case is is that what I said was, yes, we will be borrowing, that should not—[Interruption] In fact, what I said was that, yes, we would be borrowing. That should not be a revelation to the member, because, since the dawn of time, Governments have borrowed in order to finance their activities. If the member wants information about the bond issuance that the Government is doing over the forecast period and wants to learn a bit more about how that works, she can go to the Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update on page 45, where it outlines those intentions.

explanation: Asked a binary counterfactual: would day-to-day borrowing be higher or lower absent interest deductibility and the tax package. She never says higher or lower. The response pivots to the debt-to-GDP goal, the questioner's own past comments, and a comparison of operating allowances. Despite the aside that she is 'trying to help the member with the answer', the core of a narrow question is left untouched.
question: Would the borrowing for day-to-day costs, as confirmed by the Minister in the Finance and Expenditure Committee (FEC) today, be higher or lower if she had not restored interest deductibility and was not pursuing her tax cut package?
statement: This Government has set a clear goal of having net core Crown debt reduce as a proportion of GDP, in stark contrast with other members in this House, including the one who just asked a question, who said that she would be comfortable with debt increasing. So the position we have is a member opposite who is concerned, suddenly, about structural deficits, and what I would point out to her is that if the Government continued the pattern of extraordinary ineffective spending that has been the case in recent years, the structural deficit and, therefore, borrowing would have to grow considerably. I can also say—[Interruption] I am trying to help the member with the answer to the question—that we have committed to a lower operating allowance than that committed to by the previous Government.

explanation: Asked whether she accepts debt would be at least $11 billion lower under a specified counterfactual. She does engage the counterfactual, arguing it is not coherent to assume the tax relief away while holding the spending savings fixed — that is a rejection of the premise, not a pivot. But she never says whether she accepts the figure, and much of the answer is programme rhetoric and a jab at Labour. Partial engagement, core left unresolved.
question: Does she accept that if she did not restore interest deductibility or pursue tax cuts, debt would be at least $11 billion lower, with all things being equal?
statement: Well, with all things being equal, we would be continuing to plough billions more dollars into wasteful programmes. And the deal we did with New Zealanders was this: we said we’re going to spend their money more effectively, we’re going to reduce the amount of money on back-office bureaucracy, we’re going to stop subsidies for private firms to decarbonise, and we’re going to take those savings and we’re going to invest them in tax relief. What the member now wants the House to accept is that we would do one without the other. Actually, if she’s saying that Labour’s suddenly woken up and thinks savings are a good idea, then what a great revelation that is!

explanation: Asked whether she accepts a specific ANZ economist's counterfactual claim about offsetting the drivers of higher debt. She confirms only that she has seen ANZ's response and reports a different finding from it — that the fiscal track is more restrictive than the last Government's. That answers an adjacent question, not the one asked; the proposition put to her is never accepted or rejected.
question: Does she accept that ANZ senior economist Miles Workman is correct that there is a counterfactual that if the Government did not deliver those tax cuts, and cut spending as it says it will, it would offset the economic drivers of higher debt, as reported in Stuff?
statement: I have seen the ANZ’s response to the Budget policy update, in which it identified that the fiscal track and the approach being taken by the incoming Government is more restrictive on spending than the last Government.

explanation: Asked whether MSD recommended the 50,000 target and, if not, who did. The answer says scenarios were looked at and that she is proud to have landed on 50,000 — the passive framing never names MSD or anyone else, so neither half of a narrow factual question is answered.
question: Did the Ministry of Social Development recommend the target of 50,000, and, if not, who did?
statement: A number of scenarios have been looked at in terms of coming up with a target. We’ve balanced it with being really ambitious in terms of supporting the number of people into employment, and I’m really proud to have landed on 50,000.

explanation: Asked whether jobseekers with a health condition or disability will be excluded from the 50,000 reduction. "We don't discriminate" functions as an implicit "no" and carries a reason, but she never states plainly that this group is included, so the core is only reached obliquely.
question: Will those on jobseeker support - health condition or disability be excluded from the proposed 50,000 reduction; if not, why not?
statement: All job seekers deserve the same opportunities to get support and service to focus them on the rewards that work provides. We don’t discriminate. We want to use every single day that is available to support people towards work.

explanation: Asked how she intends to cut work-ready jobseeker numbers by nearly half while unemployment rises. She engages the tension by accepting the economic conditions and points to a "far more active" MSD, which is a mechanism of a kind, but the "how, given rising unemployment" core is gestured at rather than answered.
question: How does she intend to reduce the amount of people on jobseeker support - work ready by nearly 50 percent at a time when unemployment is expected to rise?
statement: I accept that we are in really challenging economic conditions that we have inherited as a Government, but I don’t shy away from the fact that every person who is either on jobseeker benefit now or may lose a job in the coming weeks and months ahead, MSD, the welfare system will be far more active in supporting people to be ready for work or in work.

explanation: Asked whether the 50,000 counts only exits into work or also exits via prison, emigration, superannuation or death, and if the latter why she calls it a work target. Saying success is measured as 50,000 fewer on the benefit implicitly concedes it is a headcount, but she never says so squarely and ignores the second limb entirely.
question: Will the reduction of 50,000 beneficiaries be purely based on those who exit into work, or will they also include those who exit because they go to prison, move overseas, change relationship status, reach age of eligibility for superannuation, or, sadly, die, and, if all of the above, why does she keep saying the target is about supporting people into work?
statement: We have nearly 190,000 people today on the jobseeker benefit. This Government is absolutely and deliberately focused on supporting people into employment, and the way we measure our success is to have 50,000 fewer people on the jobseeker benefit by 2030. It won’t be easy, but it is a challenge that this Government embraces because we know the opportunities that having a job provides.

explanation: A tightened re-ask: purely exits into work, yes or no? She clarifies which benefit is in scope — a different question than the one asked — and restates the headcount goal. The restatement leans towards "no", but after "I don't think I can be any clearer" the yes/no is still withheld.
question: OK. Will the reduction of 50,000 beneficiaries be purely based on those who exit benefit into work?
statement: I don’t think I can be any clearer. This is about those who are currently on the jobseeker support benefit—not main benefits; jobseeker support. We want to see 50,000 fewer people receiving the jobseeker benefit support by the year 2030.

explanation: Asked what recent rental-market announcements he has made. He names the three specific Residential Tenancies Act changes announced that day. Directly and completely answered; the closing swipe at the previous government doesn't detract from the engagement.
question: What recent announcements has he made on steps to improve the rental market?
statement: Today, I’ve announced changes to the Residential Tenancies Act to encourage landlords back into the rental property market. We are reintroducing 90-day no-cause terminations for periodic tenancies, returning landlords’ notice periods for ending a tenancy to 42 days in certain circumstances, and we are reintroducing landlords’ ability to give notice to end a fixed-term tenancy at the end of a term without giving a reason. We know that waging a war on landlords just ends in pain for tenants—part of the reason why rents have gone up by $170 a week in the last few years. We want to bring balance back to the rental market and bring landlords back into the market.

explanation: Asked how reinstating 90-day no-cause terminations improves conditions for renters. He gives the causal mechanism — the backstop makes landlords willing to take on marginal tenants — which addresses the question as asked, whether or not the reasoning holds up.
question: How will reinstating 90-day no-cause terminations improve conditions for renters?
statement: Well, over the last few years, we have heard from many landlords that without the backstop of 90-day no-cause terminations, they’re just unwilling to take a chance on tenants who might have otherwise missed out on the rental market—people leaving prison, for example; people with criminal records; or people at the edges of the rental property market. Giving landlords the backstop of being able to end a tenancy will mean more of them giving people a fair go with the reassurance that if things don’t work out, they can end the tenancy.

explanation: Asked what the changes mean for Queenstown. He answers about Queenstown specifically — the fixed-term rollover pushing properties to Airbnb — before widening to other hotspots. Squarely engaged, with some drift at the end.
question: What will these changes mean for Queenstown?
statement: Well, very positive changes for Queenstown. One of the effects of the 2020 changes to the Residential Tenancies Act to, basically, make the ending of a fixed-term tenancy almost automatically roll over to a periodic tenancy was the complete reduction in the number of landlords being willing to offer short-term rentals in a market like Queenstown. Instead, landlords decided it was all too hard, and instead those properties ended on Airbnb, actually, which has contributed to people sleeping in tents down by the foreshore in Queenstown, and other cases of hardship. I’m also advised that there are other holiday hotspots where this happens, including Waiheke Island and places like Dunedin with the student rental property—

explanation: Asked what else the Government is doing on housing. He enumerates the five-point plan: rental settings, urban limits, infrastructure, growth incentives, social housing and RMA reform. Direct and responsive to an open question.
question: What else is the Government doing to fix the housing crisis?
statement: Well, the Government has a five-point plan to fix the housing crisis. We need improvements to the rental market to make it easier to be a landlord and to be a tenant, but most fundamentally we need to smash the urban limits that are holding our cities back, fix infrastructure settings, and introduce incentives for cities and regions to go for growth. My colleague Minister Chris Penk is working on building and construction changes. We are going to deliver better social housing, and, most importantly, we are going to fundamentally reform the Resource Management Act 1991. Where the last Government failed, we will succeed.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statement about the media's role. She opens with "Yes" and affirms the proposition; the added sympathies are surplus, not evasion.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “Media plays a very, very important role in our democracy”; if not, why not?
statement: Yes, the media provides an important role in disseminating information and content for the benefit of New Zealand. I’d like to take this opportunity to actually say it has been a deeply distressing time for many journalists, production staff, and longstanding members of the media community this week, and my deepest sympathies lie with them and their families as they navigate the situation.

explanation: Asked why there is nothing for the media sector in the second-quarter action plan. She offers sympathy, a general commitment to modernisation, and "there is a process under way" — the last is a faint gesture at a reason, but the plan's omission is never addressed.
question: Why, given that statement and the unfolding crisis in the media sector, is there nothing for the media sector in the Government’s full second-quarter action plan?
statement: The impact of the commercial decisions made by TVNZ and Newshub and other media operators across New Zealand is incredibly sad and I want to acknowledge how much of a distressing time it is for everyone involved. I’m focused on helping the industry modernise and innovate so the industry can be more profitable going forward. There is no silver bullet to fix the current situation that TVNZ and Warner Bros. Discovery are facing at the moment. There is a process under way, and I’ll have more to say when that process has concluded.

explanation: Asked whether she has the confidence of the media sector and what she says to Bill Ralston's criticism. She switches the subject from herself to the Government ("the sector can have confidence in the Government") and never responds to the quoted criticism — both limbs dodged.
question: Does the Minister think she has the confidence of the media sector, and, if so, what does she say to former TVNZ boss and TV3 political editor Bill Ralston, who, I quote, said, “The Minister has no idea what she is doing”?
statement: I can say that the sector can have confidence in the Government who actually listen to the people. I take no pleasure in the situation happening in Warner Bros. Discovery and TVNZ. There are challenges across the sector, like in many other parts of the New Zealand economy, due to the cost of living crisis. I am committed to working with the sector to support them to modernise and innovate so they can be more commercially viable. There is a process under way, and I will have more to say once that process has concluded.

explanation: Asked (loaded, yes/no): does she have no plan and is she waiting for Winston Peters to do her job? Lee answers "No" — a direct, complete response to a yes/no question, then declines responsibility for the member's comments. Blunt and unhelpful in content, but the question was engaged rather than dodged.
question: Is it the case that, actually, the Minister has no plan, no one supports or believes her, and she has to wait until Winston Peters gets back to do her job for her?
statement: No. I have no responsibility for that member’s comments as well.

explanation: Asked: what recent announcements on speed limits in Kāpiti? Brown names the announcement (NZTA proposal to lift the Mackays–Peka Peka and Peka Peka–Ōtaki sections to 110 km/h), the date and the consultation start. The question's core is squarely and completely met.
question: What recent announcements has he made on speed limits in Kāpiti?
statement: Great news. On Tuesday, I announced that the New Zealand Transport Agency has proposed to increase speed limits on the Mackays to Peka Peka and Peka Peka to Ōtaki sections of the Kāpiti Expressway to 110 kilometres per hour, with consultation on these changes beginning 22 April. This road of national significance, started by the previous National Government, was designed to a safe standard suitable for 110 kilometres per hour, and enabling these expressways to have this speed limit is part of this Government’s plan to speed up our economy.

explanation: Asked: what reports has he seen on the safety benefits of the Kāpiti Expressway? He engages the substance of safety benefits (no deaths since opening, a claimed 70 percent reduction) but never identifies any report he has seen. Partial: the topic is addressed, the specific thing asked for — the reports — is not.
question: What reports has he seen on the safety benefits of the Kāpiti Expressway?
statement: This particular road, which is having a proposal to increase the speed limit to 110 kilometres per hour, is incredibly safe; started by the last National Government, designed and constructed to a high safety standard. Since the expressway opened, no one has died in a crash on this expressway, and there’s been a 70 percent reduction in roads in the Kāpiti district. The coalition Government is committed to delivering safe and new roads of national significance across the country to get people and freight where they need to go, quickly and safely.

explanation: Asked: how does the speed-limit change fit the Government's plan to get New Zealand moving? He states the fit directly — reversing blanket reductions, enabling 110 km/h on roads of national significance, weighting travel times and economic impact alongside safety. The connection asked about is actually drawn.
question: How does the proposed change of speed limit on the Kāpiti Expressway fit in with the Government’s plan to get New Zealand moving again?
statement: Well, the coalition Government is stopping the previous Government’s blanket speed limit reductions and is enabling new and existing roads of national significance to have speed limits of 110 kilometre per hour. Rather than forcing people to slow down, our plan ensures that, when speed limits are set, economic impacts, including travel times and the views of road users and local communities, are taken into account alongside safety.

explanation: Asked: does she stand by all her statements and actions on firearms reform? Answer opens "Yes" and then elaborates on one statement in particular. Direct and complete; the added argumentative material does not displace the answer.
question: Does she stand by all of her statements and actions in respect of firearms reform?
statement: Yes, especially my statement regarding the fact that semi-automatic firearms were never banned under his Government. The fact of the matter is that there are over 6,600 licensed firearm owners in New Zealand who have licence endorsements which can allow them to possess a semi-automatic firearm. Semi-automatic firearms were never banned under that member’s Government; many were merely transferred on to other firearm licence endorsements such as “prohibited”, “pistol”, and “collector” endorsements, among others.

explanation: Asked: does she stand by the quoted statement? "Yes, I do stand by that statement." Complete answer in one line.
question: Does she stand by her statement regarding reintroducing semi-automatic weapons like those used in the Christchurch mosque attack: “I’m not reintroducing anything. Those firearms [are] already here. In fact, we have 6,600 people who have endorsements to be in possession of those firearms”?
statement: Yes, I do stand by that statement.

explanation: Asked: which of the two figures is correct, the Minister's 328 or hers of 6,600? She answers explicitly — "Both those statements are correct" — and explains the distinction between endorsements and prohibited licences that reconciles them. The condescending offer of "education" is a civility matter, not a dodge.
