explanation: Asked what advice has been seen on why reported dolphin captures rose 700 percent since cameras were installed. No advice is described, the 700 percent figure is never engaged, and the answer drifts to generalities about wildlife interaction being 'already in the model' before closing on a joke about a stray dolphin. A narrow factual question left unanswered.
question: What advice, if any, has he seen on reasons why the reported number of dolphin captures has increased by 700 percent since cameras were put on boats?
statement: Obviously, a great deal of focus is now upon dolphins, but inevitably when the fishing industry interacts with the sea of Tangaroa, from time to time there will be captures. This is already in the model. It’s called the wildlife interaction with industry. The Minister before me, and other Ministers before her, received advice as to how initiatives can be sharpened to lessen the impact on vulnerable mammals. One was recently seen in Rongotai on its way to the Chathams!

explanation: A two-part question — agreement with a quoted statement, and commitment to a broad accessible franchise. Both get an explicit 'yes', the first with an explanation of the original context and the second with a stated qualification about legislative scope. Direct and complete; the partisan jab at the end does not affect this attribute.
question: Does he agree with the statement of Paul Goldsmith that “One of the pillars of democracy is that every adult has an equal say in who governs them, and through that vote, an equal say in important government decisions affecting their lives”, and is he committed to an electoral system in which the franchise is as accessible and broad-based as possible?
statement: In response to the first part of the question: yes. My comment was in response to the previous Government moving away from the fundamental principle of equal voting rights in the Canterbury regional council Act, which this Government has indicated it will overturn. In relation to the second one: yes, within the scope of appropriate legislative rules. For example, we have no plans to broaden the base to enfranchise murderers currently spending time in prison, which I understand is the Greens’ policy.

explanation: Asked whether election-day enrolment by 110,000 voters is considered a success. Answered directly in the first line — 'I'm not sure it was necessarily a success' — and the rest explains why, citing the Auditor-General's report and the pressure election-day registration puts on the system. A clear position, mildly hedged.
question: Does he consider it a success that 110,000 voters, the population of Dunedin, enrolled on election day and thereby had a say in important Government decisions affecting their lives?
statement: Well, I’m not sure it was necessarily a success. I would say that it’s been a significant change over the last two elections to enable people to enrol on election day. Yesterday, we had the delivery of a report from the Auditor-General which outlined many, many problems with the election result and count in 2023, where quality checks weren’t done or they weren’t done with the rigour required, and then the national quality assurance checks weren’t carried out with the information required, and then the processes weren’t in place. So that was a very concerning report, and it’s concerning because all New Zealanders need to have confidence in the electoral system. One of the issues raised in that report was the extra pressure in the system caused by election-day registration.

explanation: Asked whether the flagged changes meant removing election-day enrolment. The 'disenfranchisement' framing is squarely rejected, which answers part of it, but the substantive question of whether that specific change is intended is left open behind process talk about forthcoming reports and 'considering all those things'. Half engaged.
question: When he said to Mike Hosking this morning that “Every three-year cycle there’s a law to review the election and we’ll be making some changes.”, was he referring to disenfranchising the 110,000 voters by removing their ability to enrol on voting day?
statement: Well, certainly I reject any such suggestion around disenfranchisement. There are two steps that happen, actually. We’re going to be getting a report in the next week or so from the Electoral Commission, which is a standard report within six months of the election, which outlines some of the issues that were raised. I think everybody in this House is aware that a number of problems were experienced through the election. Whole boxes of votes were lost, there were dual votes not counted, and there were a whole range of issues that need to be dealt with. So every three-year cycle, Parliament considers the situation and makes sure that our electoral laws are in shape, and I have indicated that we should be considering all those things.

explanation: Asked whether the implications of a universal healthcare commitment for Māori women, given disproportionate maternal and infant inequities, had been considered. The reply restates the commitment, adds 'including Māori women', then moves to a facility opening and a neonatal unit. It never says whether those implications were considered — a pivot to announcements.
question: When he committed to providing “timely access to quality healthcare for all New Zealanders”, did he consider the implications of this generalisation for Māori women, who suffer disproportionate rates of maternal and infant inequities compared to non-Māori women?
statement: Oh, boy. I’ve so got to go to the gym! This Government is committed to providing timely access to quality healthcare for all New Zealanders, including Māori women. In fact, I was honoured to be asked to officially open Te Kotuku extension last month in Whangārei. This facility will provide in-patient care for tamariki from birth until their 15th birthday. In addition, the new neonatal unit will provide comprehensive care for unwell or premature babies. This Government cares about the health needs of all children and parents.

explanation: Asked whether a named Māori-led initiative is critical, and if so whether resourcing will continue. The reply substitutes a different service, downgrades 'critical' to 'useful', and drops the funding commitment entirely. The 'What I agree with is...' construction engages a question adjacent to the one asked, not the one asked.
question: Does the Minister agree that Māori-led health initiatives such as Ngā Wānanga o Hine Kōpū, a wānanga run in Te Tai Tokerau for hapū māmā are critical for the health and wellbeing of our people, and, if so, will he continue resourcing these types of initiatives?
statement: What I agree with is that the use of activities such as Hapū Wānanga, which is a free kaupapa Māori antenatal service, is useful to help reduce some of the uneven harms that we have in mortality for New Zealand women.

explanation: Asked whether racism and oppression are accepted as contributors to Māori women receiving less antenatal steroid treatment. Racism and oppression are never addressed; the answer restates outcome statistics from the Health Status Report. Declining to accept the proposition would have been a forthright answer, but the position is never actually stated.
question: Does the Minister accept that racism and oppression are contributors to the fact that Māori women in pre-term labour are less likely to receive the full and necessary amount of antenatal steroids?
statement: What I accept is what the Health Status Report tells us, which is that birth complications are more common for Māori, Pacific, and Indian women, and that these groups are more likely to have pre-term births and require blood transfusions after delivery.

explanation: Asked what reports have been seen about the $1.9 billion Corrections announcement. Answers 'Many', identifies a specific report by title, and summarises its contents (bed numbers at Waikeria, funding shortfalls, rehabilitation, back office to front line). A patsy question, but the question put is answered directly and completely.
question: What reports has he seen about the recent announcement of a $1.9 billion investment in Corrections?
statement: Many. The one I was most proud to see was one titled “Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announces $1.9 billion plan to make … [New Zealand] safer.” That plan includes financing to deliver 810 new beds at Waikeria, taking its total capacity to over 1,860. It meets the funding shortfalls Corrections is currently grappling with, gives the system extra capacity and staff to provide real consequences for crime, provides rehabilitation, and moves money from the back office to the front line of Corrections. The Government is working hard to restore law and order and get New Zealand back on track.

explanation: Asked what changes the Government is making to rehabilitation. The answer names the change — extra funding to extend rehabilitation access to remand prisoners under the 100-day plan. Engages the question directly.
question: What changes is the Government making to rehabilitation?
statement: As part of our investment in Corrections, there will be additional finding for the department to deliver on our 100-day plan commitment to provide access to rehabilitation for remand prisoners, which has the potential to benefit 1,400 prisoners at any given time.

explanation: Asked how much is being invested in rehabilitation for remand prisoners. The answer gives a figure ($78 million within the $1.9 billion package). Direct and complete.
question: How much is the Government investing in delivering rehabilitation to prisoners on remand?
statement: As part of our $1.9 billion announcement, $78 million has been set aside to ensure that the remand population has access to, and is provided, the critical rehabilitation programmes that they need. This is to ensure that the time remand prisoners spend in the corrections system gives them the best chance of rejoining society in a positive way.

explanation: Asked what programmes remand prisoners will access. The answer states which category of programme each class of remand prisoner gets (non-offence-based for accused, full suite for convicted). It answers in kind; the absence of programme names is a specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: Last supplementary: what programmes will remand prisoners have access to?
statement: Thanks to this investment, alongside our recent 100-day plan, remand accused prisoners will be provided access to non-offence - based programmes. Remand convicted prisoners can expect to be provided the full suite of rehabilitative programmes.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made. The answer identifies the speech given today and summarises its content and framing, but describes an approach rather than naming announcements. Engaged, slightly short of the core.
question: What recent announcements has she made?
statement: Today, I delivered a speech to the Hutt Valley Chamber of Commerce, setting out the approach that the coalition Government will be taking to Budget 2024. It will be a different approach to those seen in recent years because the country simply cannot afford another Budget that is long on good intentions and short on delivery. As the OECD survey released earlier this week confirmed, the economy is ailing and there has been a substantial deterioration in New Zealand’s fiscal position in recent years. This Budget can’t provide an overnight fix, but it will lay the groundwork for improving New Zealand’s prospects.

explanation: Asked whether the Government is pessimistic about the economic outlook. Answer opens 'No, not at all' and then explains. A plain yes/no to a yes/no question.
question: Does this mean the Government is pessimistic about New Zealand’s economic outlook?
statement: No, not at all. There is no country in the world in which I would rather live and raise my family. But the fundamentals need to be sorted: getting Government spending under control; delivering better value for money; and creating an environment in which businesses want to invest, innovate, take risks, hire people, build things, and make things. The Government is doing that, and things are going to get better.

explanation: Asked whether she made any announcements in her speech. Answer is 'Yes' followed by the specific announcement (a stand-alone Social Investment Agency). The subsequent talking points do not displace the answer, which is given first.
question: Did the Minister make any announcements in her speech?
statement: Yes. I announced that the Government is establishing a new stand-alone Social Investment Agency to deliver positive change for the most vulnerable New Zealanders. I would like to congratulate the Opposition member Ginny Andersen, who has already taken the title of social investment spokesperson, in respect of this change. The Government currently invests more than $70 billion a year in social services. But despite that investment, many people are not getting the help they need when they need it, and we see evidence of that in increasing welfare dependency, declining school attendance and achievement, poorer health outcomes, and rising rates of youth and violent crime. What this demonstrates is that good intentions are not sufficient to change outcomes. Just chucking money at problems doesn’t work.

explanation: Asked what difference a social investment approach will make. The answer describes the mechanism (data-directed investment, early intervention, redirecting funds) and claims materially improved lives for vulnerable citizens. It reaches the question but stays at the level of expected effect rather than stated difference.
question: What difference will taking a social investment approach make?
statement: Taking a social investment approach, as I just said, means using data, evidence, and modern analytics to direct investment where it will actually make a difference. The data is already being collected and it gives us a pretty good idea, but not absolute certainty, about which children are likely to be in greatest need of help. There is an opportunity to intervene early to break cycles of dependency and despair. Doing so will involve taking some risks. Not all interventions will prove successful. But if the Government redirects investment away from programmes that are not delivering, and into programmes that are achieving, it can materially improve the lives of some of New Zealand’s most vulnerable citizens. The Government is resolved to do exactly that.

explanation: Asked what announcements have been made on earlier intervention for jobseekers. The answer names the initiative (Kōrero Mahi) and states the new obligation. Squarely answered.
question: What recent announcements, if any, has the Minister made about earlier interventions for those on the jobseeker support benefit?
statement: This morning, I announced a new initiative called Kōrero Mahi – Let’s Talk Work, which will help people who come on to the jobseeker benefit get back on their feet quickly. All new jobseeker beneficiaries who have work obligations must now meet with the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) within two weeks of starting their benefit to determine their next steps towards finding work. This initiative is part of the Government’s plan to make the welfare system more proactive and to check on job seekers to make sure they’re getting the right support and they’re on the right path.

explanation: Asked what happens when a jobseeker attends a Kōrero Mahi seminar. The answer walks through what occurs and the branching outcomes. Direct.
question: What will happen when a job seeker attends a Kōrero Mahi work seminar?
statement: They will attend a group seminar with MSD and figure out the best way forward and the steps that they need to take. If they are work-ready, they could be connected with job vacancies straight away. If they need retraining or upskilling, they could be referred to a programme that can help them. The important thing is they are taking the steps they need to to return to the workforce as quickly as possible to avoid getting trapped on welfare.

explanation: Asked why the early intervention is being introduced. The answer begins 'Because' and gives the stated reason — jobseekers previously went months without MSD contact, with only 53 employment case managers. Answers the question asked.
question: Why is the Minister introducing this early intervention for people on jobseeker benefits?
statement: Because, before now, some people on jobseeker benefits could go many months without interacting with MSD, because the requirement to do so didn’t exist. Of about 188,000 people who are currently receiving the jobseeker support benefit, only 53 of them have employment case managers at any given time, so this early intervention is crucial for making sure that all job seekers are taking the steps they need to find work.

explanation: Asked whether sanctions will apply to the non-compliant. The answer confirms attendance is a work obligation and non-attendance without good reason could bring a sanction, then bounds where sanctions do not apply. Directly answered.
question: Will sanctions apply to those who are uncompliant?
statement: Kōrero Mahi will be considered a work obligation for those on the jobseeker support, and failure to attend without a good and sufficient reason could result in a sanction being applied. But I want to be clear. I want to be clear: no one is sanctioned if they can’t find a job. If the work isn’t there, their benefit will remain. The welfare system, under this Government, will support those in need, but there are rights and responsibilities that come along with being a New Zealander receiving benefits, and there will be consequences for those who don’t play their part.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statements and actions on Budget 2024. Answer is 'Yes', with the statements enumerated. Complete.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions in relation to Budget 2024?
statement: Yes, including the statements I made this morning in a speech titled, “Getting back on track”. My statements included: that workers have endured 14 years without any adjustment to tax brackets; that Government spending went up 80 percent; that even with this increase in spending, health waiting lists have grown, educational achievement has fallen, and violent crime has soared; that this year’s Budget won’t be an instant fix but that, instead, it will lay the ground for steady progress for today, tomorrow, and the longer term.

explanation: Asked whether the 17 percent getting no direct benefit are immune from the cost of living crisis. Willis opens with "No, they are not" — the yes/no core is answered outright before she pivots to economic-management talking points and a counter-attack on Labour's position. The pivot follows the answer rather than replacing it, so it does not pull the score down; the trailing partisan material is a Focus concern, not a Forthrightness one.
question: Are the 17 percent of New Zealanders that are going to see no direct benefit from her tax cuts immune from the cost of living crisis?
statement: No, they are not, and that is why they are grateful that they have a Government that is focused on the strong economic management needed to get inflation tracking down and interest rates tracking down too. I’d also remind the member that her position is that the other 83 percent of New Zealanders don’t deserve tax relief either.

explanation: A two-part question: is she committed to data and evidence, and what evidence shows the landlord tax breaks will reduce rents. She answers both — "Yes", then names Treasury advice as the evidence. She does not summarise what the advice says, but thinness of detail is Specificity, and whether the advice actually says that is Veracity; the question asked what evidence she has and she identified it.
question: Is she committed to using data, evidence, and analytics; and if so, what data or evidence does she have that her tax breaks for landlords will reduce rents?
statement: Yes. I have advice from the New Zealand Treasury that our proposals will put downward pressure on rents.

explanation: Asked how many economists, if any, support her tax cuts. The response gives no number, no name, and no engagement with the premise — it turns the question back on the questioner about Labour's spending. The question was narrowly factual and countable, which makes the avoidance of its core complete rather than partial.
question: If she is so committed to data, evidence, and analytic, how many, if any, economists support her tax cuts?
statement: I would invite that member to tell this House how many economists think it was wise for the Labour Party to invest billions in the middle of an inflation spiral.

explanation: A loaded yes/no about whether she dreads the forecasters because her own actions are causing the deterioration. She answers "No" and then states what she does dread and why, which engages the substance of the premise she rejected. The closing jab at the member is a Civility matter and the accuracy of the economic account is Veracity; the question itself was met.
question: Does she “dread what comes out of the forecasters’ mouths” because she knows her actions are causing the deteriorating economic conditions and her Budget will do nothing to fix it?
statement: No. I dread it when I see declining growth in our economy and declining revenue because I know what that means in the lives of everyday people. What it means is they are struggling. What it means is that there are fewer customers coming through the doors of small businesses. What it means is that inflation has eaten away at their purchasing power. What it means is that high interest rates are hurting them when they go to pay their mortgage. If that member would like to actually read a chapter from real life, she’d understand that declining Government forecasts are bad for all of us, and she shouldn’t be smug about it.

explanation: A stand-by-your-statement question. "Yes", followed by the reasoning behind it. Direct and complete — the classic maximal case for this attribute.
question: Does he stand by his statement in relation to fossil gas that “the reality in terms of storage is we don’t have significant storage in New Zealand”?
statement: Yes. I’m advised that we don’t have significant gas storage in New Zealand. There is one dedicated gas storage facility, but only 6 petajoules of the 12 petajoules it can store can be used, as the rest is needed to maintain reservoir pressure. Six petajoules is around 15 days of gas supply for the New Zealand market.

explanation: Asked whether the previous Government's multi-technology dry-year business case is still being progressed. "Well, no" answers it squarely; everything after is justification and attack on the prior Government. The volume of talking-point material is high, but it comes after a plain answer rather than in place of one.
question: Is the detailed business case funded by the previous Government on a multi-technology or portfolio approach of flexible geothermal, demand response, grid-scale batteries, and hydrogen biomass solutions to find an alternative to gas to address the dry-year problem still being progressed by his Government?
statement: Well, no, because the last Government was very much focused on picking winners rather than letting the market actually build the energy that New Zealand needs. They banned oil and gas exploration and then they spent the last number of years on pumped hydro down the bottom of the South Island, a project that wasn’t even going to come on stream until 2040. We have a low residual notice for energy shortage tomorrow morning, with New Zealanders being told they have to turn the heaters off tomorrow morning. How would a pumped hydro in 2040 help them?

explanation: A narrow binary: was the cut funding reprioritised into other dry-year or renewable work, or returned to centre? Neither branch is ever chosen. The response substitutes a general position about not picking winners and a Transpower warning, never touching where the money went. Dodging a question this precisely framed is a worse failure than missing part of a sprawling one — and the questioner's follow-up confirms the core was left untouched.
question: Was the funding that was cut from exploring the portfolio approach, not pumped hydro, reprioritised into alternative dry-year risk or renewable work programmes, or was it returned to centre?
statement: Well, the answer to that question is the Government is not taking the approach the last Government took, which was to pick winners and to force technologies into the market, but to make sure that the market settings are right to drive investment. And the market was telling that Minister that by putting all the eggs in one basket or focusing on picking winners, there was a chilling effect on investment in our energy market. We now have a Transpower warning that there is going to be low energy available tomorrow morning—customers told not to charge their electric vehicles, turn the heaters off—that is a direct result of that last Government’s policies.

explanation: "Where's the money?" — and this time he says it: "yes, the money was returned". The answer arrives inside a long stretch of Lake Onslow attack material and a prop graph, but the question asked one thing and that thing was stated. Detail and partisanship belong to other attributes.
question: Well, where’s the money?
statement: Well, the member’s asked the question and I made it very clear that we have put an end to that particular project, and what we are focusing now on is making sure the market settings are correct. So, yes, the money was returned, because we’re not going to waste taxpayers’ money like the last Government did on ghost projects like Lake Onslow, which weren’t going to come until 2040, when we have information such as this [holds up graph], where the number of low residual notices from Transpower have increased dramatically from zero up to 15 per year since that last Government cancelled oil and gas exploration.

explanation: Asked again where the dry-year business case money went. Answered explicitly — "It's been returned... to the centre". The surrounding ghost-projects rhetoric does not dilute the fact that the question's core was reached and stated plainly.
question: Where did the money that was budgeted for the detailed business cases for dry-year risk go?
statement: Well, I think I’ve answered that question multiple times. It’s been returned, because we’re not going to waste money on ghost projects. We’ve returned it to the centre, because we’re not going to waste it on ghost projects which have left New Zealand with energy insecurity—a direct result of that last Government’s policies. They banned oil and gas exploration in 2018. They then focused on a ghost Lake Onslow project which wouldn’t have come into effect till 2040. How is that going to help keep the heaters on tomorrow morning?

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken to support NZ trade; names two concrete actions (EU-NZ FTA entry into force, launch of UAE CEPA negotiations). Squarely engages the question.
question: What actions has the Government taken to support New Zealand trade?
statement: It’s been an important month for New Zealand exporters. Not only did the EU-NZ free-trade agreement officially enter into force last week, many months sooner than expected, but on Tuesday, I announced on behalf of the Government the launch of negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA) between New Zealand and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE is an important bilateral partner for New Zealand, and this launch of formal negotiations is an exciting step towards growing our trade and economic relationship.

explanation: Asked what opportunities a UAE agreement would create; answers with the opportunities — a growing $1b export market, openings in agriculture, food production and sustainable energy, jobs. Promotional but on-question.
question: What opportunities would this trade agreement with the UAE create?
statement: The UAE is a key export destination and a hub in the Gulf region. Currently, we export around $1 billion worth of goods and services to the UAE, an increase of 17 percent over the last year. By investing in this relationship, we’ll open up further opportunities for New Zealand businesses and enhance cooperation across a range of fields, including agriculture, food production, and sustainable energy. This will help grow the economy and create higher-paying jobs for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked how an agreement would benefit NZ; lists benefits (returns to business, jobs, cost of living, diversification). Leans on stock lines but the stock lines are responsive to what was asked.
question: How would an agreement with the UAE benefit New Zealand?
statement: A CEPA with the UAE will contribute towards the Government’s vision of becoming an export powerhouse for New Zealand, to our target of doubling exports by value over 10 years, and help rebuild our economy. By strengthening our trade relationship with the UAE, we can bring increased returns for New Zealand businesses, support job creation, reduce the cost of living, diversify the economy, and put more money in the pockets of everyday consumers in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked what else has been done on Middle East trade; identifies the GCC free-trade negotiations and the Saudi visit advancing them. Directly answers.
question: What else has the Government done to support New Zealand trade with the Middle East?
statement: Not only would this CEPA strengthen economic ties between New Zealand and the UAE but it will also complement our ongoing negotiations towards a free-trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). I was pleased to advance these discussions during my recent visit to Saudi Arabia last week, and my discussions with the Saudi and GCC counterparts. Trade agreements are an important tool in this Government’s plan to rebuild our economy, and a strong economy means we can provide the quality public services that New Zealanders expect.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her answers, and if so why; "Yes" answers the primary limb completely but leaves the "why" limb untouched.
question: Does she stand by all of her answers to oral question No. 5 on Wednesday, 8 May; if so, why?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet had taken a formal decision to disestablish Te Pūkenga by 30 November 2023; answers "Yes, Cabinet had made a decision" — engaged and affirmative, but substitutes a vaguer object for the specific decision asked about.
question: When she made her expectations clear in the meeting with the chair and CEO of Te Pūkenga on 30 November 2023, had Cabinet taken a formal decision to disestablish Te Pūkenga; if not, what decision with regard to Te Pūkenga had Cabinet taken at that stage?
statement: Yes, Cabinet had made a decision.

explanation: Asked whether she indicated she expected a detailed disestablishment plan already; "No." A complete answer to a closed question.
question: Did she indicate to the chair and the chief executive of Te Pūkenga at her meeting with them on 30 November 2023 that she had expected they would have already presented her with a detailed plan for Te Pūkenga’s disestablishment?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether she received advice about personal grievance risk; "No." Direct and complete.
question: Did she receive advice from Te Pūkenga or any other officials that her expectation could give rise to personal grievance claims on the part of affected current, former, or potential employees?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked why she can't explicitly rule out having directed the chair and CEO to begin disestablishment; recites her "expectations" at length without ever addressing why she won't rule it out. The core of the question is stepped around.
question: Why can’t she explicitly rule out in this House that she directed the chair and the CEO to begin disestablishing Te Pūkenga?
statement: I made my expectations clear that Te Pūkenga should cover the disestablishment of Te Pūkenga, as was the Government policy. I made my expectations clear that Government would begin disestablishing Te Pūkenga within the first 100 days, that Te Pūkenga should operate in a manner that was consistent with Government plans, and that Te Pūkenga should support as much regional decision-making as possible. I also made my expectation clear that Te Pūkenga should ensure vocational education and training continues and staff and students were supported.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on restoring democracy in Tauranga; states the announcement — elections restored this year with election day 20 July.
question: What announcements has he made on restoring democracy in Tauranga?
statement: Great news for the people of Tauranga: the coalition Government is committed to democracy, and that’s why we’ve announced that—no ifs, no buts—democracy is being restored to Tauranga this year with election day taking place on 20 July. I want to encourage the people of Tauranga to vote in their upcoming council elections, or even stand to be elected, as democracy is restored and Tauranga moves forward.

explanation: Asked how exactly the Government plans to meet the COP28 tripling/doubling pledge; restates what the pledge is and says NZ will "play our part", offering no plan or mechanism. The "how" is never reached.
question: How exactly does the Government plan to meet its pledge at the COP28 Climate Change Conference to triple renewable energy generation and double renewable energy efficiency by 2030?
statement: At COP28, New Zealand signed a commitment with 132 other countries to triple the world’s renewable energy generation and double energy efficiency by 2030. This is a global pledge and recognises that some countries are starting from different places than others. New Zealand plans to play our part, including our commitment to double our renewable energy.

explanation: Asked why the Government blames consenting when ~2,000MW is consented but unbuilt. The answer restates that regulation is the barrier without ever engaging the unbuilt-consents point that contradicts it — the core of the question is left untouched.
question: Why is this Government blaming the consenting framework for holding back renewable electricity generation when there are approximately 2,000 megawatts of unbuilt but consented wind and solar?
statement: What is clear is that this country does need to significantly increase the amount of renewable energy available in this country, and one of the major barriers in order to increase that investment is through regulation, and this Government has recognised that and is implementing legislation to reduce that regulatory burden.

explanation: Asked what steps he has taken on retailer market barriers. He responds directly that the matter is outside his delegation — a plain, complete response of the refusal type — then pads with unrelated renewables talking points. The disclaimer answers; the padding neither helps nor is a dodge.
question: What steps, if any, has the Minister taken to remove the regulatory barriers to independent and social retailers entering the electricity market and competing on a level playing field, as recommended by the energy hardship panel?
statement: Those aspects as described by the member are not within my ministerial delegation; however, what I am committed to do, in working with my Cabinet colleagues, is to ensure that we do deliver upon our coalition commitments to double renewable energy by 2050.

explanation: A two-part question (agree with the report? support loans and grants?). Neither part is reached: no agreement or disagreement, no mention of loans or grants — only a general commitment to more renewable energy.
question: Does the Minister agree with the Rewiring Aotearoa report that home energy efficiency, full electrification, and solar is a key part of the solution to reducing emissions, and, if so, does he support loans and grants to enable greater uptake?
statement: What is clear, and what this coalition Government is committed to, is to increase significantly the amount of renewable energy in this country, and the reality of what that will deliver for New Zealanders is the electrification of transport and other aspects of businesses in their communities, and that will ensure that we meet our climate targets that we are committed to delivering.

explanation: Asked whether the fund will be extended. "That's not within my ministerial delegation" is blunt and gives no substance, but it squarely and completely disposes of the question rather than talking around it. Unhelpfulness is not evasion.
question: Will the Community Renewable Energy Fund be extended beyond July 2027 and expanded; if not, why not?
statement: That’s not within my ministerial delegation.

explanation: Asked what advice he has received about fast-track consenting and mining. He describes his role in RMA reform and pivots to energy security; no advice, received or not, is ever mentioned.
question: What advice, if any, has the Minister received regarding the fast-track consent process leading to the development of more mines for more renewable energy projects, on balance?
statement: The role that I participate in as part of that broader programme of reform is as part of the ministerial oversight in regards to Resource Management Act reform. What is very clear is that we need to deal with both the challenges we have around energy security today, but also prepare for a future of energy security in the future, and doubling renewable energy will ensure that we are prepared for the energy security requirements in the future.

explanation: A yes/no confirmation request, answered with an explicit confirmation ("I can indeed confirm... that was the outcome") before moving on. The question is engaged head-on.
question: Can the Minister confirm that the acronym GIDI refers to a fund that took emissions revenue off everyday working New Zealanders and used it to pay large subsidies to profitable corporates, including many offshore businesses?
statement: I can indeed confirm to the member that that was the outcome of that policy, and, as a result of that, this Government has clearly signalled that we will not continue untargeted spending in regards to what was previously done by the last Government. We are focused on doubling renewable energy and implementing realistic projects at pace to meet our climate targets.

explanation: Asked why the rebuild was scaled back. He disputes the framing but then supplies the actual reason — phasing learnt from other infrastructure projects, allowing earlier commissioning. That is a responsive explanation of the decision, even though it is wrapped in Government messaging.
question: Why has Te Whatu Ora signalled a scaled-back project for the Nelson Hospital rebuild?
statement: I reject the characterisation in the question. This Government is absolutely committed to the people of Nelson and to delivering a hospital that will meet their needs. That is why Health New Zealand has learnt from other large-scale infrastructure projects, and are now looking to phase this build. This potentially allows for buildings to be commissioned earlier and patients to be seen sooner, all whilst work on the remainder of the site continues. This Government is committed to delivering better public services, and that means getting smarter on how we deliver key infrastructure projects.

explanation: Asked why separate buildings are preferred when the advice said a full rebuild was clinically preferred. He gives a rationale for phasing (risk, earlier commissioning) but never addresses the clinical advice the question was built on, so only half the question is engaged.
question: Why is he signalling a preference for small, separate buildings when advice provided last year was that a full rebuild was the clinically preferred option?
statement: Health New Zealand has learnt from other large infrastructure projects, and we are now of a view that looking to phase these projects will reduce risk and potentially—as I mentioned in my reply to the primary—allow earlier commissioning of sites.

explanation: A specific guarantee was sought about IL4-grade housing of beds and laboratory services. He neither guarantees nor declines to; "still in design phase" and "fit for purpose" imply no commitment is available but never say so, and the IL4 and Alpine Fault specifics go unmentioned.
question: Can he guarantee that all beds and critical services like laboratory services will be housed within an IL4 grade building that can continue to support clinical patient needs when the Alpine Fault ruptures?
statement: This project is still in design phase towards a business case, but we will deliver a facility that is fit for purpose and serves the needs of the people of Nelson.

explanation: Asked why demand modelling needs redoing when it was done in 2023. Citing 2018 bed-modelling data points gestures obliquely at a reason but never states why the 2023 work is being redone; the rest is a slogan.
question: Why does demand modelling need to be redone when it was only completed in 2023, and Nelson’s population isn’t getting any younger or smaller?
statement: I have seen data points for bed modelling from 2018, and we want to deliver a facility that is fit for purpose.

explanation: Three specific commitments were sought: 2031, on budget, 255 beds. None is accepted or refused — the reply asserts the project is "on track" and describes moving power generation, leaving all three asks unanswered.
question: Will he commit to completing the new hospital by 2031 on budget and with at least 255 beds?
statement: I can confirm that the current project is on track, including the enabling works, which, as I understand it, involve movement of the power generation from one side of the road to the other—surely a good signal that we will build this facility and have it fit for purpose.

explanation: "Does he stand by all of his Government's statements and actions?" is answered with "Yes" as the first word. Complete; the subsequent attack on the previous Government is a Focus/Civility matter, not evasion.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to fix the legacy of misery and financial mismanagement left by the previous Government at Kāinga Ora (KO). Having loaded KO up with billions of dollars in debt and wasted time on broken policies like KiwiBuild, rents soared, social housing wait-lists exploded, and we have more children in motels on their watch. We’re taking action to fix Kāinga Ora, we’re holding unruly tenants to account, and we’re cutting red tape so that we can deliver much more housing.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of Auckland Council's five lead indicators, including no-cause evictions. He never says whether he is aware or engages with the indicators at all — he pivots to a list of Government supply actions. Talking-point pivot, core untouched.
question: Is he aware Auckland Council have identified five lead indicators that his Government has direct control over, including the return of no-cause evictions, which are likely to increase homelessness in our largest city?
statement: What we are determined to do is increase the supply of rental properties, and there is a range of actions that we’ve undertaken: restoring interest deductibility, removing the brightline test back to two years, and—importantly—getting the balance right in tenancy laws between landlords and tenants.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that no one will be made homeless by reinstating no-cause evictions. He borrows the word 'guarantee' but substitutes a different object — guaranteeing effort rather than the outcome asked about — and repeats the supply line twice. A plain 'no, I can't guarantee that' would have scored high; this avoids yes or no.
question: Can he guarantee no one will be made homeless by his Government’s decision to reinstate no-cause evictions?
statement: Well, what I can guarantee is that we are working incredibly hard to make sure that we avoid homelessness in this country. Part of that process is making sure we increase the supply of rental properties so that people can actually access and rent a house. That is why we’re very committed to making sure we increase the supply of rental properties in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee about homelessness arising from the Kāinga Ora tenant-behaviour directive. The answer never mentions the directive or the guarantee, opening with 'what is important is' and returning to tenancy-law balance. A near-total dodge of a narrow question.
question: Can he guarantee that no one will be made homeless by his Government’s directive on tenant behaviour that Auckland Council says means that they are “expecting Kāinga Ora evictions”?
statement: Well, what is important is we are getting the balance right in our tenancy laws so that we encourage landlords to put more houses up and make them available to more tenants so we avoid homelessness.

explanation: Asked to choose between 'unwilling' and 'unable' to say his policies will increase homelessness. 'What I am willing to say is...' acknowledges the framing and functionally declines, which is some engagement, but he neither picks a limb nor states outright that he won't answer, and slides into a record comparison. Partial at best.
question: Is the Prime Minister unwilling or unable to say that his Government’s policies will increase homelessness in this country?
statement: What I am willing to say is that we have a housing crisis in New Zealand, and—unlike the Labour and the Green Government that did nothing about it, and outcomes got a lot worse—we are working each and every aspect to increase the supply of houses available, houses available to rent, and social housing supply, as well.

explanation: Asked whether he is proud of the $2.9b landlord tax cuts given the homelessness consequence. He answers a pride question he was not asked — proud of tackling the housing crisis — and drops the $2.9b figure entirely. The grammatical form matches; the substance is redirected.
question: Is the Prime Minister proud of his decision to hand $2.9 billion in tax cuts to landlords on the one hand, but on the other hand, making decisions that will by all accounts increase homelessness in this country?
statement: Well, I am very proud that our Government is actually going to tackle the housing crisis we have in this country and homelessness. I would love that member to come in and support our efforts, because what we’re doing, actually, by unwinding interest deductibility is we’re making a lot more houses available for renters. We’re putting downward pressure on rents, and I’d encourage the member to join us and pass that legislation.

explanation: Asked what she has announced about the Budget 2024 operating allowance. Answered directly: under $3.5 billion, with the comparison point and an explicit statement that the exact figure comes on Budget day. Withholding the number is stated plainly rather than evaded, and the question was about the announcement made.
question: What announcements has she made about the operating allowance for Budget 2024?
statement: I said in the Budget Policy Statement that the operating allowance for Budget 2024 will be less than $3.5 billion—$3.5 billion, members may recall, was the operating allowance for Budget 2024 set by the previous Government. I will announce the actual number on Budget day, but I can confirm today to the House that it will be under $3.5 billion.

explanation: Asked what the operating allowance covers. Answered squarely with a definition and its scope — discretionary spending and revenue initiatives, net of savings. No pivot.
question: What does the operating allowance cover?
statement: The operating allowance is the amount available in the Budget for discretionary spending and revenue initiatives. Importantly, allowances are a net concept. They include savings as well as spending. The operating allowance in Budget 2024 will cover spending increases and revenue reductions, as well as offsetting savings initiatives and some revenue-raising. The total of all of these adds up to less than $3.5 billion.

explanation: Asked whether tax relief will be funded through savings. 'Yes,' followed by confirmation of the mechanism. Complete.
question: Will tax relief be funded through savings?
statement: Yes. Tax relief in the Budget will be fully funded through savings and revenue initiatives. These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party’s tax plan, with some adjustments to reflect coalition agreements. There will also be other savings in the Budget. These savings will be directed towards Government priorities, including front-line public services.

explanation: Asked how a sub-$3.5b allowance compares to recent years. The response starts exactly on the comparison (Budget 2022's allowance) but the record cuts off before any figure lands. Scored for engaging the question directly while not delivering the comparison; the truncation, not a pivot, is what leaves it incomplete.
question: How does a less than $3.5 billion operating allowance compare to those in recent years?
statement: The allowance for Budget 2022, which members will recall was the year when inflation hit 7.3 percent—

explanation: Asked the standard 'does he stand by all statements and actions'. 'Yes' — a complete answer to the question posed. The talking points that follow are surplus, not evasion; the question was fully engaged.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to shift money out of the back office and the bureaucracy, and into the front line. For the size of the public service surge in recent years, we’re getting money into the areas where it can make a big difference—things like structured literacy, permanent funding for Pharmac drugs, and big investments in law and order to keep our streets and our people safe. After years of financial mismanagement, we know a good Government can invest in the front line, support families with the costs of living, and get spending back under control.

explanation: Asked to guarantee at least as many State houses at term's end as at the start. He does offer a guarantee, but for an increase in 'social houses' — a different and broader category than State houses. Engages the form of the question squarely while shifting the metric, so partial rather than a dodge.
question: Will he guarantee that there will be at least as many State houses at the end of this parliamentary term as there were at the start of it?
statement: What I can guarantee is that there will be an increase in the number of social houses in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts there was a net loss of State houses under the last National Government. He neither accepts nor denies it, pivots to what this Government won't do, and turns on the questioner's own record. The historical fact asked about is never addressed.
question: Does he accept that there was a net loss of State houses under the last National Government?
statement: Well, I can tell you what we’re not going to do is we’re not planning to sell off 10,000 State houses, because your Government—that member’s Government—borrowed $10 billion more, and loaded that up on Kāinga Ora (KO), and they quadrupled the social house wait-list, and they had more children growing up in motels. So we’re going to solve the problem, we’re going to fix KO—it’s a badly run organisation. We’re going to fix it.

explanation: Asked why tax cuts are being chosen over infrastructure. Willis rejects the either/or premise and states it will be both — that engages the question's core head-on rather than pivoting, but the 'why' behind the trade-off is left unaddressed. Dismissive tone is Civility, not Forthrightness.
question: Why is she choosing tax cuts rather than the major infrastructure works like State housing, schools, and hospitals when the construction industry is facing significant uncertainty?
statement: How facile it is to suggest that it’s one or the other. It will be both.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with reports that repealing 7AA could cripple trust and endanger children. Answers 'No, I do not agree' immediately and then addresses what the underlying document actually said. Direct and complete.
question: Does she agree with reports that the repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 could cripple trust built up with Māori communities and put vulnerable children at greater risk?
statement: No, I do not agree with reports that have stated this. I assume the member is referring to an article with that headline. What that was referring to was a regulatory impact statement that actually said, “a repeal of section 7AA may undo some of the progress that Oranga Tamariki has made in building trust, relationships, and accountability in the communities we work with.” However, the regulatory impact statement also says that the repeal “may increase levels of confidence in the Department’s decision-making for some members of the public”.

explanation: Asked what specifically about the 7AA provisions is not in tamariki's best interests. The reply implies the objection is decision-making 'based on race', which brushes the question, but no specific provision is engaged — a restatement of position where a specific was asked for.
question: What specifically about the 7AA provisions, which give practical effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, is not in the best interests of tamariki?
statement: I have stood here and made it very clear time and time again that the best interests and the safety of our children should be first and foremost in all decision making of our young people, not based on their race.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with official advice and, if not, what counter-evidence she has. She says she will check the advice and come back to the member — a straight, non-evasive acknowledgement that she is not answering now, but the question itself is left unanswered.
question: Does she agree with official advice that stripping Treaty provisions “may worsen the safety, stability, and well-being of our children with the greatest needs.”, and, if not, what counter evidence does she have?
statement: I will have to go back and check that advice and then come back to the member with an answer

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with a specific quoted statement from Tama Potaka and National. The reply never touches the quote or the contradiction it raises, retreating to intentions about children's safety and the coalition agreement — a pivot to talking points.
question: Does she agree with Tama Potaka and the National Party, who voted down her member’s bill making the same repeal of 7AA, that “It would be contradictory of us to dismiss this provision entirely, which is intended to be a genuine option to address and meet the best interests of the child in State care.”?
statement: I have said time and time again that my intentions here are to make sure that our young people in this country are safe, cared for, and loved, and they deserve to be treated with the greatest of respect. And no matter what we do here today, this is part of the coalition agreement to make sure our young people have the best start in life.

explanation: Asked whether she can guarantee no resources or programmes will cease. She says plainly she cannot make that guarantee, then states the narrower guarantee she can make. An explicit 'no' is a direct answer, however unwelcome.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Can she guarantee that no resources, programmes, or initiatives delivered by strategic partnerships for the benefit of tamariki in care will cease because of this repeal?
statement: As far as that relates to the primary question, I can’t make guarantees like that. All I can guarantee is whatever is working in the best interests of our kids will continue and whatever is not, won’t.

explanation: Asked what assurances, if any, she can give that the repeal will not worsen tamariki Māori welfare or Crown–iwi trust. The reply describes her consultation activity instead of naming any assurance; it gestures at the topic without reaching the question.
question: What assurances, if any, can she give that the repeal will not worsen the welfare of tamariki Māori or a breakdown in trust between iwi and hapū Māori and the Crown?
statement: As far as that relates to the primary question, I am working hard, around the country, speaking to iwi, hapū, and community organisations about how we move forward to make sure that our young people are safe and every decision we’re making around their care is based on their safety.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on roads of regional significance. He states the announcement, the counts, and what they replace. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What recent announcements has he made on roads of regional significance?
statement: The Government has announced roads of regional significance to sit alongside roads of national significance as part of our plan to get transport back on track. Two roads of national significance and 10 roads of regional significance will replace roading projects in the New Zealand Upgrade Programme. The New Zealand Upgrade Programme’s roading projects were subject to significant cost blowouts that resulted in project cancellations and delays across the country. These changes get these roading projects back on track.

explanation: Asked why the Government changed NZ Upgrade Programme road projects. He gives the reason — a funding gap of up to $1.5 billion — and how the projects were reallocated. Directly responsive.
question: Why has the Government made changes to road projects in the New Zealand Upgrade Programme?
statement: Well, when we came to Government, we were advised that there would be a significant funding gap of up to $1.5 billion to deliver the roading projects in the New Zealand Upgrade Programme. The Government has made tough choices to get this programme of roading projects back on track. Two of these projects will now be delivered as roads of national significance. Ten will be delivered as roads of regional significance. Two will be progressed to be delivery-ready with funding decisions made once procurement for major projects within the package are confirmed, and two will be prioritised for funding within the Government policy statement on transport.

explanation: Asked why decision making on scope and delivery was delegated to NZTA. He answers with the stated reasons: certainty of delivery, budget control, risk management, value for money. Complete on the question's terms.
question: Why has the Government delegated decision making on project scope and delivery to the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA)?
statement: Well, our Government has delegated decision making on project scope and delivery to NZTA to provide much-needed certainty of delivery to communities across the country and to ensure the programme stays within budget. This ensures decisions can be made by the NZTA board on budget cost and scope, they can appropriately manage the risk, and ensure value for money for taxpayers. We expect the New Zealand Transport Agency board to deliver these projects within the $6.5 billion funding envelope for this programme.

explanation: Asked how roads of regional significance fit into the transport plan. He answers that they sit within the plan to boost productivity and rebuild the economy by giving delivery certainty. Thin on detail, but detail is Specificity — the question is engaged.
question: Can the Minister tell us how roads of regional significance fit into the Government’s transport plan?
statement: Our Government is focused on delivering a transport system that boosts productivity and economic growth. Prioritising the delivery of roads of national significance and roads of regional significance across New Zealand provides much-needed certainty of delivery to communities across the country. It is a part of our plan to rebuild the economy.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Prime Minister's 8 May statement about West Wind. He answers 'Yes' and substantiates the eight-year timeline. Unambiguous and complete.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister’s statement on 8 May referring to West Wind: “Well, what I am very well aware of is it took eight years to consent a simple wind farm not very far from this place here in Wellington”?
statement: Yes. Preparatory work started on this consent in 1999. A range of assessments had to be undertaken so they could submit a consent application; have a reasonable chance if granted a workable consent. The work was not optional. The final decision to grant the consent was made by the Environment Court in July 2007—eight years after the work began on the consent from the applicant. West Wind took two years to construct, so the total time, end to end, in developing it into a wind farm was 10 years. As the Prime Minister has outlined, it takes too long and costs too much to get resource consents in New Zealand to build the infrastructure New Zealand needs, including renewable energy. It’s one of the reasons why we’re committed to a fast-track, one-stop-shop piece of legislation.

explanation: Asked a yes/no question — does he accept there was a net loss of State houses under the last National Government. He never says yes or no: he disclaims personal involvement ('I wasn't part of that last National Government') and pivots to the coalition's plans and attacks on the questioner's record. The core of the question is left untouched.
question: Thank you. Does he accept that there was a net loss of State houses under the last National Government?
statement: Well, I hope that member would understand—I’ve been here for three and a bit years, so I wasn’t part of that last National Government. But what I can tell you is that the Government that I am leading—this coalition Government—is incredibly focused on making sure we expand social housing in New Zealand. We have a supply problem created by that member and his former Government, and we’re not loading up $10 billion on KO in six years, we’re not quadrupling the wait-list, and we’re not putting kids into motels. We’re going to solve the problem that he created.

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree with Willis's 2020 statement, and how many additional State houses will he commit to. He effectively answers the first ('We are going to continue to build State houses') but supplies no number for the second, offering only 'a lot more' before pivoting to Kāinga Ora's finances. Half the question is engaged, the specific commitment asked for is avoided.
question: Does he agree with the then National Party housing spokesperson, Nicola Willis, who said, in 2020, “The Government needs to build state houses, and what I would like to see is the Government continuing to build state houses. That’s absolutely a policy that either Labour or National needs to continue in the years ahead”; if so, how many additional State houses will he commit to building?
statement: We are going to continue to build State houses, and—and, not or—we’re going to continue to power up community housing providers to build more social houses as well. The aggregate, one plus one, is going to equal a lot more social houses available. But I can tell you, under that member, and the way that he left Kāinga Ora, they are faced with a sell-off of 10,200 houses in order to make the finances work because of the mess that you loaded them up with.

explanation: The supplementary pins him on the word 'State houses' in the pledge. He responds squarely: he will honour the commitment, but with the substitution of 'social housing'. That is a direct answer to the point being pressed — he concedes the change of terms openly rather than talking past it. Whether the substitution is legitimate is a matter for other attributes.
question: —if not, why not? State houses—the pledge says, “State houses”.
statement: We are very happy to honour that commitment with the change that it’s social housing.

explanation: 'Will he rule out extracting a dividend from Kāinga Ora?' — answered 'Yes' at the outset. Complete and unambiguous. The lengthy attack that follows is off-topic and combative, but the question itself was answered first and fully; incivility and padding are other attributes.
question: Will he rule out extracting a dividend from Kāinga Ora as the last National Government did?
statement: Yes. But what I’m also going to say to you: what we are ruling out is actually a board that has mismanaged Kāinga Ora, a Minister that mismanaged Kāinga Ora. We are going to fix it. How on earth do you have a board that doesn’t even have a financial statement? How do you actually have a board that just accepts the Government’s going to tip $10 billion and load $10 billion of debt up on KO, making it not financially sustainable and leading to a sell-off—as that previous Government planned—of 10,200 State houses?

explanation: The question is a disjunction — keep the same wait-list criteria, or change them? A bare 'Yes' cannot resolve an either/or, and nothing in the remainder returns to criteria; it moves to board refreshes, turnaround plans and blame. The nominal 'Yes' gestures at engagement but the actual question is left unanswered.
question: Will he commit to keeping the same criteria for someone to be placed on the social housing wait-list, or will he reduce the wait-list by changing the criteria, as the previous National Government did?
statement: Yes. What I’d say to that member, though, is we are in a conversation here about social housing. We want to see more social houses available in New Zealand. We want to see more State houses built and we want to see more community housing providers build more houses as well. But the first thing to do is, rather than putting good money after bad, we’re going to take stock of the KO organisation, make sure that it actually has a board refresh, make sure it has a turnaround plan in place by November, and make sure it gets on a financially sustainable footing. That is the first job that we have to do to clean up the mess that that member and his Government left us.

explanation: Asked what announcements he made regarding the independent review. He states them directly: a series of immediate actions announced yesterday, the review's findings on financial performance and governance, seven recommendations, four adopted immediately. The question is squarely engaged and covered.
question: What announcements has he made regarding the independent review into Kāinga Ora?
statement: Yesterday, the Government announced a series of immediate actions in response to the independent review of Kāinga Ora. We had significant concerns about the financial performance and governance of the agency. These concerns have been borne out by the independent review. The review finds that Kāinga Ora is underperforming and not financially viable without significant savings, as well as funding and financing changes. The agency’s had easy access to debt but insufficient focus on fiscal discipline and low levels of accountability. And, secondly, the wider social housing system is not delivering the results New Zealand needs and is lacking in transparency and accountability. They’ve made seven major recommendations which propose significant changes to Kāinga Ora and the system, and we’ve agreed to immediately adopt four of those recommendations.

explanation: Asked what the initial steps were. He enumerates them: Simon Moutter appointed chair from 4 June, a refreshed board by July, a new letter of expectation, and a turnaround plan due by year's end. Direct and complete on exactly what was asked.
question: What were those initial steps the Government took in response to these findings?
statement: Cabinet has appointed Mr Simon Moutter as the new chair of Kāinga Ora. He will be no stranger to many in this House, with extensive change leadership experience at Powerco, Auckland Airport, and Spark New Zealand. He steps into the role on 4 June, where he’ll be tasked with leading a refreshed board which we expect to be in place in July. Ministers are then going to issue a new letter of expectation, which makes clear our expectations regarding a focus on fiscal sustainability, value for money, and a back to basics approach, and we’re going to ask from the refreshed board a turnaround plan to Ministers by the end of the year to focus on returning Kāinga Ora to financial sustainability and eliminating losses.

explanation: Asked what the review said about governance. He confirms it raised concerns about the board's governance and performance, which engages the question, but then redirects members to read the review themselves rather than relaying what it found, and moves to the remedy. Partial engagement — the topic is addressed but the substance asked for is deferred elsewhere. The thinness of content is not itself penalised here.
question: What did the review have to say about the governance of Kāinga Ora?
statement: The review laid out a number of concerns about the governance and the performance of the board. As the Minister, alongside the Minister of Finance, I am responsible for ensuring the board is well-functioning and performing its governance role appropriately. I encourage members to read the review done by Sir Bill and his team around some of the governance failures at Kāinga Ora over the last few years. We are going to refresh the board and take action, and we expect a turnaround plan to fix the problems at Kāinga Ora.

explanation: Asked what the other recommendations were. He identifies their subject area — the wider social housing system — which is a start, but then pivots to the ideological divide across the House and a list of community housing providers without ever stating the recommendations. It reaches the edge of the question and stops.
question: What about the other recommendations of the review?
statement: The other recommendations in the review relate to the wider social housing system. One of the divides between the House has become apparent within that review: on this side of the House, we do not believe that the State is the answer to all of New Zealand’s housing problems; actually, the wider housing system needs to be addressed. We believe, on this side of the House, that the community housing sector, groups like the Salvation Army, the Community of Refuge Trust, Emerge, Dwell Housing Trust, and the community housing sector—

explanation: Two parts. The first — what reports confirm the conditions — is answered squarely with a named ANZ report and quotations. The second — will she commit to tax cuts applying from 1 July — is explicitly declined ('wait for nine more sleeps'), which is a plain, if conventional, refusal to say rather than a pivot. One part fully answered, one openly withheld.
question: Fãiåk se’ea, Mr Speaker. What reports, if any, has she seen to confirm that the economic conditions are right for delivering tax cuts, and will she commit to them applying from 1 July 2024?
statement: To the second part of the question, I will say what all Ministers of Finance say at this time, which is that the member will have to wait for nine more sleeps. To the first part, I saw an ANZ report on the Budget this morning, which said, “We expect the net impact of discretionary fiscal policy changes (tax and spending cuts) to be broadly neutral from a fiscal outlook perspective.”, and, “we think the net impact of tax and spending cuts are likely to be marginally contractionary on balance, insofar as households save a portion of their tax relief or spend a greater proportion on imports than the Government would have.” To make it simpler for the House, our tax relief won’t require additional borrowing, and our tax cuts will reduce inflationary pressures. Those seem like pretty good conditions for tax relief.

explanation: Asked why she chooses tax cuts rather than policies to minimise job losses. She argues at length why tax relief is justified but never engages the comparison — job losses are not mentioned once, so the 'rather than' at the heart of the question goes unaddressed. Half the question answered, the contrastive core skipped.
question: Why is she choosing tax cuts rather than policies that will minimise job losses, which many are predicting to go well over 5 percent?
statement: I would like to remind the member of the economic and fiscal conditions which New Zealanders face. We are in a situation where there have been no adjustments to personal income tax rates or thresholds for 14 years, other than a new rate being added at the top. Now, we are a country which is one of the few outliers in the OECD that hasn’t adjusted thresholds for fiscal drag. We’re a country where the average tax rate for a median full-time salary and wage earner—by definition, someone right in the middle of the income distribution—has gone up more than five percentage points. And we are a country where someone working full time on the minimum wage is now facing a marginal tax rate of 30 percent. These conditions justify tax relief. It is a shame the Labour Party can’t see it.

explanation: Asked why tax cuts rather than productivity policies. She meets the trade-off head-on by contesting it — she argues tax relief is itself a productivity measure because it rewards hard work. That is a direct engagement with the question's premise rather than a pivot, followed by a brief partisan jab that does not displace the answer.
question: Why is she choosing tax cuts rather than policies that would increase productivity when business confidence is currently plummeting?
statement: I happen to believe that one of the greatest things we can do for productivity is send New Zealanders the message that there will be reward for their hard work. And that is what tax relief will do. Under Labour, it may be that workers are always the last to get served, but under this Government, we’re making sure they get what they deserve.

explanation: Two-part question: what does she say to the forum, and can she name a supporting iwi/Māori organisation. The naming half — narrow and factual — is never touched; no organisation is named or an inability to name one conceded. "People are entitled to have their opinions" glances at the first half before pivoting to mandate and campaign talking points. Mostly a dodge, with a sliver of engagement.
question: What does she say to the National Iwi Chairs Forum and the Pou Tangata Iwi Leaders Group, who are united against the proposed repeal of section 7AA, and can she name an iwi or Māori organisation, including any strategic partnerships with Oranga Tamariki, that supports the repeal of section 7AA?
statement: People are entitled to have their opinions. At the end of the day, this is a coalition agreement, something that I campaigned on, an issue that I promised to fix while I went around the country and heard the horrific stories of how our young people were put at risk because it was based on their race, not their safety.

explanation: She engages the question's premise directly by disputing it — the 21 roles are still a proposal out for consultation — which is a real response to the "despite slashing" framing. But the core ask, HOW partnerships will be established and maintained, is left unanswered; "a very clear direction" is a substitute, not a mechanism. Partial engagement.
question: How will Oranga Tamariki meet her expectation to establish more partnerships with Māori and continue current strategic partnerships, despite repealing section 7AA, when she is slashing 21 Māori roles at Oranga Tamariki, including the very roles that support engagement—such as the regional Māori practice coaches and senior iwi and Māori engagement advisers—as well as the Treaty response unit and the Māori practice advisers?
statement: Those roles that the member is speaking of are still a proposal, still under consideration, and still out for consultation. What we are doing right now is making sure that Oranga Tamariki and all the people that work with our young people have a very clear direction that the care and protection and safety of our young people come first.

explanation: "Charter schools are back." names the recent announcement in the first sentence, which is exactly what was asked, then elaborates. The Vanguard anecdote is padding but the question was reached before it. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has he made about lifting educational outcomes?
statement: Charter schools are back. [Interruption] That’s right. Once again, New Zealand communities—be they business, be they iwi, be they community groups that have insight into how to engage children currently disengaged from education, those educators and those innovators will have a vehicle where they can create schools where those disengaged students want to go. I’ll tell you a story that I used in my maiden statement in this House 10 years ago of one student, a child who was literally called Hope. She was at Vanguard Military School and she said, “I never knew I was smart till I came here.”—I never knew I was smart till I came here.

explanation: He heads straight at the question, citing the CREDO/Stanford evidence base as the source on charter school success — no pivot, no counter-attack. But the response as recorded is cut off before any actual finding is stated, so the question is engaged without being answered. Scored mid on engagement-reached-but-not-delivered, not penalised for a dodge that didn't happen.
question: What success have charter schools had?
statement: You know, it’s interesting to look at what the data and evidence from around the world said. For example, the gold standards of studying charter school success comes out of Stanford University, the Center for Research on Educational Outcomes—

explanation: A "why" question given a why answer: attendance and achievement are failing, so new options are needed, closing with "That's why we need them." The swipe at the former Labour Minister is a Civility/Focus matter and does not reduce forthrightness — the question's core was squarely met.
question: Why is there a need for charter schools in New Zealand?
statement: The sad reality is that nothing determines our future more than how much knowledge we transfer from one generation to the next for every kid, and we’re failing. We’re failing to get kids to school and we’re failing to have them learn valuable knowledge for their future when they’re there—that is the truth. After years of denial, where the Labour Minister of Education, for example, was absolved from responsibility for misleading the House because she didn’t know where the educational data on attendance was, we are now fronting up, we’re publishing the data, and we’re creating new options so that kids can be engaged by people with insights in their community about what will get them to school and get them engaged. That’s why we need them.
