explanation: A stand-by-your-statement question, answered with an explicit "yes", plus the source he was paraphrasing and his own reading of it. The qualification ("I wouldn't want to overstate the impact") narrows the claim but comes after the yes rather than in place of it. The Budget-countdown quip at the front is padding, not evasion.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “our tax cuts will reduce inflationary pressures”?
statement: Only seven sleeps to go till the Budget, and, yes, as the member knows, I was paraphrasing an ANZ preview of the Budget that said, “We think that the net impact of tax and spending cuts are likely to be marginally contractionary on balance, in so far as households save a portion of their tax relief or spend a greater proportion on imports than the Government would have.” I agree with ANZ’s economists. I wouldn’t want to overstate the impact, but since tax relief will be fully paid for, it should, at the margin, take a bit of pressure off inflation, given that households may save some of their tax relief rather than spend it all.

explanation: Asked whether the Minister agrees with a specific RBNZ line that rates may have to stay restrictive longer. The answer says "I agree with the Reserve Bank" but then substitutes a different quote about Budget effects being unassessed, and closes on a Budget countdown. The quoted proposition is never engaged — the apparent agreement is with something else.
question: Does she agree with the Reserve Bank that “Interest rates may have to remain at a restrictive level for longer than anticipated in the February Monetary Policy Statement.”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister, I agree with the Reserve Bank, which said in their Monetary Policy Statement, “Any impact of potential changes in the forthcoming Budget to Government spending or private spending due to tax cuts remains to be assessed.” It’s seven more days till the Budget. Not long to go.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees the spending reduction from job cuts is less deflationary than expected. The answer says only that the Budget's impact is yet to be seen, then moves to "seven more sleeps" and tax relief. The job-cuts/deflation proposition is never addressed.
question: Does she agree with the Reserve Bank that the reduction in Government spending from her job cuts is less deflationary than expected; if not, why not?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, the Reserve Bank made it very clear in their Monetary Policy Statement that the impact of the forthcoming Budget is yet to be seen because it hasn’t yet been released. So I just say to the members on the other side of the House: seven days to go—seven more sleeps. And I have great news for the hard-working taxpayers of New Zealand that tax relief is coming in this year’s Budget.

explanation: Asked whether she is aware the inflation forecast excludes the tax cuts. The answer re-quotes the MPS line that the tax-cut impact "remains to be assessed", which does glance at the premise (i.e. not yet factored in), but never states awareness or engages the question as put, and ends on the countdown. Partial engagement at best.
question: Is she aware that the higher inflation expected by the Reserve Bank doesn’t even factor in her inflationary tax cuts?
statement: Well, I don’t know whether the member has read the Monetary Policy Statement. I’ll quote it again, on behalf of the Minister: “Any impact of potential changes in the forthcoming Budget to Government spending or private spending due to tax cuts remain to be assessed.” Only seven more sleeps to go.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Treasury advice that a fiscally neutral package may still be inflationary. The answer cites contrary Treasury modelling (tax reductions modestly reducing interest-rate pressure because some is saved) — an implicit disagreement with reasons, so the core is engaged — but it never says yes or no and tails off into an attack on the Opposition.
question: Does she agree with Treasury advice that a revenue package that is fiscally neutral “may still have an inflationary impact given lower-income individuals are likely to have a higher marginal propensity to consume out of additional income”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister, Treasury has been advising that their modelling suggests the impact of tax reductions on surplus spending is likely to modestly reduce pressure on interest rates due to the fact that not everybody will spend all of that money. Some of it may be saved. That is in line with exactly the statement I made at the beginning from the ANZ. But what I just want to point out to the House is that that party on the other side of the House hate tax cuts and will always vote against them.

explanation: Asked why families must pay higher interest rates for longer. The answer offers the Budget countdown and an attack on the questioner's party over past tax policy. No part of the question is engaged.
question: Why must New Zealand families pay higher interest rates for longer because of the information provided to the Reserve Bank, on which they have provided the Monetary Policy Statement?
statement: Well, it’s seven days to go—seven sleeps to go—until the Budget. But what I would just say to members on the other side: they will say and do anything to oppose tax relief for working New Zealanders. They cancelled the last tax relief in 2017 that was last legislated. They hate the idea of letting New Zealanders keep more of what they earn, and New Zealanders rejected that at the last election.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken to reduce regulatory burden on the primary sector. The answer names the action directly — an RMA amendment bill introduced today changing national freshwater regulations. Squarely responsive.
question: What actions has the Government taken to reduce regulatory burden on the primary sector?
statement: Today, the Government has introduced the first Resource Management Act amendment bill to the House, which will start to deliver on our commitment to reduce red tape and cost for farmers by changing national freshwater regulations. The bill proposes a range of changes that will reduce regulatory burden that have been holding back our rural sector and imposing unnecessary and significant on-farm compliance costs on to our world-leading farmers, whilst focusing on better environmental outcomes.

explanation: Asked what changes in the bill will help farmers. The answer identifies changes (removing the low-slope map, leaving stock-exclusion decisions to councils and farmers). Directly on the question.
question: What are some of the changes in the bill that will help farmers?
statement: We’ve heard concerns from the farm gate and are making sensible changes to allow farmers to get on with the job. We’re proposing to remove the problematic and ineffective low-slope map, which imposes a significant cost for minimal environmental benefits, especially for low-stock farms. Regional councils and farmers are best to determine where stock need to be excluded, based upon risk. The focus is on farm-level and regionally suitable solutions, which will ultimately reduce cost for farmers and be better for the environment.

explanation: Asked how else the bill reduces regulatory burden. The answer gives further measures — repealing intensive winter grazing regulations, rebalancing Te Mana o te Wai in consenting. Directly responsive.
question: How else will this bill reduce regulatory burden?
statement: We’ll also be repealing ineffective intensive winter grazing regulations in time for the 2025 season. Effective non-regulatory measures are already in place to support the continued improvement of winter grazing practices, with sector groups confirming their continued and collective commitment to working alongside farmers and regional councils to ensure good outcomes. Where councils have already adopted their own rules, these will remain in place. We’ve also heard how Te Mana o te Wai hierarchy of obligations is being applied inconsistently, so we’ll be starting the process to rebalance the rights of all water users in respect of consent applications.

explanation: Asked why the Government is making these changes. The answer gives the rationale — regulations should be fit for purpose, primary-sector efficiency boosts exports. Answers the question asked, with a slogan appended.
question: Why is the Government making these changes?
statement: Well, regulations need to be fit for purpose and not place unnecessary costs on our most productive sectors. By improving primary sector efficiency, we can boost our largest export sector and deliver for all New Zealanders. We want an efficient primary sector that works with Government for better environmental outcomes. There’s a lot more work to do, but these changes are an important first step in our commitment to get Wellington out of farming.

explanation: Asked what update he can provide from his recent South Island trip. The answer reports the trip — Canterbury, Otago, Southland, PGF and climate-resilience sites visited. It wanders into flood-protection advocacy, but the open question is engaged and answered.
question: What update can he provide from his recent trip to the South Island?
statement: I did get stuck in the Clinton pub on Friday night—those electric cars that you have issued us are problematic in rural areas. But last week, I travelled across Canterbury, Otago, and Southland to see regional development and investment in action. Regional New Zealand is the backbone of our country, and through initiatives such as the Provincial Growth Fund (PGF) and the climate resilience fund, we can see tangible benefits coming to fruition. I was hosted by Environment Canterbury and I visited Kānoa-funded climate and flood resilient sites. Flooding is the most common natural hazard in New Zealand. Events like the Auckland floods, Cyclone Gabrielle, and the Canterbury floods just show how extensive this damage can be. Government investments in stopbanks, such as Taradale stopbank in Napier, can avoid devastating damage to our local communities. Research shows that for every $1 invested in flood protection, it is estimated between $5 and $8 in direct losses is avoided. This is why core investment in resilient infrastructure such as flood protection projects are so important.

explanation: Asked what steps the Government has taken via the Customer and Product Data Bill. He names the step (introducing the bill), states what it does — controlled secure data access opening banking and electricity to competition — and engages the competition framing squarely. Slightly promotional rather than a list of steps, but the question is reached.
question: What steps has the Government taken to encourage greater competition through the introduction of the Customer and Product Data Bill?
statement: I thank the member for the question. In short, the introduction of this bill allows for controlled and secure access to data, creating a pathway for greater competition in the banking and electricity sectors. This bill lays the foundation for open banking and open electricity which will make it easier for innovative start-ups to compete with established companies. Choice and competition are good things as they ultimately lead to lower prices.

explanation: Asked for examples of benefits to New Zealanders. He gives a concrete one (Australian customers getting an online mortgage in 10 minutes versus the manual NZ process) plus the 300-companies figure. Directly responsive.
question: What are some examples of how this bill will benefit New Zealanders?
statement: There are many innovative products that are available overseas which cannot operate in New Zealand without consumer data rights. A recent report highlighted that there are as many as 300 companies waiting to do business in New Zealand. One specific example I know of: Australian customers of major banks can get a new home mortgage online within 10 minutes; meanwhile, Kiwi customers of the same banks still have to go through that lengthy manual process to get a loan.

explanation: Asked how the transfer of data will be kept safe and secure. He answers with the mechanisms: sharing is voluntary, users must be accredited, consumer permission is required, heavy penalties for non-compliance. Squarely on the question.
question: How does the Minister intend to make sure the transfer of data is safe and secure?
statement: It’s natural for people to be concerned about their personal data and how it’s shared, but Kiwis should be and can be assured that allowing access to your data is voluntary, and those using your data must be accredited. Any data can only be shared with the permission of the consumer, and failure to comply with these security measures will be subject to heavy penalties.

explanation: Asked which sectors the framework will apply to. Answered exactly: banking first, then electricity, then telecommunications in time. Complete.
question: What sectors will the Minister be introducing the framework to?
statement: The bill will first apply to the banking sector, followed by the electricity sector. These are two areas right now where New Zealanders are hurting with high costs. In time, we will look to apply the bill to the telecommunications sector. New Zealand is lagging behind the rest of the world. There are significant opportunities for encouraging competition which will ultimately benefit all New Zealanders by lowering cost and creating more choice.

explanation: Two-part question: why the criteria changed, and does she accept that many rely on flexible funding. The first part is answered directly — the change reflects Whaikaha's view that Education funds support during school hours. The second part is met with sympathy and a pending review rather than a yes or no, so the acceptance question is hedged around rather than reached.
question: Why have disability support funding criteria changed recently to now exclude the use of funding during school hours, and does she accept that many disabled people and children rely on flexible funding to be able to access critical support?
statement: Multiple Government agencies have responsibilities for funding disability support, including the Ministry of Disabled People - Whaikaha, and the Ministry of Education through its learning supports. The recent changes to the purchasing guidelines reflected the Ministry of Disabled People’s view that the Ministry of Education is responsible for funding support during school hours. I sympathise with all children and families who may have different support due to the changes and I acknowledge that this may have caused distress. The independent review of disability support funding will be looking into how the whole-of-Government supports work together so that disabled people get the essential support they need.

explanation: Asked what she says to a specific mother whose daughter loses a one-to-one therapy class. She offers a general expression of sympathy, then redirects to the previous question's framing and to the Government's school-attendance target. The core — a response to this family's loss of support — is largely stepped around.
question: What does she say to the mum whose 11-year-old daughter diagnosed with autism and ADHD and chronic health challenges, who relies on a special one-to-one gymnastic therapy class to help improve her muscle tone and regulate her anxiety levels, will no longer be able to access support because of this new change?
statement: As I said, I sympathise with the impact that any changes may have had. The primary question was about the use of funding during school hours, and our Government recognises the importance of school attendance, so much so that we have set a target to ensure children are attending school—this is all children, and an expectation that all children get the education they deserve.

explanation: Asked what she says to a mother whose son attends a during-school-hours programme. She acknowledges the difficulty and, unlike the prior answer, does implicitly respond to the case — the service operating during school hours is the problem because children should be in school. That engages the question's premise, but never really addresses what happens to this child.
question: What does she say to the mum whose 12-year-old son attends Mockingbird, that helps autistic children cope with school and is offered only during school hours, who says—and I quote—“The only thing helping my child hold on is knowing he has Friday at Mockingbird where he can relax and be himself, and now this is being taken away from him.”?
statement: As I said, I understand how challenging it is for parents. Having navigated the system as a parent of a child who needed additional support at school, I understand how challenging it is. But our Government is committed to ensuring that children are at school during school hours and that education provides a support and assistance while children are at school. It is unfortunate that important services like this are operating during school hours when we actually want children to be in school and get the support for their education at school.

explanation: Asked whether she is committed to continuing the EGL transformation and how the changes are consistent with EGL principles. The consistency half is answered head-on by quoting the 'mainstream first' principle. The commitment half is replaced with a commitment to a different thing (DSS not substituting for other agencies), so half the question is reached and half is deflected.
question: Is the Minister committed to continuing the transformation of the disability support sector in line with the Enabling Good Lives (EGL) approach, and, if so, how are these changes consistent with EGL principles?
statement: Well, one of the principles in Enabling Good Lives is the concept of mainstream first. And to directly quote: “Disabled people are supported to access mainstream services before specialist disability services.” A review of the disability support services is under way, clearly because there were challenges in the ministry being able to live within its financial means. Additional support has been provided up to 30 June this year. Our commitment is to ensure that Disability Support Services is not a substitution for other Government services and that we are able to consistently and deliberately deliver the essential services that disabled people need.

explanation: A narrow factual yes/no: has she sought confirmation from the education Minister about school funding, and if not, why not. She never says whether she sought it, or why not; the reply is agency responsibilities, school visits and sympathy. A specific question wholly avoided.
question: Has the Minister sought confirmation from the education Minister that her Government will fund schools to cover the cost of these programmes now that they can no longer be claimed through disability support funding, and, if not, why not?
statement: As I said, there are different Government agencies that deliver services for disabled people. For disabled school children, the expectation is that they are at school. I’ve visited a number of schools who go so far above and beyond to ensure that the disabled children in their schools get the support they need. That’s exactly what we are committed to. I accept fully that it is incredibly challenging for some families.

explanation: Asked whether she is aware of The Education Hub report and how she justifies the cut given it. She never says whether she is aware of the report, and pushes the substance to the Minister of Education. A partial justification does appear (DSS should not substitute for other agencies' funding), which keeps it just above a total dodge.
question: Is the Minister aware of a report by The Education Hub released recently that said there are a growing number of neurodivergent children at schools but that inadequate resourcing, lack of knowledge, and training about how best to support neurodivergent children is taking a substantial toll, and, if so, how can she then justify cutting what little support these children currently have to be able to cope with school?
statement: As I said, I know it is incredibly challenging, and this growth in neurodiverse students in our schools is creating some challenges. If the member has specific questions that relate to education, I’d invite her to put those to the Minister of Education. My responsibility, and what the review will look at, is how to ensure that the Disability Support Services is sustainable; that it delivers for disabled children, people, their families, and their carers; but that it is not substituting funding that is available in other Government agencies that are providing disability support.

explanation: Asked for his response to the Waitangi Tribunal's finding that the Crown breached the partnership principle by failing to consult. He restates the Government's objective and notes the report will be available to the select committee, but never engages the breach finding itself. The specific charge is left untouched.
question: What is his response to the Waitangi Tribunal’s finding regarding his bill to reinstate binding polls on Māori wards that “the Crown has breached the Treaty principle of partnership by prioritising coalition agreement commitments and completely failing to consult with its Treaty partner or any other stakeholders”?
statement: The Government’s objective is to give communities the final decision about whether their district or region will have Māori wards rather than councillors. The Waitangi Tribunal report will be available for the select committee to consider alongside the bill. We look forward to viewing the select committee’s recommendations. This Government is restoring local democracy.

explanation: Asked for his response to the mayors and council chairs who criticised the bill. He gives one directly — they should focus on core issues, and if they believe in localism they should not fear a public vote. Combative and dismissive, but the question asked for his response to those critics and he supplies it, which is forthright regardless of tone.
question: What is his response to the more than 50 mayors and regional council chairpersons who have criticised this legislation, stating that it is an overreach on local decision-making, a distraction from the real issues councils are facing, and undermines the important contributions that Māori are making?
statement: Well, I say to those mayors who wrote to this Government that they should focus on those core issues, and I also say to them: why should they be afraid of what the public have to say about Māori wards? What is wrong with local democracy? Ultimately, they come into my office and they write letters to me and say, “We believe in localism.” Well, the ultimate localism is giving local people the right to have their say through the ballot box.

explanation: Asked why the referendum requirement targets Māori wards and not rural wards. He gives the asymmetry directly: rural wards are appealable to the Local Government Commission, which has the final say, whereas appeal rights for Māori wards were removed by the last Government. That is a stated reason for the difference, so the core of the question is engaged.
question: If this is really about restoring democracy and allowing voters to decide the make-up of their local councils, why are you only going after Māori wards but not rural wards?
statement: Well, I make this very clear point: when it comes to the rural wards, which seems to be the only argument that some people have against our policy, the Local Government Commission can take appeals on those wards. And, by the way, the Local Government Commission has the final say on those wards. What we’re saying when it comes to Māori wards is that the last Government took away the ability for any appeal rights, not even to the Local Government Commission, and we are giving the right to local communities to make that decision for their community.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about the open letter from 50+ mayors and chairs, and if so why he is overriding local government. He opens with a flat "No, I am not concerned" — a direct answer that disposes of the conditional second limb — then states his rationale. Blunt and dismissive of the mayors, but not a dodge.
question: Is he concerned that over 50 of the country’s mayors and regional council chairpeople have signed an open letter opposing mandatory referendums for Māori wards; if so, why is he introducing legislation that directly overrides local government?
statement: No, I am not concerned. The Government is committed to local democracy. We’re not removing the right to establish Māori wards. However, we want each community to decide whether they want one or not. This is a decision for local people in local communities to make their own decisions about local representation, and my message to those mayors is: what’s wrong with some localism—letting local communities make decisions for once? [Interruption]

explanation: Asked how he responds to the Hastings Mayor's statement that councils and communities should be trusted rather than central government leading. He does respond to it, by splitting the two things the quote joined: he says communities are trusted, through the ballot box, rather than councils deciding for them. Sneering about a "patsy question" is a civility matter, not evasion; the substance of the quote is met.
question: How does he respond to Hastings Mayor Sandra Hazlehurst: “This should not be central government-led. Local councils and communities should be trusted to determine what the best representation for their community is.”?
statement: Well, I thank the former Her Worship for the patsy question. Ultimately, we trust local communities to make these decisions. We agree local communities, through the ballot box, should be able to make decisions. We are going to entrust local communities to be able to vote on whether or not they should retain—or not—Māori wards in their communities. What’s wrong with some democracy?

explanation: Asked which other representation decisions (councillor numbers, rural wards, boundaries) will require compulsory referendums, or whether it is only Māori wards. He reaches the answer by a roundabout route: compulsion applies only to councils that established these wards without a referendum, other ward decisions stay with the Local Government Commission's checks and balances, and councils may hold voluntary referendums. Effectively "only Māori wards," though he never says it in those words.
question: How many other representation decisions will he require compulsory referendums for—for the number of councillors, for rural wards, for the boundaries, or is it only Māori wards?
statement: As the member knows, what we’re doing here is we’re requiring those councils which put in place these wards without a referendum to have a referendum. Following that, if a council wishes to put in place a Māori ward, petitioners can petition for a referendum. But, ultimately, councils, when they’re setting up other wards—their checks and balances are in place with the Local Government Commission having those checks and balances. And I would encourage local councils, if there are issues that they also wish to put to referendum, put them to referendum.

explanation: Asked whether mandatory referendums are reasonable for councils that have already consulted, given ratepayers bear the cost, and how that squares with responsible spending. He addresses the cost limb obliquely — the referendums will be held alongside the next local elections, which is a real answer to the expense concern — but never says whether he considers it reasonable and never engages the responsible-spending framing, closing on an attack on the other side of the House.
question: Does he consider it reasonable for councils who have already consulted and voted on Māori wards to have mandatory referendums when councils have stated that the costs of these referendums will be worn by ratepayers; if so, how does this reflect the Government’s supposed commitment to responsible spending?
statement: Well, this Government will be ensuring that councils can have those referendums at the same time as the next election for local councils. And so the voters will be able to vote for their mayor and their councillors at the same time as voting for whether or not they want to retain those mayors. And I say once again to members on the other side of the House: what’s wrong with some democracy? Because clearly they don’t believe in that on the other side of the House. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what he meant by his Waitangi Day statement that the obligations Te Tiriti imposes "on both sides will always be with us." He does answer a meaning question with a meaning — the Treaty is the founding document and will continue to be honoured — but the distinctive part of the quote, obligations running on both sides, is glossed over rather than explained. Thinness alone would not cost him; the unaddressed core does.
question: What did he mean when he stated on Waitangi Day 2024 that the obligations Te Tiriti imposes “on both sides will always be with us.”?
statement: Well, just that—that it’s actually the founding document of New Zealand; we’ll continue to honour it.

explanation: Asked how removing Treaty-principles references from 40+ pieces of legislation meets his Tiriti obligations. He contests the premise and describes the intent (making references specific to each Act's application), which is partial engagement, but never connects that to the obligations the question was about. The narrow "how does this meet X" is left unanswered.
question: How is removing references to Treaty principles from over 40 pieces of legislation meeting his Tiriti obligations?
statement: Well, I think that question mischaracterises what we’re doing. What we’re asking for is, actually, making sure that when there are references to the Treaty in legislation, that it’s actually very specific to the application of that legislation.

explanation: Asked how five named policies meet the Crown's obligations under Te Tiriti. He rejects the characterisation, says he could take each issue in turn and then does not, offering one example (the Māori Health Authority) justified on health-outcome grounds rather than on Tiriti obligations. A sprawling question given a fragment of a reply that sidesteps its actual test.
question: How do policies such as the Fast-track Approvals Bill, the Treaty Principles Bill, the removal of section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, the ministerial alienation of te reo Māori, and the disestablishment of Māori wards and the Māori Health Authority meet the Crown’s obligations to Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: Well, I reject the characterisation of that question. What I’d say to you is I could take each of those issues and say why we’re making the changes that we are. We don’t believe a Māori Health Authority actually delivers better health outcomes for Māori—period. We think there’s other ways to deal with that. We think we can do that through working and partnering with local iwi health organisations, as an example. So I just—you know, that’s our position, we’re very clear about it.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of the Department of Internal Affairs advice that polls were an almost insurmountable barrier to establishing Māori wards, and whether the policy is a deliberate tactic to reduce Māori representation. He neither confirms nor denies awareness of the advice and never touches the allegation of intent; the reply is generalised local-democracy talking points ending in "what's wrong with a little bit of democracy?"
question: Is he aware that the advice he received on this bill from the Department of Internal Affairs stated that the polls proved to be an almost insurmountable barrier to establishing Māori wards, and, if so, is this a deliberate tactic to reduce Māori representation in local government?
statement: Ultimately this is about local democracy, local communities making a decision on whether or not to have a ward based upon ethnicity. That is a major constitutional change for a council and, ultimately, on this side of the House, we’re of the view that communities should make those significant decisions rather than the council. And what’s wrong with a little bit of democracy? Those councils should be right behind this, actually supporting their communities being able to have their say.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with all his Government's statements and actions. Answered "Yes" and then expanded on one. A formulaic set-piece, but a clear question given a complete direct answer.
question: Talofa e te Pīka. Does he agree with all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our commitment to support working families with the cost of living crisis through tax reduction. After 14 years, this is a Government that is finally delivering income tax relief to hard-working New Zealanders in the Budget. The last Government’s response to inflation was more spending, more taxes, and more debt. We’re getting wasteful spending under control so that we can rebuild the economy and get New Zealand back on track.

explanation: Asked whether consulting affected parties is crucial and, if so, why local government representatives were not consulted as noted in the regulatory impact statement. He never says whether consultation is crucial and never mentions the regulatory impact statement or local government; he pivots to the general election as a "national conversation" that supplied a mandate. That is at best an implicit excuse for not consulting, offered in place of the answer.
question: Does he believe that consulting with affected parties is crucial when developing legislation and, if so, why was this not done with local government representatives as indicated in the regulatory impact statement?
statement: There was a thing on 14 October called an election, and the parties on this side of the House went out and campaigned on this policy, and the public, all 5.5 million New Zealanders—or not all of them could have a vote—but all 5.5 million New Zealanders were able to be part of a national conversation. They’ll all be able to have their say one day. And, ultimately, they decided on 14 October to elect the Government. And what we’re doing is implementing the policy that we were elected to do and then giving local communities the ability to have their say.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government will take to uphold its ICJ obligations. Luxon restates a February position and says NZ upholds international law and expects Israel to comply, but names no action the Government will take. Touches the subject without reaching the question.
question: What actions will his Government be taking to uphold his obligations to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in response to Israel’s continued assault on civilians and children in Rafah, including the murder of over 50 people last night?
statement: Well, I think you heard us declare in February—and we partnered with both Australia and Canada at the time—that we did not want to see Israel undertake military operations in Rafah, because it would have catastrophic implications and impact on people. Obviously, we are a country that upholds international law and we expect Israel to be compliant with the ICJ ruling.

explanation: Asked what recent Budget announcements she has made. Willis names the announcement (yesterday's savings programme with the PM) and its content. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has she made about the Budget?
statement: Yesterday, I joined the Prime Minister to outline further details of the Budget 2024 savings programme. In the same way that households have adjusted their budgets and their spending, as a Government we have had to do the same. Ministers have gone line by line through the funding they are responsible for to evaluate whether it represents the best use of precious taxpayer dollars. As I said yesterday, this line-by-line process has uncovered more than 240 individual saving initiatives for inclusion in Budget 2024.

explanation: Asked what the savings will be used for. She says explicitly 'two things' — tax relief and investment in Government priorities including front-line services. Answered, though a swipe at the Opposition is spliced into the middle.
question: What will the savings be used for?
statement: The savings will be used for two things—the members opposite laugh at the New Zealanders who are paying higher rates of tax than they have in 14 years, because it’s their view that they can always spend it better than New Zealanders can in their own families. But on this side of the House, we are making savings so that they can be both used to provide long overdue tax relief for hard-working New Zealanders and also be used to invest in Government priorities, including front-line services. On Thursday, members will see examples of careful reprioritisation in almost every area of Government, freeing up cash to go towards things—

explanation: Asked where savings have been made. Partly deferred to the Budget, but she then lists concrete sites (Corrections, Defence, income insurance, ITPs, Lake Onslow, Clean Car Discount, LGWM, school lunches). Squarely engaged.
question: Where have savings been made?
statement: That will be announced in the Budget, and I can tell the member that the Government has already announced decisions to stop some lower-value spending. This includes finding $442 million in savings at Corrections so we can reinvest in our prisons and front-line corrections officers; finding $99 million from within the New Zealand Defence Force to reinvest in defence personnel and equipment; stopping work on the income insurance scheme, another name for a job tax; stopping work on so-called industry transformation plans; stopping work on Lake Onslow; repealing the Clean Car Discount; exiting the Crown’s contribution to Let’s Get Wellington Moving, otherwise known as “Let’s Slow Wellington Down”; and continuing the school lunch programme left unfunded by the outgoing Government, and delivering it in a way that saves taxpayers approximately $107 million a year.

explanation: Asked about announcements on Public Service job losses. She gives the figures directly — ~2,250 roles, ~1,150 vacancies, 500+ further — before moving to talking points. The core was answered first.
question: What announcements has she made about the impact Budget 2024 will have on the job losses in the Public Service?
statement: The increase over the past six years in the number of back-office Public Service roles was unaffordable and needed to be reined back. According to the most recent advice I have received, the Government’s baseline savings exercise will remove around 2,250 roles from Government departments, as well as closing around 1,150 vacancies. Further savings initiatives additional to our baseline exercise will remove a little over 500 roles. The number is subject to change and will remain so after Budget day. My heart goes out to anyone losing their job but Budget 2024 has required us to carefully reprioritise taxpayers’ dollars. The members on the opposite side of the House seem to think there’s a magic money tree at the end of the garden—or at least, if it’s not at the end of the garden, that magic money tree is New Zealand taxpayers whose pockets they never give up on fleecing. But we, on this side of the House, have reprioritised funding to support more workers on the front line, including nurses, doctors, police, teachers, and corrections officers. The list goes on, and I’ll have more to say on Thursday.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his own $250-a-fortnight statement. He says 'yes' (qualified by context) and confirms tax relief is coming, then pivots to attacking Labour. The yes/no was given.
question: Talofa lava. Does he agree with the then Leader of the Opposition, Christopher Luxon, who stated on 19 September 2023, regarding the National Party’s proposed tax cuts, that “for an average household income family with young kids, that would mean $250 a fortnight”?
statement: In the context that that statement was made, yes, and I can confirm that this Government will be delivering tax relief in this year’s Budget, supporting Kiwis with the cost of living, with more detail to come on Thursday. And like him—though I don’t agree with Labour’s tax policy at the election; he’s already flip-flopped on capital gains tax, and my bet is he’s going to flip-flop on GST too.

explanation: Asked how many families will get $250 a fortnight. Answered only with a quip ('Two more sleeps to go'). An implied deferral rather than a plain refusal, and the question is never engaged.
question: How many families will benefit from $250 a fortnight in tax cuts as a result of this year’s Budget?
statement: As your former finance Minister used to say, “Two more sleeps to go.”

explanation: Asked how many extra dollars per week a minimum-wage worker keeps. He defers to Thursday — an explicit, if partial, response — then pivots to talking points about supporting workers. No engagement with the figure asked for.
question: How many extra dollars per week will a minimum-wage worker keep, thanks to his Government’s tax cuts?
statement: Again, you’ll have to wait till Thursday, but what I can say to that member is that this is a Government that believes, after 14 years, that working New Zealanders, low and middle income workers, the same people the Labour Party and the New Zealand Council of Trade Unions used to care about, actually need support. And I’d just encourage that member and his party and say, vote for the tax relief that we’re going to be delivering on Thursday evening.

explanation: Asked to confirm the $2-a-week figure from National's own calculator. Neither confirmed nor denied; deferred to Thursday and turned the calculator reference into a plug. The core is dodged.
question: Can he confirm that according to the National Party’s own tax calculator, which has mysteriously been removed, minimum-wage workers can expect an additional $2 a week?
statement: Well, again, the member will have to wait until Thursday, but what I appreciate is the question about the tax calculator, because I do want to say to the few people that are watching this broadcast today, get on board, go check out the official tax calculator on Thursday, and see how much benefit you’re going to get.

explanation: Asked how many extra dollars per week a typical property investor keeps. He says it depends on individual circumstances — a reason for not answering that at least addresses the question — then pivots to interest deductibility and brightline. No figure, but the question is acknowledged.
question: How many extra dollars per week will a typical property investor keep, thanks to the Government’s tax cuts?
statement: Again, that’ll be dependent upon their individual circumstances, but what’s great is that we have restored interest deductibility, we’ve reduced the brightline test, and we’re balancing laws between tenants and landlords so we get a greater supply of rental properties in the housing market.

explanation: Asked to confirm a specific figure ($288/week per property, 144x a minimum-wage worker). The answer is entirely about solving the housing crisis and the previous Government's record. A narrow factual question completely avoided.
question: Can he confirm that a typical property investor can expect to keep an additional $288 per week per property, or 144 times what a minimum-wage worker can expect to keep?
statement: Well, what I can confirm is that this is a Government that is going to solve the housing crisis, unlike his Government that had six years to do it and didn’t deliver. We’re here to deliver. We want an increase in supply in new houses being built, an increase in supply in rental properties, and an increase in supply in social housing.

explanation: Asked to guarantee the Budget won't trigger Reserve Bank rate hikes, and if not, why not. The response attacks the questioner's record throughout and never addresses the guarantee or gives a reason.
question: Will he guarantee that this year’s Budget will not lead the Reserve Bank to hike up interest rates again, leaving families worse off; if not, why not?
statement: Well, look, I really appreciate the member’s interest in tax relief. It’s the most animated I’ve seen him discussing it. He had six years to deal with it. He didn’t touch it at all. And I’m just thinking of all those low and middle income workers out there that are working incredibly hard and still can’t get ahead because of the economic vandalism and mismanagement that his Government created. And help is on the way on Thursday.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that the Budget won't trigger further OCR hikes, and why not if he can't give one. He never says whether he will guarantee it. The closing line about the Reserve Bank being independent brushes against the 'why not', but the bulk is a pivot to Budget framing and attacks on the previous government. Gestures at the core without reaching it.
question: Will he guarantee that this year’s Budget will not lead to the Reserve Bank hiking interest rates again, leaving families worse off; if not, why not?
statement: What I can say to him is our Budget is designed to lower Government spending, to lower inflation so we lower interest rates, get the economy growing, and we actually keep people in employment. The tragic reality of the previous administration was Government spending went up 84 percent, inflation hit an all-time high, interest rates hit an all-time high, the economy’s in recession, and rising unemployment. The Reserve Bank has an independent—we have an independent policy with the Reserve Bank.

explanation: A yes/no on whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' with a light qualifier ('in the context they were given'). Direct and essentially complete; the qualifier shades it just below a bare 'Yes'.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context they were given.

explanation: Asked whether more coalmining and oil and gas drilling is consistent with a livable planet and his stated climate goals. He redirects to a colleague's speech and argues minerals are needed for EVs, solar and wind — an implicit case that mining is compatible, but he never engages coal, oil and gas or the climate-goals test that was actually put to him. Partial engagement with an adjacent question.
question: Does the Prime Minister believe that more coalmining and oil and gas drilling is consistent with a livable planet or meeting our climate goals, as he has said that he is committed to?
statement: Well, what I’d just say to that member is I would encourage her to read an excellent speech given by the Minister for Resources, Shane Jones, in the last week. It’s an actually thoughtful speech and it talks about the role that mining will play in New Zealand in helping us make that transition. Here’s the deal: every electric vehicle (EV), every smartphone, every solar panel, every wind farm needs minerals. We can’t just make them out of thin air.

explanation: A narrow factual awareness question: is he aware the speech he cited is premised on rapid fossil-fuel phase-out and an end to coalmining? He repeats that the speech is thoughtful and that minerals are needed. The awareness question is never touched — a specific question squarely avoided.
question: Is he aware that that very speech he’s referencing of the Hon Shane Jones where he repeated the International Energy Agency’s assessment that the world needs six times more rare minerals for green transition is premised on a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels and an end to coalmining?
statement: Again, what I’d say to you is that it’s a very thoughtful speech and there’s no way we can deliver our transition to a clean economy without minerals.

explanation: Asked who he is getting his advice from, given he disagrees with the IEA, the Climate Change Commission and mainstream science. No source is named, no adviser identified; he restates the minerals-for-transition talking point. The question's core is a name, and none is offered.
question: If he disagrees with the International Energy Agency and the independent Climate Change Commission and the world’s top scientists that there is no future in fossil fuels or coalmining, from who is he actually getting his advice?
statement: Well, look, I think the member would understand that actually mining is very important for helping us actually adopt EVs, to use smartphones, to adopt solar panels, and to make sure we get wind farms. We need minerals for that process and that transition.

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree with S&P on unabated mines as stranded assets, and with his own infrastructure line. He explicitly answers only the second part, then pivots to fast-track legislation. He is transparent about which part he is taking, but the substantive core — the S&P stranded-asset assessment — is left unanswered.
question: Does he agree with Standard & Poor’s that “unabated mines face the risk of becoming stranded assets as the global economy works towards decarbonisation” and his idea of “a modern, reliable infrastructure in New Zealand”?
statement: I certainly agree with the last part of that question, which is I do want to see a modern, reliable infrastructure emerge here in New Zealand. That’s why, again, I keep saying to the member that I encourage her and her party to support our fast-track legislation.

explanation: Asked whether the kiwi-habitat framing accurately represents his Government's policies. 'I reject the premise of that question' is a real, direct answer to that — it says no. He then leaves it there and returns to the minerals talking point rather than saying what the accurate representation is. Half the question engaged.
question: Does the Prime Minister think that sacrificing the habitat of the great spotted kiwi at the altar of coalmines is an accurate representation of his Government’s economic and environmental policies?
statement: Look, I reject the premise of that question, but what I’d just say to that member is, look, here’s the deal: we need minerals—we need critical minerals—in order to make the transition to a clean future. That’s all that the Minister was putting out on the table in an excellent speech last week. I encourage all members to read it.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on social housing places; he states the announcement — $140 million for 1,500 new social homes via community housing providers. Squarely on the question asked. (A patsy question, but patsy-ness is not this attribute.)
question: What announcements has he made regarding social housing places?
statement: Last week, I was proud to announce that Budget 2024 allocates $140 million to funding 1,500 new social homes. This investment underlines the Government’s commitment to housing New Zealanders in need in a fiscally sustainable way. We will be funding these places to community housing providers. They do an outstanding job housing people in need, currently providing over 13,000 social houses around New Zealand, and they have the capability, expertise, and desire to grow further. We’re committed to growing the social housing sector.

explanation: Asked when/where the new places will be prioritised. He gives a timeframe ('the next two years'), says roughly 500 come quickly from the existing pipeline, and states the prioritisation criteria and target. Directly addressed; the swipe at the questioner and the loose 'when vs where' reading keep it a shade off full marks.
question: When will he prioritise these new social housing places?
statement: No, in the next two years—you should listen up, mate; I answered that last week. Currently, social housing is procured from community housing providers on a project by project basis. What we have said is that around 500 new homes of the 1,500 will be allocated quickly, using the existing pipeline of community housing provider opportunities, with three objectives in mind: firstly, value for money from Government investment; secondly, contributing towards our target of getting people out of emergency housing motels; and a balanced approach between achievability and building capability in historically underserved regions. In short, this means we will be prioritising social housing places where it will make the biggest difference and get people out of motels.

explanation: Asked what happens to the remaining places. He says the balance of about a thousand will go through an active-purchaser approach developed over the rest of 2024, and explains what that means. Complete and on point.
question: What about the rest of the 1,500 new places?
statement: The balance of the 1,500 places, which will be about a thousand, will likely be allocated using an active-purchaser approach, which officials will be developing throughout the rest of 2024. This is a concept developed in the independent review of Kāinga Ora, and it refers to the Government developing a much more sophisticated understanding of current and future housing needs at a national, regional, and cohort level; taking a social-investment approach to improving housing outcome; and, potentially, outcome-based contracts. Subject to ministerial agreement, officials will be looking at developing longer-term strategic partnerships with some community housing providers to achieve specific social and housing outcomes, rather than looking at single proposals one by one.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a quoted statement. She says she stands by it and restores the fuller quote. That is a yes with context, not a dodge — the question is engaged head-on.
question: Malo le soifua manuia, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by her statement, “These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party’s tax plan, with some adjustments to reflect coalition agreements”?
statement: I stand by the full statement I made in question time last Tuesday, which was, “Tax relief in the Budget will be fully funded through savings and revenue initiatives. These savings and revenue initiatives are the same as those in the National Party’s tax plan, with some adjustments to reflect coalition agreements. There will also be other savings in the Budget [and] these savings will be directed towards Government priorities, including front-line public services.”

explanation: Asked where the coalition agreement mentions an increase to the visitor levy. "It doesn't" is a complete, direct answer — nowhere. Blunt and unelaborated, but the question is squarely answered.
question: Where in the coalition agreement does it say that the international visitor levy will increase?
statement: It doesn’t.

explanation: Asked where the agreement provides for a ute tax. The opening "That's not being considered" engages the premise and implicitly answers "nowhere", but the bulk of the response pivots to trailing the Budget matters document — an announcement, not the answer. Partially answers, then moves off it.
question: Where in the coalition agreement does it say that she will introduce or consider a tax on utes as outlined in advice received by the Minister of Revenue?
statement: That’s not being considered. Now, I can see that the member is very interested in the funding of our tax plan. So what I want to announce to the House is that those interested in that can look forward to the Budget matters document, which will be released on Thursday. I can advise the member that—I think it’s page 3 or 4 of that document—there will be an itemised outline of the savings and revenue measures being used to support our fully funded tax package that’s going to put cash back in the pockets of hard-working Kiwis.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to fund 13 cancer treatments, and why not if not. Never says yes or no; defers to Budget day and pivots to Pharmac funding and the previous government. The closing line that not all coalition commitments land in the first Budget gestures at the "why not" limb without reaching it. Deferral rather than refusal — it does not settle the question.
question: Will she commit to funding the 13 new cancer treatments promised in her fiscal plan; if not, why not?
statement: I have told that member a few times over the last few weeks that she will have to await Budget day to find the full set of commitments that we are progressing. There’s two comments that I would make. The first is we are a Government that was left with a massive hole where funding for the Pharmac budget should have been—they left massive fiscal cliffs so that we have already announced our commitment to a $1.8 billion boost for Pharmac. The second thing I would say is that across the coalition agreements that the National, New Zealand First, and ACT parties have formed, there are a number of commitments and not all of them will be delivered in our first Budget.

explanation: "No." answers the primary question completely and directly. The second limb ("if not, why not?") is left untouched, which is the only thing keeping this off 1.0 — the brevity itself is not a mark against forthrightness.
question: Will the Minister be hosting a social services budget lock-up this year; if not, why not?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether the calculator was taken down for a stated reason. "No" answers directly, and the follow-on about an official Treasury calculator from 2 p.m. Thursday stays on the subject rather than pivoting away.
question: Has she taken down the tax calculator because she knows New Zealanders will not receive the $250 per fortnight in tax cuts that they had promised?
statement: No. There will be an official Government tax calculator. It will be hosted on the Treasury website, it will be available from 2 p.m. on Thursday, and you should go and check it out.

explanation: Asked what progress had been made on attendance data availability. The answer names the dashboard, its launch date and its update cadence — a direct, complete response to what was asked.
question: What progress has he made in making student attendance data more available?
statement: On 7 May, I announced a new online data dashboard which makes daily attendance data available to the public and parents in a more timely way. The interactive dashboard will be updated once a week to show a national average and also regional breakdowns of how many students attended school each and every day. [Turns laptop toward members of the House]

explanation: "Does he stand by his statement?" answered "Yes." One word, complete, nothing avoided.
question: Talofa lava, Mr Speaker. Does he stand by his statement that the review into Kāinga Ora was “thorough”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how the review can be thorough given Kāinga Ora's account of limited engagement. He engages the challenge head-on by attributing it to the agency and preferring the reviewers' findings — but that resolves whose account he believes, not how the review was thorough. Addresses the question's territory without reaching its core.
question: How is it thorough when the organisation under review has stated, “There was relatively limited engagement with our organisation, leading to some review conclusions appearing to be based on analysis informed by anecdotes rather than independently considering the performance of the organisation.”?
statement: Well, that, unsurprisingly, is Kāinga Ora’s perspective. I prefer the findings of the independent review.

explanation: Asked why the Cabinet paper omitted Kāinga Ora's concerns. "Because I didn't agree with Kāinga Ora's perspective" gives a reason for the omission directly. It does not cover the "how is it thorough" framing, but the substantive ask — why leave it out — is met.
question: How is it thorough when he in paragraph 56 of the relevant Cabinet paper omitted that there were serious and credible concerns raised in Kāinga Ora’s response, instead stating, “the Board is broadly comfortable with the review recommendations”?
statement: Because, unsurprisingly, I didn’t agree with Kāinga Ora’s perspective on the review.

explanation: Asked when he approached Sir Bill English. "Soon after the election" answers the when. It is imprecise, but vagueness is Specificity — the question was engaged, not deflected.
question: When did he approach Sir Bill English to chair the review into Kāinga Ora?
statement: Sir Bill and I talked soon after the election about whether or not he could help out in reviewing Kāinga Ora. Ultimately, that is what happened, alongside two other very credible and expert reviewers.

explanation: Asked whether he advised against involving Kāinga Ora. "No" answers directly, and the rest substantiates by listing who the reviewers met. Nothing sidestepped.
question: Did he advise Sir Bill English not to involve Kāinga Ora in the review?
statement: No, and they were involved in the review. He met with Kāinga Ora alongside community housing providers, a range of people in the social sector, developers, and builders across a range of organisations in the social sector.

explanation: Asked how he can be confident the report is credible. He does engage: he rebuts the question's premises and asserts the concerns are not credible or serious, which is a partial answer to the confidence question. But the closing turn to the member's motives and the previous government's record is a pivot away, and the basis for his confidence is asserted rather than given.
question: How can he be confident this was a credible report when it ignored serious and credible concerns raised by Kāinga Ora, the details of which were omitted in the Cabinet paper, and he instructed the review not to involve Kāinga Ora?
statement: Well, there are a number of factual inaccuracies there. Firstly, I didn’t ask the reviewers not to involve Kāinga Ora—you should have listened to my last answer. The reviewers did talk to Kāinga Ora. And in relation to the first part of his question, the concerns that the member relays as apparently or purportedly credible and serious are not credible and serious. I appreciate that the member wishes to defend the record of Kāinga Ora under the last Government; this Government has a different attitude to that, and the public can see for itself the financial disaster that is that organisation.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions; answered "Yes" outright. The trailing "in the context they were given" is a minor qualifier, not an evasion — the question was engaged and answered.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and in the context they were given.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the statement (answered "Yes, we do") and how many times the processes have been used on the Fast-track Bill (never answered — no count, no attempt at one). He pivots to the select committee process and a defence of the bill. Half the question squarely met, the narrow factual half squarely avoided.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “we have well-established processes for managing ministerial conflicts of interest”, and, if so, how many times have those “well-established processes” been used during the development of the Fast-track Approvals Bill?
statement: Yes, we do. And as I said before, and as you’ve heard the Minister for Infrastructure say, the process is before select committee. If there’s any sensible builds and improvements that can be made to the legislation, we’ll happily take that on board. But we make no apologies for adapting something that David Parker brought in the previous Government to actually fast-track and get things done in this country. We’re going to build things.

explanation: A narrow factual question — was a conflict-of-interest process used for Minister Jones' undisclosed dinner with coalmining executives, and if not why not. The answer never mentions the dinner, the Minister, or any process being used or not used; it goes straight to select committee feedback and "we're going to get things done". Neither limb touched.
question: Was a process for managing perceived or real conflicts of interest used in relation to the previously undisclosed dinner Minister Jones had with coalmining executives, including those from Te Kuha coalmine project, and, if not, why not?
statement: What I’d just say to the member is that we’ve got a bill that’s through the select committee process right now. We’re taking feedback in the select committee process to see if it can be strengthened. If there’s anything that people think that we can improve, we’re happy to take that on board. But I make no apologies. We are going to stop the talking and we’re going to get things done in this country. New Zealanders are expecting us to deliver more infrastructure, more windfarms, more renewable energy. And I keep calling on that member and her party to support this legislation.

explanation: Asked whether a process was used for the Oceans and Fisheries Minister's dinners with fishing executives. "I reject the premise of the question" is a real engagement move rather than a pivot, and "we have processes in place to manage conflicts" gestures at the topic, but he never says whether a process was used in this instance or why not, then turns to the merits of the legislation.
question: Was a process for managing perceived or real conflicts of interest used for the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries’ dinners with fishing executives who may be looking to use the fast-track consenting process and who have previously donated to Minister Jones’ election campaigns, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, I reject the premise of the question. We have processes in place to manage conflicts. But, most importantly, we are going to get this fast-track legislation done because it matters to New Zealanders. It improves the economic productivity of this country, it improves social outcomes, and it improves environmental outcomes too.

explanation: Asked for a specific commitment: change the bill to give the panel ultimate decision-making power. He neither commits nor declines — he restates that the Minister for Infrastructure is "open to sensible changes", which is adjacent to the question but never reaches it, then attacks the previous Government. A flat "no" would have scored far higher.
question: Will the Prime Minister commit to changing the Fast-track Approvals Bill so that the panel has ultimate decision-making powers to prevent any conflicts of interest in decision making, considering a Minister in his Cabinet was lobbied by the mining industry before the bill was even introduced?
statement: Well, again, the member didn’t listen to my earlier answers to earlier questions which was that the Minister for Infrastructure has said that he is open to sensible changes to the legislation that can improve it. But, again, I make no apologies. We are going to get things done because we’re not going to spend the time like the last six years of a Labour-Greens Government that just talked a lot, a lot of bumper stickers, and didn’t get stuff done. New Zealanders want delivery; they want things to happen.

explanation: Asked what would constitute a conflict of interest under the Cabinet Manual. The answer says only that policies exist for managing conflicts — restating that there is a process is not saying what counts as a conflict — and closes by telling the questioner to manage her own personnel. The definitional core is untouched.
question: What would constitute a conflict of interest under the Cabinet Manual if none of these instances from his Ministers warrant concerns from the Prime Minister?
statement: Look, again, I just say to the member: we have policies, as you well know, through the Cabinet Office for managing conflicts, perceived or real. I would just encourage that member maybe to think and focus on managing her own personnel, not ours.

explanation: Asked what recent pre-Budget education announcements she has made; she names the announcement ($53m over four years for teacher supply) directly. Question engaged and answered.
question: What recent pre-Budget education announcements has she made?
statement: Last week, I announced $53 million over the next four years to attract, train, and retain teachers—the greatest asset that we have in our education system and an essential part of our plan to lift student achievement. This investment will support an additional 1,500 teachers into the workforce and help to give our kids a world-leading education. Budget 2024 is unashamedly about the front line, and you don’t get more front line in education than the teachers who stand at the front of the classroom every day, shaping the lives of our young people.

explanation: Asked why teacher training is a priority; the response gives reasons (reports of unprepared graduates, projected shortage of up to 680 secondary teachers, ERO findings) and states the conclusion. Whether those reasons are true or well-argued is Veracity/Rigor, not this.
question: Why is investment in teacher training a priority for this Government?
statement: Multiple recent reports indicate that the system is letting teachers down. Newly graduated teachers do not feel confident, supported, or prepared for the classroom. We’re also faced with a projected shortage of up to 680 secondary school teachers in the next three years. The Education Review Office (ERO) found that half of our graduating teachers felt unprepared for the classroom. This Government is listening. Lifting achievement means investing in our teachers and improving the delivery of initial teacher education and developing the workforce of the future, and that is a priority for this Government.

explanation: Asked what the investment will deliver; the answer enumerates what it delivers (1,200 on-site training places, stipend, fees, host-school funding, relocation grants, scholarships). Squarely on the question asked.
question: What will this investment in the front line deliver?
statement: This funding includes 1,200 new on-site teacher-training places, a stipend for the trainees, contribution towards their tuition fees, and funding to support host schools. ERO recently reported that trainees who spend two or more days per week in schools were more prepared to enter the classroom upon graduation. On-site training provides an opportunity to spend more time in the classroom and to incentivise people with specialist skills and high-quality graduates to consider training as a teacher while receiving a stipend towards their cost of living and having their fees contributed to. We’re also investing in relocation grants for an additional 300 overseas teachers, supports for schools in early childhood education with teacher recruitment costs, and 670 scholarships and awards for teachers.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has seen; she supplies feedback she has seen, quoted from the PPTA president, a new teacher and a principal. That the feedback is selectively favourable does not make it a dodge of this question.
question: What feedback has she seen about this announcement?
statement: I’ve received strong support from the education sector. Post Primary Teachers’ Association president, Chris Abercrombie, said, “In-class training is a really good option and it’s a really good step from the Government to be looking at addressing the supply issue.” One new teacher, Hugo Miller, said, “I would have loved [to have spent] more time in schools.”—during his in-class training—“I really took so much away from that and from the guidance of a mentor teacher or an associate teacher.”, and David Ferguson, the principal of Westlake Boys High School, said that their experience with on-site training was a real success. He also said, “We think by exposing trainees to more in-class practising, watching really good teachers teach, that’s a better way of preparing them than being at university full time.”

explanation: Asked how many, if any, teachers will lose their jobs. The answer does engage the job-loss question — contracts not renewed, 271 FTE roles affected, retraining offered, teachers "may not necessarily lose their jobs" — but hedges around the core and never gives a number or a straight "none". Partial answer with the count avoided.
question: Talofa, Mr Speaker. How many, if any, teachers will lose their jobs due to cuts to Reading Recovery?
statement: I recently announced $67 million of investment into structured literacy approaches to ensure that Kiwi kids are learning to read using evidence-based approaches proven to lift achievement and close the equity gap. As a result of this, reading-recovery contracts due to expire at the end of this year will not be renewed as this Government commits to consistent use of best practice in our schools. Teaching staff who are employed under the ministry-allocated 271 full-time equivalent reading-recovery roles have already been offered the opportunity to retrain using structured approaches to literacy, and many have already taken up this offer. The ministry advise that, therefore, current reading-recovery teachers may not necessarily lose their jobs.

explanation: Asked how many children will lose access to reading recovery. The answer opens with "good news" and describes replacement tier 2/3 structured literacy interventions — a different question (what replaces it) than the one asked (how many lose access to it). No number, and no direct statement about loss of access to the programme named.
question: How many children will lose access to reading recovery as a result of cuts to the reading recovery programme and its teachers?
statement: Well, good news: this Government is introducing a tier 2 and 3, which is small group and one-on-one interventions using structured literacy so all children at primary school who are falling behind in their reading will have access to proven methods of intervention consistent with classroom teaching and structured literacy intervention.

explanation: Asked whether she is aware of the report and why she is cutting the programme. She engages the report head-on (disputes what it compares) and gives her reason for cutting — reading recovery teaches 'the habits of poor readers'. The 'are you aware' half is answered implicitly rather than stated, but the core 'why' is squarely met. Truth of the claim about the research is a Veracity matter, not scored here.
question: Is the Minister aware of the Government’s own report that found that children who partake in the reading recovery programme made double the normal progress expected; if so, why is she cutting the successful programme?
statement: I will not continue to fund a programme that, at the core of its philosophy, believes in teaching children the habits of poor readers. That research that that member is quoting is taking a look at reading recovery compared to what they’re doing now, which is a little sprinkling of structured literacy. So what we know is when you do structured literacy, you get better results. So how about we just do structured literacy and see what happens, because we know the evidence backs that up.

explanation: Asked what she says to a named expert's specific argument — that reading recovery works regardless of the classroom programme because it is individually driven. She opens by declining to move ('I'll go back to my main point'), restates her prior position, and closes by quoting the questioner back at herself. She responds to the general dispute but never engages Gaffney's actual claim, so the core of the question is only glanced at.
question: What does she say, then, to Professor Janet Gaffney, who led the introduction of reading recovery at Illinois successfully, where structured literacy programmes were the programmes of the day, and said, “Because reading recovery teachers plan based on the child’s strengths, it doesn’t matter what classroom programme is happening, the individual nature of the remedial programme means that observation and assessment drive the teaching.”?
statement: I’ll go back to my main point that I made in my last answer. At the heart of reading recovery, they believe in teaching children the habits of poor readers. The three-cueing system: look at the picture, guess the word. Those are the habits of poor readers. We know from all of the evidence from structured literacy in-class teaching that the need for remedial reading drops by up to two-thirds. So we know that structured literacy is the approach that’s going to work for most of our kids. I would also like to quote a very learned person, in fact a very learned teacher, who said that structured literacy was one of the best things that she had seen in her lifetime of teaching. And that person was Jan Tinetti. [Interruption]

explanation: A yes/no guarantee was sought and 'Absolutely' gives it, unconditionally and completely. One word, no hedging, nothing left dangling. Whether the guarantee is credible or wise is a different attribute.
question: Will she guarantee that any future remedial reading programme will be funded at the same amount as reading recovery and have the same, if not better, results than reading recovery?
statement: Absolutely.

explanation: Asked what she says to a teacher who wants to know why trained teachers are being taken from the students who need them most. She addresses the teacher directly and answers implicitly — they are not being removed, they are being offered retraining into tier 2/3 interventions. The 'why' is met obliquely rather than stated, but the response is aimed at the question rather than away from it.
question: What does she say to Paula, who is one of the very many reading recovery teachers who have contacted me and will be losing her job at the end of the year, who says, “Why would you take trained teachers away from those students who need them the most?”
statement: Well, my message to that woman is firstly, thank you so much for being a teacher. We value you. The ministry has already contacted all of those reading recovery teachers, offered them retraining in evidence-based structured literacy, and many of them are taking that up. So what I would say to that teacher is “Please take up the opportunity to retrain in structured literacy and be part of the tier 2 and tier 3 interventions using a structured literacy method.”

explanation: Asked what comments he has seen. Nearly the whole answer is the funding announcement itself, not comments; only the final clause ('heartening to read so many supportive comments') touches the question, and it cites none. It gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: What comments has he seen regarding his recent announcement about Gumboot Friday?
statement: Budget 2024 will provide $24 million over four years to contract the I Am Hope Foundation to provide young people aged between five to 25 years with free mental health counselling services through the Gumboot Friday initiative. This will enable Gumboot Friday to provide more than 15,000 young New Zealanders access to free mental health counselling services each year. We know that mental health issues are one of the biggest issues facing New Zealanders each year.
