question: Is it correct that her decision to halve the excise tax on heated tobacco and delay safety requirements on vapes benefit only the tobacco company Philip Morris?
statement: I will state clearly, as we seem to be relitigating this issue and we’ve traversed it thoroughly, that we are committed to achieving Smokefree Aotearoa 2025. I will yet again confirm that we are choosing to do a programme of work that will ensure that there are tools available to achieve the target audience quitting smoking. We will continue to do so. There is no relationship with the tobacco industry. We are committed to a programme of work, and we will achieve Smokefree Aotearoa 2025—highly likely that will be achieved this year.

explanation: Asked to name one thing done for New Zealanders' health greater than the benefit to Philip Morris. She opens by attacking the Opposition's fixation, but does name actions (raised excise tax first as Minister, meeting quit-smoking providers). Partially answers the 'name a thing' half; ignores the comparison.
question: Can the Minister name a single thing she has done for the health of New Zealanders that is greater than the benefits she has provided for Philip Morris?
statement: The Opposition seem to be fixated on tobacco companies. They seem to have lost sight of the people we are trying to help, which is those who are currently smoking. They ignore the fact that the first thing I did as a Minister was raise excise tax, and that we are continuing to meet with quit-smoking groups to ensure they have the best tools. The main audience for this change are the quit-smoking providers, all of whom I will be meeting with over the next month to discuss the best way to continue to reduce smoking rates and achieve our smoke-free 2025 target.

explanation: Asked what changes have been made to support young people into work. She names the change (phone-based case management for 4,000 jobseekers aged 18–24) and its roll-out. Directly answers.
question: What changes has the Government made to support young people into work?
statement: Last week, I announced that 4,000 additional job seekers aged 18 to 24 will receive support from a case manager over the phone. Fifteen hundred young people were receiving this new service at the beginning of July, and the roll-out to 4,000 young job seekers will be complete in two months. This is one of the many actions the Government is taking to make the welfare system more proactive and to support people into work, because we are not prepared to accept the current forecasts that under-25-year-olds on a jobseeker benefit will spend two decades of their life on welfare.

explanation: Asked why the support is being provided NOW. Upston answers the timing question squarely: inherited economic conditions meant jobseeker numbers were due to peak in early 2025, and young jobseekers are more vulnerable, so help is going in now. The 'why now' is the core of the question and it is reached directly.
question: Why is the Government providing young job seekers this additional support now?
statement: The challenging economic situation that we have inherited means that job seeker numbers were always due to increase and to peak at the start of 2025. We know that young job seekers are more vulnerable to tougher labour market conditions, and we want the welfare system to proactively help as many job seekers as possible in the current economic climate. Getting more direct help to young people now will mean they are better prepared to enter the workforce and take up job opportunities as they arise.

explanation: Asked how phone-based case management will work. The answer describes the actual mechanics — contact at least every 28 days, a set appointment time, tailored advice, and the obligation failure/sanction consequence for missing it. Complete engagement with the mechanism asked about.
question: How will phone-based case management work for young people?
statement: Ministry of Social Development (MSD) case managers will contact young job seekers at least once every 28 days. There will be a set appointment time for the phone call. Having a case manager means that young people will have tailored advice and support that suits their unique circumstances. This additional support of course comes with obligations. If a young person misses their assigned phone appointment without good reason, an obligation failure will be initiated, which may result in a sanction.

explanation: Asked whether phone-based case management is the only action taken. Answer opens with a flat 'No' and then names the other actions (sanctions regime, work-focused appointment in the first two weeks, six-month re-engagement). Direct yes/no plus the substance behind it.
question: Is phone-based case management the only action the Government has taken to make the welfare system more proactive at supporting people into work?
statement: No. We have set out our expectations that, along with the additional support we are providing, there will be consequences, including sanctions when people fail to fulfil their obligations to become work-ready and to take steps to find work. We are also requiring those with work obligations to have a work-focused appointment in their first two weeks of being on benefit, and if they’re still on benefit after six months, they will need to meet MSD again. The Government believes that work is the best pathway to independence and to further opportunities, and we will continue to take more actions over the coming months to support more New Zealanders into work.

explanation: A two-part question: in what specific sectors did overspending occur, and was it raised with him during the observer's appointment. Reti confirms the observer raised issues with him and identifies the hospital sector, so both limbs are touched, but 'specific sectors' gets one broad sector rather than the breakdown asked for and the eight-month timing is left vague. Partially answered.
question: In what specific sectors of Te Whatu Ora has overspending occurred, and was this raised with him in the last eight months of the Crown observer appointment?
statement: The Government appointed a Crown observer in December, given our longstanding concerns about the implementation of the health reforms that created Health New Zealand. The Crown observer has highlighted numerous issues to me, including a lack of focus on the current financial situation, particularly in the hospital sector. Hospitals are a critical sector in the health system and is one reason why this Government has taken significant action by appointing a commissioner to ensure all New Zealanders get timely access to quality healthcare.

explanation: Asked how cutting up to 3,000 jobs helps get more doctors and nurses on the front line. The answer gives the actual claimed mechanism — the cuts target back-office staff who are not patient-facing, freeing funds to redistribute to the front line. Whether that is true or persuasive is a Veracity/Rigor matter; as a response it addresses the question asked.
question: How will slashing up to 3,000 jobs from the organisation that employs doctors and nurses help to get more doctors and nurses on the front line to serve our people?
statement: The commissioner has expressed that we will streamline the back-office staff that are not directly patient facing so that we can redistribute funds towards the front line and deliver better outcome for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts health funding fell 4.5 percent per capita and, if so, whether he will increase it. He answers neither limb: 'What I accept is the biggest contribution to health of roughly $16.67 billion' substitutes a favourable aggregate for the per-capita figure put to him and never reaches the funding commitment. A narrow factual question redirected to a different metric.
question: Does he accept that the overall health Budget funding has actually reduced by 4.5 percent per capita, and, if so, will he increase funding to sustainable levels so that our health system isn’t on its knees?
statement: What I accept is the biggest contribution to health of roughly $16.67 billion across three Budgets in our last Budget.

explanation: Asked whether he really thinks a relentless focus on cost savings is the right brief for the commissioner. He replies with what he does think — that timely access to quality healthcare matters — which is not responsive to the question about the cost-savings mandate. The core proposition is stepped around rather than accepted or rejected.
question: Does he really think that a relentless focus on cost savings for our new commissioner is what he should be looking for when our health system is chronically underfunded and does not deliver for those who are most in need?
statement: What I think is that it’s important to deliver timely access to quality healthcare for New Zealanders to improve life expectancy and quality of life.

explanation: Asked what he will say to senior doctors at the GP conference. He states what he will say: thank them for their work, tell them the Government backs them, and that they are looking at ways to ameliorate the issues raised. It is thin on substance, but the question asked for his message and his message is given, so the thinness is a Specificity deduction, not a dodge.
question: What will he say to senior doctors this weekend at the GP conference who have told us this morning that they are doing administrative tasks themselves because the back-office staff reductions at Te Whatu Ora are impacting them?
statement: What I will do is thank them for their work and tell them that this Government backs them and that we’re looking at ways to ameliorate some of the issues that they’re raising with us. That’s what I’ll say to them.

explanation: Asked for a promise, given on the spot, about prioritisation within the public health system. He neither gives nor refuses the promise, pointing instead to the Government policy statement and asserting it covers what the member is asking. A plain 'no, I won't promise that' would have scored high; deflecting to a document leaves the question unanswered.
question: Will the Minister make a promise to New Zealanders right now, in this Whare, that he will never prioritise any part of our public health system?
statement: The Government policy statement, which I’ve announced, explores a wide range of actions that this Government will take, including what that member is asking now.

explanation: Asked what action is being taken to boost Police recruitment. Costello names the specific action — eligibility criteria changes admitting restricted licence holders and residence visa holders into the recruitment process. Exactly the action asked for.
question: What action is being taken to boost Police recruitment?
statement: Last week, Police announced changes to their eligibility criteria, with individuals on their restricted driver’s licence and those holding a residence visa now allowed to start the recruitment process. These are examples of common-sense changes that will open the door for thousands more New Zealanders who want to serve their communities.

explanation: Asked whether she was aware of a noticeable response to the changes. She says it's early but gives the response figure — 630 applications in the last week. Engages the question directly and supplies the fact it was fishing for.
question: Is the Minister aware of a noticeable response to these changes?
statement: Although it’s too early to claim victory, I can advise that over the last week, Police received 630 applications.

explanation: Asked for other updates on recruitment and retention. The answer delivers exactly that: applicant averages, processing staff, and attrition (cut off mid-sentence by the transcript, not by evasion). Squarely on the question.
question: Has the Minister received any other updates on recruitment and retention?
statement: I have been advised that Police are continuing their efforts to work closely alongside recruitment applicants to ensure that those who meet the required standards have the best possible chance of making it to the Royal New Zealand Police College (RNZPC). In terms of applicant numbers, I’m advised that in the first six months of 2024, Police have received an average of 526 applications per month. This is 53 percent higher than the monthly average over 2023. Additional recruitment staff are currently in place and being hired to ensure that applicants can be processed, cared for, and supported as quickly as possible. Retention of staff also remains promising, with the average attrition rate—

explanation: Asked about further plans to boost recruitment. Much of the answer describes what Police already do rather than future plans, but it closes with a specific forthcoming item — a new recruitment campaign live within a couple of weeks. Reaches the question, slightly around the edges of 'further'.
question: Is the Minister aware of further plans to boost recruitment?
statement: Police continues to attract potential candidates through its online digital platforms, including the New Cops website and district recruitment activities and marketing activity. I’m advised that 10 of the 12 police districts currently have district recruitment leads in place who are working alongside the operational recruitment teams to deliver fitness, academic, and candidate support to both applicants and potential applicants. They also run localised events, including information evenings and community recruitment activities. I’m also aware that the community patrols have increased efforts to engage with ethnic communities on the opportunities available through a career in policing. Finally, to support further recruitment, I’m advised that a new highly visible recruitment campaign will be live within the next couple of weeks.

explanation: Asked how many people had used the tax calculator. The number is given precisely — 513,000. Preamble and a partisan sign-off don't displace the answer.
question: How many people have used the Budget 2024 tax calculator?
statement: Since Budget day, when the Government announced its programme of tax relief, the Budget website has hosted a tax calculator. This calculator shows how much tax relief people will get based on their personal and family circumstances. It has been very popular. I am happy to tell members that the number of people using the tax calculator has recently reached half a million—to be precise, 513,000 people have used the calculator to see what they will be getting in long overdue tax relief that the other side of the House voted against. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked when tax relief would be delivered. Answered with a date: one week's time, 31 July, plus the already-live FamilyBoost start date. Direct and complete.
question: When will tax relief be delivered?
statement: Income tax relief will be delivered in one week’s time. Changes to personal income tax thresholds, the in-work tax credit, and the independent earner tax credit will apply from next Wednesday, 31 July. On top of those changes, the new FamilyBoost payment, which reimburses families for a portion of their early childhood education fees, was launched on 1 July.

explanation: Asked what the elements of the tax relief are. Enumerates all three — threshold shifts, in-work tax credit, independent earner tax credit. Directly responsive.
question: What are the different elements of tax relief?
statement: From next Wednesday, personal income tax thresholds will rise from $14,000 to $15,600, from $48,000 to $53,500, and from $70,000 to $78,100. The effect of these increases—these long-overdue increases in thresholds—is to reduce a person’s income tax by up to $40 a fortnight. In addition, the in-work tax credit, which helps support low to middle income working families with children will increase by $50 a fortnight; and eligibility for the independent earner tax credit, which is for people who don’t receive a benefit or Working for Families, has been extended from $48,000 a year to $70,000 a year of income. Parties on this side of the House are backing the workers.

explanation: Asked how much people will get. She answers 'it depends on individual circumstances' and refers the questioner to the calculator rather than giving any figure or range — a genuine but incomplete engagement, since a typical or maximum amount could have been stated (and was, in an earlier answer).
question: How much will people get in tax relief?
statement: That depends on a person’s individual and family circumstances. These circumstances differ widely, which is the whole reason for the Budget tax calculator. I would encourage New Zealanders who haven’t already done so—and half a million people already have—to go to budget.govt.nz and check out their own situation in the tax calculator.

explanation: The standard 'does he stand by his statements' question. Answered 'Yes' immediately; the subsequent campaigning material is surplus, not a substitute for the answer.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our commitment to deliver tax relief to low and middle income working New Zealanders, which takes effect next week. It is not radical to believe that tax brackets should be adjusted periodically to reflect inflation, and, after 14 years, it’s great that we’re finally doing it. It’s practical, it’s fair, it’s affordable, and it’s common sense. And I’m proud that this Government will do exactly that on Wednesday next week, when tax brackets are adjusted for the first time in 14 years. For an average income household, that means up to $102 a fortnight and an additional up to $150 a fortnight if they have young kids in childcare. And my message to the squeezed middle is this; it’s pretty simple: after years of struggling through more taxes, more spending, more inflation, this Government has your back. We’re lowering the cost of living. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should have confidence in the 500-officer commitment given a 124-officer drop. The reply never addresses the drop or offers a reason for confidence beyond restating intent — 'ambitious and aspirational goals... we're going to get more police.' It touches the topic but not the question's core.
question: Why should New Zealanders have confidence in his Government’s commitment to increase the number of police by 500 sworn officers, when nearly a quarter of the way through the parliamentary term, police numbers have actually dropped by 124 during his tenure as Prime Minister?
statement: We have ambitious and aspirational goals. We are determined to lower crime in this country. You cannot have a huge increase in retail crime, a huge increase in ram raids, a huge increase in violent crime and gang membership, without more police. That’s what we’re doing. We’re going to get more police.

explanation: Asked whether unemployment and jobseeker numbers had increased or decreased. Answered outright: 'It has increased.' The blame-shifting that follows is separate; the binary was given without hedging.
question: Has the number of people unemployed and on a jobseeker benefit increased or decreased since he became Prime Minister?
statement: It has increased, and it’s happened because the previous Government increased Government spending by 84 percent. It drove up domestic inflation. When that happens, it raises interest rates. That slowed the economy, and it’s risen to high levels of unemployment. This Government’s determined to kill inflation to get it under control. It’s great to see last week it’s at 3.3 percent. We expect interest rates to come down when we get it back in the band. That will grow the economy, and that will keep people in work.

explanation: Asked to confirm a specific claim that Government decisions added half a percent to inflation. The reply is entirely an attack on the questioner — 'crocodile tears', 'the arsonist who lit the fire' — with no confirmation, denial, or engagement with the figure.
question: Well, can he confirm that his Government’s decision to increase the cost of car registration, reintroduce prescription fees, scrap public transport subsidies for young people, scrap affordable water reforms and other changes that increase costs for Kiwis has actually added half a percent to inflation in the last quarter, meaning we would already be within the 1 to 3 percent target inflation range now if they hadn’t done those things?
statement: Oh my goodness! These are crocodile tears, aren’t they? Aren’t they? I mean, I’ve described that member as the arsonist who lit the fire, shows back up at the scene of the crime, and then blames us and the fire brigade for putting it out. That’s exactly what’s happening here, sunshine. That’s a bit rich coming from you.

explanation: A two-part question: has the unfunded Paris liability increased or decreased, and will the Government buy international carbon credits. Neither part is answered; the reply pivots to a general statement that lowering emissions is the best approach.
question: They don’t like the facts. Has New Zealand’s as yet unfunded emissions reduction liability under the Paris Agreement increased or decreased since he became Prime Minister, and is it his Government’s intention to purchase international carbon credits to offset any outstanding liabilities that aren’t met through domestic emissions reductions?
statement: Well, I can tell you the best way to deal with that problem is actually to lower emissions, and that’s what we’re planning to do.

explanation: Asked (a) whether the unfunded Paris liability has risen or fallen since he became PM, and (b) whether the Government intends to buy international carbon credits. Neither half is touched — the answer pivots to fast-track legislation and a jibe about David Parker leading Labour. Two narrow, checkable questions completely avoided.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Has New Zealand’s as yet unfunded emissions reduction liability under the Paris Agreement increased or decreased since he became Prime Minister, and is it his Government’s intention to purchase international carbon credits to offset any outstanding liabilities that aren’t met through domestic emissions reductions?
statement: Our Government’s intention is to reduce emissions, and what we’re going to do is pass fast-track legislation. I think that was a genius idea by the gentleman at the back—David Parker—who actually should be the leader of the Labour Party because he actually is principled and he actually cares about something. Fast-track legislation is the way in which we lower our emissions. I’d encourage that member to support us.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his rent-deductibility statement and, if so, by how much rents have dropped. He neither affirms nor withdraws the statement, and the number is never given; instead he cites rent rises under the previous government and restates the supply strategy as future intent. He stays on the topic of rents, which is the only engagement here, but the core — the figure — is squarely dodged.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “what we’re doing on interest deductibility is making sure we lower you know, we … actually put downward pressure on rents for renters.”; if so, by how much have rents dropped across New Zealand since he became Prime Minister?
statement: Well, what I can tell that member is, in the previous administration, rents went up $175 a week. What we are doing is making sure that we increase the supply of houses being built, the supply of rental properties being available, and the supply of social housing being available. If we can do that, we can put downward pressure on rents. We can make sure that people get affordable housing.

explanation: Asked which of five listed outcomes best demonstrates his 'laser-like focus'. A loaded menu question, but it seeks a response and gets one — and the response picks none of the options, attacks the questioner's record, and pivots to quarterly scorecards and transparency. The question asked is not the one answered.
question: Which of the following best demonstrates his so-called laser-like focus on outcomes: fewer police on the beat, more people unemployed, inflation staying higher for longer, increasing greenhouse gas emissions, or higher rents?
statement: Again, it is rich taking a lecture from that member on outcomes—this was a Government that spent more money, hired more people, delivered worse outcomes completely. You can’t hide from that record. We’re determined; we publish it every quarter. We’re very transparent with the New Zealand people. We have a quarterly plan. We actually announce our scorecards. We announce our progress against our targets. We’re going to keep doing it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. Answer opens with an unambiguous 'Yes'. The rest is unsolicited roading material, but the question was fully answered in the first word — the padding is a Specificity/Focus matter, not a dodge.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially the moves that we are making to deliver world-class infrastructure and to rebuild the New Zealand economy. We know the difference that world-class roads can make to local communities—helping Kiwis move faster and supporting growth and investment across the country. So it was absolutely fantastic news yesterday that this Government is accelerating work on a four-lane expressway from Auckland to Whangārei as part of our hugely successful roads of national significance. We know the difference that roads like Waikato expressway and the Kāpiti expressway have made for the regions, and now we’re bringing that to Northland. Whether you’re driving an EV or a truck, running a business or going on holiday, great roads matter, and our coalition Government’s going to build them.

explanation: Asked to name just one policy in the draft emissions reduction plan that makes it cheaper for households to cut net emissions. He offers doubling renewable energy via fast-track consenting — a policy direction in the right domain, but not identified as being in the draft plan and not connected to household cost. It gestures at the question without landing the single named item that was requested.
question: Can the Prime Minister name just one policy in the Government’s draft emissions reduction plan that will “make it cheaper for households to reduce net emissions”?
statement: Well, what will happen is that we are going to double the amount of renewable energy in this country, and we’re going to do that by accelerating our fast-track, one-stop shop legislation. I encourage that member to support it.

explanation: Asked to choose between more fossil extraction and 100 percent renewables. He does not name a side outright, but he engages both limbs directly — doubling renewables and faster consenting, plus an explicit defence of ending the oil and gas ban on gas-security grounds. That amounts to a stated position on the choice, so the question is largely met even though the binary is never resolved.
question: Does the Prime Minister believe that our pathway to a climate-friendly future lies in more extraction of coal, oil, and gas, or ensuring 100 percent renewable energy, or is he intent to keep talking out both sides of his mouth?
statement: What I’d say to you is that we are going to double the amount of renewable energy in this country. It is unacceptable to take eight years to consent a wind farm and then two years to build it. I would encourage that member and the Labour Party to actually support that legislation so we can get renewable projects consented in one year and built much quicker. I’d also say to that member, you’re well aware that under the ending of the oil and gas ban, we now have some energy security challenges around gas supply, and I’d encourage that member to also support that legislation too.

explanation: Asked whether he knows or cares that the draft plan's headline policies offset only about a third of the emissions increase from reversing the oil and gas ban. The reply is purely procedural — the plan is a draft, submissions are open, a final version comes at year end. The arithmetic claim at the heart of the question is neither accepted, disputed, nor acknowledged.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does the Prime Minister know or care that if you add up the emissions reductions of his Government’s so-called key policies in the draft emissions reduction plan, they make up a third of the emissions increase that his reversal of the oil and gas ban will create?
statement: What I’d just say to that member is we are consulting on a draft emissions reduction plan. I encourage the New Zealand public to submit on it, and we’ll have a final plan announced at the end of the year.

explanation: Asked how he feels knowing his decisions have taken New Zealand off track for its climate goals and will worsen inequality. He does not address the feeling or the inequality limb, but he meets the central premise head-on by asserting the Government remains on track for emissions budgets one and two. Brief and contested, but a direct contradiction of the question's core rather than a pivot.
question: How does the Prime Minister feel knowing that his Government’s decision under even just the emissions reduction plan alone has taken us off track to meet our climate goals and will increase inequality?
statement: Well, we remain on track to deliver the emissions reductions budget one and emissions reduction budget two.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on the four-lane roads of national significance between Auckland and Northland. He states the announcement directly — accelerating the four-lane expressway between Auckland and Whangārei, made yesterday. A friendly question, but the question asked is the question answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made on the four-lane roads of national significance between Auckland and Northland?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Yesterday, I was pleased to announce that the coalition Government is accelerating work on the new four-lane expressway between Auckland and Whangārei. For too long, the lack of resilient transport connections between Northland and the rest of the country have been a handbrake on the regions’ economic development. Planning for a replacement to the Brynderwyns was abruptly stopped by the last Government and it’s left Northland far too often in a vulnerable disruption. That’s why we’re moving at pace to get this project back on track, and I acknowledge the New Zealand First - National coalition’s commitment to this project.

explanation: Asked how the Government is accelerating the roads of national significance. Answer names the mechanism: an accelerated delivery model using a progressive public-private partnership, treating three roads as three stages of one project. Squarely responsive.
question: How is the Government accelerating work on these roads of national significance?
statement: As part of our Roads of National Significance programme, we have agreed to an accelerated delivery model to deliver this project faster and more efficiently. Our accelerated delivery strategy includes a progressive public-private partnership model that will achieve efficiencies and innovation in planning, procurement, design, and construction across the entire roading corridor between Auckland and Whangārei. It will do this by treating the three roads of national significance as three stages of the same project and incentivising the partner to deliver excellence in design, construction, finance, maintenance, and operation for each phase of the expressway. This Government is focused on getting infrastructure built.

explanation: Asked what benefits the accelerated delivery model will have. Answer lists them — avoiding multiple procurement processes, integrated design/construction/maintenance, scale efficiencies, delivery up to 10 years faster. Directly on the question.
question: What benefits will this accelerated delivery model have on these roads of national significance?
statement: There is great news for the hard-working people of Northland. Our accelerated delivery model means the New Zealand Transport Agency will avoid multiple procurement processes and will deliver integrated design, construction, and maintenance operations across the entire Northland Expressway and allow greater efficiencies through scale to deliver the project up to 10 years faster than traditional processes. The coalition Government is delivering for Northland.

explanation: Asked what benefits the Northland Expressway will bring to Northland. Answer gives them: a reliable Northland-Auckland link, an NZIER estimate of $497 million annual GDP for one section, plus AA and mayoral endorsements. Fully engaged with the question put.
question: What benefits will the Northland Expressway bring to Northland?
statement: Well, once the Northland Expressway is completed, it will provide a modern, reliable, and efficient link between Northland and Auckland, unlocking economic growth and boosting productivity. Last year, a report by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research found that the Warkworth to Wellsford section of the expressway alone would increase New Zealand’s annual GDP by $497 million including benefits for Northland. The AA has said, following this announcement, that this would be a “game changer” for Northland. Whangārei’s Mayor Vince Cocurullo has said it was awesome news and a project that “Northland welcomes with open arms”.

explanation: Two-part question. Part one ("does she stand by it") is answered with a flat "Yes" — complete. Part two asks for a specific initiative; she disputes that framing but does not leave it empty: she points to the 240-plus savings initiatives and to Treasury's BEFU finding. The question's core is engaged and argued with rather than sidestepped, though the single named initiative asked for is deliberately never given. Detail and truth of the Treasury citation are not my concern here.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “The Budget we delivered in May was a careful combination of investment in frontline services whilst also continuing to do our bit to keep inflation down”; if so, what specific initiative in her Budget, if any, can she point to that will reduce inflation?
statement: Yes. And to the second part, the member seems to fundamentally have a misunderstanding, because the significance of the impact of the Budget on inflation is not about individual initiatives but rather the overall impact of spending and revenue decisions taken together—for example, the more-than-240 savings initiatives progressed by this Government in the Budget. I refer the member to Treasury’s analysis in the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update, which says—and I quote—“The decisions taken through Budget 2024 will on balance reduce the contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure.”

explanation: A narrow request — name one Budget initiative that reduces rates. The answer names nothing, offers no reason why it can't (that comes only in the next answer), and retreats to "spending wisely" and general inflation pressure. This is the talking-point pivot: it restates a slogan where a specific item was asked for. Marked low because the question was tightly framed and its core was fully avoided.
question: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 2024 that will reduce rates that are up an average of 9.6 percent?
statement: I can point to the fact that this is a Government that is spending wisely and that, therefore, the overall impact of our Budget is to reduce pressure on inflation.

explanation: Squarely engaged on both fronts: she first answers why the premise is misdirected (she does not set insurance levies), then actually supplies a named Budget 2024 initiative — the Regional Infrastructure Fund and its flood-mitigation projects — with an explicit causal link to insurance risk pricing. She also loops back to the earlier rates question. Whether the causal link is sound is Rigor, not Forthrightness; the question was answered.
question: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 2024 that will reduce insurance that is up 14 percent, with some families paying an additional $2,000 per year or $45 per week extra?
statement: Well, as with the answer to the previous question, I do not set rates, nor do I set insurance levies. And if the member thinks it would be appropriate for the Minister of Finance to set insurance levies, then there’s a much broader discussion we can have about that. However, what we are seeing across New Zealand is that many insurers are introducing risk-based pricing and are looking at the risks which exist in our insurance market. One of the most significant risks is the risk of climate change and the more extreme weather events that are created by it. A specific initiative in Budget 2024 is the establishment of the Regional Infrastructure Fund. And the first set of projects that that fund will support are flood-mitigation projects, including stop banks across our regions, which is intended to reduce the risk of major climatic events, which, in turn, will help the context in which insurance rates are set. And to the earlier question in terms of rates, again, we do not set rates, but we are a Government that is ensuring we are providing uplifts and support for local roading projects, for many of the projects that local government are trying to carry out, and we are supporting growth in our regions.

explanation: Opens with a redirect to her earlier answer, but then explicitly turns to the question ("In answer to the question specifically about rents") and identifies restored interest deductibility as the Budget measure bearing on rents. A specific initiative was requested and one is given. The counterfactual framing ("rents would have increased faster") makes it a weaker fit to the question as posed, which is why this sits below the b06-2 answer.
question: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 2024 that will reduce rents that are up 4.8 percent—and the medium rental is $600 a week?
statement: I do think it’s important that the member continues to reflect on my answer to the first question, which is that we know the cumulative impact of the initiatives in Budget 2024, in Treasury’s advice, is to reduce inflation pressure. In answer to the question specifically about rents, I can tell you this: increasing costs on landlords through removing their interest deductibility increased pressure on rents. And so the corollary is this: in an environment where interest deductibility was not restored, I guarantee rents would have increased faster.

explanation: The "why" is addressed in the first sentence — her claim is that the pressure was downward relative to the counterfactual of higher landlord costs. That engages the apparent contradiction the question puts to her. The remainder drifts to housing supply and closes with a KiwiBuild jab at the questioner, which dilutes but does not replace the answer. The attack arrives after the question has been met, so it is not the b06-5-style substitution.
question: Why have rents increased by 4.8 percent when she said her $2.9 billion tax break for landlords would put “downward pressure on rents”?
statement: As I just said, I am confident that it has put downward pressure relative to the alternative, which was ratcheting up costs on landlords. What that Government had budgeted for was to grossly increase costs on landlords, which, I believe, would have been passed on to tenants in the rents that were charged. But, furthermore, what we are doing as a Government is the most fundamental thing we can do, which is move our levers to increase housing supply. Ultimately, we want a situation where landlords are competing much more robustly in the rental market so that, actually, there is maximum downward pressure on rents, and that’s about fixing the Resource Management Act, it’s about fixing constraints on land supply, and it’s about the changes Chris Penk is making in the building and construction portfolio to make it cheaper to build a house. And I’ll tell you what we’re not doing: we’re not going around New Zealand promising people we’ll build 100,000 KiwiBuild homes.

explanation: The literal question — will she continue to claim responsibility — is never answered yes or no. What she does do is engage the embedded charge that her actions did nothing, citing Treasury and market analysts. So the substance is contested rather than dodged, but the question as asked goes unanswered and the close ("the plan is on track") is slogan. Partial engagement, hedged around the core.
question: Will she continue to claim responsibility for the decrease in inflation, as set out in her media release last week, when her actions have done nothing to cause it?
statement: I once again point the member to the Treasury analysis, an institution she used to speak very well of. The decisions taken through Budget 2024 will, on balance, reduce the contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure. I would also point her to market analysts who agree that inflation is now lower than it had been forecast to be at this point in the cycle. The plan is on track, and New Zealand is getting back on track.

explanation: A patsy question, but scored on the same basis as any other: he was asked what he recently announced about conservation funding and he lists the announcements with figures — $25m total, $5m Cathedral Cove, $6m tracks. Direct and complete. The promotional framing at the end is Focus territory and does not move this score.
question: What recent announcements has he made about conservation funding?
statement: I have recently announced the projects that will be funded by the international visitor levy. The funding has provided a $25 million funding boost to conservation, including $5 million for Cathedral Cove, Mautohe, and $6 million for enhancing tracks and expanding Department of Conservation’s (DOC’s) network of short walks and day hikes. These are major projects that will protect and enhance our country’s majestic landscapes, flora, and fauna and make it easier for New Zealanders and our visitors, our manuhiri, to experience nature—toitū te taiao. We know that nature is one of the key reasons people choose to visit Aotearoa New Zealand, and it’s important the international visitor levy funding supports these outcomes.

explanation: Asked how the announcement benefits the Coromandel, he answers it: $5m of visitor levy funding for Cathedral Cove delivering walk-in access by summer 2024-25, with the damage context that motivates it. The opening scene-setting about the region delays but does not displace the answer.
question: To the Minister: how will this announcement benefit the beautiful Coromandel?
statement: He whenua taurikura a Moehau, Te Tara-o-te-ika. [Coromandel is a paradise.] Coromandel is an iconic place, and Cathedral Cove is one of the most spectacular beaches, not just in New Zealand but in the world. Before COVID-19, Mautohe Cathedral Cove was the fourth most visited DOC site in New Zealand. In 2023, the walking track was significantly damaged by successive weather events, having a big impact on the local economy and regional economy. I’ve approved $5 million of international visitor levy funding for Cathedral Cove to deliver walk-in access to the cove by summer 2024-25.

explanation: Asked what other projects were announced, he enumerates them — $6m tracks and short walks, $4.2m huts over four years, $5m advocacy over three years. A direct, complete response to exactly what was asked.
question: To the Minister: what other projects has he announced that encourage New Zealanders to get out into the great outdoors and connect with nature?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Six million dollars will go towards enhancing tracks and expanding DOC’s network of short walks and day hikes so more people are encouraged to enjoy a great day out in nature, in the taiao. The tracks are spread across the country and will promote tourism and export receipts that our country desperately needs. A new programme to support the maintenance and management of huts of recreational importance through partnerships will benefit from funding of $4.2 million over the next four years. And, over the next three years, $5 million will be invested in information and advocacy activities to connect people to te taiao and manuhiri experiences across the country, making it easier for people to get involved through activities like donating, volunteering, and investing.

explanation: Asked how the announcement relates to his portfolio priorities, he states the priorities (high-value conservation areas, revenue generation, fiscal responsibility) and explicitly connects the Cathedral Cove and day-walk investments to them. The question is met. The closing swipe at the Opposition is a Civility and Focus matter, not a dodge, and does not reduce the score here.
question: To the Minister: how does this announcement relate to his priorities for the conservation portfolio?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. My vision for conservation is to encourage more visits by tourists and New Zealanders to our iconic landscapes, activate commercial opportunities of public conservation land, and, ultimately, to enhance biodiversity across our country within the fiscal responsibility championed by our Government and manu pūtea, Minister Willis. My priorities for conservation include focusing greater efforts on high-value conservation areas and ensuring we’re generating additional revenue for conservation. So targeting efforts in high-conservation areas, both in terms of biodiversity and the manuhiri network, means spending money wisely, ensuring investments are providing high benefits, and returns on investment. Targeting investment and visitor infrastructure at some of our busiest locations, such as Cathedral Cove or other day hikes and short walks, means more people can continue to interact and enjoy the environment around them, and places that are easy for them to access. I hope members of the Opposition will spend more valuable time on our DOC estate rather than beavering away in their little chains. Kia ora.

explanation: "Yes" answers the first limb outright. The second limb — why beneficiary numbers keep rising — is also answered directly: numbers were forecast to rise until January 2025, are running slightly ahead of forecast, and she attributes this to a weak economy and fewer vacancies. She concedes the tracking-ahead point rather than avoiding it. The list of work programme measures front-loads the answer before it reaches the "why", which is the only reason this is not higher.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “We are focused on lifting New Zealand families out of hardship and giving them more opportunities to get ahead by helping all who can work into jobs”; if so, why has the number of beneficiaries continued to rise across the country?
statement: Yes. The Government has already delivered a range of measures to help people into work, including requiring job seekers to have a work-focused appointment with the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) inside their first two weeks on benefit, and six months. Just last week, we announced that an additional four thousand 18- to 24-year-olds will be case-managed over the phone. The Budget Economic and Fiscal Update always forecast benefit numbers to rise until January 2025, and we acknowledge the current numbers are tracking slightly ahead of these forecasts. This is the result of challenging economic circumstances that we inherited. The economy has been weak for two years, which inevitably means there are fewer job vacancies for those on welfare to move into. We remain committed to our target of reducing the number of people receiving the jobseeker benefit by 50,000 over six years, and we’ll take further actions to make sure the welfare system is more proactive in helping New Zealanders into work.

explanation: Asked how she can claim to be focused on work outcomes given 20,000 more people on benefits. She opens by attacking the questioner's own record, never engages the 20,000 figure, and only glancingly touches the core tension by citing 'two years of very challenging economic times' before returning to commitment language. Mostly a pivot with a fragment of an answer.
question: How can she claim that she’s focused on getting beneficiaries into work when there are over 20,000 more people on benefits since she took office?
statement: I’m really thrilled that that member is finally interested in benefit numbers, given the six years she was in office, there was a 51 percent increase in the number on jobseeker benefit. As I said, we have two years of very challenging economic times. We are absolutely focused on ensuring that we support more New Zealanders into work. We’re not going to wait until economic conditions improve; we’re doing the work now to ensure job seekers are ready when those jobs are there.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned about only 297 jobseekers exiting into work. She does say she is 'always concerned' — which addresses the concern question — but immediately swaps the metric to overall benefit numbers and never engages the exits-into-work figure that was the point of the question. Partial: the yes/no core is answered, the specific subject of the concern is not.
question: Is she concerned that only 297 jobseeker support recipients exited into work, as reported in the most recently published weekly update—a worse result than even at the height of COVID?
statement: As I said, I’m always concerned about the number that are on the jobseeker benefit and on main benefits across the board. We are doing what we can. That’s why economic recovery is job number one. Fighting inflation is job number two, because we know New Zealanders are doing it tough and we want to ensure that jobseeker numbers come down. We have to recognise the economic conditions we are in today, and the forecasts show, unfortunately, those numbers are due to get worse before they get better.

explanation: Asked why she chose a 50,000 headcount-reduction target instead of the exit-into-work target officials recommended. She gives a direct reason: she cares about inflow onto welfare, not just the current stock, which an exits target would not capture. She does not concede the 'ignored advice' framing, but the 'why did you choose this target' core is squarely answered.
question: Why did she ignore advice from the Ministry of Social Development when she picked a 50,000 reduction target for jobseeker beneficiaries rather than an exit into work target as was recommended by officials to her?
statement: Because I’m not just interested in those who are on the benefit today; I’m interested in the numbers who are coming on to welfare as well. If we are not managing the flow on to benefit, we’re not reducing the overall number of New Zealanders in hardship, and I want to see more Kiwis off welfare and into work.

explanation: Asked whether the plan is to hit the target simply by sanctioning people off. Answered 'No' outright, then explained what the plan does rest on (work obligations). Direct yes/no plus supporting content — the question was engaged head-on.
question: Is it the Minister’s plan to achieve her target of 50,000 people off the jobseeker benefit by simply sanctioning them until they leave?
statement: No. We are really clear that there are a number of steps that job seekers need to take to improve their chances of finding a job. That’s why we have work obligations. They’re quite simple: have a CV, turn up to a job interview, take a job that’s offered, meet with MSD on a regular basis. Those are fairly simple things that will improve someone’s chances of finding a job.

explanation: A narrow, closed question — would she sanction someone who didn't show up to work without explanation. The response restates that work obligations exist and that the Government wants people off welfare, without ever saying yes or no. A specific question left entirely unreached.
question: Would she sanction someone who didn’t show up to work with no explanation?
statement: We’ve been really clear about the fact that there are work obligations. We want to ensure that New Zealanders are getting off welfare and into work.

explanation: Asked what announcements had been made about remote inspections. He states the announcement: requiring building consent authorities to use remote visual inspections as the default. Directly and completely responsive to what was asked.
question: What announcements has the Government made about remote inspections?
statement: The Government is progressing work to require building consent authorities to use remote visual inspections as the default approach, so building a home in New Zealand can be easier and more affordable. It is an exercise in increasing productivity.

explanation: Asked why the Government is progressing the work. He gives the reasons — inconsistent and cumbersome consenting, delays, costs pushed onto end-users and the construction sector. Squarely on the question asked.
question: Why is the Government progressing this work?
statement: Well, a constant frustration getting in the way of those doing the building work is a cumbersome consenting system and an inconsistent one, including as to building inspections. Some councils typically conduct these in person, but others are much more forward-looking in using remote visual inspections. Where there are massive delays in consenting, this forces builders and other tradies to delay their work, in turn pushing up the costs for the end-user and making it difficult for our already struggling building and construction sector to get on with the work that they need to do.

explanation: Asked what benefits remote inspections have over in-person ones. He enumerates the comparative benefits: no inspector travel, more inspections per day, cross-region working, lower transport cost and emissions. Direct and complete.
question: What benefits do remote inspections have compared to traditional in-person inspections?
statement: Remote visual inspections, including through various apps that are already available, offer significant productivity gains, making it easier and cheaper to build. These include lowering costs by removing the need for inspectors to travel to site, reducing delays by enabling more inspections per day and allowing inspectors to work in other regions remotely, and reducing transport-related costs and emissions. The use of remote visual inspections is currently inconsistent across the country, and so it’s our intention to consult on ways that we can ensure we have an efficient, productive system by ensuring that these are used as the default method and determining exactly the circumstances in which they shouldn’t be.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she had made about charitable lotteries. She states the announcement — the temporary online-operation exemption for not-for-profit fundraising lotteries is being made permanent — with the background to it. Fully responsive.
question: What recent announcements has she made about lotteries for charitable purposes?
statement: Yesterday, I announced that fund-raising lotteries run by not-for-profits such as the Heart Foundation, the Coastguard, the Auckland Rescue Helicopter Trust, and many more throughout New Zealand will be able to operate online permanently. During 2020, a temporary exemption was granted but only until October of this year, after which charities would be required to return to selling tickets via the post or in person. I am pleased to say this Government will now be making the exemption permanent so charities can continue to fund-raise effectively for causes that benefit the community.

explanation: Asked what impact the change will have for non-profits that fundraise via lotteries. She answers with the impacts on those organisations: wider audience, time and money saved, safer for staff and volunteers, no reliance on cheques and post. Directly on point.
question: What impact will this change have for non-profit organisations who fund-raise using lotteries?
statement: Allowing charities to advertise and run their lotteries online will allow them to reach a wider audience as well as saving time and money in selling tickets to participants. It is also safer for their staff and volunteers to not have to sell tickets in person. These lotteries are a significant source of funding for well-loved Kiwi charities, and this change ensures they are not forced to use increasingly outdated systems such as bank cheques and the postal service.

explanation: Asked what impact the change will have for communities. She answers in terms of communities — they benefit from services provided by these charities, and the change lets that fundraising continue. Thin and largely a restatement, but it does engage the question asked rather than sliding to another one (thinness is Specificity, not Forthrightness).
question: What impact will this change have for communities?
statement: Many communities throughout New Zealand benefit significantly from the services provided by charities that fund-raise through lotteries, such as large organisations like the Heart Foundation, through to your local hospice in regional New Zealand. This change means charities can continue to fund-raise to provide these services to the community.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the statement and how many of the 513,000 calculator users are unique individuals. She says "Yes" to the first part and squarely engages the second: the 513,000 figure counts users (now 517,024), distinguishes users from views, and explicitly states that one person looking repeatedly counts as one user — i.e. users are unique individuals. Padding and self-congratulation don't change that the core was reached.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “The rising number of visitors to our tax calculator reflects Kiwis’ keen interest in understanding how the Budget will personally affect them through the savings we’ve achieved and the tax relief we’re implementing”; if so, how many of the 513,000 people that have used the calculator are unique individuals?
statement: Yes. Look, I thank the member for her question, because I absolutely stand by that statement. To the second part, the 513,000 refers to users. I’ve been advised that the calculator has now been used by 517,024 users, up 3,928 users since just yesterday. Separately to the question, I am advised that the number of users is different from the number of views. The number of views is far greater at 759,588. I’m also advised that in the Wellington region alone, in which her electorate is based, there have been more than 65,000 unique users of the website. So I’m advised that the one person sitting at home on their computer or phone, looking over and over again at how much tax relief they will get and thanking the Government for standing up for working people, represents just one user.

explanation: Asked how many calculator users found they are worse off. She engages directly — "extremely small" — and supplies the relevant number (~5,000 who get no fortnightly reduction and may get a smaller refund). She does not give a count of calculator users specifically, so it lands slightly short of complete, but the core of the question is addressed rather than dodged.
question: How many of those users that have viewed the calculator found out that they are, in fact, worse off because of her tax cuts?
statement: That number would be extremely small. The reason for that is that there is, as the member has previously been advised, a small group of people, around 5,000, who will receive no reduction in the income they get each fortnight—they will receive the same income—but who at the end of the year may be eligible for a slightly lower tax refund.

explanation: Asked how many will receive the full $250. After a short preamble about 3.5 million benefiting, she gives the requested figure: fewer than 3,000 people would benefit by $250 a fortnight. Narrow factual question, narrow factual answer.
question: How many, if any, will personally benefit by receiving the full $250 as promised by the leader of the National Party?
statement: Well, I’m advised that more than 3.5 million New Zealanders will benefit from tax reduction. The amount of tax reduction will vary depending on their personal and family circumstances, which is why I recommend they visit the tax calculator. And I’m advised that fewer than 3,000 people would benefit from $250 a fortnight.

explanation: Asked how many will receive the full $271. "I don't have that information" is a direct and complete response to a factual question she cannot answer — under this rubric that is forthright, not a dodge. She then adds an anecdote and a jab at the Opposition, which is padding but comes after the question has already been answered.
question: How many, if any, will personally benefit by receiving the full $271 as promised in her Tax at a Glance brochure?
statement: I don’t have that information. But, actually, that scenario was not one that I campaigned on. It was a scenario that, when I was advised by my tax officials, I said, “Well, look, the maximum anyone could get is $250.” They said, “No, Minister, you’re wrong. Some people will benefit by more.” And I said, “Isn’t that great?” At the same time, I thought to myself, “Isn’t it sad that members opposite have voted against every single dollar of tax relief?”

explanation: Asked how many calculator users are net better off once insurance, rates, prescription and transport costs are counted. No number, no engagement with the net-position framing — she asserts "every single New Zealander is better off" and pivots to attacking the questioner's vote. Talking points substituted for the question.
question: How many users that have used the calculator are net better-off under her Budget when some are facing a $45 per week increase in insurance, an average of 9.6 percent increase in rates, higher prescription fees, and higher public transport costs?
statement: Every single New Zealander is better off with a Government that’s getting on with rebuilding the economy, who’s getting on with restoring value for money in Government spending. If the member wants to cry crocodile tears about not enough tax relief, why did she vote against it? Working people will remember that.

explanation: Asked what she would say to a named survivor about two specific claims. She addresses him directly ("I am truly sorry") and then engages both claims on their substance — that children are not generally placed with strangers (70% in whānau placements), and that harm also occurs within family, hapū and iwi. Whether one accepts the answer is a Veracity/Rigor matter; the question itself was engaged.
question: What does she say to Tupua Urlich, a survivor of abuse in State care, who said of the proposal to repeal section 7AA from the Oranga Tamariki Act, “We know time and time again they place children with strangers who go on to physically, sexually and mentally abuse these children.” and “Whānau means more than mum, and dad and uncles - we have a wider hapū and iwi. There is no way the state can turn around and say there is no one safe enough to look after these children”?
statement: I would say that I am truly sorry for what he has been through. Some members in this House, as well as members of the public, may not be aware that just because a child is in the custody of Oranga Tamariki, it does not mean they are placed with strangers. In fact, around 70 percent of children in care are placed with whānau in what are called remain or return to home placements, or in whānau care placements, and this means they are being looked after by family or whānau. We know from reports such as the Independent Children’s Monitor’s Returning Home From Care report in 2023 and Oranga Tamariki’s own Safety of Children in Care reports that children in these placements were being harmed or abused, and are still at risk of being harmed or abused. A child must be safe first. If this can be with family, hapū, or iwi, then this should happen. However, unless we face up to the fact that harm happens everywhere, including within family, hapū, and iwi, then we will never properly address this national shame. Too often, a child is killed in this country by someone they know, someone that is meant to protect them, and someone who is meant to love them.

explanation: Two-part question: was the royal commission report considered before announcing the repeal, and why not wait for recommendations. The first part is never answered — she never says whether it was considered. The second is answered obliquely (delay has historically been the failure), which gestures at a rationale without stating it as one. Partial engagement at best.
question: Was the royal commission of inquiry into abuse in care considered prior to announcing the intent to repeal section 7AA, and, if so, why did she not wait for the recommendations before moving forward with the bill?
statement: I do not take that report lightly, but what that report also showed us was that for far too long, Governments and Ministers and people in places of power took too long to take action, and didn’t do what was right because they feared the backlash or they feared that they may not succeed. But what I will say to you is that I will do everything in my power to succeed, and everything I do is with the safety and the best interests of children at the forefront of my mind.

explanation: Asked how she reconciles the repeal with the report's specific finding that care-settings legislation should give effect to te Tiriti. The response acknowledges past failures and restates a safety-first principle; the reconciliation asked for is never attempted and te Tiriti is not mentioned. The core of a pointed question is left untouched.
question: How does she reconcile the proposed repeal of section 7AA with the report’s finding that “The State did not take the steps it should have when it saw signs its care system was failing people in care. Those steps should have included: … legislation specific to care settings to give effect to … te Tiriti o Waitangi, particularly tino rangatiratanga”?
statement: I once again acknowledge the failures of the past, and I can’t take back the failures of the past, but what I can do is make sure that we are doing the right thing for our young people and putting their safety and best interests as the first point of order when we are making decisions around their safety in care. To me, that is the right thing to do.

explanation: Asked for a yes/no — does she agree section 7AA applied correctly would redress the report's finding — and, if not, why not. She never says yes or no. She does supply something adjacent to a "why not" (the repeal is about clarity of purpose; partnerships are unaffected), which keeps this above a pure pivot, but the question as framed goes unanswered.
question: Does she agree that section 7AA, when applied correctly, would redress the report’s findings that, “Critical rights, such as those guaranteed to Māori in te Tiriti o Waitangi and human rights, that should have protected people in care, were ignored and overlooked altogether.”; if not, why not?
statement: The repeal of section 7AA is about wanting there to be clarity within Oranga Tamariki that the interest in safety and the wellbeing of children and young people are at the forefront of all decision making. This is the core purpose of Oranga Tamariki, to care for and to protect children and young people. Oranga Tamariki continues to work in partnership with providers, communities, Māori, iwi, hapū, and whānau, and nothing about the repeal of section 7AA will affect the support services and the programmes Oranga Tamariki provides for Māori or the partnerships it has and will continue to develop.

explanation: Asked what she would say to survivors who reported that disconnection from whakapapa compounded their abuse. She answers in the form asked — an apology — and speaks to the whakapapa point specifically, affirming its importance while stating her ordering of priorities. Responsive to the actual question.
question: What would she say to the survivors who not only experienced neglect, abuse, and torture at the hands of the State but also shared in the report that disconnection from whakapapa and te ao Māori “compounded the impacts of the abuse and neglect they suffered.”?
statement: Once again, I would say I am sorry for what they have suffered. Nobody should suffer anything of what they have experienced. I would never ever say that people should not have their whakapapa connection. I have never said that and I have constantly said that I find it important that young people know where they come from, but their best interests and safety must come first.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to discharge the bill, and if not, why not. She neither commits nor declines in terms, and never mentions the bill; she repeats the safety-first formula. An implicit refusal with an implicit reason is buried in there, but a plain "no, because…" would have been forthright — this talks around the ask instead of reaching it.
question: Will she commit to discharging the bill to repeal section 7AA as a sign of good faith to survivors and their moemoeā; if not, why not?
statement: I cannot say this enough and I will keep saying the same thing: the best interests and the safety of our young people need to be the very first thing we are considering when it comes to the care of our young people. This does not mean that whānau, hapū, and iwi are not a consideration; it just means that safety and wellbeing come first.

explanation: Narrow factual question about when rates or thresholds were last adjusted. Answered directly with a date (1 April 2021), plus the clarification that as a genuine adjustment the answer is 1 October 2010. Direct and complete; the partisan framing around it doesn't bear on this attribute.
question: When was the last time personal income tax rates or thresholds were adjusted?
statement: The last time personal income tax rates or thresholds changed was on 1 April 2021, when the top tax rate of 39 percent was introduced. However, this was, of course, a tax increase. Finance Minister Steven Joyce did announce personal income tax relief in Budget 2017, but this was reversed later in the year by Grant Robertson, so personal tax rates and thresholds have not, in fact, been adjusted since 1 October 2010, 14 long years ago. That will change next Wednesday.

explanation: Asked how much people will get in tax relief. She opens by rebuking the questioner and asserting they'll get more than the other side promised, then concedes only that it "depends on individual circumstances." That last clause brushes the question, but no amount or range is ever offered — the core of a "how much" question is dodged.
question: How much will people get in tax relief?
statement: To the member opposite who said a phrase that is not very parliamentary, I’d say that they’ll get a lot more from us than you were promising them. It does, of course, depend on individual circumstances.

explanation: Asked how households will benefit. She answers squarely with household counts and fortnightly amounts, including averages. Directly and completely engaged.
question: How will households benefit?
statement: As I said, people and families are in a wide variety of circumstances; hence, the calculator. But, in summary, I can tell the member that an estimated 727,000 households will benefit by at least $75 a fortnight; 187,000 will benefit by at least $100 a fortnight. On average, households will benefit by $60 a fortnight, and households with children by $78 a fortnight.

explanation: Asked how many people have used the tax calculator. She gives the number (513,000 as of yesterday) and notes it has since risen and that visits exceed unique users. The tacked-on jab about "14 long years" is off-topic but the question was answered first.
question: How many thousands of people, again, have now used that Budget tax calculator?
statement: Obviously, I was asked this patsy question earlier. As I told the House yesterday, that number was 513,000 yesterday. It has risen overnight. I’m sure it will rise overnight again, the more we talk about it, but, actually, the number of visits to the website has increased several more than that, because that is the number of individual users as opposed to the number of visits, which has been a much larger number. My reflection would be that New Zealanders are very interested in tax relief, because they haven’t seen it for 14 long years.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. "Yes." One word, complete, no evasion.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A two-part question: do any of the 10 boys have a care and protection history, and what does she say to the survivor's quoted criticism. She answers the first part ("yes, I would assume"), and explicitly flags she is doing so; the second part is not touched at all. Half the question engaged.
question: Do any of the 10 boys in the boot camp pilot have a history of care and protection, and, if so, what does she say to abuse in care survivor Tupua Urlich, when he says “Part of acknowledging the harm that has been done is taking a more empathetic approach to the healing for our young people. You don’t just inflict trauma and abuse upon them and, when those signs and symptoms of your failures show up in the community, lock ‘em up.”?
statement: To the first part of the question, yes, I would assume that they have had care and protection before, because they are in a place that has care and protection under Oranga Tamariki.

explanation: Asked for specific examples of a te ao Māori approach. The answer offers "a wide range of activities," assessments, and "people who have come forward... even in te ao Māori space" — themes where examples were asked for. Not scored down for vagueness as such, but the question's core demand (examples) is never reached.
question: What are specific examples of how the boot camps will incorporate a te ao Māori approach when nine out of 10 of the young people participating are Māori?
statement: There will be a wide range of activities, and there’ll be a wide range of things that these young people will take part in. Each young person will have a full assessment before they come into this programme, and we will make sure that everything that is done around these young people is done to their needs and their best interests. We have many people who have come forward to bring their skills, and even in te ao Māori space, to make sure that these young people get everything they need.

explanation: Asked for specific examples of day-to-day military-style activities. She states plainly that she does not have them in front of her and that the programme won't be one-size-fits-all — a direct admission rather than a pivot. A candid "I can't give you that" engages the question, so it scores well above the talking-point dodges, though she also never supplies any part of what was asked.
question: What are specific examples of the day-to-day military-style activities that young offenders will participate in, in the boot camps that she launched last week?
statement: I do not have the exact activities in front of me, but I have set the expectations that those will be made available to the young people. It may look different on a day-to-day basis. This is not something that will be a one-size-fits-all approach and we must be able to adapt as we go along, and that’s all I have to say.

explanation: Asked to guarantee that reported youth justice abuses have been addressed and won't recur at the boot camp. She engages the subject substantively — acknowledges the behaviour, cites her visits, says changes have been made — but never gives or refuses the guarantee that was requested. Answers around the core rather than at it.
question: Can she guarantee that the issues that have been reported in youth justice facilities recently, such as roughing up children, silencing informants, and inappropriate relationships with staff, have been addressed and will not occur at the boot camp at Te Au rere a te Tonga?
statement: We know, just as recently as last year, that this behaviour was happening. We cannot accept that that is happening, and I have been to visit these facilities personally more than once to make sure that they know that this behaviour will not be tolerated. Changes have been made, and we will make sure that there is transparency and availability of support when needed.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about the commuter rail lines. He states the announcement, who made it, the 18 new trains and the funding agreement. Directly answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about the Wairarapa and Manawatū commuter rail lines?
statement: This morning, I announced alongside the Hon Nicola Willis and the Hon Chris Bishop that the coalition Government is investing into the Wairarapa and Manawatū commuter rail lines, which will deliver a fleet of 18 new trains as part of a funding agreement between the Government and the Greater Wellington and Horizons regional councils. This Government is investing in the lower - North Island commuter rail network to improve service reliability, reduce congestion, and support economic growth, and now we’re getting on with getting the work done. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked about impacts on travel times between Wairarapa and Wellington. He gives the speed increase (90 to 110 km/h) and a 15-minute saving on the Wellington–Masterton trip. The promotional framing doesn't obscure a direct answer.
question: What impacts will this have on travel times between the Wairarapa and Wellington?
statement: Well, this investment comes as welcome news for hard-working people in the Wairarapa region, with passengers travelling on the Wairarapa line set to receive many benefits, including higher-frequency services and travel-time savings. Speeds on the Wairarapa line will be increased from 90 kilometres per hour to 110 kilometres per hour on the train line with these upgrades, resulting in significant travel-time savings of 15 minutes for passengers travelling between Wellington and Masterton.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statement. "Yes," with a narrowing of the context in which it was said. A qualified yes is still a yes — the question is engaged, not deflected.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “I expect people to be able to get the right response for their needs”?
statement: Yes, in the context in which I said it, which was in an answer to written questions regarding family harm call-outs.

explanation: A narrow factual question — when was she informed that police are stepping back from family violence call-outs. The answer never names a time, or acknowledges being informed at all; it pivots to general reassurance that police will still respond and a warning against undermining public confidence. A specific "when" squarely avoided.
