question: How does making Te Tiriti o Waitangi and te reo Māori a lower priority for schools—than they currently are—align with the Government’s commitment to honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: As I’ve already said, we are putting student achievement at the heart of every single thing that we do. If we want to honour the Treaty, it means closing the equity gap so that the decades of disparity that have pervaded our system in the disproportionate representation of tamariki Māori and rangatahi Māori in the lower quartiles of our education and achievement system is closed. It is my utmost belief that education can and should be the primary protective factor for our kids and a way in which they can break through intergenerational cycles of poverty and disadvantage and live the life that they want, choose, and deserve.

explanation: Asked what she says to 11 education bodies claiming the Government is demoting Te Tiriti. She said directly: that is completely untrue, and gave her reason. A flat rejection is still a complete answer to "what do you say to them".
question: What does she say to the 11 education organisations—including the Teaching Council, NZEI Te Riu Roa, PPTA Te Wehengarua, New Zealand Principals’ Federation, and Te Akatea—who say that the Government is proposing to, “demote the place of Te Tiriti o Waitangi”?
statement: I would say that that is completely untrue. I’ve already stated that putting educational achievement at the heart of our work programme to make sure that rangatahi and tamariki Māori are achieving to their full potential is giving effect to the Treaty of Waitangi.

explanation: A two-part question: lack of consultation on downgrading te reo in the Act, and the defunding of Te Ahu o te Reo Māori. She addressed only the funding half ("not good value for money") and left the consultation grievance — the substance of the question — untouched, explicitly recycling an earlier answer.
question: What would she say to Māori communities who were not consulted on downgrading te reo in the Education and Training Act before this was put out for public consultation, or the defunding of Te Ahu o te Reo Māori, and may feel that their language, culture, and rights are being undervalued by this Government?
statement: I would say what I’ve already said to this House many times today, that the course was not good value for money. We can contract much better in the future.

explanation: Asked for an update on the Make it Count action plan. She gave the update: four named suppliers of ministry-funded maths resources from term 1, 2025. Squarely on target.
question: What update can she provide to her Make it Count action plan?
statement: Yesterday, I was delighted to announce the four suppliers of ministry-funded maths resources freely available to State schools across New Zealand from term 1 of 2025. Schools will have the option to select from a range of flexible packages from PR1ME, Maths - No Problem!, Numicon, and Oxford University Press that include online resources, teacher guides, student workbooks, lesson plans, games, and activities. I’m really delighted that the Government has committed these resources directly to teachers and students to lift achievement and support the implementation of the new maths curriculum.

explanation: Asked what resources will be available in te reo Māori. She said the ministry will fully fund curriculum-aligned pāngarau resources for teachers and students. Thinner than the question invited, but thinness is Specificity — the question was engaged, not dodged.
question: What resources will be made available in te reo Māori as part of the maths action plan?
statement: To ensure those learning through te reo Māori have the same opportunities to engage with the updated pāngarau curriculum, the ministry will be fully funding resources for teachers and students in te reo Māori that are curriculum-aligned and reflect best practice around the OECD. For the first time, I am proud that everything we are doing in structured maths and structured literacy is also being delivered in te reo Māori to ensure equitable access across our education system to high-quality resources.

explanation: Asked what other supports go to schools under the plan. Named two: the curriculum brought forward to term 1 2025, and $20m of professional learning funding. Directly responsive.
question: What other supports are being provided to schools as part of the maths action plan?
statement: The maths action plan brought forward the introduction of the new maths curriculum for the year 0 to 8 students from term 1 of 2025. This puts in the hands of our teachers a knowledge-rich, year-by-year, world-leading curriculum document, now supported by a substantial resource package. In addition, this Government has committed $20 million of professional learning and development funding to support teachers to unpack and embed the new curriculum and these resources in their classes.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has received. She quoted a teacher and a principal. That is the feedback asked for — complete, whatever one makes of the selection.
question: What feedback has she received?
statement: The feedback has been heart-warming. From a teacher: “Thank you for the transformational changes you are making to literacy and maths for our tamariki.”, and from a principal: “We have been using PR1ME maths for about five years, and the difference it has made for our learners is incredible. We are thrilled that you are investing in this programme across New Zealand. All our learners will benefit. Our school budget will also benefit. We are very grateful.”

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Commissioner's submission that the Bill lacks environmental safeguards. Answered "No" and stated where the safeguards sit. A one-word answer plus grounds; nothing avoided.
question: Does he agree with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment’s submission on the Fast-track Approvals Bill that “The Bill lacks many of the environmental safeguards its predecessor legislation contained. Even the much-maligned National Development Act 1979 had more environmental checks and balances”?
statement: No. The Fast-track Approvals Bill is still before the Environment Committee. It includes environmental safeguards throughout the process, including at the referral stage and the panel decision stage.

explanation: Asked how he can stand by "we've replicated the same law Labour adopted" given that law never overrode the RMA, Wildlife or Conservation Acts. He asserted it is true and described the shared COVID-era process, and picked up the wind/solar/housing examples — but the overriding of those three Acts, the crux of the challenge, went unanswered. Engaged around the core without reaching it.
question: How can he stand by his statement in this House on August 27, regarding fast track, “We’ve replicated the same law that Labour adopted.”, when that law contained projects like wind farms, solar farms, housing, and rest homes without ever overriding the Resource Management Act (RMA), the Wildlife Act, or the Conservation Act?
statement: Well, I can stand behind it because it is true. We have taken the process, or the extremely similar process, from the COVID-19 fast-track legislation in which the Government legislates projects and then they go off to an expert panel for consenting. As the member will be aware, the Government has recommended to the select committee that the panels have the ability to decline projects. In relation to the projects that the member’s just mentioned around wind farms and solar farms, he might have missed the announcement a few days ago, but we’ve announced 149 of them and 22 of the projects of the 149 were renewable energy projects. There’s a whole bunch of housing developments in there, as well.

explanation: Asked whether he claims the bill is the same because he conceded to NZ First's push for private mining. He began by disputing the premise ("I'm not claiming the bill is exactly the same") and the response as recorded is cut off there — the mining question is never reached. Scored on what exists: premise contested, question unanswered.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Is the reason he’s claiming this fast-track bill is the same as the previous bill because he agreed to New Zealand First’s push for private mining projects, which will not have proper public or environmental scrutiny?
statement: Look, I’m not claiming the bill is exactly the same as the—

explanation: Asked whether he received a specific paper on seabed mining/offshore wind incompatibility. He engages the question openly — says he has had hundreds of fast-track papers and cannot answer accurately, and offers to check if it is put in writing — but never reaches a yes or no, then fills the remaining time with wind/mining talking points and a jab at the questioner's party. Honest non-answer plus pivot: half credit.
question: Did he receive a paper stating that seabed mining and offshore wind are incompatible as it disrupts the seabed floor, potentially delaying Taranaki offshore wind development until the 2070s?
statement: Well, I’ve had literally hundreds of papers on fast track, so I can’t give the member an accurate answer. If he wants to put it down in writing, I’m happy to go away and have a look at it. What I would say, though, is that wind and mining both have futures in New Zealand, and it is possible to do both in this country. It is possible to build wind farms, as it is possible to have mining for coal and for other minerals that we need in New Zealand. New Zealand’s future is in doing all of the above, not closing our mind off to extractive industries that provide jobs and growth in regional New Zealand. That member’s party started life in a part of regional New Zealand founded on the mining industry; we are now the party of the workers.

explanation: Asked how he can call the legislation balanced when it resurrects previously-failed projects. He goes straight at the premise — the projects are not being 'rammed through' but referred to an expert panel that can decline them if adverse effects cannot be managed — which is a direct account of where the balance is said to come from. Contesting a loaded premise is engagement, not evasion. Marked below full because he addresses the 'rammed through' framing rather than the seabed-mining-specific charge.
question: How can he pretend that this legislation is balanced when it resurrects projects like seabed mining off Taranaki, projects that have already failed under normal environmental safeguards but are now being rammed through on his watch?
statement: Well, firstly, there are a couple of factual errors there. Firstly, they’re not being rammed through; they’re being referred to an expert panel for consenting. As we’ve indicated, the expert panels will have the ability, if they can’t manage the adverse effects, or the panel decides that the adverse effects from a project can’t be managed, those projects could be turned down.

explanation: Two-part question: what changes, and why needed. He explicitly answers both parts in order. The 'why' half is answered squarely (housing crisis, long overdue). The 'what' half is answered with guiding principles — easier building, streamlined proportionate regulation, liability placement — rather than named changes, so the core of the first part is only partly reached.
question: What changes is the Government making in the building and construction portfolio, and why are these changes needed?
statement: To the first part of the question, the Government has a big year of building reforms already and we are just getting started. Our guiding principle is that building needs to be easier and regulations need to be streamlined, proportionate to the risk, and consistent nationwide, and place liability where it is most appropriate. For the second part of the question, we know that change is desperately needed and long overdue, including because of the housing crisis in this country, which has been a longstanding challenge and issue, one that the Government is utterly committed to solving through, among other things, the Going for Housing Growth programme of my friend and colleague Chris Bishop.

explanation: Asked what specific initiatives are under way. He names three: removing barriers to overseas building products, consent-free builds up to 60 square metres, and restructuring the building consent system. He declines to list all of them but says so plainly rather than substituting themes for the list. The question was engaged and substantially answered.
question: What specific initiatives are under way to make building easier in New Zealand?
statement: The Government has announced a range of initiatives from small common-sense changes to larger, more structural reforms, all with the goal of letting good tradies get on with the job. I won’t list them all here today, because I know you wouldn’t allow me to, but the most significant ones include removing barriers to overseas building products to drive competition and reduce prices, allowing granny flats and other structures up to 60 square metres to be built without a building consent or resource consent per the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement—extremely popular; not only with grannies, at that—and commencing a major reform of the structure of the building consent system to improve efficiency, certainty, and consistency across the country.

explanation: Asked how important the sector is to the economy. Opens with 'Extremely important' and supplies the figures — 20 percent of all jobs, $99 billion in sales. The question is answered before the red-tape commentary begins, so the pivot follows the answer rather than replacing it.
question: How important is the building and construction sector to the economy?
statement: Extremely important. So, notwithstanding the construction recession that we inherited, a recent report found that the building and construction sector contributed some 20 percent of all jobs in New Zealand, and $99 billion in sales. The system that we did inherit was a jungle of red tape through which builders were forced to fight for even the most simple project. Much of the regulation added no meaningful protection for consumers.

explanation: Asked how the sector has responded to the changes. Answers directly: he meets the industry regularly and the sector is 'extremely supportive' of the red-tape reduction. Whether that characterisation is accurate is a Veracity question and does not move this score; the question asked was answered.
question: How has the sector responded to the changes?
statement: I meet regularly with building industry, from large corporations to small business and sole operators all over New Zealand. Overall, the sector is extremely supportive of the Government’s approach to reducing red tape so that they can get on with building. For years, the sector has wanted a Government bold enough to make significant reforms in the building and construction sector, and now they have one.

explanation: Asked what role Whānau Ora plays for all whānau, Māori and non-Māori. He describes the role — a holistic, whānau-centred delivery model — and addresses the Māori/non-Māori element of the question explicitly, citing a Pasifika commissioning agency. Some framing and origin-story material, but the question's core is reached.
question: What role does he believe Whānau Ora plays for all whānau in Aotearoa, both Māori and non-Māori, who choose to engage with its services?
statement: Whānau Ora is a visionary kaupapa—Government-enabled, locally led, and whānau-centred—launched by Te Pāti Māori and the National Party together nearly 15 years ago. It’s a holistic approach to facilitating and delivering outcomes through a whānau delivery model focused on the needs of Māori and, actually, all New Zealanders. It’s inclusive of Māori and non-Māori, and it’s been exciting for me to see, for example, a Pasifika commissioning agency over the past few years.

explanation: Asked why he is fragmenting the network when the current model works. He supplies an actual reason: after ten years with no formal procurement process, an engagement and procurement round was judged necessary for value for money against new government priorities. He rejects the 'fragment' framing rather than conceding it, but he does answer the 'why', which is what was asked.
question: Why does the Minister think it is necessary to fragment the Whānau Ora network, creating uncertainty for the hundreds of providers and the people they serve, when the current model is a proven success?
statement: This Government believes in the Whānau Ora kaupapa, hence why we have continued to commit the same budget level for Whānau Ora over the next few years as has been committed in the last year. But we’re also cognisant of the need to ensure that we have value for money in the delivery of better public services, and after 10 years of no formal procurement process, we thought it was important to undertake an engagement and procurement process for Whānau Ora, especially in light of the new targets, priorities, and objectives of this Government. But what I can also assert and observe is that many of the Whānau Ora providers do not just rely on the allocation through the Whānau Ora allocation under Vote Māori Development but actually engage themselves in Votes across Government, including Vote Health—and I acknowledge Dr Reti for his commitment to two-year-old immunisations in the last year through Whānau Ora.

explanation: Asked for his response to providers worried they will have to compete with organisations like the Salvation Army for alternative funding. He acknowledges that similar concerns exist across portfolios and promises a defensible process, then hands the matter to 'the operational end of Te Puni Kōkiri'. That responds to the concern's existence without engaging the substance of it — competing for alternative funding is never addressed.
question: What is his response to Whānau Ora providers who are concerned that they will now have to compete with the likes of the Salvation Army for alternative funding as a result of the uncertainty he has created?
statement: As I’ve mentioned, there is a procurement and engagement process that’s under way, and there are a number of providers throughout the delivery of Government services, not just in Whānau Ora but across many portfolios and appropriations, that have evidenced similar concerns. However, we will run a defensible and credible process, and that matter currently is at the operational end of Te Puni Kōkiri.

explanation: Asked how a fourth commissioning agency will be sustained given funding cuts to the existing three. He addresses the first half by denying the premise — there is no predetermined outcome and a fourth agency is not certain — which is a legitimate answer to a conditional question. But the funding-cut half is left entirely alone, replaced by generic process assurance.
question: How will this Government sustain a fourth commissioning agency when he has cut funding for the three that already exist?
statement: I would observe that there is no predetermined outcome for the current process under way and it is not absolutely certain that there will be a fourth commissioning agency. However, what I will say is that we will go through a defensible procurement process and ensure that the needs of Māori and any others who engage in Whānau Ora services are provided for by way of the commissioning agencies and Whānau Ora providers.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the Public Service workforce. She names the source (Public Service Commission workforce data) and reports its contents in detail — reductions in clerical and policy roles, increases in contact centre, regulatory and frontline staff. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent reports has she seen about the Public Service workforce?
statement: The latest workforce data released by the Public Service Commission shows a significant shift in back-office resources towards the front line. The data show a 10.8 percent year-on-year reduction in the number of clerical and administrative staff in the Public Service, and an 8.3 percent drop in policy advisers. This has been offset by annual increases in service delivery roles, including a 16.9 percent rise in contact centre workers who are often the first point of contact for members of the public; and there’s been a 5.7 percent increase in the number of inspectors and regulatory officers; and a 1.5 percent increase in the number of social, health, and education workers. This Government promised to shift resources from the back office to the front line, and we are delivering on that promise.

explanation: Asked what is happening to the overall size of the workforce. Gives the number outright — 63,537, up 0.7 percent to 30 June — and then breaks it into the two halves of the year. The comparison to previous governments is added after the answer, not in place of it.
question: What is happening to the overall size of the Public Service workforce?
statement: Over the course of the year to 30 June, the number of public servants grew slightly, to 63,537—a 0.7 percent increase. But when you drill into the details, it is a year of two halves. The first half of the year, under the previous Government, saw a continuation of strong growth in Public Service numbers through to December. The second half of the year, under this Government, saw a decline of 3.3 percent. While this makes up an overall annual increase of 0.7 percent, this compares to average increases of almost 5 percent of the previous five years as growth ballooned with no corresponding improvement in outcomes. The steps this Government is taking to restore discipline to public expenditure and drive more value for money are working.

explanation: Asked what is happening to contractor and consultant spend. She states it fell by $274 million / 13 percent and names the $400 million reduction target — the question is engaged squarely and completely. The closing swipe at the previous Government is a Focus/Civility matter and does not lower Forthrightness.
question: What is happening to contractor and consultant spend by the Public Service?
statement: I’m delighted to see that the brakes have also well and truly been put on contractor and consultant spending. The workforce data shows this operating spending fell by $274 million, or 13 percent, when compared to the previous year. The Government is targeting a reduction in contractor and consultant operating spending of $400 million, and good progress is being made towards this. Contractor and consultant spending was another area that blew out under the previous Government, and this Government is bringing it back under control.

explanation: Asked what other changes she has seen in the Public Service workforce — a very broad question. She names one concrete change: the appointment of Sir Brian Roche as Public Service Commissioner from 4 November. That is a responsive answer to what was asked; only a mild deduction because a single leadership appointment engages the question narrowly rather than surveying workforce changes.
question: What other changes has she seen in the Public Service workforce?
statement: On Monday, the Prime Minister announced that Sir Brian Roche will be the next Public Service Commissioner. Sir Brian is a highly respected New Zealander, and I am delighted that he will be stepping into this crucial leadership position on 4 November. He brings a wealth of experience in both public and private sector roles, and a proven track record of leadership and delivering results. Sir Brian also knows how to develop talent and drive performance—two things that will be critical for the Public Service over the next few years. I want to thank and acknowledge members of other parties in Parliament who have welcomed Sir Brian’s ascension to this role, and I’m sure that the House joins with me in wishing him all the best and in also thanking Heather Baggott—who has done a great job acting as Public Service Commissioner.

explanation: Two-part question: does she stand by the 50,000 target, and how many are on jobseeker today versus when she took office. She answers 'Yes' to the first and gives the number for the second — an increase of 20,895 since taking office. Both halves reached, including the unflattering figure.
question: Does she stand by the Government’s plan to have 50,000 fewer people on jobseeker support; if so, how many people are on jobseeker support today compared to when she took office?
statement: Yes, in April this year, the Government set a target to reduce the number of people on jobseeker benefit to 140,000 over the next six years, from a baseline of 190,000 in December 2023. One of the reasons for setting this target was the fact that, over the previous six years, the number of people on jobseeker increased significantly, rising by over 66,000, or 55 percent, between December 2017 and December 2023. When this target was set, officials expected jobseeker numbers would continue to rise for some time due to the poor state of the economy, which had seen little to no growth for the previous two years. Since taking office, as expected, the number of people on jobseeker support has continued to increase, rising by 20,895. We expect this number will rise further due to the lagged effects of high inflation, high interest rates, and the recession on employment. We’re confident the steps we are taking to improve the welfare system, such as increased engagement with job seekers through case management and the introduction of the traffic light system, will pay off through reduced benefit dependency as economic conditions improve.

explanation: Asked to acknowledge that rising unemployment and jobseeker numbers are causing increased hardship for whānau. She acknowledges the rise in unemployment but never addresses hardship — the actual core of the question — and pivots to the Government's focus on work and an exits-into-work statistic. It gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: Does she acknowledge that escalating unemployment and jobseeker beneficiary numbers are leading to increased hardship for whānau?
statement: I acknowledge that two years of low to no growth led to unemployment, which is why we are seeing, unfortunately, rising numbers of unemployment. That is why our Government is absolutely focused on getting people into work so they have their own income, and I’m proud to advise the House that, in the last three months, we have seen an increase of 2,457 people exit the jobseeker benefit into work compared to a year ago.

explanation: Asked why she ignored advice about increasing RSE worker numbers given MSD's difficulty placing job seekers. She does supply a reason — regions need short-term seasonal labour and it is a balance against job seekers spread around the country — so the 'why' is engaged. She does not address the advice she was said to have ignored, leaving part of the question's core untouched.
question: Yes, Mr Speaker. Why did she ignore advice about increasing the amount of Recognised Seasonal Employer scheme (RSE) workers entering the country when the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) is already struggling to find job seekers meaningful employment in the regions?
statement: As that member will know, many regions require RSE workers for short periods of time, so there is always the balance when we are trying to get the economy up and running again, to ensure that there is short-term supply of labour for required workforces at the same time as balancing the needs of job seekers, who are spread around the country.

explanation: Asked why she did not allow beneficiaries on a non-financial sanction to access hardship assistance. She gives a direct reason in the first clause: consistency with the current sanction regime. Whether that reason is sound or true is Rigor/Veracity; as a response it answers the question asked.
question: Why did she ignore officials’ advice and not allow beneficiaries on a non-financial sanction to access hardship assistance given the dire state of unemployment and the cost of living crisis?
statement: Because I thought it was really important to ensure that there’s consistency with the current sanction regime. I will note for the House that our Government hasn’t changed the sanction regime—all we’ve done is actually use it. So the advice for the new one, which is non-financial, actually will mean people are better off because they will get their full benefit.

explanation: Asked when she will take responsibility for the outcomes listed. She never engages the question of responsibility at all, opening with pride in the Government's record and reciting the same exits-into-work figure. Classic pivot to talking points; the question's core is entirely avoided.
question: When will she take full responsibility for increased jobseeker beneficiaries, increased hardship for New Zealanders, and decreased assistance for that hardship given she has ignored the advice of her own officials because she thinks she knows better?
statement: I’m really proud of the record that our Government has despite incredibly challenging economic times and unemployment that follows a period of high Government spending, high inflation, and high interest rates. We have 2,457 job seekers in the last three months who’ve exited into work, which is an increase on the year before. That’s what I’m proud of. And, actually, our side of the House doesn’t necessarily think it is a bad thing when hardship grants reduce. That means that households are able to look after themselves, and that is a direct result of lower inflation and a lower cost of living.

explanation: Asked for an update on the Government's progress — an extremely broad patsy. He begins answering in kind ('delivering across the board', fast-track consenting bill) before being cut off. The direction is responsive but the answer is truncated after a single item, so it only partly discharges even this loose question.
question: What update can he provide on the coalition Government’s progress?
statement: We are just 11 months, delivering across the board, injecting life back into New Zealand with the fast-track consenting bill—

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken on equal citizenship and democracy. He enumerates actions: Cabinet expectations on need not race, stopping He Puapua, phase two of the COVID-19 inquiry, Sport NZ guiding principles, and the marine and coastal area Act. Whether these genuinely constitute 'upholding equal citizenship' is a contestable claim, not a dodge — the question was answered with actions.
question: What actions has the coalition Government taken to uphold equal citizenship and democracy?
statement: Cabinet communicated our expectations for public services being prioritised on the common-sense basis of need, not race. Unfortunately, it was necessary to clarify that race or personal identity is in fact not a proxy for need; anyone who understood poverty would know that. We have stopped He Puapua, which set New Zealand on a path of racial separatism, because we believe in one standard of citizenship for all New Zealanders, regardless of when you arrived here. We are now into phase two of the COVID-19 inquiry, which will rework the utterly inadequate terms of reference which we inherited. Sport New Zealand will be updating its guiding principles to ensure that we have fair competition above woke values being signalled, and we are sorting out the marine and coastal areas Act so that we can get back to a solution we had when every coastal iwi agreed to it.

explanation: Asked what has been achieved in restoring law and order. Despite the heckling asides and jibes at the Opposition, he names achievements: gang membership as an aggravating factor at sentencing, heading towards 500 more front-line police, a surge in applications and expanded recruitment wings. The rudeness is a Civility matter; the question itself is engaged.
question: What has the coalition Government achieved so far in restoring law and order?
statement: Ha, ha! Willie Jackson says “Nothing”. He’s talking about any common-sense idea he might evince. We are empowering our police and courts to hold criminals to account. Gang membership is now an aggravating factor during sentencing. Instead of giving money to the gangs, we are coming down hard on them, because Māori are the greatest victims of them. We are heading towards 500 more front-line police on the streets. A surge in applications—[Interruption] Instead of hearing cheering over there because they pretend to be for law and order, they’re jeering. Well, as they say, they came to jeer, but they’ll be starting to cheer. A surge in applications and expanding recruitment wings is also a signal that our Government is serious about law and order and putting—even you—victims first.

explanation: Asked how the Government is supporting workers. The response asserts 'this is a Government for working people' and that 'some of us know what hard work looks like' — an identity claim and a jab, with not one action, policy or measure named. Nothing in it reaches the 'how'.
question: How is the coalition Government supporting workers?
statement: This is a Government for working people, because some of us know what hard work looks like. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked specifically about plans for essential infrastructure like Marsden Point. The answer states the Government understands the vital need to invest in infrastructure and is cut off before any plan — and Marsden Point is never mentioned. A narrow, specific question met with a general sentiment.
question: What are this Government’s plans for much-needed essential infrastructure like Marsden Point?
statement: This is a Government that understands the vital need for our country to invest in our infrastructure. Critical infrastructure—

explanation: Asked what information sources she relies on. Names three sources directly — ministry advice, an independent evaluation, provider completion data. Terse but complete; the question is fully engaged.
question: What information source or sources is she using for her claims about what the evidence shows regarding Te Ahu o te Reo Māori?
statement: The Ministry of Education advice, an independent evaluation, and provider completion data.

explanation: Asked who is correct — the Minister or the 87/77 percent of participants. She concedes some participants enjoyed the course and then argues the quantitative value-for-money case, which amounts to an implicit "I am, on the measure that counts," but she never squarely resolves the contradiction she was handed. Partial engagement with hedging around the core.
question: Who is correct, then: the Minister, who said Te Ahu o te Reo Māori is a very expensive, poorly performing contract; or the 87 percent of participants who said the programme helped them to build the confidence they needed to use te reo Māori in the classroom, and the 77 percent who said it supported them to apply tikanga in educational contexts?
statement: I’ve no doubt there are some people who did the course and very much enjoyed the course. But as a steward of public money, when we spent $100 million and only 60 percent of people completed the course, and when it was 2.3 times more expensive than comparable courses, as someone in charge of public money, it’s important for me to look at this from a systems perspective. The quantitative data showed that that was not good value for money and we can contract much better in the future, and we will.

explanation: Asked what evidence she uses to discredit the programme given the evaluation's glowing findings. She does identify her evidence — the quantitative cost data, 2.3x more expensive — and directly addresses the qualitative/quantitative distinction the question rests on. Incomplete only because the answer is cut off by interruption, and it does not engage the specific passage quoted.
question: What evidence is she using to discredit the programme when the evaluation report says, “Te Ahu o Te Reo Māori has engaged a cohort of exceptional providers to deliver this initiative. Combined, these providers have an extraordinary level of experience and expertise in the development and delivery of high-quality Māori language programmes. Participants were nearly unanimous in their glowing reviews of providers and their programmes, with most noting the providers’ outstanding skills in delivering engaging and effective learning content.”?
statement: There are two kinds of data: there is qualitative and quantitative. That member might like to focus on the qualitative data, but the quantitative data is also very important. When something is 2.3 times more expensive than a similar course—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked what she compared the course to for the 2.3x claim. She answers the evidence question squarely — Ministry of Education officials' advice that comparable courses are 2.3 times cheaper. She sidesteps the questioner's premise that no comparable courses exist, but the question asked was engaged.
question: What evidence is she comparing Te Ahu o te Reo Māori to when she says that the course was 2.3 times more expensive when there are no other courses that are the same or even similar?
statement: I received advice from my Ministry of Education officials, who said that comparable courses are 2.3 times cheaper than what was contracted under Te Ahu o te Reo Māori.

explanation: Asked what evidence supports treating pronunciation and everyday phrases as an acceptable proficiency level. She restates that these things are important to her personally and pivots to future contracting — a values statement and a forward-looking plan where an evidential basis was asked for. The core of the question is left untouched.
question: What evidence does she rely on to say whether or not pronouncing Māori names and using everyday common phrases is an acceptable level of proficiency?
statement: When I made those comments, I said that those things are important to me as an education Minister. I want teachers to use everyday, commonly used Māori phrases in their teaching, and I want them to be able to pronounce Māori names correctly. That is important to us, which is why, in the future, we will recontract this, but we will do so with much better contracts, making sure we are getting good, quantitative data reporting and good evaluative frameworks built into those contracts.

explanation: Asked for an update on the inquiry. Gives the update: report released, came in early and under budget, and lists its findings. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What update can she provide about the Ministerial Inquiry into School Property?
statement: Earlier this month, the Government released the inquiry’s report, which came in early and under budget. It’s confirmed we inherited a struggling system with a pipeline of unfunded school upgrades that weren’t able to be delivered. The report found the ministry’s processes are bureaucratic and inefficient, its internal governance structures for property investments are not robust, funding decisions lack transparency, and its organisational structure does not provide the right level of focus or accountability. This resulted in a huge loss of confidence in the system and significant uncertainty for school communities, and we’re fixing it.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing in response. Lists the actions taken — instructions to the ministry, offsite modular builds with figures, a value-for-money review. Squarely on the question.
question: What is the Government doing to respond?
statement: Even before the report was finalised, we took decisive action to sharpen school property delivery. I instructed the ministry to improve communications with schools and focus on offsite manufacturing solutions. In the first six months of this year, 72 percent of additional classrooms entering construction were being delivered as offsite modular builds, compared to the 18 percent which were delivered in the same period last year. The ministry has also completed a value-for-money review to ensure a much more fiscally responsible approach has been taken using repeatable designs, modular builds, and a reduced number of bespoke designs.

explanation: Asked for next steps. Enumerates them: functional chief executive appointment, independent investment panel, a possible new entity. Direct and complete.
question: What are the Government’s next steps?
statement: We are working at pace. We’re in the process of appointing a functional chief executive with infrastructure expertise who will be responsible for operational aspects of school property, who will report to me; a new independent investment panel is also being stood up to provide expert advice on future property decisions; and a new entity for operational school property will be considered in coming months. Schools deserve transparency and predictability; taxpayers deserve value for money; and our tamariki deserve warm, dry classrooms.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has received. Relays feedback from a principal and an architect. Selective and self-serving, but that bears on other attributes — the question asked was answered.
question: What feedback has she received?
statement: A principal said this inquiry is long overdue. There are some truly dire stories out there of mouldy, damp classrooms, and, at the other end of the scale, there are rebuilds and new builds that are just over the top, and we need balance. An architect who’s designed over 100 schools said, “Great job. You’ve hit the nail on the head. The focus should be on delivering safe spaces that children can learn in, to a budget, with a low level of maintenance, and it’s totally possible to procure schools faster and better than the current process and ensure that results are cost-effective.” This Government is committed to delivering just that.

explanation: Asked why the academies are being made a sentencing response before the pilot finishes and is evaluated. Opens with talking points about caring and her visits, but does reach the question's core with "We can't wait any more for more reports" — an actual, if thin, answer to why she is proceeding pre-evaluation. Partial: the reason is given, buried in padding.
question: Why is the Government developing military-style academies as a sentencing response before the pilot has finished and before a full evaluation has assessed their impact on the children participating?
statement: Because this Government cares about these young people and we want to give them every opportunity possible to succeed and turn their lives around. I feel privileged and proud to have met with these young people. I have seen the difference that this pilot has already made in terms of their confidence and their belief in themselves, and I can’t wait to see more young people get this opportunity. I invite the member and all members in this House to join me in supporting these young people to succeed, rather than willing them to fail. We can’t wait any more for more reports. These young people can’t afford for us to wait.

explanation: Asked how many young people remain in the pilot. Gives the number: 10. Complete.
question: How many young people remain in the pilot programme?
statement: There are 10 young people in the pilot programme.

explanation: Asked how the figure can be 10 given a reported drop-out. Explains directly: an extra participant was accepted. Squarely resolves the discrepancy put to her.
question: How can it be 10 young people remaining in the pilot when it was publicly reported on 13 August that one person had dropped out of the boot camp already?
statement: Because one extra young person who put their name forward was accepted to join the pilot programme.

explanation: Asked for a count of remaining participants; answered "Nine." A one-word, complete, direct answer to a narrow factual question.
question: How many of the original 10 young people that were a part of the pilot project remain in the pilot?
statement: Nine.

explanation: Asked why she is proceeding given a dropout. She does supply an implicit reason for continuing (she has seen the programme change these young people), so it is not a pure pivot, but the core of the question — the dropout and what it says about the experiment — is never touched, and the answer drifts into thanking staff.
question: Why is she proceeding with her boot camp experiment when already one child has dropped out, representing a 10 percent failure rate of her experiment? [Interruption]
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I think I’ve made it very clear in my first answer that I have seen the difference that this pilot programme has made to these young people—their confidence and their belief in themselves, and just the change is inspirational. I’d like to thank all the staff, all the agencies, who had a role to play in this, who came together for the betterment of these young people.

explanation: Asked how she reconciles apologising to State-care abuse survivors with proceeding with boot camps. She engages the premise head-on: this pilot is not the boot camps in the royal commission report, and says why (era, trained staff, oversight, setting). The attack on the questioner's motives is rude but irrelevant here; the deduction is for leaving the "unevaluated and unevidenced" half unaddressed.
question: How can she look survivors of abuse in State care in the face and say “Sorry” next month while at the same time ploughing ahead with unevaluated and unevidenced military-style boot camps that they want gone?
statement: This pilot is completely different to the boot camps that were mentioned in the royal commission report. These were run decades ago with untrained staff, no proper oversight, and in an isolated setting. I’m kind of disappointed that we are using the survivors of abuse in State care for political gain instead of actually supporting these young people to be as successful as they possibly can. This is comparing apples with oranges—apples with oranges. For an evidence-based party, I am disappointed in you comparing apples with oranges. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what recent Anzac Day announcements he had made; he states the announcement — a bill amending the Anzac Day Act to recognise service since 1966. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding Anzac Day?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The Government is making changes so that more veterans who have served New Zealand will be formally recognised as part of official Anzac Day commemorations. What many people don’t realise is that, as a matter of law, Anzac Day currently doesn’t commemorate the contribution that New Zealand forces have made in conflict since 1966, which was when the Anzac Day legislation was last updated. The final conflict mentioned in that Act is the Vietnam War. The Government is doing something about this by progressing a bill to amend the Anzac Day Act so that the day will officially recognise those who have taken part in more recent operations, including our peacekeeping forces, as well as those from previous wars.

explanation: Asked how Anzac Day has evolved. He gives the starting point (Gallipoli) and gestures at broadening to all who have served, which is an answer, but most of the reply slides into gratitude and back to the bill rather than tracing the evolution asked about.
question: How has Anzac Day evolved over time?
statement: Anzac Day commemorations were originally designed to commemorate those who had fallen at Gallipoli. Kiwis are grateful for the courage, comradeship, and commitment of men and women of the services, not only of the past but also, of course, the present, and Anzac Day is of course one of the key ways that we are able to express that as a nation. The service personnel of today are part of a long and proud tradition therefore, and so we think it’s important to acknowledge that all of those who have served New Zealand in time of war and other operations be officially recognised, and it is appropriate to do that through amending the Anzac Day Act.

explanation: Asked when the changes take effect; gives the timeline — bill introduced before Anzac Day next year, law ahead of Anzac Day 2026. Direct and complete.
question: When will the changes to the Act take place?
statement: We’re keen to make these changes as soon as possible. The Anzac Day amendment bill will be introduced to the House prior to Anzac Day of next year, and then pass into law ahead of Anzac Day 2026. I’d like to acknowledge with thanks the support of my colleague and friend the Hon Paul Goldsmith as Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, in whose name the bill will currently sit.

explanation: Asked why recognition of veterans matters; answers with a reason — veterans say recognition is the most meaningful thanks for sacrifice that cannot be repaid. The trailing plug for future initiatives does not displace the answer.
question: Why is the recognition of veterans important?
statement: Veterans often tell me that recognition is the most meaningful form of thanks, and I suspect that colleagues across the House have probably heard similar sentiments expressed to them as well. Serving their country has come, in many cases, with great personal sacrifice that can never be fully repaid, but recognising the service personnel through official commemorations like Anzac Day does, of course, go some way indeed. I’m also looking forward to progressing other initiatives in due course alongside fellow Ministers and other veterans-supporting organisations such as the Royal New Zealand Returned Services Association, to ensure that we can better recognise the contributions of all those who have served New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a quoted statement. He disputes the questioner's characterisation, which is engagement with the premise rather than a talking-point pivot, but the yes/no actually asked is never given and no correction of the record is offered.
question: Does he stand by his statement that it was “nothing new” for Police resources to be distributed according to the Government’s priorities; if so, why?
statement: The member’s characterisation of that statement is not factual.

explanation: Asked whether he requested more Police in the Auckland CBD; answered "No." One word, complete.
question: Did he ask for Police to increase numbers on the ground in Auckland CBD in order to counter retail crime and public disorder?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether he expected redeployment from neighbouring areas. He answers a different question — his expectation of operational independence — which implies he holds no view on deployment without ever saying so. The specific expectation asked about is left unstated.
question: Was it his expectation that Police staff would be redeployed from neighbouring Police areas into Auckland CBD?
statement: It is my expectation that the Police and the commissioner will always operate with complete operational independence and decide where staff are deployed, and that’s exactly what they do.

explanation: Asked why Police consider staff ring-fenced. He plainly says he has not seen those statements and does not know their source. That is a direct, complete response of the "I cannot answer that, and here is why" kind, not a dodge — the question rests on a claim he disputes having seen.
question: Why is it that Police consider that operational staff have been “ring-fenced” and not able to be deployed to demand, therefore creating a crime displacement?
statement: Well, I mean, I haven’t seen any of those statements. I’m not sure where the member is getting that from.

explanation: Asked whether the Police Association delegate was correct that officers fear other crime priorities will be forgotten. "He absolutely raised a genuine concern" concedes the fear is real, which is a partial yes, but he then moves to what he told the delegate rather than saying whether the substance — that family harm will be deprioritised — is correct.
question: Is the Palmerston North Police Association delegate at yesterday’s conference correct when he said, “There is fear among officers that the Government gang disruption units will mean that other crimes that had been priorities for Police, such as family harm, will be forgotten.”; if not, why not?
statement: He absolutely raised a genuine concern, and I was able to allay those concerns by saying that this Government takes all forms of crime and violence in the community seriously, and we’ve got a big piece of work to deal with family and sexual harm.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Police Association representative's claim that rural policing is being hung out to dry, and if not, why not. He never says agree or disagree; he describes listening to officers, praises rural police and asserts good support and more operations. The praise implies disagreement and gestures at a reason, but the yes/no core is left unstated, so it is a partial answer rather than a dodge or a direct one.
question: Does he agree with the Police Association representative from South Canterbury, who said yesterday, “There is an increased fearfulness that rural policing is being hung out to dry as officers were redeployed into urban areas.”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, I listen to everything that front-line police officers tell me. I spend a lot of time on the ground, getting around and seeing them, and I have to say that the job that our rural police are doing is outstanding, and they get great support from their provincial colleagues. I’ve seen an increase in the operations that the police are running to protect rural communities, especially those with boy racers.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about a growing view in Police that politics influences operational deployment. He opens with a flat "No, I don't" — the question is squarely answered — then adds talking points about what he thinks the growing view actually is. The subsequent padding is a Focus/Specificity matter; the question itself was engaged and answered.
question: Is he concerned that there is a growing view within New Zealand Police that politics is directly influencing operational deployment decisions?
statement: No, I don’t. I think there’s a growing view within our police service that we’re getting back to basics, that they’ll be given the tools, and they’ve got a Government that supports them, to get out there and actually do their job, roll up over the top of gangs, start to suppress boy racers, and get on top of violent retail crime. They know that this Government is supporting them to do that.

explanation: Asked how he justifies including in the Fast-track Bill projects the courts previously declined. He gives an actual justification: prior declines were under different Acts with different tests, applicants may amend and reapply, listing grants no approval, and expert panels still apply the new test. Whether the reasoning is sound is Rigor; as an answer it addresses the question directly and completely.
question: How does he justify his proposed inclusion of projects in the Fast-track Approvals Bill that have previously been denied by the courts?
statement: The Fast-track Approvals Bill, which is currently still before the Environment Committee, will facilitate delivery of infrastructure and development projects with significant regional or national benefits. Where projects have previously been declined by the courts, they will have been considered under different Acts—for example, the Resource Management Act (RMA), the exclusive economic zone Act, or the Conservation Act—which all contain their own particular tests. That should not preclude them from being considered under the Fast-track Approvals Bill, which has its own particular legal test. It’s important to note that under New Zealand’s planning system, applicants who have had proposals turned down by courts are fully within their rights to amend those proposals and try again. The other thing to note is that listing projects in Schedule 2 of the bill does not automatically grant approvals for those projects. Expert panels will still need to consider the substantive applications against the tests in the final version of the Act. To help address this concern, Cabinet has agreed that applicants will be required to include information on previous decisions by approving authorities, including previous court decisions, in their applications.

explanation: Asked why Cabinet chose to fast-track court-declined projects like dams and seabed mining over named hospital developments. He says the Government thinks it can do a lot with the projects in the bill, declines to pre-empt the select committee, and notes a future referral power. The comparison at the heart of the question — why those and not the hospitals — is never engaged; it pivots to process and future possibility.
question: Why did Cabinet choose the fast-tracking of projects previously declined by the courts on environmental grounds, like dams and seabed mining, over projects like hospital developments for Nelson, Tauranga, Hawke’s Bay, Whangārei, Wānaka, and Palmerston North?
statement: Well, it’s the Government’s view that we can do a lot when it comes to the projects that are in the bill. It’s not to say that there may not be other projects in the future. I don’t want to preclude the final decision making of the select committee when the bill has not yet been reported back to the Parliament, but the Government has recommended that there will be the ability for the Minister for Infrastructure to refer projects in the future into the fast-track process.

explanation: Asked whether he will take personal responsibility for environmental damage from previously declined projects, and if not, who will. "That's not the way our legal system works or indeed our ministerial system" is a clear no to the first half. The second half is only implicitly addressed by describing the expert panel's power to decline, and the answer is cut off by interruption, so the "who will" is left hanging.
question: Will the Minister take personal responsibility for any environmental damage that occurs if projects that have previously been declined by the courts are now able to go ahead, and, if not, who will?
statement: That’s not the way our legal system works or indeed our ministerial system. But the point I’d make in a general sense is that the Government is proposing that Parliament list 149 projects. Those projects will then be referred to an expert panel. The expert panel has the ability to decline those projects—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked what recent announcements the Government has made about the Confirmation of Payee service. He states directly that the banks responded to his direction and agreed to introduce confirmation of payee, and describes what it does. The question is answered squarely and completely.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made regarding the Confirmation of Payee service?
statement: I am pleased to share that, last week, the banks responded to my direction that I set out earlier this year and agreed to enhance protection of their customers by introducing a confirmation of payee service. Confirmation of payee allows customers to verify that the account name matches the account number, providing a crucial safeguard against scams like investment fraud where money is sent to fake business accounts. It also helps prevent common errors where people mistakenly send payments to the wrong account.

explanation: Asked for the timeline and how the service will be introduced. He gives both: banks reported back by end of September, roll-out begins next month, in place across 13 banks by Easter 2025. Directly and completely answered.
question: What is the time line for rolling out this service, and how will it be introduced?
statement: In February of this year, I instructed the banks to report back to me by the end of September and I’m pleased to confirm that they have delivered. The roll-out of the confirmation of payee service will begin next month and will be in place across 13 banks by Easter 2025.

explanation: Asked how the system will improve payment security for individuals and businesses. He answers the mechanism directly — name-to-account verification before payment, checked against the details the customer was given — which is squarely what was asked.
question: How will the confirmation of the payee system improve payment security for individuals and businesses?
statement: The confirmation of payee system adds an extra layer of protection by verifying the payee’s name matches the account number before a payment is made. As members of this House will know, investment scams are a common form of scam, and it is one that is personally devastating to many people. Now customers will be able to check that the name of the bank account matches the information they’ve been provided with before they make a payment.

explanation: Asked how the service compares to similar systems in other countries. He names the UK and Australia, says NZ follows the same international practice, and cites a 31 percent UK fraud reduction. The comparison asked for is delivered directly.
question: How does this service compare to similar systems in other countries?
statement: New Zealand’s confirmation of payee system follows international best practice and is similar to what has been implemented in the United Kingdom and Australia. Both countries have seen significant reductions in scams and errors. By way of example, the UK reported a 31 percent reduction in bank transfer fraud within the first few months of its implementation. I’m pleased that New Zealand banks will soon be catching up with the rest of the world, and Kiwis will benefit from enhanced modern security systems.

explanation: A two-part question: was New Zealand asked to co-sign the letter, and if so did he or his office contact other Government party leaders before deciding. He addresses the first part — the letter was circulated to all member States and MFAT judged a separate statement preferable — but the second part, about contact with coalition party leaders, is never touched. Half the question is answered, the more pointed half avoided.
question: Was New Zealand asked to co-sign the letter from 104 United Nations member States in support of the UN Secretary-General António Guterres after he was declared persona non grata by Israel; if so, did he or his office have contact about this issue with other Government party leaders or their offices prior to New Zealand’s decision about whether to co-sign it?
statement: New Zealand made a public statement on 14 October which included the following quotes: “declaring diplomats persona non grata, is precisely the wrong direction … New Zealand supports the role of @antonioguterres, as UN Secretary-General, to travel widely around the world to support peace and prosperity and foster dialogue and understanding.”, and “We regret Israel’s decision to declare the Secretary-General persona non grata.” As for the letter, my understanding is that it was circulated in New York to all UN member States. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade judged that it was preferable that New Zealand express our views on the issue in our own voice and make our own statement of support of the UN Secretary-General. And that is what we did and this is what it looks like. [Holds up printed statement.] And it went out, so that’s the answer.

explanation: Asked whether the failure to sign is made worse by Israel's bombardment of the UN peacekeeping mission. He restates the sequence on the letter and calls the bombardment "an ancillary matter," which amounts to rejecting the link rather than conceding or denying that it is worse. Rejecting the premise is engagement of a kind, but he never reaches the comparative judgment he was asked for.
question: Isn’t New Zealand’s failure to sign the letter in support of the UN Secretary-General made worse by the recent bombardment by Israel of the UN peacekeeping mission on the Israel-Lebanon border?
statement: We’re dealing with the issue of the letter that was co-signed by a number—and dare I say it, at the beginning it looked like there weren’t many signatories to it. By that time, I had already commissioned the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade to put our own statement out, which is what I’ve just shown you now. That is an ancillary matter that’s happened, about which we’ve also made a public statement.

explanation: Asked why he is not progressing recognition of Palestine six months after saying it was a question of when, not if. He gives a reason: a recognition with no prospect of taking effect is futile, and the practical questions — whether it can be established and who would govern — still have no answers. That is a direct response to "why not," with the list of foreign ministers as padding around it.
question: Why is he not progressing formally recognising Palestine six months after he said it was a question of when, not if, given that like-minded countries, including Spain, Ireland, and Norway, have since done so?
statement: Because it’s one thing to make a statement because it’s an aspiration, but when it doesn’t have any chance of actually going into effect, the futility of that is as frustrating for the population you’re concerned about as it is for everybody else. We are not on a different page; we’re just far more common sense and practically aligned. For example, I’ve spoken to the foreign Ministers for Jordan, the Palestinian Authority I’ve spoken to, the Egyptians I’ve spoken to, the Turkish I’ve spoken to, and the Gulf States—a whole lot of countries have been spoken to; all aligned. But on this practical question—as to when you make a statement, can it happen and can it be established, and who will be the Government—there are still no answers.

explanation: Asked (a) what progress NZ has made in concluding who was responsible for the Lebanon device explosions, and (b) whether he will now condemn the act. The response addresses neither limb: it offers a justification of the act by reference to rocket attacks, then trails off into a general statement about New Zealand's long-standing advocacy. No attribution progress is reported and no condemnation is given or refused. A narrow two-part question entirely sidestepped.
question: Well then, given that the UN Secretary-General said he was “deeply alarmed by reports that a large number of communication devices [that] exploded across Lebanon”, killing, blinding, or injuring more than a thousand people, including children, what progress has New Zealand made in concluding who was likely responsible for that, given his answer to a primary question on 26 September saying it was too early to tell, and will he now condemn that barbaric act?
statement: Well, when that act happened, of course, it was as a result of the people who perpetuated it being the recipients of hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of rockets going on for month after month after month as though somehow there would be no consequences. The reality is we’re here in New Zealand and advocating—and have been for a long time, consistently across the political—

explanation: A yes/no question about standing by his Government's statements and actions, answered with an unambiguous "Yes" in the first word. Everything after it is unrelated promotional padding, but padding does not undo an answer — the question was engaged and completely resolved.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to deliver modern, reliable infrastructure for New Zealand. I was absolutely thrilled on Monday to announce—alongside the Minister of Transport, Simeon Brown—that work had started on our Government’s first road of national significance this week, which of course is the Hawke’s Bay Expressway. Roads of national significance have made a massive difference for local economies, whether that’s the Waikato Expressway or the Kāpiti Expressway, and now that’s coming to the Hawke’s Bay. The good news is that early works are starting now and that will bring forward the time of completion by 12 to 15 months, ensuring that the project is delivered faster so that Kiwis see the benefits sooner. It’s all part of our plan to rebuild the economy and get New Zealand back on track. And Mr Speaker, given the recent remarks, it would be remiss of me not to acknowledge the Thames Valley Swamp Foxes for their win in the Meads Cup on the weekend as well. Thank you. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why the Minister's conduct warranted no formal sanction. The answer does supply a reason: he was disappointed and it fell short of his standards, but the Minister apologised, acknowledged the wrong and gave assurances. That is a responsive account of why no sanction followed, even though it never uses the word sanction. Docked slightly because the sanction decision itself is only implied rather than stated.
question: Why does a Minister in his Government calling somebody a “loser” for working late and telling him to “Take some wine and [eff] off” not warrant any formal sanction from him as Prime Minister?
statement: Well, as I’ve said publicly, I was disappointed in the Minister’s conduct. It didn’t meet my standards; it didn’t meet the standards of what we expect from Ministers. But he has subsequently genuinely apologised, acknowledged the wrong, and assured me it won’t happen again.

explanation: Two-part question: is he confident no alcohol was consumed, and will he commit to removing the warrant if it was. Neither is answered — the response restates that the Minister accepts his behaviour was unacceptable and defers to a question on notice from another member. Pointing at a future answer is not answering; the confidence question and the conditional commitment are both left untouched. Small credit for engaging the surrounding topic rather than attacking the questioner.
question: Is he confident that Andrew Bayly had not consumed any alcohol when he berated an export worker for the very fact that he was working, and, if not, will he commit to removing Mr Bayly’s ministerial warrant if it’s proven that he indeed was under the influence of alcohol when he behaved inappropriately?
statement: Look, the Minister accepts that his behaviour was not acceptable and he accepts the overall account of the events. I understand the member has a fellow colleague who’s asking a direct question to the Minister and I’m sure he’ll give a fulsome answer to that question on notice.

explanation: A narrow factual question — had the Minister visited a brewery immediately beforehand? The response recycles the apology talking points and never touches the brewery, offering neither yes, no, nor a refusal to say. A specific factual question met with prepared lines is the sharpest form of dodge.
question: Had Andrew Bayly visited a brewery immediately prior to the business visit where he called a warehouse worker a “loser”, made ‘L’ signs on his forehead, and told him to “[eff] off and go home”?
statement: Well, as I’ve said, the Minister has accepted that his behaviour was unacceptable and fell short. He’s actually apologised to the person concerned. He’s apologised to me and reassured me it won’t happen again.

explanation: Same factual question, and this time the response engages it squarely: "I'm not aware of that." A plain statement of not knowing is a direct response to a question of fact, not a pivot. Not a complete answer (it neither confirms nor denies the underlying event, and does not say he will find out), so short of the top band, but the question was addressed rather than avoided.
question: Had Andrew Bayly visited a brewery immediately prior to the business visit where he called a warehouse worker a “loser”, made ‘L’ signs on his forehead, and told him to “[eff] off and go home”?
statement: I’m not aware of that.

explanation: The te reo form of the standard "does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions" question, answered "Yes" up front. The subsequent fast-track energy material is unrelated advocacy and includes a jab at the Greens, but neither the padding nor the jab bears on whether the question was answered — it was, directly and completely.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to unleash renewable energy through fast track. We know that New Zealand needs more renewable energy to unleash growth, to keep electricity prices down, and to ensure that we achieve our emissions targets. That’s why it’s so exciting—very exciting—that the fast-track bill includes 22 renewable energy projects enabling 3 gigawatts of generation, or about 30 percent of current capacity, for New Zealand’s grid. Those projects include seven wind farms, 10 solar farms, and five hydro schemes. The Greens say they care about climate change. We’ve heard the talk, now it’s time to walk the walk. Support the fast-track bill.

explanation: Asked what, in his opinion, the difference is between running a company and a country. "They're completely different things" merely asserts that a difference exists without naming any part of it, so the core of the question — what the difference is — goes unanswered. Scored above the pivot band because the reply stays on the question's subject rather than switching topics; scored low because it contains no responsive content. Brevity itself is not the problem here (a one-word "Yes" would score 1.0 elsewhere); the problem is that the thing asked for is absent.
question: What, in the Prime Minister’s opinion, is the difference between running a company and a country?
statement: They’re completely different things.

explanation: Asked what the benefit to everyday New Zealanders is of public ownership of hospitals, schools, roads, transport, infrastructure and a bank. The answer never mentions ownership at all, pivoting to incomes, law and order and public service delivery — a different question about Government priorities. Classic talking-point substitution.
question: What, in the Prime Minister’s opinion, is the benefit for everyday New Zealanders having public ownership of things like hospitals and schools and roads and public transport, infrastructure, and a bank?
statement: Everyday New Zealanders expect us to be able to deliver an economy that’s raising their incomes, and we are doing exactly that. They expect us to restore law and order and they also expect us to deliver better public services, particularly in health and education.

explanation: Asked whether under-funding is setting assets up to fail in order to pave the way for a sell-off. The reply denies the premise's endpoint directly: "we have no plans to do any asset sales." That is a squarely responsive denial of the allegation. The "dark and conspiratorial" jibe is a civility matter and does not lower the score here, since the answer is given rather than replaced by the attack. Slightly short of the top band because the under-funding limb of the question is not addressed.
question: Are the Government’s choices to under-fund critical infrastructure like our hospitals, our schools, and our ferries essentially just setting them up to fail to pave the way for an eventual sell-off of these crucial assets that we all own?
statement: The member is in a very dark and conspiratorial mood today. I just say, we have no plans to do any asset sales.

explanation: Asked for a commitment not to sell or partially privatise State assets, and if not, why not. "That is not on our agenda" describes current intentions but is not the commitment sought and is not a refusal to commit either; the explicit "why not" limb is ignored entirely, with the reply moving to quarterly action plans and delivery. Partial engagement — the topic is acknowledged and a near-relevant statement offered — but the core ask, a commitment or a stated reason for withholding one, is glided past.
question: Is the Prime Minister today committing to not selling off or partially privatising at all any of our State-owned assets, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, again, that is not on our agenda. What we are focused on is our quarterly action plans. We take delivery and execution very seriously, on this side of the House. It’s a coalition Government that’s getting on with the task at hand and that’s what we’re working our way through.

explanation: A tightened re-ask for a straight commitment not to sell any current public assets. "That is not part of our plan" again substitutes a description of present plans for the yes/no commitment requested, then pivots to the quarter four action plan. The narrowing of the question makes the avoidance more pointed than on the previous attempt, hence marginally lower.
question: Will the Prime Minister commit to not selling off any current public assets?
statement: Again, that is not part of our plan. Our plan is to focus on our quarter four action plan. We’re working our way through it exactly so that we deliver for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on Government finances. She names the specific report (Treasury's financial statements for the year ending 30 June 2024) and reports its contents. Squarely answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen on Government finances?
statement: Earlier this month, Treasury released the financial statements of the Government for the year ending 30 June 2024. These showed that in 2023-24, core Crown expenses were $139 billion. That is a big number. It means core Crown expenses are 73 percent higher than they were just six years earlier. This increase in expenses is far greater than the increase in revenue over the same period. The financial statements show core Crown revenue of $133 billion in 2023-24, an increase of 54 percent.

explanation: Asked what this means for the operating balances. She goes straight to the balance figures — a $5.8b core Crown deficit before gains and losses, and the total Crown OBEGAL — which is exactly what was asked. Direct and complete.
question: What does this mean for the operating balances?
statement: Core Crown expenses were $139 billion, and revenue was $133 billion. This means there was a core Crown operating deficit before gains and losses of $5.8 billion. The Government’s headline operating balance indicator—the OBEGAL—is, however, a total Crown measure, which means it also includes revenue and expenses from Crown entities and State-owned enterprises. In 2023-24, Crown entities collectively made an operating deficit that was larger than the core Crown, at $6 billion before gains and losses. In terms of sectors, this was the biggest contribution to a total Crown operating balance before gains and losses (OBEGAL) of $12.9 billion.

explanation: Asked what is behind the Crown entity operating deficit. She identifies ACC as the biggest contributor, quantifies it at $4.1b, and explains why its expenses swing. The core of the question is met head-on.
question: What is behind the operating deficit from Crown entities?
statement: ACC is the biggest contributor by far. In 2023-24, its deficit before gains and losses was $4.1 billion. ACC is, essentially, self-funding, in that it funds its activities over the long term through levies.
