explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen on the stalking proposal. He cites the Leader of the Opposition's "about time" and a quote from the Coalition for the Safety of Women and Children. Directly responsive; the selectivity of the feedback quoted is a Veracity/Focus matter, not an evasion.
question: What feedback, if any, has he seen on the Government’s proposal to make stalking an illegal and jailable offence?
statement: I’ve seen—I just heard one from the Leader of the Opposition: “about time”, and also from the Coalition for the Safety of Women and Children, who said, “This bill is a message that stalking is unacceptable [and] that it’s not OK”. They’ve called for change and this Government is delivering it.

explanation: Asked whether she accepts the officials' advice, with a fallback branch if not. She opens with an explicit "Yes, I do" and then explains how that advice shaped the pilot, so the binary is answered and the fallback branch is moot. Engaged squarely.
question: Does she accept advice from officials that “New Zealand and international evidence indicates military academies have limited effectiveness in reducing offending”; if not, what evidence can she name that supports her approach to youth justice?
statement: Yes, I do, which is why, when designing the pilot programme, we took on lessons from examples in New Zealand and internationally. In fact, in this process, over 75 formal lessons were identified and collated from these reviews of previous programmes, both in New Zealand and internationally. These lessons mean that the military-style academy pilot programme is different to what we have seen in the past. For example, each young person received a comprehensive assessment from a clinical psychologist prior to starting the programme.

explanation: Asked whether she sees the present justification as similar to the historical moral panic described in the abuse in care report. She never says yes or no and never touches the historical comparison; she does implicitly reject the "moral panic" framing by asserting the offending is real, which is a partial engagement, but the core of the question is left untouched in favour of an appeal about dairy attacks.
question: Does she see that the moral panic around youth delinquency that was used to justify the boot camps of the past, outlined in the abuse in care report, is similar to moral panic being whipped up to justify the boot camps?
statement: This Government and myself have committed to reducing youth crime within our communities, and to say that it’s just a moral panic—tell that to the people who have been attacked in their dairies and have been attacked doing their jobs every day and are left injured and traumatised by some of the crimes that these young people have committed. Our job is to make sure that these young people face consequences for that behaviour, but also make sure that we provide a rehabilitative programme on the other side.

explanation: A narrow question: what evidence would make her pause. She names no such evidence and instead offers evidence for continuing (a 90 percent pass rate) — answering the opposite question. The specificity of the question makes the dodge worse.
question: What evidence or experience would she need to see to make her pause and reflect on whether to proceed with boot camps or not?
statement: I think a 90 percent pass rate from the first part of the pilot programme shows that it’s actually done a pretty damn good job. Now our focus is down in the community making sure that the transition from residential to community is as smooth as possible. So I’m looking forward to seeing the positive results that these young people show for their future.

explanation: Asked whether she is saying children who have offended do not deserve safe environments. She answers directly — "I don't recall saying that or even implying that" — and states the contrary position. A complete denial; the added material about the omnibus bill is elaboration, not evasion.
question: Is she saying that children that have committed a crime in their lifetime are not deserving of safe environments and protection by the State because of the things that they have done?
statement: I don’t recall saying that or even implying that. I think that young people deserve to be in a safe environment, which they call their home, which is why in response to the abuse in care inquiry and to that report, I have tabled, in the omnibus bill yesterday, ways to keep young people safe within these facilities—because I know the damage that can be done from being abused, neglected, and traumatised, and I will not oversee any situation where I’m not making my best efforts to make sure that that doesn’t happen.

explanation: Asked whether she accepts a historical pattern: ministers claiming their boot camp is different and getting the same result. She restates that this one is different because of the 75 lessons — which is precisely the claim the question anticipated — without ever saying whether she accepts the pattern. Slight credit for conceding that past mistakes exist.
question: Does she accept that almost every time a new boot camp initiative has been launched for the last 60 years, Ministers have claimed that their boot camp is different to the ones in the past, but that the result has been the same?
statement: That’s why, when we were designing the pilot programme, we made sure that we looked at examples from New Zealand and internationally. That’s the reason why we found 75 formal lessons that were collated from this to make sure that we don’t repeat any mistakes from the past and make sure that we can add value to these young people’s lives.

explanation: A two-part factual question: how many expressions of interest, and how many approved over a manager's objection. Both numbers are supplied (863 and 224). The preamble about operational matters does not displace the answer.
question: How many Te Whatu Ora staff members have now expressed interest in accepting the voluntary redundancy first offered in August, and how many, if any, have had their request approved despite their local manager recommending against it?
statement: Decisions about voluntary redundancies are an operational matter for Health New Zealand and applications will not necessarily be accepted. However, I’m advised that 863 expressions of interest have been received from staff. To the second part of the member’s question, I’m assured by Health New Zealand that a clear process was established for considering all applications. As at 8 November, Health New Zealand advises that 224 offers have been made to people whose applications were originally declined by their immediate managers.

explanation: A yes/no factual question about whether Northland emergency doctors were asked to do registration paperwork and reconsider 777 calls. The reply neither confirms nor denies, offering only a general assurance that staffing and patients are safe. A narrow factual question completely avoided.
question: Is it correct that emergency doctors in Northland have been asked to fill out patient registration forms themselves and even reconsider whether they really need to put out 777 calls for in-hospital medical emergencies because of insufficient clerical staff in the department at night?
statement: I’m assured by Health New Zealand that the net front line of clinical staff is safe, that patients are safe, and that outcomes will improve work.

explanation: Two parts: does he stand by the quote, and if so why were local managers overridden in over 80 percent of accepted redundancies. He answers the first plainly ("I do agree with those statements"). The second is deflected to "an operational matter" plus an assurance that leaders consider such things — the why is never given. Half answered.
question: They’re doing paperwork. Does he stand by his statement “Local circumstances require local solutions rather than national bureaucracies.”; if so, why have the objections of local service managers in the Bay of Plenty been overridden in over 80 percent of voluntary redundancies that have been accepted?
statement: I do agree with those statements—that reflected the previous Government’s position—and what I would say is that voluntary redundancies are an operational matter for Health New Zealand. But I’m assured that senior leaders take wider strategic matters, including the one the member raises, into account when they make their decisions.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the decentralisation statement, and how decentralised the system is given the 10-positions-a-week approval cap. The "Yes" answers the first part cleanly. The second part gets a counter-assertion about four regions and a jab at the previous Government; the specific constraint raised is never addressed.
question: Does he stand by his statement “We believe in decentralising as close to the home and hapū as possible.”, and, if so, how decentralised is the health system today when the deputy chief executive will only permit Bay of Plenty district to seek approval to recruit for 10 positions a week?
statement: Yes. And we have decentralised the four regions, but that previous Government did not.

explanation: A loaded "when will he admit" question. He redirects to what he will admit instead, which functions as a refusal of the premise rather than a pivot to an unrelated topic — but he never engages the substance (whether the cuts have tied clinicians up in paperwork or will cost more). Credit only for the implicit refusal.
question: When will he admit the impact of his cuts has tied up clinicians and paperwork and will ultimately cost the system more in the long run?
statement: What I admit is that we’re fixing the botched reforms of the previous Government and looking to improve patient outcomes.

explanation: An open question about recent emergency housing announcements. He names the target, Priority One and the social outcomes contracting trial announced that day. Directly and completely responsive to what was asked.
question: What recent announcements has he made about emergency housing?
statement: The Government has set a target of reducing the number of people in emergency housing by 75 percent by 2030. We established Priority One to focus on whānau with tamariki, and it had indicative progress—blue shoots—to 30 September in getting 726 households, including 1,452 tamariki, moved from emergency housing into social housing under Priority One. Now we are putting in place a new practical initiative to help those in emergency housing without tamariki to move into more permanent housing. Earlier today, I announced the social outcomes contracting trial aimed at singles and couples without tamariki in emergency housing. We will start those in emergency housing for over 12 months in Wellington—Te Upoko o Te Ika—and Hamilton—Kirikiriroa.

explanation: Asked why the trials are limited to Wellington and Hamilton. He gives the reason — those two cities had the most emergency housing households, with the relevant counts and the singles/couples share. The question's core is met head-on.
question: Why are the trials in Wellington and Hamilton only?
statement: As at end September 2024, Hamilton and Wellington had the most households in emergency housing. In Kirikiriroa, there were 225 households in emergency housing, and around two-thirds are singles or couples with no tamariki. In Te Upoko o Te Ika / Wellington, there were 216 households in emergency housing; the overwhelming majority were singles with no children.

explanation: Asked what outcome is sought and how this differs from other contracts. Both parts answered explicitly and in order: the outcome is improved housing stability, and the difference is outcome-linked rather than service-delivery-linked payments.
question: What outcome is being sought, and how is this different to other contracts?
statement: To the first part, the outcome being sought is improved housing stability. To the second part, the social outcomes contract will link some payments to the achievement of specified outcomes rather than most Government housing contracting, which ties funding to the delivery of specific services. Providers will have flexibility in how they tailor their wraparound tautoko for these clients and may receive incentive payments for getting the singles and couples out of emergency housing, supporting them to stay out of emergency housing for three, six, and 13 months.

explanation: Asked how many people will participate and how the trial will be monitored. Both answered: 50-100 people across two regions over two years, monitored via the Integrated Data Infrastructure and an evaluative process with the Social Investment Agency.
question: How many people are expected to participate in the trial, and how will you monitor the trial?
statement: The trial’s expected to support between 50 and 100 people total across both regions over the two years. The trial will help us understand the particular needs of the eligible individuals and what it takes to tautoko them out of emergency housing and to stay out. Officials will use the Integrated Data Infrastructure from data received from providers and set up an evaluative process alongside the Social Investment Agency to inform future insights and actions.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on progress in social investment. The answer reports a specific recent development (the new Social Investment Board, its chair and members, and a meeting held today), which squarely engages the question.
question: What recent reports has she seen on progress in social investment?
statement: Last week, I announced an important step in the Government’s implementation of social investment. That is the new Social Investment Board, chaired by former Treasury Secretary Dr Graham Scott, and made up of highly skilled people with a diverse range of expertise and known to many members of this House. They are Laura Black, the Hon Te Ururoa Flavell, Helen Leahy, Katie Murray, Julie Nelson, Debbie Sorenson, Mike Williams, and David Woods. I met with the board earlier today, and I know it will make a valuable contribution to bringing about better outcomes for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what social investment is. The answer gives a definition — funding, delivering and measuring the impact of social services for the most vulnerable. Direct and complete as a definition.
question: What is social investment?
statement: Social investment is about funding, delivering, and measuring the impact of social services in a way that ensures better results for the most vulnerable New Zealanders. Despite decades of good intentions, multiple strategies, and thousands of contracts, Government efforts have not had the impact required. Social investment is more than simply delivering better value for money; it is about improving people’s lives.

explanation: Asked how social investment will be implemented. The answer addresses implementation — partnership with providers and iwi, a named new chief executive, and three workstreams under way — but at a thematic level rather than naming mechanisms. Engaged, not fully reached.
question: How will social investment be implemented?
statement: Social investment will only come to life by the Government working closely together with others. That means drawing together grassroots providers, iwi, experts, and others, and empowering providers to do what works. I’m delighted that Andrew Coster has this week taken up his role as chief executive of the Social Investment Agency. He has the skills and experience to foster those partnerships. Work has already begun to create a social investment fund, create a new way to commission social services, and, most importantly, to identify investments that will make a difference to the lives of the most vulnerable New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what other progress is being made. The answer names a further concrete item, a social investment hui in Lower Hutt with 100+ participants, which is what was asked for.
question: What other progress is being made in implementing social investment?
statement: Tomorrow, I will attend a social investment hui in Lower Hutt, bringing together more than 100 people who work, lead, and support the delivery of social services in New Zealand. There will be grassroots providers at the hui with deep experience and knowledge. There will be iwi representatives, experts, philanthropists, Public Service leaders, and others with an interest in getting better results for our most vulnerable. The hui will discuss how we collectively push ahead with social investment. I’m looking forward to those discussions, and, more importantly, I’m looking forward to getting on with delivering solutions for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all the Government's statements and actions. Answered 'yes'. One word, complete.
question: Does he stand by all the Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the specific 'disservice' statement, and why not if not. The blanket 'I stand by all my statements' does deliver the yes the question sought, though it reaches it by covering everything rather than the named statement.
question: Does he stand by his statement that the Treaty principles bill is a “disservice” to the Treaty; if not, why not?
statement: I stand by all my statements.

explanation: Asked what he meant by calling the bill 'divisive' and how introducing it reflects on the Prime Minister. The answer supplies neither: it pivots to the coalition agreement and National's voting intention. The core of both parts is untouched.
question: What did he mean when he said the bill is “divisive”; and how does it reflect upon the Prime Minister that he is willing to introduce legislation he describes in those terms to secure a coalition?
statement: Speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, the Government in its coalition agreement has agreed to support this bill to the select committee process, and we are doing so. The National Party has indicated it will not support this bill becoming law.

explanation: Asked how the bill is 'very simplistic' and whether he acknowledges detrimental effects on Crown-Maori relations. Neither is reached — no account of 'simplistic', no engagement with Crown-Maori effects — but the answer does state the bill is not the way to achieve equal citizenship, which grazes the first part.
question: How is the Treaty principles bill “very simplistic”, as he described it this morning, and does he acknowledge the complex and detrimental effects it is having on Crown-Māori relations?
statement: Well, we believe in equal citizenship and equal opportunity for all New Zealanders, but we do not believe that this bill is the way to achieve that.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with 42 King's Counsel that the bill and referendum are 'wholly inappropriate', and why not if not. The answer states only that National will not support the bill becoming law — already-traversed ground that is not the agree/disagree that was asked for.
question: Does he agree with 42 King’s Counsel that the Treaty principles bill and the intended referendum on the implementation of the bill is “wholly inappropriate” as a way of addressing such an “important and complex constitutional issue”; if not, why not?
statement: Speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, and as has been traversed in this House many times, it is not the intention of the National Party to support this bill becoming law.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned the bill is disturbing the business community. The business community is never addressed, but the answer does state a substantive objection to the approach ('a crude way to handle a very delicate subject'), which half-answers whether he holds a concern.
question: Is he concerned that the bill is disturbing even the business community, with a director telling the Mood of the Boardroom survey last month that “[Mr Seymour’s] divisive approach needs to end; this is not the Kiwi way”?
statement: As we have set out, it is a bill that is required through a coalition agreement to be supported to a select committee. What I have said before is that I do not think it makes sense or will be enduring for Parliament to simply set down its interpretation of the Treaty and then seek a majority of the public to confirm it in a referendum. That is a crude way to handle a very delicate subject.

explanation: Asked what her leader's silence over Seymour's "clearly nervous"/"afraid of hard issues" remarks says about his leadership. Willis engages the core rather than pivoting: she attributes the statements to Seymour and flatly calls them "wholly incorrect", which is a direct rebuttal of the accusation. She never reaches the second limb — why nothing was done to dissuade the public of the notion — so it is responsive but not complete. Brevity and combativeness are not counted against it.
question: What does it say about his leadership when his soon-to-be Deputy Prime Minister accused him of being “clearly nervous” about the bill and the National Party of being “afraid of taking on hard issues”, with him doing nothing to dissuade the public of that notion?
statement: Well, of course, David Seymour is responsible for his own statements. In this case, they are wholly incorrect.

explanation: Asked whether the Prime Minister supports all the statements and actions of his Government. Answer: "yes." One word, but it is exactly the answer the question called for — direct and complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, yes.

explanation: A two-limb question: does he stand by calling the bill "divisive", and if so does he take personal responsibility for the division. The first limb gets a hedged yes — "I stand by my statements in the context in which they are given" qualifies rather than affirms — and the second limb, personal responsibility, is not touched at all. Half the question engaged with a hedge, half unaddressed.
question: Does the Prime Minister stand by his statement both yesterday and earlier today that the Treaty principles bill is “divisive”, and, if so, does he take personal responsibility for the division currently amplifying across this country?
statement: Speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, I stand by my statements in the context in which they are given.

explanation: Narrow question: does the Prime Minister take personal responsibility for the division the bill is causing. The answer reframes the verb onto a different object — "what I take responsibility for is the coalition agreement" — and then volunteers National's position on the bill's later stages. No yes or no on responsibility for the division. A squarely-put question answered by substituting a more comfortable one; the substituted material is on-topic, which is the only thing keeping it above zero.
question: Does the Prime Minister take personal responsibility for the division that the Treaty principles bill is causing across this country?
statement: What I take responsibility for is the coalition agreement which I am honouring by supporting the first reading of the Treaty principles bill. As I have made clear in this House on several occasions, we in the National Party will not support it becoming law.

explanation: A narrow, checkable question — does the Prime Minister have the constitutional power to block his MPs from voting their conscience. The reply, "The member is confecting things that haven't occurred," disputes the questioner's framing and never addresses whether the power exists. Dismissing the premise is not the same as answering; a factual question this specific being sidestepped is a serious dodge.
question: Does the Prime Minister have the constitutional power to block National Party MPs from voting with their conscience on the Treaty principles bill?
statement: The member is confecting things that haven’t occurred.

explanation: Asked whether National members are free to vote their conscience this afternoon. "The vote this afternoon will be a party vote" resolves the question substantively — a party vote is by definition not an individual conscience vote — even though it never says the word no. The listener is left in no real doubt, so this is engagement rather than evasion, marked down only for leaving the inference to be made.
question: Is the Prime Minister there saying that members of the National Party are free to vote with their conscience this afternoon on the Treaty principles bill? [Interruption]
statement: The vote this afternoon will be a party vote.

explanation: Asked whether we should take it that the Prime Minister is blocking his MPs from exercising conscience. Answer: "no." Direct and complete; whether the denial is accurate is a Veracity matter and does not move this score.
question: Are we to take from that that the Prime Minister is blocking his MPs from exercising their conscience on one of the most significant constitutional votes that has come before this House in living memory?
statement: Speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, no.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on the Kāpiti Expressway speed limit. He names the announcement, the sections, the new limit and the date it took effect. The trailing credit-claiming about the previous National Government is surplus, but the question itself is fully answered before it.
question: What recent announcements has he made on the Kāpiti Expressway speed limit?
statement: Good news for Kāpiti: on Monday, I announced that the speed limit on the Mackays to Peka Peka and Peka Peka to Ōtaki sections of the Kāpiti Expressway would increase to 110 kilometres per hour from yesterday. [Interruption] This road of national significance, built by the previous National Government, was designed to a safety standard suitable for 110 kilometres per hour. Enabling these types of expressway to have speed limits of 110 kilometres per hour is part of our Government’s plan to get New Zealand moving again.

explanation: Asked what support he has seen for the 110 km/h limit. He answers with the consultation result — 93 percent of 3,313 submissions in support. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What support has he seen for having a 110-kilometre-per-hour speed limit on the Kāpiti Expressway road of national significance?
statement: Well, a lot of support. In April, I announced that the New Zealand Transport Agency was consulting on the new 110-kilometre-per-hour speed limit on the Kāpiti Expressway road of national significance. The results are in: 93 percent of the 3,313 submissions received supported the new 110-kilometre-per-hour speed limit, and this has now been delivered for those travelling through Kāpiti.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on the safety benefits of the expressway. He supplies the substance the question was reaching for — no deaths since opening, a 70 percent reduction in district road deaths — without ever identifying a report as such. The core is engaged; the literal "what reports" framing is passed over, and the closing commitment line adds nothing to the answer.
question: What reports has the Minister seen on the safety benefits of the Kāpiti Expressway road of national significance?
statement: Incredible safety benefits. The Kāpiti Expressway, started by the previous National Government, was designed and constructed to a high safety standard. Since this expressway opened, no one has died in a crash, and there has been a 70 percent reduction in road deaths in the Kāpiti Coast District. Our Government is committed to delivering safe, and new roads of national significance across the country to enable people and freight to get where they need to go quickly and safely.

explanation: Asked which other roads of national significance are proposed for 110 km/h. He names Ōrewa to Warkworth and the Christchurch Southern Motorway. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What other roads of national significance are currently proposed to have a 110-kilometre-per-hour speed limit?
statement: Good news: there are currently proposed speed limit increases to 110 kilometres per hour between Ōrewa and Warkworth, and on the Christchurch Southern Motorway road of national significance to reduce travel times for those travelling on these routes. The roads of national significance are some of New Zealand’s best highways that are unlocking economic growth and improving safety.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is foundational to the country. He answers "Āna—yes" and confirms the position. The question is answered outright at the first word; everything after is elaboration.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “Te Tiriti o Waitangi is foundational to our country”; if not, why not?
statement: Āna—yes. Te Tiriti o Waitangi—the Treaty of Waitangi—is foundational for our country, past, present, and future. Whilst there are other important documents, like the Magna Carta 1215, the National Party recognises that the Treaty is fundamental in our constitution by stating recognition of the Treaty of Waitangi as the foundational document of New Zealand as one of our 10 party values.

explanation: Asked why the Government is letting the Treaty principles bill proceed. Potaka gives the actual reason — National agreed to take it to select committee as an output of MMP coalition negotiation — and states the endpoint, that they will vote it down. He ignores the embedded premise about discrimination against Māori, which keeps this off 1.0, but the core 'why is it proceeding' is answered directly.
question: If Te Tiriti is foundational to our country, why is his Government allowing the Treaty principles bill to proceed when all the evidence shows that the bill will discriminate against Māori?
statement: First, I want to acknowledge that there’s significant opposition to this bill. Second, National supports the process to take this bill through first reading to select committee. This was the output from negotiating coalition Governments in an MMP environment. However, as you know, National’s focus is to rebuild the economy, reset law and order, and deliver better public services. This bill does not strengthen that focus. As a result, we will not support this bill beyond select committee and will vote it down.

explanation: A closed question — has he read the Cabinet Manual. 'I have read that manual.' Direct and complete; the conditional second half falls away. Brevity is not evasion.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Has the Minister read the Cabinet Manual, which provides a framework for policy formation and decision making and recognises the Treaty as a major source of the constitution which accords special recognition to Māori rights and interests, and, if not, when does he plan to read it?
statement: I have read that manual.

explanation: Asked why Prebble was appointed ahead of two named alternatives given his record against the tribunal. Potaka does supply a reason for Prebble (former Minister, acquainted with the House, therefore appropriate), so the question is partly reached. But he opens with a whataboutism about Mike Williams and never engages the comparison with O'Regan and Fox or Prebble's advocacy against the tribunal — the sharpest part of the question.
question: Why did he choose to appoint former ACT Party leader Richard Prebble to the Waitangi Tribunal ahead of the brilliant Dr Hana O’Regan and our foremost broadcaster Derek Fox—why was that appointment made given that Mr Prebble has actively advocated against the tribunal and also said that he thinks there should be a Treaty principles debate, which he is on record as saying?
statement: A number of members from across our communities are appointed to different boards, such as the former Labour Party president Mike Williams being appointed to the Social Investment Board. As a former Minister of various Labour Governments and someone who is well acquainted with the machinations of this House, Richard Prebble is an appropriate person to be appointed to the tribunal.

explanation: Asked how he can call himself an advocate for Māori rights having done nothing to stop the bill. He rebuts the factual premise — that he has done nothing — by asserting he advocates in caucus and Cabinet where the member cannot see. That engages the core claim rather than sidestepping it, though he offers nothing about what that advocacy was and closes by calling the member presumptuous, leaving the question half-met.
question: How can the Minister for Māori Development stand there and look our people in the eye and tell them that he is an advocate for Māori rights when he has done nothing to stop the Treaty principles bill proceeding?
statement: The member presumes what happens in caucus and Cabinet and various other places where I advocate for various matters, and I think that is very presumptuous.

explanation: Asked what it will take before he does something, or has he given up. The opening — National will not vote for the bill beyond select committee, and a referendum would be divisive — is a partial answer to 'does something'. He then pivots to Māori unemployment under the previous Government and attacks the questioner's standing to lecture him, never reaching 'what will it take' or the 'given up' charge.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What will it take before this Minister actually does something, or has he given up because—and I will quote him—he’s “way down … the food chain” and has no influence at all?
statement: As we’re aware, National will not vote for this bill beyond select committee. Our long-held position is that a referendum on the Treaty would be divisive. It is unrealistic for that member, who was part of a former Government that saw an increase of unemployment across Māori by over 30 percent, to come and give me a lecture on tikanga or anything else.

explanation: Asked what funding announcement had been made for front-line volunteer services. Names it immediately: a $23.1 million package over four years, announced last month with the Minister of Transport. The summer-safety padding around it does not displace the answer. Scored on engagement only — that this is a friendly question to a Minister of the same side is irrelevant to Forthrightness.
question: What recent announcement has the Government made regarding funding support to strengthen front-line volunteer service organisations?
statement: More good news. Last month, the very hard-working Minister of Transport and I announced a $23.1 million funding package over four years to boost critical front-line volunteer services. Heading outside for a day of fun is part of the Kiwi life, I’m sure you’ll agree, Mr Speaker, particularly as we head into the busy summer season. However, with that comes risk. That is why our Government is making this investment so we can better equip and prepare organisations to continue saving lives, communities, and livelihoods when faced with emergency situations.

explanation: Asked which organisations benefit. Names both with amounts: Surf Lifesaving New Zealand $14.6 million, Coastguard New Zealand $3.1 million. Complete.
question: What organisations are set to benefit from this announcement?
statement: Oh, good question. More good news. Surf Lifesaving New Zealand will receive $14.6 million over four years. Coastguard New Zealand will receive $3.1 million. These two front-line agencies provide critical water safety services for Kiwis, and their services are delivered almost entirely by volunteers. Let’s have a big shout-out for our hard-working volunteers in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked what the funds will be used for. Answers concretely — repairing and replacing assets damaged in the 2023 North Island weather events, a replacement Bethells Beach club, Mangawhai Heads landslide repairs. Slightly short of complete because it covers only the Surf Lifesaving share and says nothing about Coastguard's.
question: What will these funds be used for?
statement: Oh, another good question. Surf Lifesaving will use this funding to repair and replace Surf Lifesaving assets that were damaged in the 2023 North Island weather events, including a replacement for the Surf Lifesaving Club at Bethells Beach and repairs to the Mangawhai Heads club that was damaged following a landslide.

explanation: Asked what other actions the Government has taken. Opens with a talking point about reducing wasteful spending, but does reach a second, distinct action: the Budget 2024 boost of $63.644 million over four years to Coastguard and Surf Lifesaving. The preamble delays the answer without replacing it.
question: What other actions has the Government taken to support front-line volunteer service organisations?
statement: Well, what we have here is a Government that’s focused on reducing wasteful spending so we can reinvest that into critical front-line services. So that’s why you see in this funding package an addition to early investment that the Government announced for Coastguard and Surf Lifesaving New Zealand. Through Budget 2024, Coastguard and Surf Lifesaving received a funding boost of $63.644 million over four years to keep Kiwis safe in, on, and around the water.

explanation: Asked what recent steps had been taken on small-business payment times. Answers directly: from 1 January 2025 the Government's 135 agencies must pay small businesses more promptly, announced with Minister Lee. The $50 billion procurement figure is context, not deflection.
question: What recent steps has the Government taken to improve payment times for small businesses?
statement: My colleague the Hon Melissa Lee and I recently announced that the Government is committed to supporting faster payments for small businesses, especially given that the Government spends over $50 billion annually with its suppliers. From 1 January 2025, the Government’s 135 agencies will be required to pay small businesses much more promptly, providing these businesses with the timely cash flow they need to grow and succeed.

explanation: Asked for the timeline. Gives dated, staged milestones: 90 percent of trade invoices within 10 business days from 1 January, rising to 95 percent in 2026, and mandatory e-invoicing with five-working-day payment from 2026 for agencies over 2,000 domestic invoices. Squarely and fully answered.
question: What is the time line for implementing faster payment requirements for Government agencies?
statement: From 1 January next year, the 135 agencies must pay 90 percent of trade invoices within 10 business days, increasing to 95 percent in 2026. Secondly, as part of the Government’s focus on encouraging greater digitisation of the economy, from 2026, Government agencies processing over 2,000 domestic invoices annually must use e-invoicing, ensuring payment within five working days.

explanation: Asked what steps will ensure compliance; answer names the steps directly — quarterly reporting by agencies, publication on the MBIE website, and reporting failures to the responsible Minister. Squarely answered.
question: What steps will the Government take to ensure compliance with these payment rules?
statement: To ensure compliance, we will require Government agencies to report their payment results quarterly. These results will be published on the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment website. This will allow anyone to check the compliance of relevant Government departments. These agencies will also have to report why they have failed to meet the payment requirements and front up to their respective Minister.

explanation: Asked about the impact on small businesses' day-to-day operations; the answer engages that directly (cash flow, ability to hire, upgrade equipment, expand) rather than pivoting. It stays at a general level, but low detail is a Specificity matter, not evasion. The closing line about Government support is a small drift.
question: How will these new rules impact the day-to-day operations of small businesses?
statement: These rules are set to make a substantial difference. We know that for small businesses, cash flow is critical, and waiting extended periods for payment can hinder growth or even threaten survival. By mandating shorter payment times, we’re providing business owners with the resources they need to invest in their operations, whether it’s hiring more staff, upgrading equipment, or expanding services. This is all part of the Government’s support for small businesses.

explanation: A stand-by question with a 'why' rider. The answer opens 'I stand by this answer' and then supplies reasons — settlement prioritisation, tax cuts, the $25m Kurahaupō payment. Both halves engaged; whether the reasons are good is Rigor, not Forthrightness.
question: Te Arawhiti: Does he stand by his answer to oral question No. 11 on 7 November 2024 that “There are a number of matters that have strengthened the Māori-Crown relationship”; if so, why?
statement: I stand by this answer, and, as mentioned, people like Minister Goldsmith are prioritising outstanding Treaty settlements in the vein of previous Ministers for Treaty of Waitangi negotiations. Minister Willis has continued to support Māori back pockets through tax cuts, resulting in hundreds of millions of dollars staying with whānau. Of course, we are expediting purely settlement delivery matters, like the payment of $25 million to Kurahaupō iwi last week for the failure to deliver the airport to them. Constructive relationships do require work. There is a lot more mahi to do no matter who is the Kāwanatanga.

explanation: Asked what he says to a named critic who called his answers dishonest and duplicitous. He does speak to that person, but the substance of the accusation is never touched — he answers with thanks and praise instead. The core of the question is avoided; not an attack on the questioner, hence not the lowest band.
question: What does he say to Ngati Toa leader Helmut Modlik, who described his answers last week as “so dishonest, duplicitous, and dishonourable”?
statement: Thank you, Matua Helmut. I know you are pono. I know you are genuine, and I know you carry the international responsibilities of our people of Ngāti Toa Rangatira, and thank you for your tautoko of Te Kahu o Te Raukura here today and every day.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether the Treaty principles bill is one of the strengthening matters. He never says yes or no, but the answer is squarely on the bill and his stated view that it is too blunt and simplistic amounts to a clear implied 'no'. Partial: reaches the question by implication without stating the answer.
question: Is the Treaty principles bill one of the matters the Minister has referred to that has strengthened the Māori-Crown relationship?
statement: As we’re aware and as I’ve mentioned today, the bill is the result of a coalition arrangement between the National Party and the ACT Party in order to get a stable Government in an MMP environment. But, as you know and I know, our view from the National Party is that this bill is too blunt, is too simplistic, that it fails to address equal citizenship and equality of opportunity for iwi members, Māori, and all New Zealanders, and that our quest is to ensure equal citizenship and equality of opportunity for Māori and for everyone.

explanation: Asked for a specific commitment — that every Minister direct their agencies to uphold Te Tiriti obligations. He confirms National will vote the bill down and affirms obligations 'need to be upheld... by agencies', but does not commit to the directive that was asked for. Engages the subject, stops short of the commitment.
question: Should the Treaty principles bill be voted down, will he commit to ensuring that every Minister directs their agencies to uphold their Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations?
statement: National will vote this bill down at its second reading, and it is absolutely clear to us that the Treaty responsibilities and obligations, whether they come from a settlement arrangement or otherwise, need to be upheld and pursued by agencies across this Government and future Governments.

explanation: Two-part question. Part one — who is correct, the PM or Seymour — is answered directly ('I stand by the Prime Minister's comments'). Part two, what the divided opinions mean for the Māori-Crown relationship, gets an aspirational line about kotahitanga rather than an answer.
question: Who is correct: the Prime Minister, who says the Treaty principles bill is “divisive”; or David Seymour, who says the bill is not divisive, and what does he think that these divided opinions mean for the Māori-Crown relationship?
statement: I stand by the Prime Minister’s comments and say this: the Treaty of Waitangi—Te Tiriti o Waitangi—can be and should be and will be a force for kotahitanga.

explanation: Asked whether the bill threatens the continued existence of the relationship. He states it 'cannot and will not wipe out the responsibilities of rangatiratanga and Kāwanatanga' — an effective 'no' — and explicitly flags 'in response to the question'. Not a flat yes/no, but the core is reached.
question: Te Arawhiti: Does he consider that the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill threatens the continued existence of the Māori-Crown relationship?
statement: E te Māngai, e mihi ana ki te pātai. [Mr Speaker, I acknowledge that question.] First, I wanted to acknowledge that there is significant opposition to this bill across many communities—tangata Māori, tangata Tiriti, tangata Pasifika. Second, in response to the question, this bill cannot and will not wipe out the responsibilities of rangatiratanga and Kāwanatanga, along with the quest to achieve equal citizenship and equality of opportunity. National supports the process to take this bill through to select committee. That was the output from negotiating the coalition Government; however, as you know, National will not support this bill beyond select committee and will vote it down.

explanation: Asked what message he is sending to iwi Māori and the mokopuna in the gallery. He first pivots to the coalition-negotiation rationale, but does end with an actual message addressed to them — come to the select committee with full force. Partial: the core is reached late and only after a detour.
question: What message is the Minister sending to te iwi Māori and ngā mokopuna in the gallery today that it is OK to compromise the mana o Te Tiriti?
statement: As we know, and as I’ve discussed today, we have taken this matter forward as a result of negotiating a coalition arrangement, in light of an MMP environment and to ensure that it wasn’t left for other parties to create an unstable situation. However, what I can also add and say is that, please mauria mai ō pūkana, ō arero, ō tetē, tō ihi tō wehi tō wana [bring your bulging eyes, your protruding tongue, your clinging teeth, your fearlessness, your power, and your prowess] to the select committee process.

explanation: Asked how he can be a Minister and allow the bill to proceed. The response acknowledges hurt and pain but is cut off by interruption before addressing the 'how can he' core. On the record as it stands, the question is not answered; the truncation is why this is not scored lower.
question: How can he be a Minister of this Government and allow the Treaty principles bill to viciously attack te iwi Māori?
statement: I can acknowledge that there is genuine hurt and pain across many communities as a result of this bill, but what I will say is—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked how he would use his position in the event of a referendum. He repeats the vote-down commitment, which implicitly treats the referendum scenario as not arising, but never engages the hypothetical he was asked about — and says so knowingly ('I can repeat it as many times as you like').
question: How will the Minister use the position to fight for te iwi Māori if there is a referendum?
statement: As we’ve said many times, whilst the National Party is a part of this coalition Government, we will vote down the proposed Treaty principles bill immediately after the select committee and at the second reading. That is what we will do, and I can repeat it as many times as you like in this Whare this afternoon.

explanation: Asked whether he has confidence the Government is upholding the rule of law. Answer opens 'Yes.' — direct and complete. The subsequent swipe at the questioner's party leader is a Civility/Focus matter and does not displace the answer, which was already given.
question: Does he have confidence that the Government is upholding the rule of law and Aotearoa’s constitutional arrangements?
statement: Yes. The Government is committed to upholding the rule of law and New Zealand’s constitutional arrangements. I’m also confident that our constitutional arrangements have the strength to withstand unhelpful comments, such as those by that member’s party leader that we have “A criminal justice system that we all know only serves to produce more harm, more crime, and more victims”, which is a slap in the face for the tens of thousands of Kiwis who work every day in the justice system to keep our communities safe.

explanation: Asked how the Government's alleged unilateral change to te Tiriti's meaning is constitutionally consistent. Goldsmith engages the core by denying the premise on two grounds — it would only occur if a law passed, the Government won't pass it, and it doesn't do what she claims. The opening jab at the member's understanding is a civility matter, not a dodge. Loses a little because he asserts rather than explains the constitutional consistency.
question: Thanks, Mr Speaker. How is it consistent with upholding our constitutional arrangements for the Government to, in the words of the most senior legal counsel in our country, “unilaterally [change] the meaning of te Tiriti”?
statement: Well, the member opposite doesn’t seem to understand the processes of the Parliament—that would only happen if a law was passed and it did indeed do what the member claims. We won’t be passing it, and it doesn’t even do what the member suggests.

explanation: A yes/no question: does he agree with the 40 King's Counsel that the bill rewrites the Treaty? He never says. He retreats to a generality about lawyers always disagreeing and their entitlement to views. The core — his own position on the claim — is squarely avoided, and the question was narrow.
question: Does he agree with the open letter to the Government from 40 King’s Counsel stating that the Treaty principles bill seeks to “rewrite the Treaty itself.”?
statement: Look, the very nature of the law is that there is a wide variety of opinions, and lawyers always argue over every piece of legislation. They’re perfectly entitled to their views, and they’ll have an opportunity, no doubt, to discuss them.

explanation: Asked whether this letter specifically gave him pause or concern. 'I'm always pausing and I'm always reflecting' is a generic non-answer that never touches the letter, followed by a pivot to attacking the Greens over welfare sanctions. A sliver of engagement keeps it above zero, but the specific object of the question is never addressed.
question: Has the open letter signed by the most senior legal counsel in this country given him pause for reflection or concern at all as the Minister responsible for the rule of law, constitutional arrangements, and protecting our democracy?
statement: I’m always pausing and I’m always reflecting, but I won’t be taking lectures on the rule of law from that party, which has the view—it’s campaigned on removing welfare sanctions on people who are on the run. I mean, I know it’s expensive to be on the run, but I don’t think that strengthens the rule of law in this country.

explanation: Asked whether he will heed the call to abandon the bill. He never says yes or no, but 'the Government is also committed to its coalition agreements' functions as a recognisable soft no on the actual question. Partial: the core is reachable by inference rather than stated.
question: Will he heed the call of these 40 King’s Counsel and the Waitangi Tribunal and the tens of thousands of people currently in the hīkoi across the nation to “act responsibly now and abandon the Bill.”
statement: Well, I’m always willing to listen to the views of all New Zealanders, and the Government is also committed to its coalition agreements.

explanation: Two-part question — committed to the Act's Treaty purpose, and if so how. 'Absolutely' answers part one outright, and she supplies a 'how' (attendance, achievement, closing the equity gap, collective responsibility). One may dispute whether that constitutes honouring te Tiriti, but that is a Rigor/Veracity judgement; as a response it engages both halves directly.
question: Is she committed to the purpose of the Education and Training Act 2020 that establishes and regulates an education system that “honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relationships”; if so, how?
statement: Absolutely. As I have said many times, raising achievement and closing the equity gap is at the heart of everything that we do. For Māori students in mainstream education, the outcomes are of great concern to me. Regular school attendance rates are 39.1 percent, 12 percent of Māori students at the end of year 8 are at curriculum for maths, over a third of rangatahi Māori left without NCEA level 2 last year. Everyone has a part to play—parents, iwi, Māori leaders, schools, the Crown, and both sides of this House. This Government’s relentless focus on lifting attendance and achievement of tamariki Māori is an utterly essential way in which we must collectively honour the Treaty.

explanation: Asked what tino rangatiratanga in article 2 means for Māori education — a question about a concept. She never engages the concept at all, reframing to 'this Government is about choice in education' and listing kaupapa Māori spending and structured-literacy work. The length and detail of the answer are irrelevant here; a different question was answered.
question: What does tino rangatiratanga in article 2 of Te Tiriti o Waitangi mean for Māori education?
statement: Well, there was a comment to my right that mentioned charter schools. It is also this Government’s commitment to kaupapa Māori education—[Interruption] In answer to the question, this Government is about choice in education. We are massive supporters of kaupapa Māori education, as evidenced by my support for Te Rūnanga nui o ngā Kura Kaupapa Māori o Aotearoa and Ngā Kura ā Iwi o Aotearoa, who I meet with regularly and have an excellent relationship with, and I’m rebuilding that relationship. It’s evident in the fact that we have also set aside $100 million for kura kaupapa property because of the state of their buildings. It’s evident in the fact that everything that we have done in structured literacy and maths in the mainstream, we have also provided in te reo Māori for rumaki and for kura kaupapa as well. We have delivered the world’s first structured literacy phonics checks in te reo Māori because we are supportive of choice in education.

explanation: Asked how she can claim to honour te Tiriti given named education bodies' united opposition to the bill. She restates her honouring-through-achievement case, which glances at the 'how can she say' half, but the stated opposition of those organisations — the pivot of the question — is turned around into their concern about achievement and never confronted.
question: How can she say that she is honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi when national education leaders including Te Akatea, NZEI Te Riu Roa, New Zealand Principals’ Federation, New Zealand Post Primary Teachers Association, Teaching Council of Aotearoa New Zealand, and others have said, “As a group of national education organisations, we are united in our opposition to the Treaty principles bill.”?
statement: All of those organisations are also extraordinarily concerned about the achievement of our tamariki and rangatahi Māori. Every single one of those educational groups has talked about the fact that things like 66 percent of the young people in alternative education are our rangatahi Māori, because we are utterly failing them. This is a Government that is putting educational outcomes and the achievement of young Māori at the heart of everything we do so that they can go on to live the life that they want.

explanation: Asked how she honours te Tiriti while removing it from Te Mātaiaho and scrapping the te ao Māori science expert group. She contests the factual premise head-on: only English and maths are released, the full curriculum isn't out, so nothing has been removed. That directly engages the question. Docked for ignoring the science-expert limb entirely.
question: How is she honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supporting Māori-Crown relationships when she is mainstreaming the curriculum by removing Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the curriculum framework, Te Mātaiaho, and scrapping the group of experts contributing te ao Māori knowledge to the science curriculum?
statement: There have only been two parts of the curriculum that have been released, English and maths, and also in Pāngarau as well. Now, the full curriculum with all of the details has yet to be released. So that member’s assertion that things have been taken out is not true, because we haven’t released the full document yet.

explanation: Asked how 'rebalancing' histories honours te Tiriti and Māori-Crown relations. She begins on the rebalancing rationale (ERO found too little national history, too little consistency) but is cut off before connecting it to the Treaty half. Genuinely started toward the question; only the first half was reached.
question: How is rebalancing Aotearoa histories in school curriculum honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supporting Māori-Crown relationships?
statement: That’s an excellent question. One of the problems that the Education Review Office determined in their report into the New Zealand histories curriculum was that there wasn’t enough of our national history being taught. There wasn’t enough consistency in the curriculum. For example, there are certain—

explanation: Asked whether Te Akatea was consulted on this specific matter. The answer confirms consultation with a wide group "including Te Akatea", but in general present tense — it engages the question without confirming consultation on the thing at issue. Partial.
question: Did you consult them on it?
statement: And the ministry and I both consult with a wide group of principals and groups who represent unions, teachers, including Te Akatea.

explanation: Asked what announcements the Government has made on removing infrastructure roadblocks. The answer names a concrete announcement (independent expert panel reviewing the Public Works Act, now reported back). Squarely addressed.
question: What announcements has the Government made on removing roadblocks to building infrastructure?
statement: The Government is committed to making it easier to build infrastructure in New Zealand. As part of a suite of efforts to achieve this, we have appointed an independent expert advisory panel to review the Public Works Act. This important legislation allows the Government to acquire land for critical infrastructure, of course while also respecting and acknowledging property rights. I’m pleased to say that the panel has now reported back to me on recommendations for improving the fairness and efficiency of the Act.

explanation: Asked why the Public Works Act requires review. The answer gives the reasons directly — infrastructure deficit, no substantial amendment since 1988, delays and cost blowouts. Direct and complete.
question: Why does the Public Works Act require a review?
statement: New Zealand has a widely acknowledge infrastructure deficit which is holding us back socially, environmentally, and economically. We’re determined to do something about that, and, in particular, to improve our levels of productivity, lift our standard of living, and so we need it to be easier to build infrastructure such as schools, hospitals, public transport facilities, water facilities, and flood mitigation works. The Public Works Act has not been substantially amended since 1988. It’s outdated in several key respects, leading to long delays and cost blowouts.

explanation: Asked what the review focused on. The answer states the focus (efficiency, effectiveness, clarity) and illustrates it. Addresses the question asked.
question: What did the review focus on?
statement: The independent expert advisory panel has completed a short, sharp review of the Act, focusing on areas in which the efficiency, effectiveness, and clarity of the Act can be improved. Modern, large-scale infrastructure projects often create a knock-on effect where existing infrastructure must be upgraded or moved to accommodate the new project. For example, the current version of the Public Works Act does not allow for this and nor does it allow for collaboration between local and central government agencies.

explanation: Asked when the changes come into effect. The answer gives a timeline for introducing an amendment bill (mid next year) and an announcement "shortly", but never reaches when changes take effect. Engages, falls short of the core.
question: When will these changes come into effect?
statement: We are moving at pace—you’ll be pleased to hear. The Government is considering the panel’s recommendations, and I hope to make an announcement shortly. An amendment bill will likely be introduced into this Parliament in the middle of next year.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. Answer: "Yes." One word, complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how he can claim to represent all New Zealanders while refusing to front the hīkoi. He responds to the fronting charge (a delegation was sent, position stated) but not to the representation claim. Partial.
question: How can he say that this Government represents all New Zealanders when he refuses to go outside and front the tens of thousands of New Zealanders gathered here today?
statement: Our position is very clear. We had a delegation from the National Party representing our position, receiving the hīkoi, and making clear our point of view, which is that we’re not supporting the bill beyond first reading, therefore it won’t become law.

explanation: Asked why the crowd was not sufficient reason for him to go out personally. He rejects the premise and repeats the delegation answer; the "why not you" core is never engaged. Mostly a dodge, though not an attack on the questioner.
question: Why is that crowd of tens of thousands of people not good enough for him to go out there and front the decision that he just made?
statement: I reject the characterisation of that question. As I said, the National Party sent a delegation out, representing our position, to receive the hīkoi. I’ve also met with iwi leaders up and down the country and will continue to do so.

explanation: Asked what the point of meeting iwi leaders is when their demand is unmet. He explicitly answers the first part — the point is improving outcomes — and illustrates it, but leaves the "their demand is to kill the bill" half untouched. Partial.
question: What’s the point of meeting with iwi leaders across the country when their clear demand is for the Government to kill the bill and he has not done that, with all of the opportunities that he has had to abandon this bill?
statement: In answer to the first part of your question, the reason I meet with iwi leaders is because we want to improve outcomes for Māori and non-Māori. When we see 12 percent of Māori getting to high school at the standard they need to be for on mathematics because of the previous Government, that’s not great. When we see the number of Māori young kids in emergency motel accommodation and the work that we’ve done subsequently since coming to Government to take them out of there to put them into a proper house, that’s the stuff that we talk about. When we work with Waikato-Tainui to make sure we’re working on social housing, that’s the work that we’re interested in—making sure we improve outcomes for Māori, not this stuff.

explanation: Asked why he would give false hope given the bill's fate. He explains the reasoning behind the position (MMP compromise, no support beyond first reading), which touches the "why", but never engages the false-hope charge. Partial.
question: Why would he give false hope to New Zealanders that their voice matters when he has said that the bill will be killed at second reading?
statement: Well, it’s been a longstanding position of the National Party. We came to a compromise under an MMP environment in forming a coalition Government. We agree on many, many things between the three parties in this coalition Government; we don’t agree on this. We came to a compromise. We’re not supporting it beyond first reading. It won’t become law.

explanation: Asked how people can trust him having compromised on the Treaty in a coalition deal. The answer pivots to the economy, incomes, housing, education — talking points that never reach the trust question as posed.
question: How are people supposed to trust him when he’s willing to compromise on the founding document of our country in his coalition agreement?
statement: Well, New Zealanders can trust us that we’re going to deliver on improving outcomes for Māori and non-Māori. That is why this Government is working so incredibly hard to rebuild the economy, because Māori want higher incomes, Māori want better quality housing, Māori want much better quality education outcomes, and they want access to timely quality healthcare as well. That’s what this Government’s focused on.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has seen on the bill. He names two specifically — the first reading and referral, and the select committee opening submissions. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has he seen regarding the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill?
statement: Two of note in the last few days: one being that the bill was read a first time, agreed to by the House, and referred to the Justice Committee. The second announcement was just this morning, that the Justice Committee is now seeking public submissions from all New Zealanders on their views on the bill. This is the first time in our history that all New Zealanders have been offered an equal chance to have a say on what our constitutional future means under the Treaty of Waitangi, and I’d encourage people to get along to the Justice Committee website and have their voice heard.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on the bill's first reading. He confirms there has been extensive reportage and characterises it, so the topic is engaged, but he never identifies a single report and slides into a contrast between 'rational debaters' and 'name callers' — a talking point where a characterisation of the reports was asked for. Partial engagement with a sprawling question.
question: What reports has he seen on the first reading of the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill?
statement: Well, I have to say there’s been quite a lot of reportage on the topic, but if I was to try and boil it down it would be a contrast between people who want to have a respectful and rational debate about our constitutional future and the way the principles of the Treaty have evolved in recent years, versus people who resort to name calling, abuse, and theatrics but not actually engaging with the argument, and I think that contrast is perfectly clear for New Zealanders, and I think there’ll be some people in this House who want to review which side of that divide they’d like to be on.

explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can have their say. He names the mechanism (submissions to the Justice Committee) and the deadline (11.59 p.m., 7 January). Directly and completely answered; the surrounding exhortation to submit respectfully doesn't displace the answer.
question: How can New Zealanders have their say on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill?
statement: Well, as I mentioned, from now until 11.59 p.m. on 7 January, the Justice Committee will be accepting submissions, and I think it’s very important that people have a view on this bill and the issues surrounding it; actually have their say, and make sure that they do it in a respectful and constructive way with a view to how our country can work together under this Treaty principles bill, perhaps with improvements suggested by people at select committee. Having this kind of debate and reflection is healthy for New Zealand, and I invite people to make those submissions to the Justice Committee.

explanation: Two-part question. Part one ('does she stand by the statement') gets a flat 'yes'. Part two ('is the business community on board with the bill') gets a disclaimer of portfolio responsibility followed by an actual answer — a variety of opinions, i.e. not uniformly on board. Both parts reached, the second with hedging around the core.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “We know that to be successful in driving growth we need you and your colleagues in the business community on board”; if so, is the business community on board with the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, to the first part of the question, yes. To the second part of the question, I don’t have responsibility for either the business community or, indeed, the bill, but what I will say is that my sense from the business community is that, much like the rest of the country, there are a variety of opinions on the bill.

explanation: Asked whether she has received advice on the bill's impact on the sovereign risk rating. Answer: 'no.' One word, squarely responsive, nothing left dangling. Its unhelpfulness is a specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: Has she received any advice about the impact of the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill and associated divisiveness on New Zealand’s sovereign risk rating?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, no.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with a specific Newfield quote about moving away from divisive issues. He says he generally agrees with what Newfield has to say — an answer, but pitched at the man rather than the proposition, and then redirected to the Government's growth agenda. The specific claim about divisive issues is hedged around rather than met.
question: Does she agree with Morrison & Co CEO Paul Newfield that “We need to move away from small-minded divisive issues and focus on building a better New Zealand together”?
statement: Well, I generally agree with what Mr Newfield has to say. He’s a very smart man. What I would say is that this Government is intensely focused on building a New Zealand that is more productive, smarter around how it uses capital, and drives economic growth for the future. I know Mr Newfield shares those ambitions.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees that Seymour is the wrong person to wear the growth badge. No yes/no is ever given, but the substance is a direct rebuttal — walk and chew gum, National differs on the bill, Seymour is leading investment and red-tape reform. The core proposition is engaged by counter-argument rather than avoided, but the agree/disagree asked for is never stated.
question: Does she agree with Foodstuffs North Island CEO Chris Quin: “If Seymour is really focused on long-term economic growth and productivity, that would be fine, but his obsession with divisive social issues that energise people on the fringes of the New Zealand political debate make him the wrong person to wear that badge”?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, it’s possible to walk and chew gum at the same time, and while the National Party has a different view to one of the governing parties in the coalition on the Treaty principles bill—that’s been well canvassed—what I can say in a ministerial context is that Minister Seymour is intensely focused on productivity and is leading the charge on foreign investment reform inside the Government and on a range of red-tape - busting initiatives to get Government off the back of businesses, who are just trying to make an honest buck in the world and grow this economy.

explanation: Asked how the Government can claim economic focus while distracted by the bill. He denies the premise by turning the charge on Labour, then delivers an extended statement of the Government's growth mission. Contesting the premise is a form of engagement, so this isn't a pure dodge, but the bulk is talking points and the specific tension raised is never addressed.
question: How can her Government claim to be focused on supporting the economy and growth when it is distracted with the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, the only person who, I think, has got very excited about it and distracted is members of the Labour Party, including herself. This Government’s driving mission—this Government’s driving ambition and mission—in politics, and the reason why it was elected almost a year or so ago, is to lift our ambitions as a country, get out of the mire of low growth, both in growth and productivity, and get this economy growing again, because, ultimately, the only way to build a prosperous and ambitious country that New Zealanders want to stay in and not leave and to build the types of public services that New Zealanders demand—the only sustainable way to create that—is economic growth and getting this joint going again, and that’s what we’re focused on.

explanation: Asked what announcement he has made on contactless payments in Auckland. He states what was announced, with whom, when, and who funded it. Directly and completely answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about contactless payments on Auckland’s public transport network?
statement: On Thursday, I announced alongside the Mayor of Auckland, Wayne Brown, that the Government and Auckland Council have delivered contactless payments on Auckland’s public transport network, to enable commuters to tag on and off public buses, trains, and ferries travelling across the region. The New Zealand Transport Agency and Auckland Council have jointly funded the delivery of contactless payments on the Auckland transport network, which provides Aucklanders with more travel choices to get where they need to go.

explanation: Asked what payment options Aucklanders now have. He enumerates them: HOP cards, contactless debit and credit, Apple Pay and Google Pay on phones and watches. Exactly the question asked, fully covered.
question: Excellent. What options do Aucklanders now have to pay on public transport?
statement: From Sunday, Aucklanders have more ways to pay on Auckland’s buses, trains, and ferries. In addition to HOP Cards, Aucklanders and visitors to the city are now able to tag on and off using contactless debit cards, credit cards, as well as Apple Pay and Google Pay on their smartphones or smartwatches. This is fantastic news for Aucklanders and it takes away the hassle of needing cash or a HOP card.

explanation: Asked how the roll-out will benefit Aucklanders. He gives the benefits — convenience, easier use, more transport choices. The promotional framing doesn't displace the answer; the question's core is met.
question: How will the roll-out of contactless payments benefit Aucklanders?
statement: Rolling out contactless debit and credit card payments for public transport users will be a game-changer. Not only will it make public transport services more convenient and easier to use but it will also help give Aucklanders more transport choices. It’s all part of our Government’s plan to increase travel choices and help people get where they need to go quickly and safely.

explanation: Asked what plans exist to roll out contactless payments nationally. He answers with the programme (National Ticketing Solution) and a timetable: Timaru and Christchurch in early 2025, other regions by end of 2026. Squarely responsive.
question: What plans does the Government have to roll out contactless payments across the country?
statement: Good question. The roll-out of contactless payments in Auckland’s public transport network is the first step delivering New Zealand’s one National Ticketing Solution. Contactless payments on public transport are common elsewhere around the world, and this will ensure New Zealanders have the same standard of service. The roll-out of contactless payments will expand to Timaru and Christchurch in early 2025 and it will reach other regions by the end of 2026.

explanation: Asked how he assesses the bill's impact on the Crown's ability to honour completed settlements. 'With great care' is a quip that supplies no assessment, and he then points to another Minister holding the responsibility. The portfolio deflection is stated plainly, which lifts it above a pure pivot, but the question's core — the assessment itself — is never reached.
question: How does he assess the impact of the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill on the Crown’s ability to honour its Treaty obligations with Treaty settlements that have been completed, particularly regarding partnership, protection, and participation?
statement: With great care, although I should note that ministerial responsibility for post-Treaty settlement issues lies with the Minister for Māori Crown Relations, which I’m sure the Opposition spokesperson’s well aware of.

explanation: Asked what steps he is taking so the Treaty principles bill does not undermine Crown-iwi trust. He does name an action — continuing in-depth conversations with Treaty settlement groups — so a 'what steps' answer of sorts is given, but the core of the question (the bill and its effect on goodwill) is never touched; the bill is not mentioned at all. Partial engagement.
question: What steps is he taking to ensure that the proposed Treaty principles bill does not undermine the trust and goodwill between the Crown and iwi, who are currently engaged in Treaty negotiations?
statement: The steps we’re taking are carrying on the in-depth conversations, with goodwill, with many Treaty groups that are wanting to advance their settlements, and they are scattered all about the country. I can inform the House that we are making steady progress on those issues.

explanation: A yes/no question with an explicit 'if not, why not'. He never says whether he agrees with Finlayson and gives no reason; 'grain of salt' and 'entertaining to hear what he has to say' gesture at disagreement while sidestepping both halves. Close to a full dodge, with only a faint implication standing in for the answer.
question: Does he agree with former Treaty of Waitangi negotiations Minister Christopher Finlayson, who has said that National is risking damaging its relationship with Māori by agreeing for the Treaty principles bill to go through a select committee process; and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, I always take the comments of former colleagues with great interest but also with a grain of salt, because things have sometimes moved on from where they were when they were in the House.
