But that former Minister has a lot to say on many issues, and it’s always very entertaining to hear what he has to say.

explanation: A narrow disjunctive question — Finlayson, Shipley, or all former National MPs? Real and answerable despite its loading. He names nobody and pivots to the party's tradition of robust debate and conducting itself with good grace. The specific core was squarely avoided.
question: When he stated, “some former MPs sometimes feel they can chip in and tell the current ones what to do”, was he referring to Christopher Finlayson, Jenny Shipley, or is it just all former National MPs who are pointing out this Government’s mistakes?
statement: Well, of course, on this side of the House, we have a long tradition of robust debate within the National Party. We’re not sort of all having to believe the same thing at the same moment at the same time, and I think that’s what we’re seeing across the country. There are a wide variety of views on these things, but the most important thing is that we conduct ourselves with good grace, listen to the other side, and have a good, honest conversation, and that’s what we’re about.

explanation: Two-part question: does she stand by the commitment, and if so how. She answers the first explicitly ('yes') and then addresses the 'how' by naming closing the equity gap for tamariki Māori as what honouring the Treaty means in her portfolio. The 'how' is thematic rather than itemised, but that is a specificity matter; both parts were engaged.
question: Does she stand by her absolute commitment to honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi and support Māori-Crown relationships, as set out in the purpose of the Education and Training Act 2020; if so, how?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes. In answer to the second part of the question, we are putting student achievement at the heart of every single thing that we do. If we want to honour the Treaty, it means closing the equity gap so that decades of disparity that have pervaded our system and the disproportionate representation of tamariki Māori and rangatahi Māori in the lower quartiles of our education and achievement system is closed. It is my utmost belief that education can and should be the primary protective factor for our kids and the way that they can break through intergenerational cycles of poverty and disadvantage and live the life they want.

explanation: Asked to explain how Te Tiriti is embedded in the refreshed curriculum. She engages directly by rejecting the premise with a reason — Te Mātaiaho is only a shell, not yet written, only English and maths released, and it will be consulted on. Disputing the premise on stated grounds is a response, not a pivot; she does not reach the dismissal-of-advisers part.
question: Can she explain how Te Tiriti o Waitangi has been embedded and authentically reflected in the refreshed curriculum following the outright removal and erasure of Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the curriculum framework Te Mātaiaho and dismissal of Māori advisers on the curriculum refresh working group?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, I answered this last week, and I’ll repeat myself: Te Mātaiaho has not been developed yet. There are only two learning areas—English and maths—that have been put out. What has been put out in terms of the framework which is Te Mātaiaho is only a shell. We are working on that framework and it will be consulted on in the same way that all of the learning areas are being consulted on. But I’ll reiterate: it hasn’t been written yet, so the member needs to understand that.

explanation: Asked why she mandated science of learning while ignoring Māori ways of knowing. Both halves are met: the 'why' is answered (well-documented, well-evidenced way to improve outcomes) and the 'ignoring' charge is met by pointing to Te Marautanga o Aotearoa also being refreshed and to Better Start Literacy results for tamariki Māori. Engaged, if partly by counter-assertion.
question: Why has she taken the unprecedented move to mandate an unrecognised concept for science of learning as the teaching and learning approach for all, ignoring Māori ways of knowing, teaching, and learning?
statement: That’s why we have the New Zealand Curriculum and also Te Marautanga o Aotearoa. Te Marautanga is also being refreshed, as well as the New Zealand Curriculum. The science of learning is a well-known, well-documented, and well-evidenced way to improve the outcomes of our students. If that member wants to see some evidence of that, she should go and look at the structured literacy Better Start Literacy Approach results for tamariki Māori, because they are outstanding.

explanation: Asked what she will do to keep Māori learners safe from racism once the NELPs are scrapped. She answers the 'what will she do': section 127 duties remain and more guidance for boards is coming, plus a reason the NELPs are being dropped. The guidance is vague, but vagueness is a specificity failing, not evasion — the question was addressed.
question: What will she do to ensure that Māori learners and other children from minority cultures are safe from racism and discrimination when she plans to scrap the National Education and Learning Priorities (NELPs)?
statement: There are many things that boards of trustees need to take into account when it comes to keeping children safe at school. One of those things is section 127 of the Education Act. We will be developing more guidance for boards in the future, but the NELPs are something that only need to be given regard to and they are cluttering up the things that school boards need to pay attention to.

explanation: Asked why tamariki are at a hīkoi rather than relying on her to honour Te Tiriti. She never addresses the 'why', instead asserting schools should be open and children should be in class. That implicitly rejects the premise, which is some engagement, but the question's core — her own failure to honour the commitment — is left untouched.
question: Why do tamariki have to attend a hīkoi today instead of relying on an education Minister to live up to her promise to honour Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: As I said today, all schools should be open for instruction, and the most important thing for our tamariki Māori is that they are in front of a teacher, learning, every single day that they possibly can if we’re going to close the equity gap.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he made about crime statistics. He states what he announced yesterday and enumerates the figures. Direct and complete; a patsy question, but that does not change whether it was engaged.
question: What recent announcements has he made about crime statistics?
statement: Yesterday, I announced some of the progress that we have made as a coalition Government in our first year. I highlighted a 3 percent reduction in victimisations, an increase of over 30 percent in foot patrols, ram raids dropping by 60 percent, and aggravated robberies down by 11 percent. As I said, there is a lot more work to do to make New Zealand the safest country in the world and to restore law and order, but this coalition Government is committed to deliver on that promise.

explanation: A narrow comparative question — this year's gang membership growth versus last year's. He gives both figures (1 percent to October, against 10 percent for the same period last year) and the comparison. Exactly the question asked, answered fully.
question: How does gang membership growth compare this year to last year?
statement: Gang membership recorded on the National Gang List grew 1 percent to October this year. Last year for the same period, it grew by 10 percent. Under this coalition Government, gang membership growth has slowed tenfold.

explanation: Asked what a reduction in overall victimisations means. He answers directly: it is a significant early sign that things are getting better and that the country is becoming safer. The framing is self-serving, but interpretation of the meaning is what was asked for and it is supplied.
question: What does a reduction in overall victimisations mean?
statement: Victimisations reducing across the board by 3 percent this year is a significant early sign that things are getting better. While there are still areas of improvement, and the job is by no means done, to see a reduction in total victimisations by 3 percent is a sign that we are becoming a safer country.

explanation: Asked whether the job of restoring law and order is done. Answers 'No.' outright, then elaborates. A complete, unhedged response to the question put.
question: Thank you. Is the job done in restoring law and order?
statement: No. Despite the progress that has been made, we must remain relentlessly focused on some growth areas like retail crime. I was appointed police Minister to help restore law and order. That job is not yet done, but I’m firmly committed to seeing it through with my ministerial colleagues inside our coalition Government and with our combined desire to make New Zealand the safest country in the world.

explanation: Asked what recent actions the Government took to boost the economy; the answer enumerates concrete trade actions (EU FTA entry into force, UAE CEPA, GCC agreement, APEC signing) and ties them back to growing the economy. It is a friendly question answered squarely. Slight deduction only because 'the economy' was answered entirely through the trade portfolio, leaving other economic levers untouched — but the question was engaged, not dodged.
question: What recent actions has the Government taken to boost New Zealand’s economy?
statement: It’s been a big year for New Zealand in trade negotiations. In May, the European Union free-trade agreement (FTA) entered into force many months sooner than predicted, providing $46 million of tariffs saved for Kiwi exporters this year that they would otherwise have missed out on. In September, we concluded the New Zealand - United Arab Emirates Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, our first FTA in the Middle East, giving Kiwi exporters commercial advantage in that growing market. Last month, we concluded a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)—unfinished business for successive Governments over 18 years—with a particular focus on goods and services trade. And last week, at APEC in Peru, we signed the agreement on trade with sustainability with Costa Rica, Iceland, and Switzerland; particularly good for our sheep farmers and wood producers. Growing New Zealand’s trade relationships is part of the Government’s plan to grow the economy, lift incomes for all Kiwis, and create jobs.

explanation: Asked how the Middle East agreements will benefit Kiwi exporters; the answer states the benefit mechanism directly — 98.5% tariff elimination on entry into force rising to 99%, duty-free access for 99% of exports over ten years, tariffs removed on 51% of Gulf exports on day one — and names the sectors that gain. Direct and complete response to the question as asked.
question: How will these trade agreements with the Middle East benefit Kiwi exporters?
statement: Well, as I said, in September—after just four months of negotiation—we concluded a trade deal with the UAE delivering 98.5 percent tariff elimination on New Zealand exports on entry into force, rising to 99 percent after three years. Just three weeks ago, in Doha, we concluded a high-quality trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council, having significantly reengaged with them in February of this year. The GCC agreement delivers duty-free access for 99 percent of New Zealand’s exports over 10 years and, when combined with the UAE agreement, removes tariffs on 51 percent of our exports to the Gulf on day one. These two agreements secure market access in a highly competitive market for beef, lamb, dairy, manuka honey, fish, and many, many other goods, and contribute towards their ambitious goal of doubling exports by value over 10 years.

explanation: Asked what additional provisions the GCC agreement contains; the answer lists them (customs procedures, services access, intellectual property, transparency, sustainable development, labour standards, climate, CEDAW commitments, Treaty of Waitangi exception). The question asked for provisions and provisions were given.
question: What additional provisions are included in the Gulf Corporation Council agreement?
statement: The NZ-GCC FTA includes provisions that will make doing business easier, with preferential access for our primary sector exporters, streamlined customs procedures, reduced trade barriers, and commitments to level the playing field for Kiwi services businesses entering the market. The agreement also includes chapters and provisions on intellectual property; transparency and trade and sustainability of sustainable development; and includes commitments to international labour standards, climate, and women’s economic empowerment, committing to the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women. New Zealand also secured our Treaty of Waitangi exception to allow us to meet Treaty obligations.

explanation: Asked what additional actions were taken to double export value and grow trade; the answer describes the 70-company China delegation to CIIE and Guangzhou, 24 agreements worth $340 million, and the NZ-China FTA services upgrade. These are actions responsive to the question. The closing 'a big year for trade negotiations' is padding but does not displace the answer.
question: What additional actions has the Government taken to double export value and grow trade?
statement: Two weeks ago, I led a business delegation of over 70 companies to China—our most significant economic relationship—to attend the China International Import Expo (CIIE) in Shanghai and then on to Guangzhou. This was the largest number of companies to attend or exhibit at the CIIE, and New Zealand’s largest footprint and presence there. The companies and their products were very well received and built on New Zealand’s reputation for producing high-quality, safe, environmentally friendly food and fibre. Twenty-four agreements and memorandums of understanding between New Zealand and Chinese companies were signed during the visit, worth an additional $340 million in export revenue to New Zealand over the next three years. Also, earlier this year, with the Chinese Government, we announced and committed to upgrading the services we compounded of the NZ-China FTA. As I said, a big year for trade negotiations.

explanation: A standard 'does she stand by her statements and actions' question, answered 'Yes' and then elaborated with the maths pilot. The yes/no core is delivered unambiguously before any elaboration, which is the complete answer to what was asked.
question: E tautoko ana ia i āna kōrero me āna mahi katoa?
statement: Yes, especially my recently announced maths pilot to lift student achievement and close the equity gap. From term 1 and 2 next year, around 2,000 year 7 and 8 students who need the most help will take part in an intensive programme to support them to progress towards the required curriculum levels in mathematics.

explanation: A two-part question: (a) is specific hapu/iwi consultation part of meeting Te Tiriti obligations, and (b) what specific consultation was undertaken on removing Te Ahu o te Reo Maori and the section 127 changes. The Minister answers only the first part, and hedges it ('in certain circumstances, yes'). Part (b) was the narrow factual core — a request to name the consultation actually undertaken — and it goes wholly unaddressed. A specific factual half avoided entirely scores low even though the response is brief rather than a talking-point pivot.
question: Does she believe that specific consultation with hapū and iwi on decisions affecting Māori is part of meeting obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi; and if so, what specific consultation did she take on removing Te Ahu o te Reo Māori and changes to section 127 of the Education and Training Act?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question: in certain circumstances, yes.

explanation: Again two parts: (a) does she recognise the Crown's section 9 responsibility, and (b) how is not consulting Maori consistent with that. The answer is 'In answer to the first part of the question: yes' — the yes/no half is answered cleanly, but the substantive 'how is this consistent' half, which is the entire point of the question, is left untouched. Answering the easy half and stopping is a dodge of the core.
question: Does she recognise the Crown’s responsibility to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, as established in section 9 of the Education and Training Act, and, if so, how is not consulting with Māori about any of the changes I mentioned in education consistent with this?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question: yes.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to release the full consultation report. 'If it's required by law then yes we will' engages the question directly and gives a determinate answer under a stated condition — it is not a pivot to talking points. But it stops short of the commitment that was sought, converting a yes/no into a contingency without saying whether the law does in fact require it. Partial answer that hedges around the core rather than avoiding it.
question: Will she commit to releasing the full report of the consultation that she conducted on the removal of Te Tiriti o Waitangi as a primary objective under section 127 of the Education and Training Act?
statement: If it’s required by law then yes we will.

explanation: Asked whether attending the hikoi is consistent with the section 5(4)(c) objective of instilling appreciation of Te Tiriti, and if not, why not. The Minister never says whether she agrees or not, and never touches section 5(4)(c). Instead she pivots to a different provision of the Act — achievement and being in school in front of teachers — which gestures at disagreement without ever stating or justifying it. The 'if not, why not' limb is never reached.
question: Does she agree that for ākonga to attend today’s hīkoi is entirely consistent with section 5(4)(c) of the Education and Training Act objective “to instil, in each child and young person, an appreciation of the importance of … (iii) Te Tiriti o Waitangi”; if not, why not?
statement: There are many things in the Education and Training Act, one of which is to make sure that students are achieving to the best of their abilities, and in order to do that, they need to be in school in front of their amazing teachers.

explanation: Asked why she wants to deprioritise upholding Te Tiriti in schools. 'We're not deprioritising it' rejects the premise the question was built on, which is a direct engagement with the question rather than an evasion of it — once the premise is denied, the 'why' has no subject left to answer. Marked slightly below the top because no reason is offered for the denial in the face of the cited Whanaketia recommendation, but the question was met head-on, not sidestepped.
question: Why does the Minister want to deprioritise upholding Te Tiriti o Waitangi in schools, despite the recommendation of Whanaketia that “The government should partner with hapū, iwi and Māori to give effect to te Tiriti”?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question: we’re not deprioritising it.

explanation: 'Does he stand by all of his Government's statements and actions?' answered 'Yes.' One word, unambiguous, and a complete answer to the question asked. Brevity is not evasion — nothing about the question was left unaddressed.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Shipley's "civil war" warning, and (if so) why the select committee process. He answers the first part squarely — no, he does not agree, there is no civil war risk, the language is inflammatory. The second half was conditional on "if so", so the failed antecedent voids it. Blunt and short, but the question asked was engaged head-on.
question: Does he agree with former Prime Minister Dame Jenny Shipley: “I caution New Zealand - the minute you put the Treaty into a political framework in its totality, you are inviting civil war.”; if so, why is his Government asking a select committee to spend the next six months attempting to do exactly that?
statement: In answer to part of the question, no, we’re not at risk of civil war in New Zealand. That’s inflammatory language.

explanation: A narrow "why" question, given a direct causal answer: because it is part of the coalition agreement. Thin on detail, but detail is Specificity, not this attribute — the core of the question is reached and answered.
question: Why is the Government asking a select committee to spend the next six months attempting to put the Treaty into a political framework in its totality?
statement: Because it’s part of our coalition agreement.

explanation: The quote had several elements (malicious, politically motivated, fundraising-motivated); he explicitly flags he is answering "the first part" and addresses only the fundraising element, leaving the "malicious/politically motivated" core untouched. The "if so" follow-up is voided by his disagreement. Partial engagement rather than a dodge or a pivot.
question: Does he agree with Dame Jenny Shipley “this sort of malicious, politically motivated, fundraising-motivated attempt to politicise the Treaty in a new way should raise people’s voices, because it is not in New Zealand’s immediate interest.”; if so, why did he prioritise the Government’s political interests over the best interests of New Zealand?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, I don’t believe it’s linked to fund-raising.

explanation: "No" is offered, but it is not clear which part it answers — the agreement with Shipley's contract framing, or whether the bill rewrites the Treaty — and he then moves to a general statement about upholding Crown obligations that engages neither directly. Hedging around the core rather than an outright pivot.
question: Does he agree with Dame Jenny Shipley, who said, when speaking about the Treaty, “this was an agreement, a contract - and you do not rip up a contract and then just say, ‘Well, I’m happy to rewrite it on my terms, but you don’t count.’ ”; if so, does he agree that the bill currently before the Justice Committee rewrites the terms of the Treaty?
statement: No, what I expect is the Crown to uphold our obligations under the law and under the Treaty.

explanation: The standing "does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions" question is answered "Yes" in the first word; that is complete. The gang-policy material that follows is unsolicited padding, but padding after a direct answer does not make it a dodge.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to crack down on gang activity. At midnight tonight, a raft of tough new laws will take effect. Gang insignia will be banned in all public places, courts will be able to issue non-consorting orders, and police will be able to stop criminal gang members from associating and communicating. Greater weight will also be given to gang membership at sentencing, enabling courts to impose more severe punishments. Gangs aren’t community groups. They’re not Rotary. They thrive on destroying the lives of other New Zealanders, whether that’s by peddling drugs or through brutal acts of violence that leave communities in fear. We promised to restore law and order, and tomorrow, police will have more powers to do exactly that.

explanation: Neither part is answered: he never says whether he stands by the statement, and never says whether he is comfortable with smoking and vaping rates having risen by 16,000 daily smokers. "The Minister is working incredibly hard" and "we've got a great plan" are talking points that route around a specific, checkable question.
question: Does he stand by his statement: “Casey Costello is very focused on lowering smoking rates and I’m comfortable”; if so, is he comfortable with the news that both daily smoking and vaping rates have risen under his watch, with 16,000 more daily smokers?
statement: Well, I’d just say that the Minister is working incredibly hard to make sure that we deliver on Smokefree 2025, but we know that the last group of smokers to come off daily smoking is going to be incredibly hard to move. But we’ve got a great plan and we’re working hard at it.

explanation: Asked whether the alternatives-based approach is working, he lists four things the Government is doing (quit attempts, quit support, staying smoke-free, reducing uptake) and never says whether any of it is working. Activity offered where an assessment was asked for — the core yes/no is left untouched.
question: Does he stand by his statement that he and Casey Costello will “deal with that really hard-core group of smokers as we try and get that target down to 5 percent. All she’s done is propose alternatives”; if so, are efforts to target that hard-core group by proposing so-called alternatives working?
statement: Well, what I’d say to the member is we’re very focused on four attempts as we try and deal with this last, hard-core group of smokers. That involves us increasing quit attempts, it means we’re improving access to quit support, it means that we’re supporting people to stay smoke-free, and we’re going to reduce the uptake of smoking.

explanation: Asked for the return on investment on $216 million, he opens and closes with attacks on the questioner, but in between does engage the substance by disputing the premise — it is an accounting accrual for forgone excise, not a tax break. He addresses the object of the question without ever reaching the question, and the figure asked for is never given.
question: What is the return on investment on the $216 million tax break to tobacco companies his Government has given, apparently to encourage smokers to quit, when it has demonstrably failed, with the first rise in daily smokers in New Zealand’s recent history?
statement: Well, again, the member has difficulty understanding economics, and that was clearly obvious by the economic mess that he left behind after six years in Government. What we have accrued, as you know, is an accounting accrual, essentially, for a loss of excise tax, should we be super successful in taking people off cigarettes and into alternatives. That’s a good thing. We’re just making sure that we are fiscally prudent and managing the economy well—as we do—instead of the mess that you left behind.

explanation: "No" answers the yes/no put to him directly, and the follow-on clarifies what he is asserting instead. The clarification is self-serving, but self-serving is not evasive — the question was engaged and resolved in one word.
question: So is he asserting that the fact that more people are smoking now than when he became Prime Minister, and the Government is, therefore, collecting more tax from that, is a sign of success?
statement: No. What we’re saying is that we have more work to do with a very strong cohort of daily smokers. We need to redouble our efforts and work even harder. It’s a harder task, but we’re doing everything we can to do that.

explanation: "I reject the characterisation of that question" does convey a refusal to admit he was wrong, which is a form of answer, but he then pivots to talking points about the previous Government rather than addressing either specific decision he was asked about. Half a refusal, half a pivot.
question: Will he admit that he was wrong to submit to New Zealand First and scrap New Zealand’s world-leading smoke-free legislation, just as he was wrong to submit to the ACT Party and support the Treaty principles bill?
statement: I reject the characterisation of that question. I’m proud of our coalition partners and I’m proud of the work that this coalition Government is doing to clean up the ungodly mess that that member left behind after six years of economic mismanagement, letting crime get out of control, and delivering worse outcomes for New Zealanders.

explanation: The reply is a bare premise rejection with nothing said about his negotiating skills or his priorities. A stated refusal is not automatically a dodge, but this rejects the framing without answering, refusing, or engaging the substance at all — closer to declining to participate than to "no, I won't".
question: What does it say about his negotiating skills or, indeed, his priorities that he is willing to provoke conflict between the Crown and Māori and increase the number of Kiwi smokers just to form a coalition with parties who had nowhere else to go anyway?
statement: I reject the characterisation of that question.

explanation: She engages the topic substantively — partnerships should continue, nothing in the bill prevents them — but does not give the commitment asked for, and on the specific select committee recommendation defers to considering advice. She does say why she is not committing now, so this is hedging around the core rather than avoiding it. Length here is Specificity; it does not lift the score.
question: Will she commit to retaining strategic partnerships with iwi and Māori organisations, as recommended in the select committee report on the repeal of section 7AA; if not, why not?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. The repeal of section 7AA is about ensuring the safety and wellbeing of children in care is at the forefront of all decision making. I’ve always said that strategic partnerships should continue, and I’ve made my expectations clear to officials that they should continue the good work that is being done in this space, if the agreement is working in a positive way to the betterment of children. I also made it very clear in my first reading speech that nothing in this bill prevents Oranga Tamariki from retaining its current strategic partnerships or from entering new partnerships with iwi, hapū, and Māori organisations. In regards to specific recommendations in the select committee report, I want to thank those who made submissions and those who appeared before the committee in person, and I also want to thank the select committee for their careful deliberation and consideration on the bill. I will consider the recommendations and take advice before making any decisions on next steps.

explanation: Asked why she doesn't recognise the value of reporting on outcomes/disparities for tamariki Māori. She engages by disputing the premise — enumerating the reporting channels that already exist (Independent Children's Monitor, National Care Standards, annual OT report, s448B). Rejecting the premise with reasons is engagement, not a dodge. Held below high because the 'disparities' core and the 'why not' framing are addressed only obliquely; the detail of the list does not raise the score (that is Specificity).
question: Why does she not recognise the value of reporting on outcomes and disparities for tamariki Māori, given she has now recognised the need for strategic partnerships?
statement: In regards to reporting, we have a number of ways that can be reported on issues in that space. We have a report from the Independent Children’s Monitor in this space, we have the National Care Standards report that reports on outcomes for Māori and young people and their whānau, we have an annual Oranga Tamariki report that reports in this space, and under section 448B of the Oranga Tamariki Act, the Minister for Children is required to report on whether the legislation and Government policy meets the needs of children and young people.

explanation: A two-part question — (a) does requiring the CE to report on Māori outcomes limit the ability to serve tamariki Māori, (b) if not, would she reconsider retaining 7AA. The answer gives neither. It restates what she thinks the CE should focus on (safe, healthy, loved), which is a talking point adjacent to the question, and part (b) is untouched. A narrow yes/no was asked and avoided.
question: So does she believe that requiring the chief executive of Oranga Tamariki to consider and report on outcomes for Māori limits the ability to serve tamariki Māori, and, if not, would she also reconsider retaining this 7AA requirement?
statement: In regards to the first part of the question, what I think is important for the CE of Oranga Tamariki to concentrate on is making sure that the children that come into the care of Oranga Tamariki are safe, healthy, and loved.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to reconsider other aspects of the repeal in light of select committee evidence, Whanaketia and Waitangi Tribunal findings. The response never reaches commit-or-not; it pivots entirely to a general statement that Māori children are no different to any other child. The specific evidentiary grounds named in the question are not engaged at all.
question: Will she commit to reconsidering other aspects of this repeal to better reflect select committee evidence, Whanaketia, and Waitangi Tribunal findings that tino rangatiratanga over kāinga and protection and active partnership must be enshrined in care, and, if not, why not?
statement: When it comes to Māori children in care, I can tell you: Māori children are no different to any other child. They want to feel safe, they want to feel loved, and they want to feel like they belong. And they want to know that when they wake up tomorrow, they’re going to be safe.

explanation: Part one is answered squarely and immediately: 'No, I don't disagree' — she accepts the Fitzmaurice proposition and adds that she has never claimed a clash. Part two ('how can she go ahead with repealing') gets only an implicit answer via the safety-first rationale, not a direct one. Direct on half, gestural on half.
question: Does she accept Dr Luke Fitzmaurice’s select committee submission argument that “There is no clash between tikanga and safety … In reality, the two are intertwined.”, and, if so, how can she go ahead with repealing any aspect of 7AA?
statement: No, I don’t disagree, and I’ve never said that the two clash. What I have said is that the safety and wellbeing of children must be first and foremost when we’re making decisions about all children in care. Every child deserves to feel safe and loved.

explanation: Asked to admit the bill was a mistake, and if not, why not. She says plainly 'no, I stand by my decision' and supplies the why — redirecting Oranga Tamariki to its core purpose. Both limbs of the question are met. Whether the reason is persuasive is Rigor, not Forthrightness; the small deduction is for the hedge that precedes it ('I will consider the recommendations'), which softens the core before answering it.
question: Will she admit, now select committee has reported back, that it was a mistake to introduce a bill that would fully repeal section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, and, if not, why not?
statement: As I’ve said, I will consider the recommendations and take advice before making any decisions in the next step. But, no, I stand by my decision, because I’m proud of the fact that we are redirecting Oranga Tamariki back to their core purpose, which is the safety and wellbeing of children.

explanation: Both parts answered explicitly. He stands by the statement (quoting it in full), then flags the second limb and answers it in one word: 'In answer to the second part of the question, no.' Signposting which part is being answered is the opposite of a dodge.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “we had set a very clear plan that it will allow the books to return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2027/28”; if so, is she committed to reaching an OBEGAL surplus no matter the cost?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I stand by my full statement, which was, “we had set a very clear plan that it will allow the books to return to an OBEGAL surplus in 2027-28. If we had stuck to the spending plans of the last Government, that date would have been pushed out until 2031, an unacceptable outcome.” In answer to the second part of the question, no.

explanation: A closed question — is the Chief Economic Adviser correct that the implied speed and size of the decline is unprecedented? The answer never says correct or incorrect. It restates fiscal-target framing, concedes generally that forecasts have deteriorated, defers to the half-year update, and redirects to a speech the adviser is giving tomorrow. The concession about deterioration is the only contact with the question; the specific 'unprecedented' claim is left unaddressed.
question: Is the chief economist of Treasury correct when he said, in order to reach that goal, that the “implied speed and size of this decline is generally unprecedented in recent history in New Zealand.”?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, as the fiscal strategy report in Budget 2024 makes clear, the Government is not going to be a slave to a surplus target. It is correct that over the last few years each update to the economic forecast has involved a deterioration in the outlook, which then flows through into the fiscal forecast. The member will have to wait and see what happens in the half-year update. I’m also advised that the person that the member just quotes, the Chief Economic Adviser of Treasury, is giving a speech tomorrow which gives the background to some of the forecast revisions, and in particular the role of Treasury’s assumptions about underlying productivity trends. I know the member will be reading it.

explanation: Asked whether she plans to shift more services to user-pays. The answer engages head-on: not ruling it out, states the general principle that beneficiaries should pay, and names a live example (toll roads). It stops short of a plan-or-no-plan commitment, which is what keeps it off the top, but the question is squarely taken up rather than sidestepped.
question: Does she plan to shift more services to user-pays to help reach surplus?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, I’m not ruling out revenue measures like user-pays. The Government, as a general rule, believes that people who benefit from services should pay for them. For example, we have outlined a programme of work around toll roads, which the member will be well familiar with, all of which is designed to align the beneficiaries of infrastructure investment paying for it. That is one example of user-pays: toll roads.

explanation: Asked whether shifting health/education to the private sector would help reach surplus. He rejects the premise and states the Government runs public health and education services — which answers the intent behind the question but not the question asked (whether it would help). The subsequent contrast with the last Government is off-target, but I have not let that lower the score, as targeting is Focus.
question: Would shifting publicly run services like education or health to the private sector help her reach a surplus?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, I reject the assumption behind the member’s question. The Government has a public health service and a public education service. We are focused on driving better performance and delivery out of those two very significant items of State spending. The Ministry of Education is extremely focused on our education system actually (a) getting kids to attend school, and (b) making sure when they’re there they learn how to read and write, unlike the focus of the last Government. The man sitting next to me is very focused on delivering better value for money out of the health system.

explanation: A narrow request for a guarantee of no front-line reductions. No guarantee is given or refused — the answer describes the Government's 'driving focus' on shifting spend from back office to front line, which is a statement of intent, not the yes/no asked for. A blunt 'no, I won't guarantee that' would have scored high; talking past the ask does not.
question: Will she guarantee no reduction in front-line services to reach surplus?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, the driving focus of this Government’s fiscal reprioritisation so far has been to make sure that services flow not to the back office but to the front line.

explanation: Asked what the latest Quarterly Investment Report shows, and the answer states what it shows: 198 investments in delivery worth $85.7 billion, 176 in planning near $80 billion, plus the report's finding on incomplete agency data. Directly and completely responsive to the question posed.
question: What does the latest Quarterly Investment Report show?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, the latest QIR shows the significant investment activity across the pipeline. There’s 198 investments in delivery with a combined budget of $85.7 billion, and 176 investments in planning worth close to $80 billion. I do want to say, though, that the data also shows there are still issues with the quality and completeness of data reported by Government agencies. It’s not good enough. Good data is critical for good decision making. We are a Government that is focused on better long-term planning, more fulsome reporting, and stronger monitoring. We will be demanding, as a Government, better information from central government agencies to allow Cabinet to make better decisions.

explanation: Asked HOW quarterly investment reporting holds agencies to account. Bishop names the actual mechanism — chief executive attestations as a formal signal of whether agencies meet Cabinet rules — which is a real answer to 'how'. He then drifts into asset management commentary that is not accountability machinery, so the answer reaches the question and then wanders past it. Engaged, not fully carried through.
question: How will quarterly investment reporting hold agencies to account?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, today’s release includes chief executive attestations. These are a formal signal as to whether or not agencies’ investment practices meet Cabinet rules. It’s really important that we learn what Government agencies are following Cabinet rules and what Government agencies are not. One example, to pick up some data from the report, is asset management. It is true to say that agencies and, by extension, decision makers do not know enough about the condition or age of the Crown’s assets and plans to maintain them. This is something the Government is extremely focused on and doing a lot of work on. Asset management and asset maintenance have been something that has been underdone by central government for too long.

explanation: Asked how projects are tracking on time and on budget. Bishop gives both figures squarely: 83 percent on budget with $2b cost escalation, 87 percent to current time frames, 54 percent to original. Direct and complete on both halves of the question; the surrounding commentary about the previous Government is extra, not a substitute.
question: How are central government projects tracking for on-time and on-budget delivery?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Finance, we all want on-time and on-budget projects. The latest data shows that 83 percent of investments are on budget and there’s still $2 billion of cost escalation, and the September QIR shows that 87 percent of investments are tracking to their currently approved time frames, but only 54 percent are tracking to their original time lines. There’s a long history of grand pronouncements, including by the previous Government, where projects are meant to be delivered by a certain date but then exceed those. It is true to say that we need to do a better job across the Government around this. We have work under way to improve project cost and time lines. This is business as usual, good standard investment practice. We are fixing the foundations of our infrastructure investment system.

explanation: Two-part question: does she agree with her own 2023 quote, and if so why are school bus routes closing nationwide. She re-contextualises the quote as an Auckland public-transport remark rather than saying whether she agrees, and disposes of the second half by disclaiming ministerial responsibility for public buses — a scope narrowing that leaves the ministry-run school routes the question was actually about untouched. She engages the framing but never reaches either core.
question: Does she agree with National MP Erica Stanford, who, in May 2023, said, “The public and school bus systems are failing us. Every day buses are cancelled leaving people stranded. Kids are being left behind when trying to get to school”; if so, why are school bus routes to close up and down the country?
statement: As the member knows, I made that comment as the local member of Parliament for East Coast Bays in relation to a public meeting that I held in my electorate when a shortage of bus drivers was impacting Auckland Transport, both public bus and public school bus routes. The quotation is directly in relation to the provision of public transport for children. To the second part, Auckland Transport does not operate up and down the country; public buses and public school buses do—however, I do not have ministerial responsibility for those.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with a parent's complaint and, if not, why not. She never states agreement or disagreement, but she does supply the 'why not' content: policy unchanged, eligible children still get transport, and the three specific circumstances in which a route closes. The substance of the second limb is delivered even though the yes/no is skipped.
question: Does she agree with Claudia Heaps, a Hawke’s Bay mother, who said that “I can’t believe they would make something as basic as getting to school a challenge for kids, especially in the light of talking about improving attendance records.”; if not, why not?
statement: I would say to that mother and all parents across the motu that these decisions are operational. The policy has not changed and if a child is eligible for the ministry’s transport assistance, they will get it. The only time that a ministry-operated bus route will close is because a public bus has been established, the number of students has dropped below eight—where, then, we pay members of that family a conveyancing allowance—or if a route was merged with another route.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees that rural areas have no transport alternatives, and why rural routes are being allowed to close. She answers only by pointing back to her previous answer. That prior answer covers general closure criteria, so a little is incorporated by reference, but the rural-specific core — that the 'a public bus has been established' rationale cannot apply where no public transport exists — is not touched at all.
question: Does she agree with Rural Women New Zealand president Gill Naylor, who said, “In rural areas, there’s no public transport options, there’s no footpaths or cycleways, our roads are not safe for kids to be biking to school.”, and, if so, why is she allowing rural school bus routes to close?
statement: I would say to that person the same answer I gave to the person in the second question.

explanation: Asked what options exist for schools whose routes were cancelled and whose students are now stranded. She does name one concrete option — the conveyancing allowance where numbers drop below eight — which is a genuine answer for that case. But she restates the closure reasons instead of addressing the other scenarios, and answers for families rather than for the schools asked about. Half the question is reached.
question: What options are there for schools who have had their school bus routes cancelled and now have students stranded at home and unable to learn?
statement: As I said in my second question, if a route is stopped it is for those reasons, and what we do when the numbers of children drop below eight is we pay families a conveyancing allowance to help them get their children to school.

explanation: Asked why she is taking no steps to protect rural school bus routes. She contests the premise directly and names the step: a work programme instigated in February to make bus services fair and equitable across the country. That is a squarely responsive answer. The closing jab at the questioner's own record is a Civility and Focus matter and does not displace the answer already given.
question: Why is the Minister not taking any steps to protect rural school bus routes and is allowing them to be cancelled on her watch?
statement: We are taking responsibility and that’s why in February of this year I’ve instigated a work programme to make sure that bus services for eligible students are fair and equitable across the country, and that work programme is under way. I would also like to point out that the member who asked the question had six years to sort it out and did nothing.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made. Seymour names the announcement — consultation opening on the regulatory standards bill — with its four components and the closing date. A friendly question, but eligibility turns on whether a real question got a real answer, and it did: direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has he made?
statement: With great pleasure I’d like to inform the House that yesterday I announced the next steps in the Government’s plan to improve the quality of regulation by opening consultation on the proposed regulatory standards bill. To lift productivity and wages, the Government’s agreement is to include a commitment to pass the regulatory standards bill. This bill has four components: a set of principles for responsible regulation, a mechanism to ensure regulations are consistent with the principles, justified departure from the principles, and a recourse to enable New Zealanders to seek an independent assessment when a regulation does not meet the principles and statutory powers for the ministry. Consultation on the proposed regulatory standards bill is open until Monday, 13 January 2025.

explanation: Asked what the principles of responsible regulation are. He gives all three categories — design and content of legislation, good lawmaking, regulatory stewardship — each with an illustration. The question asked for the principles and the principles were supplied.
question: What are the principles of responsible regulation?
statement: The principles fall into three categories. The first is the principle relating to the design and content of legislation, such as the importance of the rule of law and that fair compensation should be paid for the taking or impairment of private property. Second is the principle of good lawmaking, such as ensuring regulation should produce benefits that exceed the cost of imposing that regulation. The third is the principle relating to regulatory stewardship, such as eliminating regulatory burden and compliance costs and ensuring that regulatory systems are fit for purpose.

explanation: Asked how the bill will improve the quality of new regulations. He answers the causal question directly: the bill compels regulators to consider the principles and publicly justify departures, raising the political cost of bad lawmaking. He even volunteers that nothing in the bill compels compliance, which engages the question rather than evading it.
question: How will the regulatory standards bill improve the quality of new regulations?
statement: The regulatory standards bill is fundamentally an exercise in transparency. There’s nothing in the bill that requires the regulator to follow the principles of regulation. However, it does require regulators to consider the principles and publicly justify why they shouldn’t apply to any particular rule that they’re imposing upon New Zealanders. If we raise the political cost of making bad laws by allowing New Zealanders to hold politicians and regulators accountable, the outcome will be better lawmaking, higher productivity, and better wages for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what new tools Police will have from tomorrow. Mitchell lists them: the patch and insignia ban from midnight, non-consorting orders, and dispersal notices. Direct, complete, and confined to what was asked.
question: What new tools will Police have from tomorrow to crack down on gangs?
statement: At midnight tonight, it will be illegal to wear or display gang patches and insignia in public in New Zealand. Police will also be able to issue gang members with non-consorting orders and issue dispersal notices. The coalition Government promised a gang crackdown; tomorrow, that will be in full force.

explanation: Asked what action the Government is taking to restore Canadian dairy access. McClay names the action: a further formal step compelling Canada to meet and either change or pay compensation, with tariff sanctions reserved. The background recital is padding, but the actual action asked for is stated.
question: What action is the Government taking to restore Canadian dairy access?
statement: Well, Canada continues to fail to meet its obligations to New Zealand under the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership in respect of dairy exports to Canada. Last year, under the previous Government, New Zealand started a formal dispute procedure under this agreement with Canada, and we won a panel ruling in our favour. Unfortunately, Canada continues to not comply with their obligations, and, as a result, New Zealand dairy farmers are missing out on market access that was negotiated and granted under that trade agreement. This is a matter of principle. New Zealand takes its obligations seriously and we expect others to also do so, and we will stand up for New Zealand farmers and exporters. We’ve therefore taken further action which forces Canada to meet with us formally to make changes to allow exports or to pay New Zealand compensation for the trade harm they are causing. The ball is now squarely in Canada’s court. The New Zealand Government reserves the right to take any action we deem appropriate, including imposing tariff sanctions on Canadian exports to New Zealand. I say the time is running out for Canada to honour their obligations to New Zealand farmers.

explanation: A yes/no standing-by question. Answered 'Yes' in the first word; the law-and-order material that follows is surplus but the question itself is squarely and completely engaged.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to restore law and order. A year ago, Kiwis demanded fresh leadership and a new approach to a major rise in violent and retail crime that occurred in recent years. Since then, we’ve made big changes and we’re already seeing results. Foot patrols have increased 30 percent, ram raids are down 60 percent, serious assaults have dropped 3 percent, and aggravated robberies are down 11 percent. There are more changes coming: tough new gang laws take effect tonight and stronger sentencing is on the way. There’s always more to do, but the signs suggest that restoring law and order means that we’re getting New Zealand back on track.

explanation: Asked for a definition of tino rangatiratanga. The answer talks only about the bill's legislative fate and never attempts a definition — a narrow, specific question completely sidestepped.
question: Can he define what tino rangatiratanga means, given his Government has introduced a bill to redefine tino rangatiratanga?
statement: Well, as I’ve said, the bill is being introduced at first reading, it won’t be supported at second reading, and therefore it won’t become law.

explanation: Same definition question, put again. This time a definition is given ('unqualified exercise over land and taonga'). Terse, and whether it is a good definition is a Veracity/Specificity matter — as an answer it lands directly on the question.
question: Can he define what tino rangatiratanga means?
statement: Unqualified exercise over land and taonga.

explanation: Asked why he did not welcome the hikoi to Parliament. He gestures at a reason — the organisers were affiliated with Te Pati Maori — but then moves to accountability in the House, his message on the bill, and his engagement with Maori generally. It brushes the question without squarely answering why he did not appear.
question: The Prime Minister was respectfully welcomed at marae across all the country, so why couldn’t he offer Māori the same respect when welcoming them to Parliament yesterday?
statement: Well, as I said yesterday, many of the organisers were affiliated with that member’s party, Te Pāti Māori. You can hold me to account on this Parliament many days in any given week. My message to the hīkoi was very straightforward, which is the bill is being supported at first reading but not beyond that and won’t become law. And the last thing, as I say, is I engage with Māori up and down the country on a range of issues.

explanation: A clarifying yes/no: will he never meet Te Pati Maori members or affiliates? Answered 'No, I'm not saying that' — direct and complete, with a brief supporting fact.
question: For clarity, is the Prime Minister saying that any members of Te Pāti Māori or members of the public who affiliate to Te Pāti Māori will never be met with by the Prime Minister?
statement: No, I’m not saying that. We sent a delegation out from the National Party that represented our position, received the hīkoi here at Parliament—it was good.

explanation: Asked how he will repair damage to the Crown-Maori relationship after missing the hikoi. He answers a reframed question — how he builds the relationship generally (incomes, housing, health, education) — never engaging the specific damage or the absence, and closes by attacking the questioner. Partial engagement at best.
question: How will he reconcile the damage he has done to the Crown’s relationship with Māori after not showing up to the largest hīkoi in the history of New Zealand?
statement: Well, what I’d say is that the way that we build a stronger relationship with Māori and the Crown is by focusing on things that matter most to Māori. And what matters most to them is how they lift their incomes, how they secure better housing, how they get timely, quality access to healthcare, how they improve educational outcomes. Those are the things that matter to Māori and to non-Māori, and that’s what this Government is doing. And, you know, frankly, I haven’t heard anything from that member talking about why only 12 percent of Māori students are at the standard they need to be at going into high school. That kind of matters.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he had made on the National Infrastructure Plan. He names the announcement (the Commission's discussion document) and lists its four components. Directly responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made on the National Infrastructure Plan?
statement: Earlier this month, I welcomed the release of the Infrastructure Commission’s discussion document on the National Infrastructure Plan. It gives everyone an opportunity, including Government agencies, local government, private sector, iwi, and NGOs, to have their say on what the plan should include. It’s got four components: an infrastructure needs assessment, a strengthened national infrastructure pipeline, an infrastructure priorities programme, and recommendations for priority system reforms.

explanation: Asked the role of the needs assessment within the plan. He states its role: assessing needs over five to 30 years and setting a benchmark against which the infrastructure deficit is measured. On point.
question: What is the role of the needs assessment as part of the National Infrastructure Plan?
statement: I think the country broadly agrees that we need to do a better job of long-term planning, particularly over the near- and long-term horizon. So the infrastructure needs assessment is about looking at our needs over the next five to 30 years and looking at demand drivers, including population growth, renewals, inflation, resilience, and increasing living standards. The needs analysis will set a benchmark so that we can look at what we have against that need and then what we need to do to close that infrastructure deficit over the long term.

explanation: Asked how the infrastructure priorities programme works. He describes the mechanism — open submission via the Commission website, independent expert assessment, then referral to Government decision makers. The question's core is answered.
question: How does the infrastructure priorities programme work?
statement: We’re picking up some ideas that have been used overseas, most notably in parts of Australia where independent agencies take a structured, independent assessment of priority problems and projects. I want the independent experts at the commission to give us their best estimates and assessments of what projects are worth doing. Anyone can submit a proposal through the Infrastructure Commission website into the Infrastructure Priorities Programme—the IPP—and then that will go to the Government, and it will be, ultimately, over to the decision makers to make investment decisions. But we need to be well informed by good data and good evidence around that.

explanation: Asked for next steps. He lists them in sequence: workshops, feedback close, drafting, formal consultation next year, then a parliamentary debate. Squarely answered.
question: So what are the next steps for the National Infrastructure Plan?
statement: The commission’s been running plan workshops around the country with experts, and after the feedback closes on the discussion document towards the end of this next month, the commission will work on drafting a plan. There will be formal public consultation next year. It is something that I would like to see the whole of Parliament get behind and so I’m encouraging all political parties to meet with the Infrastructure Commission to be briefed on the plan. I know some political parties have taken up that opportunity already and I really welcome that and encourage them to do that. And then it is the Government’s intention to hold a debate in Parliament on the plan once it’s presented to the Government later next year.

explanation: A yes/no standing-by question, answered 'Yes, with the usual caveats.' The caveat is a mild hedge on completeness, but the question is answered directly in a single line.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, with the usual caveats.

explanation: Asked how non-consorting orders help police fight organised crime. Answer states the mechanism directly — court-issued orders against known gang offenders preventing them communicating/consorting — and what it enables. Squarely on the question.
question: How will non-consorting orders help police fight organised crime?
statement: Non-consorting orders are able to be issued by the court against known gang offenders, preventing them from communicating and consorting with each other to commit violent and organised crime. These have proved very effective in other jurisdictions at preventing the flow of illegal activity and will enable police to dismantle gangs from the inside.

explanation: Asked what benefit dispersal notices have for the public. Answer names the benefit directly: police can disperse gang gatherings and avert public disruption, with the seven-day mechanism. Directly responsive.
question: What benefit will dispersal notices have for the public?
statement: Police will be able to issue a dispersal notice to any known gang offenders congregating in a public place. This will mean that police can disperse gang gatherings and avert disruption to the public before it happens, by telling members to go home and not come back for seven days.

explanation: Asked whether police are ready to enforce the new laws. "Yes, they are." — one word, complete, no dodge. Brevity is not evasion.
question: Are police ready to enforce the new laws?
statement: Yes, they are.

explanation: Asked whether he is confident the Human Rights Commission is politically independent, and why. Answers "Yes" and gives the why (s19 of the Human Rights Act requires independence). Both halves engaged; the reason is thin but that is a Specificity matter, not evasion.
question: Is he confident that the Human Rights Commission is politically independent; if so, why?
statement: Yes. As the member will know, section 19 of the Human Rights Act 1993 requires the Human Rights Commission to act independently in performing its statutory functions and duties.

explanation: Asked whether an ACT-recommended nomination is consistent with the Paris principles duty of independence. Answers "Yes, perfectly" and gives his reasoning — anyone may nominate, Cabinet decides. Direct yes plus grounds; whether the reasoning holds up is Rigor, not this.
question: Does the Minister consider that it is consistent with the duty to ensure the independence of the commission under the 1993 United Nations Paris principles, that the appointee is the Chief Human Rights Commissioner, Dr Stephen Rainbow, who was recommended to him for appointment by the ACT Party?
statement: Yes, perfectly. Everybody in this country’s free to nominate somebody and then Cabinet makes the decision about that.

explanation: Asked whether he acted consistently with the independence duty given the panel found Rainbow not appointable. Answers "Yes" and explains the divergence — panel recommendations taken up in one case, Cabinet sought a different skill set for chief commissioner. The closing jab at the previous Government is off-point but the core was reached first.
question: Does the Minister consider that he acted consistent with the duty to maintain the independence of the commission, as required by the Paris principles, when Dr Stephen Rainbow was recommended for appointment by the Minister, despite the fact that an expert interview panel found that he did not have the skills and qualifications to be a viable appointment and did not consider him appointable?
statement: Yes. We’ve been over this before. The independent panel are very senior legal people who I respect greatly. They made some recommendations, and in one case we took up that recommendation with Gail Pacheco. In terms of the chief commissioner, ultimately Cabinet made the decision that they were looking for a slightly different set of skills, and in particular a focus on communicating effectively in terms of human rights. So we went with Dr Rainbow. And I’m proud to say I’ve got every confidence that he’ll do a better job than appointments from the previous Government.

explanation: Asked what actions he took after Rainbow was told he wasn't preferred that led to Rainbow re-entering the process. Answer disputes the premise (he didn't inform Rainbow; any such notification was premature) but never states what actions he took. Denying a premise is genuine engagement, so not a zero, but the question's core — his actions — goes unanswered.
question: What actions did the Minister take after Dr Stephen Rainbow was informed that he wasn’t a preferred candidate for the Chief Human Rights Commissioner role that led to Dr Rainbow re-entering the selection process?
statement: Well, I certainly didn’t inform Mr Rainbow about that. And if he was informed by anybody, they were obviously premature, because no decision had been made until the decision to appoint Dr Stephen Rainbow.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: did he take any action to ensure Rainbow re-entered the selection process. He recasts "the action I took" as merely continuing the process and recommending to Cabinet, never answering yes or no to the specific action asked about, then pivots to the three appointments and the vacant Race Relations role. Touches the question, then leaves it.
question: Did the Minister take any action to ensure that Stephen Rainbow re-entered the selection process after he’d been told he wasn’t the successful candidate?
statement: Well, the action that I took was to continue the process and to develop a recommendation to Cabinet to appoint a person for the Chief Human Rights Commissioner. The member may go deeper and deeper into the weeds on this; the reality is that we’ve made three excellent appointments to the Human Rights Commission. The Race Relations Commissioner had been empty for more than a year after the resignation of Meng Foon—remember Meng Foon? We’re very confident that those three appointments are going to give some real strength to the commission and they will carry on in a politically independent way to safeguard and stand up for human rights in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he is confident the commission will retain its A accreditation. "Yes, I am quite confident" — direct answer to the question asked. The Geneva/Russia material that follows is padding and doesn't bear on accreditation, but the question itself was answered up front.
question: Is the Minister confident that the commission will retain its A accreditation by the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions under the Paris principles, given that Dr Rainbow was nominated by a governing political party, he was put on a shortlist by the Minister against advice, and his appointment was made despite an independent panel saying he was not a viable appointment?
statement: Yes, I am quite confident. We went to stand up and defend our human rights in Geneva in April this year. We did face some criticism on our human rights record from Russia, but I’m confident that we’ll be able to continue to have a very high regard in the international sector.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken to grow the economy and lift farm-gate returns. Answer names the actions — a programme to resolve non-tariff barriers, 16 resolved this year covering $733m of exports. It is a friendly question answered on its own terms, which scores the same as any other.
question: What actions has the Government taken to grow New Zealand’s economy and increase farm-gate returns for farmers and growers?
statement: The Government is relentlessly focused on reducing trade barriers, unlocking new markets, and supporting Kiwi businesses to grow. A big part of this is reducing non-tariff and technical barriers (NTBs) to trade, which we estimate affect $9.8 billion worth of New Zealand exports each year, with the primary sector facing the greatest impact. This is why we have started a programme to resolve trade barriers and increase farm-gate returns for farmers and growers. This year, the Government has successfully resolved 16 barriers to trade, affecting $733 million worth of exports. This directly supports our ambitious target of doubling exports by value in 10 years; and with one in four jobs tied to trade, it returns more money to the back pocket for thousands of New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what actions support primary exports and reduce other barriers. Answer enumerates them one by one — EU wine/spirits, Mexico medical devices, Indonesia onions, India logs, Korea blueberries, China deer velvet, the EU deforestation reprieve. Squarely responsive.
question: What actions has the Government taken to support primary exports and reduce other barriers?
statement: Well, we’re returning more value to the primary producers and other exporters. Since June, we’ve reduced regulatory burdens on wine and spirits exports to the EU; resolved barriers on medical device exports to Mexico; restored onion exports to Indonesia, New Zealand onions’ largest market; restored access for up to $250 million worth of log exports to India; extended tariff-free access for New Zealand digital exporters to all World Trade Organization members; resolved compliance measures to secure blueberry access to Korea; restored $88 million worth of frozen deer velvet exports to China; and achieved a 12-month reprieve for costly EU deforestation regulations, saving farmers and exporters up to $200 million. Reducing these barriers is part of the Government’s plan to grow the economy, to lift incomes for all Kiwis, and to create jobs.

explanation: Asked what additional actions the Government is taking on trade barriers. Answer lists the forward targets — EU deforestation exemption, Australian structural timber, China cosmetics, Canadian dairy. Opens with an export-total statistic that isn't asked for, but then reaches the question.
question: What additional actions are the Government taking to address trade barriers?
statement: New Zealand exported $98.2 billion worth of goods and services this year to June 2024. Over the next 12 months, we will continue to focus on targeting over $900 million worth of NTBs, including seeking a permanent exemption to EU deforestation regulations, removing a ban on structural timber exports to Australia, restrictions on cosmetic exports to China, and we’ll continue to take action against Canada dairy restrictions. We’re focused on removing barriers to trade and making it easier for farmers and growers to supply high-quality, safe food to the world.

explanation: Asked which of three named colleagues is correct about Treaty principles. The reply is a Latin quip ("res ipsa loquitur") that names none of them and takes no position — the question is never engaged.
question: Who is correct: David Seymour, who thinks Treaty principles should be unilaterally rewritten by the Crown; Winston Peters, who thinks they don’t even exist; or Christopher Luxon, who thinks they are “Partnership, protection, and other things”?
statement: That’s a case of what I might call “res ipsa loquitur”—the thing speaks for itself.

explanation: Two-part question: did Jones push for ring-net fishing over Potaka's objection, and if not, why was he overruled. Most of the reply rebuts the questioner's framing of Potaka's standing, but the closing line — "by a process of consultation, they came to a conclusion together" — does glance at the substance by implying no override occurred. It never confirms or denies the push, so the core is only brushed.
question: Did Shane Jones push to allow commercial ring-net fishing in the Hauraki Gulf marine protection bill, overriding conservation Minister Tama Potaka’s push to protect that area, reflect Potaka’s self-described lowly position in the food chain; if not, why was he overruled?
statement: Well, the difference between some political parties and ones on this side of the House is that we treat every member as an equal. We don’t think we’re superior. So to describe Minister Potaka that way I think is so unmeritorious of that usually generous member over there. The second thing is: by a process of consultation, they came to a conclusion together.

explanation: Two-part question: agreement with the Costello quote, and concern at the 16,000 rise in daily smokers. The agreement half is ignored entirely, but the concern half is squarely engaged — he disputes the year-on-year reading, gives trend figures, and makes clear he is not concerned. Partial: one core answered, one dropped, plus a stretch of credit-claiming. Detail and truthfulness were held out of this score.
question: Does he agree with Casey Costello that “We know we want to deliver. We need some clear, logical conversations about what we’re trying to achieve, which is smoke-free.”; if so, is he concerned that the number of daily smokers has risen by 16,000 people year on year, the first such jump in recent history?
statement: We are so pleased that member asked that question. First of all, the results are a retentive survey looking at the trend, rather than year on year. Over the last five years, the Māori smoking rate has halved, while smoking rates are lowest in our young people, signalling a generational shift away from cigarettes. The smoking rate for 18- to 24-year-olds is now down to 4.2 percent, for 15- and 17-year-olds it is down now to less than 1 percent, and daily smoking rates have declined amongst all people. But here’s the point: we’re in the first three in the world, and we got there with legislation—not Labour’s, but designed by New Zealand First. That’s why it’s a five-year survey. Every change that Labour made between 2020 and 2023 was never coming into effect until 2027, so they can take no credit whatsoever. New Zealand First—with Action on Smoking and Health, I might add—can take all the credit.

explanation: Asked whether he expects Peters to engage with Willis, or will go over her head again. The "over the head" clause is denied directly ("no one goes over their head"), which addresses half the question; the expectation of engagement in the Budget process is never stated, and the reply drifts into self-praise about "bespoke wisdom".
question: Does he expect Winston Peters to engage with Nicola Willis during the next Budget process, or will the foreign affairs Minister defy convention and go over the finance Minister’s head once again?
statement: Again, that’ll be news to Nicola Willis because no one goes over their head, and everyone on this side of the House knows that. The second thing is that when you are presenting policy and plans that are bespoke wisdom, it usually is quite persuasive.

explanation: Asked WHY non-rail-enabled ferries are being considered given the coalition agreement and the Deputy PM's statement. The reply recites a 2017-20 rail record and defers to a decision due before 11 December — no reason is given. The answer is cut off mid-sentence, but nothing in what exists reaches the question.
question: Why is he considering non - rail-enabled ferries when the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement says they must “facilitate the development and efficiency of ports and strengthen international supply networks.”, and his Deputy Prime Minister has stated “Rail is vital national infrastructure”?
statement: Again, I’m very grateful for that question, because, first of all, it’s based on some experience in rail, where we turned it around between ’17 and ’20, and we saved rail in this country. The second thing is that there’s decision that’s going to be made by this Government before 11 December—

explanation: Asked what the point of the Regional Infrastructure Fund is. After an economic-inheritance preamble, he restates and answers the question outright: the purpose is to invest seriously in the provinces. The "action man" material is padding, but the core was reached. Vagueness about which communities is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: What is the point of Shane Jones’ Regional Infrastructure Fund when communities are crumbling due to the collapse of industries, like timber mills and meat works?
statement: The reality is that we inherited a seriously failing economy, much worse than many people thought, and a power system that was the most costly in the world. All these things are staggering. I understand what the member’s saying, but what is the purpose of Shane Jones’ mission? It is to do what so many Governments have not done, and that is to invest seriously in the provinces and return us to where the country once was: in the top three in the world. Mr Jones is quite different from a lot of people in this Parliament; he’s an action man. Some talk and some act. Mr Jones is an action man. If you don’t know that, go down to Ōpōtiki, go down to Hawke’s Bay—[Interruption]
