explanation: Asked what announcements he has made about regional summits; he states he has announced 15 nationwide summits and describes the associated fund allocations. Direct and complete on the thing asked.
question: What announcements has he made about regional summits?
statement: It is best that this answer is heard in silence. I have announced a series of 15 nationwide summits, where the audiences have applauded the fact that, at long last, after three years of absence, a regional development Minister willing to be bold and make allocative decisions has arrived. Over 150 applications for the Regional Infrastructure Fund have been received, and in those regions, work is already taking place on fixing up the neglected flood management systems as a consequence of the Budget allocation of $100 million initially, up possibly to $200 million. That is what the regional summits reflect.

explanation: Asked what he can report on the Southland summit; he reports who was met, what was announced, and what was visited. The closing pun does not displace an answer that was already given.
question: What can he report regarding last week’s Southland regional summit?
statement: Last Thursday, sadly for the dignity of the House, I was absent. We engaged with Ngāi Tahu and the civic leadership of Southland Murihiku. We shared the occasion with Ngāi Tahu, where the many thousands of hectares of aquaculture space, as a consequence of the historic aquaculture settlement, was announced. We also visited a host of developments, and I can say that in Bluff we saw pāua being grown, and it was a day in Murihiku where I celebrated whitebait. Yet, in other parts of the country, white were being baited.

explanation: Asked what he planned to discuss at the Taranaki summit; he lists ironsand mining, vanadium and other minerals, and the oil and gas ban repeal. Squarely responsive.
question: What did he plan to discuss at the Taranaki regional summit tomorrow?
statement: I’m looking forward to going to Taranaki, as we have already allocated a $5.8 million grant at historic site Parihaka. But I am also proud we’re going to Taranaki, because I’m going to extol the virtues of ironsand mining. I’m going to remind the audience that vanadium and other minerals are essential for the climate change journey. Unlike other MPs, we’re prepared to make the hard trade-off decisions. I’m also going to share with the Taranaki audience that soon the oil and gas ban, which destroyed the oil and gas industry, by the last Government will pass through Parliament.

explanation: Asked why he thinks visiting the regions matters; he gives a reason — demonstrating willingness to co-invest and giving regions confidence their solutions will not be squashed by Wellington. The parting jab at the Opposition is a Civility/Focus issue and does not reduce engagement with the question.
question: Why does the Minister think it is important to visit the regions and hold these summits?
statement: So much of politics is about hope. Underlying these regional summits and the existence of the pūtea—$1.2 billion—is a demonstration on the part of our Government that we are willing to co-invest. We believe in public-private collaborative efforts, and from time to time, there will be, on the rare occasion, projects that do require a modest level of grant funding. But people have to have confidence that solutions that are discovered in the regions won’t be squashed by Wellington advisers or timid politicians, far too many of whom sit on the other side of the House.

explanation: Asked what recent reports he had seen about Police. He names two specific reports he saw (the Hastings insignia enforcement, the Chambers appointment). Squarely responsive to an open question; the promotional framing is Focus, not Forthrightness.
question: What recent reports has he seen about Police?
statement: This morning, I saw reports that in Hastings, only three minutes into the insignia ban coming into effect, police took enforcement action against a gang member for displaying gang insignia on the dashboard of his car. I’ve also seen extensive coverage of the recent announcement of Richard Chambers as the incoming Commissioner of Police. Mr Chambers will be an outstanding leader for our police and I look forward to working closely with him to continue to restore law and order.

explanation: Asked for further examples of the patch ban in effect. He supplies two further examples (Wairoa, Papakura) plus a compliance characterisation. Directly and completely answers what was asked.
question: Has there been any further examples of the patch ban in effect?
statement: Apart from the enforcement action at 2.03 this morning, I’m advised that there has been a high level of compliance with the ban. I’m told that this morning a gang member was arrested in Wairoa for wearing gang insignia to the supermarket and a patched gang member was arrested standing on the street in Papakura. Both patches have been seized.

explanation: Asked what feedback he had seen from officers. He states the feedback: they are happy to have the new powers. Thin and unsourced, but thinness is Specificity — the question was engaged head-on.
question: What feedback has he seen from police officers about the new laws?
statement: Feedback from police officers around the country is that they’re happy to have new powers that enhance their ability to police organised criminal groups.

explanation: Asked what the new commissioner said about enforcing the ban. He relays what the commissioner said. Responsive; whether the relay is accurate is Veracity.
question: What has the new commissioner said about enforcing the gang patch ban?
statement: The commissioner said that much has been made of Police’s response, but it is important to acknowledge that the gangs have a question to answer: what choices are they going to make? Because if they comply with the new law, then they will not feel the full force of the law.

explanation: Asked what advice he gave the Minister of Conservation. He disclaims responsibility for the bill, declares himself a champion of the fishing industry, and says consultation happens 'from time to time' and Cabinet discussions are 'tapu'. Never says what advice he gave, nor plainly refuses to say — a clean 'I won't disclose that' would have scored high, but this only gestures at confidentiality after two pivots.
question: What advice did he provide to the Minister of Conservation about the decision to allow specific companies to commercially fish in high protection areas?
statement: Yes, well, obviously, I’m not responsible for the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill. However, I am a champion of the fishing industry. Consultation, from time to time, does take place between Ministers, but, of course, decisions are made by Cabinet, and those discussions are tapu.

explanation: Narrow factual question: did he tell the Minister about Leigh Fisheries? Answer is an unambiguous no ('At no time have I shared the name of that company'). Direct and complete.
question: Did he advise the Minister of Conservation that one of the largest quota owners of kahawai, trevally, and mullet—the stocks targeted with this decision—is Leigh Fisheries, a wholly owned subsidiary of Foodstuffs (NZ), who sells to supermarkets throughout the whole upper North Island?
statement: At no time have I shared the name of that company with that Minister.

explanation: Asked what assurances he can give on affordable prices in South Auckland. He effectively concedes he can give none ('the price of fish is slightly beyond my grasp') and offers an expectation that value will fall. That engages the assurance question but substitutes a forecast for it, and the South Auckland/Ponsonby core of the question goes untouched.
question: What assurances can the Minister give that the fish caught by commercial operators in these high protection areas will actually be sold at affordable prices to communities in South Auckland, as promised by the Minister of Conservation, and not, for example, at Ponsonby New World?
statement: Well, obviously, the price of fish is slightly beyond my grasp. However, as a consequence of quota allocation decisions, not the least of which is a massive expansion of the catchable amount of snapper in New Zealand, I imagine that the value of fish is going to shrink.

explanation: Asked if he is confident Cabinet colleagues were fully informed. Opens with 'Yes' and then addresses the substance by minimising the changes as tiny refinements. The closing 'my party didn't campaign on it' is a pivot, but the question was answered before it.
question: Is he confident that his Cabinet colleagues, including the Prime Minister, were fully informed in making the decision to allow commercial fishing in the high protection areas despite official advice based on Fisheries New Zealand data clearly stating that the commercial operators could still catch fish in the over 90 percent of the Gulf outside of the high protection areas with “minimal impact on their businesses”?
statement: Yes, these harmless refinements that were introduced at the point of which the Cabinet discussions process was taking place, as you’ve referred to, are like a beauty spot: they are so small. The vast majority of the Tīkapa Moana reserve areas remain as they were originally introduced. But I would say to the member: that piece of proposed legislation was not something that my party campaigned on.

explanation: Asked whether it is fair that late Seafood NZ changes overrode a decade-long collaborative process and a unanimous select committee. He never addresses fairness or the process at all, restating the 'vast majority remains protected' line and the kaimoana benefit. A pointed question met with prepared talking points.
question: Does he think it’s fair for community, hapū, and industry to go through more than a decade-long collaborative process to then have the Minister allow late changes by Seafood New Zealand to trump community and the unanimous select committee recommendations that supported the bill?
statement: As I’ve said, the vast majority of the Tīkapa Moana protected areas are going to be made available for those who wish to recreate and not see fishing there. Tiny, beauty, star, little infinitesimal points will enable four or five additional fishers to provide kaimoana during the months of winter, and it will be thoroughly appreciated by working-class families in “Strugglers’ Gully” that they will have access to affordable kaimoana.

explanation: Asked for his message to New Zealanders given the official advice quoted. He gives no message; he disputes that officials used that language. Contesting the premise is some engagement — it responds to the advice half — but the question asked was left unanswered.
question: What is his message to New Zealanders who love the Gulf and want to see its health and mauri restored when they hear the official advice that allowing the continuation of commercial fishing in their new marine protected areas is “incompatible with the purpose”, will “undermine biodiversity outcomes”, and “create significant equity issues.”?
statement: There is too much hyperbole in that rendition of official advice. I couldn’t imagine officials would use such imaginative and wild language.

explanation: A stand-by-statement question answered 'Yes, I do'. Complete. The attack on the previous Government that follows is Focus/Civility and does not reduce forthrightness.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “We’ve seen our police officers having to deal with more and more firearms related incidents, and we’ve got to do something about that. And we can’t be a country that just accepts that’s the way it’s going to be”?
statement: Yes, I do, because the previous Government accepted an increase in gang-related violence, and this Government doesn’t.

explanation: Asked if he is concerned about the Police Association claim that police cannot inspect ranges, and if not, why not. He answers the 'why not' directly by denying the factual premise: police will be able to inspect and access gun ranges. He never uses the word 'concerned', so it is a shade short of complete, but the core was met, not dodged. Whether the denial is correct is Veracity.
question: Is he concerned that the Police Association has stated publicly that they are aware of patched gang members using shooting ranges, and that police won’t be able to control that or inspect the ranges under the new arms amendment bill; if not, why not?
statement: Police will be able to inspect and have access to gun ranges.

explanation: Asked how he reconciles his earlier statements with the 9 September police email. He gives a direct reconciliation — at the time of the question, that was the advice he had. Terse and self-serving, but it engages the exact contradiction put to him rather than pivoting away. Marked below 1.0 because it addresses only the 'how do you reconcile' half and leaves the specific email unremarked.
question: How does he reconcile telling the House on two separate occasions that gang members were not practising on gun ranges when a police email on 9 September 2024 released under the Official Information Act states, “I’ve included images of those gang members shooting .50 calibre in the South Island, one being overseen by a senior NZ pistol shooter.”?
statement: Because at the time the question was asked, that’s the advice that I had.

explanation: The question is narrow and evidentiary: the information was in May and June briefings and a 9 September email, so why did he not have it on 18 September, 19 September and 7 November? The reply restates the general principle that he answers with the information he has at the time, which is the same line as before and does not engage the claim that the information had already been given to him. The specific dates are never touched. Partial credit only because it amounts to an implicit denial rather than a change of subject.
question: Why was the information that was captured in briefings to him in both May and June in an email from police on September 9 provided to him before he answered the questions in the House on 18 September, 19 September, and again on 7 November; how does he explain not having that information when it was provided to him in briefings on those occasions?
statement: When the member asks me a question in the House, I’ll respond with the information I’ve had at the time. It’s very simple.

explanation: Asked why he failed to incorporate police advice into Cabinet decisions. He answers by rejecting the premise and describing what he did — police advised, he forwarded recommendations, Cabinet decided. That squarely addresses whether he failed to incorporate the advice. Short of full marks because the 'why' about the outcome is closed off with 'that's the end of it' rather than answered.
question: Why did he fail to incorporate police advice into Cabinet decisions about the arms amendment bill, despite police intelligence that included images of gang members shooting .50 calibre in the South Island, overseen by a senior New Zealand pistol shooter?
statement: Police did provide advice, and I forwarded my recommendations to Cabinet. Cabinet’s made a decision and that’s the end of it.

explanation: Two parts: does he expect the House to believe he was unaware of the police intelligence, and what is the point of banning patches while ignoring gang shooting practice. He answers only the second, and only as a set-piece justification of the patch ban; the awareness question — the substantive one — goes untouched. Credit is for engaging the rhetorical half at all, not for reaching the core.
question: Does he seriously expect the House to believe that while police disclose they held intelligence of gangs using gun ranges, that he was not made aware of this at the time when his Government was taking decisions to weaken gun club regulations, and what is the point of banning gang patches when he is turning a blind eye to them practising their shooting skills on gun ranges?
statement: We’re banning gang patches because for a gang member to have a gang patch, they have to have shown they have a propensity to commit violent crime. So there is a trail of tears and victims sitting behind each one of those gang patches. They’re designed to intimidate the communities that they operate in, and that’s why we ban them.

explanation: A friendly question with a matching answer: he names the announcement made with Minister Potaka, the awareness campaign, and who it targets. The question asked what he had announced and he says what he announced.
question: What recent announcements has he made about preparing for avian influenza?
statement: The H5N1 strain of avian influenza, or bird flu, has been spreading around the world since 2020. Although we’ve never had a case and our isolation has protected us so far, we won’t be able to rely on that for ever. This particular strain is well adapted to spread into wildlife. The primary risk for New Zealand is from migrating birds; they come from other parts of the world. It is not feasible to protect our border against incursion through this pathway, so we must be prepared. Last week, Minister Potaka and I announced the start of an awareness campaign that encourages New Zealanders to take steps to be ready for bird flu. We are focusing on the thousands of New Zealanders that are owners of backyard chickens and pet birds, as well as lifestyle-block owners and poultry farms.

explanation: Asked what poultry farmers can do; the answer is a list of things poultry farmers can do — enclosures, distance from waterways, feed and water security, staff hygiene, wild bird control. Directly and completely on the question asked.
question: What can poultry farmers do to prepare for avian influenza?
statement: The best way to keep chickens safe is to take steps to reduce the risk of contact with infected birds or contaminated material. Work on that should start now before we get the bird flu in New Zealand. Poultry farmers should be taking steps to enhance on-farm biosecurity such as investing in secure enclosures to keep birds away from wildlife and from open waterways where wild birds tend to gather. Good on-farm biosecurity and animal husbandry practices like good maintenance, security of feed and water supplies, staff hygiene, and wild bird control have the potential to make a big difference in avoiding infection and limiting spread. The message is simple: don’t wait. Make the effort now and it will pay off if we have to respond to a bird flu incursion.

explanation: Asked how the Government is supporting the industry to prepare; he describes MPI's work with wildlife hospitals, industry groups and vets, the surveillance programme, testing kits, and business continuity planning. The question is engaged head-on.
question: How is the Government supporting the poultry industry to prepare for an incursion?
statement: Early detection is the key here. The Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) is working closely with New Zealand’s wildlife hospitals, poultry industry groups, and vets to raise awareness and get people to look for the signs of bird flu. We are carrying out a nationwide surveillance of birds in New Zealand for exotic diseases and working with Fish & Game to conduct annual summer field surveillance programmes. So far this year, we have tested 30 different species of birds. Testing kits have also been provided to people in Antarctica to use when they spot deaths that look like bird flu. To make sure we’re ready when it does arrive, MPI is also working in partnership with the poultry industry on business continuity and resilience planning.

explanation: Asked about the impact on native birds. He answers the question — the impact is uncertain, but overseas experience shows serious effects on colony-nesting wild birds — then moves to DOC's vaccination trials and a public appeal, which is a different question. The core is reached before the drift, so this sits well above a dodge but short of a complete answer.
question: How will avian influenza impact New Zealand’s native birds?
statement: The potential impact on New Zealand’s native species is uncertain, but certainly around the world we have seen serious impacts on wild birds, especially those that live closely together in large colonies. The Department of Conservation is undertaking vaccination trials on a targeted number of endangered birds in captivity and is asking the public to keep an eye out so we can detect bird flu early. In particular, we are asking the public to report any time you’re outdoors and see several sick or dead birds in a group.

explanation: A closed question — does she stand by her answers — met with 'Yes.' One word, and it is the whole answer. Brevity is not evasion.
question: Does she stand by her answers to oral question No. 5 on 20 November?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked what transport options exist for rural kids whose routes were cancelled. She names the options: Ministry assistance, either a bus or a conveyancing allowance. The question is answered. The circular 'if eligible students are in fact eligible' framing narrows it to eligible students without saying whether the affected kids are eligible, which is why it is not higher — but the vagueness of the options themselves is a Specificity matter and has not been counted against it here.
question: What public transport options, if any, are there for kids in rural communities who have had their school bus routes cancelled?
statement: If eligible students are in fact eligible, they will be provided Ministry of Transport assistance. That may be in the form of a bus; it may be in the form of a conveyancing allowance.

explanation: Two direct questions — does she stand by the statement, and does she think the allowance is sufficient. Neither is answered. The reply pivots to the allowance being unchanged since the previous Government, which is a point about who set the rate, not about whether it is enough. The sufficiency question is the core and it is stepped around entirely.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “we pay families a conveyancing allowance to help them get their children to school.”; if so, does she really think this allowance is sufficient for the costs parents face where the routes have been cancelled?
statement: I would note that the amount of conveyancing allowance hasn’t changed since the previous Government, so that member should know.

explanation: Compound question: (a) does she stand by the statement, (b) why is she refusing to take responsibility. 'Yes, I do stand by my statement' answers (a) directly and completely, but (b) is left entirely untouched. Half the pair engaged. Brevity itself is not penalised — a bare 'Yes' to a single-part standby question would be 1.0 — but here a second, distinct question was asked and never reached.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “I would say to that mother and all parents across the motu that these decisions are operational.”, and, if so, why is she refusing to take responsibility for school bus routes closing under her watch?
statement: Yes, I do stand by my statement.

explanation: 'This is an operational matter for the Ministry of Education' is a genuine answer to 'why is she allowing this': the stated reason is that the decision is not hers. That is a refusal-shaped but responsive answer, which scores high by this rubric. The follow-on about 29 routes cancelled under the questioner's government is an attack, but it is appended to an answer rather than substituted for one, so it dilutes rather than negates. Incivility and whataboutism are not this attribute's business.
question: Why is she allowing the cancellation of school bus routes when it means parents have no safe option to get their kids to school, given her claims that she is focused on improving attendance?
statement: As I said, this is an operational matter for the Ministry of Education. I would also like to point out that in 2023, under that member’s Government, 29 routes were cancelled. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what announcement was made; states the announcement (a coordinated cross-government approach to online financial scams, launched for Fraud Awareness Week, with himself as lead Minister). Squarely on target. The added scale figures are surplus detail, which is Specificity's concern, not Forthrightness's.
question: What announcement has the Government recently made about combatting scams?
statement: To launch Fraud Awareness Week, we announced that the coalition Government will be taking a much more coordinated approach to tackling online financial scams, which cause so much distress to Kiwis. Scams are a huge problem for New Zealand—reported losses are about $200 million a year, but the estimated cost is well in excess of $1 billion. To put this issue in perspective, worldwide it is estimated that cyber-crime is the third-largest economy, after the US and China. I’ve been appointed as the lead Minister to tackle this problem.

explanation: Asked what measures he will take; gives three enumerated components (information sharing across agencies, industry-led solutions with telcos/platforms/banks, regional engagement with Australia and Singapore). Direct and complete against the question as posed. Whether the measures are adequate or true is Veracity/Rigor, not this.
question: What measures will the Minister be taking to combat scams?
statement: My plan includes three key components: first, better information sharing across Government and its agencies; second, work with telcos, social media platform providers, and banks to develop industry-led solutions; and, third, engage with ministerial counterparts in Australia and Singapore to look at regional solutions.

explanation: 'Great question. [Interruption] Thank you. [Interruption]' — the question of why a lead Minister is needed is never addressed in the response as transcribed. Scored low on the text present, but flagged: the content appears lost to interruption rather than deliberately withheld, which is a transcript-quality issue rather than evasion. If responses that are majority interruption markers can be detected upstream, this pair is better excluded than scored.
question: Why is a lead Minister needed?
statement: Great question. [Interruption] Thank you. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what other work he is doing; answers with concrete further work — pressure on banks, confirmation of payee by Easter, a compensation scheme for victims, and forthcoming pressure on telcos and platforms. Engages the question fully. The 'this is for Mr Willie Jackson' aside and the closing slogan are noise that belong to Focus/Civility, and were not allowed to move the score.
question: What other work is the Minister doing to tackle scams?
statement: Lots. I’ve been explicit with the banks—this is for Mr Willie Jackson. I have been explicit with the banks that they must improve their customer safety. Banks have agreed to implement confirmation of payee, which will be in place by Easter next year, and I’m working with them on a compensation scheme for scam victims. I’m also about to apply similar pressure to telcos and social media platform providers. Tackling online financial scams is part of our plan to rebuild the economy and crack down on crime by supporting Kiwis to safely transact and to do business.

explanation: Asked 'does she stand by the commitment; if so, why'. Both halves are answered: 'Yes', followed by a why (the government's four priorities and their claimed impact on older New Zealanders). The why is generic, but genericness is Specificity — the question was engaged on both limbs.
question: Does she stand by her commitment to “improving the lives of older New Zealanders”; if so, why?
statement: Yes. The Government is committing to improve the lives of all New Zealanders through rebuilding the economy, easing the cost of living, restoring law and order, and delivering better public services. These priorities have tangible impacts on the lives of older New Zealanders, and I am committed to delivering on them.

explanation: A narrow factual question — what actions did she take when advised in May to progress the review with a 'lighter touch'. The answer never addresses that advice, that month, or any action taken in response to it, substituting a general account of engaging with two sector associations. A specific factual question with its core wholly avoided, which this rubric treats as a worse failure than a sprawling question partly covered.
question: What actions did she take, if any, when the Associate Minister of Housing, Tama Potaka, advised officials in May to progress the long-overdue Retirement Villages Act review that she’d committed to with him, with a “lighter touch”?
statement: I have engaged strongly with the Retirement Villages Association and the Retirement Villages Residents Association to ensure we achieve positive outcomes. There is a tough issue to deal with, and we have found common ground. So there is work to be done in this space. I’m confident we’ll achieve a positive resolution, and I am meeting with both of the organisations in the next week.

explanation: Asked how a 2029-at-earliest timeline improves seniors' lives. She does not defend the timeline, but she does engage its premise: legislation is not always the answer, and the outcomes are being pursued without the legislative process — which is a responsive way of saying the timeline is not the operative path. It gestures at the question and reaches its edge without landing on it. Rejecting a question's premise is engagement, not evasion, so this sits mid-scale rather than low.
question: How does she think the time line for actual change for residents of 2029 at the earliest improves the lives of seniors?
statement: I think we can agree that legislation is not always the answer to every problem. There is common ground with both parties, and we are working to achieve those positive outcomes without the need for the legislative process. There is opportunity and definitely appetite for the groups to come together and achieve those resolutions.

explanation: Asked what she says to residents struggling to pay for rest home care while waiting for a licence-to-occupy to sell. The affordability core is untouched, but the answer does reach one limb of the question — the nine-month average for sale of occupancy rights speaks to the waiting period the question describes. Partial engagement with continued meetings offered where a response to affected residents was asked for.
question: What does she say to residents who continue to struggle to pay for rest home care while waiting for the licence to occupy to sell their retirement village unit because of unfair rules?
statement: I will continue to—and do—meet with the residents’ association to identify those key issues, and when that occurs, I will of course enter into engagement. I am encouraged by the Retirement Villages Association’s commitment to addressing these issues, and, on average, the sale of those occupancy rights has been within the nine-month period.

explanation: Asked why the review was deferred to the next parliamentary term. No reason for the deferral is given at any point; the answer restates 'common ground' and work under way — the same talking points already used in the two preceding answers. This is the pivot-to-talking-points pattern: it never says why.
question: Why has she allowed the retirement villages review to be kicked into the next parliamentary term when many of those who need it will not live long enough to benefit from the protections?
statement: As I have said, there is very good common ground. A lot of the initiatives that we’re hoping will be achieved under this legislation are under way or in action. There is common ground, and I appreciate that there are discussions continuing, and that is why I’m continuing to meet with those groups and addressing those practical issues to get the job done.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. He opens with "Yes" — a complete answer to a sprawling formulaic question. The economic recital that follows is padding, and its self-serving tone belongs to Focus/Civility, not here. The question was engaged and answered.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our actions to rebuild the economy, given the economic mismanagement of the previous Government. This is a Government that is on the side of working New Zealanders. And the progress that we are making by offering tax relief for the first time in 14 years, having inflation at 2.2 percent to have wages growing faster than inflation for the first four quarters of this Government versus 13 under the last one where it went backwards, having the official cash rate and interest rates down, having actually business sentiment and confidence up and consumer confidence up—we’re making good progress. A long way to go, but we’re on the right track.

explanation: Two parts: does he stand by the stable-rents claim, and how does he reconcile it with Stats NZ's 4.5 percent. He confirms the claim ("that is the case") and names the reconciliation — he is using tenancy bond data, not the Stats NZ series. That squarely addresses both halves. Whether the bond data actually supports him is a Veracity question; the Labour comparison is a minor pivot but does not displace the answer.
question: Does he stand by his claim, “We haven’t had a single rent increase; it’s been stable rents over the last 12 months.”; if so, how does he reconcile that with Statistics New Zealand’s annual rent inflation figure of 4.5 percent over that time, over twice the rate of headline inflation?
statement: Because that is the case. We have actually had stable rents under this Government versus $180 per week under Labour. Our source of data, from memory, is the tenancy bond data.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: is he saying Statistics New Zealand is wrong? He never says yes or no. Restating "stable rents based off the data we've been using" implies a disagreement between sources without ever conceding or denying the point put to him, and he tacks on the $180 Labour line. Partial engagement, core hedged around.
question: So is he saying that Statistics New Zealand is just wrong?
statement: I’m saying that we’ve had stable rents based off the data that we’ve been using, compared to the $180 per week increase under his Government.

explanation: Asked how a 4.5 percent rent rise squares with his promise that rents would fall. He disputes the premise — rents are stable — and gives reasons (costs off landlords, brightline change), which is a legitimate way of engaging. But the promise to reduce rents is never addressed, and the answer opens by turning on the questioner. Rejecting the premise gets it partway; the core of the question is left untouched.
question: Given he promised New Zealanders rents would decrease as a result of reintroducing interest deductibility for landlords, how is rents going up 4.5 percent during his tenure as Prime Minister something for New Zealanders to celebrate?
statement: I find it ironic, from that member, getting lectured about rent increases, don’t you think? It’s $180 per week that it went up under his Government. We have stable rents under this Government. Why is that? Because we’ve taken the costs off landlords, we’ve actually got the balance right between tenants and landlords, and we’ve pulled the brightline test back to two years. I’ll just say to that member: rents are stable. They went up $180 under his Government. We’re doing the opposite.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee the new ferries will cost less than the cancelled $551 million contract, and why not if he won't give it. He guarantees something else — less than $3.2 billion — silently swapping the benchmark. He neither gives nor explicitly refuses the guarantee asked for, and offers no reason for withholding it. Answering a different question than the one asked, on a narrow and specific ask.
question: Crikey! Will he guarantee that the new inter-island ferries Cabinet has agreed to fund will cost less than the $551 million contract with Hyundai that his Government cancelled; if not, why not?
statement: Well, I can guarantee that member they will cost less than the $3.2 billion he let that project grow out to. It’ll be less than that.

explanation: Asked to assure that the Government will not liberalise MSSA sale and supply, or say why not. "We haven't had that conversation in Government" is a real response to the "why not" limb — no position has been formed, so no assurance can be given. He then substitutes a generic assurance about public safety, which is not what was sought. Partial: half the question reached, half deflected.
question: Will he assure the New Zealand public that his Government will not liberalise the sale and supply of military-style semi-automatic weapons; if not, why not?
statement: We haven’t had that conversation in Government, but I can assure you we are focused on improving public safety.

explanation: Two limbs. "I don't agree with that" answers the first directly and completely. The second — why should New Zealanders respect his leadership — is answered loosely rather than dodged: he points to what the public can see the Government delivering. That is a responsive line of argument, thinly made, so it lands short of full engagement but well clear of a pivot.
question: Does he agree with his Deputy Prime Minister, Winston Peters, that he is struggling in the job of Prime Minister, and, if he doesn’t, why should New Zealanders respect his leadership when his own deputy clearly doesn’t?
statement: Well, I don’t agree with that, but I’ll just say to you members: the New Zealand public can see that this is a Government that’s getting the work done. They can see that inflation’s down, they can see that interest rates are down, they can see that crime is down, and—compared to the ungodly mess that that Government left us—they can see we’re making progress. That’s why they think the country is heading in the right direction, not the wrong direction as it was under your Government.

explanation: Asked what recent banking announcements she has made. She states the announcement — Kiwibank capital access, up to $500 million, who will be approached. Directly and completely responsive. The oligopoly commentary at the end is editorial but comes after the question has already been answered.
question: What recent announcements has she made on banking?
statement: Yesterday, the Government announced it is proceeding with plans to provide Kiwibank with access to more capital. The Treasury and Kiwibank’s parent company, Kiwi Group Capital, will talk to New Zealand KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment institutions, and New Zealand professional investor groups about a potential investment of up to $500 million in the bank. Additional capital would enable Kiwibank to compete more vigorously against the “big four” Australian-owned banks. As the Commerce Commission reported earlier this year, the banking sector is a “highly profitable, two-tier oligopoly”, and New Zealanders are not well served by what could be characterised as a cosy pillow fight between the “big four” banks.

explanation: Asked what benefit more capital would bring. She gives the benefit in terms: $500 million supporting up to $4 billion of business or $10 billion of home lending, and the Treasury estimate of consumer savings. Squarely on the question.
question: What benefit would there be in providing Kiwibank with access to more capital?
statement: Kiwibank has been growing faster than the market average for six years, but it is still a relatively small player. To keep growing, it needs more capital. I’ve been advised that an additional $500 million of capital could support up to $4 billion of business lending or $10 billion of home lending. That is sufficient to add competitive pressure to the market. Treasury calculates that even a 0.25 percent drop in personal and business lending rates across all banks would save customers $1.5 billion to $2 billion a year.

explanation: Asked when the decision will be made. She gives the timeline — advice around the middle of next year, Cabinet decision after, offer window October next year to June 2026. A direct and complete answer to a narrow timing question.
question: When will the Government make a decision on access to additional capital?
statement: Around the middle of next year, Kiwi Group Capital and the Treasury will report to me on options. Cabinet will then make a final decision on whether to proceed with a capital raising. If a decision to proceed is taken, it is expected that Kiwi Group Capital will launch a formal offer to raise new capital from suitable New Zealand investors between October next year and June 2026.

explanation: Asked whether Kiwibank will be floated on the open market. She answers it: not this term, the offering is limited to named institutional investors, and a public offering is not possible before the 2028 systems upgrade. She addresses both the near term and the longer-run possibility rather than leaving the question hanging.
question: Will Kiwibank be floated on the open market?
statement: A future Government may consider the possibility of a public share offering at some point, but, at this stage, the potential offering would be limited to KiwiSaver funds, New Zealand investment institutions, and New Zealand professional investor groups. I’m advised that Kiwibank would not be in a position to conduct a public offering until it has completed upgrading its systems and technology. That is not scheduled to happen until 2028. Therefore, the Government is not considering a market float during this term of Government.

explanation: Two limbs. "Yes" plus the context of the KiwiRail funding decision fully answers whether she stands by the statement. The second limb asked for confidence that the alternative ferries will cost less than the cancelled $551 million Hyundai contract; she expresses confidence against a different figure — the $3 billion iReX blowout — so the comparator she was asked about is never engaged. Half answered, half answered as a different question.
question: Fa‘afetai tele lava, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by her statement that “We have a responsibility to ensure the public gets value for its money”; if so, is she confident that the Government’s alternative ferries will be less than the $551 million contract with Hyundai that was cancelled?
statement: Yes. I stand by the statement which was referring to the Government’s decision to decline a request from KiwiRail to contribute additional funding to the iReX project. And, yes, I’m confident that the Government’s alternative ferry solution for the Cook Strait will cost less than the iReX project that was started under the previous Government and which blew out to a cost of at least $3 billion.

explanation: Asked whether a $900m tagged contingency was set aside. Willis explicitly declines to answer and states why (an announcement is coming this week). That is a plain refusal, not a pivot — she engages the question and closes it off rather than talking around it. Scored high per the refusal rule; not full marks only because the refusal defers rather than settling the matter.
question: Has she set aside a tag contingency of $900 million for the procurement of two smaller, non - rail-enabled ferries?
statement: I do not believe it is in the public interest to answer that today. The member will just have to wait until an announcement is made later this week.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question: has a cost-benefit analysis been undertaken? She labels the question speculative, never says whether such an analysis exists, and moves to what Cabinet 'had in mind' (safety, reliability, value for money). That is answering a different question. The 'I do not have a need to respond' is not a clean refusal to disclose — it is a dismissal followed by substitute material, so it earns a little credit but not much.
question: Has she undertaken a cost-benefit analysis to understand the increase in cost to users, freight operators, port operators, and the wider transport system as a result of her decision to not support rail-enabled ferries?
statement: That question contains speculation which I think I do not have a need to respond to. What I can say is that Cabinet, in considering a ferry replacement option, has had in mind safety, reliability, resilience, compatibility with rail, and value for money, not just for freight users and passengers but for New Zealand taxpayers as well.

explanation: Asked whether $300m was set aside for Hyundai cancellation costs. She states the negotiations are unconcluded and commercially sensitive and says outright 'I won't be disclosing details about that.' A direct, complete refusal with its reason — the question was engaged and answered in the forthrightness sense, even though the number is withheld.
question: Has she set aside $300 million to cover the cancellation cost with Hyundai?
statement: The negotiations with Hyundai are yet to conclude. The details of those negotiations are highly commercially sensitive. It is my responsibility to protect the taxpayer and so I won’t be disclosing details about that.

explanation: Asked whether she regrets refusing extra KiwiRail funding given the resulting costs. She answers about a different regret entirely — recasting it as regret at the situation the previous Government left. The core (does she regret her own decision) is never touched; the response is a reframing into talking points about the failing project.
question: Does she regret making the political point by refusing additional funding for KiwiRail now that her alternative deal for the new, smaller ferries could cost $900 million, the sunk costs on winding up the project are around half a billion, and the break fee could be upwards of $300 million?
statement: I regret and will always remember an incoming Government being faced with a situation where they were set a deadline of a matter of weeks to determine whether we would shovel more cash into a failing project that had had multiple cost blowouts, that had gone completely off the rails, and that the last Government had not acted on. For an incoming Government—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether the half-billion write-off plus a potential $300m cancellation cost is a good deal for New Zealanders. She answers the counterfactual instead — that continuing iReX would not have been a good deal — and closes by attacking the questioner. There is an implicit 'better than the alternative', which is partial engagement, but the write-off itself is never assessed. Note the attack and the truth of the $3bn figure are deliberately not weighed here.
question: Is it a good deal for Kiwis that around half a billion dollars has been written off the Government’s financial statements and potentially a $300 million cancellation cost as a result of her Government’s decision to cease the iReX project?
statement: As I have said, it would not have been a good deal for New Zealanders to have shovelled more cash at a failing project which had blown out to more than $3 billion in cost, and I would say was destined to blow out even further; where there were still questions about whether the ships could pass through the Tory Channel; where there were still questions about whether berths would be delivered on time. It was a failed project, and the member’s defence of it tells me that she does not take value for taxpayers’ money seriously.

explanation: Standard 'does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions?' answered 'Yes.' One word, direct, complete. Nothing is dodged.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: The same stand-by question put in te reo Māori, answered 'Yes.' Direct and complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: is the Government committed to meeting the NDC? The answer — 'we're going to work incredibly hard to deliver on our climate commitments and goals' — substitutes effort language for the commitment being asked about and never says yes or no. Gestures at the topic without reaching the question.
question: Is the Government committed to meeting our nationally determined contribution (NDC) to the Paris Agreement to limit global warming below 1.5 degrees?
statement: Well, we’re going to work incredibly hard to deliver on our climate commitments and goals.

explanation: The question was re-put in narrower form after the first dodge, and the answer ('we're going to do everything we can to meet some very ambitious goals') retreats further from a yes/no. A tightly specified question squarely avoided a second time, which is the worse form of failure under this rubric.
question: Is the Prime Minister and his Government committed to meeting our nationally determined contribution?
statement: We’re going to do everything we can to meet some very ambitious goals.

explanation: Asked whether his prior answer should be read as the Government not being committed to the NDC. Answered 'No.' A one-word direct response to a yes/no question — complete engagement, whatever one makes of its consistency with the two answers before it (consistency is not this attribute).
question: Is that answer to be taken that this Government is not committed to meeting our nationally determined contribution to the Paris Agreement?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of the MfE/Treasury forecast of up to $24 billion in offshore mitigation costs. The answer is a restatement of commitment to net carbon 2050 and NDC 2030 — awareness of the forecast is never confirmed, denied, or addressed. A factual question about knowledge answered with a position statement.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware that the Ministry for the Environment and Treasury last year forecasted that we could be on the hook for up to $24 billion to pay other countries to reduce their emissions if we refuse to do it here at home under our nationally determined contribution?
statement: Our Government’s very committed to delivering on our net carbon 2050 goals and doing everything we can to deliver on NDC 2030.

explanation: Asked whether the public should be concerned at his refusal to commit to the 2030 NDC. The reply lists emissions budgets and a forthcoming plan — a defence of the record that implicitly says 'no', but the question's core (should there be concern about the refusal) is not engaged. The loaded framing does not excuse the dodge; it remains a real, answerable question.
question: Should the New Zealand public be concerned that the Prime Minister of this Government is refusing to commit to meet our nationally determined contribution out to 2030, only promising that he is hopeful that we will do so?
statement: Well, this Government is committed to net carbon 2050. That’s our commitment. That’s what we’re working towards. Our emissions budget 1 puts us on track to do that. Emissions budget 2 puts us on track to do that, and you’ll hear more about that with the emissions reduction plan announced this week.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statements and actions, and why. She says "Yes" outright and then names the specific statements she stands by, which supplies the "why". The qualifier "in the context in which I said and did them" is a mild hedge but does not withhold the answer.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions in relation to the Military-Style Academy Pilot and young offending; if so, why?
statement: Yes, in the context in which I said and did them; in particular, my statements that Oranga Tamariki does not have the ability to restrict the movement of these young people, or the choices they make once they leave the residence and return to the community, and also my statement that we have already seen success with the military-style academy, including involvement for the participants in jobs, education, and training.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by a specific quote about "12 months in, 12 months out", and why. She never says yes or no. She does engage the substance by describing the duration the legislation permits (three to 12 months), which is adjacent to the quoted claim, so this is a partial answer that hedges around the core stand-by question rather than a full pivot.
question: Does she stand by her statement in relation to the young serious offenders legislation that “Then we can actually have a more intensive programme where it’s not just three months in, nine months out; it’ll be 12 months in, 12 months out with the option of extra time if the young person still needs it.”, and, if so, why?
statement: The new legislation will allow the ability for a judge or a court to decide on the level of intensive response that is needed for a young person based on their needs. It is to be no less than three months, but no more than 12 months. Each young person has their own issues that they are dealing with and may need a different level of intervention.

explanation: Asked to rule out NZDF or Corrections involvement in any future military-style academy. "I'm not responsible for Corrections or Defence" declines on portfolio grounds without saying whether she would rule it out — and the academies are her portfolio, so the boundary does not dispose of the question. Blunt, but it answers a different question (who is responsible) than the one asked (will you rule it out). Not scored down for terseness.
question: Will she rule out any involvement of the New Zealand Defence Force or Corrections in any future military-style academy?
statement: I’m not responsible for Corrections or Defence.

explanation: Asked for a total count of alleged reoffending and breaches of in-community transition plans. She gives a number — three young people with accusations of reoffending — which squarely answers the main limb, and flags upfront that parts may be outside her knowledge. The breach limb goes unanswered, so it is short of complete. The count's accuracy is a Veracity matter and did not move this.
question: How many participants, in total, have allegedly reoffended, including offending not involving police, or breached the conditions of their in-community transition plan?
statement: There’s some questions in there that I may not be able to answer because they may not be to my knowledge, but there have been three young people that have had accusations of reoffending.

explanation: Asked whether Oranga Tamariki had advised her of any other incidents — a yes/no. "Nothing that was in the public interest currently that I can speak to" neither confirms nor denies; it is a hedged non-answer that leaves open whether other incidents exist. A plain refusal ("yes, but I won't discuss them") would have scored high; this avoids committing either way.
question: In relation to the previous question I asked, has Oranga Tamariki advised you of any other incidents?
statement: Nothing that was in the public interest currently that I can speak to.

explanation: Asked for a promise to shut the academies down if harm is found. She talks about her motivations, historical harm and safety mechanisms, and closes on what the previous approach did not do — but never engages whether she would make that promise. Talking points offered in place of the yes or no asked for.
question: If she sees any harm being done to children in the military-style academies—in residence or in the community—will she promise to shut them down?
statement: In all seriousness, I came into this role to make the lives of young people better. Children and young people have been hurt and harmed for over 20 to 30 years. The royal commission report has brought this to our attention. What I can say is I will put all safety mechanisms that I can in place to keep these young people safe, but we cannot continue to do what we were doing, which was absolutely nothing.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he had made on transport accountability in Auckland. He names the announcement, when it was made and with whom, which is what was asked. That the question was a friendly one from his own side does not change whether it was engaged.
question: What recent announcements has he made on restoring democratic accountability to transport in Auckland?
statement: On Friday, I announced, alongside Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown, that our Government is restoring democratic accountability to transport decision-making in Auckland, ensuring voters can hold their elected representatives accountable for the city’s transport policies. The changes we’re making will ensure that transport policies have democratic legitimacy and democratic accountability, something that has been sorely lacking in Auckland.

explanation: Asked what reforms the Government is making to Auckland transport decision-making. He enumerates four specific reforms. Direct and complete against the question asked.
question: What reforms are the Government making to transport decision-making in Auckland?
statement: Well, our reforms will return regional transport policy and planning to Auckland Council; establish a new Auckland regional transport committee, which will develop a 30-year integrated transport plan for Auckland, designate Auckland Council as Auckland’s road-controlling authority, and empower Auckland Council to have control over its council-controlled transport organisation.

explanation: Asked why the Government is restoring democratic accountability. He gives reasons — Aucklanders' frustration, the 29 percent satisfaction figure, and accountability at the ballot box. The question asked for a rationale and a rationale is what he gives.
question: Why is the Government restoring democratic accountability to transport in Auckland?
statement: Aucklanders have become increasingly frustrated with how transport decisions are being made and how little their views have been taken into account. Even Auckland Transport’s recent annual report highlighted that only 29 percent of Aucklanders felt the organisation listens and responds to their needs. To address these concerns, we’re restoring democratic decision-making for transport in Auckland, and if Aucklanders continue to feel the transport system isn’t working for them, they can hold their local elected representatives to account at the ballot box.

explanation: Asked what the reforms mean for Aucklanders. He answers with the consequences — long-term planning, a delivery-focused CCO, and local accountability over decisions like car parks and cycleways. Squarely on the question.
question: What do these important reforms mean for Aucklanders?
statement: Well, these reforms will mean there’ll be greater long-term planning between central and local government, with a 30-year integrated transport plan; focus on delivery with a transport council-controlled organisation focused on delivering transport services and infrastructure; and accountability over decisions made in local communities, such as removing car parks, installing speed bumps, putting cycleways in place. Aucklanders will be able to hold their elected members to account at the ballot box.

explanation: Asked whether she is comfortable with the decision and, if so, why. "Unsurprisingly, yes, I am" answers the first limb outright, and the funding rationale answers the second. She frames it as a refocusing rather than a cut, but she does not dodge the question; whether that framing is accurate is a Veracity question, not this one.
question: Is she comfortable with her decision to cut social sciences and humanities research from the Marsden Fund, and, if so, why?
statement: Unsurprisingly, yes, I am. Last week’s changes to the around $78 million Marsden Fund ensure our limited funding is focused on the areas of science research with the greatest potential to grow our economy while enhancing quality of life for New Zealanders. The Marsden Fund will continue to support blue-skies research, but will now focus on those core science areas more likely to lead to scientific breakthroughs.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the 'science with a purpose' statement and whether she is confident the system can still address pressing challenges. She says 'Yes' to the first, states she is confident the science will be better, and engages the premise directly (only ~50 percent of applications need an economic-growth case; blue-skies research remains). Both limbs reached.
question: Does she stand by her statement that the Marsden Fund should “focus on core scientific research that helps lift our economic growth and contributes to science with a purpose.”, and, if so, is she confident that the science system will still be able to address the most pressing challenges facing Aotearoa today, when it is simply funding a narrow and politically manufactured definition of a science system, based purely on economic gain?
statement: Yes, thank you, Mr Speaker. Look, I’m very confident that we’ll be going to be doing even better science than what we have been doing. And, certainly, it’s wrong to say that the entire focus will be on economic gain; only 50 percent of the applications, or around that, will need to show that they can actually start to grow the economy and they have potential to do so. There is still blue-skies research, but it will be on science.

explanation: Asked whether housing, poverty, mental health and similar research fails to 'contribute to science with a purpose'. She answers the substance squarely — most of those are not science in her view, though they are important and funded elsewhere — and names the other funding channels. The detour to who funds them does not displace the answer.
question: Is she saying that research on housing, homelessness, poverty, poor achievement in schools, racial hatred and terrorism, crime rates, violence, discrimination, the marginalisation of groups in society, social cohesion, mental health, addiction, and poor health outcomes does not “contribute to science with a purpose.”?
statement: I don’t want to pick on any particular area that the member’s raised, but I will say that most of those that he’s named are not science. They are, however, very important, and many of those are already funded through the funding that the universities get—if I think about things like, for instance, the Performance-based Research Fund, the centres of research excellence, and tuition subsidies. In addition to that, many Government departments commission research to support policy objectives, including some of those that the member’s raised, social and cultural outcomes—for example, the Treasury; the Reserve Bank; the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment; the Ministry for Primary Industries; the Ministry for the Environment; the Department of Conservation; and others. In essence, this is targeted funding for science, and it will be staying with science while I’m the Minister.

explanation: Asked to explain what she means by 'science'. She engages directly, giving the school-subjects framing (chemistry, biology, physics) and then a list of funded projects she counts as science and one she does not. Ostensive rather than a definition, so the core is approached by example rather than stated, but the question is not dodged.
question: Can the Minister explain what she means by “science”?
statement: Well, I think it’s really important to go back—so, I mean, when I was at school, we learnt about maths; so we learnt chemistry, biology, physics. We learnt about science. We also understood that in order to deal with some of the big issues of the world—whether it’s climate change, whether it’s pollution, whether it’s those sorts of issues—we need to go to science. So, you know, when I look at some of the things that I would like to talk to him about, and you mentioned some of the things that I consider science, that have been funded this year through Marsden—“Mapping how viruses get into and travel around B cells and lymph nodes”; that’s science. “Producing next-generation materials that can capture methane”—that’s science. “The molecular mechanisms driving gastric cancer survival rates: understanding the role of nuclear immune systems”—yes, no, no, that’s science. “Unleashing the potential of titanium as a replacement for precious metal catalyst by fixing it to solid supports”—yeah, no, that’s science too. And I’d also say that there’s quite a lot of science that’s currently being funded, but I do not think $360,000 of taxpayer money to look at what are the implications of policing climate justice activism—nah, that’s not science.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by 'no payback at all for the New Zealand taxpayer' for social sciences and humanities, or sees value in climate-adaptation research combining modelling with social research. She never addresses the quoted statement and never touches the climate-adaptation example; she restates that social science is funded elsewhere and pivots to mocking a roadside-sculptures grant. Only the funding-boundary edge of the question is engaged.
question: Does she stand by her statement regarding social sciences and humanities research that “There is actually no payback at all for the New Zealand taxpayer.”, or does she see value for taxpayers in research which helps Aotearoa avoid costly climate change adaptation impacts by combining modelling and science with social research?
statement: Well, I think I made it really clear that social sciences—research into those—there’s already loads of funding for that. It’s in various areas but it’s not going to be coming out of my science budget; I want to make that really clear. These are the things I’ve listed off what I think is science—I do actually accept that they need to be funded. I’m not happy with things like $360,000 going for Big Things, Complex Shadows: Investigating Intersecting Stories Of Place, Identity, And Erasure Through Aotearoa’s Large Roadside Sculptures in Aotearoa. And this is all about, basically, the carrot outside Paeroa. No, I don’t think that’s science, sorry.

explanation: Asked how the Marsden changes align with Crown obligations under Te Tiriti to protect Māori knowledge. The single responsive clause is that Vision Mātauranga-relevant applications remain eligible; Tiriti obligations themselves are never addressed, and the answer turns to ridiculing a proposed study and the questioner's likely next suggestion.
question: How do these changes to the Marsden Fund align with the Crown’s obligations under Te Tiriti o Waitangi to actively protect and promote Māori knowledge and development?
statement: Look, what I think is really important to realise is that if there are science applications or science research applications that are relevant with Vision Mātauranga policy, that’s fine, too—they’re still relevant—and I think that’s really important. But I don’t think that Māori or anyone else in New Zealand, apart from a few, might be that excited about the fact that they want to look at the history of big things that were put outside towns in the 1980s. I mean, next thing the member will be suggesting that we fund a study into those great big pou that are around those wonderful roads of national significance, but I actually don’t think that’s science. It might be interesting—ain’t science.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements the Government has made on work-focused support for jobseekers. She names the announcement directly — expanded phone-based case management for 10,000 more, 70,000 total, needs assessments and job plans. Complete and on point.
question: What recent announcements has the Government made regarding new work-focused support for people on jobseeker benefits?
statement: I’m pleased to say that we have recently expanded the Ministry of Social Development’s (MSD) phone-based case management service to support 10,000 job seekers. This has increased the total number of people who are being supported by an MSD employment case manager at any time to 70,000. All 70,000 will now be eligible to receive a new, more comprehensive needs assessment of the challenges that might be holding them back from finding work and a personalised job plan to overcome them. These new supports add to the ever growing suite of welfare initiatives that we have introduced in our first year and demonstrate our commitment to delivering better public services and supporting more people to move off welfare and into work.

explanation: Asked how individual job plans work. She describes the mechanism end to end: work-readiness assessment, the barriers examined, case manager plan and timeline, referral to services. Squarely answered.
question: How do individual job plans work?
statement: Individual job plans will begin with a comprehensive work-readiness needs assessment that will go beyond someone’s work experience, availability, and career aspirations. It will examine any barriers to employment that they may have, such as their reading and writing skills, childcare needs, driver-licensing requirements, and how comfortable they are with digital technology, as well as any physical or mental health issues that they may have. Their case manager will work with them to come up with a personalised plan to address these issues and for a time line to complete them. The job seeker will then be referred to any training programmes or support services as required.

explanation: Asked why the Government considers the new support necessary. She gives reasons: slowing benefit exit rates, forecast lifetime years on welfare for under-25s, and specific employment barriers. The 'why' is directly supplied.
question: Why does the Government consider new work-focused support necessary?
statement: Slowing benefit exit rates in previous years has contributed to a significant increase in the amount of time people on benefits are predicted to spend on welfare. For instance, people under the age of 25 who come on to a main benefit are currently forecast to spend an average of about 20 future years on welfare over their lifetime. This is a 49 percent increase over the figures in 2017. We also know that many people on jobseeker support have complex backgrounds, and not being able to read instructions properly or take the company van out to run errands because they don’t have a driver’s licence is holding them back from finding work. We want MSD assessing the needs of job seekers early so that they can identify issues and get the help they need to overcome them faster.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement about delivering change in his first year, and if so why. He says 'Yes, I do' and then supplies the reasons — the crime measures he says are down, patrols up, gang patch ban, polling. Both the yes/no and the 'why' are answered; the swipe at the previous Government does not replace the answer.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “Having considered my performance over the last year in Government, I believe that I have delivered on my promise for New Zealanders to see change in my first 12 months as Police Minister”; if so, why?
statement: Yes, I do: victimisations are down, ram raids are down, aggravated robberies are down, serious assaults are down, burglaries are down, crime in the Auckland CBD is down. Foot patrols are up. Police are back on their core role, keeping communities safe. Gang patches are banned. The gangs have found out that they’re not above the law, and police do outstanding work every day reminding them it’s them who control the streets. Earlier this year, TVNZ polled the public and asked if they felt safer; they did it again last night. The good news is more people feel safer. I recognise that there’s still a lot of work to do. We’ve inherited, as an incoming Government, a terrible situation left by the previous Government, and it’s going to take a lot of hard work to get on top of that, and we acknowledge that, but we’re seeing good movement in the right direction. There was one poll that was taken when the previous member was Minister of Police—

explanation: Asked whether the Deputy Commissioner was correct that 500 more police would be achieved when a wing graduates on 26 June 2026, and if not why not. He does not say correct or incorrect about the delivery claim — he substitutes a different proposition (that the deputy was correct about funding running to June 2026), asserts a November target instead, and turns to the previous Government's record. The narrow yes/no put to him is left unanswered.
question: Was the Deputy Commissioner of Police correct about the delivery of 500 more police at the annual review when he stated, “When that wing graduates on 26 June 2026, we’re projected to have achieved that by that date.”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, he was correct in stating that the funding by this Government goes through to June 2026. That’s how appropriations work. But he would also agree with me and say that under this coalition Government, an excellent recruitment policy brought by our partners New Zealand First for 500 additional police officers is to be delivered in November of this year, unlike the previous Government, who promised 1,800 and only delivered 1,500.

explanation: Asked whether the Commissioner was wrong to say he was confident 500 more police would be delivered in 2026, and if so why. He never says wrong or not wrong; he asserts the commissioner agrees with him and that the target is November of this year. That implies a position on the timing but sidesteps the direct question about the Commissioner's statement.
question: Was the Commissioner of Police wrong when he told One News that he was confident that 500 more police would be delivered in 2026; if so, why?
statement: Because he knows that there’s going to be a lot more police on the street in 2026. But the reality of it is that the commissioner agrees with the deputy commissioner and agrees with me that our target is to deliver 500 additional police officers in November of this year.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Commissioner's statement that extra time would be taken to produce the best recruits, and if not why not. No explicit agree or disagree is given, but the reply is partly responsive on the merits — standards matter and the college course moved from 16 to 20 weeks — before pivoting to praise of the appointment and the November target. It circles the question without landing on it.
question: Do you agree with the Commissioner of Police’s statement “if it takes us a little bit of extra time to produce the best men and women of our organisation for the front line, then we’ll take that [time].”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, I think we’ve got an outstanding Commissioner of Police, and we were very, very pleased to make that appointment. I think that he recognises, as do we, that standards are extremely important. That’s why the Police College is now delivering a 20-week course instead of a 16-week course. The commissioner agrees with me that we have our target, an aspirational target, a very good target, delivering 500 additional police officers in November.

explanation: Asked which of two people was correct. He answers the question head-on — "they're both right" — and gives the reconciliation (November 2025 delivery is also 500 more in 2026). Choosing "both" is a real answer to a who-is-correct question, not a pivot; whether the reconciliation holds up is a Veracity/Rigor matter, not Forthrightness.
question: Who is correct: Casey Costello, who said, “I think it’s really important to get the context of what the commissioner was saying.”—and it was that he had said there was no deviation from the commitment to achieve November 2025—or the Commissioner of Police, who publicly stated on the national news that Police will have 500 more police in 2026?
statement: Well, they’re both right. Casey Costello’s absolutely 100 percent correct, as we are committed to delivering 500 police officers in November of this year. The Police Commissioner is also correct in saying there’ll be 500 additional police officers in 2026, because there will be—they would’ve been delivered in November 2025.

explanation: Asked which of three stated timelines (three years / two years / three years) was correct. He attacks the questioner's credibility ("rambling mumbo-jumbo") and pivots to public-safety talking points and the previous Government. The question's core — which timeline is right — is never touched.
question: Who is correct: the police Minister on 30 January, who said it would take three years to deliver the 500; the police Minister, who said, the next day, after a phone call from Winston Peters, that the 500 would be delivered in two years; or the Commissioner of Police, who said just last week it would take three years?
statement: The problem the member has is she’s got no credibility around her information sources and figures, so that’s a whole lot of rambling mumbo-jumbo. I just want to say that on this side of the House, in this coalition Government, we are deadly serious about public safety and we are focused on making sure that we’re a safer country. We inherited a shambles from the previous Government that wasn’t focused on that. We are laser-focused on it, and we’ll deliver our police officers and we’ll make New Zealand a safer place.

explanation: Asked whether he regrets not fronting up to scrutiny week. "Oh no, don't worry. I front up all right" is a direct denial of both the regret and the premise, so the core is engaged; but he then turns to an attack on Hipkins and Andersen and is cut off before saying anything about scrutiny week itself, leaving the specific occasion unaddressed.
question: Does he regret not fronting up to scrutiny week and showing some leadership now that he is left with no other option but to gaslight New Zealanders about the broken promise to deliver 500 more police in two years?
statement: Oh no, don’t worry. I front up all right—don’t worry about that. I get around the country and I constantly get asked, “Where’s that Chris Hipkins and Ginny Andersen that walked around with—

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on reducing building cost. He names a specific announcement made yesterday (changes to insulation/energy-efficiency installation standards) and its cost effect. Squarely responsive.
question: What announcements has he made around reducing the cost of building?
statement: We’ve made many such announcements, but yesterday we announced that we’re proposing sensible changes to the installation standards for energy efficiency that will enable a more flexible approach to be taken to achieve the same standards but in a more nuanced fashion that will have the added benefit of reducing cost.

explanation: Asked why the change was needed. He gives the reason directly: construction costs up 40 percent since 2019, including costs imposed by last year's rules, hence a search for a more flexible route to the same standards.
question: Why was change needed?
statement: The context is that since 2019, the cost of construction increased by 40 percent. That was due to many different factors, including additional costs imposed by the rules in the form that they were imposed that came into effect late last year.
