So our approach was to consider ways that we might be able to achieve the same standards in a more flexible or nuanced way, relying on the calculation and modelling methods as opposed to the more prescriptive schedule method in the building code.

explanation: Asked what changes are proposed to the installation standards. He names them — removal of the schedule method, regional/climatic flexibility, adjusted minimum R-values in walls. Directly on the question asked.
question: What changes are being proposed to the installation standards?
statement: I’ve referenced the proposed removal of the schedule method, meaning that in different parts of the country with different climactic conditions, we will allow designers and builders to take account of the requirements in those areas in a way that makes sense for those conditions. We are adjusting the minimum R-values in the installation, for example, in the walls, so that the overall building design can get us to the place that we need to be for the purpose of energy efficiency, respiratory health, energy efficiency and therefore cost, all without increasing the additional cost that had been imposed in the rules in the form that they had been introduced last year.

explanation: Asked what impact the changes will have on building costs. He answers the direction (reduce considerably) and the magnitude (up to $15,000 per new build, per MBIE figures). Complete response to what was asked.
question: What impacts will these changes have on building costs?
statement: We hope and expect that they will reduce the cost considerably in many cases. The figures provided by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment in relation to the first part of the consultation ahead of the public consultation that will now take place indicates that up to $15,000 may be saved in the case of each new build. So we think it’s a very positive result and we’re grateful for the engagement that’s got us to this outcome.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on fuel security. He gives the announcement — new rules requiring at least 10 days of jet fuel at the busiest airport. Padded with blame of the previous Government, but the announcement asked for is actually delivered.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding fuel security?
statement: Fuel security is at the apex of our concerns in terms of our economy. Sadly, the security was undermined as the closure of the Marsden Point refinery was green lighted by the Labour Government. To reverse that imperilment, what we have done is announce that new rules are about to be put in place to ensure that we have at least 10 days of jet fuel at the country’s busiest airport. Sadly, this was due to be implemented over the last three to five years and has taken the arrival of the matua to address this problem.

explanation: Asked why fuel security matters. He does supply reasons — broader energy security, avoiding diverted planes and lost connectivity, the 2019 inquiry finding — though a large share of the answer is spent on Labour's oil and gas decision rather than on the why. The core is reached, if indirectly.
question: Why is fuel security important?
statement: Fuel security is an important part of broader energy security, and no one, sadly, when that unwise decision to cancel the oil and gas industry, ever imagined it would depend on Indonesian coal. We cannot afford to recreate a situation where jet fuel supply was undermined and we had planes diverted, reducing our connectivity with the rest of the world. A 2019 Government inquiry into the fuel supply disruption concluded that regulations and a remedy needed to be found in a rapidly short period of time. Sadly, this lingered. That has undermined perceptions about our resilience. Consequently, we will no longer allow our energy sector, in relation to fuel security, to be imperilled further.

explanation: Asked when the new rules come into place. "The new rules will be in place by November 2026" — the date is given immediately and unambiguously; the rest is surplus commentary that does not qualify the answer.
question: When will the new rules come into place?
statement: The new rules will be in place by November 2026. This is to ensure that no indiscriminate decisions are made which have unintended consequences, as was the case with the Labour Government’s closure of the oil and gas industry in New Zealand. Therefore, we are working with the fuel companies, but they know that there is no time left—no opportunity for wriggle room. They have to respect that if they want their social licence to be esteemed in New Zealand, they have to step up to the plate and not further undermine our fuel security, as, sadly, was the legacy of the Labour Government.

explanation: Asked what other actions he is taking on fuel security. He lists further actions: the 21-day stockholding cover, an independent study on Marsden Point's role, and possible bespoke planning regulations for the site. Directly answers the "what other" question.
question: What other actions is he taking to ensure fuel security?
statement: Well, obviously the oil and gas industry is about to be re-established, but I’m confident that the 21-day cover for diesel or for jet fuel as a stockholding rule will boost our resilience. We are also completing an independent study on the options as to how Marsden Point may further play a role in respect of fuel security, and indeed whether there’s a case for a bespoke set of planning regulations to protect the strategic importance of that site, given it was trashed over the last three years.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the economy. She names one — the Reserve Bank's 50 basis-point OCR cut, the 125-point cumulative reduction and the forecast track — and its relevance. Exactly what was asked for.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Two weeks ago, the Reserve Bank made a 50 basis-point reduction in the official cash rate (OCR). The bank has now reduced the OCR in three consecutive meetings by a total of 125 basis points. It’s forecast OCR track indicates another reduction at the next meeting in February and further falls in 2025. Reductions in the OCR, of course, affect mortgage and business lending rates, which have a direct impact on New Zealand families and businesses.

explanation: Asked how OCR cuts affected businesses. Willis names a source (ANZ Business Outlook), gives the direction of confidence, own-activity expectations and experienced activity, and links it to rate cuts. Squarely on the question asked; the aggregate-rather-than-firm-level framing is a mild hedge, not a pivot.
question: How have OCR reductions affected businesses?
statement: Every business is unique, but a good aggregate picture is shown in the monthly ANZ Business Outlook survey. Business confidence is high. Firms’ expectations of their own future activity is high; their experienced activity, compared to a year ago, is negative but steadily improving, suggesting that interest rate reductions are changing actual behaviour, not just expectations. As ANZ itself points out, the economy is clearly still weak, but things are starting to turn.

explanation: Asked how OCR cuts affected households. Answers with the transmission channel (mortgage rates) and a concrete magnitude ($140/fortnight on a $500k mortgage). The tax-relief and FamilyBoost additions are surplus talking points but come after the question has already been met.
question: How have OCR reductions affected households?
statement: OCR reductions will directly impact households through lower mortgage rates. For someone with a $500,000 mortgage, the difference between an 8 percent mortgage and a 7 percent mortgage is around $140 a fortnight, depending on the term. And that comes, of course, on top of tax relief, which took effect on 31 July this year, and the FamilyBoost childcare payments that many households are now receiving. While each family has its own set of circumstances, many will be feeling better off than they were a year ago.

explanation: Standard "does he stand by" primary. "Yes" is a complete answer to a yes/no question; everything after it is volunteered advocacy about fast track. The padding is off-topic but nothing was dodged.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to unleash growth and investment so that we can rebuild the New Zealand economy. Last night, the next stage in the passage of the Fast-track Approvals Bill kicked off—critical legislation designed to unshackle investment in infrastructure, renewable energy, housing, and a raft of industries that are hungry to grow. We are serious about growth and infrastructure on this side of the House, and fast track is a big part of delivering that vision, and it’s good to see that we’re not alone. It was fantastic to see Labour MP Rachel Boyack give an impassioned speech this morning on one of those projects on the fast-track list: the Hope Bypass. As I’ve said many times before: like many of the fellow Labour MPs, if he’s serious about the future, don’t play politics; support fast track.

explanation: The question was WHY, a year on, no replacement decision. Luxon answers a different question — what today's plan is (two rail-compatible ferries, 2029) — which does implicitly assert the decision now exists, but the year of delay is never addressed. Half-engaged: it lands adjacent to the question rather than on it.
question: Why, over a year after cancelling, via text message, the $551 million order for two new Interislander ferries, has the Government still not decided what’s going to replace them?
statement: Well, I’m very proud that today we announced an incredibly fantastic, incredible plan to actually ensure we have a resilient, safe, and reliable crossing on the Cook Strait, at a reasonable cost. I’m very proud of the plan that we’ve got. We’ve got a great plan: two rail-compatible ferries, an opportunity to improve it even further between now and March, and, importantly, the new ferries will be operational, on time, on the 2029. And isn’t it fantastic to have a new Minister for Rail who’s got the expertise—it’s not his first rodeo.

explanation: Two-part question: how much, and why won't Willis say. Neither is answered — no figure beyond "a lot less than $3.2 billion heading to $4 billion", and the non-disclosure point is ignored entirely in favour of a recital of iReX cost history. A narrow factual ask deflected into a history lesson.
question: How much will the new Interislander ferries cost, and why wouldn’t Nicola Willis share that with the public, given David Seymour seems happy to announce it via Twitter?
statement: What I’d say is it’s going to cost a lot less than the $3.2 billion heading to $4 billion. And maybe, for the member’s benefit, we could just take him through a bit of the history, because in November 2018, the cost was originally $775 million; one year later, 19 November, it doubled to $1.4 billion; February 2023, it was up at $2.6 billion; and by the time we got to November last year, it was actually $3 billion; and then, in July last year, they were told it’s actually closing approximately $4 billion. So what I can reassure that member is that you won’t see the Labour playbook that we’ve seen on ferries and Dunedin and Kāinga Ora; we’re actually going to do it a lot cheaper than that.

explanation: A specific question about whether costs shifted to ports, ratepayers and users count against the comparison. The reply — "do not worry, we have a fantastic Minister for Rail" — engages with none of it. "On time, in full, under budget" is an assurance, not an answer about cost transfer.
question: Will the Government’s commitment to delivering the new ferries for less than the estimated cost of the iReX project include costs transferred to other parties such as the port companies, ratepayers, and users?
statement: I’d just say to that member: do not worry, we have a fantastic Minister for Rail; he will deliver it on time, in full, under budget.

explanation: Asked what the portfolio transfer says about his confidence in Willis. "Absolutely false" rejects the premise head-on, and "the best Minister of Finance this country has seen" is a direct statement of confidence in her. But the actual subject — why responsibility moved to Peters — is skipped, and the middle of the answer is a Labour attack. Half answered.
question: In that case, what does it say about his confidence in Nicola Willis that he’s transferred responsibility for rail and the Interislander to Winston Peters, who set up the iReX project that Nicola Willis cancelled, creating this mess in the first place?
statement: Absolutely false. The first thing is that the new Minister for Rail signed up to a project at $775 million, not close to $4 billion, because when Labour people get in charge, they don’t run the money well and they let it blow out. And I’d just say we have the best Minister of Finance this country has seen for a very long time.

explanation: Asked why he can't disclose cost, builder, timing, rail capability and user costs. He gives an actual reason — commercial sensitivity in contract formation — which answers the "why can't you" core directly, even if only for the cost limb and none of the other four. The jab about economic illiteracy is rudeness, which does not move this score.
question: If he’s so confident that the new Interislander ferries are going to be such better value for money, why can’t he tell New Zealanders, one year on, how much they’re going to cost, who’s going to build them, when they’re going to arrive, whether they’re going to be able to have trains on them, and what the costs for other users are going to be?
statement: That member’s question just illustrates the economic illiteracy from the other side. Because if you knew anything about forming contracts and getting capital approved, you don’t reveal—for commercial sensitivity reasons—the actual budget. That’s quite normal commercial practice. But I appreciate nobody on the front bench has actually run stuff, understands how it works. But I just say to you, I’m very confident we’re going to get a great project and a great result.

explanation: Asked whether he will now disclose the cancellation cost. "Our budgets are commercially sensitive" is a plain refusal with a stated reason — a refusal is a forthright answer. Marked down from ~0.9 only because the second half abandons the question for the arsonist metaphor; whether the sensitivity claim holds for a sunk cancellation cost is a Veracity question, not this one.
question: One year after cancelling the order for the previous Interislander ferries, will he now tell the New Zealand public how much the decision to cancel the ferries has cost?
statement: As I said, our budgets are commercially sensitive—for the reasons I’ve just tried to outline to that member. But what I find quite outrageous is the Leader of the Opposition is the arsonist who lights the fire and then criticises the fire brigade for trying to put it out.

explanation: Te reo primary of the same "does he stand by" form. "Yes" is complete. The climate material appended afterwards is unsolicited but displaces nothing the question asked for.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to deliver on net zero 2050. Whatever we hear about climate change from the other side, and it’s often bad news, we’re not pushing up prices higher by turning off natural gas.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware the final ERP performs worse on emissions than the draft. He never says yes or no to the awareness question, but he does contest the substance of it — claiming the deficit halved between draft and final, and conceding more work on EB3. That is engagement with the draft-versus-final comparison at the heart of the question, arrived at obliquely and prefaced with the net-zero talking point.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware that his Government’s final emissions reduction plan published today somehow does even a worse job for emissions reduction than his draft version?
statement: What I’d say to that member is we are committed to delivering on net zero 2050. ERP 2, which we released today, confirms that we are in good shape on EB 1. Emissions budget 2, we’re in good shape. We’ve got more work to do on emissions budget 3, but ever since the draft plan was announced and where we got to today, we’ve actually halved the deficit or the progress that we need to make in that space. That doesn’t kick in till 2031 to 2035. We’ve got some time to sort that out.

explanation: Asked why the ERP takes NZ off track for emissions budget 3. He engages by rejecting the premise ("I disagree") — a direct response — but then substitutes EB1/EB2 and 2050/2044 and never addresses EB3, the specific budget asked about. Half the core is reached.
question: Why is his Government’s emissions reduction plan actively taking us off track to meet emissions budget 3?
statement: I disagree. It’s delivering EB 1 and EB 2, which is the pathway that gets us to net zero 2050. Equally, it’s encouraging to see that we may be able to reach that goal much quicker, in 2044, six years earlier.

explanation: Asked (a) is he aware of the ~81 Mt of extra emissions from three named reversals, and (b) will he take responsibility. Neither part is touched: he restates ERP2/EB2, offers a line about Indonesian coal, and turns to urging the Greens to back his bills. A pivot to talking points.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware that his Government’s policy decisions to reverse the oil and gas ban, which he just mentioned; cancel the Clean Car Discount; and encourage consenting of new coal mines in its fast-track process will increase emissions by, at a minimum, an extra 81 million tonnes, and will he take responsibility for the long-term impacts of those emissions on behalf of everyone in Aotearoa?
statement: ERP 2 delivers on EB 2. That’s the pathway by which we hit net zero 2050. I’d just say to that member, we don’t believe in importing Indonesian coal and not having domestic gas as we make that transition. I’d encourage the Green Party to support the end of the oil and gas ban, support us on fast track, and support us on our gene tech legislation as well.

explanation: Asked whether any Government policy, statement or action would prevent non-executive Government MPs from supporting the bill. He answers about the bill (hasn't seen it, will look) and about NZ's settlements position — a different question. The question was about constraints on his backbenchers, and that is never reached, though 'I haven't seen it' is at least a real reason offered.
question: Is there any Government policy, statement, or action that would prevent non-executive members of Parliament from the Government side from supporting the Unlawful Occupation of Palestine Sanctions Bill?
statement: I haven’t seen the nature of the bill that I understand that member has just announced in the time we were coming into the House. I’m happy to look at it, but what I’d just say to you is that our position has been that those settlements are illegal under international law. The best way forward, as you know, is a two-State solution, and we’ve been taking sanctions against extremist settlers.

explanation: Asked to confirm Government MPs are free to vote their conscience on the bill. He does not confirm, but he says squarely why not — the bill was only just proposed and he hasn't seen it. That is engagement with the ask rather than a pivot, but it stops short of the yes/no requested (and the answer is cut off).
question: Will the Prime Minister then confirm that his Government MPs are therefore free to vote with their conscience on the Unlawful Occupation of Palestine Sanctions Bill?
statement: I don’t know how to explain this, but as I understand it, the member has just proposed a bill. We haven’t seen the bill, so—

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree with the Finance Minister's statement, and what is the total Crown contribution versus $2.2 billion. Part one is answered outright ('Yes, I agree'). Part two is not: he disputes the $2.2b baseline with the Treasury $4b figure but never gives a cost for the alternative.
question: Does he agree with the statement of the Minister of Finance that “the Government’s alternative ferry solution for the Cook Strait will cost less than the iRex project”; if so, how much will the total Crown contribution be, compared to the $2.2 billion Crown contribution that was planned for project iRex?
statement: Yes, I agree with the Minister of Finance. But in answer to the second part of her question, the member asserts that the Crown’s contribution would have been $2.2 billion for Project iReX, but that seriously understates what had been the case, and Treasury, under the Official Information Act that this information was made available to that member, said it could go past $4 billion.

explanation: Asked whether he is confident the total Crown contribution will be under $2.2 billion. 'Most assuredly' is an unambiguous yes; the Little River Band line is padding, not evasion. Direct answer to a yes/no question.
question: Is he confident that the total Crown contribution will be less than the $2.2 billion agreed under the previous Government for Project iReX?
statement: The answer to that is most assuredly, or, as Little River Band sang, “Hang on, help is on its way.”

explanation: Asked whether he will keep the rail-enabled ferry option open. 'We'll look at every option we possibly can' covers the asked option only by implication and never commits to it specifically — the question is brushed rather than dodged outright.
question: Will he keep the option of rail-enabled ferries open, even though the ferries may be smaller?
statement: The reality is that all aspects going forward, having picked up this mess that we inherited, are going to be looked at. We’ll look at every option we possibly can.

explanation: Asked for the estimated cost of the minimum viable option for the Picton wharves. He gives no figure, no refusal and no reason — only a general profession of frugality with taxpayer money and industry approval. The core of a narrow costing question is entirely avoided.
question: What are the estimated costs of the minimal viable option for the wharves used by KiwiRail in Picton, given they reach their estimated useful life in 2029?
statement: My answer to that member’s question is that in every aspect we will be frugal and sensible and wise about public expenditure. We’ll be as careful about spending the taxpayer’s money as if we are spending our own money, and that’s why you can be assured that out there in the industry, they’re cheering from the rafters at the change.

explanation: Asked for the estimated annual cost of an extra 55,000 container wagon moves. He declines, and gives the reason — you don't disclose your position mid-commercial-negotiation — closing with 'We're not going to do that'. That is a stated refusal, which is forthright, though it is wrapped in an attack on the questioner and the refusal is left implicit rather than said plainly.
question: What is the estimated cost of an extra 55,000 container move-on, move-off wagons in Wellington and Picton, per year, over the lifetime of the ferries.
statement: Can I just say that the first aspect of any business negotiation is not to tell the other party what you want. The very advice being given over there shows a certain innocence—no commercial skills, don’t know how to close a deal, don’t know how to start the deal, and, first of all, you’re spending taxpayers’ money while you learn on the job. We’re not going to do that, are we?

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that KiwiRail operations will not be privatised. He responds on point — there have been no discussions of it — but substitutes a statement of current fact for the forward guarantee that was requested, so the core ask is only half met.
question: Can he guarantee that the operations currently being undertaken by KiwiRail will not be privatised?
statement: Let me just say that there have been no discussions about that whatsoever on this side of the House.

explanation: Asked whether he can assure the public he will do better than the Minister of Finance. No assurance is given at all; the answer relocates to the inherited iReX blowout, Treasury advice and the previous government's transparency. It is a pivot, though the question was a loaded, sprawling one and 'we've got a chance to save rail' gestures faintly at the ask.
question: Can he assure the New Zealand public that he will do a better job than the Minister of Finance, who, in a year, has only delivered an announcement?
statement: The reality is that the Minister of Finance inherited a disaster. We had hardly come into Government, and there was Treasury saying, “Look, this could blow out. It’s already got to $2.8 billion and it could possibly blow out to $4 billion.” That’s all in the Treasury advice that they had, and they should have shared it with the public as they were coming into the 2023 campaign. Were they transparent? No, they never told the public a darn thing about it, and we picked up this absolute mess. So I’m not blaming the previous Minister at all; I’m just saying, though, that we’ve got a chance to, again, save rail.

explanation: Asked what benefits New Zealanders would see. He names them directly — 55,000 houses, 143,000 tonnes of aquaculture/farming, 180 km of transport, 3 GW of renewables. The question's core is squarely met; the closing swipe at 'years of mismanagement' is a Focus/Civility matter, not a dodge.
question: What benefits does he expect New Zealanders to see as a result of this bill?
statement: Well, there are enormous public benefits to New Zealanders from these regionally and nationally significant projects. The projects listed in the bill, in the schedule agreed in the committee of the whole House earlier this morning, enable 55,000 houses; 143,000 tonnes of aquaculture and farming projects; 180 kilometres of new road, rail, and public transport; 3 gigawatts of additional renewable energy generation; and a significant boost to our resources sector. These projects will help rebuild and grow our economy after years of mismanagement.

explanation: Asked what benefit the 55,000 homes will have. He answers a different, adjacent question — why the homes are hard to build and how fast track will unblock them. Ending the housing crisis and affordability are gestured at, so it is not a clean pivot to talking points, but the benefit itself is never stated.
question: What benefit will those 55,000 homes have?
statement: Well, this Government has inherited a housing crisis, which has been driven by unnecessary planning barriers in place of new housing developments. Report after report has said that our planning system is at the heart of our housing affordability challenge. Our Going for Housing Growth plan will help, so will fast track and making sure that private developers—because the vast bulk of housing in New Zealand is built by the private sector—can get out there and build houses that they want to build and that New Zealanders want to live in. And fast track is about removing those red-tape and green-tape barriers that get in the way of houses New Zealanders need.

explanation: Asked what he says to those concerned about fast track. He says it: the environment can be protected while the economy grows, then makes the case. The question was open and soft; he engaged its core rather than avoiding it. Sloganeering does not lower forthrightness.
question: What does he say to those who are concerned about fast track?
statement: Well, I say to those that are concerned that we can protect the environment and grow our economy at the same time. If we want to end our housing crisis, support fast track. If you want more jobs in our cities and our regions, support fast track. If you want more renewable energy, support fast track. If you want modern roads, rail, and public transport, support fast track. If you want a growing economy, fast track is where it’s at.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, complete, no evasion available or attempted.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A narrow counterfactual — would Cabinet still have signed off on the 149 projects knowing of the consent breaches? He never touches it, pivoting entirely to enthusiasm for fast track and blame for the previous Government. Neither yes, no, nor a refusal to say.
question: Would he and his Cabinet have signed off on all 149 projects to be included in the Fast-track Approvals Bill if he had been aware of the ongoing environmental breaches from some of those companies, detailed as recently as this morning in an RNZ article titled “Second audit finds more consent breaches by OceanaGold’s Otago Macraes mine”?
statement: Well, I’m very excited about fast track, for the reason that the Minister for Infrastructure just outlined. We need to grow our way out of a recession caused by the Labour-Greens Government, and one of the ways we do that is we get modern, reliable infrastructure in this country. We’ve got to build things faster and at lower cost and quicker, and fast track’s cracking through the system, it’s breaking the system to get things done.

explanation: Same counterfactual, this time about the SFO-investigated founder. 'I'm not going to comment on individual projects' is a stated refusal, which counts for something, but it answers a question that was not asked — the question was about the Cabinet's own decision, not about a project's merits — and the rest is talking points.
question: Would he and his Cabinet have signed off on all 149 projects to progress through the Fast-track Approvals Bill if they had known about the founder of a company associated with one of those fast-track projects having been previously investigated by the Serious Fraud Office?
statement: Well, I’m not going to comment on individual projects, but what I will comment on is the excitement that we could have 55,000 new homes; the excitement that we could have 180 kilometres of new roads in this country, which would be brilliant; 30 percent growth in renewable electricity generation. They’re all good things, designed to get our regional and national economy growing.

explanation: Asked whether he is comfortable continuing the committee stage despite the Clerk's advice. He deflects the procedural half to the Speaker but does answer the comfort question — he is 'very proud that fast track is moving through the House exactly as it should.' The Clerk's specific objection goes unaddressed, so the core is only partly reached.
question: Is the Prime Minister comfortable with continuing to progress the Fast-track Approvals Bill through the committee stage, despite advice from the Clerk that his Government’s Amendment Paper could be in the nature of private legislation and the subsequent ruling that stated, “It is undesirable, in principle, for Parliament to make law that is only for the benefit of specific private persons.”?
statement: Again, that’s a matter for the Speaker, but I’m very proud that fast track is moving through the House exactly as it should, and that’s incredibly exciting.

explanation: A precise quantitative question; he gives a precise answer — 'In answer to the question: none' — and then says who did the modelling. Whether 'none' is correct is a Veracity question and does not move this score.
question: What proportion of total emissions cuts projected between the period 2026-35 are attributed to unproven or disproven technologies?
statement: In answer to the question: none. Experts in the Ministry for the Environment completed the modelling for the Government’s second emissions reductions plan (ERP). They worked closely with technical experts across the Government and private sector to ensure that all projections were justified and reasonable.

explanation: Asked how he can have confidence in the assumed capture rate. He gives grounds for that confidence: Norway's decades of storage, industry advice on feasibility, CO2 already separated in production, conservative official modelling. He never engages the 100 percent figure or the 10–72 percent real-world range that was the sting of the question, so it is engaged but not fully met.
question: How can he have confidence in carbon capture and storage achieving the 100 percent capture and storage of emissions from the Kapuni gas field that is assumed in his plan’s modelling, given globally not a single carbon capture and storage project has ever reached its target carbon dioxide capture rate, and no existing project has consistently captured more than 80 percent of carbon, and real-world capture rates range from 10 to 72 percent?
statement: Well, what is interesting is that internationally, countries like Norway are already storing carbon dioxide and have been doing so for several decades, and we understand from industry that this process is feasible here in New Zealand. This is credible as carbon dioxide is already removed as part of the existing production process, leaving the natural gas remaining. Our officials have been and taken a conservative approach to modelling the expected removals. Carbon capture, utilisation, and storage is real and happening all over the world today.

explanation: A narrow factual question — what changes were made to the baseline projections because of the NZ Steel deal. The reply says officials 'worked through the modelling' and 'took into account all of the changes' without naming a single one. A specific question answered with a description of the process is a dodge, and a narrow question dodged is a worse failure.
question: What changes were made to baseline projections from the interim projections in the ERP 2 discussion documents to the final plan as a result of the New Zealand Steel deal achieving more emissions reductions faster than initially projected?
statement: Officials have worked through the modelling and taken into account all of the changes that were made in regards to different aspects of the economy. Our plan reflects the best estimate in terms of where those initiatives are at, and that includes all aspects across our broader economy.

explanation: Asked why GIDI was scrapped in favour of unproven policies. He calls the questioners 'grinches' and celebrates the plan's 2044 net-zero pathway. No reason for the decision is offered at any point; the reply attacks the questioner and substitutes a different subject.
question: Why has his Government chosen to scrap proven emissions reduction strategies such as the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry Fund, which produced the 1.8 megatonne increase in baseline projections, and instead rely on policies that are best described as speculative and unproven?
statement: Well, unlike the grinches on the opposite side, this side of the House today is celebrating an emissions plan that puts us on track and on a pathway for net zero as early as 2044. That is a success and that demonstrates the confidence and capability on this side of the House to ensure that we are managing emissions reduction in this country while also protecting our economy.

explanation: Asked whether taxpayers deserve a plan not reliant on speculative technology. Watts never says yes or no, but he does engage the core premise — he disputes that the technology is unproven and argues it is already in development here. Partial: the challenge is met, the question is not answered.
question: Do New Zealand taxpayers, who may face liabilities of up to $24 billion if the Government fails to meet its international climate targets, deserve a plan that relies on more than just speculative technology advancements to cut more than half of the emissions projected in the plan he released today?
statement: Well, I am proud that this Government today has reflected and published an ERP 2 plan that shows that we are on track for the first two emissions budgets and, most importantly, net zero by 2044 at the earliest. The technology that the member references that is unproven—and this is an example of what that technology could look like, that will go into cows to reduce biogenic methane—is happening under development in this country already by scientists and innovators, and we should back those individuals and we should back our agricultural sector and not always put them down.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: does he agree with McClay that the Government won't buy overseas carbon credits? He praises McClay, restates a commitment to being 'on track', and says they will look at the international components soon — which sidesteps the agreement question entirely. A specific question squarely avoided.
question: Does he agree with Todd McClay, who says the Government won’t buy overseas carbon credits to meet emissions targets?
statement: I always will acknowledge and reflect the positions of the very wise Todd McClay. It is clear that we need to ensure that we are on track in terms of all of our targets, and we will be looking at the international components very soon.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, direct, complete.
question: Does he stand by his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his own 'probably worse' comment on Crown-Māori relations. He talks about strong feelings on the Treaty principles bill and blames the previous administration for division; he never affirms or retracts the comment.
question: Does the Prime Minister stand by his comments that Crown-Māori relationships are “probably worse” than they were a year ago?
statement: As I’ve said, I think the discussion around the Treaty principles bill—there are strong feelings on all sides of that topic. I’d also say that the previous administration built a lot of division and a lot of frustration across New Zealand with some of its actions that it didn’t make the public case for and didn’t take the public on.

explanation: Asked what role he played in worsening the relationship. He describes a coalition difference of opinion and an MMP compromise, which obliquely gestures at his position but never identifies any role of his own. Mostly a dodge.
question: What role does he think he has played in making the relationship worse?
statement: Well, again, as I’ve explained before, we have a difference of opinion within the coalition Government about this issue. Neither party got what they wanted but, in an MMP environment, we found a very sensible compromise and we’re working our way through it.

explanation: Asked why he still invokes the coalition agreement when the bill wasn't an ACT bottom line. He does supply a 'why' — MMP means making space for coalition partners — but ignores the bottom-line premise the question turned on. Thin but genuine partial answer.
question: Why is the Prime Minister still using the coalition agreement as an excuse for the division the Treaty principles bill has caused when it wasn’t even a bottom line for the ACT Party?
statement: We’re in an MMP environment—and a modern, mature MMP environment—and we make space for all the parties in our coalition Government.

explanation: Asked when, if ever, he will support sanctions on Israel. He answers about travel bans on extremist settlers in the occupied territories — adjacent sanctions activity, but not sanctions on Israel, and no timing is given. Answers a narrower, different question.
question: Given he has accepted the International Court of Justice ruling to issue an arrest warrant on the Israel Prime Minister, when, if ever, will the Prime Minister support sanctions on Israel?
statement: Well, we have been very clear about sanctions—travel sanctions, travel bans on extremist settlers in the occupied territories. That’s been a longstanding position and we’ve continued, through the course of this year, to ratchet that up.

explanation: Asked how the Government proposes to strengthen the three-strikes bill. She names the mechanism directly: an Amendment Paper carrying strikes from the repealed regime into the new one. Direct and complete.
question: How is the Government proposing to strengthen the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill?
statement: This week, I intend to table an Amendment Paper to the House to strengthen the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill. The amendment ensures that strikes recorded under the original three-strikes regime repealed by the previous Labour Government are carried over into the new regime. Offenders who have committed repeat sexual and violent crimes should not escape accountability for their previous actions. This change reflects our Government’s commitment to public safety by ensuring that repeat serious offenders are kept off our streets and out of our communities.

explanation: Asked what support she has received for the amendment. She identifies submitters and their stated concern, which does answer who backed it and why, though it is framed as their fears rather than as an account of support. Substantially responsive.
question: What support has the Minister received for this amendment?
statement: Submitters feared that without this change, offenders who had already received warnings under the previous regime would not face consequences under the new regime until they reoffended and received a new warning. To address these concerns, I will table amendments at the committee of the whole House stage to ensure that consistent strikes are carried through into the new regime, holding repeat offenders accountable and protecting communities from their offending.

explanation: Asked how carried-over strikes are kept consistent with the new regime. She answers the mechanism precisely: old strikes carry across only if they meet the new qualifying criteria, per the Justice Committee recommendation.
question: How is the Minister ensuring that strikes carried over from the previous regime remain consistent with the new regime?
statement: While the Justice Committee supported the reactivation of strikes from the previous regime, it also recommended that only warnings consistent with the new qualifying sentence thresholds be reactivated, and I agree with this approach and have amended the bill to clarify that strikes issued under the old regime will only be carried across if they meet the qualifying criteria of the new regime. This ensures fairness and consistency while upholding the objective of the legislation.

explanation: Asked the likely impact on prison population. She gives the estimate — 130 to 210 more prisoners over ten years — before adding a talking point. The question is answered squarely.
question: How is the reinstatement of the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Bill with these changes likely to impact on prison population?
statement: It’s estimated that the prison population will increase by 130, to 210 prisoners over the next 10 years due to the reinstatement of the three-strikes regime. We make no apologies for locking away the worst offenders for longer.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken to protect highly productive land. He names the action: rules limiting farm-to-forest conversions entering the ETS. Direct, with a partisan coda that doesn't displace the answer.
question: What actions has the Government taken to protect highly productive food-producing land in New Zealand?
statement: Last week in Southland, the Prime Minister and I announced the Government will set clear rules to limit farm-to-forest conversions from entering the emissions trading scheme (ETS). These changes deliver on a key Government commitment to protect food production for farmers while providing ETS certainty for foresters. They also address the previous Government’s failed ETS policies that incentivised large-scale conversions, created ETS complexity, and undermined our world-best primary producers. [Interruption from gallery]

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken to protect productive land. He names a specific action — the announced rules limiting farm-to-forest ETS conversions — which squarely answers it. The transcript cuts off mid-pivot to the previous Government, but the core was reached before that; the pivot costs Focus, not Forthrightness.
question: What actions has the Government taken to protect highly productive food-producing land in New Zealand?
statement: Last week in Southland, the Prime Minister and I announced the Government will set clear rules to limit farm-to-forest conversions entering into the emissions trading scheme. These changes deliver on a key Government commitment to protect food production for farmers while providing ETS certainty for foresters. They also address the previous Government’s failed ETS policies that incentivised—

explanation: Asked what policy measures were announced. He lists them: the LUC 1-5 moratorium, the 15,000 ha cap on LUC 6, the 25 percent planting allowance, LUC reassessments, Māori land exemptions and transitional exemptions. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What policy measures did the Government announce to protect food production in New Zealand?
statement: Well, the Government announced several clarifying changes to limit farm-to-forest conversion from entering the ETS. These include a moratorium on exotic forest registration for land-use classification (LUC) one through five farmland that’s actively farmed; an annual registration cap of 15,000 hectares of exotic forest registering on land six farmland; the ability of farmers to plant up to 25 percent of LUC one through five land in forestry while maintaining flexibility and choice; property-level LUC reassessments for land categorising ensuring accuracy and fairness; exemptions for certain Māori-owned land categories to honour Treaty obligations while ensuring pathways for economic development; and also transitional exemptions for landowners with intention to plant trees prior to 4 December 2024. These changes strike the right balance between protecting productive farmland and ensuring sustainable forestry development.

explanation: Asked why the changes were made. He gives reasons — the previous settings incentivised large-scale conversion, created ETS complexity, contributed to failed carbon auctions — and states what the new rules fix. That the reasons are framed as an attack on the predecessor government is a Focus matter; the 'why' was answered.
question: Why did the Government decide to make these changes to farm-to-forest emissions trading scheme rules?
statement: Well, as I said in answer to the primary question, the previous Government’s ETS policies incentivised large-scale land conversions and they created ETS complexity, which was one of the reasons why the carbon auction failed so many times before the last election. They also led to undermining world-best primary producers. These new rules address these significant challenges. They provide much-needed certainty for ETS participants, enabling farmers, foresters, and investors to plan ahead with confidence. At the same time, these changes preserve New Zealand’s ability to produce high-quality, safe, sustainable food that is demanded globally whilst protecting the rural economy.

explanation: Asked what additional measures were announced for farm and rural productivity. He names one: $995,000 co-investment expanding the Land for Life pilot in Hawke's Bay, with its purpose and projected returns. Direct answer to the question asked.
question: What additional measures has the Government announced to improve farm and rural productivity?
statement: Well, last week, I announced, with the full support of hard-working local MPs Katie Nimon and Catherine Wedd, that the Government is co-investing $995,000 to expand the Land for Life pilot project in the Hawke’s Bay. This programme helps farmers and growers plant trees on low-quality farmland so they can adapt to changing conditions, prevent erosion, and generate additional income through carbon credits and timber on low-quality farmland. We estimate that this will benefit $380 million in cumulative economic gains for participating farmers over 30 years, and $1.5 billion in avoided cost from reduced landslides. This is just another way the Government supports our rural sector.

explanation: A 'does he stand by' question, which asks for yes or no. He opens with 'Yes' and then adds supporting examples. The question was answered in the first word; the subsequent 'outcomes, not outbursts' framing does not retract it.
question: Te Arawhiti: Does he stand by his statements regarding the Māori-Crown relationship?
statement: Yes, and this Government is committed to outcomes, not outbursts over Māori-Crown relations. There are many people out there that don’t like the fact that we support over 20 Māori-led or partnered projects through the fast-track process, that we have recently offered, through Minister “Metekōura”, the Kororipo Pā to Ngāti Rēhia on behalf of Ngāpuhi, or that Matua Tararā, Minister Jones, has offered support to Waitangi, Parihaka, and Rātana through the Regional Infrastructure Fund. But we’re into action, not acting up.

explanation: An either/or: who is correct, him or the Prime Minister. He answers it explicitly — 'The Prime Minister is correct, and I am also correct' — and reconciles the two, that the relationship can be at a low ebb while still strengthening. Answering 'both' to an either/or is a real engagement rather than a dodge, though it sidesteps the forced choice, and the tail drifts into unrelated examples.
question: Who is correct: Tama Potaka, who said in response to my oral question on 7 November that the Māori-Crown relationship had been strengthened under this Government, or the Prime Minister, who said that the relationship was probably worse under this Government?
statement: The Prime Minister is correct, and I am also correct. We can have things at a low ebb but continue to strengthen Māori-Crown relations. It’s in this vein that I turn to Minister Mātauranga, Minister Stanford, with her great Māori Education Action Plan, and the work that my erudite colleague Minister Watts is doing with the Pou Take Āhuararangi or the climate change pou or the national Iwi Chairs Forum to ensure adaptation of many, many marae to climate change.

explanation: Asked which specific bill he has introduced that strengthened the relationship. He names one, the Ō-Rākau bill, which is the specific thing requested. Marked down slightly because he describes supporting and progressing it rather than introducing it, so the question's exact terms are met only approximately — but a named bill is not a dodge.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What specific bill, if any, has he introduced in his capacity as Māori-Crown relations Minister that has strengthened the Māori-Crown relationship?
statement: I continue to support and lead the ongoing progress of the Ō-Rākau bill, which was fomented as a result of Prime Minister John Key and Minister Christopher Finlayson to ensure that that particular piece of property—whenua—is returned to the three iwi around that: Maniapoto, Raukawa, and Waikato.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree with Modlik's 'so dishonest' remark, and if so is that why the Government was uninvited from iwi chairs meetings. He never says whether he agrees, and the uninvitation is not addressed at all. He corrects Modlik's job title and asserts Modlik was later supportive — adjacent to the subject and an implicit rebuttal, but the core of both parts is left unanswered. The bluntness of the fact-check is not what lowers this.
question: Does he agree with Ngāti Toa chair Helmut Modlik, who said that he found the Minister’s response to be “so dishonest that he couldn’t sit there and listen to that a moment longer”, and, if so, does he think this is the reason why the Government has been uninvited from any future iwi chairs meetings?
statement: Can I just correct the honourable member’s comments: Helmut Modlik is actually the CEO of Ngāti Toa Rangatira and not the chair of Ngāti Toa Rangatira—fact-check. The second thing is that Ngāti Toa CEO Helmut Modlik returned to the Whare the week after that particular comment and was very supportive and enthusiastic about my responses in relation to a number of questions that were of a very similar nature.

explanation: A narrow factual question: what risks did Te Arawhiti officials outline about Ministers attending Waitangi 2025. He concedes 'various risks' were outlined but names none, then pivots to the upsides of engagement and a swipe at 'acting up and outbursts'. The specific thing asked for is never supplied, and a precise question dodged is a worse failure than a broad one partly covered.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What risks have Te Arawhiti officials outlined regarding Ministers attending Waitangi 2025?
statement: A number of officials, as well as iwi leaders and others, have outlined various risks but also the enormous upsides of the continued engagement between the Ministers of the Crown, the Cabinet, and other members of this Government attending various events in the Māori calendar—but also ensuring that we are absolutely focused on delivering on the needs of Māori, rather than various acting up and outbursts that we often see.

explanation: Asked whether he will recommend the Prime Minister stop the Treaty Principles Bill progressing. He replies that he supports the Prime Minister's decision and that his party does not support the bill advancing beyond select committee — a clear statement of the position the question sought. Short of a full 1.0 because he states a party position rather than saying outright whether he will make that recommendation. Answering in te reo Māori does not affect the score.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Will he recommend to the Prime Minister to immediately stop the Treaty principles bill from progressing any further to prevent further division in this country?
statement: Kei te tautoko au i tā te Pirīmia i whakatau ai. Kāore tēnei rōpū, te pāti kahurangi, i te tautoko i te anga whakamua o te Pire Mātāpono Tiriti ki tua o te komiti arotake.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he made about Mautohe Cathedral Cove. He names the announcement and its date — restoration of public walking access, 1 December 2024 — and elaborates. Complete and on point.
question: What recent announcements has he made about Mautohe Cathedral Cove?
statement: On 1 December 2024, I attended and announced the restoration of public walking access to Mautohe Cathedral Cove in time for the summer tourist season. Mautohe Cathedral Cove plays an important role in supporting the local economy in the grand electorate of Coromandel. And this reopening is an exciting step in the region’s tourism recovery following storms and COVID-19 lockdowns. Manuhiri to the area are predicted to bring an estimated $12 million into the region annually. I’ve committed to Ngāti Hei and community leaders to ensure this first stage was delivered in time for the high numbers expected this tourist season. I want to thank everyone—Te Papa Atawhai, other officials, those that worked on it, contractors—for delivering on this commitment.

explanation: Asked how important these attractions are for regional economies like the Coromandel, specifically naming tourism and employment. Potaka supplies evidence of tourism volume ("significant numbers of international manuhiri") which speaks to half the question, but never addresses employment or the regional economy as such, and the back half of the answer drifts to weather resilience and DOC's finite resources — a different subject. It reaches the question's edge without landing on it.
question: How important are these kinds of attractions for regional economies like the Coromandel, including tourism and employment?
statement: As I regularly am reminded by the member for the Coromandel, it’s very evident at Mautohe Cathedral Cove. In the Punangairi visitors centre I recently opened at Paparoa National Park, significant numbers of international manuhiri come to see our spectacular coastal views, unique flora and fauna, and learn about tangata whenua relationships and responsibilities. Adverse weather events are increasingly impacting the safe operations of these kinds of attractions. The Department of Conservation (DOC), Te Papa Atawhai, is considering the second stage of development at Mautohe, which is intended to provide more resilient access to better withstand some of these ongoing issues. These are the challenges that we have to deal with at DOC while simultaneously applying its finite resources to protecting biodiversity, heritage landscapes, and other matters.

explanation: Asked how DOC will meet these challenges in future. Potaka answers directly with the actual mechanism — a live consultation on modernising conservation management — and lists what it covers (simplifying rules, fit-for-purpose processes, commercial/recreational benefits, land exchange flexibility) plus the submission deadline. The question is squarely engaged; short of 1.0 only because "we are consulting on options" is a step removed from how the challenges will be met.
question: How is the Department of Conservation going to meet these kinds of challenges for areas like the Coromandel in the future to ensure that we can continue to enjoy the beauty and richness of our landscapes and creatures?
statement: Thank you for that pātai. We are now actively seeking—through consultation, hui, and submissions—public views on options for modernising conservation management. This includes simplifying conservation rules, ensuring that processes are fit for purpose so businesses and others can more easily ensure quality experience, maximising benefits from commercial and recreational activities on conservation land to support nature and local communities, and increasing flexibility for land exchanges or disposals that align with conservation and community and other needs. And I’m encouraging everyone to have their say and to submit by the end of February 2025.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. "Yes, with the traditional caveats" is a direct yes with a stated qualification. One line, complete, no dodge.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, with the traditional caveats.

explanation: Asked whether Willis was not up to the job, and whether that is why the portfolio went to the person who first signed off the original ferries. Peters opens by calling the questions laughable but then engages both halves: he addresses the signed-off point (the $400.1m price that blew out to $3.2bn) and rejects the premise on Willis by calling her cancellation "the most compelling and brilliant decision". The disagreement is substantive rather than a pivot, though he never states a plain no.
question: Would the Prime Minister agree that Nicola Willis was not up to the job, which is why he’s had to give it to the person who first signed off on the original ferries?
statement: Those are, seriously, laughable questions. Of course, to answer the second question first: the Minister who originally signed off, he signed off to a total purchase price of $400.1 million, which blew out to $3.2 billion on the way to $4 billion, according to the Treasurer, in both cases. Minister Willis made the most compelling and brilliant decision when she cancelled the contract.

explanation: Asked two things: did Seymour's disclosure contradict the wishes of the PM, finance Minister and Rail Minister, and if so will he now be open with taxpayers. Peters answers neither. He argues Seymour was careful to say "approximate" — a defence of the disclosure that implies no indiscretion, which is the only reason this is not near zero. The contradiction question goes unanswered and the commitment to openness is never touched.
question: Did David Seymour’s public disclosure of indicative costings for the new ferries contradict the wishes of the Prime Minister, the finance Minister, and the Minister for Rail; if so, will he now be open with New Zealand taxpayers, given the cat is out of the bag thanks to Seymour’s indiscretion?
statement: Words matter in politics, and no more when you were acting as a Prime Minister, and Mr Seymour was very careful to point out to the media of this country that he used the word “approximate” and how wide that approximation could be.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Willis's "good deal" statement and how inferior, smaller vessels at greater cost three years later constitute one. Peters relitigates the previous contract's cost escalation instead. The implied argument — anything beats $4bn — is a sideways brush against "how is this a good deal", but he never addresses the inferior/smaller/later specifics and never says whether he agrees with the quote.
question: Does he agree with Nicola Willis, who said last year that she wants to “look taxpayers in the eye and say this is a good deal; we’re doing this right’”; if so, how does delivering inferior, smaller vessels at far greater cost at least three years later represent a good deal?
statement: If you start by turning back a deal that began at $401 million, blew out to $3.2 billion and is heading for $4 billion, and where the actual cost of the ferries would be then about 14 percent of the total plan that was announced as being a plan for ferries, you’ll get the drift of things. That’s why we are able to say to those people—

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Mainfreight CEO's characterisation of Seymour, and what measures he will take to prevent ferry privatisation. The response is a jab about the member's Celebrity Treasure Island appearance — an attack on the questioner with no engagement with either half of the question.
question: Does he agree with the CEO of Mainfreight that David Seymour’s aspiration to privatise interisland ferries makes him “a bit off the planet”; if so, what measures will he take to ensure the ACT Party can’t act on their impulse to pawn off vital national infrastructure to their mates at bargain basement prices?
statement: Look, I’m certain that when that member was getting ready for leadership at Celebrity Treasure Island, she would have learnt on the way through—

explanation: Asked whether he is confident Peters can follow through on his assurance, given Willis's lack of progress on the ferries. Most of the answer is a retrospective on the inherited contract and the previous government's spending. He explicitly declines part of it — "some questions cannot be answered now" — and closes with a promise that the rail turnaround will "very shortly be back on track", which is a partial expression of the confidence asked about. The core question is grazed, not met.
question: Is he confident that Winston Peters will be able to follow through with his assurance that “That’s not the way. If I was in charge of it, I’d have done it anyway.” when looking back at Nicola Willis’ inability to make any meaningful progress in securing new ferries?
statement: The reality is that the Minister of Finance was left with an awful prospect of something that we did not need and could not afford. And what happened downtown was they were asked to get two ferries and they decided, “Here’s a chance to add every other feel-good thing we want and make the taxpayer pay.” And then, coming to Government was a group of rational, sane, and experienced people in politics who understand the very character and nature of business. And that’s why some questions cannot be answered now and some will have to wait. But what I can promise is the turnaround and restoration of rail circa 2017 and 2020 is going to be very shortly back on track.

explanation: Asked why he could not commit to rail-enabled ferries and what "rail compatibility" means instead. He gives neither: no reason for the non-commitment, no definition of rail compatibility. Instead: "all matters are on the table", speaking to everybody, "we were the inheritors of a disaster", and the $4 billion cost. Both halves of a two-part question are left untouched — a pivot to inherited-mess talking points.
question: Why was he unable to commit to the ferries being rail-enabled and what does rail compatibility mean instead?
statement: What was being told to the media and the country yesterday was that all matters are on the table in terms of consideration. And we’ve got to ensure that we speak to everybody who can possibly help here. We were the inheritors of a disaster. Can anyone seriously believe that $4 billion or worse was what the project should have been about and what was needed to ensure rail, which is all over this country—

explanation: A loaded but answerable question: will more of Willis' responsibilities be handed to Peters? He never says yes or no, but he does engage the core by rejecting its premise — the three examples are "the inheritance", and the Minister of Finance "is doing a fine job" and will keep doing so, which functions as an implicit no. Partial engagement, ending in a jibe rather than the plain answer. Scored on the dodge alone; the sneer at "unarmed opponents" is a Civility matter and was not counted.
question: OK. Will more of Nicola Willis’ responsibilities be passed on to Winston Peters to clean up; perhaps some of the responsibilities like the rising unemployment rate, record company liquidations, and an anaemic economy ravaged by austerity?
statement: Well, could I just say that the three examples that the questioner used are all examples which were part of the inheritance the present Government received, and now we’re being blamed for it. The reality is the Minister of Finance is doing a fine job at the moment. I want to make it very clear: she shows all the signs of doing a fine job in the future in the most difficult of circumstances. And the last thing I want to say is I don’t want to have a duel of wits with a whole lot of unarmed opponents.

explanation: "When will the next Budget Policy Statement be released?" — the answer begins "I will release—" and is cut off by interruption. The opening is squarely on the question, not a pivot, but the record contains no date, so the question is not answered in the text available. Scored mid-range on that basis; the shortfall is transcript truncation rather than evasion, so it should not be read as a dodge.
question: When will the next Budget Policy Statement be released?
statement: I will release—[Interruption]

explanation: "Will these documents show any changes to the economic outlook?" — answered yes in substance: there are always changes, and recent updates have been "progressively revised downwards". She states the direction of the change and why. Slight deduction only because the answer generalises about forecasts before landing on the specific documents asked about. The partisan swipe at the previous Government's assumptions is Focus, not Forthrightness, and did not lower the score.
question: Will these documents show any changes to the economic outlook?
statement: There are always changes to the economic outlook. Forecasts are inherently uncertain and rely on assumptions that change. I have learnt that it doesn’t pay to get too attached to a particular set of numbers in the forecasts. In recent updates, the economic outlook has been progressively revised downwards, independent of Government policy. That is because Treasury has been winding back some assumptions made when the previous Government was in office that, in hindsight, were far too optimistic about future economic growth. At some point, the series of downside revisions will end, and I look forward to that day.

explanation: "Will there be any changes to the fiscal outlook?" — "Yes, downward revisions to the economic outlook will flow through to the fiscal outlook." Direct yes on the first word, with the mechanism. Answer is cut off mid-elaboration, but the question was already fully answered before the interruption.
question: Will there be any changes to the fiscal outlook?
statement: Yes, downward revisions to the economic outlook will flow through to the fiscal outlook. Forecasts of GDP, for example, affect tax forecasts. Taxes by far—

explanation: "Will there be any changes to the Government's fiscal strategy?" — she answers that the strategy stands as set out in the Fiscal Strategy Report and that two flagged reviews "could result in minor changes", then names both reviews. That is a real answer: essentially no major change, possibly minor ones. Not a full 1.0 because it stops short of committing to whether the changes will in fact be made. The length and technical detail are Specificity and did not raise the score.
question: Will there be any changes to the Government’s fiscal strategy?
statement: The Fiscal Strategy Report released in May set out the Government’s fiscal strategy. It also stated there would be two reviews, and these could result in minor changes to the strategy. One was of the multi-year capital allowance introduced by the previous Government—another tool that was used to fuel gross amounts of spending. The other was of operating balance indicators used in setting the Government’s short-term fiscal intentions. As noted in the Fiscal Strategy Report, having Crown entity deficits in the current operating balance before gains and losses measure risks undesirable fiscal policy responses. This is because some entities, like ACC, are set up to be self-funded and financially sustainable over the long run, even when running large deficits in particular years.

explanation: Two parts. Part one — does he stand by "it will be, and can be, rail-enabled"? — is never addressed; the phrase "rail-enabled" does not reappear. Part two is engaged, but by redefining the comparison: asked to beat $551m for ferries, he answers that the whole project was over $3b and that this Government will deliver "for much less than the previous Government signed New Zealand up to" — a different benchmark than the one asked about. Half-engaged on a shifted basis, so a partial. The correction about what $551m covers may well be accurate; truth is Veracity's business, not this attribute's.
question: Does he stand by his statement regarding the new Cook Strait ferries that “It will be, and can be, rail-enabled”; if so, is he confident that he can deliver them for less than the $551 million that was under contract with Hyundai Mipo Dockyard?
statement: I want to thank the member for that question because, with all the controversy going on about this issue, the facts, after all this time, are still not out there. The $551 million the member refers to relates solely to the cost of the two ferries contracted under the iReX project. It does not take into account the extra landside cost required to accommodate the ferries, which pushed the total cost of the project, according to Treasury, past $3 billion and potentially up to $4 billion. We are very confident that this Government will deliver a safe, reliable, and resilient service for much less than the previous Government signed New Zealand up to. But going back to the point, two ferries were ordered. When the whole thing was over in terms of their contracting ability, the ferries were barely 20 percent of the total project. Which part of that did those guys up there miss?

explanation: "Can he guarantee that he will announce the actual procurement of new ferries in March next year?" — he supplies the timing asked about ("by the end of March or before") but stops short of the guarantee, hedging with "working with all the speed we possibly can". The core is reached, not squarely: a soft commitment where a guarantee was sought.
question: Can he guarantee that he will announce the actual procurement of new ferries in March next year?
statement: The reality is we are working with all the speed we possibly can put behind this so that sometime by the end of March or before, we’ll be telling the public with great transparency what we’re going to do.

explanation: Two narrow questions — guarantee of 2029 arrival, and how much extra KiwiRail is spending on the current fleet. The dollar figure is never given at all. The 2029 date returns only as "2029 as a possibility", the opposite of a guarantee. Most of the reply disputes the word "nursing" and tells the member when he should have asked his questions. A narrow factual question (the KiwiRail spend) dropped entirely, which the rubric treats as the worse kind of failure.
question: Can he guarantee that the new ferries will arrive in 2029, and how much more are KiwiRail having to spend to nurse the current Interislander fleet along until new ferries arrive?
statement: First of all, they’re not nursing anything to do with the current fleet. They are going to be required to do their job with the utmost professionalism and not have the kind of thing that happened recently when it ran aground in the Sounds. That’s when the member should’ve been asking those questions, right back then. What they’re going to do is ensure that we can perhaps answer those questions well before, in terms of delivery, 2029 as a possibility.

explanation: Asked why the PM claimed a solution today but did not announce one yesterday. He does not answer why, but he does respond squarely to the premise: he didn't hear the PM say it, will check with him, and offers a reading (the solution sits within "all-up considerations"). Declining to confirm a quote you didn't hear is a legitimate response rather than a pivot, but the speculative gloss is not the requested explanation. Middle of the range.
question: Why did the Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon, say today that the Government has a solution but did not mention the solution yesterday at the Government’s announcement?
statement: Well put. Well, for a start, I didn’t hear the Prime Minister say that, and I’ll check it out with him because he may have meant that as part of the all-up considerations there is a solution in there, and that, really, is obvious as well.

explanation: Asked whether the PM's quoted statement is correct. He gives an explicit, plain refusal to confirm — "until I do, I will not confirm what I should make of it" — and per the rubric a stated refusal is a form of answering, not a dodge. Pulled down from there because he does not simply stop: he appends unprompted praise of the PM being "in the best possible space" and the "grievous fiscal wrong", drifting toward talking points on a question requiring a yes or no.
question: So is the Prime Minister correct when he said today, “But, for right now, we’ve got a good solution, and if we can improve on it, great, and if not, we move forward with that solution.”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, again, I have to confess that I did not hear the Prime Minister say that, and until I do, I will not confirm what I should make of it, other than to say the Prime Minister’s in the best possible space at this point in time, because he has got the main solution, a united Government that is setting out to correct a grievous fiscal wrong.

explanation: Asked whether Cabinet has confirmed a preferred ferry replacement option. Answered "no" outright, which fully resolves the question and moots the conditional "if so" clause. Maximally terse and unhelpful in content, but a complete direct answer — exactly the case the rubric says to score high.
question: Has Cabinet already confirmed a preferred replacement option for the Cook Strait ferries; if so, what is it?
statement: The answer to the question is no.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government is taking on stalking. Named the specific bill introduced and the penalty it creates, then gave rationale. The named action directly answers "what actions" with nothing withheld.
question: What actions is the Government taking to make stalking an illegal and jailable offence?
statement: The Government’s introduced the Crimes Legislation (Stalking and Harassment) Amendment Bill, which will make stalking an illegal and jailable offence for up to five years. Stalking and harassment pose a threat of serious harm to victims and can be a precursor to more serious and violent crime. We want to ensure that the harm victims experience is recognised and prosecuted effectively, as the current settings do not adequately respond.

explanation: Two-part question: what measures, and were they adequate. The first part is answered concretely ($48m in Budget 2024, a letter of expectation to the board). The second part is sidestepped by reassigning responsibility to the board and management rather than assessing adequacy. Half the question squarely engaged, half deflected.
question: What measures, if any, has the Government taken to ensure the financial sustainability of Whakaata Māori, and have these measures been adequate?
statement: Whakaata Māori has received nearly $48 million in Budget 2024. The Minister of Finance and I, as shareholding Ministers, have issued a letter of expectation to the Whakaata Māori board. The board chief executive and management of Whakaata Māori are responsible for its financial sustainability, and it’s important to understand that the sustainability of any media organisation is dependent on its ability to meet audience needs and providing relevant content on platforms that can be accessed by anyone anywhere at any time.

explanation: Two direct questions — does he agree the Crown-Maori relationship is "probably worse", and will ending the bulletin improve or worsen it. Neither is touched. The reply pivots to whose discretion the content decision is and expresses confidence in the board, which answers a question about decision-making authority that was not the one asked.
question: Does he agree with the Prime Minister that the Crown’s relationship with Māori is “probably worse” than a year ago, and is the Whakaata Māori news bulletin ending tomorrow after 20 years going to improve or worsen that relationship?
statement: Thank you for that pātai. The selection or the choice of moving content online is one that is at the discretion of the Whakaata Māori board and/or management, and we’ll leave that discretion with them. But I tautoko and have great confidence that the board and management will make those decisions very carefully.

explanation: Asked why he couldn't find a few million dollars for Whakaata Maori. Opens with a dismissal of the premise as "financial conjecture" — but rather than stopping there as a refusal (which would score high), it continues into shared-challenge framing, audience-needs boilerplate repeated from an earlier answer, and an unrelated aside about Olympics coverage. The "why" is never reached.
question: Why couldn’t the Minister find a few million dollars for Whakaata Māori’s budget, like the last Government did, or are the only broadcast Te Reo channel and te ao Māori evening news just the acceptable casualties of the Government’s cost-cutting drive?
statement: I won’t be trifling today with the chicanery of financial conjecture.
