And the cherry on the top, former Labour Minister for Economic Development Stuart Nash, who launched the visa in 2022, coming out to congratulate us, to say, “We got a couple of things wrong, I admit that.”, but this Government has “done a really good job on this.”

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his statements and actions. "Yes." One word, complete, no dodge.
question: E tautoko ana ia i āna kōrero me āna mahi katoa?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether the funding cut has reduced lunch quality. He never touches quality — pivots to expanded access for 10,000 more children and savings redirected to education and health. Classic talking-point substitution for the question asked.
question: Does the Prime Minister agree that his Government’s decision to cut funding for school lunches by up to 75 percent per child has reduced the quality of those lunches?
statement: I think what’s important is that we actually are expanding access for 10,000 more kids, and the money saved is actually going into delivering better resources in education and healthcare.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware the procurement change cost ~2,000 local jobs and reduced food quality. The reply ("What I'm excited about is that any savings...") answers a different question entirely; neither jobs nor quality is acknowledged even to deny them.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware that his Government’s choice to stop contracts with local providers and procure school lunches from a large corporation has cost approximately 2,000 local jobs in communities, as well as a reduction in the quality of this food?
statement: What I’m excited about is that any savings made are being redirected to our kids so they get a better education and they get better healthcare.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware how much of the food is going to landfill. He declines by referring the member to the relevant Minister. It is a plain, non-weaselly deferral rather than a talking-point pivot, which lifts it above the two preceding answers — but unlike "No, I won't release that", it neither answers the awareness question nor gives the number, so it remains a dodge.
question: I’ll repeat the question: is the Prime Minister aware of how many of these lower-quality lunches procured by his Government are now ending up in landfill as a result of them being inedible for our kids?
statement: I just encourage the member to direct the question at the relevant Minister.

explanation: Asked how many homes were approved; gives the number directly ("around a thousand") up front, then adds context. Question squarely answered.
question: How many homes has this Government approved through the Māori housing programme at the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development?
statement: Since coming into administration in November 2023, including this recent announcement, this Government has enabled the delivery of around a thousand homes for whānau to be built across the country through the Māori housing programme. The delivery of these homes will complement the delivery of 1,500 social housing homes by community housing providers by the end of June 2027 and many Kāinga Ora homes by the end of June 2026, as announced in Budget 2024.

explanation: Asked when and where; answers both halves explicitly — end of June 2027, and named priority regions (Te Tai Tokerau, Te Tairāwhiti, Waikato). Complete on both axes.
question: When and where will these homes be delivered?
statement: These 1,000 homes are intended to be delivered by Māori housing providers by end of June 2027. In terms of where: the developments are focused but not exclusive to high-needs priority rohe against the backdrop of severe housing deprivation and acute shortage of quality affordable rental homes. Priority regions include Te Tai Tokerau, Te Tairāwhiti, and the mighty Waikato.

explanation: Asked how this impacts Government housing priorities. Spends most of the answer on deprivation statistics before reaching the point, but does connect the projects to the priority (addressing inequality, sitting within Going for Housing Growth). Sprawling question, partly covered.
question: How does this impact on Government priorities for housing?
statement: We know from the 2021 housing economic survey that around half of Māori households spend more than 30 percent of their disposable income on housing costs and more than a third spend more than 50 percent. Māori are overrepresented in the cohort of whānau struggling to get into warm, safe, and affordable homes. These Māori housing projects will go some way towards addressing that inequality of opportunity. This mahi sits within the Going for Housing Growth renaissance, led by the indomitable “Manu Pīhopa”—Minister Bishop—and the “Manu Pūtea”—Minister Willis.

explanation: Asked for a submission count; states the number is confidential until tabled and gives the rule that makes it so. A stated refusal with its basis is a direct, complete response, not a dodge — marked slightly below a plain answer only because he offers no figure at all.
question: How many submissions, if any, have been received on the Gene Technology Bill?
statement: I’ve been advised by the clerk of our committee that the number of submissions received by a committee is confidential until the submissions have been tabled by the committee, as the act of tabling is the act of receiving them, and until the decision to table has been taken, it is a matter before the committee. Submissions are open until Monday, 17 February.

explanation: Asked whether the stakeholders' extension request will be brought before the committee. He answers a different question — who has authority to decide — and restates the existing 17 February deadline, so the yes/no about putting the request to the committee is never given. Engaged with the topic, missed its core.
question: Will the request of an extension period by agricultural stakeholders, DairyNZ, Beef + Lamb New Zealand, the New Zealand Meat Industry Association, and the Dairy Companies Association of New Zealand be brought before the Health Committee?
statement: It is not for the chair to decide on a matter such as that. The committee had unanimously determined that the submission period will be open until 17 February. That is longer than an eight-week period. That is where we stand on that. Thank you, ma’am.

explanation: Asked how many submissions; answers "5,342". Exact figure, nothing else needed.
question: How many submissions, if any, have been received on the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill?
statement: The committee has tabled and released 5,342 submissions.

explanation: Asked whether he would call a committee meeting to consider extending hearings. Replies that timing is for the committee rather than the chair alone, plus a confidentiality reminder — on-topic but never says whether he would call it. A narrow will-you question left unanswered.
question: Would the chairperson call a meeting of the committee to consider extending hearings for organisations that have had their submission time cut to five minutes, like Te Kāhui—
statement: Decisions on matters of timing are a matter for the committee, not the chairperson alone. I would remind the member that proceedings in committee which are excluded from the public are confidential to the committee until it is reported back to the House.

explanation: Asked how many submissions; answers "3,533". Direct and complete.
question: How many submissions, if any, have been received on the Social Security Amendment Bill?
statement: The Social Services and Community Committee has tabled and released 3,533 submissions.

explanation: Asked why no additional meeting was called. Opens by invoking confidentiality, but then does supply a reason — the committee had more time available yesterday than there were submitters to use it. Reaches the "why", though obliquely and without addressing the named organisations.
question: Why did the chair not call for an additional meeting so there would be enough time for full submissions, full 10-minute submissions, from organisations like the Child Poverty Action Group, Coalition of Community Law Centres Aotearoa, Disabled Persons Assembly, and the Salvation Army, and the individual submitters who wanted to speak to their submission but were unable to due to the decision to limit the time for the oral hearings?
statement: I would refer the member to Standing Order 390(4), which is that matters of the committee in private are confidential to that committee until it reports back to the House. But going beyond that, the committee is determined to hear as many submitters as possible. In fact, yesterday, we had more time available for submitters than there were submitters available to make oral submissions.

explanation: Asked what recent economic reports she has seen; names the Westpac quarterly forecasts and summarises them. Exactly what was asked for.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: This morning, Westpac released its latest quarterly economic forecasts. The report is called Turning the corner, and that is precisely what their forecasts show. Westpac expects growth in the economy to be positive in the December quarter of last year, and it is forecasting growth to pick up across 2025, and reach 3 percent in 2026. It also expects inflation to stay within the 1 to 3 percent target band and expects the current account deficit to narrow.

explanation: Asked for other recent reports; names the ANZ Truckometer and its January figures. The partisan closing line is a Focus/Civility matter and does not move this score — the question itself was answered.
question: What other recent economic reports has she seen?
statement: This morning, ANZ released its monthly Truckometer report for January. The Truckometer is useful because truck numbers and weights can be measured in real time and are a useful indicator of economic activity. A heavy traffic index continues to trend upwards, being 4.1 percent higher than a year ago on a three-month rolling average. That is consistent with a pick-up in economic activity over the end of last year and the beginning of 2025. I hope that members across this House welcome that, because economic growth is the best way to deliver good jobs for New Zealanders, rising incomes, and more financial security.

explanation: Asked when the next Treasury forecasts land; a caveat about forecasts precedes it, but the date is given plainly — 22 May, alongside the Budget. Preamble delays the answer without withholding it.
question: When will the next Treasury forecasts be released?
statement: I should stress that forecasts aren’t reality, and as the shifting GDP figures show, even reality can be hard to pin down and measure. But forecasts do contain valuable information for people and businesses making economic and financial decisions, including the Government. Treasury will release its next set of economic forecasts alongside the Budget on 22 May, and the next Reserve Bank forecasts will come out next Wednesday as part of the Monetary Policy Statement (MPS).

explanation: Asked what the market expects from next week's Monetary Policy Statement. Answered directly: a 50-basis-point OCR cut to 3.75 percent. The added commentary on mortgage rates doesn't detract — the core was answered squarely.
question: What is the market expecting from next week’s Monetary Policy Statement?
statement: Well, good news. The key part of the MPS is the Monetary Policy Committee’s decision on the Official Cash Rate (OCR). That is entirely a decision for the committee, but the market and most economists are expecting a 50-basis point reduction in the OCR. That would take the OCR down to 3.75 percent, supporting lower retail interest rates, lower mortgage rates, which in turn will support a growing economy.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' immediately; the subsequent economic material is elaboration on an already-complete answer, not a substitute for one.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and, in particular, the action we’re taking to get our economy moving. We know that life is still tough for a lot of Kiwis, but there are encouraging signs that we are making progress. Wages are rising faster than inflation, goods exports in December were up 17 percent, average mortgage rates have fallen now for two months in a row, and economists—as you’ve just heard from the Minister of Finance—are now predicting we’ll have more interest rate relief very, very shortly. So inflation is low, interest rates are falling, wages are rising, and our farmers and growers are kicking the recovery into gear. There’s a long way to go, but we’re heading in the right direction.

explanation: Asked why it was acceptable for a Minister to ignore warnings, deny being told, and criticise the guard. The reply refers the matter to the Speaker and pivots to an attack on the questioner over Michael Wood. The 'why acceptable' core is never engaged.
question: Why is it acceptable for a Minister in his Government to ignore repeated warnings that he’d not been given approval to drive a Land Rover up the steps of Parliament and do it anyway, to deny he’d been told not to, and to criticise the security guard who stopped him, or has he replaced standards of ministerial conduct with Health New Zealand’s new mantra of “fail early and fail often”?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, the Speaker has dealt to the issue, but we don’t need to take 12 to 16 contraventions of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood.

explanation: Asked whether Seymour's conduct meets his expectations of ministerial conduct. The reply says it is a matter for the Speaker. Deferring jurisdiction is not the same as a refusal to answer the question put — he never states whether it meets his expectations.
question: Does David Seymour’s conduct, in driving a Land Rover up the steps of Parliament, despite repeated warnings not to, along with his criticisms of the security guard who stopped him and his insistence that he should have been allowed to, meet his expectations in terms of ministerial conduct?
statement: As I’ve said before, this is an issue for the Speaker, and the Speaker has comprehensively dealt with the issue.

explanation: Same question about whether the conduct meets his expectations. Again routed to the Speaker, but 'I have every confidence in all of my Ministers' gets partway to the point by implication. It answers around the core rather than at it.
question: Does David Seymour’s conduct, in driving a Land Rover up the steps of Parliament, despite repeated warnings not to, along with his criticisms of the security guard who stopped him, and his insistence he should have been allowed to, meet, as Prime Minister, his expectations in terms of ministerial conduct?
statement: As I’ve said before, that’s an issue for the Speaker to talk about the Parliamentary Service. But with respect to my Ministers, I have every confidence in all of my Ministers.

explanation: Asked HOW driving up the steps meets his expectations of ministerial conduct. The reply reports that he has expressed views publicly and met the Minister, then restates confidence. It describes process taken, not the how that was asked for.
question: How does driving a Land Rover up the front steps of Parliament meet his expectations around appropriate ministerial conduct?
statement: I have expressed my views publicly on both the issues around the letter and the parliamentary steps. I have met with the Minister and had a positive and constructive conversation about it. And I have every confidence in all of my Ministers.

explanation: Asked whether three specific statements (McClay, Jones, Peters) meet his expectations, and if so why. He explicitly answers only 'the last part', and even there offers praise for the Deputy Prime Minister rather than a judgment on the statement. Two of the three named items go unaddressed.
question: Does Todd McClay’s statement to another MP, “You’re not in Mexico now”; Shane Jones’ statement, “Send the Mexicans home”; and Winston Peters’ statement that immigrants should “show some gratitude” meet his expectations of ministerial conduct; if so, why?
statement: Well, in answer to the last part of that question: I have huge confidence in the Deputy Prime Minister, who really believes in the Mexico - New Zealand relationship and visited the country and cares deeply about those relationships.

explanation: Asked whether Jones' funding threat meets his expectations of ministerial conduct. The reply says members spoke in the heat of the moment and have admitted their language wasn't perfect — an implicit concession that engages the subject matter, but it never states whether the conduct met his expectations.
question: Does Shane Jones’ threat to cut funding to organisations that disagree with the Government meet his expectations, as Prime Minister, of ministerial conduct, particularly given a backbench MP in the Key Government was made to apologise for doing the same thing?
statement: I think you’ve actually heard from, in all of those cases, members expressing in the heat of the moment in this place that they may not have got their language perfect, and they’ve admitted as much.

explanation: Asked whether three specific Government decisions contributed to New Zealand's lowest-ever Corruption Perceptions Index rating. The reply asserts pride in New Zealand's standing and then turns to attacking the questioner's own record. The causal question is never touched.
question: Does he think his Government’s decision to adopt tobacco lobby suggestions as Government policy, add projects sponsored by donors to the coalition parties to the fast-track list, and appoint a gun lobbyist as firearms Minister have contributed to New Zealand getting its lowest ever rating in Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index?
statement: I’m proud of the standing that New Zealand has in the world around transparency and no corruption. We are a high-performing country. I’ve just actually had meetings this morning talking about exactly that with ASEAN members as well. I’d just say to the member, it’s a little bit ironic, as I said yesterday, that we’re being lectured by someone who took 16 goes of contravention of the Cabinet Manual to get rid of Michael Wood. Meka Whaitiri didn’t even tell him she was leaving while he was travelling. We’ve got Stuart Nash with a multiple series of issues before he got sacked as a Minister, and you want to talk to me about conduct of my Ministers.

explanation: Asked whether he is surprised that more than half the country think the country is heading in the wrong direction. Rejecting the premise is a direct, non-evasive move and engages the question head-on rather than filibustering, but the actual question — is he surprised — is left unanswered.
question: If he’s willing to accept a Minister breaking the rules and driving up the steps of Parliament, accept his foreign affairs Minister and his trade Minister making anti-immigrant remarks, accept a senior Minister threatening charities, and watch New Zealand’s international reputation crumble, and his only solution seems to be to carve the country up and sell it to overseas investors, is he surprised in any way that more than half the country think New Zealand’s heading in the wrong direction under his leadership?
statement: Yeah, I reject the premise and the conflation of all those issues in that question.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about the minerals sector. Names the announcement — the launch of the inaugural Minerals Strategy at Waihī. The rhetorical flourish and jab at Labour are irrelevant to this attribute; the question was answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding the minerals sector?
statement: On behalf of our pro-growth Government, I have been to a goldmine, located at Waihī, to launch New Zealand’s inaugural Minerals Strategy. Whilst I was there it was evident that economic seeds are germinating, buds are developing; no longer will this sector be shackled in green tape. No longer will people be able to carry on talking on smartphones, dependent on minerals—rare earth minerals imported into the country—when we have them in our own country. Also it’s my pleasure to tell the House that most of the people there reminded me they never left the Labour Party; the Labour Party left them.

explanation: Asked why the Minerals Strategy and Critical Minerals List matter for the sector's growth. Offers a reason of sorts — a measurable $3 billion target by 2035, delivered via fast track — but wraps it in metaphor and partisan asides, reaching the question only partly.
question: Why is the Minerals Strategy and the Critical Minerals List so important in ensuring the continued growth of this crucial sector?
statement: So the New Zealand economy may be conceived as a quiver of arrows and each arrow must strike a target. Consequently, the $3 billion target that has been set for this sector—clear and measurable—will achieved by 2035, but it will only be achieved as we operationalise fast track, an idea that is driven by growth, prosperity, and embraced and improved, based upon the model of the Labour Party.

explanation: Asked what reactions he had seen; he gives four named reactions (the Mayor, Weenink, Woods). A soft patsy question, but the question asked is answered squarely and completely.
question: What reactions has he seen about the Brougham Street upgrades?
statement: Let me quote the Mayor of Christchurch, His Worship Phil Mauger: “This is a truly fantastic day for Christchurch.” It’s going to be a game-changer for Brougham Street. Vanessa Weenink, a very hard-working local MP, said residents in her electorate and in the wider region have told her it’s an important route. And it was great to welcome the congratulations from the member for Wigram, the Hon Megan Woods, saying it was a huge win for the local community—of course delivered under this hard-working coalition Government.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the statement, and how is zero growth 'every lever'. 'Yes, and we haven't' answers the first directly and rejects the premise of the second. Denying the premise is an engagement, not a dodge; terse, but terseness is a Specificity matter.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “We are focused on using every lever at our disposal in the housing market to improve affordability”; if so, how is opting for zero growth of the public housing stock using every lever?
statement: Yes, and we haven’t.

explanation: A 'why' question that gets an actual reason — Kāinga Ora's funding ran out. The answer is cut off mid-jab at the questioner, but the causal answer is already delivered before the swipe.
question: Why has Kāinga Ora cancelled at least 103 public housing projects—comprised of 965 much-needed houses, including 398 houses in the last five months—if the Government is using every lever?
statement: Well, Kāinga Ora’s housing funding ran out, as that member knows—well, the member may not know—

explanation: Asked to reconcile ruling out a mass sell-off with a 2,000 percent increase in sales. He offers a partial reconciliation (selling high-value stock to reinvest is not a sell-off) but never touches the 2,000 percent figure or the earlier statement. Engages the core without closing on it.
question: How does the Minister reconcile his statement ruling out a mass sell-off of State houses when he is increasing annual State house sales by 2,000 percent, compared with 2017 to 2023?
statement: Well, what we’re doing is taking a sensible approach to the housing stock that Kāinga Ora owns. For example, I don’t know many New Zealanders who think it is an economic use of land and houses for Kāinga Ora to own around 200 houses, most of them in Auckland, worth $2 million or more. Actually, what Kāinga Ora can do with those houses is divest themselves of those houses and use the proceeds to reinvest in many more houses. The Leader of the Opposition himself said, around a week or so ago, it makes sense for Kāinga Ora to sell houses in places where they don’t make sense, to sell houses where the houses have come to end of life, and that when that is reinvested in building greater density, for example, and making much more economic use of the land, that makes a lot more sense. I agree with him; that is exactly what we are doing.

explanation: Asked whether he will implement the 1,000-per-year commitment; 'We will honour that commitment' is an explicit yes. The 'including beyond 2026' clause is left unaddressed, and the trailing 'should we not trust' clause is rhetorical.
question: Will the Minister implement Nicola Willis’ pre-election commitment to building net 1,000 new public houses in Auckland every year, including beyond 2026, and, if not, should we just not trust any commitment his colleagues make to forums of over 500 community organisations?
statement: Well, it’s a three-year term in Government. We are 15 months in, and since 27 November 2023, when this Government took office and we got sworn in as Ministers, over 2,000 net new social houses have been built in Auckland. So we’re well on the way to meeting the 1,000 per year commitment and we’re 15 months in. Three-year commitments are not broken within 15 months; you’ve got to wait till the end. We will honour that commitment.

explanation: A narrow question about a specific year — will there be 1,000 net new public homes in 2026. He restates the 15-month total, reasserts the commitment generally, then redefines 'public housing' to include the community sector. Hedges around the core rather than answering for 2026.
question: Will there be 1,000 net new public homes in 2026, as promised by Nicola Willis and the Prime Minister just now?
statement: The member needs to listen to the answers I’m giving: I just said we have delivered over 2,000 net new social houses in only 15 months. Again, we will honour that commitment, because we are going to grow social housing, but if you define public housing as “houses owned by the Government”, that is one thing; we have a broader view of social housing in this country, and we think public housing includes not just Government-owned houses through Kāinga Ora but also the community housing sector. [Interruption]

explanation: 'Yes, in the context in which they were given or made' answers the standing question directly. The follow-on attack on the previous Government is surplus, and Civility/Focus failings do not count here.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given or made. In particular, I stand by my statement that economic growth means more and better-paying jobs for Kiwis. This should of course go without saying, but it is a good reminder for some members of this House who seem to believe that if only the Government borrowed more, taxed more, and spent more, nirvana would come. Well, the past Government tried that, and we are still cleaning up the wreckage it left.

explanation: Answers 'No' first, then explains. The unemployment forecasts she cites are supporting material, not a substitute for the answer.
question: When she said she was going for growth, did that mean growing the number of people that are unemployed?
statement: No. My desire is to see as many Kiwis who want to work and can work in good-paying jobs. But I would remind the member of this statement: at the pre-election update, forecasts were released for where unemployment would be right now, and rather than interpreting for myself, I will refer to a statement by the previous finance Minister, who said, “Unemployment is forecast to remain below the long-term average of 5.8 percent - peaking at 5.4 percent before declining to 4.6 percent at the end of the forecast period.” We are tracking exactly to those forecasts, and I would highlight to the member that the previous finance Minister was quick to note that we remain below the long-term average.

explanation: Asked why HYEFU has unemployment at 5.4 percent; she supplies the matching pre-election forecasts and a causal account (inflation, then rate rises, constraining activity). A real 'why' is given. Whether that account is true is Veracity, and the partisan attribution is Focus.
question: Why, then, in the HYEFU, is unemployment due to grow to 5.4 percent?
statement: Well, at the pre-election update, we had the following forecasts for unemployment. It was to be 5.4 percent in 2025; HYEFU has it at 5.4 percent for 2025. It was to be 4.8 percent for 2026; HYEFU has it at 4.8 percent for 2026. It was to be 4.6 percent for 2027, and HYEFU has it at 4.5 percent. So if the member is suggesting that somehow it is the actions of this Government that have led to unemployment, she needs to explain why her previous Government was forecasting exactly the same levels of unemployment that are occurring today. I suggest to the member that the basic economics are this: when you let inflation get out of control, when interest rates have to surge to get it back under control, you constrain activity in the economy, and you put people out of jobs. Your party chose to do that, and we’re cleaning it up.

explanation: A loaded question that presupposes she caused the recession. She rejects the causal premise and gives her account of the cause — that is engaging the core, though she never addresses the 'going for growth' framing or the liquidation figures.
question: Was she going for growth when she put the country in the deepest recession for the last 30 years with the exception of COVID, and the accelerating number of company liquidations and closures?
statement: It is a shame to me that I have to give this explanation to that member. The situation our economy is in today is not a result of actions taken by this Government. It is a result of an extraordinary set of decisions made by a Labour-led Government which saw inflation surge to generational highs, all while they spent more, which saw interest rates having to be cranked up at such pace by the Reserve Bank that it killed off all sorts of activity in the economy. So what has happened since we have come into office? Well, interest rates are coming down fast, inflation is back in the target range, and growth is forecast to return. I don’t take responsibility for making your mistakes; I take responsibility for fixing them.

explanation: Asked how the strategy was received by the sector. Jones gives a direct answer — "universal acclaim", including conservationists — before drifting into DOC/stewardship-land material that goes beyond the question. The core was reached in the first clause; the padding is a Focus/Specificity issue, not a dodge.
question: How has the strategy been received by the sector?
statement: So I can say with characteristic modesty, universal acclaim, that this is an area where even the conservationists, the green lobby realised that we cannot import minerals from the Congo whilst our own children and families know that profit, jobs, and opportunity exist in the mineral estate in New Zealand. Not only will Freddy the frog be protected because the mineral companies know that social licence is important, and guard rails will ensure that there’s the right balance, but there is also the opportunity for suitable locations in the Department of Conservation (DOC) estate to be opened up for economic development, once again within guard rails, because, as we’ve said on numerous occasions, stewardship land is not DOC land.

explanation: Asked what other steps are being considered. He names concrete ones — the Crown Minerals Amendment Bill (with drafting improvements underway), RMA changes, fast track — so the question is engaged, though most of the reply is polemic about the oil and gas ban rather than further steps.
question: What other steps are being considered to support the sector?
statement: Of course, the Crown Minerals Amendment Bill has been introduced. Some drafting improvements are being worked upon as we speak, and this will overturn the worst energy decision made in the history of New Zealand, where an entire oil and gas sector was snuffed out by juvenile, childish green thinking, which is now being proven to have been shallow and irrelevant because the power companies today are now underwriting the importation of Indonesian coal. So that shows that not only our Resource Management Act improvements and our fast track but even our friends from the gremlin community know without coal, there will both be dole and no lights.

explanation: Closed yes/no question about confidence in all his Ministers. Answered "Absolutely" — direct and complete. The subsequent fast-track advertising is surplus, but the question itself was squarely answered.
question: Does he have confidence in all of his Ministers?
statement: Absolutely, and especially all our Ministers taking action to promote growth and investment across our economy, as you’ve just heard. Just take fast track: it’s now open for applications for regionally and nationally significant projects. We’ve got roads, we’ve got energy, we’ve got housing, quarries, and aquaculture—more than a hundred projects that will make a big difference to our economy. And it doesn’t stop there, because applications are now also open for projects with significant regional or national benefits. It’s all part of our plan to get the economy moving again, and I can’t wait to see many of those projects kick off—and I hope the Greens support them.

explanation: Asked whether he has confidence in the Minister for Child Poverty Reduction given the Salvation Army findings. "Absolutely" answers it outright, and he engages the poverty premise directly with a counter-figure. Whether that figure is true is Veracity, not Forthrightness.
question: Does he have confidence in the Minister for Child Poverty Reduction to meet child poverty targets, considering the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation report found that, in the past year, most of the indicators monitored showed worsening or unchanged outcomes for children and youth?
statement: Absolutely, and that’s why this year’s Budget package takes 17,000 children out of poverty compared to the last year of the Labour-Greens Government, which put 23,000 more children in poverty.

explanation: Asked how he can have confidence given the 7AA repeal. He addresses the repeal head-on, giving the rationale (child safety paramount), which is the substantive core. He never engages the two-thirds-in-care statistic and closes on an unrelated youth-offending boast, so it is answered but not completely.
question: How can he have confidence in the Minister for Children, considering she is repealing the protections for tamariki Māori in section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act, despite the Salvation Army finding that tamariki Māori still make up more than two-thirds of children in care?
statement: Well, the clause is being repealed because we want the paramount focus to be on the safety and safeguarding of a child. That matters above and beyond everything else. I just say to the member I’m also very proud to see in the Salvation Army report that youth offending is coming down, which that Minister’s been a great advocate for.

explanation: Asked how he can have confidence in the Minister for Māori Development given the tamariki Māori hardship rate. He does supply grounds for confidence (motels, Māori social housing), which is what "how can he have confidence" asks, but the hardship-rate premise is never touched and half the reply is directed at the Opposition's record.
question: How can he have confidence in the Minister for Māori Development when the material hardship rate for tamariki Māori was found to be more than twice the rate for European children?
statement: Because that Minister—Minister Potaka—has done an exceptionally good job getting almost 2,000 children out of motel accommodation in emergency motels. He has also delivered $200 million recently to Māori social housing. And what was the record of a Labour-Greens Government for that member, who was responsible for homelessness? A lot of reports. But in 12 months, Minister Potaka has got it done, and I think the Opposition should just simply say, “Thank you. Well done, Tama Potaka, getting 2,000 children out of motels, bringing the households from 3,151 down to 591. Thank you, Tama Potaka.” That’s all that’s needed. [Interruption]

explanation: A two-part question — is he confident in the Minister, and will he admit his Government's decisions worsened food insecurity. Neither part is answered: no statement of confidence, no engagement with the quoted remark or the admission sought. The entire reply pivots to blaming the previous Government and listing measures the Opposition did not support.
question: Is he confident in his Minister for Social Development and Employment, when, in 2024, her response to questions regarding funding for food banks was: “If we’re serious about dealing with the cost of living crisis, we have to pull Government spending back.”, and, if so, will he then admit that it is his Government’s decisions that led to sharply worsening food insecurity in 2024?
statement: Well, again, what has created difficulty and hardship for New Zealanders has been economic mismanagement from a Labour and Greens Government that let inflation out of control, drove interest rates up, put the economy in recession, and helped people lose their jobs. We care about people. If you cared about working people—I don’t remember the Greens or the Labour Party supporting tax relief or Working for Families relief recently. I don’t remember you actually supporting the more funding that’s going into healthcare. I don’t remember you actually supporting the more support going to Māori social housing.

explanation: A narrow yes/no on confidence in delivering 1,000 net new public homes in Auckland in 2026. "Yeah, look" reads more as discourse filler than an answer; he cites 2,000 houses already built (not the question asked) and swerves into the last Government's record before being cut off. The questioner having to re-ask confirms the target was not hit.
question: Does he have confidence in the Minister of Housing to build 1,000 net new public homes in Auckland in 2026?
statement: Yeah, look, he’s built 2,000 houses already. What I’d say to you is what he’s not going to do—is that housing was an abject failure under the last Government—

explanation: Same narrow question re-put. "Yes, and we're on track to do that" answers it directly and completely. The following attack on the previous Government trails the answer rather than replacing it.
question: I will; thank you. Does he have confidence in the Minister of Housing to build 1,000 net additional new public homes in Auckland in 2026?
statement: Yes, and we’re on track to do that. But what we will not be doing is driving up house prices 50 percent, adding $180 of rent per week, having a fourfold increase in the social house wait-list, and putting 3,000 to 4,000 families into motel accommodation in emergency motels. We care about New Zealand’s most vulnerable folk, and we want to help them out of those situations, and that’s what we’re doing.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on Christchurch transport connections. He names the specific announcement — SH76 Brougham Street upgrades, announced last week. Direct and complete.
question: What announcements has he made regarding better transport connections in Christchurch?
statement: Some more good news in the transport space, Mr Speaker. I’m delighted to tell the House that last week we announced the delivery of upgrades to State Highway 76 Brougham Street in Christchurch—I’m sure you’re familiar with that site, sir. We are committed to delivering transport infrastructure to boost economic growth and productivity and reduce congestion. Brougham Street carries 45,000 vehicles per day, a critical route servicing the commercial, industrial, and residential areas of Christchurch.

explanation: Asked what the project delivery includes. He begins listing exactly that — intersection upgrades and corridor interventions — before the transcript cuts off. The answer is on the question; the truncation limits completeness, not engagement.
question: What will be included in the delivery of this project?
statement: It’s a very important project. It includes intersection upgrades and other interventions along the corridor to improve—

explanation: Asked how the project drives economic growth. He supplies the mechanism — improved productivity, reduced congestion, freight efficiency on the main route to Lyttelton. Slogan-heavy, but it reaches the question rather than circling it.
question: How does this drive economic growth?
statement: We are committed to delivering transport infrastructure that boosts economic growth. State Highway 76 upgrades are going to improve productivity and reduce congestion. It is the main freight route to the South Island’s largest port at Lyttelton. Getting freight to places as efficiently as possible is a key part of our plan to grow the economy.

explanation: Asked how we can trust she is going for growth given a list of adverse indicators, and why half the country doubts her. Willis explicitly takes up the second part (the poll question) and answers the trust question with a theory of her role plus Treasury/Reserve Bank endorsement, so the core is engaged — but every enumerated indicator (unemployment, construction roles, liquidations, homelessness) goes untouched and she closes by turning on the questioner. Partial engagement.
question: How can we trust that she is going for growth, when we have record unemployment, 13,000 less construction roles in the economy, record net migration, record company liquidations, more hungry children and homelessness, all because of her choices, and half the country doesn’t think she’s up for that job?
statement: Well, in reference to the second part of the question, the question that she refers to asked whether Nicola Willis will deliver good economic growth over the term of this Government. I don’t know about that member, but I have a slightly more humble view of the role of the finance and economic growth Minister. My job is to create the conditions in which growth can occur. Do you know who’s going to deliver it? It’s not you and it’s not you; it’s the New Zealanders who get up in the morning, the farmers who milk their cows and get more for their milk, it’s the businesses who choose to hire more people, it’s the entrepreneurs who decide to start a new business. This is a Government that is on their side. I am confident that with us on their side, the economy will grow, and the Treasury backs me up on that, the Reserve Bank backs me up on that. The only one who wants to say the sky is falling is you, Barb.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made about outcomes for Maori students. She names the announcement directly — te reo Maori maths resources into 310 classrooms. Squarely the thing asked for.
question: What recent announcements has she made about driving better outcomes for Māori students?
statement: Right now, for the first time ever, we are delivering, to 310 classrooms across the country, nationally consistent maths resources including student workbooks, teacher guides, and tactile materials in te reo Māori. These world-leading, curriculum-aligned resources, grounded in the science of learning, will benefit 27,000 ākonga across the country, learning in immersion settings. And as the Minister responsible for a bilingual education system that strives for excellence and equitable outcomes, I’m being intentional about replicating my English medium work in te reo Māori so that all Kiwi kids can reach their full potential.

explanation: Asked how these resources set up akonga for success. She answers the 'how' on its own terms: structured/sequenced materials raise achievement, support kaiako, reduce workload, make progress visible to whanau. Engaged and complete for the question's breadth.
question: He rawe [That’s great]. How are these resources setting up ākonga for success?
statement: Well, structured and sequenced resources grounded in the science of learning will help deliver on the Government’s commitment to teaching the basics brilliantly and raising student achievement. As we introduce the refreshed Te Marautanga o Aotearoa Curriculum, it’s essential to support kaiako with high-quality, curriculum-aligned resources. This not only reduces teacher workload but helps build confidence, capability, and consistency in the classroom. Whānau will be able to walk into classrooms and see these workbooks and know more about how their tamariki are progressing.

explanation: Asked how the decodable books and phonics check support better outcomes for tamariki learning in te reo Maori. She describes the monitoring tool and its checkpoints and closes the loop to outcomes via targeted literacy interventions. Reaches the question, though the decodable books specifically are left aside.
question: How will the new decodable books in phonics check Hihira Weteoro support better outcomes for tamariki learning into te reo Māori?
statement: From right now—this term—kura and immersion units can use newly developed purpose-built tools used to monitor student progression in reading in te reo Māori. Students will be checked at 20, 40, and 55 weeks of schooling to see how they’re progressing with identifying sounds, letters, and words, if they can segment and write words, and whether or not they can read sentences comparing basic sight words. Data from these phonics checks will help us better target structured literacy interventions to those learning through te reo Māori.

explanation: Asked what feedback she has received from schools using the resources. She supplies exactly that — a named school and a quoted letter. Direct and complete.
question: He pātai mutunga [A final question]. What feedback has she received from schools who are benefiting from these new resources?
statement: Just today, Dr Sarah Brown from Kerikeri Primary School wrote to me about the new te reo maths resources being used in her bilingual classrooms. She said, “The content is both relevant and comprehensive, making it a valuable asset for structured learning in literacy and maths.” She said, “Our tamariki are finding the resources motivating and easy to engage with. The kaiako—teachers—have reported that they are being seamlessly incorporated into daily lessons. It is clear that these resources are making a real difference in our classroom. We truly appreciate your work and dedication to the future of te reo Māori education.”

explanation: Two-part: does he stand by the statement, and if so what is his reaction to the Salvation Army finding of rising homelessness. He answers part one 'yes' (with a stated qualifier), and does react to the finding rather than sidestep it — conceding severe housing deprivation rose 10 percent while setting his own numbers against it. Both parts reached.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “those people who have a genuine need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation known as emergency housing have a pathway to do that”; if so, what is his reaction to the finding in the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation 2025 report that “there are rising numbers of people who are homeless”?
statement: Āna. Kei te tautoko au i tāku i kī ai, ki te nuinga o ngā tāone me ngā tāone nui i roto i a Niu Tīreni. [Yes. I support what I said, in the majority of the towns and cities within New Zealand.] A lot of whānau are doing it tough, and often because of the cost of living challenges and other health challenges that they face. But I acknowledge the Salvation Army and their very supportive mahi, particularly at Grandview Road in Hamilton West. I’ve not read their whole report, but note that it does report on the number of households in emergency housing being the lowest in eight years, and reducing over 80 percent. We are proud of this reduction and the reduction of over 5,000 households on the Housing Register. These reductions have happened, notwithstanding the increase in the number of people being reported as in severe housing deprivation, which rose by 10 percent between 2018 and 2023.

explanation: Asked whether he expects people to believe the need has reduced when providers say the drop is caused by his gateway policy. He never engages the causal claim at all, pivoting to the cost-of-living crisis and a list of housing programmes. The core of the question is untouched.
question: Does he seriously expect New Zealanders to believe his claim that the need for emergency housing has reduced when front-line providers such as the Salvation Army have shown that the real reason emergency housing numbers have dropped is due to his policy to stop people getting in?
statement: I do believe that most New Zealanders recognise that there has been a severe cost of living crisis that has contributed to a number of housing challenges throughout the country. A lot of people are doing it tough. There continues to be a number of avenues for people to access better housing support, whether or not that’s Housing First, Rapid Rehousing, transitional housing, or, indeed, when there’s a genuine need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation in most towns and cities for emergency housing.

explanation: Asked whether he feels ashamed celebrating the reduction given a specific rough-sleeping case. He states a feeling — 'very concerned' — which glances at the question, but never addresses shame or the celebrating, and turns to inherited legacy. Gestures at it without reaching it.
question: Does he feel ashamed celebrating the reduction in emergency housing costs when a pregnant woman sleeps not in a social house, nor in emergency housing, but in the doorway of the Salvation Army’s Rotorua base?
statement: I am very concerned by the number of people with severe housing deprivation throughout the country, and this is some of the legacy that we’ve inherited over the last 15 months.

explanation: Asked why he will not admit the drop is a crock, that his policies increased homelessness, and that this is cost-saving. He effectively refuses and says why — he disputes the premise and is proud of the reduction, citing improved tracking of where people go. Refusal-with-reason counts as engagement, but the cost-saving and homelessness limbs are dropped.
question: Why won’t he just admit that the drop in emergency housing numbers is a crock, that his policies have led to increased homelessness, and, actually, all this is about is saving costs, not housing people?
statement: I’m actually very proud—indeed whakahīhī, in a humble way—that we have committed our efforts, our energies, the taxpayers’ resources, and our networks to ensure that we can reduce the number of whānau and households living in emergency housing by over 80 percent. What I’d also acknowledge is this: when we arrived, we knew where about 50 percent of people were going to once they left emergency housing; now we know where there’s more than 80 percent. I think that’s progress; don’t you?

explanation: Asked why New Zealanders should take him seriously given three named broken promises. He offers a partial answer to 'why take us seriously' via current build commitments, but declines the specific allegations with 'we've traversed these matters' — the substance asked about is never engaged.
question: Why should New Zealanders take him seriously when he has broken his promise to build more houses than the previous Labour Government; when Chris Bishop broke his promise to build enough houses to eliminate the housing waiting list; and when this pledge, signed by Nicola Willis, promised a net increase of 1,000 State homes in Auckland but demonstrates that her word is worth nothing?
statement: We’ve traversed these matters at various times during the last hour and, of course, over the last 15 months, but what we do know is that we continue to be committed to facilitating the use of taxpayer funds to build houses through community housing providers—1,500 by June 2027, Kāinga Ora is probably 2,650 by June 2026, and the numbers of Māori housing projects that we continue to facilitate using taxpayer funds. We’re actually very proud of that. We’re also very proud of the reduction in numbers of households and whānau living in dank, dark motels in far out places like Masterton.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about Kainga Ora. He names one — ending the Sustaining Tenancies framework and the new rent debt policy — with supporting figures. Answers the question, stretching 'recent' to March 2024.
question: What recent announcements has he made about Kāinga Ora?
statement: In March 2024, this Government instructed Kāinga Ora to end its Sustaining Tenancies framework and introduce a new rent debt policy with fairer consequences for tenants who do not pay their rents and meet their obligations. Between 2017 and 2023, Kāinga Ora tenant debt increased from $1 million to $21 million, with some whānau struggling to repay their debt. We are seeing blue shoots on action with disruptive tenants, and we want to continue that momentum to ensure that Kāinga Ora tenants pay their rent.

explanation: Two-part: what the new rent debt policy is, and what difference it will make. He sets out the policy's content and the changes it produces, including earlier tenancy termination. Both parts addressed.
question: What is Kāinga Ora’s new rent debt policy, and what differences will it make?
statement: The new policy focuses on preventing tenants from getting into rent debt, acting quickly when rent payments become overdue, preventing large debts in the future. Kāinga Ora will continue to support tenants who fall behind on rent but are making genuine attempts to get back on track. Kāinga Ora will also be firm with tenants who regularly skip payments and refuse to work with Kāinga Ora to address the debt challenges. In those situations, and if necessary, Kāinga Ora will take steps to end the tenancy. The new approach will endeavour to ensure that tenants who get into more than 12 weeks’ worth of rent debt when their tenancy has ended—this means that Kāinga Ora will begin that process of ending the tenancy earlier than in the past.

explanation: Asked a direct yes/no — does he have confidence in the health system — he never says either. He describes the system's problems, blames the previous government, and lands on 'my focus is on patients'. The core of a narrow question is left untouched; this is a pivot to talking points.
question: Does he have confidence in New Zealand’s health system?
statement: Our health system is faced with significant challenges. We know that Kiwis are waiting too long to be seen at emergency departments, to receive first specialist assessments, or have elective surgeries. There has been a steep decline in delivery in recent years, exacerbated by members on the other side of the House who thought removing health targets and reforming the health system in the middle of a pandemic was a good idea. My focus is on patients and backing our health system to turn this around. New Zealanders rightfully expect access to timely, quality healthcare, and that’s what my absolute focus is on.

explanation: Opens with 'I have confidence in the commissioners and the work that they are doing' — the yes/no is delivered immediately and unambiguously. He does not engage the embedded 'failing often' quote, and the rest is an attack on the questioner's side, but the question asked was about confidence and that was answered squarely. The partisan pivot afterwards is a Focus/Civility matter, not a dodge.
question: Does he have confidence in health commissioner Lester Levy, given that under his programme of funding cuts, teams within Health New Zealand have been told that, “Failing often and failing early is the way to succeed.”?
statement: I have confidence in the commissioners and the work that they are doing to get Health New Zealand back on track and focusing back on delivering for patients. You cannot manage what you don’t measure, and they got rid of the health targets, and I just say shame on them. People are waiting too long to get an elective surgery, waiting longer at emergency departments, immunisation rates declining. They need to look at the mirror and actually look at the results that they left, and we’re fixing it.

explanation: Two-part question, both parts engaged. The count is given exactly ('one commissioner; three deputy commissioners'), and the second part's premise is rejected head-on — he says he does support the commissioners rather than accepting 'why won't he'. Marked down slightly because the answer then runs off into waiting-list statistics rather than finishing the support point, but the question was reached.
question: Can he confirm how many health commissioners there are in New Zealand and why won’t he support Mr Levy, who was hand-picked by the Prime Minister to be health commissioner?
statement: Well, there is one commissioner; there are three deputy commissioners. I support the commissioners in the work that they are doing to deliver on the Government’s priorities. I put it to you, Mr Speaker, when the last Government came into office in 2017, there were 918 people waiting longer than four months to get their first specialist assessments. When we came to office, it was 59,000—

explanation: 'He has my confidence.' The question asked him to name Levy as someone with his confidence and he does exactly that, by name, in one sentence. Direct and complete.
question: Can he state to the House and name Mr Levy as a person with his confidence?
statement: Well, Mr Levy is the commissioner of Health New Zealand. He has my confidence and he is focused on delivering on the Government’s priorities.

explanation: A jibe in the form of a confirmation question, but it does ask him to confirm something specific, and he neither confirms nor denies it — he deflects with a joke about being called many things. The response is good-humoured rather than evasive in tone, but tone is not what is measured here: the question was not engaged. Scored low rather than omitted because it is put as a question to the Minister and is answerable.
question: Can the Minister confirm: is he the “one vanilla-flavoured brown-bag common cheap solution per problem” that Health New Zealand leaders are describing in their presentations?
statement: Well, I have been called many things in my career in politics and I’m sure that’s probably not the worst.

explanation: 'Āna, yes.' The yes/no arrives in the first two words, followed by a list of instances offered as support. He also concedes the qualification that the Government will not always agree with rangatira. Directly and completely answered.
question: Does he believe this Government is upholding its obligations to Māori under Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: Āna, yes. In the past week alone, we’ve seen many examples of this Government upholding the responsibilities under Te Tiriti o Waitangi—for example, Minister Goldsmith attending Kororipo Pā to encourage the return of Kororipo Pā to Ngāti Rēhia as a catalyst for the Ngāpuhi settlement; Minister Stanford announcing structured literacy and numeracy materials in te reo Māori out at Panguru; Minister Mitchell and Minister Watts attending Mātihetihe Marae, out at Mitimiti, to activate further funding for a climate change pilot project; Minister Jones announcing various Regional Infrastructure Fund support for marae up in Northland; Minister Seymour and other Ministers, old and new, from many sides of this House, attending the reopening of Tipene in Bombay and announcing it as a charter school. As kāwana, we won’t always agree with rangatira throughout the motu. We could all do better. But the key is to keep engaging respectfully, in the same waka, in a timely manner, to uphold the responsibilities of Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

explanation: The question is a counterfactual — would this debate be happening if MPs had Tiriti training. He answers a different, easier question: that he encourages everyone to have a basic understanding. He stays on the topic of Tiriti education, which is more than a bare pivot, but the counterfactual at the core is never reached.
question: Does the Minister believe that we would be having the current debate around the Treaty principles bill if elected members of Parliament were required to undergo elementary, basic history and Te Tiriti training?
statement: I am absolutely encouraging of all members, and in fact all New Zealanders, to have a very basic and fundamental understanding of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi, a bilingual and bicultural document, which is the founding document of this great nation.

explanation: A narrow request for a guarantee about a specific bill. He uses the word 'guarantee' but attaches it to something else entirely — his quest for equality of opportunity and citizenship. The Public Works Act is never mentioned and no guarantee about land is given or refused. A flat refusal ('no, I can't guarantee that') would have scored high; substituting a different guarantee is a squarely avoided question.
question: Kei te pai, ka haere tonu. [That’s OK, I’ll continue.] Can he guarantee te iwi Māori that the proposed changes to the Public Works Act won’t result in more Māori land being confiscated by the Crown?
statement: As I have announced in this Whare on many occasions, I can guarantee that my quest, and my parliamentary experiences now and into the future, is to ensure equality of opportunity and equal citizenship and to ensure that Te Tiriti o Waitangi is recognised as the founding document of this nation.

explanation: Asked whether he would support a parliamentary commissioner for Te Tiriti, and if not, why not — so both a yes/no and a reason were requested. He answers neither, talking instead about supporting Treaty settlements. The proposed commissioner is not acknowledged at all.
question: Would he support the establishment of a parliamentary commissioner for Te Tiriti o Waitangi to ensure that all future legislation is compliant with Te Tiriti o Waitangi; if not, why not?
statement: I am absolutely committed to ensure I support Minister Goldsmith and others in this House to progress the settlements for various many historical Treaty claims. That is what I am absolutely supportive of.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about infrastructure growth; he names one — the international investment summit in March, with who is attending. A friendly question, but that is irrelevant here: it was asked and it was answered.
question: What recent announcements has he made about going for growth in infrastructure?
statement: On Monday, the Prime Minister and I announced we’ll be hosting an international investment summit in March, with about a hundred of the world’s highest-profile investors in super funds, construction companies, engineers, and business leaders coming. At the summit, we will be showing that New Zealand is a country worth partnering with and is indeed open for business.

explanation: The purpose is stated — showcasing infrastructure opportunities and the long-term pipeline, and highlighting policy and legislative changes that make investing easier. Marked down a little because it takes a lap through general growth rhetoric before getting there, but the question is reached and answered.
question: What is the purpose of the investment summit?
statement: As has been a theme this year so far, we have to go for growth, because it’s growth that provides the higher living standards that New Zealanders need. That means investment. That means being welcoming of foreign investment into New Zealand. It means saying yes to investment, innovation, ambition, and growth. We will be showcasing upcoming infrastructure opportunities for partnership and investment, as well as the Government’s long-term infrastructure pipeline, and that pipeline is very important to give stability and certainty so that people have confidence in investing in New Zealand. We’ll also be highlighting some changes to policies, regulation, and legislation to make it easier to invest here, and we’ve already seen some of the changes under way by my good colleague Erica Stanford and other Ministers already, and there’s more to come.

explanation: Asked which other sectors will be involved and he lists them: renewable energy, advanced transportation, cleantech future fuels, resources, aquaculture, plus a feature on the Māori economy. The question asked for sectors and sectors were named.
question: What other sectors will be involved in the summit?
statement: It’s not all about the Government. Actually, it’s ambitious Kiwi businesses and iwi who are looking for better opportunities for them and New Zealanders. So the summit will be covering some growth sectors that the Government is excited about: renewable energy, advanced transportation, cleantech future fuels, and, of course—and Minister Jones will be pleased about this—the resources sector and the aquaculture sector, which, unlike other members in this House, the Government sees as real areas for potential future growth. We’re also very excited that there will be a real feature on the Māori economy at the summit, and we have some exciting opportunities lined up there as well.

explanation: Asked why NZ needs the summit. Bishop gives an actual answer to 'why': the country's failure to embrace opportunities has produced weak growth, and the summit signals NZ is open for business across infrastructure, energy, aquaculture and resources. The rhetorical framing ('saying no is easy') is a preamble, not a substitute — the core of the question is reached.
question: Why does New Zealand so desperately need this summit?
statement: Well, saying no is easy. Actually, what New Zealand needs to do is say yes to more things. Our 30-year failure to embrace opportunities has produced anaemic levels of growth and lower productivity growth than we need to drive higher living standards. So this summit is about putting down a marker to the rest of the world and saying that New Zealand is here, we have fantastic opportunities here across infrastructure, across energy, across aquaculture, across resources, and we are here and ready to do business with the rest of the world, and we’re going to start saying yes to these opportunities so we can grow our economy.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. He says yes. The 'usual caveats' formula is a standard qualifier rather than an evasion; the question gets a clear affirmative.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: With the usual caveats, providing the premise is made in the same and providing the facts were made in the same, yes.

explanation: Asked whether driving a car up Parliament's steps meets the standards expected of an incoming Deputy PM. He refers the matter to the Speaker instead of answering. This is not a refusal ('I won't say') but a redirection that leaves the question entirely untouched.
question: Does driving a car up the steps of Parliament, after repeatedly being told that was prohibited, meet the standards that are expected of an incoming Deputy Prime Minister?
statement: I think the answer to that question lies with the person three over to your right in the Speaker’s Chair.

explanation: Same question repeated. 'All the comments the Prime Minister wishes to make on this matter have been made' points elsewhere and offers no view on whether the conduct met the standard. Nothing of the question is engaged.
question: Does driving a car up the steps of Parliament, after repeatedly being told that was prohibited, meet the standards that are expected of an incoming Deputy Prime Minister?
statement: All the comments the Prime Minister wishes to make on this matter have been made. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether advocating for a suspect in a murder investigation meets the standards expected of an incoming Deputy PM. He engages the substance by disputing the premise — the standard applies to sworn Ministers, and these acts were done as a backbencher, so different criteria apply. That is a real response to the standards question, though he never states a verdict and closes by deflecting to another member.
question: Does advocating for a potential suspect in a murder investigation, thereby undermining the justice system’s independence, meet the standards that are expected of an incoming Deputy Prime Minister?
statement: The reality is that the judgment being made on that standard is set against the actions of a sworn Minister of the Crown. In this case, they weren’t; they were made by a backbench member of Parliament, and the standards and criteria are massively different. I suggest you ask Willie Jackson about that because he’d be very knowledgable about it.

explanation: Asked whether directing an abuse survivor to the party's lawyer rather than police meets the expected standards. He concedes the proper place of complaint lay elsewhere, which touches the question, but then dissolves it into 'people have their own experience' and 'not everybody's a lawyer' without saying whether the standard was met.
question: Does directing a child sexual abuse survivor to speak with the ACT Party’s lawyer, rather than the police, after being abused by the ACT Party’s then president, meet the standards that are expected of an incoming Deputy Prime Minister?
statement: It has been pointed out that the proper place of complaint lay elsewhere. But, you know, people have their own experience, they all learn, and not everybody’s a lawyer.

explanation: Asked whether he will loosen rules for foreign non-residents buying existing homes. 'Not a matter that's currently on the present agenda' is a partial answer — it indicates no current plan without committing to yes or no on will-he — and the rest pivots to Labour's 2002 Singapore deal.
question: Will he loosen the rules to allow foreign non-residents to buy existing homes in New Zealand?
statement: The reality is that that is not a matter that’s currently on the present agenda. The last time that happened, of course, was in 2002, when the Labour Party did precisely that in their free-trade deal with Singapore.

explanation: Asked which of two conflicting ministerial positions on English-language requirements he agrees with. He rejects the premise (the two were speaking about different matters), which is a legitimate form of engagement, but he never indicates his own position and finishes with a joke about choosing between geniuses.
question: Does he agree with Winston Peters that “English should be a basic requirement of anyone coming into the country, unless they are genuine refugees”, or does he agree with Erica Stanford that it’s insulting to expect that of migrants who are “worth millions of dollars” and that “we don’t need them to speak English”?
statement: Well, the reality is that those two Ministers were making statements about different matters. It’s an awful conflict when you have to choose between two geniuses!

explanation: Asked which industries' perceived interference explains NZ's worst-ever corruption index rating. He names none of the listed options and instead argues NZ's historical ratings were unjustified. Attacking the instrument glances at the question but leaves the 'which of these' core unanswered.
question: Is New Zealand’s worst ever rating on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index a result of perceived interference from the tobacco industry, the mining industry, the fishing industry, the real estate industry, the childcare industry, the pharmaceutical industry, or all of the above?
statement: With the greatest respect, and this is a more personal answer, the reality is that over many years the New Zealand rating was unjustified. Smack in the middle of the wine-box inquiry and the BNZ inquiry and every other fraud I saw, we were still rating number one and we’ve only slipped to number four.

explanation: Same question. This answer engages more of the list — fishing (new control regime), tobacco (complaining about changes, so not corrupt) — and effectively argues 'none of the above, the index is artificial'. That reaches part of the question, though most of the listed industries go unaddressed and no direct attribution is made.
question: Is New Zealand’s worst ever rating on Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index a result of perceived interference from the tobacco industry, the mining industry, the fishing industry, the real estate industry, the childcare industry, the pharmaceutical industry, or all of the above?
statement: The reality is that New Zealand is at number four at the present moment. The fishing industry has had the most comprehensive control regime set around it, announced the other day, and I’m shocked it got so little publicity, being the most comprehensive plan, and supported massively by people of this country who are concerned about the fishing industry. As for the tobacco industry, if they’re complaining massively about the changes, then they can hardly be guilty of any corruption—only someone who doesn’t understand how the world works would make those allegations now. The other thing I want to say is, when we were at the top of the so-called index, then the sharemarket crashed, of course—a period that member might remember—and of the world’s worst 10 we had the sixth, and of the world’s worst, we had all four. So here we go again with a judgment that was artificial all along, and rather than make these proud boasts, I think our country should be doing better to be a more corruption-free land.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made about the traffic light system. She states exactly what was announced: two non-financial sanctions, and what each requires. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has she made about the new traffic light system?
statement: Last week, I announced the addition of two non-financial sanctions to the traffic light system. Non-financial sanctions allow job seekers who fail to meet obligations for the first time to continue receiving their full benefit payments while still being required to complete activities such as the new Report Job Search, where job seekers must perform a minimum of three job-search activities every week for four weeks and report this to the Ministry of Social Development, and upskilling, where job seekers must attend and participate in employment-related training for at least five hours a week over a four-week period. It’s important that beneficiaries who can work are taking reasonable steps to re-enter the workforce or remain work-ready, and that consequences exist for those who don’t.

explanation: Asked why the Government is introducing these sanctions. She gives the reason — to reduce welfare dependency and get more people into work on the view that a stronger economy depends on employment. The 'why' is squarely answered.
question: Why is the Government introducing these sanctions?
statement: This Government believes that a stronger economy depends on more people being employed. By introducing these sanctions, we aim to reduce welfare dependency and increase the number of Kiwis entering the workforce and then sharing in the benefits of economic growth.

explanation: Asked the goal of the sanctions. She states the goal outright — accountability, reasonable work-search effort, skills — and adds the retained-benefit point. Squarely engaged; the extra promotional framing doesn't dodge anything.
question: What is the goal of adding these sanctions?
statement: The goal is to hold beneficiaries accountable and ensure that they are making reasonable efforts to seek employment. The sanctions also aim to help individuals gain skills that will improve their chances of finding work so that they can be part of New Zealand’s economic growth. It also means, and I remind the House, that job seekers can retain the full amount of their benefit instead of it being reduced.

explanation: Asked how the traffic light system is tracking. She gives tracking figures directly: 33,000 off jobseeker, 22 percent increase, and the compliance/orange/red breakdown. Direct and complete.
question: How has the traffic light system been tracking?
statement: There have been some really positive early results. Between July and December, more than 33,000 people moved off the jobseeker benefit into work, a 22 percent increase compared to the same period in 2023. It’s also positive to see that 98.6 percent of clients are complying with their obligations, while only 0.4 percent are in orange and 1 percent in red.

explanation: Asked (a) whether she agrees with the Salvation Army's claim that access was reducing and (b) failing that, her expectations for how applications are assessed. She never says agree or disagree; 'eligibility requirements haven't changed' is an implicit answer to (b) only, and the bulk of the response pivots to inflation and the inherited cost of living crisis. Half the question reached, the core comparison avoided.
question: Does she agree with the Salvation Army’s State of the Nation 2025 report that “During 2024, access to hardship grants was reducing as Work and Income tightened eligibility for assistance, at the same time as the number of children living in families needing this assistance was increasing”; if not, what are her expectations for how applications for hardship assistance are assessed and granted?
statement: Eligibility requirements for food and other special needs grants haven’t changed, and I have no plans to change them. As I said in the House yesterday, we have seen a reduction in applications, so I would encourage people who need help to get in touch with the Ministry of Social Development (MSD), as there is assistance available. Times remain tough due to the cost of living crisis we inherited, and while we’ve worked hard to reduce inflation from 7.3 percent to 2.2 percent, and that’s helping to bring costs down and put more money in people’s pockets, we do recognise that some are still feeling the pain of the cost of living and high inflation. As interest rates continue to reduce and the benefits of this start to flow through, more New Zealanders will feel the positive impact of the hard work we are putting in. This will grow the economy and help more people into work.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: does she disagree with the Salvation Army that access to hardship assistance was decreasing. She answers a neighbouring question instead — eligibility rules unchanged, applications declined — which is about demand, not access, and never states agreement or disagreement. Partial engagement with a question that had a one-word answer available.
question: Does she disagree with the Salvation Army, who, in their report, stated that “access to hardship assistance was [decreasing]”?
statement: As I said in my primary answer, eligibility requirements have not changed, but I recognise that demand and the number of applications has declined.

explanation: Asked whether it is acceptable for a family in immediate need to be declined a grant, and if so why.
