We’re putting more money in, we’re fixing the system, and we will deliver health outcomes that you failed to do in six years, including three years with an absolute majority.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all the statements and actions of his Government. "Yes" answers it completely; the housing material that follows is volunteered elaboration, not a substitute for the answer.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to deliver affordable housing to help Kiwis with the cost of living. For many, the cost of housing is incredibly difficult; it’s their biggest expense—whether it’s their mortgage payments each week or whether it’s their weekly rent. The good news is: whichever way you look at housing, we’re actually making sure we’re bringing interest rates down so that Kiwis have more money in their pockets, we have stable rents, we have a reduction in people on the social housing wait-list, and, most importantly, we have 2,000 kids out of emergency housing in good, safe, dry homes.

explanation: Asked how, if at all, he will ensure growth is fairly distributed. Tax relief is named, which brushes the distribution question, but the bulk is a list of things the Opposition did not support. The mechanism for fair distribution — the core of the question — is never given.
question: How, if at all, will the Prime Minister ensure that this growth that his Government is chasing will be fairly distributed among New Zealanders?
statement: Well, what we’re not going to do is run the economy into the ground like the Labour-Greens Government did in the last administration. That’s why we are working hard to give tax relief to everyday working New Zealanders. But I don’t remember the Labour and Green Government supporting that. I don’t remember the Labour-Green Opposition supporting an increase of $17 billion into our healthcare system. I don’t remember the Labour-Greens Government fixing emergency housing, and saying it’s OK to have 3,200 households raising their kids in motels. We find that unacceptable.

explanation: A deliberately narrow yes/no: does he think it is the job of Government to reduce inequality. He restates the job of Government in his own terms (lifting incomes), which implies a declining answer without ever giving one. A pointed question was reframed rather than answered, and the narrowness of the question makes the miss worse.
question: I’ll put it simply: does the Prime Minister think that it is the job of Government to reduce inequality?
statement: It is the job of Government to lift incomes for every New Zealander, and that’s what we are doing. We are offering them tax relief, inflation relief, and interest rate relief. We are managing the books well because if you care about vulnerable people, if you care about low and middle income, working New Zealanders, you run the economy well—not into the ground like you lot did.

explanation: Asked why the top 10 percent hold almost 60 percent of the wealth after years of growth. The answer criticises the premise of the question, praises ambition, and pivots to the Opposition having no policy ideas. No explanation is offered, and the wealth-share figure is never engaged.
question: Why, after years of increases in economic growth, do the top 10 percent in this country hold almost 60 percent of the wealth?
statement: I mean, again in that question, what you see is not celebrating people who have been successful, you know? That is good. We want more ambition in this country. We want more aspiration. We want people to be successful; we want to celebrate that. That is a good thing. We have a fair tax system, as has been said before. But I’m telling you, what’s interesting is: what’s the one policy idea we’ve had from the Opposition? We actually haven’t had one. What we’ve got is a conversation about a capital gains tax or a wealth tax, and Chris Hipkins won’t make a decision on it, but that’s all that they want to talk about. I tell you, that’s not going to work for New Zealand.

explanation: Asked why he is convinced benefits will trickle down given the OECD's caution against relying on that. He never engages the OECD point, but the closing assertion — that growth is what helps low and middle income New Zealanders get ahead — is a bare direct response to the trickle-down premise. Partial engagement, with the specific challenge sidestepped.
question: Why, in the face of the OECD stating—and I quote—“Focusing exclusively on growth and assuming that its benefits will automatically trickle down, may undermine growth in the long run.”, is the Prime Minister convinced, somehow, that, this time, it will all just trickle down?
statement: What I’m convinced of is that running the economy like Labour-Greens did over six years, into the ground—we need growth in this economy. That is not a conversation point any more. We need to grow so that we can actually create higher-income jobs, more jobs, put more money into people’s pockets so they can deal with the cost of living. That’s what we’re focused on each and every day in this Government. That member may not believe in growth, but growth is actually what helps low and middle income vulnerable New Zealanders get ahead.

explanation: Asked, in loaded form, whether going for growth means growing inequality, poverty, homelessness and emissions. He answers the "what does it mean" core by rejecting the framing and stating what he says it does mean, which is a genuine response, but none of the four named consequences is addressed. Roughly half the question is engaged.
question: By going for growth, does the Prime Minister mean growing inequality, growing poverty, growing homelessness, growing climate-changing emissions?
statement: It means lifting incomes for New Zealanders, which is what they care most about so they can get ahead, they can work hard in a country, get ahead, they can actually feel safe in a country, they see great education, great healthcare. That’s what we want for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked WHY coal was added to the critical minerals list, given coal is a fossil fuel not a mineral. Luxon praises the Minister, cites 37 minerals / 21 domestic, then offers a partial rationale — coal and metallurgical coal are 'really important for our mining industry'. That gestures at a reason, so it is not a pure pivot, but it never engages the categorical objection at the core of the question. Partial engagement.
question: Why has he added coal to the critical minerals list when coal is not a mineral but a fossil fuel?
statement: Well, I mean, I think the Minister’s done a very good job, actually, identifying 37 critical minerals, of which 21 of them we think are actually in this country. Importantly, coal and metallurgical coal and gold are actually really important for our mining industry.

explanation: Asked whether he is AWARE of a specific emissions comparison (66.5Mt from one fast-track project vs a 42Mt reduction commitment). The answer never says aware or unaware and never touches the numbers; it pivots entirely to wholesale electricity prices and the previous Government's oil and gas ban. A narrow factual question squarely avoided.
question: Is he aware that the coal set to be mined by just one of his fast-track projects would increase emissions by 66.5 million tonnes, meanwhile his latest international commitment to reduce emissions is just 42 million tonnes?
statement: Well, I just say to that member: the bumper sticker of the Labour-Greens Government of ending the oil and gas ban led to wholesale electricity prices of $1,500 last winter. That actually put huge pressure on businesses and people lost their jobs on the back of that. So, actually, a consistent, good energy policy that actually helps grow our economy, doubles the amount of renewables we have in it, but keeps our lights on with affordable, abundant electricity is exactly what we’re doing in this Government.

explanation: Asked why the PM thinks Rod Carr made a particular statement. The response calls the conversation 'outrageous' and pivots to economic growth and electricity prices, including a counter-question to the Greens. The Carr remark is never addressed. A real supplementary question (not procedural), so eligible, and it is a clear dodge.
question: Why does the Prime Minister think that Rod Carr, former chair of the Climate Change Commission, in his final hearing before this Parliament, said that those who promote the combustion of fossil fuels are “committing crimes against humanity”?
statement: I mean, this is an outrageous conversation we’re actually having here, because this country needs to grow. We need to have economic growth. Are the Greens not for economic growth? I mean, what’s the position? You have to grow an economy. You need to have energy to do it. And we need to make sure we make it affordable, abundant, and we’re not having $1,500 wholesale electricity prices next year—period. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what the benefits for biodiversity are. The answer names the $19m investment and enumerates the specific biodiversity outcomes — wallaby containment, deer/goat control, predator control for southern dotterel, wilding pine removal. Squarely on the question and complete.
question: What are the benefits for biodiversity?
statement: We are investing $19 million into protecting biodiversity by reducing the spread of pests, predators, and weeds. This includes stopping the spread of wallabies in renowned and spectacular places like the Te Arawa Lakes district; managing deer and goat populations, especially nanny goats, in national parks and visitor areas like the Kaimanawa Range to allow nature to thrive; targeted predator control to protect native species, especially the critically endangered tuturuatu, or southern dotterel birds, in Rakiura National Park; and stopping and removing wilding pines from our majestic landscapes like the Mackenzie Country.

explanation: Asked what the benefits for tourism are. The answer states the benefits (jobs supported, export receipts, relieving pressure at popular sites) and backs them with the $11m infrastructure programme. It leans more on what is being spent than on the benefit itself, but it reaches the question. Note the answer's detail is a Specificity matter and did not raise this score.
question: What are the benefits for tourism?
statement: Tourism is a critical part of this Government’s focus on economic growth and supports nearly 200,000 jobs—and, might I say, 15,000 jobs in Māori tourism businesses. Improving tourism infrastructure is good for the economy, helping export receipts and mahi. To manage pressures at our most popular visitor sites, the Government is investing $11 million, including upgrades to huts in Aoraki / Mount Cook; Rangitoto Island, Ngā Pona-toru-a-Peretū; and Motutapu Island, Te Motutapu a Taikehu; safety upgrades to various cable structures including suspension and swing bridges—we’ll build those and get through them—and investment at Goat Island, Te Hāwere-a-Maki, to improve beach access, car-parking, and reflect the area’s significant cultural heritage. “Mook” Hohneck will be pleased. These investments will help a top-notch manuhiri experience at some of our most popular visitor sites.

explanation: Asked what the benefits for international visitors are. The answer identifies the problem (infrastructure not keeping pace) and names the benefits — health and safety, recreation, wairua, better experiences at Aoraki and Tongariro. Thinner than the previous two and partly hedged into 'and all New Zealanders', but it answers the question asked.
question: What are the benefits for international visitors?
statement: Our manuhiri infrastructure is not keeping pace with growing tourist numbers or providing the experiences expected at world-renowned sites like Aoraki and Tongariro. Investments in improving visitor or manuhiri experiences benefit international tourists and all New Zealanders now and into the future for their health and safety, their recreation, and their wairua. Kia ora tātou.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the economy. The answer immediately names one — the Reserve Bank's 50 basis-point OCR reduction announced shortly before. The transcript is cut off mid-sentence by an interruption, but the answer reaches the substance before the cut, so this is scored on a complete response.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: I understand that a short time ago, the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee announced a 50 basis-point reduction—[Interruption]—in the official cash rate (OCR)—

explanation: Asked what the Reserve Bank said about FUTURE OCR changes. The answer goes straight to the revised forward track and states the bank is signalling faster reductions than previously. Directly on the core of the question.
question: What did the Reserve Bank say about future OCR changes?
statement: This is where it gets interesting, because today’s 50-point reduction was widely anticipated. Probably of more interest to economists and financial markets is the bank’s revised track for the official cash rate going forward. In today’s release, the bank is signalling faster reductions than it has previously—

explanation: Asked what this means for ordinary New Zealanders. The answer addresses exactly that — falling mortgage rates, the 55 percent of lending floating or short-fixed that benefits soonest, and the estimated household spending effect. Direct and complete.
question: What does this mean for ordinary New Zealanders?
statement: Falling mortgage rates boost household budgets when borrowers are on floating rates or when they come to refinance a fixed mortgage. Currently, 55 percent of mortgage lending is either floating or is fixed for six months or less, so that means that many people are set to benefit when the official cash rate falls. Infometrics has previously estimated that by the end of this year, as a result of lower mortgage rates, households will have another $45 million to spend every week. That is, of course, good news for families who, in recent years, have suffered a protracted cost of living crisis.

explanation: Asked what the Reserve Bank's latest economic FORECASTS show. What is on the record is a reply to an interjection ('that was an extremely astute interjection') conceding there are always risks to the outlook — it never reports what the forecasts show. Scored on the record as captured; note this excerpt is truncated mid-sentence, so if the response continued past the cut this score is soft.
question: What do the Reserve Bank’s latest economic forecasts show?
statement: Obviously, that was an extremely astute interjection, because, yes, there are always risks to the economic outlook—

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. The first word is 'Yes' — a direct, complete answer to a yes/no question. The rest is partisan talking points about the previous Government, but that is a Focus and Civility matter and must not pull down Forthrightness; the question was engaged, not dodged.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to take pressure off inflation and interest rates and to support working Kiwis with the cost of living. The last few years have been incredibly tough with all the wasteful spending, the high inflation, the high interest rates, the low economic growth and the rising unemployment—thanks to the last Labour Government. We are working hard to take sensible economic action, sensible spending, personal tax relief—which Labour never supported—inflation relief, interest rate relief, and I just wish the Leader of the Opposition would celebrate with us the great news for working New Zealanders today.

explanation: Asked for the difference between the Health Assurance Unit and the task force. The reply only restates who set the Unit up and never draws any distinction between the two bodies — a narrow factual question left unanswered, though it does at least stay on the named subject.
question: Can the Minister be more specific about the difference between the Health Assurance Unit he just spoke of that has been set up by the Public Service Commission and the task force that he spoke of?
statement: Well, the Health Assurance Unit is what the Public Service Commission has set up.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the quote, and why fund a task force rather than clinical staff. He gives a partial answer to the second part (the team advises him over three months) but never says whether he stands by the statement, and closes on ED-wait-time talking points about the previous government.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “What I won’t stand by is bureaucracy, bureaucratic processes, and constant centralisation”, and, if so, why are people being appointed to a new task force to fix the Government’s failing plan when this money could have been better spent hiring doctors and nurses to staff New Zealand’s struggling emergency departments (EDs)?
statement: Well, the Public Service Commission has set the health assurance team up to provide advice to me over three months. I would also note that in 2020, the last Government established the health transition unit housed within the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to design and advise on the health system reforms. What I would say is we’re focused on getting results and performance out of the system after years of decay by the last Government and, for example, ED wait times, which declined from 89.2 percent of people being seen within six hours when National left office to 67.5 percent when Labour left office. We’re focused on outcomes.

explanation: Asked whether the Government will admit running the health system is not as simple as running an aeroplane. He labels the question cynical and pivots entirely to performance statistics under the previous government; the admission asked for is never addressed either way.
question: Can his Government finally admit that after firing the Health New Zealand board, overseeing a health leadership exodus, and appointing one man who has delivered nothing but cuts, running the health system is not as simple as running an aeroplane?
statement: What a cynical question from the Opposition. What I would say is we are focused on outcomes and delivery and results after six years of reorganising the bureaucracy and seeing decline, decline, decline. ED wait times: declined. First specialist assessments: declined. Elective surgeries: declined. Children’s immunisations declined under their watch. We’re focused on results; we increased the funding for Health New Zealand. That’s what this Government is focused on doing.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to restore primary-sector confidence and growth. He engages it — common-sense policies lifting productivity and farm-gate returns, reducing spending to bring inflation and interest rates down — plus evidence that confidence has risen. Some of the reply reports the outcome rather than the doing, but the core is met.
question: What is the Government doing to restore confidence and drive growth in the primary sector?
statement: We’re turbo-charging growth to return confidence to the primary sector through common-sense policies that are driving up productivity and driving up farm-gate returns. The latest Federated Famers confidence survey has seen rural confidence rise to the highest level in over a decade, with one of the largest one-off improvements of 68 points since the question was introduced in that survey in 2016. The Government has been reducing wasteful spending to bring down inflation, which in turn means lower interest rates for our farmers and every New Zealander.

explanation: Asked what has been done to improve farmer confidence. He answers squarely: over 20 actions to cut red tape, then names four of them. Directly responsive to the question as put.
question: What has the Government done to improve farmer confidence?
statement: Farmers and growers are the backbone of the New Zealand economy, contributing over $10 billion in export revenue for New Zealand. This is why we are laser focused on better rules and getting the cost of these rules down. Already, the Government, in slightly more than 12 months, has taken over 20 actions to slash red tape and get Wellington out of farming. This includes restricting full farm-to-forest conversions, taking agriculture out of the emissions trading scheme, working to replace the National Policy Statement for Freshwater Management, and a commitment to not close down farms or send jobs and production overseas.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to further support farmers. He answers with what is planned this year — regulatory burden, water storage and irrigation, trade access, Te Mana o te Wai. On point throughout.
question: What is the Government doing to further support farmers?
statement: This year, we are going for growth in the rural sector by further slashing regulatory burden and reducing on-farm costs, boosting productivity by improving water storage and irrigation, we’re improving trade access, rebalancing the hierarchy of the obligations of Te Mana o te Wai, and strengthening support for our rural communities, because we back rural New Zealand.

explanation: Asked how supporting farmers is key to economic growth. He opens on forward plans before reaching the link asked about — 80 percent of goods exports, 360,000 jobs, hence crucial to the economy. It arrives at the question's core after a detour.
question: How is supporting farmers key to economic growth?
statement: Well, looking ahead, we’re focused on leveraging trade opportunities, including the recently concluded United Arab Emirates and Gulf Cooperation Council agreement, and delivering more permissive regulatory conditions for farmers to be able to meet their obligations whilst growing their businesses. The primary sector generates more than 80 percent of New Zealand’s goods exports and directly employs almost 360,000 people in New Zealand. Ensuring its continued success is crucial to every Kiwi’s economic future. The positive momentum we are seeing now is just the beginning; when rural New Zealand is confident, all of New Zealand can be confident.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about Māori development. He describes a specific recent event — last Friday's launch of the BERL report on Māori tourism — which is responsive, though it is one launch attended rather than a survey of his announcements.
question: What recent announcements has he made about Māori development?
statement: Last Friday, it was my pleasure to attend the launch on Tumunui land, south of Rotorua, at Te Pā Tū, the launch of the Business and Economic Research Ltd report on the value of Māori tourism. This report provides a fact-based and data-driven analysis of the economic contribution of Māori tourism to the New Zealand economy while also highlighting the unique aspects that define Māori tourism experiences. As you know, nature and culture are major drawcards for international tourists, and the report observes that Māori tourism emphasises the relationships between Māori; whenua, or land; and manuhiri, visitors.

explanation: Asked why Māori tourism is so important. He answers directly: second-largest export earner, $1.2 billion of productive GDP in 2023, 23 percent growth since 2018. The question's core is engaged head-on.
question: Why is Māori tourism so important?
statement: The Prime Minister is clear that our Government’s focus is on economic growth, and tourism makes an important contribution as New Zealand’s second-largest export earner. The Government is firmly focused on creating the right conditions for businesses, organisations to grow, to create jobs, and to lift incomes. The report identifies that, in 2023, Māori tourism contributed $1.2 billion of productive GDP to the New Zealand economy, an increase from $975 million in 2018. That 23 percent growth is a clear indicator of the great value-add of Māori tourism to the tourism sector and the wider economy.

explanation: Two-part question: which resourcing/clinical-capacity factors HNZ cited, and what was being done about them at the time of the June 2024 referral. The first half is engaged squarely and on the record (coding error; operational pressure from an extended clinician absence). The second half — what was being done at the time — is never reached; the remedial action described (HNZ investigation, HDC referral) is all after the fact. Substantively answers about half of what was asked.
question: What were the departmental resourcing and clinical capacity factors that Health New Zealand said led to delays in the assessment of Daniel Walker’s cancerous lump on his testis, and what, if anything, was being done to address these factors at the time of Mr Walker’s referral to Nelson Hospital’s urology service in June 2024?
statement: This case is deeply regrettable, and I acknowledge the significant distress it has caused Mr Walker and his family. I’m advised that the delay in treatment resulted from a combination of factors. Initially, the referral was triaged as urgent, but a human coding error led to it being downgraded, causing a delay. I’m also advised that Health New Zealand is investigating this incident to prevent this error from happening again. Additionally, I’m advised that Health New Zealand has identified that operational pressures in the system played a role in this situation because of the unexpected extended absence of a key clinician. As this case is currently before the Health and Disability Commissioner, it would be inappropriate for me to comment further on the specifics.

explanation: A narrow, closed factual question (was a locum being sourced; had the vacancy been approved for recruitment). The response supplies neither fact and defers to a written question. It is a plain, non-deflecting deferral rather than a pivot or an attack, which keeps it above zero, but the question's core is left wholly unengaged — and per the rubric a narrow factual question left unanswered is the worse kind of failure. Note this is a deferral, not a refusal: a refusal resolves the question, a promise to revert does not.
question: Is it correct that Nelson Hospital was trying to source a locum urologist in June 2024, when Mr Walker was referred, and, if so, had approval been given for the vacancy to be recruited into?
statement: Well, that’s a specific question. I’d invite the member to put that in writing, and I’ll come back to her in regard to the specifics of that question.

explanation: Asked to explain an apparent inconsistency between the ACC-response account (resourcing) and the current account (administrative error). The answer does address the contradiction on its own terms — it asserts both factors were in play, so the two accounts are not exclusive. That is a real engagement with the core, though largely by restating the primary answer rather than accounting for why the earlier response named only one. Judged on engagement, not on whether the reconciliation is persuasive.
question: Why did Health New Zealand, in its response to Mr Walker’s ACC claim, say that the delay was due to resourcing factors if they are now saying that it is due to an administrative error?
statement: Well, I repeat what I said in my primary answer, which was there were two particular factors at play here. The first was a human coding error; the second was an operational pressure in relation to the unexpected extended absence of a key clinician, so there were two factors. As I’ve also said, Health New Zealand is investigating this incident to prevent this error from happening again, and it is also before the Health and Disability Commissioner, as well.

explanation: The question raises a specific chronological objection: the recoding occurred on 19 July, by which point the clinically acceptable timeframe had already passed, so the coding error cannot explain the delay. The response restates the coding-error narrative verbatim and adds that the downgrade 'took time until that was then noticed' — it never engages the date or the timeline problem. Near-total restatement of a prior answer in place of addressing the point put.
question: How can the administrative error be involved in the delay when the fact is that it was on 19 July that the recoding of Mr Walker’s clinical condition occurred, when he was already beyond the limit for the clinically acceptable time for his condition to be seen by a specialist?
statement: Well, as I said in my primary answer, the case is deeply regrettable. I’m advised that one of the reasons for the delay was the fact that the referral was triaged as urgent, but then a human coding error led to it being downgraded, and, of course, that took time until that was then noticed. That is deeply regrettable and I acknowledge that it is, and that is why I’ve also been advised that Health New Zealand is investigating this incident to prevent this error from happening again. There are investigations also under way by the Health and Disability Commissioner.

explanation: A closed factual question about whether the Government removed Nelson Hospital staff's power to approve recruitment. The answer expresses regret about the case and points to an HNZ investigation — it addresses the patient's situation, which was the premise, and never touches the recruitment-authority proposition, which was the question. A pivot to sympathetic framing with the substantive core untouched.
question: Is it correct that while Mr Walker’s cancer care was delayed for lack of a surgeon, the lump on his testis grew and spread, and the Government removed the power for Nelson Hospital staff to approve recruitment?
statement: Well, what I would say is that this situation is deeply regrettable and the delays did cause a significant impact on Mr Walker, and that is why there is now an investigation under way by Health New Zealand into this incident.

explanation: Asked what announcements he had made about vintage vehicles and motorhomes; states the announcement directly — consultation on reducing WoF/CoF inspection frequency from six-monthly to annual. Directly and completely responsive. The supporting statistics are extra detail, which is a Specificity matter and does not lift or lower this score.
question: What announcements has he made regarding vintage vehicles and motorhomes?
statement: Earlier this month, I announced at the British and European Car Day in Trentham, the Government will soon consult on reducing the frequency of warrant of fitness (WoF), and certificate of fitness (CoF) inspections for vintage light vehicles, and private heavy motorhomes. There are 128,000 vintage vehicles in New Zealand and about 40,000 private motorhomes. They have to spend time and money getting a WoF or a CoF every six months. That is despite the fact that they travel less compared to modern cars. Evidence shows faults in these vehicles are half as likely to contribute to serious crashes. So we’re consulting on changing the rules to make it annually rather than every six months.

explanation: Asked what specific changes NZTA is consulting on; names them — reduced WoF frequency for vehicles over 40 years old including motorcycles, and CoF frequency for privately owned motorhomes moving from six months to a year. The question is answered squarely and in full.
question: What specific changes are the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) consulting on?
statement: NZTA will soon begin consultation on reducing the WoF check frequency for vehicles over 40 years old, including both cars and motorcycles—I received quite a bit of correspondence about motorcycles—and they’re reducing the CoF check frequency for privately owned motorhomes from six months to one year. Our view is this is a sensible approach to making sure that vehicles continue to be safe while not going overboard on compliance.

explanation: Asked what feedback the Minister has received; he reports feedback received, with named sources. Directly responsive. The selection is plainly favourable and unrepresentative, but whether the account is one-sided goes to Veracity and Focus — on the single question of whether the question was engaged, it was.
question: What feedback has the Minister received on the proposal?
statement: The feedback has been quite extraordinary. Let me quote Antonio, “Bloody brilliant. Thanks for the common sense.” Selwyn: “It’s a no-brainer.” The New Zealand Motor Caravan Association, Bruce Lochore: “It’s never made sense…these vehicles do a fraction of the mileage of normal vehicles, they have a fraction of the serious accident[s] … it’s an over-exaggeration of compliance”. Garry Jackson, president of the New Zealand Federation of Motoring Clubs, said, “We’re just delighted.”

explanation: Asked when the changes take effect. The answer gives the consultation window precisely (opens Monday, closes 4 April) but resolves the actual question — the commencement date — only as 'soon after' a Government decision. The core is reached and answered conditionally rather than avoided, but it is hedged rather than settled; a genuine partial.
question: When can Kiwis expect these changes to come into effect?
statement: I’ve got good news for Greg O’Connor and all other owners of vintage motor vehicles. Public consultation will begin next Monday. I encourage people to have their say. I know that the member of Parliament for the West Coast with their vintage hot rod will be submitting. Please go to nzta.govt.nz; the last day is 4 April. Once consultation has gone through and Government has made a decision, it will take place soon after that.

explanation: Two-part question: has a taskforce been established, and when will it finish. Both are answered — a unit has been established by the Public Service Commission, and it runs for three months. Marked down because the answer renames the body (Health Assurance Unit) without confirming or denying the specific premise put, that its purpose is to review and potentially replace Levy's reset plan. The closing swipe at the previous Government is a Civility/Focus matter and does not move this score.
question: Has a taskforce been established to review and potentially replace the health system reset plan put forward by Health New Zealand Commissioner Lester Levy; if so, when will it complete its work?
statement: This Government is focused on delivering a health system that prioritises timely and quality healthcare for patients. The Public Service Commission has established the Health Assurance Unit to provide advice to me and to ensure performance across the health sector so that it can deliver upon the Government’s health priorities. The task force is established for three months. Unlike the previous Government, which prioritises restructuring during a pandemic, we’re focused on delivering better healthcare for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether the reset plan will be public and on what date; neither is answered. Responsibility is assigned to the commissioner and the plan's status reported as still being finalised. This is a deflection by attribution rather than a talking-point pivot, and it gives the questioner a small amount of relevant information, but a straightforward two-part question is left unresolved on both parts.
question: Will Health New Zealand’s reset plan be publicly available, and, if so, on which date?
statement: That is a matter for the commissioner, but I understand the commissioner is continuing to work with Health New Zealand to finalise the reset plan.

explanation: Asked for the value-add of Māori tourism. The answer does name what it contributes — manaakitanga, connection to whenua, accommodation/experiences/events "not replicated elsewhere" — so the question is engaged, but it drifts into heritage narration and a Te Matatini plug rather than staying on the value-add. Its vagueness is a Specificity matter, not counted here; the partial score reflects the drift off the asked point, not the lack of figures.
question: What is the value-add of Māori tourism?
statement: Māori tourism boasts a rich herstory and history. Before the word “tourism” was coined, our tūpuna deployed manaakitanga, and a profound connection to the whenua—land; thank guides Sophia Hinerangi and others in Te Arawa. Māori tourism continues to thrive on manaakitanga and whenua. Māori collectors, in particular, offer a diverse range of accommodation, experiences, and events that are prominent on our tourism must-do lists and are not replicated elsewhere, like the greatest Māori show on earth Te Matatini next week in Taranaki, where I hope to see as many members of this House as possible supporting the Waikato kapa haka teams!

explanation: Asked how productive Māori tourism enterprises are. The answer goes straight at it: better than non-Māori tourism businesses 2010–2020 on labour productivity and GDP per worker, with contributing factors. The extra material on jobs and local multipliers is additive, not evasive. Squarely answered.
question: How productive are Māori tourism enterprises?
statement: Between 2010 and 2020, Māori tourism businesses generally performed better than non-Māori tourism businesses in terms of labour productivity, GDP per worker, and relevant industry groups. Contributing factors could include the higher-average salaries of employees for Māori tourism businesses and operational efficiencies in these businesses. The economic impact of Māori tourism extends beyond revenue and pax numbers. They have 15,000 jobs, often in regions where job prospects may be limited. Māori businesses often prioritise local businesses and suppliers, creating a multiply effect that directly benefits the local and regional economies.

explanation: A narrow factual question — how many social houses were funded through Budget 2024 — met with the number and nothing else: "1,500." Complete.
question: How many social houses were funded through Budget 2024?

explanation: Asked in what years the funding would be allocated. He answers the allocation timing ("now") and gives the delivery window, 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2027. The allocation half is answered briskly rather than year-by-year, but the core of the question is reached directly.
question: In what years will that funding for those 1,500 houses be allocated in?
statement: In terms of allocation, the funding is being allocated now and they are for delivery from 1 July 2025 through to 30 June 2027.

explanation: Asked how many houses built since the 2023 election were funded by this Government. Answer opens with the number — "none" — and explains the funding lag. The "look at a calendar" jab is a Civility matter and does not displace the answer, which was given first and in full.
question: How many of the social houses built between the 2023 general election and today were funded by this Government?
statement: Well, none, because, as the member knows, funding is allocated two or three years out from when the funding starts, and the Government took office on 27 November 2023, so it’s a little bit difficult to allocate funding and have a house built the day or the month afterwards. I invite the member to look at a calendar.

explanation: Asked why he had claimed credit for the 2,000 houses. He engages the premise directly: he says the earlier question was how many houses had been built since taking office, and 2,000 was the answer to that — i.e. he denies claiming credit. That reaches the core. The election jab at the end is padding, and the score is held below 0.9 only because he restates rather than fully accounts for the earlier framing.
question: If that is the case, why did he stand in this House and say to members here and the country that he takes credit for the 2,000 houses that have been built up to now?
statement: The member asked me how many houses had been built since this Government came to office, and the answer is what I gave, which is over 2,000. The member might not like the fact that they lost the election and we won, but that’s what happened.

explanation: Asked whether it is the Government's position that anything after the 2023 election is its doing — a yes/no. He never states the position. The Transmission Gully, City Rail Link and SkyCity examples are on-topic to attribution and imply "no, and nor did you", so this is not a pivot to unrelated talking points, but the question is answered by analogy rather than reached. Partial.
question: Is it the position of this Government that anything that happens after the 2023 election is its doing?
statement: The simple reality is that stuff that happens in one Government often comes to fruition in another Government. For example, the National Government in 2014 started the funding for the Transmission Gully motorway. It finished in 2022, but I noticed that didn’t stop Jacinda Ardern and Grant Robertson riding out in the Crown limos to spend up roughly $400,000 opening Transmission Gully, even though they campaigned against it in the first place. The City Rail Link project was funded in 2014 and has taken so long we have had an entire new Government from National come around, so the fifth National Government when it started life under the fourth National Government. Another example is the SkyCity convention centre, which was funded back in 2013 and 13 years later will open. Things take a while. House building takes a while as well.

explanation: "Does she stand by all her statements and actions?" — "Yes". Complete answer in the first word; the material that follows is elaboration, not avoidance.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and, in particular, my actions to deliver excellent and equitable outcomes for tamariki Māori. I was really proud to launch our first nationally consistent, high-quality structured literacy and numeracy resources in te reo Māori, benefiting 27,000 ākonga across the country. I’m advised that the kura umbrella group Ngā Kura ā Iwi, at their recent hui, made comment on the high quality of the resources, the comprehensive nature of the content, and the clear link to language acquisition. Finally, I’m further advised that teachers from outstanding kura, including seven from the member’s electorate—including that member’s own former wharekura—were involved in the development of this curriculum and supporting resources.

explanation: Asked why she believes Māori-medium and mainstream should or should not get equal treatment. She states the position plainly — equitable resources and outcomes for both — and gives a reason (a bilingual system the Government is committed to fully funding), with mirroring in both mediums as evidence. The opening deflection to the primary question shaves a little off, but the position and its grounds are given.
question: Can the Minister explain why she believes that Māori-medium education and mainstream education should or should not receive equal treatment?
statement: I think that the answer in the primary question answered the member’s question. There should be equitable resources and outcomes for both Māori-medium kura kaupapa and tamariki Māori in the mainstream, which is why every single thing that I have done in the English medium, we have mirrored in the Māori medium, as well. For the first time, we have nationally consistent pāngarau—or maths—resources available to every child learning in te reo Māori, no matter where they are learning, because we have a bilingual education system and we are committed to fully funding that.

explanation: Asked how she justifies $100m for one mainstream school against $100m for all kura kaupapa projects. She justifies the Wellington Girls' College side — spread over years, largely pre-dating this Government, earthquake-prone buildings — which engages half the comparison, but never addresses the kura kaupapa side that gives the question its force. Answer is cut off by interruption; scored on what was said.
question: How does the Minister justify the allocation of $100 million to one mainstream school when the entire budget for all kura kaupapa projects is $100 million?
statement: The member is referring to Wellington Girls’ College, and an explanation of the $100 million is that that is over a long period of time; in fact, much of that money pre-dates this Government—investment that was required for buildings that were earthquake-prone and, in fact, were rather dangerous, and that work needed to happen. Further work needs to happen in order to make that school—

explanation: Two-part question: does she agree kura kaupapa buildings are dilapidated, and if so why have they not been prioritised. She contests the premise of the second part head-on — they are being prioritised, $100m set aside — which is a legitimate direct engagement, but the first part (standing by her own prior statement) goes unaddressed. Partial.
question: Does the Minister agree with her previous statement that kura kaupapa buildings “are in an extremely dilapidated state”; if so, why have kura kaupapa buildings not been prioritised for repairs?
statement: Well, kura kaupapa buildings are being prioritised. We have set aside $100 million that we are continuing to top up, and—

explanation: Asked why 20 kura kaupapa projects were deprioritised or cancelled. She begins giving the actual reason — 250 unfunded projects inherited on taking office — before being cut off by interruption. As far as the answer runs it is on the asked point, not a pivot; truncation by the House is not a dodge.
question: If the Minister agrees that kura kaupapa need to be prioritised, can she explain why 20 kura kaupapa projects were deprioritised or cancelled last year?
statement: I can exactly tell that member why things had to be put on a different train, and that is because when we turned up in Government, we had 250 projects that were unfunded—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the economy; the answer names yesterday's Monetary Policy Statement and states its finding (CPI sustainably in the 1-3 percent band). A specific report is identified and characterised, which is exactly what was asked. The added editorialising about 2021-2023 inflation does not displace the answer.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Yesterday’s Monetary Policy Statement confirmed annual Consumers Price Index inflation is sustainably within the 1 to 3 percent target range, giving the Reserve Bank confidence to continue lowering the official cash rate (OCR). In other words, the era of high inflation is over, and, of course, New Zealanders hurt a lot between 2021 and 2023, when inflation went over 7 percent, eroding people’s wages and savings. Spending constraint and price stability is back.

explanation: Asked how the Government is helping keep inflation under control; the answer names the mechanism -- spending discipline and declining government expenditure as a share of the economy -- and cites the Reserve Bank's assumption of that decline. The opening caveat that the Reserve Bank holds primary responsibility is framing, not evasion, and the question's core is reached.
question: How is the Government helping to keep inflation under control?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Finance, of course, the Reserve Bank has primary responsibility for controlling inflation, but the Government of the day can either help that task or hinder it through decisions around tax and spending. This is a Government that is helping. We’ve introduced discipline to Government spending after years of largesse, and the Reserve Bank says, in the Monetary Policy Statement, that Government expenditure is still assumed to decline as a share of the economy over the medium term, reducing inflationary pressure.

explanation: Asked by how much households benefit from lower rates; after a brief and reasonable caveat that circumstances vary, the answer gives a concrete worked figure -- roughly $150 a fortnight on a $500,000 mortgage per 1 percentage point. A quantified response to a quantitative question.
question: By how much will households benefit from lower interest rates?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, people’s circumstances vary, so there is no one exact answer, but to give an illustration that helps demonstrate the point, for someone with a $500,000 mortgage over 25 years, a 1 percentage point drop in their interest rate reduces their required repayments by around $150 a fortnight. That is a significant reduction that could be used elsewhere in the household budget. So a decline in the OCR has a real, material impact on households’ budgets and helps New Zealanders get ahead.

explanation: Asked for the Reserve Bank's growth forecast for the next year; the answer states it directly as 2.4 percent over 2025, plus corroborating bank forecasts. The exact figure requested is supplied without any detour.
question: What is the Reserve Bank’s forecast for economic growth in the next year?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, more good news: the Reserve Bank expects economic growth to have returned in the December quarter of last year, then forecasts growth of 2.4 percent over 2025. This is in line with other forecasts, including Westpac’s, which expects growth of 2.5 percent this year. BNZ expects 2.6 percent, and ANZ expects 2.7 percent. This economy is back in growth, and we need to accelerate that from this point on.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions; the answer is an unqualified yes. One word, complete, nothing avoided -- the textbook maximal case.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: As I have said over 300 times, yes.

explanation: Asked to choose between the Peters and Seymour positions on the country's name, or admit to silence. The answer engages the subject at length and implicitly leans toward the Peters position, and it does resolve the related question of whether a name change will happen, but it never states which colleague he agrees with. The specific choice put to him is left unmade.
question: Who does he agree with: Winston Peters, who said, “The name of this country is New Zealand. This person who came here in 2006—you’re not going to change it.”, or David Seymour, who said that “while I prefer to use New Zealand, I’m not here to stop other people saying Aotearoa.”, or will he maintain his silence on this issue?
statement: As an answer that’s based on intellectual and academic integrity, the name of this country was always New Zealand, until Pember Reeves decided in the 1880s that he would call it Aotearoa, which is a massive insult to the people of Ngāi Tahu—that’s not their name—and we are going to not make a name change for this country until, in the democratic conventions of this great nation, we first consult and get the agreement of the New Zealand people.

explanation: Asked whether Peters' comments imply migrants should have fewer rights and, if so, whether he would condemn them. The answer denies the premise squarely -- Peters made no such suggestion, and it is not an attack on any immigrant -- which answers the first branch and makes the conditional second branch moot. A denial that meets the question head-on is a direct answer, not a dodge.
question: Do Winston Peters’ comments suggest that New Zealanders who were born overseas should have fewer rights than those who were born here, and, if so, will he condemn that?
statement: Look, it is very, very clear that Mr Peters made no such suggestion at all, but he paralleled the fact that in 2006, an application was made to a country called New Zealand, and that is still the same country that that person came to. Now, that’s not an attack on any immigrant, at all.

explanation: Asked whether he will discipline Peters and Jones. The answer declares the question fallacious and says it does not bear a response, which disputes the framing but never says whether he will or will not act. Unlike a plain refusal such as 'No, I won't', this declines to reach the will-or-won't at all, so the core of a narrow question goes unaddressed despite the bluntness.
question: Will he stick up for migrant communities by disciplining Winston Peters and Shane Jones for their repeated attacks on members of Parliament based entirely on their country of origin, or will he continue to keep his head down by pretending that his Ministers’ comments are not his problem?
statement: The simple answer to that is that if you get a fallacious statement like that, it doesn’t bear a response at all.

explanation: Asked how the 500-officer commitment will be achieved given 72 fewer officers now. The answer supplies the mechanism -- up to 650 recruits starting training in the first half of 2025, more than the whole of 2023-24 -- which addresses the 'how' with figures. It sidesteps the embedded claim about the current shortfall, so one limb of a two-part question is left untouched.
question: How will he achieve the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to train no fewer than 500 new front-line police by 27 November 2025 when there are now 72 fewer police officers than when he became Prime Minister?
statement: I thank the member for that question. The current police planning is for up to 650 recruits to commence training in the first half of 2025. This is 75 more than in the entirety of the 2023-24 year, which the previous Government was responsible for. We, in short, are on track.

explanation: Asked to choose between Peters' claim and the Police Commissioner's assessment that the target slips to 2026. The answer asserts confidence that the target is on track, which does address the underlying question of whether it will be met, but it reaches that by citing Peters' past record and never engages the Commissioner's position it was asked to weigh against. The comparison requested is not made.
question: Does he agree with Winston Peters that the target of 500 additional police by 27 November 2025 would magically be met if police officials would merely read the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement, or does he agree with the Commissioner of Police, who has all but admitted that the target won’t be met until 2026 at the earliest?
statement: Given the very, very remarkable record of Mr Peters on this matter, where the last tranche of such training was a commitment for 1,800 but it ended up being successfully 2,338 in that tranche, we are setting out for the same performance this time around. So that’s why we’ve got confidence that on this matter, we’re on track.

explanation: Asked whether Peters is accomplishing anything and whether he will acknowledge the approach is divisive. The answer refuses on a pretext about the questioner's use of 'Aotearoa' and offers nothing on either limb. This is a refusal to entertain the question rather than a direct answer to it, and it also turns on the questioner.
question: Is Winston Peters actually accomplishing anything for Aotearoa when he tells members of migrant communities that their views are worth less than people born in Aotearoa and he instructs officials that they can meet political targets just by reading a coalition agreement, or will he acknowledge that this is a divisive and counter-productive way to run a Government?
statement: That member will get an answer when she asks the question about a country called New Zealand, for which I’m responsible.

explanation: Asked what announcements he had made on resilient transport in Hawke's Bay. He names the specific announcement (Waikare Gorge realignment funding) and its content. The question is squarely answered; the padding about advocacy and recovery comes after the answer, not instead of it.
question: What announcements has he made regarding resilient transport connections in Hawke’s Bay?
statement: Last week, I travelled to the mighty Hawke’s Bay—thrilled to confirm the Government has approved funding to deliver the Waikare Gorge realignment project, at a cost of between $350 million and $425 million. This will deliver 4 kilometres of State Highway 2 realignment between Wairoa and Napier, including a 160 metre long arch bridge over the top of the Waikare Gorge. It was actually two years to the day since Cyclone Gabrielle, and I know it’s been a tough grind for the people of Wairoa and the East Coast. We are committed to this region and its recovery, and I want to acknowledge the strong advocacy of its fine local MPs.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statements and actions. She says "Yes" — a direct answer — with the mild qualifier "in the context in which they were made", then adds what she particularly stands by. Marginally short of the bare "Yes" that would score 1.0, but the core is engaged.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions in relation to serious youth offenders and the military-style academies?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were made at the time. I especially stand by my actions to provide funding of $30.6 million over four years to continue the fast-track youth offending programme and extend the programme to 14- to 17-year-olds, which will contribute to this Government’s target rate of a 15 percent reduction in the total number of children and young people who are serious and persistent youth offenders.

explanation: Asked a narrow factual question: are pilot participants currently missing from the in-community stage. She does not say yes or no, but she states plainly that she will not discuss these young people's activities and why. That is an explicit stated refusal rather than a pivot, which scores high — held below that because the refusal recharacterises a yes/no question about programme status as a request about "day-to-day life activities", so the core is partly sidestepped rather than met head-on.
question: Are there currently military-style academy pilot participants missing from the in-community stage of the pilot?
statement: I have said in the House many times that I will not be speaking to these young people’s day-to-day life activities, that they’re a small cohort of young people, and that we must respect their privacy.

explanation: Asked whether there is currently a matter of public safety concerning the pilot. She answers the question as put — it is not hers to determine — and names who would make that call. She engages the question directly and gives a plain reason for not asserting either way; no pivot to talking points, no attack on the questioner.
question: Is there currently a matter of public safety concerning the military-style academy pilot?
statement: It wouldn’t be for me to say whether something is or is not a matter of public safety. This would be a matter for the police, who would make the call on that.

explanation: Asked what announcements the Government has made about Defence housing. He identifies the new soldiers' flats at Papakura Military Camp and how they were delivered. Directly responsive.
question: What announcements has the Government made about Defence housing?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I recently had the pleasure of cutting the ribbon on new soldiers flats at Papakura Military Camp—by happy coincidence, within the electorate of the Minister of Defence. The project was delivered in an impressive time frame of six months and constructed offsite with modular technology. This offers an exciting insight into the future of being able to deliver more Defence housing and accommodation options on base, and mirrors the work of other ministerial colleagues to more efficiently and affordably procure more classrooms, social housing, and so on, in the same manner.

explanation: Asked why the Government invested in upgrading the flats. He gives the reason: supporting posted personnel, and an ageing stock of 1,900 homes mostly over 60 years old. The aside about the questioner's service is padding but does not displace the answer.
question: Why did the Government choose to invest in upgrading the soldiers flat at Papakura Military Camp?
statement: Defence housing is an essential way to support our personnel wearing uniform who serve our country so well—they are posted across New Zealand. Some 1,900 Defence homes, many of which—in fact, most of which—are more than 60 years old. We know that our soldiers, sailors, and aviators deserve better than they have had for very many years in this regard, and I’m sure that the member asking the question, ex-Major Weenink, having experienced those facilities herself, would share my view in that regard.

explanation: Asked what the benefit of improving Defence housing is. He answers directly: morale and discipline, feeding recruitment and retention. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What is the benefit of improving housing for New Zealand’s Defence personnel?
statement: Improving Defence housing isn’t just placing a roof over the head of our Defence Force personnel and their families, important as that is. It’s a crucial element in maintaining morale and discipline, which in turn leads to positive outcomes in terms of recruitment and retention that are going to be essential as we ensure that our personnel are well equipped to provide the national security aims, and other ways in which our Defence Force is a force for good for New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether this is the last Defence estate project. "Far from it" is an unambiguous no, followed by the forward programme. Direct and complete.
question: Is this the last Defence estate project the Government will be investing in?
statement: Far from it. In fact, it’s not even the last Defence investment in housing at Papakura Military Camp. We have an ambitious programme to deliver through the Defence Estate Regeneration Plan. For example, in the next year alone, $180 million worth of procurement of capital projects—again, better housing for our personnel and their families, modernised shared spaces like dining halls, and maintenance, of course, for the facilities that we already do have. On top of this, Budget 2024 delivered an extra $7 million of new operating funding for leasing of Defence housing so that at Devonport Naval Base, an additional 35 new houses will support those personnel. I thank all those who’ve worked hard on these projects over the year—they are coming to fruition under this Government.

explanation: Asked what phase one changes are and how they cut red tape. She names the two vehicles (the AML Amendment Bill and the Statutes Amendment Bill) and the mechanism — streamlining requirements, removing duplication, cutting compliance costs. Both halves are addressed at a general level; the thinness is a Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: What changes is the Government making in phase one of its anti-money laundering and countering finance of terrorism reform, and how will these changes cut red tape to boost the economy, if at all?
statement: Phase one focuses on cutting red tape to reduce compliance costs and grow the economy. The Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Bill and the Statutes Amendment Bill will together streamline outdated anti - money-laundering (AML) requirements, remove duplication, and reduce compliance costs, with the aim of increasing productivity.

explanation: Asked what specific changes the AML Amendment Bill makes. She gives one: removing mandatory enhanced customer due diligence for low-risk trusts, with the current position it replaces. Directly answers.
question: What specific changes are being made through the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Bill to cut red tape and grow the economy?
statement: We are removing mandatory enhanced customer due diligence for low-risk trusts such as family trusts. Currently, businesses are required to apply the same enhanced customer due diligence processes to all trusts regardless of the risk. This change will provide relief for reporting entities that will no longer have to collect information for low-risk trusts.

explanation: Asked how the Statutes Amendment Bill tackles unnecessary regulation. She names the change — removing address verification requirements in most cases — and what it fixes. Directly answers.
question: How will changes introduced through the Statutes Amendment Bill tackle unnecessary regulation and encourage growth?
statement: The Statutes Amendment Bill will remove address verification requirements in most cases. Many New Zealanders and businesses are currently required to have their addresses repeatedly verified due to the AML requirements, even if they’ve used the same bank for many years. This unnecessary regulation wastes time and money, and creates barriers for people trying to access basic financial services. Removing these requirements will also help those without a formal address, like dependent children or persons with intellectual disabilities, to open bank accounts more easily.

explanation: Asked for other examples of red tape being removed in phase one. She supplies one: the Border Cash Report requirement for already-declared cash. Exactly what was requested.
question: Can the Minister provide other examples of red tape that’s being removed in phase one of her reforms?
statement: One example is the requirement for people to submit a Border Cash Report if they receive cash from someone who has already declared it when entering New Zealand. This is unnecessary red tape, adding no value but creating more work for businesses and individuals. Phase one of my reforms will remove outdated requirements like this one to save New Zealanders both time and money.

explanation: Asked how she can have confidence in the Government's advocacy for women and why she has done nothing as Minister for Women. Collins calls it a stupid question and rebukes the questioner for belittling members; neither part of the question is engaged. Pure attack on the questioner.
question: How can she have confidence the Government is advocating for women when her colleagues mock perimenopausal women, dismiss the causes for the gender pay gap, appoint an anti-abortion lobbyist as the Minister of Health, and tell women what to put in their vagina, and why has she, as the Minister for Women, stood by and done nothing?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. What a stupid question, and the last thing we need is for women in this House to be belittling other members of Parliament who are trying to do their job. Just stand up for women when they ask you to. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' with a standard 'in the context in which they were made' qualifier and an example. Direct and essentially complete; the mild hedge keeps it just below 1.0.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were made at the time, especially my statement that the best interests and the safety of our children should be first and foremost in all decision making for our young people.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the decision to remove mandatory FGCs for young serious offenders given the Māori over-representation. She professes support for FGCs and their 'true intention' and criticises tick-box use, but never says whether she stands by the decision, and never touches the Māori disproportionality. Stays on topic while missing the core.
question: Does she stand by her decision to remove mandatory family group conferences (FGCs) for youth classified as young serious offenders, despite the fact that 80 percent of rangatahi likely to receive this classification are Māori and will be the most in need of input from whānau, hapū, and iwi?
statement: I am a real big fan of family group conferences and the intention of why family group conferences were brought in in the first place. I want to go back to the true intention of why those FGCs were brought about in the first place, not it becoming a tick-box exercise for judges to hold up the court system and allow kids to be on remand for up to 12 months at a time because of FGCs.

explanation: Asked whether she is determined to isolate mokopuna Māori from their whakapapa via removal of mandatory FGCs and repeal of section 7AA. She squarely rejects the FGC premise ('We will not be removing family group conferences') and explains what is changing, which engages half the question, but says nothing about section 7AA or the isolation charge itself.
question: Is she determined to isolate mokopuna Māori in the system for their w’akapapa—genealogy—with the removal of mandatory family group conferences and the repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act?
statement: We will not be removing family group conferences. What we’re doing is making sure that a family group conference is done right in the first place rather than having to have repeated family group conferences with no outcomes and not being done in the way that they were intended to be done.

explanation: Asked whether she wants to see a reduction in the number of tamariki Māori in care. Answered 'Absolutely' and then supported it. Unambiguous, complete engagement with exactly what was asked.
question: Does the Minister want to see a reduction in the number of tamariki Māori in care?
statement: Absolutely. That’s why I’m really proud of four of the nine partners that are now operationalised within this country showing positive results. For example, far fewer Tainui tamariki entered care and protection in 2023 compared to 2019, and there was a 61 percent reduction, all because we’ve worked together for our young people.

explanation: Asked a comparative question: would the $260,000 per child have been better spent on school lunches. She defends the boot camp spend on accountability and rehabilitation grounds — an implicit 'no' — but never engages the comparison or the alternative use put to her.
question: Would the $260,000 spent per child on these boot camps have been better spent on expanding the Ka Ora, Ka Ako - Healthy School Lunches Programme to help prevent our tamariki from offending in the first place?
statement: The money that we are investing in these young people is to help them to be accountable for the crimes that they’ve committed. They have left victims behind within the community, and there needs to be accountability for that. But it is also about making sure that we rehabilitate these young people to lessen the chance of victims in our community and also give these kids a better chance at life.

explanation: Asked what recent announcement he made about Innovation Fund money for the Mental Health Foundation. He names the recipient, the matched funding, the project and what it will do. Directly and completely responsive to the question asked.
question: What recent announcement has he made regarding funding from the Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund for the Mental Health Foundation?
statement: I was thrilled to recently announce that the Mental Health Foundation is the latest recipient of the Government’s Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund. This funding is being matched by the Mental Health Foundation to fully fund Project Wakapuāwai, an initiative that will digitise more mental health resources to allow Kiwis faster access to mental health information and support. This funding will allow for the Mental Health Foundation to redevelop and futureproof its digital platforms to improve the ways they provide crucial information about mental health, wellbeing, suicide prevention, and mental distress for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked why digitising mental health resources matters. He gives the reason — access barriers for rural and remote communities — and illustrates it. Squarely answers the 'why'.
question: Why is it important to digitise mental health resources?
statement: Well, this Government knows that access to information and support for our rural and remote communities remains a barrier, so online resources such as this are another option for those looking to support themselves or someone they care about. If you’re on a farm in Northland or a tiny town in Southern New Zealand, we know your access to mental health support can be limited. We want every Kiwi to know help is close, and this goes some way to achieving that.

explanation: Asked what other contracts have been announced under the fund. He names all three other recipients and what each will do. Complete answer to the question put.
question: What other contracts have been announced as a result of the Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund?
statement: Well, the Mental Health Foundation is the fourth contract to be awarded so far from the first round of the mental health innovation fund. The other three recipients are Youthline, the Sir John Kirwan Foundation, and MATES in Construction. Youthline will receive funding to expand its Counselling Your Way programme. The Sir John Kirwan Foundation will receive funding to scale up Mitey, a free early intervention initiative to support children’s mental health. MATES in Construction will receive funding for its community workplace-based programme. These are only the first three recipients, and I’m excited to share more recipients in the future.

explanation: Asked how the fund supports New Zealanders to access timely mental health support. He does connect the fund to front-line workforce growth and faster access, so the mechanism is reached, but much of the reply drifts into general government positioning ('more money out of Wellington') rather than the 'how'. Partial engagement with the core.
question: How does the Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund support New Zealanders to access timely mental health support?
statement: Well, the Government is focused on not only growing and improving the performance of our existing front-line services but we’re also growing and developing new front-line mental health and addiction workforces. I think it’s fantastic that the innovation fund is supporting our front-line mental health workforce and enabling more Kiwis to get faster access to timely mental health support. This fund is part of the Government’s commitment of investing more in grassroots initiatives. We came into Government to say we’d get more money out of Wellington to the front line, and that’s what we’ve done.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' up front, then elaborated on health funding. The elaboration is campaigning, but the question itself was answered directly and completely.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action in recent days to make it easier for New Zealanders to see a doctor. We know that too many Kiwis wait too long to see their GP, which is why we’re putting more funding into primary healthcare. And thanks to that funding, Kiwis will see more nurses working in primary care, more international doctors working in their community, more opportunities to enrol with their local doctors, and more choice with the roll-out of a 24/7 digital service. Fixing the healthcare system won’t be easy, but our outstanding Minister of Health is backing patients and making sure we can get them the care they need—he’s funding more, he’s growing the workforce more, and he’s getting rid of the bureaucracy.

explanation: Asked (a) does he stand by the 'safe to do these changes' statement and (b) what specific evidence on DSI impacts. He answers 'Yes' to the first and, for the second, names the source (the Ministry's interim regulatory impact analysis, publicly released) and reports what it said — that the DSI impact is hard to model. Both limbs are engaged; that the evidence is thin is a Specificity/Veracity matter, not a dodge.
question: Does he stand by his statement about speed limit increases that it is “safe to do these changes”; if so, what specific evidence has he received, if any, on the impact of reversing speed limit reductions on deaths and serious injuries?
statement: Yes. I’m advised the Ministry of Transport undertook an interim regulatory impact analysis to support the new speed rule, which has been released publicly. The ministry advised it is difficult to accurately model the impact of the rule on deaths and serious injuries.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts a specific 2024 Waka Kotahi finding. Pleading unfamiliarity with the document is a minimal but genuine engagement with the ask; he then declines to go further and pivots to mandate and popularity, never accepting or rejecting the finding. Partial at best.
question: Does he accept the findings from Waka Kotahi’s speed monitoring economic assessment, undertaken in 2024, that found corridors which had speed limits reduced prevented an average of 27 deaths and serious injuries, per corridor, each year, with travel time increases of between 12 seconds and four minutes?
statement: I’m not overly familiar with the document the member is referring to. All I would say is that the Government is reversing the blanket speed limit reductions advocated and pushed forward by the previous Government. We sought a mandate for that at the election. We are carrying that out, and it’s been broadly popular around the country.

explanation: Asked what he says to a resident who claimed a community-driven reduction had become political rather than a safety issue. He replies on the community point: the corridor may be in the 50 highways out for consultation, consultation requirements have been improved, community voice matters. That addresses the community-driven core, though it never touches the 'political not safety' charge.
question: What does he say to a Waitaki Bridge resident who said about the reduced speed limit that “The speed limit change was community-driven from the very beginning. It was fantastic that the community had managed to see the change happen, and it just seems that it’s now become a political issue rather than an actual safety issue.”?
statement: Well, as the member knows, there are around 50 State highways around the country that are out for further consultation, so that particular resident potentially is able to have their say. We’ve actually improved the consultation requirements for ongoing speed limit changes as part of the new rule that was set last year, and community voice, as part of the process, is important.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: will he let councils keep existing limits where community support is demonstrated, without reversing and re-consulting? He restates that there are new consultation requirements and pivots to the schools rule. The yes/no is never reached, and the question was tightly framed — a squarely avoided core.
question: Will he then allow road-controlling authorities, including local councils, to retain safe speed limits where strong community support has already been demonstrated, without having to automatically reverse and then consult again?
statement: There’s new consultation requirements as part of the new rule, but as the member knows, we are setting a rule, particularly around schools—that I know the member’s been very concerned about—and that is an important change that we’re making.
