explanation: Two limbs: is he aware of the New Plymouth situation, and will councils have to reverse then pay to consult again? 'Yes, I've seen the comments' answers the awareness limb completely and directly, but the substantive second limb is left entirely unaddressed. Half the question engaged.
question: Is he aware that in places like New Plymouth, for example, they’ve been told that they have to automatically reverse speed limits by July in places where the reductions had 89 percent community support, and will they have to reverse the speed limits, then spend money consulting again in order to have a speed limit that actually delivers for their communities?
statement: Yes, I’ve seen the comments from the Mayor of New Plymouth.

explanation: Asked whether he has any idea what the reverse-then-reconsult cycle will cost councils. The response turns the questioner's quoted phrase back on her and her party; no cost figure, no estimate, no engagement with the question at all. An attack in place of an answer.
question: Does he have any idea how much it will cost councils to automatically reverse all of the speed limits, then consult again should they wish to prioritise road safety instead of following his Government’s direction, described by the New Plymouth mayor as “ideologically-driven nonsense [with] no scientific basis”?
statement: The only person who generally advocates for that ideologically driven nonsense is that member and her comrades in the Green Party.

explanation: Asked whether she has confidence the Government is prioritising issues pertaining to women. 'Yes.' One word, direct, complete — nothing was asked that this fails to cover.
question: Does she have confidence that the Government is advocating on behalf of, and prioritising issues pertaining to, women?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether abolishing the Ministry for Women would help advocacy for women. 'It depends whether or not the ministry has a great Minister' gestures at the value of the ministry without answering, and the coalition-agreement line answers a different question — whether abolition will happen, not whether it would help. Partial engagement, core sidestepped.
question: Certainly. Would abolishing the Ministry for Women, as per the next Deputy Prime Minister’s campaign wish, help advocate for issues pertaining to women?
statement: Well, it depends whether or not the ministry has a great Minister, which they do in the Hon Nicola Grigg. And I’d also say, too, that the coalition agreements are what the Government is fulfilling, not every party’s campaign promises.

explanation: Asked a direct agree/disagree on Seymour's account of the gender pay gap. She speaks about her own late-night working and that women get different treatment, which brushes against the premise, then moves to a general call to stand up for women and a jab across the House. No agreement or disagreement is ever stated.
question: Does she agree with ACT Party leader, David Seymour, when he said, “The gender pay gap exists when you have to be there late at night to make the sale, put in the extra hours, and do all the extra things that women are often unavailable to do because of the way gender roles work.”?
statement: Well, I think, being one of those women who is always there late at night working, and always have been in my working life, I know that sometimes women do get a very hard time and different treatment, and that is why we stand up for women. The best thing we can all do is to acknowledge women, stand up for each other no matter what, and no matter our political affiliations, which is not something I’ve always felt from that side of the House.

explanation: Asked whether it is appropriate for the Under-Secretary to tell women what period products to use. She says she thinks it is 'amazing' and is grateful he takes an interest — an answer on the appropriateness question, in the affirmative. Flippant and dismissive in tone, but tone is Civility; the question itself was engaged, not dodged.
question: Does she think it’s appropriate for Parliamentary Under-Secretary Simon Court to tell women what period products to use to save money?
statement: Do you know, I think it’s amazing, because I don’t need to worry about those sorts of things any more, and I’m just so grateful for the fact that this man is actually interested in it, because I sure as hell am not.

explanation: Asked why he has confidence in Seymour given his Education Minister withheld hers. He does give a reason for the confidence (Seymour is the accountable Minister and is 'all over the detail'), so the 'why' is engaged, but the contrast with Stanford's position — the sharp edge of the question — is left untouched. Partial.
question: Why has he expressed confidence in David Seymour’s ability to clean up the mess he’s made of the school lunches programme, given his own Minister of Education has refused to share that confidence?
statement: Well, David Seymour is the accountable Minister. I’ve got every confidence he’s all over the detail and he’s going to make sure all the food and the meals get up to scratch.

explanation: A two-part question: was Stanford right that Seymour overstepped, and if so what did the PM do. He answers neither directly — no yes or no on whether she was correct — and substitutes a general statement about delegations. The 'what have you done' half is only implicitly answered (nothing; the delegations stand).
question: Was Erica Stanford correct that David Seymour’s announcement cancelling teacher-only days overstepped the mark; if so, what has he as Prime Minister done about it?
statement: Well, I have clear delegations and clear responsibilities. David Seymour is the accountable Minister for school lunches; he is aware of the issues and he will fix them. Erica Stanford is the accountable Minister for teacher-only days, and she will manage that.

explanation: Asked why Stanford is cleaning up Seymour's messes while he skips meetings with her. The response is a request for clarification ('which meetings?'), not an answer. It is good-faith engagement rather than a pivot to talking points, but no part of the question is answered.
question: Why is Erica Stanford being left to clean up David Seymour’s messes while he fails to show up to meetings with her, and he as Prime Minister won’t do anything about it?
statement: Sorry, can you explain which meetings?

explanation: The same question put again, explicitly. He returns to the prepared line about confidence in Seymour working through the school lunch issues, which addresses neither the missed meetings nor why he will not intervene. A near-total dodge of a question that had just been narrowed for him.
question: OK, I’ll repeat the question: why is Erica Stanford being left to clean up David Seymour’s messes while he fails to show up to meetings with her, and why will he as Prime Minister not do anything about that?
statement: Well, as I said before, I have every confidence that David Seymour is working his way through the issues around the school lunches. He’s aware of the detail, he’s on top of it, and I have every confidence that he will sort it out.

explanation: Asked why Stanford has fortitude he appears to lack. The recorded response is 'As I said—', a pointer back to the earlier confidence-in-Seymour line, which was not responsive to this question either. Note: the transcript is cut off by interruption, so this may understate what was actually said.
question: Why does Erica Stanford have the fortitude to repeatedly stand up to David Seymour that he seems to lack?
statement: As I said—

explanation: Asked whether he still expects the cheaper lunches to be as good or better, and if so when. He answers a different question entirely — who funded the programme — and turns on the questioner ('it's a bit rich'). The expectation is never restated and no timeframe is offered.
question: Is it still his expectation that the new, cheaper, mass-produced school lunches will be at least as good, if not better, than the healthy locally made lunches his Government cancelled; if so, when can hungry school students expect him to deliver on that promise?
statement: Well, I’ll just say to that member, it’s a bit rich because we saved school lunches, because that Prime Minister didn’t fund school lunches. So we are spending more on school lunches and we are giving them to more kids. That’s a good thing. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what it would take for him to step in personally. He opens with the funding counter-attack, but does reach the question: he concedes some food is 'not up to scratch' and says the Minister is working through it — in effect, nothing will make him step in. The core is answered obliquely rather than squarely, and the Marmite aside sidesteps it again.
question: If it hasn’t taken feeding children melted plastic, failing to deliver lunches at all, serving up the same food 13 days in a row, or serving pork to halal students, what will it take for him to finally step in and sort out the mess that his Government has made of the school lunches programme?
statement: Look, again, I’d just say to that member, this is a Government that has actually put together a school lunch programme that is feeding more children and is funded. He hadn’t funded it; we funded it. We’re expanding the access to it. Yes, some of the food is not up to scratch, but the Minister is working his way through the issues and I have every confidence he will resolve it. And I just say to parents that may be listening to this, feel free to prepare a Marmite sandwich and an apple for lunch. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what recent economic reports she had seen. She names a specific release (the December-quarter trade figures) and reports its contents. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Recent data releases are consistent with a growing New Zealand economy. Yesterday, for example, the latest trade figures were released. These show that in the December quarter of last year, New Zealand exported $26.7 billion worth of goods and services. That’s an increase of 9.6 percent over the same period a year earlier. Dairy was particularly strong, making up almost a quarter of our total exports in the quarter.

explanation: Asked what is driving the export increase. She names causes directly — rising volumes, rising world prices, a competitive dollar — and cites the commodity price index. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What is driving this increase in exports?
statement: Well, both export volumes and prices have been rising—that is, the amount of goods we export has been rising and the world price we get for those goods has also been going up. Furthermore, the New Zealand dollar is currently at a competitive rate for exporters. ANZ’s Commodity Price Index, which follows movements in prices for New Zealand exports like dairy, meat, horticulture, and forestry, has risen 15 percent in the past year when measured in world prices, and has risen 25 percent in New Zealand dollar terms. That is good news for New Zealand’s hard-working exporters and the people they employ.

explanation: Asked how export prices compare to import prices. She answers with the terms of trade, states the direction (exports rising faster) and the level (near-record). The comparison asked for is the comparison given.
question: How do export prices compare to import prices?
statement: Import prices are, of course, the other side of the equation. Luckily, economists have a measure of a country’s export prices relative to its import prices, and that’s the terms of trade. New Zealand’s terms of trade have been rising strongly as export prices have been rising much more strongly than import price rises. Currently, the terms of trade is at a near-record high in a series that goes back to the 1950s. Now, that is good news. As New Zealand’s purchasing power has, effectively, gone up, we are getting more in return for what we export.

explanation: Asked what other export industries are picking up. She names one — apples and pears — with figures. The question invited a plural answer and got a single case, so it is complete in kind but narrow in coverage.
question: What other export industries are picking up?
statement: Well, I’d like to share with you facts from a letter I received from New Zealand Apples and Pears, who tell me that New Zealand’s apple and pear industry has achieved $1 billion in orchard-gate returns for the very first time. I would like to congratulate the apple and pear industry, which also has revealed that this is worth $2.5 billion in revenue impact to the New Zealand economy—up 27 percent from 2023—with employment in the sector also increasing to more than 13,700 jobs, and this growth trend looks set to continue.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. He opens with 'Yes' and then elaborates on cost-of-living measures. The elaboration is campaign material, but the question itself was answered in the first word.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to support Kiwis with the cost of living. We know it’s a tough time for New Zealanders, which is why it’s so important to get on top of wasteful spending, inflation, and interest rates. We’ve made real progress: repealing the Auckland regional fuel tax, delivering tax relief, and supporting young families with FamilyBoost. But there’s more to do, and that’s why the focus this year is on unleashing growth so that Kiwis have more money in their back pocket. That’s why we’re backing farmers; that’s why we’re backing exporters; backing tourism; fighting hard offshore in trips, like to Vietnam, to make sure that we actually create more deals for Kiwi businesses, to create more jobs at home and more money in the back pockets of Kiwis.

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree with the programme's purpose, and how can he be proud of the rollout. He gives a reason for pride (this Government funded and extended it) but never touches the rollout's execution, which was the point of the question, and never engages the first half. Partial engagement wrapped in a swipe at the questioner — the swipe itself is a Civility matter, not scored here.
question: Does he agree that Ka Ora, Ka Ako is about supporting our tamariki to be healthy and well in order for them to learn, and, if so, can he tell the House how he can be proud of his Government’s roll-out of the updated school lunch programme?
statement: Well, I’m proud of it because that member was part of a Government that didn’t fund it, and this is a Government that has come in, has funded the programme, and has extended it to more children. That’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a named principal's specific claim that the programme is one of the most direct ways to tackle intergenerational poverty. He never says yes or no to the quoted claim, but does engage its substance — hunger, learning, not being consigned to welfare, future potential — which is the intergenerational-poverty argument in his own words. Half-answered: the core proposition is addressed obliquely but the direct yes/no is left out.
question: Does he agree with Ragne Maxwell, principal of Porirua College, that the Ka Ora, Ka Ako programme is “one of the most direct ways to tackle intergenerational poverty”?
statement: Well, I think it’s an important thing for kids who come to school with no lunch. We’re not willing to let them go hungry, we don’t want them not to learn, and we don’t want them ending up on, or being consigned to, welfare or other things. We want them to have potential and a future.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his own "not up to scratch" statement and what he is doing about it. The response begins deflecting to the accountable Minister and does not reach either half of the question — neither the stand-by nor the what-are-you-doing. On the record as given, this is a deflection, not an answer.
question: Does he stand by his statement made this morning that some of the lunches aren’t “up to scratch”, and, if so, what is he doing as the Prime Minister to ensure our tamariki are given on-time, nutritious, edible kai?
statement: Well, again, the Minister who is accountable—

explanation: A direct question about whether he will take personal responsibility for a failure. The answer returns to the funding/extension talking point already used twice and never addresses responsibility at all — neither accepting it nor refusing it. A plain "no, I won't" would have scored high; this does not reach the question.
question: Will he as Prime Minister take responsibility for failing to achieve the purpose of Ka Ora, Ka Ako, and feed our tamariki?
statement: Well, again, we have funded the programme and we’ve extended it to more kids.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees hunger should never be a barrier to learning. "That is why we have a welfare system and a school lunch programme" is a compressed but genuine yes — the "that is why" concedes the premise and points to the response. Short and unhelpful on detail (a Specificity matter), but the question is engaged rather than dodged; docked only because the agreement is implied rather than stated.
question: Does he agree hunger should never be a barrier to learning for the over 156,000 tamariki whose households cannot afford basic essentials, like food, and who deserve better from this Government?
statement: Well, that is why we have a welfare system and a school lunch programme.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a quoted statement. Opens with "Yes" and restates what he agrees with. Direct and complete; the added policy framing does not dilute the answer.
question: Does he agree with Mark Mitchell’s statement, “I think there’s a real risk of seeing a tragedy unfold with members of the public who have become exasperated … every week I’ve got to try and talk to people that want to take vigilante type action to actually protect themselves … That’s the worst possible thing that could happen. And I’d encourage people definitely not to go down that road”; if not, why not?
statement: Yes—and I agree that many New Zealanders have become exasperated at the high level of crime occurring in our communities and that vigilante justice is not the solution. That’s why this Government is focused on restoring law and order, so people are confident that our justice system delivers real consequences for crime.

explanation: Asked what advice Police or the Ministry of Justice gave on safety risks. He answers substantively and against his own interest — Police were not broadly in favour and had concerns about potential impacts — before the response is cut off mid-sentence. The core of the question is reached; only the fuller account of the weighing is missing.
question: What advice did Police or the Ministry of Justice provide him on the safety risks associated with the new citizen’s arrest power?
statement: There was a range of advice. The Police, quite frankly, were not broadly in favour of the changes; they had concerns around potential impacts. We weighed that up against our concerns about the current situation, where that, during the day—

explanation: A narrow question: what consultation was undertaken with the Police Association specifically. The bulk of the answer is retail-crime framing and the advisory group's provenance. Only at the end does it approach the question — the group "talked to a wide range of people" and the Police Association will have its say at select committee, which implies no prior consultation without ever saying so. A specific question substantially avoided.
question: What consultation did the Minister of Police or the Minister of Justice undertake with the Police Association regarding the impact of citizen arrest powers on front-line police?
statement: The proposals, in particular, came from the ministry advisory group led by Sunny Kaushal in response to a significant increase in retail crime over the past few years. New Zealanders are fed up with the level of retail crime that they are experiencing in our communities. That’s why this Government has considered proposals to change the rules, because if you want to have a different outcome, sometimes you have to change things, and that is what we are proposing. So, in the course of developing those proposals, the ministry advisory group talked to a wide range of people, and, of course, when we introduce this legislation it will go off to the select committee and then many New Zealanders will have their say, including the Police Association.

explanation: A narrow, factual, yes/no question: must a store owner inform a detained child's parents. The answer describes the obligation to contact police and follow police instructions, and closes on general policy justification. Parents are never mentioned. It answers an adjacent question — what the requirements are — while leaving the one asked untouched, and the question's narrowness makes that a worse miss.
question: Is a store owner required to inform the parents of a child who is being held steady or detained in a storeroom?
statement: Well, the requirements if a situation occurs when somebody is stealing from business and reasonable force is being used to detain that person—the proposal is that they would then need to contact the police and follow instructions from police. Then that is the situation. It’s already the law at five past nine at night and our proposal is to make it the law during the day, and, ultimately, every retail worker needs to consider the broad circumstances and the situation that they confront. But this Government makes no apology for coming up with new ideas and new responses to deal with the significant increase in retail crime that we experienced over the past few years. New Zealanders want change and that’s what we’re going to deliver.

explanation: The core of the question is "how do you justify the $3.6m spend", and he justifies it: retail crime costs billions, so a modest investment to source ideas outside the justice sector is warranted. That is a real answer to the actual ask. Docked because the two premises attached to the question — 72 fewer police and doubled meth use — are passed over entirely. Whether the justification is convincing is Rigor's business, not Forthrightness's.
question: How does he justify a $3.6 million spend on the retail crime advisory group when there are 72 fewer police on our streets and methamphetamine use has doubled under his watch.
statement: Well, I think people would recognise that retail crime costs our community billions of dollars, and all New Zealanders have to pay more for the things that they buy because some New Zealanders steal it and don’t pay for it. That is why we think a modest investment in a retail advisory group to come up with bold ideas—and the purpose behind the retail advisory group is to say, “Look, we have a Ministry of Justice and a whole justice sector that has continued its ways a number of times, and we’re open to radical new ideas coming from elsewhere, in order to come up with different solutions so that we can have better outcomes, and for New Zealanders to keep safe in their communities.”

explanation: Asked whether he will take responsibility if the law change costs a life. He answers the responsibility question squarely, if in the negative: responsibility lies with the person who took the life, not with him. That is a direct refusal of the premise, which counts as engagement. The attack on the questioner and the law-and-order list that follow are Civility and Focus concerns and do not lower the score; docked slightly because "I will not take responsibility" is left implicit rather than stated.
question: Will he take responsibility if someone in New Zealand loses their life because of his law change?
statement: What I can tell that member is that the only person that is responsible for losing a life in a situation like that would be the person that took the life—that swung the axe, that used the weapon to kill or hurt or maim somebody. If that member doesn’t understand that and wants to create excuses for that kind of activity, then I don’t think they understand how law and order should work in this country. We are very determined to ensure that New Zealanders are kept safe in their community, and that is why already in Government, we have brought back three strikes, increased sentencing reform, and given the police the powers that they need to deal with gangs. All of those things are designed to keep our communities safe.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on overseas investment. He names the date, the Act, the Cabinet package and the specific changes. Directly and completely responsive. That it is a friendly question from a Government member does not bear on whether the question was engaged.
question: What recent announcements has he made to encourage overseas investment into New Zealand?
statement: I thank the member for his question. On 23 February, I announced changes to the Overseas Investment Act. Cabinet has approved a package of legislative reforms that will ensure faster decision-making, greater investor certainty, and stronger national interest protections. Specifically, I announced reforms that will change the presumption of the Act to better acknowledge the benefits that international investment provides to New Zealand’s economy. It will reduce the time frames for the regulator’s assessment of most applications to 15 days unless escalated to a comprehensive assessment in more sensitive cases. These reforms will make New Zealand a more attractive place to invest, enabling businesses to access capital, grow, and create higher paying jobs.

explanation: Asked why the Government believes the reforms are necessary. He gives a direct causal answer — stalled productivity (1.4% to 0.2%), capital access, wages — which is squarely the 'why' that was asked.
question: Why does the Government believe these reforms are necessary?
statement: Because we follow economic evidence. The evidence in particular is clear around productivity. Our growth has stalled. It was at 1.4 percent per year from 1993-2013, but only 0.2 percent over the decade to date. One of the keys to improving productivity and driving growth will be reversing these trends by ensuring that Kiwi businesses get the investment they need to grow. When businesses get capital, they can invest in better technology, expand production, and pay their workers more. That’s what this Government is committed to enabling with these reforms.

explanation: Asked how the reforms compare with overseas investment regimes. He does make the comparison (NZ among the hardest to invest in; Australia/Canada/UK protect interests while attracting more FDI), but compares the status quo regime rather than the reformed one, so the comparison stops just short of what was asked.
question: How do these reforms compare with overseas investment regimes in other countries?
statement: New Zealand is currently one of the hardest countries to invest in. Other OECD countries such as Australia, Canada, or the United Kingdom protect their natural interests effectively; meanwhile, they receive billions more foreign direct investment than we do. The reality is that other countries are competing for global capital while we’ve been scaring it away. That must change and it is changing, including with these changes to the Overseas Investment Act, making us a country that actually welcomes our friends around the world sending their money and their ideas to our country so we can trade value for value, and get stronger together with higher wages and better jobs.

explanation: Asked what protections remain to safeguard national interests. The reply ('That was concise; there's just a lot of quality content') names no protection at all and appears to respond to something other than the question. Complete non-answer.
question: What protections remain in place to safeguard New Zealand’s national interests?
statement: That was concise; there’s just a lot of quality content.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the 'same quality or better' statement and why. Both halves answered: 'Yes, I do stand by that statement,' plus the reason (previous nutritional standards will be met).
question: Does he stand by his statement that school lunches would be “the same quality or better”; if so, why?
statement: I thank the member for her question. Yes, I do stand by that statement, and the reason is that the programme has been set up to ensure that the nutritional standards under the previous iteration of the school lunch programme will be met under this iteration.

explanation: Asked how melted plastic in food is the same or better. He engages the incident head-on — rejects the premise that it is part of the programme, then identifies the cause (wrong oven temperature in one regional kitchen, failed QC) and the remedy. The jab at the previous programme is a detour but the core is reached.
question: How are plastic containers melting into food the same or better?
statement: Plastic containers melting into food is not a part of the programme. For the member to claim that would be to say that every single failure, including, if I recall, seven different food safety investigations into the prior scheme, were a feature of that programme. Now, I’m sure the member wouldn’t think that the Ministry for Primary Industries investigations into the lunches she served were a part of the programme. However, in this particular instance, we have taken it very seriously and done so rapidly. We have investigated the cause, which was the overheating of plastic by using the wrong temperature in an oven in one of the 27 regional kitchens and then failing to do correct quality control before they were sent out. The people concerned have been spoken to about this and we are taking steps to ensure that it won’t happen again. And this is important because we are here to make things better every day, and we are—

explanation: Asked how undelivered meals leaving kids hungry are better. He denies the premise ('that would be no better if it were true; however, it is not'), which is engagement, but then never addresses non-delivery and pivots to standards and the previous Government's Budget line.
question: How are undelivered meals, that leave kids hungry all day, better?
statement: That would be no better if it were true. However, it is not. As I said in my primary answer, if the member heard me say that, the specifications and standards for the healthy school lunch programme are equal to those under the previous programme. But I tell you what they are much better than: they are much better than zero, because people tend to forget that when the previous Government budgeted for the healthy school lunch programme, there was a fiscal cliff where there was no money in the Budget for the healthy school lunch programme in 2025. That’s a Minister, in the past, who budgeted no money for healthy school lunch programmes; this Government is delivering.

explanation: Asked how the same meal 13 days running is better. Flippant, but it does answer the question posed — his position is that free butter chicken 13 times is not a hardship. He contests that the repetition is a defect rather than sidestepping it.
question: How is providing the same meal 13 days in a row better?
statement: I think I addressed this question, and it speaks to the issue of what people are happy to have and not. In this particular instance, I seem to recall it was actually butter chicken. Now, a lot of people I know, if someone gave them butter chicken for free 13 times, they wouldn’t be complaining. They’d actually be thrilled. Namaste.

explanation: Asked how staff buying sandwiches because lunches weren't delivered is better. He addresses delivery failure directly — acknowledges teething problems and cites 99% on-time delivery on 3 March — but never engages the 'better' comparison, and closes on the questioner.
question: How is school staff having to go to a bakery to buy sandwiches because their school’s lunches were not delivered better?
statement: Throughout this programme we’ve been upfront and honest about any teething problems we’ve had, and then we’ve fixed them. That’s what you do when you have challenges. You own it, you accept it, and then you fix it. And in terms of fixing it, yesterday on 3 March, we achieved 99 percent on-time delivery up and down New Zealand. That’s how you start off with a problem—you put on your thinking cap, you solve it, and make the world a better place. And if that member had done it when she was the Minister, we wouldn’t have to work quite so hard.

explanation: Asked about hundreds of local jobs lost to a centralised system. He answers only the 'working better' clause and says nothing whatsoever about job losses, then diverts to the member's tweet and a Young ACT rumour.
question: How are hundreds of local jobs being lost up and down the motu in favour of a centralised system that clearly doesn’t work better?
statement: I believe that it is working better. Wherever there are problems, we fix them, and in many instances, we hear from children that they believe that the food is better. There’s been some confusion. For example, that member tweeted outrage at the quality of the healthy school lunch programme, but we all know how this ends. She forgot it was a picture that had been sent to her of the school lunches that she was responsible for. [Interruption] And I’ve got something else. I’ve got news for the member. I heard a rumour that cannot be substantiated that that picture was sent to Jan Tinetti by Young ACT. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why he won't attend a meeting with the education Minister. He gives an actual explanation — the meeting was contingent on caucuses finishing on time and ACT's ran over. Self-serving, but it is a direct response to why the meeting didn't happen.
question: If his school lunch programme is better, how is it that he won’t even show up to a meeting with the education Minister, the Hon Erica Stanford, to discuss it?
statement: Well, it’s very simple. We had a meeting scheduled, contingent on our respective caucuses finishing on time. But the ACT caucus is a very tight, busy, and productive group of people, and we can’t always be ready for that.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on access to healthcare. He enumerates them: 100 clinical placements, 400 graduate nurses a year, a 24/7 digital service, $285m uplift. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made to improving access to timely, quality healthcare for all New Zealanders?
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Yesterday, the Prime Minister and I announced a boost for primary healthcare to help Kiwis access timely and quality primary care for all New Zealanders. This includes 100 clinical placements for overseas-trained doctors to work in primary care, incentives to recruit up to 400 graduate nurses per year for the next three years, a new 24/7 digital healthcare service for online medical appointments, and a $285 million performance-based uplift for general practice over the next three years. Our Government is putting patients first, and these measures will help ensure Kiwis have more access to the care they need, where they need it.

explanation: Asked why the Government is increasing overseas-trained doctors in primary care. Answered directly: more doctors are needed, and trained doctors already here are blocked by a lack of training places, which the 100 placements fix.
question: Why is the Government increasing the numbers of overseas-trained doctors working in primary care?
statement: Well, we all know that we need more doctors. That’s why we are funding a new two-year primary care training programme for up to 100 extra overseas-trained doctors. It makes no sense that overseas-trained doctors living in New Zealand who are willing to work in primary care can’t, because there aren’t the training opportunities available to them. By funding 100 clinical placements, we will provide them with the support needed to work in general practice with our most needed, putting their skills to good use so that New Zealanders have improved access to both timely and quality care.

explanation: Asked how the 24/7 digital service will improve access to timely care. The answer states the mechanism — video consultations, prescriptions and lab referrals with registered clinicians any time from anywhere — and ties it back to access. Squarely on the question; it stops short of a fully complete account of 'for all New Zealanders' (e.g. those without a device), which is the only gap.
question: How will the new 24/7 digital healthcare service improve access to timely, quality healthcare for all New Zealanders?
statement: Well, we are investing in a new digital healthcare service that Kiwis can see a doctor or a nurse, get prescriptions and lab referrals any time, anywhere, using their phone or laptop. Enabling Kiwis to access video consultations with registered clinicians at any time from anywhere will play a key role in improving access to timely, quality healthcare for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen from the sector. He names two — Dr Bryan Betty of General Practice NZ and Dr Samantha Murton of the College of GPs — and quotes both. That is a direct and complete response to what was asked; whether the reports are representative is a Veracity/Focus matter, not this one.
question: What reports has he seen from the healthcare sector about the Government’s healthcare boost?
statement: Well, good news. I’ve seen some very positive reports from the sector. The chair of General Practice New Zealand, Dr Bryan Betty, said, yesterday, that our Government’s investment will “help ensure that patients receive the care they need when they need it, while also strengthening the sustainability of the workforce.” The College of GPs’ president, Dr Samantha Murton, has backed our actions, saying that “focusing attention and resources on general practice and primary care will go a long way to turning our health services [around].”

explanation: Asked what announcements she has made about boosting front-line police numbers. She identifies the announcement — a new police training base in Auckland, announced Sunday — and its purpose. Direct and responsive; the closing 'restoring law and order' line is decoration, not a substitute for the answer.
question: What announcements has she made regarding the Government’s commitment to boost front-line police numbers?
statement: On Sunday, I announced that the New Zealand Police will be opening a training base in Auckland, increasing the training capacity of police and supporting the attraction and training of quality new officers from our largest market. This Government is committed to restoring law and order, and adding a training facility in Auckland is another example of what can be achieved with a Government that is backing police. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why another training facility is needed. The reply is mostly a restatement of commitment ('wants to do everything they can', 'a concrete example of that') and only reaches a reason near the end — delivering the additional 500 police requires expanded training capacity. The core is touched but circled first, so a partial answer rather than a dodge.
question: Why is another training facility needed?
statement: This Government wants to do everything they can to drive recruitment, increase the number of police, and make our communities safer. Opening a training facility in Auckland is a concrete example of that. This Government knows that delivering our additional 500 police is not just about delivering people but implementing the systems and providing the resources that invest in the front line, which includes expanding our training facilities.

explanation: Asked how the Auckland facility complements other recruitment work. She answers the complementarity directly: applicant numbers are at a record and an extra training location moves that existing pipeline through faster. The praise for recruitment teams is padding, but the question was engaged before the padding started.
question: How does adding a training facility in Auckland complement other work being done to boost recruitment?
statement: Police now have record numbers of applicants, and having an extra training location will support their efforts to get applicants through the pipeline and into training faster. I would like to recognise and commend the efforts of the recruitment teams and the Police front line, who have worked diligently to improve processes, create efficiencies, engage earlier with our applicants, and achieve an outstanding pipeline of quality recruits that are now entering the college.

explanation: Asked how recruitment processes are becoming more agile. She lists actual process changes — on-site recruitment days to cut wait times, the relaunched advertising campaign, an updated recruitment management system. That is the question answered on its own terms; the Round the Bays aside drifts, but the core was already covered.
question: How are Police recruitment processes becoming more agile and fit for purpose?
statement: I’m advised that Police are holding recruitment days where resources will be on site to assist applicants in moving through the first stages of recruitment processes at the time to help reduce wait time within the current processes. We have reconfigured the advertising campaign with the relaunch of the He Ain’t Heavy campaign to ensure that the quality of police is recognised and the service they deliver is recognised. We have also recently launched an updated version of the recruitment management system to allow candidates to better manage their recruitment experience and support Police to understand what options there may be for future improvements. Police are working incredibly hard, investing resources nationally and across the districts, and I would also highlight the Round the Bays efforts, which will be in Christchurch at the end of this month, where we are actively engaging with the public to attract recruitment.

explanation: A two-limb question: did he discuss the ferry cancellation, and did Hyundai raise concerns about future contracts. The reply implies a discussion occurred ('We shared with Hyundai...') but never confirms the cancellation was the subject, and the second limb — what Hyundai said about future shipbuilding contracts — is not touched at all. It pivots to the cost blowout under the previous government. Mostly a dodge, with a sliver of implicit engagement on the first limb.
question: Did he discuss in his meeting with Hyundai on Friday, 28 February 2025 the cancellation of the rail-enabled ferries; if so, did Hyundai raise any concerns about future shipbuilding contracts with the New Zealand Government?
statement: I want to thank that very sensible member for his very sensible question. We shared with Hyundai the fact that a two-ferry project in May 2020 involving $400.1 million of Government funding, when I was Minister, was on track to reach over $4 billion under his Government—that is, the Opposition now. The core objective of infrastructure to safely berth ships blew out to involve the highest possible specifications for the renewal of almost every piece of infrastructure, all at the taxpayer’s expense.

explanation: Asked whether he discussed the $300 million break fee and what Hyundai said. The first limb gets a hedged near-confirmation ('it would be unusual that a Minister... did not have that as part of the background information') rather than a yes; the second is deflected to KiwiRail and Hyundai's contractual relationship. A plain refusal would have scored higher than this hedge — but he does engage the subject matter and contest the figure rather than changing the topic, so it lands mid-range.
question: Did he discuss the $300 million break fee with Hyundai; if so, what did they have to say?
statement: It would be unusual that a Minister in that circumstance did not have that as part of the background information, but with respect to that discussion, that lies with KiwiRail and Hyundai in a contractual sense. However, that so-called $300 million break fee has been misrepresented by the questioner in the sense that there were a whole lot of infrastructural costs that made up that $300 million, not just the iReX project.

explanation: Asked how confident he is that Hyundai will bid again. He does not state a confidence level in terms, but he answers with the basis for it — an amiable meeting with S Y Park and their 'renewed interest in this tendering process'. That is substantively responsive to what was asked; the deduction is for reporting the meeting's tone in place of stating the confidence directly.
question: How confident is he that Hyundai will put in another contract bid for the new Cook Strait ferries when they are currently negotiating out of an existing contract with this Government?
statement: I’ve got some good news for the member: their head, S Y Park, was delighted to meet us. With his team, we had a very, very amiable and profitable discussion, and we were delighted to learn of their renewed interest in this tendering process.

explanation: Asked whether it is correct that his Government triggered the break fee. The answer opens 'It is correct that...' and then substitutes a different proposition — that the Government acted on a cost blowout. It concedes the action while reframing the responsibility, so the question's core is approached but not answered yes or no. Note the response is truncated mid-sentence, which caps how much can be read into it.
question: Is it correct that it was his Government that triggered the multimillion-dollar break fee with Hyundai that’s now required him to go back calling for a redo?
statement: It is correct that when this present Government realised that a $400.1 million project was blowing out past $4 billion, in the interests—

explanation: A two-limb question: did he consult Nicola Willis, and what was her response. Both limbs are addressed — consultation is affirmed, if glibly ('we're famous for consulting with each other'), and her response is given ('she wished me the very best'). The flippancy and the partisan tag are Civility and Focus concerns, not this one; the question was engaged.
question: Did he consult with the Minister of Finance, Nicola Willis, before inviting a new bid from Hyundai, and, if so, what was her response?
statement: In this Government, we’re famous for consulting with each other, and she wished me the very best and hoped that I could fix up the Labour Party’s mess.

explanation: Asked whether he is confident Willis won't pull the rug out on a future contract. He answers a different, past-tense question — whether her earlier action was justified. Confidence about the future is never addressed. A clear pivot; the truncation does not explain it, since the sentence is already committed to defending the past decision.
question: If Hyundai signs another contract for new ferries with this Government, is he confident that Nicola Willis won’t pull the rug out from under them again?
statement: The reality is that no responsible finance Minister could not take the action that the Minister of Finance took, because—

explanation: Asked what announcements he had made on infrastructure funding and financing. He names the announcement (pillar two of Going for Housing Growth) and enumerates the five improvements. Squarely and completely engaged.
question: What recent announcements has he made about improving infrastructure funding and financing to get more houses built?
statement: Last Friday, I announced pillar two of the Government’s Going for Housing Growth policy, five improvements to infrastructure funding and financing to support urban growth: replacing development contributions with development levies, regulatory oversight of those levies, increasing the flexibility of targeted rates, improving the Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act, and broadening existing tools to support value capture. We’re developing a flexible tool kit to support growth paying for growth, to allow a responsive supply of infrastructure where it’s commercially viable to build new houses. A flood of urban land coming to market plus responsive infrastructure will unlock an abundance of development opportunities, drive down the price of land, and make housing more affordable.

explanation: Asked why existing funding and financing tools need to change. He gives reasons directly — development contributions only recover costs for planned/costed growth, councils cross-subsidising growth (Drury) — before drifting into growth rhetoric. The core 'why' is reached.
question: Why do our existing funding and financing tools need to change?
statement: As I think many members around the House acknowledge and recognise, as indeed councils and developers do as well, there are significant challenges in our infrastructure system around funding and financing. Development contributions, for example, can only recover infrastructure costs for planned and costed developments, meaning councils need certainty about when and where the growth will occur. It is true that some councils have not been able to effectively recover growth costs, leaving ratepayers to pick up the cheque and cross-subsidise that growth—for example, at Drury, and there are other examples that members will be aware of around the country. We are creating an environment in which there are no ceilings on how high our cities can grow and there are no rings around how far our cities can expand. And that means the days of careful drip-feeding of land into a hot market fed by artificial scarcity, driving up land prices and therefore house prices, is over. We are creating a system where if you want to build and you can fund the infrastructure to build it, subject to normal environmental constraints, you can go for it.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answered 'Yes' — one word, complete, no dodge.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his climate Minister's specific statement that the Paris target is 'not a liability... no legal obligation'. He never says whether he stands by it; he answers a different question about effort on NDC1 and signing NDC2. The quoted proposition is left untouched.
question: Does he stand by the statement of his climate change Minister regarding the Paris Agreement that “It’s not a liability on our books, it’s intent and there is no legal obligation in the context around that.”?
statement: I agree that we are working incredibly hard to deliver on Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) 1 for 2030, and I also note that we have signed up for NDC2 in 2035.

explanation: Asked a binary: committed to meeting Paris, or does he agree NZ need only be 'seen to do its part'. Response pivots to economic growth and 'Kiwis first', closing on net zero 2050 — neither limb of the question is engaged.
question: Is the Government committed to meeting the Paris Agreement or does he agree with his climate change Minister that Aotearoa be just “seen to do its part”?
statement: What we’re committed to doing is going incredibly hard on economic growth and we’re going to make sure that it’s in our national interest to continue to do so. We’ll continue to put Kiwis first and make sure that we’re acting in our own national interest. But we are determined to drive for growth, and we are going to do everything we can to deliver on net zero 2050.

explanation: Asked why he is unwilling to use the word 'committed' about the NDC. He offers no reason at all, instead expressing pleasure that NDC2 aligns with net zero 2050. The question's core — his own reluctance — is entirely avoided.
question: Why is the Prime Minister so far unwilling to use the word “committed”, as in the Government is committed to meeting our nationally determined contribution under the Paris Agreement?
statement: Well, what I’m very pleased about is that our NDC2 2035 target now finally aligns with our internal targets for New Zealand net zero 2050.That’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked directly whether the Government is committed to meeting the NDC under Paris. He affirms commitment to a different target (net zero 2050), substituting the domestic goal for the international one asked about. Narrow question, squarely sidestepped.
question: Is the Prime Minister and his Government committed to meeting our Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement?
statement: We are committed to delivering on net zero 2050, as we have consistently said from the beginning.

explanation: Asked again about NDC commitment and for specificity. 'I've got nothing further to my previous answer' is an explicit, unambiguous close-off rather than a filibuster — that candour earns partial credit — but unlike a plain refusal it still leaves the yes/no unstated by pointing back to an answer that never gave one.
question: Is the Prime Minister committed to meeting our Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement, and can he be specific about that commitment under the Paris Agreement?
statement: I’ve got nothing further to my previous answer.

explanation: Asked for the Government's Budget 2025 priorities. She lists four priorities. Directly and completely answered.
question: What are the Government’s priorities for Budget 2025?
statement: The Government’s four priorities for Budget 2025 are: lifting economic growth through measures to address long-term productivity challenges, implementing a social investment approach, keeping tight control of Government spending while funding a limited number of policy commitments and cost pressures, and developing a sustainable pipeline of long-term infrastructure investments.

explanation: Asked for examples of policy commitments to be funded. She supplies one concrete commitment (the $1.37b/year health funding) with figures. The question asked for examples and examples were given.
question: What are examples of policy commitments that will be funded in the Budget?
statement: The Government has already announced a significant policy commitment for Budget 2025. That is the commitment of $1.37 billion a year from 2025 onwards to meet demographic, volume, and price pressures for front-line health services. In total, that comes to an additional $5.48 billion for Health New Zealand over the forecast period. Agreeing this very significant increase in funding ahead of time gave Health New Zealand certainty in its planning and demonstrates the Government’s commitment to delivering the healthcare New Zealanders need.

explanation: Asked whether other health funding had been announced ahead of the Budget. Answered 'Yes' and itemised medicines and primary care. The closing swipe at the PSA is a civility/focus matter, not a dodge; the question was answered first.
question: Has the Government announced any other funding for health ahead of Budget 2025?
statement: Yes. Budget 2025 provides just over a billion dollars of extra funding over the forecast period for additional medicines, including cancer treatments. On Monday, the Government announced measures to boost primary care, including increasing the number of doctors and nurses in primary care and a new 24/7 digital healthcare service for online appointments. These new measures will also be funded from Budget 2025. There is a myth propagated by the New Zealand Public Service Association and others that health funding is being reduced. Nothing could be further from the truth. Billions of dollars of additional funding are going into health to help ensure Kiwis have more access to the care they need where they need it.

explanation: Asked how the extra health funding fits within the operating allowance. She states the $2.4b allowance and explains the mechanism — allowances are net, savings create room — which addresses the 'how'. It stops short of showing the fit for this specific spend, and the jibe at the end is irrelevant to this attribute.
question: How will this additional health funding fit within the Government’s operating allowance?
statement: The Government has set an operating allowance for Budget 2025 of $2.4 billion. That is a tight allowance aimed at restricting growth in expenditure and reducing New Zealand’s structural Budget deficit left to us by the last Government. It is important to remember, though, that allowances are a net concept. They encompass savings and revenue initiatives as well as new spending. More savings, therefore, in the Budget equals more opportunity to invest in front-line services. That is called reprioritisation, for the benefit of members who did not experience this concept when they were last in office.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. Answered "Yes" outright, then expanded. Direct and complete; the promotional padding is a Focus/Specificity matter, not a dodge.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to make it easier for Kiwis to get access to the healthcare that they need. This morning, our excellent Minister of Health, Simeon Brown, announced more support for nurses so they can play a greater role in primary care. That comes off the back of action yesterday to train more doctors here at home, including in primary care. On Monday, we announced action to support more nurses into primary care, making it easier for international doctors to practise here, and introduce a whole system of digital 24/7 care. Kiwis deserve to be able to see a doctor as quickly as they can. We’re working hard to make that a reality. I would have thought the Opposition would want to support that.

explanation: Asked whether a lunchtime meal is a basic collective entitlement for ALL tamariki regardless of socio-economic status. Replied about helping "kids who are coming to school with no lunches" — a needs-based reframe that engages the topic but never takes a position on the universality that was the core of the question.
question: Does he agree that, regardless of socio-economic status, a meal at lunchtime is a basic level of collective care that should be afforded to all tamariki?
statement: What I believe is that we need to help kids who are coming to school with no lunches, and that’s why we saved the school lunch programme that was unfunded. We’ve got some challenges, but we’re working our way through them.

explanation: Asked whether school lunches are an important collective response, more helpful than vilifying struggling families. Answered by accusing Labour and the Greens of vilification instead — pivots to attacking the questioner's side and never touches the proposition put.
question: Does he agree that providing school lunches is an important collective response and one that is far more helpful than vilifying parents and families doing it tough?
statement: What I’d say is in the last 24 hours the vilification from Labour and the Greens, who are telling working parents across New Zealand who happen to give their kids a Marmite sandwich and apple each and every day that they are bad parents, is not acceptable.

explanation: Two-part question: agree with the principal's quote, and how many jobs were lost from the Ka Ora, Ka Ako changes. Neither part is addressed — no response to the quote, and the job-loss number is never given; instead funding and $130m of savings are asserted and the matter handed to the Minister.
question: Does he agree with Mana College principal Jeff Chapman that the previous school lunch programme “was a nice little circular local economy, and it was working great. The contractor was providing local employment and using local food.”; if so, can he tell the House how many people have lost their jobs as a result of his Government’s changes to Ka Ora, Ka Ako?
statement: Well, what I can say is that we are actually funding the school lunch programme. We are feeding more kids than the previous Government did. We are doing so, more efficiently, having saved $130 million, which has been put back into health and education for our kids. So I think it’s a win-win. We’ve got some challenges to work through. The Minister, David Seymour, will deal with that.

explanation: Asked whether he will stop pointing at his Ministers and take responsibility himself. "Well, we are" is a nominal answer, but the rest of the response does precisely what was asked about — routes the problem to the Minister — so the core of the question is left unengaged.
question: Will he stop pointing fingers at his Ministers and take responsibility, as Prime Minister, to feed our tamariki?
statement: Well, we are. We have a school lunch programme. Look, we have said that—and the Minister has said himself that—the food is in some cases not up to scratch. He’s making sure he holds those contractors to account, he’s working through the issues, and I’ve got every confidence that he will do so.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to continue Ka Ora, Ka Ako. Commits to "making the school lunch programme work" and to continuing to provide lunches to children "who need" them, but does not commit to the named programme as asked. Partially answers while hedging around the core.
question: Will he commit to continuing Ka Ora, Ka Ako?
statement: I commit, and the Minister is very committed, to making sure we make the school lunch programme work and we get what we contracted for. But, as I have said before, we will continue to provide children who need lunches with a school lunch programme. It’s important, because we know the evidence is that, if they don’t have food, they don’t learn and they end up on welfare—that’s not great.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. "Yes" — direct and complete. The cost-of-living recitation that follows neither adds to nor detracts from the answer given.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to support Kiwis with the cost of living. Two years ago, inflation was running at 7.2 percent; today, it’s 2.2 percent. Two years ago today, the official cash rate was 4.75 percent, and today it is 3.75 percent. Two years ago, food inflation was 10.3 percent, and today it’s just 2.3 percent. You know, it’s an encouraging sign that we’re making progress. We know there’s a lot more for us to do, and the best thing that we can do is grow the economy so that we can create those jobs, lift incomes, and actually create opportunities for more Kiwis so they’ve got more money in their pocket. That’s important.

explanation: A narrow factual question: on what day and at what time did he first discuss the allegations WITH Bayly. The reply gives when he was made aware of the issue (Thursday) and when Bayly resigned — a different question. Neither the day of the discussion with Bayly nor any time is supplied.
question: On what day and at what time did he first discuss allegations that Andrew Bayly had a physical altercation with a staff member, with Andrew Bayly?
statement: As I have previously said, I was made aware of the issue on Thursday, and Andrew Bayly resigned very late on Friday.

explanation: Same question re-put. This time the date is answered squarely — "I discussed it with Andrew Bayly on the Friday" — plus office contacts on Wednesday and Thursday. The "at what time" half is still not reached, so it is answered but not completely.
question: On what date and at what time did he first discuss allegations Andrew Bayly had a physical altercation with a staff member, with Andrew Bayly?
statement: My office had conversations with Andrew Bayly on the Wednesday and the Thursday, and I discussed it with Andrew Bayly on the Friday.

explanation: Asked when the resignation was formally received and in what form. "It was a phone call very late on Friday evening" answers both parts in one sentence. Terse, but complete.
question: When did he formally receive Andrew Bayly’s resignation as a Minister, and in what form was his resignation delivered?
statement: It was a phone call very late on Friday evening.

explanation: Asked whether he indicated Bayly would be dismissed if he did not resign. "No." — a flat, direct answer that disposes of the question and correctly makes the conditional second part moot.
question: Did he indicate to Andrew Bayly that, if he didn’t resign, he would be dismissed; if so, when did he do that?
statement: No. As I have said publicly, Andrew Bayly resigned, and he made the right decision.

explanation: Two-part question: WHY the Governor-General was not informed until Monday, and whether that meets his legal obligation. "Yes" answers the second half completely and unhedged, but the "why" — the substantive half — is left entirely unaddressed.
question: If Andrew Bayly resigned on Friday, why didn’t he inform the Governor-General of that resignation until Monday, and does he believe that fulfils his legal obligation to “keep the Governor-General fully informed about the general conduct of the Government”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked two narrow factual things: did he ask Bayly what he did, and was Bayly's account consistent with the staff member's. Answers neither — points at Bayly's own statement and closes with 'nothing further to add'. Not a refusal (never says he won't say), just a non-answer to both halves.
question: Did he ask Andrew Bayly what he did to the staff member who made the complaint, and was Andrew Bayly’s account consistent or different from the account of the staff member?
statement: Andrew Bayly talked in his statement about the incident, and I’ve got nothing further to add to that.

explanation: Asked whether an investigation is still open and, if so, who is conducting it. The response recites the sequence ending in resignation without ever saying open/closed or naming an investigator; the resignation is offered as a substitute for the answer.
question: Is there still an open investigation into the complaint about Andrew Bayly’s physical altercation with a staff member; if so, who’s conducting that investigation?
statement: Well, there were concerns raised, the Minister reviewed the incident, it didn’t meet his expectation, and he has resigned.

explanation: Asked what recent healthcare-access announcements he has made. The response enumerates exactly that — overseas-trained doctor pathway, extra medical school placements, nurse practitioner training. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What recent announcements has he made on improving access to timely, quality healthcare for all New Zealanders?
statement: Good news for Kiwis this week: our Government is delivering on our commitment to improve access to timely, quality care for all New Zealanders. This week, I have announced a significant healthcare boost to ensure Kiwis see a GP faster, including a range of actions to ensure overseas-trained doctors can work in New Zealand. I also announced more locally trained doctors in general practice, including increasing the total extra medical school placements to 100 each year over the course of this Government. We’re also boosting our nursing workforce by training more nurse practitioners and supporting advanced education for nurses in general practice. These initiatives will help strengthen the healthcare workforce, reduce wait times, and ensure Kiwis can receive the timely, quality healthcare they need.

explanation: Asked why the Government is increasing overseas-trained doctors in primary care. Gives the reason directly: doctors already living here want primary care work but lack training placements, so 100 clinical placements are funded. Answers the 'why'.
question: Why is the Government increasing the number of overseas-trained doctors working in primary care?
statement: Well, we recognise the need for more doctors working in our healthcare system, which is why we are funding a new two-year primary care training programme for up to 100 additional overseas-trained doctors. It doesn’t make sense that overseas-trained doctors living in New Zealand are keen to work in primary care but lack the training opportunities to do so. By funding 100 clinical placements, we will offer the necessary support to help them work in general practice, where they’re needed to help give Kiwis the timely, quality access to the healthcare they need.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to increase NZ medical school placements. States the action — already up 75 places a year, increasing to 100. Direct and complete.
question: What is the Government doing to increase the number of placements at New Zealand medical schools?
statement: Well, to reduce wait times for New Zealanders, we can’t just rely on sourcing our doctors from overseas. We must also ensure a sustainable pipeline of New Zealand - trained doctors. Under our Government, medical school placements have already increased by 75 places each year. Increasing this to 100 places will provide more opportunities for talented Kiwis to train as doctors and help ensure New Zealanders have access to the timely, quality healthcare that they need.

explanation: Asked why nurse practitioner training places are increasing. Gives the rationale (NPs diagnose, prescribe, treat; 120 places a year to work alongside GPs). The 'why' is engaged head-on.
question: Why is the Government increasing the number of training places for nurse practitioners in primary care?
statement: Well, nurse practitioners are highly skilled professionals who can diagnose conditions, prescribe medicines, and develop treatment plans for patients. By increasing the number of training places to 120 a year, we’re empowering more nurses to work alongside our hard-working GPs and deliver timely, quality healthcare in local communities. This investment will ensure more patients are seen sooner, easing pressure on the system and reducing wait times for New Zealanders.

explanation: Two parts: does she stand by the statement, and is she confident the Budget 2024 fiscal risks are manageable. Opens with 'Yes' to the first, and explicitly returns to the second ('to the second part of the question') to say risks are uncertain but will be managed. The confidence answer is hedged and detours through the previous Government first, but the core of both parts is reached.
question: Does she stand by her statement that she is looking at “changes to strengthen transparency and fiscal responsibility”; if so, is she confident that the fiscal risks in Budget 2024 are manageable?
statement: Yes. I was shocked, on becoming Minister of Finance, at the magnitude of unfunded fiscal risks left by the previous Government, such as Lake Onslow, the income insurance scheme, and Auckland Light Rail. I was also shocked by the large number of fiscal cliffs left in the accounts, where funding for an initiative had only been provided for a limited period despite a clear public expectation of it continuing, like Pharmac essential medicines. And, to the second part of the question, fiscal risks are by definition uncertain; they may or may not occur. If they do, they will be managed, and the Government has choices about how to do that.

explanation: Two parts: does she stand by the cost comparison (yes) and what will the Cook Strait resilience fiscal risk cost. Answers the first outright and answers the second by saying it depends on procurement and negotiations yet to occur — a direct 'no figure exists yet' rather than a pivot, though it stops short of any range.
question: Does she stand by her statement, in relation to the Cook Strait ferries, that “costs are expected to be much less than would have been the case with Project iREX”; and, if so, what will the cost of the fiscal risk of Cook Strait resilience be?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes, and in answer to the second part of the question, that depends on the procurement approach and commercial negotiations yet to occur.

explanation: Asked how she can be confident the alternative costs less when her own Cabinet paper says the port infrastructure cannot be confidently costed. She does give her basis for confidence — iReX as the point of comparison — so the 'how can you be confident' core is engaged, but the specific tension with the Cabinet paper's uncostable finding is left untouched.
question: How can she be confident that the alternative will cost less than the previous project when her Cabinet paper said the required port infrastructure “cannot be confidently costed”?
statement: Because the point of comparison is Project iReX, the biggest dog of an infrastructure project New Zealand has seen in many years, that blew out, members, from $750 million to $4 billion and climbing, with only 21 percent of the costs actually being for the core project of replacing the ferries. That project was terrible and was getting worse, and, by stopping, it we have saved New Zealanders money.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the Minister for Rail that the break fee costs way less than $300 million. 'I find it is wise to agree with the Minister for Rail' conveys agreement obliquely, so the yes/no is half-delivered, but she never adopts the claim in her own right.
question: Does she agree with the Minister for Rail, who said the break fee “costs us way less than 300 million”?
statement: I find it is wise to agree with the Minister for Rail.

explanation: Asked both whether she agrees Treasury predicts a $2 billion saving and whether she can confirm it. Repeating the same 'wise to agree' line glances at the agreement half and leaves the confirmation — the point of the supplementary — entirely unaddressed.
question: Does she agree with the Minister for Rail that Treasury’s prediction is that this will save $2 billion; can she confirm that?
statement: Well, as I’ve just said, I find it’s always wise to agree with the Minister for Rail.

explanation: Asked how she can be confident the fiscal risk is manageable given she has no costing, got a new figure mid - question time, and has no control over the Rail Minister. She restates the iReX comparison, which brushes the 'how can you be confident' core, then spends the rest quoting Grant Robertson against the previous Government; none of the three specific grounds in the question is engaged.
question: How can she be confident the fiscal risk is manageable when she has no idea how much the new project will cost, she got a new figure during question time from the Minister for Rail, and she has no control over what the Minister for Rail will do?
statement: Because—and forgive me for the repetition—the point of comparison was such a dog of a project that, actually, we just need to do simple things well, to do better, and to save New Zealanders money. I want to share with you a characterisation of Project iReX by someone that I think members across the House know: “KiwiRail under-scoped the landside infrastructure in 2021 meaning the decision to procure two large rail-enabled ships at that time was premature. To date, we are yet to see a satisfactory explanation for why this was the case.” That is a quote from the Hon Grant Robertson.

explanation: Asked what steps have been taken to improve school property delivery. She names steps directly: standardised repeatable designs, off-site manufactured classrooms, more maintenance investment, with delivery counts. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What steps have been taken to improve the delivery of school property for students across the country?
statement: After a ministerial inquiry found the Ministry of Education’s school property function was not fit for purpose, this Government has been driving for stronger performance and efficiency by investing far more into maintaining existing school buildings and delivering more new classrooms for less through the use of standardised, repeatable designs and offsite manufactured classrooms. In this financial year, we’ve already increased the number of cost-effective off-site manufactured buildings delivered—a 35 percent increase on the last financial year—and we’ve still got a long way to run. In 2023, only 433 new classrooms were built; in 2024, 581 were built—a 30 percent increase on the year before because we are driving efficiency, delivering results, and building more classrooms.

explanation: Asked how she is able to build more classrooms. She gives the mechanism: off-site manufacturing and standardised designs cutting per-classroom cost from $1.2m to $870k and shortening build time. Directly responsive.
question: How is she able to build more classrooms?
statement: Well, as previously mentioned, we’re delivering more off-site manufactured buildings. The average cost per classroom when we arrived in Government was $1.2 million. This is now down to $870,000—nearly a 30 percent reduction. And we are still driving this down so that more students can benefit from safe, warm, dry learning environments that support them to achieve. With our drive to use standardised designs and off-site manufacturing, we’re significantly reducing construction time and costs so more classrooms can be delivered more quickly and more efficiently.

explanation: Asked what changes, if any, she intends to make in response to the ICM report. She thanks social workers, says the Government 'did not need to wait' for the report, and lists measures already under way. That implies 'no new changes' without ever saying so, and no intended change is stated. Partial engagement.
question: What changes, if any, does she intend to make in response to the Aroturuki Tamariki | Independent Children’s Monitor’s Experiences of Care in Aotearoa 2023/24 report that found that Oranga Tamariki social workers are under significant pressure?
statement: Firstly, I just want to take this opportunity to say thank you to Oranga Tamariki social workers for what they do and also to the Independent Children’s Monitor (ICM) for what they do. I regularly talk with social workers across the country and I’ve personally visited at least 29 Oranga Tamariki sites since becoming Minister, and I’m constantly impressed by their dedication and commitment to caring for children. I know it takes a special kind of person to do the work that they do. This Government did not need to wait for this fourth report from the ICM. We already, amongst other things, secured funding of $68.5 million through Budget 2024 to upgrade the outdated case management technology system so social workers can have the tools they need, which means they can spend more time with the children and family that they work with. We’ve also recruited 33 allied support workers, which is a front-line role to support social workers by taking on tasks that don’t require a social work qualification, freeing up social workers to focus on core work.

explanation: Two-part question. The data-collection half is answered squarely (the $68.5m case management system is offered as the means). The second half — what she says to the 63 percent not receiving the minimum standard of care — is only brushed by the KPI reference and never addressed.
