question: How does she expect social workers to collect data when their workloads prevent them from visiting all tamariki assigned to them, and what does she say to the 63 percent of tamariki that aren’t receiving the minimum standard of care under the national care standards regulations?
statement: I absolutely agree that it’s difficult to collect data around young children. That is why we invested the $68.5 million into an updated case management system, which will allow them to collect that data better. And it’s why I also, in August 2024, set key performance indicators on the chief executive around the frequency of visits of children in care, timeliness around reports of concern, and supporting caregivers, because this means a lot to me and to the staff looking after our young people.

explanation: Asked what she says to the PSA's claim about 400 lost workers and higher workloads. She does respond to the quote — dismissing it as opinion — which is a form of answer, but the core assertion (staffing losses driving workload) is left untouched in favour of a spending talking point.
question: What does she say to the Public Service Association’s (PSA’s) national secretary, Fleur Fitzsimons, who has highlighted: “Decades of reviews and inquiries have consistently identified high staff workloads as a barrier to Oranga Tamariki consistently delivering on its purpose. The Government’s reckless spending cuts have seen Oranga Tamariki lose over 400 workers, meaning those remaining shoulder even higher workloads.”?
statement: I’m sure the PSA is entitled to their opinion, but, at the end of the day, this Government is committed to making sure that every dollar we spend goes towards our young people, and we are prioritising our front-line staff to make sure that they do have the tools that they need to do their job and do their job well.

explanation: Asked to confirm whether she thinks the statement was factually incorrect, or was dismissing it over its source. She answers the first branch flatly — 'I never said it was factually incorrect' — and restates her position. Terse and unhelpful, but it engages the question; the source branch is left implicit.
question: Can she confirm that she thinks the previous statement is factually incorrect, or is she dismissing it because of who the quote comes from?
statement: I never said it was factually incorrect; I said she’s entitled to her opinion.

explanation: Asked what she says to the 507 tamariki abused in care about hope for their future. She recounts her own advocacy and a 'see something, say something' campaign, ending with 'we can finally deal with the problem' — a glancing answer on the future, but the question's addressees and the four years of no improvement are never reached.
question: What does she say to the 507 tamariki and rangatahi that were abused or neglected in State care, about the hope for their future when there has been little improvement for them in the last four years, and the report stating that it is unlikely to change in the next report?
statement: Since becoming the Minister for Children, and even before being the Minister for Children, I’ve always advocated for the safety and wellbeing of our children in care. This is why I set it as a priority for Oranga Tamariki to get back to their core focus, which is the safety and wellbeing of our young people in care and those that come to the attention of Oranga Tamariki. No abuse is OK, but what I would say is I’ve spent the last year going around the country encouraging people that if they see something, say something. This report shows that we now have staff that feel they can speak up when they see something’s going wrong, and we can finally deal with the problem.

explanation: Asked whether she is confident her actions will improve achievement for all rangatahi. She answers 'I am absolutely confident' and stands by the actions. A complete yes; the supporting list neither helps nor hurts this attribute.
question: Is she confident that her actions will improve education achievement for all rangatahi?
statement: I am absolutely confident in that, and I stand by my actions to build a world-class, leading education system that delivers excellent and equitable outcomes for every child, including tamariki Māori. Right now, this term, every child learning in te reo Māori has access to high-quality, nationally consistent structured maths books benefiting 27,000 ākonga across the country. We’ve refreshed Te Marautanga o Aotearoa to be knowledge-rich year by year in te reo Māori. We’ve launched a structured programme to teach reading, writing, and speaking in te reo. We’ve developed purpose-built phonics check tools to monitor student progression in te reo. We’re delivering free decodable books that we have created in te reo Māori. We’re progressing my Māori education action plan, and I’ve established my Māori education advisory group.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by the NCEA literacy and numeracy tests given claims they are failing low-income students. She engages the premise head-on — 'the students are failing the assessments' — and defends keeping them. She never utters 'I stand by', but the position is unmistakable and the core is met.
question: Does she stand by her new NCEA reading, writing, and maths tests when these tests are failing students in low-income schools and principals at these schools have warned that these changes will create a generation of school leavers with no qualifications, most of whom will be Māori or Pasifika?
statement: Those assessments—literacy and numeracy assessments—are not failing the students. The students are failing the assessments, and it is upon this Government to make sure that every single one of those students gets the assistance that they need to get a base level of literacy and numeracy so that they can live the life that they want. If we don’t do that, we are pushing the problem down the road, and we all know what happens to young rangatahi who do not have good literacy and numeracy. This Government will not stand by and let that happen.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with a specific claim about kaupapa Māori kura and resource teachers of Māori. She answers a different proposition — that children should have choice — and never says whether she agrees with the claim or the role it defends. A narrow agree/disagree question sidestepped.
question: Does she agree with New Zealand Educational Institute President Ripika Lessels that “The evidence shows tamariki Māori succeed best in Kaupapa Māori Kura where te reo me ngā tikanga is supported. Resource teachers of Māori play a key role in supporting teachers and children in these schools.”?
statement: I agree that children should have choice. There are many families who would like to send their children to a kura kaupapa and there are many families who would like to send their children to an English-medium school. The purpose of this Government and the drive that I have is to make sure that, no matter where tamariki Māori end up, they have an excellent education and equitable outcomes.

explanation: Asked what message the Government sends by stressing literacy while considering defunding RT Māori. She justifies the consultation on distributional grounds (Southland vs Northland) rather than answering what message is sent, but the justification does engage the contradiction the question rested on.
question: What message is the Government sending to young Māori when they stress the importance of literacy, on the one hand, while considering defunding expert teachers who support literacy and te reo Māori, on the other?
statement: Well, we are out for consultation around a role, the resource teacher (RT) Māori role. The reason that we’re out for consultation is that there have been multiple evaluations that have said that this particular service delivery model is inequitable and is not optimised. I’ll give you one example of that. In Southland, there are five RTs Māori; in Northland, there are only three. Yet rangatahi Māori predominantly are in Northland, in far greater numbers than in Southland. That is the reason why we need to take a look at this resource and work out exactly how we can optimise it so more young people have access to that specialist help.

explanation: Two-part question. He answers the first directly — 'Yes, I stand by my statement', with a light 'in the context it was made' hedge — and answers the second by stating front-line health workers are critical to delivering the services. Both halves reached.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “my focus is and always will be on improving patient outcomes. Patients will be my number one priority”, and what is the role of health workers in achieving those outcomes for patients?
statement: Yes, I stand by my statement in the context it was made. My focus is and always will be on patients and improving patient outcomes. That’s why we are refocusing the healthcare system on delivering access to timely, quality healthcare for all New Zealanders through our Government’s health targets. Our Government knows that front-line health workers are critical in delivering these services. That’s why our front-line workforce—Health New Zealand—is the largest and strongest it has ever been, with over 2,000 more nurses employed at Health New Zealand since 2023, earning, on average, a salary of $125,000, comparable now with nurses in New South Wales. On this side of the House, we are unashamed that it is the patients who will always be at the heart of every decision we make, and it is the healthcare workers who are critical to delivering those services.

explanation: Asked to pick between two positions (Luxon's pay-parity statement vs his own 'not my job'). He picks one explicitly — 'I agree with the Prime Minister' — and endorses pay parity, plus explains the contested quote. The core of the either/or is squarely answered; the trailing swipe at the last Government doesn't displace the answer.
question: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, who said, with respect to nurses, “Whether they’re in aged care, whether they’re at GP community practices, or in the DHB-equivalent system they should be paid the same”, or Simeon Brown, who said nursing wages are “not my job”?
statement: Look, I agree with the Prime Minister, and the quote that was taken out of context by The Post this morning was in regards to contractual negotiations between doctor clinics and their staff. That was a quote taken out of context, but I absolutely agree with the need to make sure that there is pay parity between nurses working in our hospitals and in our primary care areas. Ultimately, we know it will take time to deliver that, but that’s why we’re focusing back on primary care, which was something the last Government didn’t.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: are these PSA-represented clinicians 'bureaucrats'? The response never says yes, no, or anything about who counts as a bureaucrat. It pivots immediately to attacking the union's leader and then to generic 'focus on patients' talking points. A specific question completely avoided.
question: Are the dietitians, the mental health nurses, the pharmacists, and the public health nurses represented by the Public Service Association (PSA) “bureaucrats”?
statement: Well, I’m very happy to talk about the PSA union, led by a failed Labour Party candidate who couldn’t even win her seat, and ultimately the union’s doing what the union does: when the National Party’s in Government, they attack the Government. That’s what they’re doing, and I completely get what they’re trying to do, but, ultimately, my focus is on the patients and getting better outcomes for them. That’s what this Government is unashamedly focused on.

explanation: Asked why he attacked the PSA's leader rather than engaging the report's contents. He glances at the framing ('I'm open to the low blow from time to time') but gives no reason, and switches to patients-vs-unions talking points. At most an implicit 'because they're a union front' — gestures near the question without reaching it.
question: Why did he attack Fleur Fitzsimons rather than respond to the contents of the PSA report; couldn’t he be the bigger man, at least metaphorically? [Interruption]
statement: Look, I’m open to the low blow from time to time, but what I would say is that this Government is focused on patients. They’re focused on the unions. They got rid of the health targets, they ran down our health system, they restructured it during the pandemic, and they forgot about the patients. We will stand on the side of the patients while they stand on the side of unions—and shame on them. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why he won't respond seriously to a report documenting specific patient harms. The response is entirely an attack on the report's author's electoral record and is cut off before any substance. Neither the 'why' nor the report's contents are touched.
question: Why, if he’s so committed to patient outcomes, won’t he respond seriously to a report that documents delays in rehab for stroke patients, malnourished cancer patients, and untreated babies left with cleft palates because of his Government’s cuts?
statement: Well, if she’s talking about the PSA union’s report, which she’s talking about again, well, I’ll tell you what: the PSA union member, who is clearly leading that organisation, who failed to win her seat—

explanation: Same question repeated without the attributed cause. This time he engages the underlying subject — concedes 'a need for greater investment' and cites funding — which is a partial response to the report's substance, but he still never addresses why he won't respond to it or any of the named harms. Themes offered where the core was avoided.
question: Why, if he’s so committed to patient outcomes, won’t he respond seriously to a report that documents delays in rehab for stroke patients, malnourished cancer patients, and untreated babies left with cleft palates?
statement: Well, I acknowledge that there is a need for greater investment in our health system, and I’m proud of the investment this Government has made. We have increased health funding by $16.68 billion over three Budgets. We are focusing the system back on front-line service delivery. That is the focus this Government is bringing in putting the patients back at the heart, not the bureaucratic change which the last Government was focused on.

explanation: Two parts: will he accept the invitation to attend a team meeting, and if not is he out of touch. He answers neither directly, but does contest the premise head-on ('There is no such thing as a hiring freeze') and cites vacancy numbers, which is genuine engagement rather than pure pivot. The yes/no invitation is left unanswered and the close is an attack on the questioner's side.
question: Will he take up the invitation posed by professionals struggling with the hiring freeze in Health New Zealand: “We’d love someone to come to our team meeting and explain why we do not have approval to advertise for the current vacancies we are holding.”, and, if not, does he worry that he is out of touch with the reality of healthcare in New Zealand?
statement: Well, there are hundreds of jobs advertised at Health New Zealand, currently online and available for people to put their names forward. There is no such thing as a hiring freeze. We are focused on front-line service delivery. As I said in my primary answer, we have the largest healthcare workforce ever in New Zealand. We have over 2,000 more nurses employed, under this Government, in Health New Zealand. We are focusing back on the delivery of services for New Zealanders, and those members should look in the mirror. When they got rid of the health targets, they saw the outcomes reduced for patients, and then they decided to restructure during a pandemic—shame on them.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he made about police work on gangs; he names the announcement, who made it, and what it covered (Gangs Act enforcement, charges, insignia seizures). Direct and complete for the scope asked.
question: What recent announcements has he made about Police’s work to tackle gangs?
statement: Last week, the Minister of Justice, and I, announced that police have done outstanding work in enforcing the Gangs Act, laying charges and seizing insignia. The Gangs Act has proven to be an enabling piece of legislation as well, providing a vehicle for police to cause further disruption to gangs through a raft of other changes, including firearms. Contrary to all the commentary prior to the implementation of the legislation, compliance has been high, and it is obvious to the public that our police are controlling the streets again, not the gangs.

explanation: Narrow factual question — how many charges under the Gangs Act. Answered with the number (385, plus 3,546 other charges) and a date. Nothing avoided.
question: How many charges have police laid under the Gangs Act?
statement: As of yesterday, police have laid 385 charges under the Gangs Act 2024, and 3,546 other charges overall against individuals on the National Gang List. This Government is committed to giving police the tools they need to significantly disrupt gangs.

explanation: Narrow two-part count question; both figures given (76 patches, 67 firearms) with an as-at date. Fully answered.
question: How many patch and firearm seizures have been made?
statement: As at 19 February, police have seized 76 patches and 67 firearms from gang members since the new legislation came into force. It has proven to be a valuable tool for police to find further evidence of offending and lay more charges.

explanation: Asked for examples; two dated, concrete examples supplied. The question is fully engaged — that it was a friendly patsy question affects other attributes, not this one.
question: What recent examples of great work and tackling gangs can he share?
statement: On Tuesday, 14 January, Napier police executed a search warrant and found a loaded firearm, ammunition, cannabis, methamphetamine, and $3,900 in cash, laying multiple charges. In the Central Hawke’s Bay, on 30 January, police arrested an Outlaws gang member and seized three firearms, including a fully loaded pistol, which was in the same bag as a quantity of methamphetamine. I want to thank all our police, who are doing an outstanding job in cracking down on gangs and organised crime.

explanation: Asked how firearms prohibition orders are intended to make NZ safer; the answer states the mechanism — expanded police search powers over persons, vehicles and premises to keep firearms from gang members and high-risk offenders. The 'how' is addressed directly.
question: How are firearms prohibition orders intended to make New Zealand safer?
statement: Last year, Parliament passed the Firearms Prohibition Orders Legislation Amendment Act to keep firearms out of the hands of gang members and other high-risk offenders. Last Sunday, that legislation came into force. This means police have more powers to search individuals subject to a firearms prohibition order, along with their vehicles and premises, to ensure that they are not in possession of firearms.

explanation: Asked how the improvements will stop future offenders accessing firearms; answer names the change (expanded qualifying criteria beyond specific violent offences to drug/firearms/other violent convictions) and the loophole it closes (senior members using prospects). Squarely on the question asked.
question: How will improvements to firearms prohibition orders ensure future offenders can’t access firearms?
statement: Previously, firearms prohibition orders were limited to offenders convicted of specific violent offences like murder, serious assault, sexual violence, and aggravated robbery. I have expanded the qualifying criteria, allowing firearms prohibition orders to be issued to gang members and criminals convicted of drug, firearms, and other violent offences. This means senior gang members can no longer avoid firearms prohibition orders by having their prospects commit offences on their behalf.

explanation: Asked what the improved search powers will mean for offenders under firearms prohibition orders. The answer states exactly that: police can search FPO subjects at any time without needing suspicion of a breach or other offence. The closing rhetoric about criminals being on notice is surplus, not evasion — the core was reached directly.
question: What will improved police search powers mean for offenders subject to firearms prohibition orders now that the new regime is in force?
statement: Police now have the power to search gang members and serious offenders subject to a firearms prohibition order at any time. They do not need to suspect they’re breaching their firearms prohibition order or that they are committing any other offence. Firearms prohibition orders are only effective if police have the power to enforce them, and I have made sure that they do. Criminals are now on notice. Illegal firearms possession will not be tolerated, and they will be held accountable for their actions.

explanation: Asked what the FPO regime means for the Government's law-and-order commitment — a sprawling, invited question. The answer engages it squarely: the regime is delivery on that commitment, and she links it to the violent-crime trend she expects to continue. It is talking-point-shaped, but the question asked for exactly that connection, so it is not a pivot away.
question: What does the improved firearms prohibition orders regime mean for this Government’s commitment to restoring law and order?
statement: I’m delivering on this Government’s commitment to crack down on crime and restore law and order. Last year, reported violent crime dropped for the first time since 2018. With these improved firearms prohibition orders now in force, I am confident this downward trend in violent crime will continue, making our communities safer, and ensuring criminals are held to account.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statements and actions on extended arrest and detention powers. Answered 'Yes' with a light contextual qualifier and a restatement of the position. Direct and essentially complete.
question: Does he stand by his statements and actions in respect of extended powers of arrest and detention for ordinary citizens?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were given. I particularly stand by my statement yesterday that “New Zealanders are fed up with the level of retail crime that they are experiencing in our communities. That’s why this Government has considered proposals to change the rules, because if you want to have a different outcome, sometimes you have to change things, and that is what we’re proposing.”

explanation: Asked whether he considered Hospitality New Zealand's health-and-safety objection before announcing the policy. Answered 'Yes' up front, then explained the rationale. The follow-on is justification rather than a dodge; the yes/no core was delivered.
question: Did he consider the opinion of Hospitality New Zealand, who told the Ministerial Advisory Group for Victims of Retail Crime that Hospitality New Zealand would consider it a significant health and safety risk to both staff and customers if we start advocating for stronger detaining abilities, before he announced extended powers of citizen’s arrest?
statement: Yes. I mean, I think the member is pointing to the fact that there is a widespread variety of views on this matter, but the point I would make is that, in the hospitality context, we have laws in place after 9 p.m. where a citizen’s arrest can be conducted, but before 9 p.m. it can’t be, and so, fundamentally, it’s about trying to rectify that situation. Of course, no hospitality worker is obliged to do anything by these proposals; it is an option that is available and can be used if the circumstances are appropriate.

explanation: Asked why he announced the proposal when the only supportive written submission was the advisory group chair's own. He answers the 'why' — because he believes it is good policy and wants to try something different — but never engages the submissions premise that gave the question its point, and closes by turning it back on the questioner. Half the question was reached.
question: Why did he announce proposals for extended powers for citizen’s arrest when the only written submissions to Sunny Kaushal’s Ministerial Advisory Group for Victims of Retail Crime that clearly supported increased powers of arrest for ordinary citizens was the submission of Sunny Kaushal in the name of the Dairy and Business Owners Group?
statement: Why? Well, because we believe it’s a good policy. The ministerial advisory group led by Sunny Kaushal has a variety of people in it, and they all have their different views. We fully expect that they will come up with proposals which are bold and which may well be pushing the boat out, but we need to experiment and come up with different approaches, otherwise we’re going to have the same outcome. I think all New Zealanders are fed up with the level of retail crime that they’re seeing in our communities. We’ve had a very significant increase over the past few years, and if the member wants to argue for the current arrangements being perfect and everything being fine, well that’s up to him, but I think we need to do something different.

explanation: A narrow factual question: did he or the advisory group consult the Police Association before announcing? He never says yes or no. He answers a different question — why the 9 p.m. distinction is illogical — then moves to select committee process and a list of other law-and-order measures. The core was squarely avoided.
question: Did he or his ministerial advisory group for victims of retail crime consult with the Police Association, whose president, Chris Cahill, said, “The idea that the public can do this safely is just putting them at risk that isn’t necessary.” before he announced his powers of citizen’s arrest?
statement: Well, I’d be interested as to how the Police Association consider it is OK at 9.05 p.m. to do something and not OK at 8.55 p.m. to do something. Anyway, that’s part of the ongoing discussion, and this legislation, when it’s introduced, will come into the House. We are sure that we’ll get a wide variety of views in the select committee process, but this is a Government that is prepared to do different things to get different outcomes, and we’re not satisfied with the situation on our streets right now. We’re not satisfied with the level of retail crime. This is one of many things that we’re considering in order to improve the situation, alongside bringing in real consequences for crime with our sentencing regime, the return of three strikes, and many other things, such as giving the police extra powers to deal with organised crime.

explanation: Two parts: was Brian Tamaki consulted, and is he concerned the powers could be misused by malicious actors. The first is answered flatly and clearly — 'Nobody asked Destiny.' The second, the concern about misuse, is never addressed; he dismisses Destiny's views rather than the risk. One part answered, one dropped.
question: Is it the fact that he or his ministerial advisory group consulted with Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki, who suggested his thugs, who have disrupted lawful activities, will use power of arrest and detention when he said, “How Excited i am That MAN UP Is about to Recieve Increased Powers to Police.. Where Law and Order has Failed”, and is he concerned that new citizen’s arrest powers may be misused by such malicious actors?
statement: Well, I did think it was a cheap shot by the New Zealand Herald to refer to Destiny being in support of this proposal. Nobody asked Destiny. Nobody is particularly concerned in the views of the Destiny Church on this matter, and we certainly don’t make our decisions as to whether to progress law and order policies based on the opinions of the good bishop, and I’d encourage that member not to pay too much attention to his views either.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned that the advisory group chair had a conflict of interest in submitting to himself. He defends the appointment on its merits and describes the dairy-owner constituency, which implies 'no' without ever saying so or touching the conflict itself. It gestures at the question from a distance.
question: Is he concerned that Sunny Kaushal, the chair of the ministerial advisory group, had a deep and significant conflict of interest when he, essentially, made a submission to himself when he submitted in his capacity as chair of the Dairy and Business Owners Group and then largely adopted the recommendations he had made to himself?
statement: Well, of course, we did appoint Sunny Kaushal because of his wide-ranging experience on the front line, dealing particularly with the dairy owners who have to deal with a horrendous level of abuse and violence in our communities. We have thoughts very much in mind, particularly for husband and wife teams working very hard in the small retail sector, trying to make a living, often coming from other countries, trying to settle in New Zealand and make a living and struggling with the level of violent and ongoing retail crime. We want to offer them solutions rather than just continuing on with the same approach that we’ve had for such a long time.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the Prebble appointment and, if so, why. He answers both parts explicitly — yes to the first, and for the second cites the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 criteria, the Crown–Māori relationship, and the members' skills and capabilities. Direct on both branches.
question: Does he stand by his appointment of Richard Prebble to the Waitangi Tribunal in light of Prebble’s comments on his resignation; if so, why?
statement: Ki te wāhanga tuatahi o tēnei pātai, āna, āna. Ki te wāhanga tuarua, i whai whakaaro mātou i ngā rārangi kōrero i raro i te ture mō Te Tiriti o Waitangi 1975, me te mea nei me āta whakaarohia, me āta tirohia hoki te hononga i waenga i te Karauna me te iwi Māori, tae atu rā ki ngā pūmanawa me ngā pūkenga o ngā mema. Nā Mr Prebble hoki i tuku mai i tāna reta rihaina. E mihi ana ki a ia me tēnā reta, ā, hoki ora atu, e Rīhari, ki Rotomā.

explanation: Asked what the Waitangi Tribunal does. He states its statutory function: to inquire into and make recommendations on claims that the Crown has acted inconsistently with Treaty principles. Complete. The jab at the member to go read the Act is a civility matter, not a dodge.
question: What does the Waitangi Tribunal do?
statement: The Waitangi Tribunal’s role is set out very clearly in the Treaty of Waitangi Act, which I suggest the member reads. It is to inquire into and make recommendations on claims that the Crown has acted in a manner inconsistent with the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi.

explanation: Asked whether he was aware of Prebble's 'one Treaty' view before appointing him, and if not why he didn't ask. He answers the operative branch — he was aware of some of Prebble's views — which makes the second branch moot. 'Some' hedges around whether that particular view was among them, so the core is engaged but not fully pinned.
question: Was he aware of Richard Prebble’s views prior to his appointment to the tribunal that there is one Treaty, despite there being both English and te reo versions which are not direct translations of each other, and, if not, why didn’t he ask him for his views before appointing him?
statement: I was aware of some of Mr Prebble’s views prior to appointment, and he’s entitled to his own opinions and his own views.

explanation: A direct question: did Māori cede sovereignty, and if not, why not. He notes there are a variety of views and pivots to what he is 'absolutely clear about' — that rangatiratanga will be protected. Neither branch is answered; the question is acknowledged and then stepped around.
question: Did Māori cede sovereignty when they signed Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and, if not, why not?
statement: As we’re all aware, there are a variety of views in relations to that matter. But what I’m absolutely clear about is that there’s one thing that existed before the Treaty of Waitangi and will continue to exist after we all leave this place, is that rangatiratanga will be protected, preserved, and enhanced.

explanation: Asked what the financial statements show about revenue and expenses. Gives both figures directly ($600m above forecast revenue, $600m below forecast expenses) plus the year-on-year expense growth. The closing spin about spending constraint doesn't displace the answer.
question: What do the financial statements show about revenue and expenses?
statement: Core Crown tax revenue for the seven months was $600 million higher than forecast in the half-year update in December, while core Crown expenses were $600 million lower than forecast. Some of that is likely to do with timing across the year, but it is interesting to compare growth and expenses in this set of accounts with a year ago. Over the seven months to January, core Crown expenses were only 2 percent higher than they were in the corresponding period a year earlier. That shows the Government’s commitment to spending constraint and turning around the poor fiscal position we inherited.

explanation: Asked what the statements show about the operating balance and debt. Both are given squarely: OBEGALx deficit of $3.7b ($1.4b better than forecast) and net debt at 42.8 percent of GDP.
question: What do the financial statements show about the operating balance and debt?
statement: The OBEGALx deficit at seven months is $3.7 billion, which is $1.4 billion better than expected at the half-year update. Let’s see how that pans out at year end, but the improvement is a positive sign so far. Net core Crown debt is in line with forecasts, at an estimated 42.8 percent of GDP. The Government’s intention remains, in the short term, to get net debt trending down towards 40 percent of GDP, and that will involve reprioritising spending over the next few years.

explanation: Asked what else would help balance the books. The answer is stated — economic growth — and quantified ($2b a year from a quarter-percent of nominal GDP). It then runs on into general pro-business rhetoric, but the core of the question was reached.
question: What else would help get the books back in balance?
statement: The economic growth is good for wages. It is good for jobs. It is good for opportunities and living standards. It is also good for the books. Additional growth of even a quarter of a percent of nominal GDP each year would boost tax revenue by $2 billion a year by the end of the forecast period. That is why the Government is committed to removing unnecessary obstacles from the path of businesses and creating an environment in which people are rewarded for investing, for innovating, for taking risks, for employing others. We do not view business as the enemy, because we know it is not the Government that ultimately creates jobs. It is business, not Government, that generates the revenue that funds public services.

explanation: Asked whether he believes the Tribunal plays a critical role in holding the Government accountable. After a long statutory preamble he lands on it explicitly: he disagrees with that characterisation. A clear 'no' to the question as put.
question: Does he believe the Waitangi Tribunal plays a critical role in holding the Government accountable for its actions or omissions that breach Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: Under the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975, the Waitangi Tribunal is empowered to inquire into and make recommendations on claims by Māori that the Crown has acted in a manner or omitted to act in a manner inconsistent with the principles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, the Treaty of Waitangi. As an independent commission of inquiry, the tribunal provides a platform for claims to be heard, ensures historical—and herstorical—and contemporary grievances are examined, and offers recommendations to help guide the Crown in upholding its Treaty obligations. As such, I disagree with the member’s characterisation of the Waitangi Tribunal as holding the Government accountable.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees the Treaty is to be honoured rather than settled, and whether the Tribunal's powers should be strengthened. He agrees instead with a proposition the question was contrasted against (that claims should be resolved and settled) and never touches the Tribunal's powers. Answers a different question.
question: Does he agree with the late Moana Jackson, one of the most profound contemporary contributors to Tiriti understanding, that the Treaty is to be honoured, not settled, and, if so, does he agree that the tribunal’s work must be ongoing and, for the sake of clarity for the nation, have its power strengthened, not diminished?
statement: I absolutely agree with the sentiment that the Crown and the Government—and, actually, everyone in this House—need to ensure that historical Treaty claims and grievances are resolved and settled. That’s why I want to mihi to Minister Goldsmith, who led the settlement of Te Korowai o Wainuiārua claims today through legislation.

explanation: Asked whether it is appropriate that New Zealand First lead the Tribunal review given their hostility. He confirms the review exists and will happen in due course, then deflects the allocation of responsibility back to the questioner. The appropriateness question — the whole point — is never engaged.
question: Is it appropriate that New Zealand First are leading a Government review of the function and purpose of the Waitangi Tribunal, given their senior Ministers have been publicly hostile towards the role of the tribunal, which already has limited powers as it is?
statement: The review of the Waitangi Tribunal that’s articulated and set out in the coalition arrangement between New Zealand First and National is one that will be undertaken in due course. As to the allocation of responsibilities in regards to that review, that’s something that the member clearly knows more about than I do.

explanation: Asked what he is doing to uphold a specific Tribunal recommendation about Treaty clauses in 28 Acts. Replies only that many recommendations have been received and 'remain for active review' — the specific recommendation and any action on it go unaddressed. A narrow question met with a generality.
question: Ka pai. Tēnā koe. Back to the Minister: what is he doing to uphold the tribunal’s recommendation that this Government abandon its coalition policy to review and potentially remove Treaty clauses from 28 pieces of legislation, as promoted by New Zealand First?
statement: We have received a number of recommendations from the Waitangi Tribunal, as Ministers, over the last 15 months, and those matters remain for active review.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on the ferries programme. Names the 4 February announcement opening the process to alternative market proposals, and says more will follow after Cabinet in late March. Directly responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made on the Cook Strait ferries programme?
statement: On 4 February, the Government opened the door to alternative proposals from the market, as we leave no stone unturned in getting value for taxpayers. We’ll have much more to say about this process after Cabinet meets at the end of March.

explanation: Asked how the approach differs from iReX. The contrast is drawn — iReX's cost escalation from ~$1b to a forecast $4b versus a worldwide search for shipyard partners. Drifts into shipbuilder interest at the end, but the difference asked about is stated.
question: How does this approach differ from the previous project, iReX?
statement: Well, the previous project was commissioned at $401 million for two ferries, and then there was an infrastructure cost contained in the forward proposal, which was promptly abandoned, and it went from just over $1 billion to, as Treasury forecast, over $4 billion. In this case, we’re announcing a worldwide search for shipyard partners, but we cannot speak for specific shipyards’ interest. But the reality is that commercial shipbuilders all around the world are showing an interest now, and we should be able to give the country far greater detail in a matter of weeks now.

explanation: Asked what the Government expects to announce after Cabinet. He describes the two options Cabinet will consider rather than what is expected to be announced, and the response breaks off mid-sentence. Engages the subject and partially constrains the answer without reaching what was asked.
question: What does the Government expect to announce on the ferries after Cabinet next discusses the topic?
statement: We were very clear on 11 December 2024 that Cabinet will be considering two firm options: cost-effective infrastructure with vessels taking vehicles and passengers—that’s one—and cost-effective infrastructure with vehicles taking vehicles, passengers, and rail wagons. The second one hasn’t been worked on—

explanation: Two parts: does she stand by the statement (answered outright, 'Yes'), and what impact international inflation has on New Zealand's growth (answered as 'it depends', with a dairy-price example). The first half is complete, the second is hedged around rather than answered.
question: Does she stand by her statement that “Recent data releases are consistent with a growing New Zealand economy”; if so, what impact does inflation in international economies have on New Zealand’s growth?
statement: Yes, and to the second part of the question, it depends. For example, an increase in world dairy prices would likely be good for the New Zealand economy.

explanation: Asked whether 31,000 more jobseeker beneficiaries is consistent with a growing economy. Never says yes or no: redirects to the unemployment rate matching pre-election forecasts, then attacks the previous Minister. The figure put to her is not addressed at all.
question: Is 31,000 more people on the jobseeker benefit consistent with a growing New Zealand economy?
statement: Well, there are two parts that we need to consider there. The first is that unemployment is running at exactly the rate that it was forecast to be when that member’s party was leading the Government prior to the election. The second part is what has changed is we now have a Minister who is dedicated to putting incentives in place so that as many people as possible who can work do work—an active welfare system. Because I am looking at members—and I’m looking at Carmel Sepuloni—who, despite record low unemployment, allowed the number of jobseeker beneficiaries to increase dramatically. What a failure.

explanation: Q: how can Māori trust his judgment after the Prebble appointment? A: "Can I just have that question again, please?" The question is never engaged — no part of it is answered. It is a request for repetition rather than a pivot to talking points, so it is not the worst kind of dodge, but nothing about the appointment or his judgment is addressed. The substantive reply arrives in the following pair, which is scored separately.
question: How can New Zealanders, and especially Māori, trust his judgment after he appointed someone to our Waitangi Tribunal who has proven themselves historically illiterate?
statement: Can I just have that question again, please? Thank you.

explanation: Q asks how New Zealanders and Māori can trust his judgment given the appointment. The answer disputes the questioner's use of the word "our" and rejects the characterisation of the Tribunal as one party's preserve. That is a quarrel with the framing, not a response to the core: neither his judgment nor the appointment is addressed at all. Note the answer's civility and its point about the Tribunal being non-partisan are irrelevant here — the question was simply not reached.
question: How can New Zealanders, especially Māori, trust his judgment after he appointed someone to our Waitangi Tribunal who has proven themselves historically illiterate?
statement: The Waitangi Tribunal is not the preserve of one party, whether or not it’s the Green Party or any other party. If the use of the word “our” is to select one particular group in this House, I reject the characterisation.

explanation: Q: does he acknowledge the appointment and immediate resignation made a mockery of the institution? The answer engages the substance squarely — it asserts due process was followed, confirms the resignation, and says he accepted it. It is a clear implicit "no, I do not acknowledge that", and it stays on the appointment rather than pivoting. It stops short of 1.0 only because the explicit acknowledgment question is never answered in terms; the rebuttal is left to be inferred.
question: Does he acknowledge that his appointment of Prebble to the tribunal, only for him to immediately resign and make a political stunt, makes a mockery of the institution itself?
statement: The appointment of the Hon Richard Prebble followed due process. Mr Prebble has resigned. I have accepted his resignation and I wish him well.

explanation: Q: does he stand by all his Government's statements and actions? A: "The answer is yes." Direct and complete. The sarcastic preamble about the "very clever question" is a civility matter and does not move forthrightness.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: I thank the member for that very, very, very clever question. The answer is yes.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree Willis delivered ferries on 11 December 2024, and if so why was he sent on a global search. The first part is never answered — no agreement or disagreement is expressed. The second is only glanced at: "the job happened to be by chance passed on to me" gestures at why he was dispatched, wrapped in inherited-mess talking points about cost blowouts. Mostly a pivot, with a fragment of the second limb touched.
question: Thank you. Does he agree with Nicola Willis that she delivered new Cook Strait ferries on 11 December 2024; if so, why was Winston Peters subsequently dispatched on a global search for replacements, including meeting with the company who was contracted to build those ferries in the first place?
statement: The reality of the matter is that the Minister of Finance inherited an absolute mess. What was meant to be $401 million for two ferries and then a total infrastructure cost under $1.4 billion, all up with the ferries, had gone from there to over $4 billion, which was a warning that Treasury gave the previous Government. So, having dealt with that, the job happened to be by chance passed on to me, and I’ve sought to rectify the matter, at a massive saving to the New Zealand people.

explanation: Q: does he agree Willis was too hasty in cancelling the ferries, as the Herald reported? The answer does engage the core by attacking the premise — it says the Herald "got it massively wrong" and points to Treasury's advice, which communicates disagreement. But he never says whether he himself agrees the cancellation was hasty, deflecting into a complaint about the newspaper's accuracy. Partial: the question's subject is addressed, its actual yes/no is hedged around.
question: Does he agree that Nicola Willis was too hasty in cancelling the ferries, as reported by the New Zealand Herald?
statement: The reality is that we will all have those sorts of criticisms being made, but the New Zealand Herald today got it massively wrong in the editorial in the second to last paragraph. I’d ask them, for goodness’ sake, to start getting their facts right for a change by reading the full story, which was told not by me, not by Nicola Willis, but by Treasury itself to Grant Robertson.

explanation: Q offers a binary: negotiate the break fee first, or pursue both concurrently. The answer picks neither, but explains why — the break fee is a matter between KiwiRail and Hyundai and not his to sequence — and then volunteers that a new deal would trigger reconsideration of the prior settlement. Rejecting the premise with a reason and supplying the adjacent fact is engagement, not a dodge; it falls short of full marks because the sequencing question is left formally unanswered.
question: Will Winston Peters prioritise negotiating the break fee with Hyundai before he enters into another contract with them, or will he pursue both negotiations concurrently?
statement: I appreciate what the member is asking, but the so-called break fee lies as a matter between KiwiRail and Hyundai; the new issue that we’re dealing on is separate. However, in our representations, it was made very, very clear to me that, while that matter is separate, if there were to be a new deal, there would be a reconsideration of the prior settlement, to which we are not a party at the moment.

explanation: A narrow quantitative question — how many millions of school lunches the break fee could have funded. The answer gives no figure and no attempt at one, pivoting immediately to a "parallel circumstance" talking point about inheriting both programmes unfunded. A specific factual question squarely avoided, which the rubric treats as the worse kind of failure.
question: How many millions of healthy school lunches could Nicola Willis’ ferry break-fee have paid for?
statement: Well, all I do know is that we’ve got a sort of parallel circumstance here: the Government inherited a school lunch programme unfunded, and we inherited a ferry programme unfunded as well.

explanation: Q: how many Kiwis are out of a job because of the Compass contract? The answer does not supply the number, but it responds to the request head-on: it says no one can answer it without speculating and offers to obtain an answer if put in writing. That is a direct, complete response to what was asked rather than a pivot — the same shape as a plain refusal, which the rubric scores high. Held below 0.9 because "on speculation" leaves slight ambiguity as to whether the figure is unknown or merely not to hand.
question: How many Kiwis are now out of a job thanks to the Government giving the school lunches contract to multinational corporation Compass?
statement: I don’t think anyone can answer that question on speculation, but, if the member wants to write a note or put it in written form, we’ll get an answer.

explanation: The question is loaded but answerable: when Willis said she had delivered, what did she mean? The answer states plainly what he takes her to have meant — the quarterly update released that morning — which addresses the question directly and implicitly rejects the three sardonic options offered. It then drifts into an economy-turnaround set piece with the ship metaphor, which is padding rather than answer. Engaged, then trailing off.
question: When Nicola Willis said she has delivered, did she mean delivering 31,000 more people to Work and Income New Zealand, delivering 72,000 New Zealanders overseas, or delivering thousands of inedible meals into rubbish bins in schools across the country?
statement: I think when the Minister of Finance was saying, “I have delivered”, she meant the answer that came in the quarterly update this morning. We have turned the circumstances of this country’s economy around. It’s the first bright news we’ve had, and, like a big vessel out at sea, it is hard to stop. It is hard to turn an economy around—

explanation: Q: what recent reports has she seen on the Government's fiscal position? The answer names the report directly — Treasury's interim financial statements for the first seven months, released today — and states what it covers, including OBEGALx and the debt position. Direct and complete. That it is a friendly patsy question does not bear on whether it was answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the Government’s fiscal position?
statement: Today, the interim financial statements of the Government for the first seven months of the financial year were released by Treasury, as referred to by the Deputy Prime Minister. The statements show Crown revenue and expenditure for the financial year up to 31 January, and they also update both the operating balance before gains and losses, excluding ACC—that is OBEGALx—and the Crown’s debt position.

explanation: Asked whether a 42% rise in consumer credit defaults is consistent with a growing economy. Willis concedes the defaults are evidence of financial stress and offers a lag explanation, which touches the premise, but never says whether the figure is or isn't consistent with growth before pivoting to inflation under the previous government. Partial engagement, core comparison avoided.
question: Is consumer credit defaults increasing by 42 percent consistent with a growing New Zealand economy?
statement: I am always concerned by New Zealanders being under financial stress, and obviously consumer credit defaults are evidence of that. But what we need to be clear about is that we had a Government that allowed inflation to be driven to 7.3 percent, that saw successive years of high inflation outside New Zealand’s target band, that saw the Reserve Bank left alone while they sprayed the money hose around to crank up interest rates at a rapid rate. That has then had a very chilling effect on the economy, and it shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone with economic literacy that it takes some time to turn a mess of that magnitude around.

explanation: Asked whether 35%/67% rises in liquidations are consistent with a growing economy. The answer is entirely a list of government actions and a message of support to businesses; the liquidation figures and the consistency question are never touched at all.
question: Is a 35 percent increase in liquidations for the North Island and a 67 percent rise in the South Island consistent with a growing New Zealand economy?
statement: I want to see New Zealand businesses thrive. That’s why, from day one in office, this Government has leaned into the actions a Government can take to make this a better place to invest and grow. That is why we are better educating New Zealand kids. That is why we are reducing red tape and regulation. That’s why we’re investing in productivity-enhancing infrastructure. That’s why we’re making sure our science system actually delivers commercially realisable opportunities. What I would say to any New Zealand business who is struggling is this: you’ve gone through a really tough few years, but you’ve now got a Government that’s on your side.

explanation: Asked whether building consents down 7.2% is consistent with a growing economy. Willis gives a causal account of why construction falls when interest rates are high, which is adjacent to the question, but she never states whether the decline is consistent with growth, and closes by attacking the questioner.
question: Is building consents being down 7.2 percent consistent with a growing New Zealand economy?
statement: Well, I want to see construction improving and increasing, and that’s why we are taking steps across the board to support that, including liberalising land markets, improving infrastructure funding and financing, reducing the complexity of getting a building consent, allowing people to import more easily. But fundamentally, the construction industry responds badly when interest rates are high, because they need to borrow for their construction projects. So Governments that allow inflation to get out of control so that interest rates are ratcheted up tend to find that construction drops off. That member, Barbara Edmonds, is sitting next to members of a Cabinet who allowed a historic level of damage to be delivered to the New Zealand economy, and now she has the cheek to blame us for fixing it. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether the listed indicators are green shoots of growth or an example of her delivery. She opens with a flat "No" and gives her own characterisation of what they are. Partisan and content-free on substance, but the question was a binary and she answered it squarely — detail and truthfulness are not scored here.
question: Is the growing number of people on the benefit, growing company liquidations, growing numbers of New Zealanders leaving for Australia, growing consumer credit defaults, fewer homes being built, the green shoots of a growing economy or, like the ferry contract, an example of her delivery?
statement: No, they are the remnants of a failed regime, a Labour-led Government that did all it could to destroy this economy, and we on this side of the House are fixing it up.

explanation: Asked what recent tourism announcements she has made. Upston names the announcements ($3m Regional Tourism Boost Fund, $9m Great Rides infrastructure) and their purpose. Direct and complete.
question: What recent announcements has she made about boosting tourism in New Zealand?
statement: I have recently announced a range of investments and initiatives to boost tourism in New Zealand. This includes a new $3 million Regional Tourism Boost Fund that will be used to attract more international visitors to regional destinations, and a $9 million boost for infrastructure upgrades and replacements on our Great Rides cycle trails. Tourism is a crucial part of our Government’s focus on economic growth, and these investments are part of our tourism boost package to bring international visitor numbers back to pre-COVID levels.

explanation: Asked why the investments are important. The answer gives reasons for each of the two investments — visitor volumes on the Great Rides, and regional tourism organisations securing funding. Squarely on the question asked.
question: Why are these investments important?
statement: Together, the 23 Great Rides receive about a million visitors a year; of whom, around 20 percent are international visitors. With those numbers expected to continue growing, maintaining and improving these trails is a must. That’s why the $9 million boost for our Great Rides cycle trails is important, so visitors can keep enjoying the unique experience of pedalling through New Zealand’s beautiful landscapes. The Regional Tourism Boost is a chance for regional tourism organisations to secure funding for activities that boost international visitation, helping local businesses and communities thrive.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by a statement and whether he is on track. "The answers are yes and yes" — both parts answered explicitly and completely, brevity notwithstanding.
question: Does he stand by his statement regarding the new Cook Strait ferries that by the end of March 2025, “We’re going to be able to announce who’s in the game, what they’re aiming for, and what the cost will be”; if so, is he on track to do so?
statement: I thank that very sensible member for his sensible two questions, and the answers are yes and yes.

explanation: Asked whether any bids have been received and how many. "No bids have been received yet" answers the first part and makes the second moot. Direct and complete.
question: Has he actually received any bids yet from shipbuilders for the new Cook Strait ferries; if so, how many?
statement: No bids have been received yet.

explanation: Asked whether he gave Hyundai assurances and what they were. Peters does recount what he told Hyundai, so he engages the "what did you say" part, but the reply is a historical anecdote about respect and trust rather than an answer to whether assurances against a second cancellation were given. Half of the two-part question reached.
question: Did he provide Hyundai with any assurances that a new contract signed with his Government would not fall through again; if so, what were those assurances that he gave?
statement: I reminded Hyundai that in 1950, when their country was under attack, my country came to their aid. When their currency collapsed in 1997 under the Asian financial crisis, my country was one of the nine that underwrote its currency. It’s a thing called respect and gratitude, and that he could go forward in the future and trust my country and me.

explanation: Asked whether the Government is in formal dispute resolution with Hyundai and, if not, why exiting the contract is taking so long. He responds by locating responsibility with KiwiRail, which is a genuine (if deflecting) response to who would know, but neither the arbitration question nor the delay question is answered.
question: Is the Government currently in a formal contract dispute resolution with Hyundai, such as arbitration, and, if not, why is it taking so long to exit the existing ferries contract that Nicola Willis cancelled?
statement: The answer to that question lies with KiwiRail—that’s in charge of the process, not the Government.

explanation: Asked whether he has confidence the total cost will come in under $2 billion. He substitutes confidence about a different threshold ($4 billion) and defers detail to later. Same subject, different question answered.
question: Does he have confidence that the total cost of ferries and infrastructure will come in under $2 billion?
statement: What we have enormous confidence in is that the Treasury forecast that was given to the Labour Party and us of it passing $4 billion is not going to happen. In short, hang on, help’s on its way, and I’ll give the details shortly.

explanation: Asked whether the preferred ferry replacements might still be purchased. The reply is a defence of Willis's decision to cancel and says nothing about whether the purchase remains possible. A complete pivot to talking points.
question: Is it still possible that Nicola Willis’ preferred ferry replacements will be purchased, or is her delivery finally dead in the water?
statement: The reality is that what Nicola Willis did was see a financial crisis and take the appropriate action when her predecessors had not.

explanation: Asked what announcement he made this week about the fund. He names the visit, the recipient (Wellington City Mission's Crisis Café) and what the funding does. Directly and completely answered.
question: What announcements has he made this week regarding the Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund?
statement: On Tuesday, I visited Wellington City Mission’s Crisis Café to announce they are one of the latest recipients of the Government’s Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund. The funding will allow the City Mission to scale up its Crisis Café to 24 hours a day, four days a week. Crisis Cafés provide an alternative place where people can go when they need support to alleviate demand on emergency departments. One of the criteria of the innovation fund is to increase access to mental health and addiction services, and this is exactly what this announcement does.

explanation: Asked what other announcement he made this week. He names Rotorua community youth centre, the service and the scale (560 young people). Squarely answered.
question: What other announcements has he made this week regarding the Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund?
statement: Oh, a good question. Yesterday, I was in Rotorua to announce that the Rotorua community youth centre would be receiving funding from the mental health innovation fund. The trust provides free primary mental health and addiction services to young people. The funding will support an additional 560 young people as well as provide a range of courses and workshops to upskill people in the community to better support youth mental health. One of the criteria of the innovation fund is to develop capacity in the mental health workforce, and this is exactly what this announcement does.

explanation: Asked what other services the fund has financed. He lists Youthline, the Sir John Kirwan Foundation/Mitey and Mates in Construction. The question is answered in full.
question: What other services has the Mental Health and Addiction Community Sector Innovation Fund funded?
statement: The innovation fund provides Government funding to match, dollar for dollar, philanthropic and other funding secured by organisations, including New Zealanders, with their mental health. In addition to the Wellington City Mission and Rotorua community youth centre, it has funded Youthline to expand its youth counselling, the Sir John Kirwan Foundation to scale up Mitey, the school-based mental health programme, and to support Mates in Construction to deliver vital suicide prevention on site. One of the criteria of the innovation fund is to deliver scalable solutions for unmet need, and this is exactly what these announcements do.

explanation: Asked how the fund supports the Government's mental health priorities. He states the priorities and links the fund to them via investment in community/NGO services — the connection asked for is made, though it drifts into a slogan at the end.
question: How does this fund support the Government’s mental health priorities?
statement: Well, this Government is laser focused on reducing mental health wait times, training more mental health workers, and investing more in prevention and early intervention. One way of achieving this is investing more in our hard-working community and NGO mental health services, who are already making a difference on the ground. This Government is committed to getting money out of Wellington to the grassroots, and that’s what we’re doing.

explanation: Two parts: does he believe State housing matters (answered 'Yes' outright) and why zero growth beyond next year (explicitly declined as pre-Budget). A stated refusal is still an answer; the intervening jab at the Opposition is a Civility/Focus matter, not a dodge.
question: Does he believe that State housing is important for growing the supply of affordable housing; if so, why is the Government opting for zero growth in State housing beyond next year?
statement: Yes. However, the Opposition’s infatuation with State ownership of affordable housing is laughable. We are very comfortable and enthusiastic with community housing providers, iwi, and others providing affordable housing where suitable. This Government’s housing renaissance, led by the energetic Minister of Finance and the exemplary Minister of Housing, is focused on fixing the housing ecosystem to grow affordable housing. In relation to the second part of this question, it’s inappropriate to get ahead of the Minister of Finance’s Budget decisions.

explanation: Two parts: has he seen the poll ('No' — direct) and will he abandon the plan (never addressed; he pivots to his own emergency-housing figures). Half the question is engaged, half is left unanswered.
question: Has the Minister seen yesterday’s poll from Public Housing Futures that shows that 72 percent of people believe the Government should address the housing crisis by building State housing at scale, and, if so, will he listen to the people and abandon their anti-growth State housing plan?
statement: No, but I have seen the tables that have seen nearly 3,000 children come out of emergency housing in the last 15 months and a reduction of 5,000 households from the social housing register. I have seen the absolute reduction in the million dollars a day that the previous Government was spending on emergency housing. Those are the tables I’ve seen. But I’m happy to get the member’s polls and materials through my office. Thank you.

explanation: Asked whether he recognises Kāinga Ora can finance social housing more cheaply than CHPs. He refuses the premise as 'fuzzy accounting' — a legible implicit 'no' — but then turns to something else and is cut off before reaching the substance.
question: Does the Minister recognise that despite the tinkering to leasing and contracts, Kāinga Ora is in a much stronger position to finance new social housing at a lower cost per home than community housing providers, who face more expensive borrowing and have far smaller balance sheets than Kāinga Ora?
statement: I’m not going to get into the member’s fuzzy accounting and math, but what I will say is this: that I have—

explanation: Same comparison put again. He answers the comparison implicitly in the negative (CHP and iwi providers 'often have better outcomes') but never engages the specific cost-of-finance/balance-sheet claim at the core of the question.
question: Does the Minister recognise that despite the tinkering to leasing and contracts, Kāinga Ora is in a much stronger position to finance new social housing at a lower cost per home than community housing providers, who face more expensive borrowing and have far smaller balance sheets?
statement: We on this side of the House recognise that community housing providers and Māori and iwi housing providers often have better outcomes for provision of housing that is affordable than utilising Kāinga Ora. We are very proud of the recent announcements that we made to support and accelerate 400 or so homes amongst Māori housing providers, utilising funds. Thank you.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about lost trade jobs from stalled State housing developments. He never says whether he is concerned nor touches the job losses; he recites the economic downturn and the Finance Minister's diligence. A pivot to talking points.
question: Is the Minister concerned about the loss of local trade jobs and contracts across the country due to the stalling and cancellation of State housing developments, when over 10,000 construction workers lost their jobs due to that last year?
statement: As we know, we have suffered a market downturn and a cost of living crisis and an economic crisis over the last couple of years, and those are the things that the Minister of Finance is absolutely and diligently and professionally ensuring that we deal with and get housing back on track.

explanation: Asked how the Government reconciles reviewing 4,000+ units with public support for building at scale. He characterises the question as revealing an ideological gulf and restates his own position; the reconciliation asked for is never attempted.
question: How does the Government reconcile putting Kāinga Ora projects comprising of over 4,000 units under review, including over 500 in Wellington, with the overwhelming support of New Zealanders for the Government to get on with building State housing at scale?
statement: The nature of that question demonstrates the absolute gulf between the Opposition’s view of how housing should be generated in this country. We have a view—a very strong view—that a number of players, including iwi Māori, community housing providers, and others, are in a position to activate more social and affordable housing. The Opposition, including the member who’s asked that question, has a very strong view that the Government should have a monopoly on the provision and we don’t agree with it.

explanation: Asked how many of the iwi/CHP homes stem from this Government's funding rather than the previous one's. He supplies a figure (1,500 IRRS places) presented as this Government's, which reaches the question, but leaves the attribution contrast and the post-2026 funding point untouched.
question: How many of those iwi Māori - led and community housing provider - led houses that he has been mentioning are a result of funding committed by this Government and not the previous Government, led by the Labour Party and the Green Party, that had already been committed to, given that Government hasn’t committed any funding to new builds beyond 2026 or the operational subsidies needed to actually run that housing?
statement: We’re very proud in ensuring that 1,500 additional social houses, income-related rent subsidy funded places, have been provided for community housing providers to deliver over the next couple of years. Actually, that’s something that we are really enthusiastic around.

explanation: Asked what impact Trump-era tariffs will have on NZ exporters and importers. She gives general channels (global inflation, lower demand, suppressed growth) and says NZ is not being singled out, but stops short of the effect on NZ exporters and importers specifically.
question: What impacts does he think the imposition of tariffs by the Trump presidency will have on New Zealand exporters and importers?
statement: Rising tariffs between the major economies have the potential to drive global inflation, lower demand in some countries, and supress economic growth. While President Trump campaigned on a tariff agenda, there’s no suggestion the US is focused on or singling out New Zealand. The embassy in Washington, DC is gathering as much information as it can, while continuously making the case to the US that New Zealand’s trade is well balanced. We are monitoring developments, taking advice on everything available to us—everything is still on the table.

explanation: Asked which of two apparently contradictory McClay statements she agrees with. She picks an option and states it plainly — both, because both were right — and gives the reading that reconciles them. The either/or was engaged head-on rather than sidestepped; whether the reconciliation is persuasive is a Rigor question, not this one.
question: Who does the Minister agree with, the Todd McClay who stated on 31 January this year that exporters will do “very well” during Trump’s second term, or the Todd McClay who stated on 6 March 2025 that “A tariff on New Zealand exports … is not a good thing for New Zealand.”?
statement: On behalf of the Minister for Trade and Investment, of course, Todd McClay was the same man on both occasions, and on both occasions he was right. New Zealand exporters do have a great future ahead of them, and of course New Zealand has consistently opposed additional tariffs on our goods.

explanation: A two-part question: does she agree with Key's claim that Trump will be better for the economy, and what should KiwiSaver holders make of it. She says only that she doesn't take responsibility for Key's comments — which answers neither part. This is not a clean refusal (she never says she won't say whether she agrees); it changes the question from 'do you agree' to 'are you accountable for it'.
question: Does she agree with the statement by Sir John Key that Trump will “be better for the economy”, and what should New Zealand KiwiSaver fund holders think about that?
statement: On behalf of the Minister for Trade and Investment, I don’t take responsibility for the comments of the Rt Hon John Key.

explanation: Asked why she cited a $5 million tariff figure and how that reconciles with Stats NZ figures implying $34 million. The first half gets a token answer — officials' advice informs her statements — but the reconciliation, which is the core of the question, is never attempted; the reply moves to praising the questioner and asserting exporter resilience.
question: Why did the Minister state that “we will face about an extra $5 million of tariffs—plus or minus” on tariffs that have already been imposed on aluminium, iron, and steel, and how does the Minister reconcile this with Statistics New Zealand figures that show a 25 percent tariff would be about $34 million a year, based on last year’s export figures?
statement: On behalf of the Minister for Trade and Investment, obviously, I take a range of advice from my officials, and that is what informs my statements. I would like to acknowledge the member asking these questions, who, alongside other members of this House, has worked hard over many years to help secure good trading relationships between New Zealand and a network of other nations around the world. I would like to remind the member that, ultimately, our exporters are resilient and will continue to find good opportunities in a range of markets.

explanation: Asked why exporters should trust the Minister's advice given the claimed lack of contact with US officials and the Meat Industry Association. The answer does squarely rebut the contact premise — officials in Washington have been instructed to engage — but never reaches the trust question and ignores the Meat Industry Association entirely. Half the question engaged.
question: If the Minister can’t get the maths right, why should exporters trust his advice at this uncertain time, considering no one in his office has contacted any US officials since President Trump’s election, and he hasn’t even contacted the Meat Industry Association about the proposed tariffs on agriculture, when the US is now our single largest meat market?
statement: On behalf of the Minister for Trade and Investment, I can assure the member that this Government is working hard through all of our channels, across multiple Ministers, to ensure as strong a relationship as possible with the United States is in place in order to ensure that New Zealand’s interests can be pursued, and that absolutely includes the interests of our exporters. Minister McClay has instructed New Zealand officials in Washington, DC to engage with the new administration to ensure that they remain aware that our trade is balanced and complementary, and that US exporters predominantly enjoy lower tariff rates into New Zealand than our exporters do into the US because we have a very low-tariff regime.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to support women. After an International Women's Day preamble, she names a concrete thing the Government did: the gender pay gap tool kit. The question was answered; the digressions at either end don't retract that.
question: What is the Government doing to support women?
statement: How fitting to address this House on this matter with you in the Chair, Madam Speaker. I want to wish all women a very happy International Women’s Day this Saturday, and I’d like to send my personal thanks and appreciation to the women across the country, who deserve to be celebrated on this day and every day. To support women, last year I launched the first ever Government-backed gender pay gap tool kit. This helps businesses to calculate their pay gap and then an action plan tailored to their individual needs. It was designed alongside business to ensure sustainable and enduring change, and I thank those involved. I encourage members across the House, instead of carping and moaning, to get on board with it and visit the resources this International Women’s Day.

explanation: Asked why this work is a priority. She gives the reason directly — the 8.2 percent pay gap and the flow-on KiwiSaver gap, and closing it as her stated top priority. A why-question met with a why.
question: Why is this work a priority?
statement: The gender pay gap, of course, sits at 8.2 percent, and the Retirement Commission has found a 36 percent gap in the amount that men and women are putting into their KiwiSaver each year, which is primarily caused by the gender pay gap rather than contribution rates. Reducing that gap, of course, can lift women to economic empowerment, which is my number one priority as Minister.

explanation: Asked what engagement has been like. Answered directly and completely: 16,000 site hits, 750 workbook downloads, positive feedback from business.
question: What has the engagement been like so far?
statement: It has been fantastic. I am very pleased to share with this House that since the day we launched it, there have been 16,000 hits to the site and 750 downloads of the workbook by individual businesses. It’s really great to hear all the positive feedback from the business community as I travel across the country sharing this resource with business and professional sectors.
