Part two, why the OECD says tax settings hamper productivity and equity, is turned into a point about what the previous Government did, so the OECD finding itself is never engaged. Half the question landed.
question: Does the Prime Minister agree with his statement that “We have a fair tax system”, and, if so, why has the OECD consistently said that New Zealand’s productivity and equity is hampered by “shares, land, and residential property being tax favoured”?
statement: The Prime Minister agrees with the statement, otherwise he wouldn’t have said it. On the second thing: the OECD’s had a lot of suggestions for this country, but if you look at it, the former Government went through this experience and decided in the opposite and, in fact, in the bonfire of inanities, the present leader of the Labour Party got rid of them.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about the gap between tax on wages and tax on wealth. The 'yes, we most certainly do' attaches to a substituted proposition — caring about working people — not to the asymmetry put to him. It reads as engagement, but the specific concern asked about is answered only by implication.
question: Is he concerned that people who earn their money from work pay a higher effective tax rate than those who make money off wealth?
statement: Being the only parties in this House that give a hoot about the working man and woman in this country: yes, we most certainly do.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about the 9.5% vs 29% figures. He disputes the premise, saying only a Das Kapital analysis produces those numbers. Contesting the figures is a real response to the substance rather than a pivot, and its dismissiveness is a Civility matter, not this one — but he never says whether he is concerned, so it stops short of complete.
question: Is he concerned that wealthy New Zealanders pay 9.5 percent tax on their economic income while New Zealanders who earn a salary of $80,000 pay around 29 percent?
statement: If one is going to do the analysis from the book Das Kapital, you’ll arrive at that sort of calculation, but nobody else has.

explanation: Two specific asks: should those workers be guaranteed a living wage, and why was that removed from procurement rules. 'We're working on it' is a minimal touch on the first; the second — the actual removal — is not addressed at all, and the reply moves to wage growth versus inflation. A narrow factual question left unanswered.
question: Should cleaners, caterers, and security guards working on projects procured by the Government be guaranteed a living wage; if so, why did he remove paying these workers a living wage in the new Government procurement rules?
statement: As someone who has ensured in the last 50 years to raise the minimum wage more than any other political influence in this country, the answer to that is we’re working on it, but at the present time the wage rises are actually in excess of the inflation rises and the worker is still in front.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken on South-east Asian trade; names actions — prioritising the Vietnam relationship, a trade mission and business delegation, an announced upgrade to comprehensive strategic partnership. Preamble about RCEP and population share pads it, but actions are delivered.
question: What actions has the Government taken to support trade with South-east Asia?
statement: Vietnam is a valued member of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership—or RCEP, as it’s commonly known—and a partner for New Zealand, and this year we are celebrating 50 years of diplomatic relations. South-east Asia, of course, is home to 9 percent of the world’s population and is critical to maintaining and building New Zealand’s prosperity. Our Government has prioritised re-energising the relationship with Vietnam, and, recently, I joined the Prime Minister in a business delegation on a trade mission there to elevate our relationship. During that trip, the PM announced a major upgrade of the relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership—the highest level available with Vietnam—making New Zealand just the 10th country in the world to achieve that.

explanation: Asked why the partnership is significant; gives the significance — 14th-largest trading partner, fastest-growing ASEAN economy, 40% two-way trade growth, named high-value sectors. Directly responsive.
question: Why is this comprehensive strategic partnership with Vietnam significant?
statement: Vietnam is our 14th-largest trading partner and the fastest-growing economy in ASEAN, therefore providing huge opportunities to us here in New Zealand. Over the last five years, two-way trade with Vietnam has grown a substantial 40 percent, and this new partnership, of course, has potential to increase it further. In New Zealand, there are great opportunities to build on partnerships with high-value sectors like premium food and beverages, agritech, technology, innovation, and renewable energy.

explanation: Asked what was achieved on the trade mission. The answer lists concrete achievements: $130m of export value across 16 deals, a new VietJet route, a 56% increase in scholarships. It goes straight at the question and covers it completely. (Whether those figures are accurate is Veracity's business, not this one.)
question: What was achieved on this trade mission?
statement: Heaps. During the trade mission to Vietnam, New Zealand Trade and Enterprise has estimated that over $130 million of potential export value over the next three years was secured across 16 export deals and commercial partnerships. It’s also been announced that the airline VietJet will be developing a new commercial route here to strengthen connectivity and build better people-to-people links. And, of course, finally, we have increased the number of Government scholarships available to Vietnamese students by 56 percent, further growing our education links with Vietnam.

explanation: Asked how the Vietnam partnership benefits New Zealanders. The answer names the benefit chain directly: Vietnamese demand for NZ food and beverage exports, more trade, growth, jobs, higher incomes. It is a promotional answer, but the question asked for benefits and benefits are what was given. No pivot.
question: How does our partnership with Vietnam benefit New Zealanders?
statement: Like trade partnerships with any other nation, strengthening our relationship with Vietnam is incredibly important to New Zealand’s economic future, with more opportunities for businesses here. As Vietnam gets wealthier, Vietnamese people want to buy high-quality products from around the world, and we, of course, have some of the best food and beverage producers and innovative businesses around. The more we trade with the world, the more we grow our economy, which translates to more jobs, higher incomes, and more money in the back pockets of everyday New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked a yes/no about whether he is committed to the same health outcomes for Maori as his predecessor. 'My focus, as was the focus of my predecessor...' gestures at continuity, which touches the core, but he never affirms or denies the commitment and moves quickly onto waiting times, health targets and the previous Government. Partial engagement, core left hedged.
question: Is he committed to the same health outcomes for Māori as his immediate predecessor?
statement: My focus, as was the focus of my predecessor, is on ensuring that all New Zealanders, including Māori, have access to timely, quality healthcare. We know that too many New Zealanders are waiting too long to be seen at emergency departments, receive first specialist assessments, and have elective surgeries. Unlike the previous Government, our approach is putting patients first and backing our health system to get health back on track. This starts with bringing back our critical health targets, which the previous Government removed, to drive better outcomes for all New Zealanders, including Māori.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree with Reti's quote, and if so what does 'powering up' the boards mean. He never says whether he agrees, and never engages the phrase 'powering up'. He does answer an adjacent version of part two by stating what the boards should do (give consistent advice, not commission services), so it is not a pure dodge, but neither part is squarely met.
question: Does the Minister agree with the Hon Dr Shane Reti when he said, “I want to see iwi Māori partnership boards powered up to support the health outcomes for your whānau and your communities.”; if so, what does powering up iwi Māori partnership boards mean?
statement: Well, my predecessor was very clear, about independent Māori partnership boards, that they should be providing consistent advice around health needs for Māori across the country and that these partnership boards should not be commissioning agencies.

explanation: Two parts: has he seen the mortality/disease evidence, and why do the targets not address it. The first part is ignored entirely. The second is genuinely answered, if implicitly: the targets are universal by design and cover Maori as part of all New Zealanders. That is a real reason, so half the question is squarely engaged.
question: Has the Minister seen the overwhelming evidence that Māori die seven years earlier, that Māori are twice as likely to die from cardiovascular disease, and that Māori are more likely to get type 2 diabetes, and, if so, why do none of his health targets specifically address any of these issues?
statement: Well, the five health targets that this Government put back in place, which the last Government removed, are for all New Zealanders. Every New Zealander expects to be able to turn up to an emergency department and be able to be seen in a timely manner. All New Zealanders expect that if they require elective surgery, they’re able to receive that in a timely manner. This Government is focused on timely, quality access for all New Zealanders, which includes Māori.

explanation: A forced-choice question: does 'healthcare for all' mean raising Maori life expectancy or lowering non-Maori. The opening clause ('improving health outcomes for all New Zealanders, for Maori and for non-Maori') does implicitly select the first horn, which is partial engagement. But he then turns to attacking the previous Government's removal of targets and ends on 'Shame on them', leaving the choice never explicitly made.
question: Does healthcare for all New Zealanders mean raising the life expectancy for Māori or lowering the life expectancy for non-Māori?
statement: Well, the Government’s focus is on improving health outcomes for all New Zealanders, for Māori and for non-Māori, and I’d just make this point to the other side: they removed health targets, and every single one went backwards for non-Māori and for Māori. All New Zealanders were worse off because of what they did when they decided to rearrange the health system in the middle of a pandemic. Shame on them.

explanation: Asked whether it means making Maori and non-Maori life expectancy the same. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, unambiguous, complete. Brevity is not evasion; this is the textbook maximum.
question: Does healthcare for all New Zealanders, for this Government, mean making the life expectancy for Māori and non-Māori the same?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether she will ensure scrapping the living wage requirement will not cut these workers' pay. 'Yes, I can assure that' is a direct yes, with a reason attached (existing contracts must be honoured by law). Terse and arguably answering only for existing contracts rather than future ones, which is the one thing keeping it off 1.0 — but the question was engaged head-on, not dodged.
question: Will she ensure that her proposal to scrap the living wage requirement in Government contracts for cleaning, catering, and security guard services will not result in pay cuts for these workers?
statement: Yes, I can assure that—it’s the law. Existing contracts have to be honoured.

explanation: Asked what message he has for the cleaners and security staff whose pay floor is being scrapped. He does supply something addressable to them (they remain covered by negotiated employment agreements), which is a partial answer, but he then pivots to removing complexity and duplication and helping businesses win contracts. The message to those specific workers is never really delivered.
question: What message does she have for the workers, like those in Parliament who clean her office and toilet and keep her safe, when she scraps the rules that ensure they are paid enough to live?
statement: What I can say is that employers that are currently employing Kiwis—and hard-working Kiwis—across this country will still be bound by the terms of employment agreements negotiated with their staff and unions. And, as we step back from this issue, I think it is important to acknowledge that the consequences of these proposed changes remove complexity and duplication, and actually make it easier for New Zealand businesses to expand and to grow by winning Government contracts. That is good for New Zealand workers, and that is good for New Zealand.

explanation: Asked for a response to a named cleaner's testimony about the living wage. He does formally direct a reply 'to that individual', which counts as engaging the form of the question, but the content is a general statement about focus on growth and the cost of living rather than any response to what Liam Shaw actually said. Mostly a talking-point pivot with the question's shape preserved.
question: What is the response to cleaner Liam Shaw, who said, “The Living Wage basically allows me to survive. Before the Living Wage came in I was really struggling to afford groceries, especially considering how high my rent was, and the Living Wage has allowed me to thrive in what would be seen as a very basic sense.”?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, what I can say to that individual is that we have a Government that is relentlessly focused on economic growth and reducing the impact of the cost of living on those New Zealanders. We are working very hard for individuals—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked how the Government expects workers to survive. The implicit answer is 'via economic growth', which is a thin but real engagement, and then he moves to removing duplication and making it easier for businesses to win Government contracts. The question was about workers' survival and the answer is about business conditions, so the core is largely sidestepped.
question: How does your Government expect workers to survive?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, what I can be clear about is that this is a Government that is focused on economic growth, which will benefit all New Zealand workers. That is the critical point. The changes which we are making here will remove duplication and complexity. It will make it easier for New Zealand businesses to get New Zealand Government contracts.

explanation: Asked what he recently announced on the FIF rules. He names the announcement and its content (a new method for calculating taxable FIF income) — direct and complete after a short preamble.
question: What recent announcements has he made on the foreign investment fund rules?
statement: Well, New Zealand should be a place where talented people want to invest and grow businesses, but right now our tax rules are making that harder. Good news: we are fixing that. Yesterday, I announced the Government’s proposed changes to the foreign investment fund rules, including the addition of a new method to calculate a person’s taxable foreign investment fund income. This change will remove a tax barrier that is stopping highly skilled migrants and, importantly, returning Kiwis from investing here.

explanation: Asked why the change is critical to facilitating foreign investment. He gives the reason — the current rules hit migrants and returning Kiwis, with double-taxation risk for US citizens. Squarely on the question.
question: Why is the change so critical to facilitating foreign investments into New Zealand?
statement: Well, the current system hits new migrants and returning Kiwis unfairly, especially those in the tech and start-up sectors where still some migrants, particularly US citizens, risk double taxation. We want New Zealand to be an attractive place to live and work in and these changes will make that easier.

explanation: Asked what reaction he has seen. He reports the reaction directly and quotes two named industry figures. Complete answer to what was asked.
question: What reaction has he seen to this announcement?
statement: We are hosting the investment summit in Auckland this week and we have had extremely positive feedback from the tech and startup sectors. Graeme Muller, the chief executive from NZTech, said that “these improvements in tax rules are exactly what we need to make New Zealand more attractive for both investors and global talents.” Similarly, Robbie Paul, the CEO of Icehouse Ventures, has said “this is a stand-up example of Government engaging on a genuine issue so we can all create … brighter future[s] for New Zealand[ers].”

explanation: Asked what plans exist for existing residents. He answers that broader reforms are being considered, naming thresholds and investment visas, though 'more to say later this year' leaves the core of it open.
question: What plans are there, if any, for existing residents?
statement: Well, the Government is looking at broader foreign investment fund reforms, including how these rules affect residents, including whether the tax thresholds should be raised and how we can support investment visas. We want to unlock investment and growth, and I’m looking forward to having more to say on that later this year.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions. 'Yes.' One word, complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked to choose between two MPs' opposed views on deterrence. He states a position — 'I tend to agree with both members' — which engages the question but sidesteps the either/or it was built around.
question: Does he agree with National MP Dr Vanessa Weenink, who, when voting against the Crimes (Theft by Employer) Amendment Bill, said, “When you make something a criminal offence, does it really deter people?”, or New Zealand First MP Mark Patterson, who, when voting for that bill, said, “There should be consequences for a crime. We fundamentally believe that, and this bill does provide that deterrence factor.”?
statement: Well, the great thing about this side of the House is that we allow people to think for themselves. We don’t have the old rule 242, which says that the party’s conscience is your conscience, and, therefore, I tend to agree with both members.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees people should be held accountable or is satisfied leading a soft-on-white-collar-crime Government. 'I can handle it' addresses neither limb; nothing of the question is engaged.
question: Does he agree with New Zealand First that people should be held accountable for their crimes, or is he satisfied leading a Government that is soft on white-collar crime?
statement: I can handle it.

explanation: Asked whether accountability applies to all or only some. He answers the first limb plainly ('we have always agreed... people should be held accountable'), then diverts the white-collar limb into a wine-box anecdote rather than answering it.
question: Does he agree with New Zealand First that people should be held accountable for their crimes, or is it just some people?
statement: We have always agreed, on this side of the House, that people should be held accountable for their crimes. Otherwise, you’d get a thing called anarchy and the utter destruction of democracy and freedom and liberty. And, on the other side of the thing on the question of white-collar crime, look at the person who took on the wine-box inquiry, who, against all odds, won.

explanation: Asked whether Parliament's guards and cleaners should continue to be guaranteed a living wage. He responds on point — they are on a contract that does that and it cannot be changed — but answers what is the case rather than the 'should it continue' that was asked.
question: Should security guards and cleaners employed at Parliament continue to be guaranteed a living wage?
statement: Well, the reality is that they’re on a contract which does just that. The contract cannot be changed.

explanation: Asked whether all Government-contracted guards and cleaners should get the same assurance. He talks about union representation, his own record on the minimum wage, and tidying up a 'conflated mess' — the yes/no on extending the assurance is never reached.
question: If security guards and cleaners in Parliament are to receive a living wage, shouldn’t all Government contracted security guards and cleaners be provided the same assurance?
statement: The reality is that the people we’re talking about have all got representation. They’ve got agencies that work for them, and someone that worked and was a delegate for the most lowly union in this country, the Labourers Union. We know something about that, and we’ve got a record, of course, having gone for the minimum wage at a higher level than any other party. Now, my point is, what we want to do is make sure that the conflated mess that is this matter is tidied up so that people can get on getting employed and getting paid properly. And they will be.

explanation: Asked whether minimum-wage pay is appropriate given enhanced citizen's-arrest duties. He rejects the premise outright ('that is not the case at all'), which is a form of engagement, but he does not say which part is false or address appropriateness.
question: Is it appropriate that those security guards should now be paid minimum wage at the same time they have been asked to perform the Police’s job with enhanced powers to perform citizens arrests, therefore putting them in harm’s way?
statement: Well, if the member begins with the premise that is false, then she’ll get the false conclusion that she has just arrived at. That is not the case at all.

explanation: Asked why the Government is reducing incomes and defending wage theft. He denies both premises specifically — the Government is not allowing employers to steal, and existing contracts will be maintained — so the loaded question is contested rather than dodged, but the 'why' is not answered.
question: Why is this Government focused on reducing incomes for security guards and cleaners and defending employers who steal money from their workers at a time when Kiwis are struggling to put food on their tables?
statement: We’ll begin with—the Government is not allowing employers to steal from their workers. That’s clear, if the member did the numbers, where things are going on that matter. So that’s number one put right. And the other matter is to do with their present, existing contracts, which will be maintained. So why this alarmism? We do not understand.

explanation: Asked (a) whether she agrees with the quoted statement and (b) how many Government contractors are on the minimum wage. Part (a) is answered with an unambiguous "Yes" plus the context she attaches to it; part (b) is plainly declined as outside her ministerial responsibility. A stated refusal on jurisdictional grounds engages rather than dodges, but the number asked for is never reached, so this falls short of complete.
question: Does she agree with Brooke van Velden’s statement, “I think a lot of people in New Zealand do live on minimum wage and we have to allow people to make ends meet”; if so, how many Government contractors are currently paid the minimum wage?
statement: Yes, in the context in which it was made, which was an RNZ interview titled “ACT: need more jobs rather than raising min wage”. If the member had listened to the full context of the interview, she would note that I’m not in favour of large increases to the minimum wage but policies that support an economy where people have jobs to go to rather than people shutting up shop. I want to make it easier for business owners to actually take a chance on someone and give them a job. In response to the second part of your question, this is not my ministerial responsibility.

explanation: Asked how removing the living-wage requirement helps incomes. The answer is a single plain statement that procurement contracts are not her responsibility — a direct, complete refusal rather than a pivot to talking points, which the rubric scores high, but it leaves the substance untouched.
question: How does removing the requirement for cleaners, caterers, and security guards to be paid the living wage help to increase the incomes of some of our hardest-working New Zealanders?
statement: It is not my responsibility to be talking about procurement contracts of this Government.

explanation: Asked whether she supports Andy Foster's commitment to the living wage, and if not, why not. The answer never says whether she supports it; it deflects into a general proposition that coalition members may hold individual opinions. A narrow yes/no question left unanswered.
question: Does she support New Zealand First MP Andy Foster’s public commitment to maintaining the living wage; if not, why not?
statement: Like my colleague Winston Peters has articulated quite nicely in the House, members on this side of the Government are entitled to their individual opinions.

explanation: Asked (a) what impact the wage cut will have on child poverty, homelessness and food-bank demand and (b) whether she has received advice. Part (b) is answered squarely — she states the advice she received. Part (a) is reframed rather than answered: she argues the minimum wage is not a poverty tool instead of giving the expected impact. Half the question engaged.
question: What impact will cutting workers’ wages by over $370 a fortnight, during a cost of living crisis, have on child poverty, homelessness, and demand for food banks, and has she received any advice on this?
statement: I thank the member for her question. In regards to things like the minimum wage as a floor for employee rights in New Zealand, I’ve had advice that the minimum wage is not a good redistribution tool for poverty reduction. This Government, alongside other previous Governments, have used more targeted responses to reduce poverty—things like the accommodation supplement, things like Working for Families, FamilyBoost. Having the minimum wage standard is not a poverty reduction tool; it is simply a floor for wages in this country.

explanation: Asked a direct belief question: does withholding wages constitute theft? The answer never says yes or no — it redirects to the sufficiency of existing civil law, the Labour member's bill, and an anecdote about a cafe owner. The core word "theft" is never engaged.
question: Does she believe that employers intentionally withholding wages from workers constitutes theft?
statement: What I do believe is that we already have civil law in New Zealand that allows for people to be paid correctly by their employer. The Labour Party’s member’s bill is not necessary for people to be paid correctly. But what I’d also say is perhaps the member would like to have some conversations with people that I’ve been speaking to recently—for example, one cafe owner that I met, just in this last week, who sold her car and her husband’s bike to keep her own employees employed. There aren’t just good and bad people; there are people trying to make ends meet who are workers and business owners.

explanation: Asked, in loaded form, whether Going For Growth applies only to unemployment queues and food-bank lines. The answer declines on responsibility grounds and names the Minister who should answer — a plain, complete refusal that reaches the question's addressee problem but not its substance.
question: Does her Government’s Going For Growth strategy just apply for unemployment queues and lines for the food bank?
statement: I’m not responsible for the Going For Growth strategy. That question is best responded to by the Minister for Economic Growth.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made on refreshing the eating disorders strategy. The answer states the announcement and what the refreshed strategy will contain. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made on refreshing New Zealand’s eating disorders strategy?
statement: As part of Eating Disorders Awareness Week, I recently announced that the Government would be refreshing New Zealand’s eating disorders strategy. The refreshed strategy will have clear and prioritised actions for implementation. Other focuses will include identifying where further efforts across eating disorder services are required and improving our understanding of eating disorder data. It will also include opportunities to grow and utilise the peer support workforce more. We know we can do a lot better in supporting individuals and their families who are struggling to get support.

explanation: Asked why the strategy needs refreshing. The answer gives reasons: the strategy is 16 years old, and a 2021 review showed demand has risen significantly. The "why" is squarely addressed.
question: Why does the eating disorders strategy need to be refreshed?
statement: Around 2,000 people access support for an eating disorder every year, and approximately 1,500, or three-quarters, of these will be young people under the age of 25, but we know there will be more need. New Zealand’s strategy has not been refreshed in 16 years, with the last strategy published in 2008. It is long overdue for an update. A 2021 review by the ministry showed that demand for eating disorder services has risen significantly since the strategy was first published over a decade ago.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen from eating disorder groups. The answer quotes two named group representatives. Exactly what was asked for.
question: What feedback has the Minister seen from eating disorder groups?
statement: Sarah Rowland, co-chair of the Eating Disorders Carer Support New Zealand, said, “The strategy will be a significant step towards improving prevention, early intervention, treatment accessibility, and long-term recovery support.”, while Rebecca Toms from WithLoveED said, “I just wanted to say thank you for paying attention to the critical issue of eating disorders in New Zealand. You know it means a lot to families like mine to see this issue finally receiving the recognition at a national level.”

explanation: Asked what other feedback he has seen. The answer supplies three further messages from members of the public. Directly responsive.
question: What other feedback has the Minister seen?
statement: I have a message by Bex, the mother of a child with an eating disorder. She said, “This makes me so happy. As a parent who almost lost her 16-year-old son to an eating disorder, the fight I had against the system almost broke me. I’m happy for families and people in the future who will get the support earlier.” Lisa from Christchurch messaged me and said, “This is so overdue. So very glad this is happening. There are way too many families struggling to care for loved ones with this disorder.” And Joseph messaged me, saying, “More people suffer from eating disorders than we realise. A lot of men as well. This is good news.”

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing for small businesses and manufacturers. Penk names a concrete programme (e-invoicing promotion, the 50,000-business milestone, mandating agency adoption) — that is the question engaged. It is a soft, sprawling patsy question and he covers only one strand of it, which is the only reason it is not higher; the narrowness of the answer is a Specificity/scope matter, not a dodge.
question: What is the Government doing to support small businesses and manufacturers?
statement: This Government is working hard to grow the economy, particularly for small businesses and manufacturers. This includes the promotion of e-invoicing. The productivity gains, the efficiency gains, and the protection against fraud are all key reasons that we are doing so. Recently, a key milestone of 50,000 businesses across New Zealand was reached for the uptake of e-invoicing, and we are asking—requiring, in fact—Government agencies to play a leadership role in adopting that technology, as well.

explanation: Two-part question: were alternative proposals received, and how many. Peters answers the first squarely ("Yes, we have had strong interest") but never gives the number, deferring it to a Cabinet briefing and then pivoting to the previous government's cost blow-out. The deferral is a stated refusal rather than a pure dodge, which keeps it mid-range, but half the question — the count — goes unanswered and the pivot to attack lines consumes most of the reply.
question: Has the Government received any alternative proposals for the procurement of new Cook Strait ferries from the private sector; if so, how many?
statement: Yes, we have had strong interest from the private sector, and we thank them for that—for their contributions, equities, and ideas. As for any details, the House will need to wait until Cabinet has been briefed, but let me remind the member that we have a task to do to tidy the issues of a $3.1 billion project that started with a Government contribution of $400.1 million, and then Treasury began warning the Government, the past Government, in 2023, that this project was going to blow out to over $4 billion. So we’re working on it and very soon, in a few weeks, we’ll give the member the answer he wants.

explanation: Asked whether he will seriously consider private-sector options, or still thinks that is "just ridiculous". The reply — looking at every option from China and Korea to Scandinavia — is about where vessels might be sourced, not about private-sector involvement, and the earlier quote is never addressed. It gestures at open-mindedness without reaching either limb of the question.
question: Will he seriously consider alternative options from the private sector for the procurement of ferry services, or does he still consider private sector involvement “just ridiculous”?
statement: The reality is we’re looking at every option all around the world, from, dare I say it, China, Korea, all the way to Scandinavia.

explanation: Asked whether the ferry service will be privatised under his watch. "I think I can give you a firm promise: under my watch, no." A direct, complete, unambiguous answer to exactly the question asked.
question: Will the Government’s Cook Strait ferry service be privatised under his watch?
statement: I think I can give you a firm promise: under my watch, no.

explanation: Asked a yes/no: will the Government pay for the required portside infrastructure upgrades. The answer compliments the questioner, relitigates the previous contract's 1:4 ratio, and says the ports each have "a certain contribution to make" — never stating whether the Crown will fund the upgrades. It circles the subject-matter without answering the funding question.
question: Will his Government pay for the required portside infrastructure upgrades that will be needed for any new ferries?
statement: Well, the reality is, that’s a fascinating question and I’m so pleased that very sensible member asked it, because that’s what the problem was with the last contract: for every $1 we were going to spend on the ferry, $4 was going to the infrastructure, and that was impossible. So what we’re doing here is looking at the infrastructure of the future, and he will know that Port Marlborough has got a certain contribution to make, the Wellington port has got a certain contribution to make, and we’re looking at how we best can make this work, reusing as much as we possibly can, which our forefathers had in mind when they were insightful runners of this Parliament.

explanation: Asked what communications he has had with Hyundai since 28 February and what they concerned. He says he wrote a letter thanking them, and characterises its content. Both limbs are answered. The reply is thin and may well be incomplete as a matter of fact, but thinness is Specificity and truth is Veracity — the question itself was engaged head-on.
question: What communications, if any, has he had with Hyundai since his meeting with them on 28 February 2025, and, if so, what were those communications about?
statement: I wrote a letter thanking them for their gracious respect in giving us their time and their expertise for a very, very meaningful discussion, which adds to the quality of information we have in making a decision as a Cabinet going forward.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Seymour's statement about private investment. He first bats away the "disaster" jibe, then does engage the quote — "that is a view, but" — and answers obliquely by endorsing the Singaporean Temasek model instead. The substance of the question is genuinely touched, but he never says plainly whether he agrees, so it lands as a hedge around the core rather than a direct answer.
question: Does the Minister agree with David Seymour that “Private investment will bring private market discipline which will lead to a better and more cost-effective service in years to come.”, or will the privatisation of the ferry service be another disaster, this time with him at the helm?
statement: It is not the history of somebody that’s at the helm ever being in charge of a disaster—quite the consequence; pointing out disasters, yes, but not starting them. In respect of Mr Seymour’s comment, that is a view, but then if you have a look at the Singaporean Temasek model, where they’ve used the best of business expertise in the interests of the nation and their savings programme, it has been a brilliant success and I do think that there are members on this side of the House who believe we need it here in our country.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she has made on air ambulance upgrades. She names the announcement made the previous day — a new helicopter in service for Waikato, Coromandel and King Country — and its features. Directly and completely responsive; the closing acknowledgements are surplus, not evasion.
question: What recent announcements has she made regarding upgrades to New Zealand’s air ambulance fleet?
statement: Yesterday, I had the pleasure, with the Minister for ACC, Scott Simpson, to announce that a brand new air ambulance helicopter is now in service for the people across the Waikato, Coromandel, and King Country. This is great news for the region and the hard-working local MPs who have so strongly advocated for an upgraded helicopter. This new helicopter offers improved safety, a more reliable service, better capacity to respond in bad weather conditions, reduced maintenance cost, greater fuel efficiency, and better operational performance. Mr Speaker, if you’d indulge me, I would also like to acknowledge the unwavering commitment of Central Air Ambulance Rescue Ltd and the trusts, organisations, and individuals who collaborate so effectively to deliver these critical services.

explanation: Asked why fleet upgrades are needed. The answer states the reasons: the oldest fleet in the developed world, sustainability and reliability risk, and demand up more than 20 percent over five years. Squarely the question that was asked.
question: Why are upgrades to the air ambulance fleet needed?
statement: The helicopter fleet is currently the oldest in the developed world. This creates sustainability and reliability risks and means that our excellent paramedics, doctors, and nurses providing treatment to patients have had to do so in constraints of the existing fleet. In addition to our ageing fleet, emergency air ambulance helicopter services have come under increasing demand, which has grown more than 20 percent over the last five years. In the last calendar year alone, the emergency air ambulance fleet flew 13,309 hours, an average of more than 36 flight hours each day. Meeting this growing demand and ensuring patients can receive the best care in their time of need is essential and requires a fleet that can spend more time in the air.

explanation: Asked when New Zealanders can expect more upgrades. She gives dates — a near-new helicopter in Auckland from mid-April, three more by end of May, nine replacements funded. The tail ("further ones will be made in due course") is vague, but the timing question was answered.
question: When can New Zealanders expect more upgrades to the air ambulance fleet?
statement: This Government has allocated an additional $14.7 million to be invested in this to enable air ambulance service providers to replace nine ageing helicopters with newer ones. On top of the brand new helicopter announced yesterday and one that’s been operational in Tauranga from mid - last year, at this stage, we are looking at a near-new helicopter to be operational in Auckland from mid-April, and three more helicopters are expected to arrive in New Zealand by the end of May. Announcements about these upgrades and further ones will be made in due course.

explanation: Asked what work the Government has done for the hunting and fishing community. Meager cites the approval of three new commercial upland game preserves and names them. That is a direct answer to what has been done; the promotional framing does not displace the substance.
question: What work has the Government done to support the hunting and fishing community?
statement: As a Government, we are strongly committed to supporting the hunting and fishing community and maximising the value of hunting and fishing as a cultural and economic resource for New Zealand. As an example, at the start of this month, the Government approved three new commercial upland game preserves. These are Mangakahia in Whangārei, Lagoon Hill in southern Wairarapa, and Grange Hill in the mighty South Canterbury. Game preserves currently constitute a $7 million per year industry, and this announcement will provide economic growth and a further boost to the sector. This is just a small part of this Government’s ambitious hunting and fishing work programme.

explanation: Asked how else the Government is supporting the community. He opens with his own consultation round rather than with government action, but goes on to list the work being progressed — herds of special interest, the Access Charter, the community hut programme, modernising Fish & Game. The "how else" is reached, just by way of a detour.
question: How else is this Government supporting the hunting and fishing community?
statement: Since becoming the new Minister for Hunting and Fishing, I have met with all 12 Fish & Game regional councils around the country as well as Fish & Game New Zealand, the Game Animal Council, New Zealand Deerstalkers Association, and many other passionate hunters. Their views reinforce the importance of progressing work on things like herds of special interest, recognising valued introduced species as a resource rather than a pest, improving access to public land through the Access Charter for Recreational Hunting and Fishing, investing in huts of recreational importance by supporting the community hut programme, and supporting and modernising Fish & Game New Zealand.

explanation: Asked for his portfolio priorities; he names his number one priority explicitly (making it as easy as possible for New Zealanders to hunt and fish) and expands on it. Direct and on-point, even though it is a patsy question.
question: What are the Minister’s priorities in his portfolio?
statement: As Minister for Hunting and Fishing, my number one priority is to make it as easy as possible for New Zealanders to go hunting and fishing. Our hunters and anglers are one of our biggest conservation resources, which is why we have invested significant funds in partnering with hunters to undertake animal management programmes throughout New Zealand, particularly in the South Island. We will never be able to manage our conservation land and improve our biodiversity without the work and support of hunters and fishers. I am proud to be the Minister for Hunting and Fishing. I am looking forward to working with Opposition spokesperson for hunting and fishing Scott Willis on how we can further support the great work of hunters and anglers.

explanation: Asked how people can get involved; he gives concrete entry points — game bird licences on sale from today, duck shooting season from 3 May, the roar and the red deer season opening. Answers the question, if slightly obliquely (seasons rather than a how-to).
question: How can people get involved in hunting and fishing?
statement: From today, game bird licences go on sale across the country and the duck shooting season starts on 3 May. I know that the member, alongside myself, will be keen to get out on the maimai. Also starting this month is the roar, with the opening of the red deer hunting season. I wish all hunters a successful season and I also encourage everyone to stay safe and follow the seven rules of firearms safety.

explanation: Asked how the Government will back up its fair-prices promise; he names an actual mechanism — a review of competition settings including the first major Commerce Act review in two decades. It reaches the 'how', though it stays at the level of a review rather than an action.
question: How will the Government back up its promise to ensure fair prices for Kiwi consumers?
statement: Increasing competition is a key pillar of this Government’s going for growth plan. Having better competition means that we can bring down the cost of living for Kiwis and lift living standards. That’s why I’m progressing an ambitious review of New Zealand’s competition settings, which includes, amongst other things, the first major review of the Commerce Act in more than two decades. Getting these core settings right is important as greater competition will lead to more innovation and fairer prices for all Kiwis.

explanation: Asked whether the Government will take action on the banks; he neither says yes nor no, deferring to the Finance and Expenditure Committee inquiry and 'wait and see'. Pointing to a live process is a partial engagement with the question rather than a squarely responsive yes/no.
question: Will this Government take action on the big banks charging Kiwis more right now, after 18 months of posturing and as a defiant ANZ, recording its most profitable quarter ever, is making $10 million a day from New Zealanders?
statement: As the member will well know, the Finance and Expenditure Committee is currently conducting an inquiry into banking, and the member will need to just wait and see what recommendations come from that committee. But she can be well assured that this Government is keeping a very careful eye on banks.

explanation: Asked when power prices will come down; no date, timeframe or direction is ever given. He pivots to generation shortages and making new renewable generation easier — a different question from the one asked.
question: When will Kiwis see their power prices coming down, given that they are going up next month?
statement: Power prices are crucial to New Zealanders and, as that member will well know, we have an infrastructure shortage in terms of power generation. So this Government is intending to make it easier for new generation to occur, particularly renewable generation. So the key to this question is in fact getting electricity supply right and the value right for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether anything in the commerce and consumers plan makes groceries cheaper; he does not say, but he states plainly why he will not — a declared recusal for conflict, with the matter passed to Minister Willis. A stated refusal to engage is more forthright than a dodge, but the question itself is left unanswered.
question: Is there anything in the Government’s plan for commerce and consumers that will make a trolley of groceries cheaper?
statement: Well, this is interesting because the member also will be well aware that my predecessor had the supermarket duopoly firmly in his sights. But the member will also be very clear that I have proactively, in accordance with the Cabinet Manual, recused myself because of a conflict to be involved in any matters relating to supermarkets or groceries. Those matters will be handled by none other than the Hon Nicola Willis, and I can think of no better Minister to do that.

explanation: Asked two things — whether Air New Zealand hiked fares by up to 300 percent, and whether he would support a select committee inquiry. He answers neither: pricing is 'a matter entirely for Air New Zealand', followed by generalities about competition lowering airfares.
question: Has Air New Zealand hiked fares for some routes by up to 300 percent in five years, and, if so, would he support an inquiry at select committee into airlines?
statement: The pricing mechanism that Air New Zealand uses is, of course, a matter entirely for Air New Zealand. That said, like all New Zealanders, I’m looking forward to greater competition on our airways and the opportunities that that will provide for lowering airfares and making better value air flights for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked why he is sitting back on banks, power and transport costs; he does not address any of the three, turning instead to the previous Government's six years and inflation. Attacks the questioner's party in place of an answer.
question: Why is he sitting back while New Zealanders are charged more by the banks, they pay more for their power, and they can’t get around the country?
statement: Well, it’s very difficult to take a lecture from a member of that party on issues relating to that sort. They had six long years to attend to these matters. They saw inflation out of control, they saw costs out of control, and the net result was that New Zealanders had a crisis of confidence in that Government. Our Government is standing up for all New Zealanders. We’re getting the economy going, we’re going for growth, and we’re back on track. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions; the answer opens 'Yes' — complete on its own terms. The lengthy growth material that follows is padding, but it does not undo the direct answer.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our actions to go for growth. Wasn’t it absolutely great news last week to see Stats New Zealand confirm that the economy grew by 0.7 percent to finish 2024, with the first increase to GDP per capita in two years. We know that growth matters, on this side of the House, and more growth means more jobs, higher wages, more opportunities for all New Zealanders to beat the cost of living and to get ahead. That’s why just in the last two weeks we’ve been at it hard, fighting hard for trade in India, making sure we’re taking action to scrap and replace the Resource Management Act, and hosting investors worth trillions of dollars here in New Zealand so that we can build the roads, energy, and homes Kiwis need to thrive. There’s always more to do, but it’s very exciting to say that growth is back, and I’m sure that member, in a bipartisan way, would fully support and endorse those comments.

explanation: Two parts: does he agree with the 2023 statement, and is he confident lunches have been improved, optimised and enhanced. The first gets a clear 'Yes'; the second is engaged with only glancingly — 'some practical issues' being worked through, plus savings — without ever saying whether he is confident on those three counts.
question: Does he agree with the statement made by Christopher Luxon in September 2023 with regard to the school lunches programme: “We’re very supportive of it. I just want to make sure that I’m sure it can be improved, I’m sure it can be optimised, I’m sure it can be enhanced.”; if so, is he confident that the school lunches programme has been “improved”, “optimised”, and “enhanced” under his Government?
statement: Yes. The free lunch programme is there so that hungry kids going to school can actually focus and get something to eat so they can learn. There’s been some practical issues, which the Associate Minister of Education’s working his way through very well, and again I just say I think it’s fantastic that savings have been generated, and those savings can be generated back into health and education to help support our kids.

explanation: Asked why Libelle and Compass were selected given both had lost large numbers of schools. He offers only 'there was a standard procurement process' and redirects specifics to the responsible Minister. That touches the 'why' at the most general level while leaving the substance of the question — the providers' track record — untouched.
question: Why did the Government select Libelle and Compass to deliver the school lunches programme, given Libelle had lost nearly 60 percent of the schools it had been serving under the old programme due to quality concerns, and Compass had lost 23 of the 53 schools that it was serving?
statement: There was a standard procurement process. But if the member wants to direct more specific questions, feel free to direct it to the Minister.

explanation: Asked why the Government ignored official advice on Compass's and Libelle's failures. Luxon does not answer the 'why', but he engages the question head-on and states plainly that he lacks the procurement detail, redirecting to a question on notice. No talking points, no attack — a clean plea of ignorance rather than a dodge, but the core still goes unanswered, so it sits mid-scale.
question: Why did the Government ignore official advice that Compass had failed to meet the nutritional standards required in more than half of the assessments of its meals under the previous programme and had prolonged issues with undersized meals and inconsistent portioning, while Libelle had been the subject of 163 complaints about food quality, food safety, and food suitability?
statement: I think the member would understand that I don’t have that detail in front of me around a procurement process, but I would encourage him to put his question on notice.

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree with his own 2023 'better delivery' statement, and why were the contracts awarded to the worst-performing providers. Neither part is addressed — the agreement question is ignored entirely, and the procurement 'why' is deferred again, this time with a pivot to savings redirected into health and education. The 'practical issues... Minister's working through them' line gestures at the topic without reaching the question.
question: Good to see he’s awake, though. Does he agree with the statement of Christopher Luxon in August 2023, with regard to the school lunches, that a Government led by him would “make sure we get better delivery and better execution”; if so, why did they award the exclusive contract to deliver school lunches to Libelle and Compass, who had amongst the highest rates of uneaten lunches and food waste in the previous programme—almost double the average?
statement: Well, again, I’d just say to the member, I’m not party to the details of a procurement process. If he wants to put his detailed questions on notice, feel free to do so. But this is a programme that has been able to generate savings that can be redirected back into health and education. Yup, there are some practical issues; the Minister’s working his way through them.

explanation: A narrow factual question — why Seymour did not pass on five days' notice of Libelle's liquidation. The answer never touches the notification at all; it substitutes a general statement of comfort with ministerial delegations and the fact that he and the Associate Minister talk often. Relevant subject matter, but the specific core is squarely avoided, and a tight factual question dodged rates low.
question: Why didn’t David Seymour bother to tell the Minister of Education that the major provider of school lunches, Libelle, was going into liquidation, given he’d found out five days before it happened, yet the Minister was left to find out about that through the media after it happened?
statement: Well, again, I’m very comfortable with the delegations and accountabilities that we have between our Ministers. The Associate Minister and I talk all the time. We’ve talked about the school lunches. We’ve talked about many other things as well. I’m comfortable with it.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his 2023 statement and why nutritional value is now lower. He answers a question he was not asked ('I agree that we are working harder on education') and then turns to attacking the questioner's record as Minister of Education. Nutrition is never mentioned. The rhetorical counter-question at the end confirms the pivot.
question: Does he agree with the statement of Christopher Luxon in September 2023: “I’d work harder on education to make sure we give people healthier choices in the school lunch programme.”; if so, why is the nutritional value of school lunches now being provided consistently lower than under the previous school lunches programme that his Government scrapped?
statement: I agree that we are working harder on education, because I remember who was the Minister of Education when kids stopped going to school, when half our year 8s are not at the standard they need to be at on reading, and 80 percent of our kids going into high school are not where they need to be at on mathematics. Who was the Minister for 5½ years?

explanation: Asked whether spending less is achieving better outcomes. The reply asserts 'more value for money' and that savings are being redirected, which brushes against the outcomes claim without ever confirming or denying it; the 'does he agree with his own statement' half is left untouched. Partial engagement at best — it hedges around the core rather than answering it.
question: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon’s statement in July 2023: “I’m not interested in how much money is being spent; I’m interested in the results that are being achieved.”; if so, is his spending less achieving better outcomes so far?
statement: What we’re impressed about is that we’re getting more value for money. The money that’s being saved is going into education and health for our kids and the issues that are being worked through are being worked through.

explanation: A standard 'does he support all his Government's statements and actions' question, answered with an unambiguous 'Yes' before elaborating. The answer is given squarely in the first word. The subsequent sentencing-reform material and the jab at a Green MP are matters for Focus and Civility, not Forthrightness, and do not pull the score down — the question was engaged.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and especially our action to crack down on criminal activity and to restore law and order. Kiwis are sick of the large discounts and the short sentences regularly handed down, even in instances of serious offending. The good news is that, this week, the Sentencing (Reform) Amendment Bill will return to the House for its third reading. That bill will cap discounts and bring in tougher consequences for serious and repeat offending. It doesn’t stop there, though, for convicted criminals, because the last few weeks have, sadly, shown the longer you spend in prison, the more likely it is you’ll get visited by a Green MP of a convicted criminal.

explanation: Asked whether the companies want to make a profit. 'Well, they may well do, and I would hope they would want to see a return' is a substantive answer to the actual question, though softened by 'may well do' where a plain yes was available. He then moves to investment enthusiasm. Answered, with hedging around the core.
question: Do the companies that the Prime Minister is asking to build our schools, roads, and hospitals want to make a profit?
statement: Well, they may well do, and I would hope they would want to see a return. But what I’m excited about is that there is massive interest from investors who want to build public infrastructure in New Zealand, and the benefits to New Zealanders economically, socially, and environmentally are profound. If we can pull forward infrastructure development, get more roads built, more wind farms built, more energy delivered, that’s only good for New Zealand.

explanation: A binary question — does paying shareholder profit on top of build cost make it more or less expensive for New Zealanders. He calls it 'a strange line of questioning', characterises the Greens as a degrowth party, and lists investment aspirations. The more/less comparison is never addressed. Attacking the questioner in place of answering is the clearest form of evasion.
question: When our country has to pay for the profit of shareholders on top of the cost of building public infrastructure like our schools and hospitals, does that equation ultimately cost New Zealanders more or less?
statement: This is a strange line of questioning, and it just speaks to the degrowth agenda of the Green Party—the degrowth agenda of the Green Party. Not only do they want to abandon prisons but they now don’t want to grow the economy. To that member: we want investment in this country. It is capital thin. We need to get public infrastructure built. Iwi want to get on and actually get projects built, and private companies in our growth sectors need support too.

explanation: Asked a clean either/or: will PPP profit stay in New Zealand or go offshore. The answer restates a focus on attracting investment, tells the questioner she is confused about economics, and lists general prosperity goals. Neither branch of the alternative is chosen; the question's core is entirely skirted.
question: Will the profit that the private companies make through his Government’s intended public-private partnerships stay in Aotearoa New Zealand or go offshore?
statement: Well, again, our focus is on attracting investment to New Zealand so we can get public infrastructure built. The member seems to be confused about how economics works. We want New Zealanders to get ahead. We need them with more money in their pockets. We want them to have higher standards of living. One of the ways we do that is we attract investment to New Zealand as well as use domestic pools of capital as well.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts that PPPs will cost more and send profit offshore. He opens with a flat 'No' — a direct, complete answer to the yes/no question asked. The rest is unresponsive argument, but the answer was already delivered. A blunt denial engages the question and scores high regardless of whether it is right.
question: Does the Prime Minister accept that his plans for public-private partnerships will ultimately, then, cost New Zealanders more and send that profit offshore?
statement: No. We are looking at the right funding and financing tools and mechanisms to support the right infrastructure. We need to get a lot more infrastructure built in this country. The member may disagree with us, but we are going to grow New Zealand because it’s good for New Zealanders. And part of that is getting infrastructure built faster, quicker, and if we can do that in partnership with private capital, we will. [Interruption]

explanation: A narrow comparative question — who borrows more cheaply, private companies or the Government. The answer never names either party as cheaper; it retreats to 'the right funding and financing mechanism', makes no apologies for partnering with private capital, and returns to the degrowth attack. A specific factual comparison completely avoided.
question: Who can borrow money cheaper: the private companies that the Prime Minister wants to build our public infrastructure, or the Government?
statement: Again, as I’ve said to that member, we’re going to find the right funding and financing mechanism that supports the right project. But I make no apologies for wanting to partner with private capital—international or domestic—to get things built for New Zealanders. You may disagree with us ideologically on that point, as a degrowth party, but we want growth in New Zealand, and that’s what we’re going to do.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on the economy. Willis names the report (Statistics New Zealand's GDP release), states the figure, and compares it against Treasury and Reserve Bank forecasts. This answers exactly what was asked. That it is a friendly question inviting a favourable answer is irrelevant here — the question was engaged directly and completely.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Last week, Statistics New Zealand released the latest GDP figures. These showed the New Zealand economy expanding 0.7 percent in the December quarter of 2024, led by a pick-up in tourism-related spending. Growth of 0.7 percent in the quarter was stronger than economists were predicting. For example, both the Treasury and the Reserve Bank were forecasting quarterly growth of 0.3 percent. In terms of per capita growth, GDP per person rose 0.4 percent in the December quarter—the first such increase in more than two years.

explanation: Asked the significance of the GDP result. Answered directly and up front — it marks a turning point, the end of the downturn and the start of an upturn — before adding partisan history. The core was reached, and the partisan padding is a Focus concern, not a dodge.
question: What is the significance of the GDP result?
statement: The significance is that it marks a turning point. It marks the end of a protracted and painful downturn in the New Zealand economy, and the beginning of an upturn, with per capita GDP having fallen around 5 percent since the third quarter of 2022. From 2021 to 2023, of course, members, uncontrolled Government spending helped push annual inflation to more than 7 percent. Interest rates were hiked to bring inflation down, and there was little to no growth in the economy over the past two years. Inflation is now back within target, interest rates have come down, and last week’s result is the confirmation that growth has returned.

explanation: Asked what more recent economic indicators show. Answered squarely with named indicators: goods exports, tourism, and the BNZ-BusinessNZ PMI. Nothing asked was left unaddressed.
question: What do more recent economic indicators show?
statement: Of course, the GDP results are backward-looking: they tell us what happened in 2024. More recent information indicates what is happening this year and identifies positive signs, challenges, and risks. On the positive side, goods exports are doing well and tourism is stronger than expected. The most recent BNZ—BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index (PMI) indicates that the manufacturing sector is continuing to expand. BNZ economist Doug Steel said that the improvement in the PMI this year is “one of several indicators that suggests the broader economy is turning for the better.”

explanation: Asked what the risks to the outlook are. Named the risk directly — the global environment, OECD-forecast tariff uncertainty deferring investment and higher prices cutting consumer spending. Complete engagement with the question.
question: What are some of the risks to the economic outlook?
statement: As members know, one of the biggest risks is from the global environment. The OECD has just reduced its forecast for global growth. In its latest economic update, the OECD warns that rising uncertainty around tariffs will lead businesses around the world to defer investment and that higher prices will reduce consumer spending. That could impact the New Zealand economy. Forecasters expect the economy to continue picking up over 2025, but the journey could be a little bumpy.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions. Answered "Yes" — complete. The jab at the questioner that follows is a Civility matter and does not reduce forthrightness, since the question was already answered.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: Yes. In particular, I tend to make the same statement to one audience as I do to another, unlike that member, who took so many positions on public-private partnerships last week that she ended up having to apologise for the confusion she’d caused.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with her own October 2023 statement given that surplus has been pushed out and debt is growing. A blanket "I stand by all my statements" formally answers the agree/disagree, but the specific tension the question was built on is never engaged; the rest pivots to Labour's fiscal conversion. Partial.
question: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, who said in October 2023 that the Government “will never hit surplus and debt will blow out even further than it is today” when she has shifted surplus out, will not deliver in the forecast period, and debt is growing under her watch?
statement: Well, I stand by all my statements, and I welcome this turn of fiscal prudence from the Labour Party, in which, suddenly, for the first time, that member, instead of encouraging me to get out the money hose, is saying that she cares about debt and surplus. Stick to those guns, Barbara.

explanation: Two-part question: does she agree the Government can't keep blaming external events, and if so why is she now concerned about international headwinds. "Absolutely" answers part one; part two is left unaddressed — she argues the last Government's inflation was not global rather than explaining her own present appeal to global conditions.
question: Does she agree with Nicola Willis, as reported by the media in July 2022, that “the government could not keep blaming external events”, and, if so, why is she now concerned about international headwinds?
statement: Absolutely, because under the last Government, what we had was a spending approach which was so excessive compared to other countries around the world that now numerous studies have shown that our inflation went higher and stayed higher for longer and that our interest rates needed to soar higher to control that, and that was not a result of global factors. It wasn’t global factors that made every former Minister sitting opposite me spend like a drunken sailor on bureaucrats, go-nowhere projects, and wasted initiatives. It was your Government that chose to do it; it drove up inflation, and it caused real pain for New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked which of two seemingly contradictory debt statements she agrees with. She engages the contradiction directly and reconciles it — debt added recklessly by the previous Government, but from a low base so still relatively low internationally. An actual answer to the either/or, though wrapped in partisan framing.
question: The Minister of Finance. Does she agree with the Minister of Finance that “we have huge amounts of Government debt”, or does she agree with her statement at the international investment summit that “We have relatively low levels of government debt compared to other countries,”?
statement: Yes—yes—another set of wise statements by Nicola Willis, because, on the one hand, the previous Government added more than $100 billion to debt with just about nothing to show from it, which I believe was pretty reckless, and, on the other hand, because of the great work by Sir Bill English and other prudent National Party finance Ministers, our debt had started in a low position, and so it ended up in a lower position than some other countries. But if that lot had stayed in, I can guarantee you this: the debt would have got out of control.

explanation: Asked why she called for more capital investment while cutting investment in schools, hospitals and housing. She rejects the question's factual premise and cites counter-figures on homes, classrooms and roads. Contesting the premise with evidence is engagement rather than a dodge, but the "we need more capital investment" half is never directly explained.
question: Why did she tell the international investment summit that “we need more capital investment” while cutting back Government investment into schools, hospitals, and housing?
statement: The member should be very cautious before she makes statements in this House that cannot be backed up by the facts, and I would sincerely ask her to go back, look at the words she used in that question, and see if she can find factual verification for them, because this is a Government that in its first Budget invested more money in school buildings, invested more money in transport infrastructure, invested more money in housing, such that we have added more than 4,000 public homes since we came to office, such that we have added more classrooms, we have built more schools, and we have more than $6 billion worth of roads under construction. So get your facts right. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why she says one thing to international investors and the opposite to the public. After a dismissive opener, she restates the reconciliation — low base from prior prudence, Labour's rise to 40 percent of GDP, hence relatively low but still needing restraint — which addresses the alleged inconsistency directly, if by repetition.
question: Why is it that she says one thing about the Government’s books to international investors but is more than comfortable to say the complete opposite to the New Zealand public?
statement: This is like patsy hour! I’ve given the member the answer, and I’ll give it to you again, which is this: on the one hand, we have had years of prudent fiscal management, including by Sir Bill English, who managed to get debt down to extremely low levels. We then had the spendthrift days of the Labour Government, who brought that debt up to 40 percent of GDP, and because we started from a good base, because of the prudent work of previous National Governments, it meant that, relatively, our debt is still quite low compared to some countries in the OECD. But I would caution the member this: New Zealand is a country that is prone to significant economic shocks, be they climatic events, be they seismic events, be they trade-related events. So it has been the longstanding position of both Labour- and National-led Governments that it makes sense to keep our debt at low levels. If the member wishes to depart from that longstanding consensus, I would suggest to her that most New Zealanders would not agree.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on replacing the RMA. Answered directly with yesterday's announcement on the shape of the replacement legislation and the Cabinet-endorsed Expert Advisory Group report.
question: What recent announcements has he made regarding the replacement of the Resource Management Act 1991?
statement: Yesterday, the Government announced that we have agreed on the shape of the Government’s replacement legislation to a far more liberal planning system with less red tape premised on the enjoyment of property rights. In our first year, we repealed the previous reforms of the last Government and made a series of targeted amendments. We also passed the Fast-track Approvals Act, and now we are getting on with the job of replacing the Resource Management Act (RMA) completely. We set 10 principles for the new system. We’ve received a report from the Expert Advisory Group; I want to thank the chair, Janette Campbell, for the reports—an excellent high-quality piece of work that Cabinet has now endorsed—and we’ll be getting on with developing the legislation.

explanation: Asked for the key features of the new planning system. Enumerated them directly — two Acts, narrower scope, property rights, national direction, environmental limits, standardisation, streamlined plans, compliance — then expanded on standardised zoning. Fully engaged.
question: What are the key features of this new, more enabling planning system?
statement: Well, Cabinet has agreed to two new Acts, a narrower scope, property rights at the core, simplified national direction, clear environmental limits, more standardisation, streamlined council plans including spatial planning, and stronger environmental compliance enforcement and monitoring. Standardised zoning will be a key feature of the new system, and it might surprise members of the House to learn that across the country there are currently 1,175 different kinds of zones; in the entirety of Japan, there are 13. It’s our view that elected representatives should spend more time focusing on and talking to their communities about where density should and should not occur, and less time focusing on the enormous number of technical details that go into regulating that density. Standardised zones make up just one part of the new system but do give a sense of the ambition that we are aiming to achieve.

explanation: Asked what benefits New Zealanders can expect. Answered with the Castalia estimate of 45 percent process-cost savings plus wider economic benefits, before broadening to the "culture of no". The question's core is reached, with some drift into rhetoric at the end.
question: What are the key benefits New Zealanders can expect to see from this new planning system?
statement: Well, there’s been some preliminary economic analysis done by Castalia which estimates a 45 percent saving in process costs compared to the RMA. There will be further economic work done as policy is developed and as bills—plural—are prepared, and that is before we consider the wider economic benefits. The broader point is this: we need to change the culture of “no” that permeates decision making in this country. Whether it’s aquaculture off the coast of the South, or a new green six-star building replacing a heritage gravel pit next to a train station in our biggest city, the RMA has obstructed growth instead of enabling it. Our aim is to change that.

explanation: Asked what response has been seen to the announcement. The answer names three specific responders (EMA, Planning Institute, BusinessNZ) with quotes — exactly the thing asked for. The trailing material about writing to Opposition spokespeople is additional, not a substitute. Direct and complete.
question: What response has he seen to this announcement so far?
statement: It’s been quite overwhelming in terms of support. The Employers and Manufacturers Association said they strongly support the direction of travel: “The proposed changes will allow for more efficient development”. The Planning Institute welcomed the announcement: “Spatial planning … is a no-brainer. This will be a game changer for proactive planning”. Business New Zealand also welcomed it. Following announcements yesterday, today I have written to the relevant spokespeople from the Opposition, from Labour and the Greens, inviting their involvement in the process to replace the RMA. Our core policy intentions remain obvious, but we do want to try and work—

explanation: A two-part question: do you agree, and if so why. "Yes" answers part one unambiguously; the follow-on (back office to front line, fewer policy roles, more front-line nurses) supplies a why. The why leans on the lanyard half of the quote and leaves the high-vis half untouched, so it is slightly short of complete, but the core was engaged head-on.
