One example is the $2.7 million meth rehabilitation programme run by patched Mongrel Mob members in the Hawke’s Bay, which ended nine months ago but is yet to produce an outcomes report. To prevent such misuse, this Government has introduced a rigorous ratings process to ensure funding proposals are complete, outcomes-focused, and fully aligned to the objective of the fund. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked how the changes contribute to the 20,000-fewer-victims target. She describes the causal route — funding short-term initiatives that stop crime escalating to violent crime or disrupt organised crime — then restates the commitment. The link to the target is asserted rather than explained, so it partly reaches the question and partly restates the goal back.
question: Thank you. How will these changes contribute to the Government’s target of 20,000 fewer victims of crime by December 2029?
statement: The updated funding criteria recognises that the drivers of violent crime are complex and often require targeted interventions to break offending cycles. This allows Government agencies to apply for funding for short-term initiatives. These must either prevent crime from escalating to violent crime, or disrupt organised crime. This Government is reinforcing its commitment to the 20,000 fewer victims of crime by 2029.

explanation: Asked whether the ferry replacement programme is on track. After setting out what the promised update covers, he states plainly "We're on track to deliver the goods in full and on time." The core question gets an explicit yes.
question: Is the Cook Strait ferry replacement programme on track?
statement: We said on 11 December that we would provide an update on this programme by the end of March this year. This means outlining, first, the type of ferries and the infrastructure plan that we will be pursuing; second, an update following our worldwide engagement with ship builders; and, third, an update following an alternative proposals process. There is a performance indicator in the freight world called a DIFOT—in short: delivered in full, on time. We’re on track to deliver the goods in full and on time.

explanation: Asked what he had learnt from stakeholder engagement. He offers one lesson — that there is no shortage of pragmatic ideas when you listen — then shifts into a roll-call of who was met and praise for the Ferry Holdings team. The question is engaged but only glancingly; most of the answer describes activity rather than anything learnt.
question: What has the Minister learnt from his engagement with key stakeholders involved in this programme?
statement: There is no shortage of good, pragmatic, sensible ideas when one is willing to listen and discuss. We have met unions representing Cook Strait mariners, engineers, masters, and crews. We have met on site with CentrePort to hear their views and see the infrastructure that has served our country for decades. We’ve met with the Mayor of Marlborough, Nadine Taylor, and enjoyed hearing the priorities of her community, and her council’s 100 percent commitment to practical, sensible solutions. The small but effective team at Ferry Holdings has met with KiwiRail, both ports’ officials, councils, and many other interested parties, and they have done an extremely good job in the service of us all in this House, and in the service of our country.

explanation: Asked how the infrastructure work is tracking. What is on the record is a remark about the "no-nonsense thinking" that comes when a Government is disciplined, which says nothing about the programme's progress. The response is cut off, but as it stands it does not reach the question.
question: How is work on the infrastructure programme tracking?
statement: It is just stunning to see the no-nonsense thinking that comes from people when the Government is disciplined—

explanation: Asked what lessons the review of the previous programme yielded. He gives a concrete one — the undisclosed $750m decision missing from the 2023 PREFU — says 21 such problems were counted, and states openly that time prevents listing the rest. That is the question engaged, not dodged; the incompleteness is flagged rather than concealed.
question: What lessons has the Minister learnt upon his review of the programme he is replacing?
statement: We were staggered to learn that the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update in September 2023 did not disclose a $750 million funding decision taken before the election, because Cabinet took this decision a week after Treasury round out the numbers, but months after the cost blowout was known to the Government. And there were cliff-face disasters like this one after the other—we’ve counted now 21. I can’t answer today because of the brevity of time in this House, but if they’ll ask me a question from that side, I’ll give you the full list.

explanation: Asked whether any options have been ruled out. The reply is a pun ("we have ruled out letting directionless, empty vessels") aimed at opponents rather than a statement about which ferry or infrastructure options are off the table. It gestures at the yes/no shape of the question while substituting a joke for the substance.
question: Has the Minister ruled out any options?
statement: Let me say this right here, right now: we have ruled out letting directionless, empty vessels.

explanation: Standard "does he stand by" opener, answered "yes" with the conventional caveat about context. One word of substance, and it is the word the question asked for.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Well, obviously, in the context and with the usual caveats, yes.

explanation: Asked whether officials are being prevented from releasing boot camp reoffending rates and why. He confirms the pilot is under way and that confidentiality until final assessment is part of the process — that is both the "if so" and the "why". The jibe about members' education and mental processes is discourtesy, not evasion, and does not lower the score here.
question: Is the Government preventing officials from releasing reoffending rates for boot camp pilot participants, and, if so, why?
statement: As the Minister has said yesterday and the countless times before, the pilot programme is going on, and confidentiality until the final assessment is part of that process. It’s not a matter of not—[Interruption] Look, sometimes it takes some people—because of their education, I suppose, or maybe their mental process—a long time for it to sink in, but the Minister has been going on for months about the fact that it’s a pilot programme and there’s a certain privacy to—

explanation: Asked whether the "tough on suppliers" objective has been achieved given a 96% rise in meth use. He contests the baseline of that statistic — arguing COVID lockdown years make a poor comparator — which engages the evidence but never says whether the objective has been achieved. Disputing the premise is partial engagement; the core yes/no is left unreached.
question: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, regarding methamphetamine: “We’re going to be really tough on that. I mean, we have to get to the suppliers.”; if so, has that objective been achieved, given that the waste-water testing suggests a 96 percent nationwide increase in meth use in the 2024 year?
statement: Now, that’s a fascinating question, because the first thing that that judgment was made about in 2024 was the COVID years, when we were locked down everywhere, and to use that as the base for comparative figures seems attractive until you realise that it had to be the pre-COVID years first, and then—

explanation: Asked whether he will work with Labour on bipartisan RMA reform. "The answer is yes", with a condition about sincere cooperation attached. Direct, and the conditional does not obscure it.
question: Will he work with Labour to build a sustainable, bipartisan consensus on reform to the Resource Management Act (RMA) through compromise; if not, why not?
statement: The answer to that is—that’s such great news that we were asked that question. The answer is yes, and as long as we get rational, sane cooperation—now, I know that some members on that side have got what it takes, and then there are some who are so difficult to cooperate with. But if that member is making a sincere offer, then of course we’re going to take the offer up and welcome it sincerely.

explanation: Two-part question: does he agree with the Collins quote, and if so why cut Defence Force roles. He answers the first part (agreeing with Collins is "very wise") and is interrupted before the second, which is the substantive half. Half the question addressed on the record.
question: Does he agree with Judith Collins that “our best assets are our people”; if so, why is the Government cutting hundreds of roles across the New Zealand Defence Force?
statement: Well, it’s very wise to agree with the Hon Judith Collins—that’s number one—

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement about frictionless immigration settings for India. He confirms he does ("of course we'd want to make it as easy and frictionless as possible") and qualifies it with the intention to keep strict policies. The qualification refines the answer rather than avoiding it.
question: Does he stand by his statement regarding immigration settings from India: “We want to make sure that we’re making it as easy and as frictionless as possible”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, the answer to that is that of course we’d want to make it as easy and frictionless as possible, and for the most obvious reasons. But, remember, that does not mean we will not adopt the same sorts of strict policies, sensible policies, followed all over Asia and, dare I say it, in India itself.

explanation: Asked why the Government refuses to acknowledge listed failings. He rejects the premise outright — the assertions are "false" — which is a legitimate direct response to a loaded why-question, but he then moves to the previous Government's cycleway and light rail rather than substantiating the rejection. Premise contested, then the ground shifts.
question: Why is this Government refusing to acknowledge its failings, with meth use almost doubling, unsustainable RMA reform, free-trade agreements that may not even survive coalition negotiations, and a defence force that’s being stripped to the bone?
statement: Well, I reject all of the background ill-researched and lack-of-foresight thinking behind that question, because everything that was said there was false. The reality is that unlike the last Government, we’re out to succeed. We will not always get it right, but we’ll never stop trying, not like the previous group, when the then Prime Minister at the time recently confessed that they had so many policies they hadn’t worked their way through. Do you remember them: $54 million for a cycleway over the Auckland Harbour Bridge—how could you get that far down? Light rail, at $1.2 million—[Interruption] And I want to thank those members—

explanation: Asked whether the average affected beneficiary could afford rent and bills. Most of the answer pivots to justifying sanctions and obligations, but the final two sentences do engage the core conditionally: if a client cannot afford rent and bills, money management would not be a suitable sanction and MSD would consider an alternative. Partial — the 'average beneficiary' question is never answered, but the affordability concern is addressed rather than ignored.
question: Will the average jobseeker beneficiary subjected to compulsory money management be able to afford their rent and bills?
statement: Someone getting their full benefit is financially better off than someone whose benefit has been reduced. Avoiding this or any other sanction is simple: beneficiaries must comply with the obligations they agreed to when they applied for assistance, such as to look for or to prepare for work. If someone does not comply with their obligations currently, they may be subject to a financial sanction, with their benefit reduced by either 50 percent or 100 percent. If a client cannot afford their rent and bills, a money management non-financial sanction would not be a suitable sanction for that person. An alternative and appropriate sanction would be considered by the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).

explanation: A narrow factual question: is the average jobseeker's housing cost share over 50 percent, and if not, what is it? The answer says nothing about any figure at all, returning instead to the suitability of money management as a sanction. A closed factual question answered with a different topic entirely.
question: Is it true that the average proportion of a job seeker’s income spent on housing costs is over 50 percent, and, if not, what is the figure?
statement: If we look at money management as a non-financial sanction, it will not be applied if it is not suitable for that particular beneficiary. MSD will have the discretion to decide what is appropriate.

explanation: Asked how she can be confident given a 41 percent misassessment rate and reports of wrongly applied sanctions. She does give grounds for her confidence — 98.6 percent compliance, and trust in front-line case managers' judgement — which answers 'how can you be confident'. She never engages the misassessment evidence the question rested on, so it is engaged but not squarely.
question: How can she be confident that compulsory money management will be adequately applied when 41 percent of benefit entitlements aren’t even assessed correctly and front-line organisations report that many sanctions are wrongly applied and subsequently overturned when a review of the decision is lodged?
statement: Because there is a very small number, which I’m proudly happy to say, of people that aren’t complying with their obligations—98.6 percent of people are at green. So there’s a very small number who are not complying with their obligations. I’m very confident in MSD’s and the front-line case manager’s ability to decide which non-financial sanction is appropriate for the client in front of them.

explanation: Asked how she can be confident given 41 percent of entitlements are assessed incorrectly. She answers directly on two fronts: she disputes the figure, and she argues entitlement accuracy is a separate work stream from sanctions, so it does not undercut her confidence. The closing line about wanting fewer people on welfare is a talking point, but it arrives after the question has been met.
question: How can she be confident when 41 percent of benefit entitlements are not even assessed correctly?
statement: Well, I’m not sure that that figure is correct. But what I will say is that there has been recognition that MSD has room for improvement in terms of accuracy of benefit entitlements. Some are overpaid and that is equally a problem as if they are underpaid. That is a separate piece of work that is very unrelated to the work on sanctions and ensuring that beneficiaries are complying with their obligations, and that is what our focus is. We want fewer people on welfare and more people in work.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether she would stake her role on no one being made homeless. The answer never says yes or no, and never touches the question of personal commitment; it restates the argument that 100 percent of a benefit beats 50 or zero. A closed question replaced with a different one.
question: Is she committing and staking her own role on no person subjected to compulsory money management being made homeless?
statement: I will say it again: 100 percent of a benefit payment is better than 50 percent or zero percent, which is the only option available today. So someone who is getting 100 percent of their benefit has got a lot less chance of being homeless than someone who’s getting zero.

explanation: Asked to confirm or deny that someone spending over half their income on rent could not keep a roof over their head under compulsory money management. The answer opens on general economic conditions, then gestures at the core by noting the sanction leaves a person on 100 percent of their benefit and that case managers decide. It neither confirms nor denies the proposition put to her; it circles the question without reaching it.
question: Is it correct that if the average person on the jobseeker benefit spends over 50 percent of their income on rent, they simply won’t be able to keep a roof over their head if they’re subjected to compulsory money management?
statement: Let me be clear: the economic conditions we have mean there are more New Zealanders who are facing incredibly challenging economic times. Those on benefit are no different from any other New Zealander who is confronting challenging times. MSD’s front-line case managers will make decisions, based on someone’s circumstances, on whether a non-financial sanction—which means a person receiving 100 percent of their benefit—is better than other options. I trust them to make that decision.

explanation: Asked how the Australian report compares with New Zealand's grocery market. Answered squarely and comparatively: similarities and differences, shared concentration and barriers to entry, and the domestic history of mergers and the 2022 market study. The aside about MPs opposing new supermarkets is a digression, but the comparison asked for is delivered.
question: How does the Australian report compare with what is happening in New Zealand’s grocery market?
statement: Well, there are similarities between the New Zealand and Australian grocery markets, and there are differences too. Like Australia, our market is highly concentrated, and there are significant barriers to entry and expansion at a national scale. Indeed, it’s even the case that some MPs oppose the building of new supermarkets. Kiwi shoppers are being poorly served by extremely low levels of competition in our grocery sector, and the lack of competition is the result of a series of mergers that have occurred over the past 20 or 30 years. This dynamic was acknowledged by the previous Government when it made changes to the sector’s regulatory framework following a 2022 market study. However, since then, in 2024, the Commerce Commission noted that despite the reforms, competition had not materially improved.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing about supermarket competition. Answered directly: the February announcement seeking a new entrant, intent to remove regulatory hurdles, and ongoing engagement with interested parties. Whether that amounts to much is a separate matter; the question was engaged.
question: What is the Government doing to address supermarket competition?
statement: In February, I announced my desire to see another competitor enter the supermarket scene to deliver more effective competition in New Zealand’s grocery sector, because I’m interested in not just addressing the effects of poor competition but materially improving competition, because that means better prices and choices for Kiwi shoppers. And I made clear, in February, that I wanted to help remove barriers that could get in the way of a new entrant, including potentially removing a range of regulatory hurdles. Since then, my officials and I have been engaging with a range of interested parties. A new grocery competitor that is able to introduce competitive pressure, not just in one niche or one region but at a national scale, would be good for our grocery market and good for Kiwi shoppers.

explanation: Asked for the Government's next steps. Opens with a jab at members opposite and a repeat of the prior answer, then does reach the question: the Commerce Commission's wholesale inquiry, land banking analysis and second grocery report due mid-year, plus a further announcement she is cut off before naming. Answered, but only after preamble that displaced part of it.
question: What are the next steps the Government will take to increase competition in the New Zealand grocery market?
statement: Well, I note that members opposite are talking about what they did. I will repeat what I said in my earlier answer, which is that the Commerce Commission has found that the changes made by the last Government have not resulted in any material change to competition. So we have a number of strands of work under way to address that issue. The Commerce Commission is continuing its work to complete its wholesale inquiry, its analysis into land banking issues, in its second grocery report, and we can expect to hear more from the commission in the middle of the year. In addition, this weekend, Duncan, I will be outlining—

explanation: A two-part question: does she stand by the statement, and if so why should the public believe future Treasury forecasts. Both parts answered explicitly — 'Yes', then a direct response to the second part reframing forecasts as predictions rather than guarantees. Whether that reframing is persuasive goes to Rigor, not to whether the question was engaged.
question: Does she stand by her statement yesterday that “The Treasury got its forecasts before the election plain wrong”; if so, why should the public believe future Treasury forecasts?
statement: Yes, and I would note that a lot of other people were wrong, too. To the second point, it’s not a matter of belief; people can be guided by economic forecasts as they are by weather forecasts, but neither of these is a guaranteed thing. They are predictions of the future, not reality.

explanation: A closed question: does she stand by the quoted statement. Answered with one word, 'Absolutely'. Complete.
question: Does she stand by her statement yesterday that the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update, which is independently produced by Treasury, was “doing all sorts of things to make the books look better than they actually were.”?
statement: Absolutely.

explanation: Asked whether Treasury forecasts are always based on the stated basis. Willis opens with a flat "Yes" — the question is answered outright. The follow-on about the PREFU being wrong and forecasts not being 100 percent accurate is argumentative padding, but it does not undo the direct answer.
question: Are Treasury’s forecasts always based on “Our observations of the economy, alongside the Government’s fiscal policy decisions”, as stated in every Treasury fiscal update?
statement: Yes. I’m not really sure what the member’s point is. As I’ve tried to explain to her: forecasts are put together; in the case of the pre-election fiscal update, it was completely wrong, for a combination of reasons. And if the member is of the view that forecasts are somehow going to be 100 percent accurate, she’s wrong.

explanation: Asked what actions the Government has taken to restore consequences for crime. Goldsmith names three: capping sentencing discounts, new aggravating factors for offences against connected homes/businesses, and ending repeated remorse discounts. Squarely responsive; the closing jab at Labour is a Focus/Civility matter, not a dodge.
question: What actions has the Government taken to restore real consequences for crime?
statement: The Government has continued to take action to restore real consequences for crime. Yesterday, we delivered on our promise to cap sentencing discounts so that those who commit horrific crimes are not given a slap on the wrist. We’ve introduced new aggravating factors to address offences against people whose homes and businesses are connected, and stopped offenders from receiving repeated discounts for remorse. Kiwis deserve to feel safer in their communities, and it’s disappointing that our friends in Labour didn’t support it.

explanation: Asked how the new gang laws are restoring consequences. Goldsmith answers the "how": extra tools for police, ability to hold gangs accountable and disrupt them before new victims. The mechanism is described only in general terms, but that is a Specificity shortfall — the question was engaged, not deflected.
question: How are the Government’s new gang laws restoring real consequences for crime?
statement: Our new gang laws have given police the extra tools they need to go after the gangs that are a scourge on our communities, to hold them accountable for the misery they inflict upon others. It has given the police the ability to disrupt gangs before they create new victims. Again, it’s incredibly disappointing that we weren’t supported in this by our friends on the other side of the House.

explanation: Asked what commentary he has seen on the need for prisons. He answers by pointing to photos of the Green co-leader in People Against Prisons Aotearoa merchandise, then gives the Government's own view. Photos of clothing are a loose reading of "commentary," so it does not fully land, but he does identify what he has seen rather than changing the subject.
question: What commentary has he seen on the need for prisons as part of our justice system?
statement: Well, I have seen some commentary, some photos of the co-leader of the Green Party, Chlöe Swarbrick, wearing merchandise from People Against Prisons Aotearoa. It’s this Government’s view that we don’t live in a utopia and that prisons are necessary to keep particularly serious violent and sexual offenders off the streets, to prevent the creation of new victims. We take public safety very seriously.

explanation: Asked what observations he has made on the response to the Government's law-and-order actions. He states an observation — the irony of Hipkins calling Tamatha Paul's view stupid while the two parties vote in lock step. That is literally an observation about the response, so the question is answered, however partisan the content.
question: What observations has he made on the response to the Government’s actions to restore law and order?
statement: Well, I have observed the irony of Chris Hipkins’ description of Tamatha Paul’s view on the police and justice system being stupid. I find it ironic because the voting record of the Greens and Labour are in lock step when it comes to law and order.

explanation: A two-part question: does she stand by the quoted statement, and did she direct Oranga Tamariki to withhold the reoffending rates. Chhour answers both limbs explicitly — "yes" to the first, "no" to the second. Complete and unambiguous.
question: Does she stand by her statement regarding the release of the rates of reoffending by participants of the military-style academy pilot that “Oranga Tamariki is of the understanding that they follow my instructions that these young people’s privacy is the most important thing, and making sure that we’re taking care of the wellbeing and the safety of these young people comes first and foremost before anything else”; if so, did she direct Oranga Tamariki to withhold the rates of reoffending by participants of the military-style academy pilot?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes, and in answer to the second part of the question, no.

explanation: Asked whether anyone in her office had indicated in any way that the reoffending figures should not be released. Chhour recounts the December agreement on milestone updates and then says that if a staff member reiterated her privacy expectation, she applauds them — a conditional that neither confirms nor denies the office contact. She engages the surrounding subject but hedges around the core yes/no.
question: Has anyone in her office indicated in any way to Oranga Tamariki that information about the re-offending figures should not be released?
statement: Last year, it was brought to my attention by Oranga Tamariki that the intense focus on this small group of young people from media and negative attention for political reasons was having a real negative effect on them, their wellbeing, and their families and whānau. Following this, in December last year, it was agreed with Oranga Tamariki that in order to balance the public interest in this matter with the need to protect the privacy and wellbeing of the young people, Oranga Tamariki would provide public updates at appropriate milestones in the programme. This position has not changed, and if one of my staff members has reiterated to Oranga Tamariki my expectation that the privacy, safety, and wellbeing of these young people comes first, then I applaud them for it.

explanation: Asked whether she is confident her officer's actions comply with Cabinet Manual paragraph 3.27. Answer: "Yes." One word, and it is the whole answer the question called for.
question: Is she confident that her officer’s actions are consistent with the Cabinet Manual, paragraph 3.27?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether she is confident her own actions comply with Cabinet Manual paragraph 3.26. Answer: "Yes." Directly and completely responsive.
question: Is she confident that her actions are consistent with the Cabinet Manual, paragraph 3.26?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether the real reason for interfering with the release is that it would show the pilot has failed. Chhour never addresses the reason: she turns on the questioner's "lack of concern" for the young people, raises privacy breaches under the previous Government, and closes on talking points. The proposition put to her is left entirely untouched.
question: Is the real reason that she is interfering with the release of the reoffending rates because it will show her military-style academy pilot is a complete failure?
statement: Oh, look, given that member’s attitude to the lack of concern for the privacy and wellbeing of these young people, I’m really not surprised about the recent findings of serious privacy breaches by Oranga Tamariki under the previous Government which had put people at serious risk of harm. This is a Government that respects people’s privacy and their safety, and I’m focused on giving these young people the best opportunity to be the best that they can be.

explanation: Asked whether she will ever make the reoffending rates public, or withhold them until her serious young offender legislation passes. She answers the first limb — public updates at appropriate milestones while the pilot runs — but gives no response to the suggestion that the timing is tied to the legislation. Half the question is met; the sharper half is not. The rebuke to "start listening" is a Civility matter and did not affect the score.
question: Will she ever make the reoffending rates public or will she continue to withhold these until she has pushed through her serious young offender legislation?
statement: I suggest the member starts listening. I have repeated this over and over again. We will provide public updates at appropriate milestones of the pilot. This pilot is still running.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen from the Public Service Commission. Collins identifies one directly — progress on the $400 million consultant and contractor savings target — and reports its findings. Exactly what was asked for.
question: What recent reports has she seen from the Public Service Commission?
statement: I have received a report on progress on the Government’s target to cut spending on consultants and contractors by $400 million by the end of June. I can tell the House that not only will we meet this target but we’re on track to double it. That’s $800 million of taxpayer funding that will now be able to be spent on areas like healthcare, law enforcement, and education.

explanation: Asked what is happening to contractor/consultant spend. Answer states directly that spend is falling and quantifies it (48% fall in six months, >$500m for the year, >$800m from baseline). The question's core is met head-on; the thank-you at the end is surplus, not evasion.
question: What is happening to contractor and consultant spend by the Public Service?
statement: Well, we are seeing a clear and sustained reduction in spending on contractors and consultants. Spending by agencies fell a further 48 percent in the six months to 31 December 2024. On current forecasts, we anticipate there will be a reduction of over $500 million for the full financial year and well over $800 million from the 2022-23 baseline. This is more than twice the targeted reduction of $400 million. I’d like to thank the chief executives of those agencies for their effort and focus on reducing spending in this area.

explanation: Asked what is happening to the size of the core Public Service workforce. Answer gives the figure: down 4 percent in the 12 months to December, back-office weighted. It opens with a definitional caveat and closes with a partisan comparison, but the number asked for is delivered.
question: What is happening to the size of the core Public Service workforce?
statement: Well, of course, the core Public Service workforce does not include teachers, police, and other front-line staff. Official data shows the core Public Service workforce decreased by 4 percent in the 12 months to December. This reduction was largely in back-office roles, with an increase in the number of front-line staff offsetting this. We simply could not continue to support the staggering 72 percent increase in salary costs that occurred before our Government. Our Government will continue to focus on getting delivery of front-line services out of the back office.

explanation: Asked what other changes she expects in the Public Service. The answer lists expectations (back to basics, core functions, value for money, plus retention of neutrality/merit/competence). The question was broad and open, and the response stays on it throughout — vague, but the vagueness tracks the question rather than dodging it.
question: What other changes do you expect to see in the Public Service?
statement: Well, I expect the Public Service to get back to basics, sticking to its core functions, and delivering outcomes for the taxpayers that we all serve. I expect it to continue to focus on getting the best bang for the taxpayers’ buck, and Government agencies need to be prudent when spending taxpayers’ money. While I do expect a great deal of change to drive improvement in Public Service performance, I also want to see core principles of the Public Service maintained, like political neutrality, like appointment on merit to all positions, and professional competence.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with S&P's stated reasons; if not, why not. He answers the agree/disagree axis by declining to take a position ("it's not for me to agree or disagree") and offers a partial reason, then moves to Government talking points. A stated non-position engages the question, but the specific causal factors S&P listed are never addressed either way.
question: Does he agree with Standard & Poor’s that their ratings downgrade of 18 councils and three council-controlled organisations “reflects factors including the quick passage and repeal of several key laws governing local councils, the cancellation of various Crown grant programmes, an increase in unfunded mandates, and recent announcements about infrastructure financing options”; if not, why not?
statement: I have seen Standard & Poor’s report. It’s not for me to agree or disagree. Rating agencies make their decisions based on a number of factors, including council performance. That is why this Government is focused on getting councils back to basics, delivering Local Water Done Well, and broadening the range of funding and financing tools available to councils.

explanation: Asked why S&P downgraded the councils. He does not give a reason; he plainly declines on jurisdictional grounds ("I am not responsible for Standard & Poor's"). It is a bare refusal rather than an answer, but it is short, plain and free of pivoting — the forthright end of not answering, not a dodge into talking points.
question: Why, then, did Standard & Poor’s downgrade the ratings of 18 councils and three council-controlled organisations?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Local Government, I am not responsible for Standard & Poor’s.

explanation: Asked whether he takes responsibility for the volatile policy environment; if not, why not. The answer never says yes or no — it substitutes a different subject ("what we take responsibility for is...") and pivots to Local Water Done Well and the previous Government. A yes/no question converted into a talking point.
question: Does he take responsibility for the volatile policy environment that led to councils’ ratings downgrades; if not, why not?
statement: Well, on behalf of the Minister of Local Government, what we take responsibility for is getting councils back to basics and putting in place Local Water Done Well, which will ensure that councils are able to borrow at a cheaper rate for water infrastructure than what would have happened under that Government’s failed three waters.

explanation: Asked whether higher borrowing costs will mean larger rates increases. He does not say yes or no, but the reply is on-point rather than a pivot: councils borrow via the LGFA, whose ratings were affirmed — an implied "no" the questioner can extract. It engages the mechanism of the question while stopping short of stating the answer.
question: Will the increased borrowing costs that local councils will now face because of the rating downgrade lead to larger rates increases in the future?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Local Government, most councils borrow through the Local Government Funding Agency (LGFA). Of course, the same report from Standards & Poor’s says we have affirmed our AA+ foreign currency and AAA local currency ratings on the Local Government Funding Agency on 18 March.

explanation: Asked whether he understands S&P's assessment that the LGFA changes are "generally negative for credit quality." The answer never engages the credit-quality finding; it restates the purpose of Local Water Done Well and cites DIA advice on borrowing cost. Adjacent subject matter, but the specific proposition put to him is left untouched.
question: Does he understand that changes made to the New Zealand Local Government Funding Agency, that he just referenced, will, according to Standard & Poor’s, “generally be negative for credit quality across the sector”?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Local Government, the work the Government is doing to deliver Local Water Done Well is to ensure that councils are able to borrow the funding needed to be able to deliver the water infrastructure that they need. And the advice from the Department of Internal Affairs is that the funding through Local Water Done Well, with the partnership with LGFA, will be cheaper than what it would have been under the last Government’s failed three waters.

explanation: Asked why he will not take responsibility for his Government's actions. The reply is entirely talking points — back to basics, the four wellbeings, the last Government — and never engages the question of responsibility. (The question is loaded, but it is a real supplementary seeking an answer, not a procedural one.)
question: Why won’t he just take responsibility for his Government’s actions, directly increasing costs for Kiwis and their households, which the international rating agency has so plainly and clearly stated?
statement: On behalf of the Minister of Local Government, this Government is focused on getting councils back to basics and focused on core delivery rather than on the four wellbeings and all of the other things the last Government was focusing councils on. We want councils focusing on the basics and giving them the funding and financing tools they need to do just that.

explanation: A two-part question: does he agree with the Minister's statement, and if so is he committed to protections in the gulf. Both parts answered explicitly — "yes, I agree" and "the Government is committed to establishing additional marine protection." Direct on both limbs.
question: Does he agree with the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries’ statement that “Locals have raised serious concerns about the decline of spiny rock lobster in the inner Hauraki Gulf, and this has been backed up by fishery-independent research. I share these concerns and … I’ve decided to stop spiny rock lobster fishing in the inner Gulf”; if so, is he also committed to protections in the Hauraki Gulf?
statement: Āna—yes, I agree with Minister Jones’ statements and welcome the closure. Locals have raised concerns and officials have given advice on kōura decline in the majestic Hauraki Gulf—te Pataka kai Tīkapa Moana. The Government is committed to establishing additional marine protection in the gulf. The announced spatial closure to the code of fisheries by our Dalmatian matua compliments the protections under the bill in restoring the health and mauri of the gulf.

explanation: Asked whether the documented declines require an equally active protection response. The reply refuses the premise by attacking the questioner's party ("I won't succumb to the Green catastrophising") and never reaches the question. Note this is scored low for dodging, not for rudeness — a blunt "no, they don't" would have scored high.
question: Does he consider the documented 57 percent decline in key fish stocks, 67 percent decline in seabirds, 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins, and the functional extinction of snapper and crayfish populations in some areas of the gulf to require an equally active response in establishing evidence-based marine protection from overfishing?
statement: Thank you for that question, but I won’t succumb to the Green catastrophising of members diagonal opposite—

explanation: Asked for the justification for permitting commercial fishing in areas his own advice said this would undermine. The answer restates a commitment to tripling protection and the legislative timetable; the conflict with official advice, which is the whole of the question, is never addressed. A narrow, well-specified question met with a general commitment.
question: What justification can the Minister provide for his decision to allow commercial fishing in the exact areas that are supposed to be set aside to allow the gulf to recover, when his own official advice stated that allowing the continuation of commercial fishing in the new high protection areas is “incompatible with the purpose” and “will undermine biodiversity outcomes”?
statement: For the umpteenth time, we are very committed to tripling the marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf—Tīkapa Moananui-ā-Toi-te-Huatahi [Hauraki Gulf and the Bay of Plenty]—and we have done this in a manner that will expedite the progress of the legislation to its logical dénouement that will result in seriously more protection than other Governments have achieved.

explanation: Asked whether he is comfortable risking the bill's purpose for $14,000/yr of commercial ring-net revenue. He signals comfort ("very proud of our pragmatic approach") and offers a proportionality rebuttal (the areas are ~3 percent of the protected zone), which glances off the core trade-off — but he explicitly declines to engage the data ("before I start quoting various points of data") and never addresses the $14,000 figure the question was built on. Partial engagement with a narrow question.
question: Is he comfortable with potentially risking the very purpose of the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill and potentially undermining his own purported biodiversity goals for the $14,000 per year that Fisheries New Zealand data demonstrated would be the commercial ring-net fishing revenue from all 12 proposed high protection areas of the gulf?
statement: As mentioned, we’re very proud of our pragmatic approach to ensuring a balanced and increased protection in the Hauraki Gulf. And before I start quoting various points of data, can I point out: of the additional 1,500 square kilometres of the Hauraki Gulf that this marine protection will protect, the areas in question comprise around 3 percent.

explanation: Asked why the public should trust National's word given an unmet commitment. The reply is a restatement of the tripling-protection talking point plus a jab at the previous Government; the trust/broken-commitment core is never reached. Only the faintest implicit answer ("trust us because we're delivering").
question: Why should Kiwis trust the National Party’s word on ocean protection when they’re failing their own commitment to “accelerate initiatives like the Hauraki Gulf marine protection and the Kermadec Ocean Sanctuary bills to ensure the effective protection of marine biodiversity”?
statement: Can I repeat, for the third time today: we are very proud and happy to progress the legislation to triple the marine protection of the gulf, something—between 2020 and 2023—another Government was unable to achieve.

explanation: Asked why industry is being prioritised over iwi, hapū, community and the Government's own commitment. He repeats the pride line but does add one on-point element — the ring-net matter has been considered and will be reviewed in three years — which touches the industry side of the question. The "why prioritise industry" core is not answered.
question: Given the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill was unanimously supported in the recent select committee process, why is the Minister prioritising industry over the wishes of iwi, hapū, and community, and his own Government’s commitment to restore the health and mauri of the Hauraki Gulf?
statement: We are very proud and comfortable in progressing the tripling of marine protection in the gulf. We have considered the appropriate review of the various matters regarding the ring-net fishing, and we’ll undertake that in three years after we pass this legislation.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with a quoted statement, and if not why not. He answers "No" outright and supplies the reasons. Direct and complete; the closing swipe at the alternative is irrelevant to forthrightness.
question: Does he agree with the statement by the member for Wellington Central that people “do not want to see police officers everywhere, and, for a lot of people, it makes them feel less safe”; if not, why not?
statement: No, that is total nonsense. This Government has invested in police and part of that has been getting them back out on the beat and back to basics, building relationships with business owners and their staff, and giving Kiwis a sense of confidence and reassurance. The country should reject any alternative that would see a serious degradation or attempted abolition of our police.

explanation: A narrow factual question — by how much have foot patrols increased — answered with the exact figures and percentage, including the district asked about. Nothing left unaddressed.
question: By how much have foot patrols increased nationwide?
statement: In 2024, there were 78,830 foot patrols in New Zealand. That’s an increase of 40 percent on the 56,134 recorded in 2023. In the Wellington district, this was an increase of 54 percent.

explanation: Yes/no question answered "No" immediately, then substantiated. The question is engaged squarely; the volume of supporting detail is a Specificity matter and does not lift or lower this.
question: Does the Minister agree that all the beat police do is pick up rubbish?
statement: No. Police do an outstanding job. Last year, on top of responding to, investigating, and prosecuting criminal behaviour, they also conducted over 2 million prevention and service activities, including 1,295 land rescues, 1,593 water and sea rescues, 4,332 sessions educating kids on road safety, 7,653 visits to schools, 191,000 family harm investigations, 2,500 emergency disaster responses, 20,000 missing person events, and gave crime prevention advice 38,000 times.

explanation: Asked what message he has for the public about the good work police do. He does deliver a message, and opens by acknowledging the police's challenging environment — but the message itself pivots to warning about a rival party rather than the good work asked about. Answered in form, drifted in substance.
question: What message does the Minister have for the public about the good work that our police do?
statement: Our police operate in a challenging environment every day and respond to the needs of the public. My message to the public is very simple: I think they should be very worried about the prospect of any Government including a party that entertains the abolition of the Police.

explanation: Asked whether he will report the bill back before all submissions are processed. He does not give yes or no, but engages the question directly by explaining it is not his decision as chair and stating what he will do when the committee resolves. That is a substantive response to the question's premise rather than a pivot, though the questioner still learns nothing about timing.
question: Will he report the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill to the House before all submissions have been processed and considered by members?
statement: Decisions about when a bill is reported back are made by the committee and not by the chair. So when the committee resolves to report the bill to the House, I will do so accordingly.

explanation: "Yes." One word, and it completely answers the question asked.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A two-part question — agreement with a quote, and why power bills are rising by up to $25 a month — met with generic cost-of-living talking points and an attack on the questioner's voting record. Neither the agreement nor the transmission charges are addressed.
question: Does he agree with Christopher Luxon, “What’s mattering most to New Zealanders out there is what we are doing to reduce to the cost of living.”; if so, why is his Government increasing Kiwi household power bills by up to $25 a month through increased transmission and charges during a cost of living crisis? [Interruption]
statement: I’m very proud of the efforts of our Government to help New Zealanders with the cost of living. That’s why we’re getting control of Government spending, that’s why inflation’s coming down, that’s why interest rates are coming down. I just note that that member didn’t support tax relief for the first time in 14 years for low and middle income workers. We’re doing everything we can to put money back in Kiwis’ pockets.

explanation: A binary question (do these specific fee and levy increases raise or lower household costs?) answered by talking about inflation, interest rates and GDP, then attacking Labour's votes. The increasing-or-decreasing core is never touched despite being answerable in one word.
question: Is his Government’s decision to increase car registration fees by $50 a year, increase taxes on parking fines, and more than double the insurance levies on motor vehicles increasing or decreasing cost of living for Kiwi households?
statement: What is improving the situation for Kiwis’ households is making sure that inflation is coming down, interest rates are coming down, and the economy is starting to grow. It was fantastic to see the economy grow at 0.7 percent in quarter four last year. Importantly, Labour didn’t vote for tax relief, Labour didn’t vote for Working for Families credits, and Labour didn’t vote for FamilyBoost.

explanation: Another increase-or-decrease question. The opening clause "We don't set insurance premiums" does engage the premise about responsibility, which is marginally more than a pure pivot, but the rest is the same macroeconomic talking points and the question itself goes unanswered.
question: Will his Government’s plan to increase annual household insurance bills by between $400 and $948 a year increase or decrease the cost of living for Kiwi households?
statement: We don’t set insurance premiums, but what we can control is the environment—which is an economy that’s incredibly well managed—to make sure that we’re bringing spending down, to make sure that we’re bringing inflation down and interest rates down, and that the economy’s growing so people have more money in their pockets and they can access higher-income jobs.

explanation: Asked a binary question: did prescription charges, transport subsidy cuts and rubbish-disposal costs increase or decrease the cost of living? The answer never says increase or decrease — it states pride in the Government's cost-of-living work and attacks the questioner's party for not voting for tax relief. A narrow either/or question answered with talking points plus an attack.
question: Did his Government’s decision to reintroduce charges for pharmacy prescriptions, slash public transport subsidies, and increase the cost of rubbish disposal increase or decrease the cost of living for New Zealand families?
statement: I’ll just say to that member: I am incredibly proud of what this Government is doing to help New Zealanders with the cost of living crisis. That member and his party did not vote for tax relief—

explanation: Asked whether below-inflation minimum wage rises increased or decreased the cost of living crisis for low-income earners. The reply pivots to entitlement indexation and aggregate real wage growth over five quarters. It touches the real-terms frame of the question but never answers increase or decrease for minimum-wage earners; partial engagement, core avoided.
question: Does his Government’s decision to increase the minimum wage by less than inflation for two years in a row—meaning those earning the minimum wage earn less now in real terms than two years ago—increase or decrease the cost of living crisis for low-income New Zealanders?
statement: I’m proud of the fact that we are increasing entitlements by roughly the amount of inflation. But what I’m also proud about is the fact that real wage growth has grown for five quarters in a row, after declining for 13 quarters in a row under that Government.

explanation: Asked (a) does he stand by his 'fees and levies are not a major focus' statement and (b) does he acknowledge the listed cost increases show his priority lies elsewhere. The answer opens by conceding it addresses only 'part of that question' and then goes to economic growth and the inherited economy. Neither limb is answered — no yes/no on standing by the statement, no engagement with the list.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “There might be just regular annual increments in some fees and levies across the piece, but that’s not a major focus.”, and, if so, does he acknowledge that increased costs for prescription charges, electricity lines charges, car registrations, car insurance levies, survey and title fees, insurance levies, and, in fact, fuel excise indicate that his priority isn’t fees and levies that impact everyday New Zealanders but rather delivering tax cuts for landlords and tobacco companies?
statement: In answering part of that question—my focus is on making sure we run a great economy so New Zealanders can get ahead. We inherited a situation where the economy was run into the ground. We are making sure that we do everything we can to get growth back into New Zealand so we get money back into Kiwis’ pockets so they can get out of the mess that we’ve inherited thanks to that last Government.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she made on supermarket competition. The answer names them directly: an RFI process to identify support for a national-scale entrant, and commissioned external advice on restructuring the duopoly. Squarely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has she made regarding supermarket competition?
statement: On Sunday, I outlined the Government’s next steps to drive more competition in the supermarket sector and deliver better grocery prices for Kiwi shoppers. I announced two things: first, a formal request for information (RFI) process to identify what is needed to support a significant, national-scale competitor to enter our grocery market. Second, I announced that I have commissioned specialist external advice on ways in which the existing supermarket duopoly could be restructured to improve competition. I would note that this approach is similar to that recommended by the last Cabinet in June 2023, when Minister Duncan Webb said that “It would make sense to consider the need for more detailed policy work on divestment to occur after the Commission makes its first report into the state of the grocery sector”. That report was delivered in September.

explanation: Asked what response she has seen to the announcement. The answer supplies actual responses — quotes from the Grocery Action Group chair and a grocery commentator — which is exactly what was asked for.
question: What response has she seen to the announcement?
statement: There have been a range of responses welcoming the Government’s announcement, including from Grocery Action Group’s Chair, Sue Chetwin, who said the announcements were “terrific news for Kiwi shoppers”. Miss Chetwin said that “While the many recent regulatory reforms of the supermarket sector have been worthwhile, none has effectively curbed the duopoly’s market power.” Well-known grocery commentator Ernie Newman said the announcements were “A significant move”, and “The good news is the sense of urgency”. He added: “That said, this is necessarily a long-term project. I hope that all parties in Parliament will endorse the direction of travel.” Of course, the Government’s announcement builds on our coalition commitment with New Zealand First to ensure that there is greater competition in the supermarket sector. There are many other responses which reinforce the sentiment that change is needed, and I agree with them.

explanation: Asked what other work is under way on supermarket competition. The answer lists the Commerce Commission's wholesale inquiry, land-banking analysis and second grocery report, plus officials' work on RFI participation. Directly on the question.
question: What other work is under way to address supermarket competition?
statement: The Commerce Commission is working to complete its wholesale inquiry, its analysis into land banking issues, and its second grocery report. My officials are also working to get as much involvement as possible in the RFI from market players, potential entrants, and investors. On that note, I was pleased to see on Sunday that Foodstuffs said in response to my announcements that it will “constructively participate in the Government’s RFI process.” I welcome their involvement.

explanation: Asked when the next steps toward better grocery competition will come. The answer gives a timeline: RFI closes after six weeks, recommendations to Cabinet mid-2025, legislation before year's end if needed. The 'when' is answered.
question: When will we see the next steps towards better competition in the grocery market?
statement: Well, the RFI is proceeding at pace and will close after six weeks. In mid-2025, once I’ve considered the evidence from the RFI and the Commerce Commission’s additional work, I will bring further recommendations to Cabinet. Depending on what I hear, I may seek Cabinet’s mandate to progress further design work on structural options to improve competition in the grocery sector. If legislation is needed, I would want to introduce it before the end of the year. We need to move fast and also with due care to ensure Kiwi shoppers get the benefits of stronger competition in our supermarket sector.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all the statements and actions of his Government. Answered 'Yes' — one word, complete, no evasion.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the Housing Minister's 'very proud of it' statement and, if so, which of two things he is more proud of. He answers the 'what are you proud of' limb, but on his own reframing (children out of motels, wait-list reductions) rather than the either/or posed, and never states whether he stands by the statement. Engages the topic without reaching the question as asked.
question: Does he stand by the statement of the Minister of Housing, who, when asked whether his Government’s emergency housing policies were a success, replied, “Yes, we’re very proud of it”, and, if so, what is he more proud of: homelessness services across the country reporting increased homelessness or siphoning money out of services that our most vulnerable people in Aotearoa need to survive?
statement: Well, I’m incredibly proud that in a very short period of time, this Government has ended what I think is one of the blights on New Zealand’s social policies—the fact that we have taken 2,000 children out of squalid motel rooms and we have put them into proper, dry homes; the fact that we have taken 5,000 people off the State social housing wait-list who are desperate to get a home—that is fantastic. And so we should be very proud about that, and I think the House would want to join with me on that.

explanation: Asked whether he will accept that his Government's decisions are causing reported increases in homelessness. The answer begins with a flat 'No' — a direct, complete response to the yes/no put to him — before adding supporting comment. The subsequent pride-in-record material is padding, not a dodge; the question itself was answered.
question: Will he accept that it is his Government’s decisions that are resulting in reports of increasing homelessness, with less people being able to access basic supports that were available even this time last year?
statement: No. Government support is still available to people who need housing assistance, and will continue to be so. But what I am incredibly proud about is that emergency motel housing has been a major challenge in New Zealand for a decade or so—we’ve talked about it all the time—and this Government has finally done something about it through good, active management and getting the job done.

explanation: Asked whether he understands that being denied MSD housing support, even for one night on the street, can have lifelong consequences for rangatahi. The reply denies the premise ('There will always be Government support') rather than addressing whether he understands the consequence described. Premise-denial is some engagement, but the question asked was not answered.
question: Does he understand that being denied housing support from the Ministry of Social Development, resulting in even just one night sleeping on the street, can have lifelong consequences for our rangatahi?
statement: There will always be Government support for people in need of housing. That has not changed.

explanation: Two-part question: (1) does he stand by the Minister's statement, (2) if so, why are community organisations saying they can't get support. The answer explicitly addresses only the first part — "In answer to the first part of the question, yes" — and leaves the substantive second half untouched. The half it answers is answered squarely and unambiguously, so this is a genuine partial, not a pivot; but the core the questioner was driving at (the contradiction with providers' experience) is simply not engaged.
question: So does he stand by the statement of his Minister of Housing that “There is always support available for people who are sleeping on the streets,” and, if so, why are community-based homelessness organisations saying that they are unable to get support for people who urgently need housing?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to properly resource community-based providers. The answer never says yes, no, or 'we'll consider it' — it opens by disputing the premise of the questioning and then recites motel-accommodation figures and the Government's housing record. The record cited may be accurate and relevant to homelessness generally, but truth and relevance are other attributes; the question of whether he will commit to resourcing providers is never reached.
question: Will he commit to properly resourcing community-based providers who are already supporting those doing it tough, or will our rangatahi continue to be abandoned to sleep on our streets?
statement: The member’s line of questioning is not acknowledging that we had 3,141 families and households in motel accommodation in New Zealand—completely and utterly unacceptable. This Government—a Government that cares about outcomes, cares about people and making sure they find housing—has reduced that to 591 families. We now have 2,000 kids out of motels and in proper houses. Whether that is State housing, social housing, transition housing, or the private rental market, that is a great outcome and we are very, very proud of it.

explanation: Two-part question (does she stand by the statement; do today's changes reflect it) answered with "Yes and yes", followed by the specific changes she has in mind. Both halves answered directly and completely.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “The Government is focusing on the things that make a difference to the quality of people’s lives”; if so, do the changes coming in today reflect that?
statement: Yes and yes, because the annual general adjustment changes coming into effect today help New Zealanders, with greater increases to payments, including those who are receiving New Zealand superannuation, veteran’s pensions, and benefits, which will help them with the cost of living. I note that for those that are adjusted according to the after-tax average wage, the increases are larger than they would have been otherwise because of the tax adjustments delivered by this Government in its first Budget.

explanation: A narrow question — does a 35c/hour rise, below inflation, make a difference to quality of life? The answer never addresses the effect on workers at all; it switches to the perspective of employers and the risk to jobs. That is a defence of the decision, not an answer to what was asked, and the yes/no at the question's core is avoided. Dodging a question this narrowly framed is a worse failure than missing part of a sprawling one.
question: Does a 35c per hour increase in the minimum wage—less than the rate of inflation—make a difference to the quality of people’s lives?
statement: Well, the first thing I would note is that our Cabinet is mindful of the fact that the minimum wage is paid by employers—small businesses and medium businesses up and down the country—and we are conscious that in recent years, they have undertaken a very difficult period in which they have faced significant inflation and rising interest rates. We want to ensure that they are now in a context where, given the choice between letting a worker go and hiring a new worker, we minimise the costs that they face and ensure that we do not put New Zealanders’ jobs at risk.

explanation: Asked how removing the living wage for Government-contracted cleaners, caterers and security guards improves quality of life. The answer does engage the 'how' — it identifies the procurement changes, and offers a mechanism (an economic impact test favouring small and medium businesses, jobs, training, community impact). It reframes away from the affected workers and never confronts their pay, but unlike the surrounding answers it supplies an actual causal account responsive to the question. Partial engagement with the core.
question: How does the planned removal of the living wage for Government-contracted cleaners, caterers, and security guards make a difference to the quality of people’s lives?
statement: The member is referring to the procurement changes which the Government is consulting on, which intend to improve the quality of New Zealanders’ lives by ensuring that when the Government is choosing who to contract with, instead of ticking a lot of boxes, small businesses and medium businesses in New Zealand are invited to submit on the impact their business will have on New Zealand as a whole, including the jobs they create, the training they create, and the positive impact they have in their community. We think this economic impact test is an important way to ensure we make the most of Government procurement.

explanation: Asked specifically about removing free public transport fares for under-25s and cutting subsidies. Public transport is not mentioned once in the reply, which moves instead to tax relief, inflation and interest rates. This is a clean substitution of a different question for the one asked.
question: Does removing free public transport fares for under-25s and reducing public transport subsidies make a difference to the quality of people’s lives?
statement: In our first Budget, what we did was we ensured that we were able to offer tax relief to millions of New Zealanders, fully funded by savings across government, and what we can say is that that has allowed many New Zealanders to have more money in their bank accounts than would otherwise be the case. At the same time, we have ensured that inflation is back in the target range, minimising the price increases that New Zealanders face across the general economy, which has allowed interest rates to reduce—again, improving the cost of living for many families.

explanation: A sprawling question listing several rising costs and ending on the 35c rise and the living wage. The answer explicitly picks up the last part and gives a substantive response to it — that abatement of Working for Families and the accommodation supplement erodes a minimum wage increase for many households. That engages one strand of the question directly. It then abandons the rest of the list (transport, registration, power, insurance, rates) for general talking points and an attack on the previous Government. Partial, with the breadth of the question working somewhat in its favour.
question: How can she stand by her statement that she “is focusing on the things that make a difference to the quality of people’s lives” when public transport costs and car registration fees are up and power prices, insurance levies, and rates are up, but our lowest-paid workers only get a 35c an hour raise or won’t receive the living wage?
statement: Well, picking up on the last part of that question, it’s important to note that minimum-wage workers are in families with a range of different household circumstances, and what we have been advised is that in many cases, those workers will be eligible for additional Working for Families and accommodation supplement support, such that in some cases, a minimum wage increase will actually be eroded by the abatement in those payments that would occur otherwise. The significance of this is that, actually, what New Zealand families want is pretty simple. They actually want jobs, and we’re ensuring our policies support that; they want a cost of living that’s under control, and we’ve ensured that a lower inflation rate delivers that; and they want to be part of an economy that’s growing so that there are more and better-paid jobs and so that their cost of living is controlled in the medium term. The alternative approach is that of the last Government, where they sprayed the money hose around, crossed their fingers, and hoped, and what that delivered was a cost of living crisis that made many New Zealanders worse off.

explanation: "Is the programme on track?" — answered "Yes", with a delivery date and specifics, before padding with supportive quotes. The padding and the swipe at another member don't bear on this attribute; the question was answered directly at the first word.
question: Is the Cook Strait ferry replacement programme “on track”?
statement: Yes. By Christmas 2029, two brand new ferries will have rail on them and it will save the taxpayer billions. This is met with positive reactions: Carl Findlay, Maritime Union, said, and I quote, “Particularly happy for the workers who now know that they have a future”. Nadine Taylor, Marlborough Mayor, said this: it’s “the certainty [that port] needs to move forward”. Anthony Delaney, CentrePort, said this “gives … surety to all the people who rely on the provision of a safe, reliable and affordable ferry service”. And Don Braid of Mainfreight said this: “It’s a pragmatic, logical, sensible decision.” And he went on to say this very important note: “there’s a good number of people, politicians included, who are a little naïve as to how much freight actually moves by rail”. And then this self-appointed economist said this: “Rail-enabled ferries are a no-brainer”—that’s Julie Anne Genter.

explanation: Asked how the Government's plan compares to previous plans. The reply is a single quip about a former Prime Minister's remark on mega ferries; it makes no comparison of the plans on any dimension — cost, scope, timing, capability. The implication that the earlier plan was poor is all that gestures at the question, and the comparison itself is never made.
question: How does this Government’s plan compare to previous plans?
statement: Well, the greatest maritime fiction, since Moby-Dick, was delivered by Chris Hipkins when he said this: mega ferries “wasn’t the wisest decision.”

explanation: Asked how the marshalling yards will differ from Project iReX. Answered squarely: iReX proposed raising both yards by a metre; this plan increases culverts to manage water and keeps the existing yards. The difference asked about is stated plainly. The closing jab at the previous Government is a Civility/Focus matter, not a dodge.
question: How will the road and rail marshalling yards be different compared to Project iReX?
statement: Well, under iReX, both yards were proposed to lift by a metre at huge expense. There’s a lot of stone and concrete with new buildings, roads, and a rail on top. It was far beyond the modest alterations we had planned in 2020. They said lifting yards would mean extreme weather events would not disturb the ferry operations. That would have cost hundreds and billions of dollars alone. Here’s the point: why build a halo around a car yard when you could increase the culverts to stop the build-up of water in the first place? This can be done at a fraction of the cost and means we can keep using existing yards. It’s blindingly obvious to some of us, but not to those in charge between 2021 and 2023, or Mr Hipkins.

explanation: Asked how the terminal buildings featured in his thinking. Answered directly — the existing buildings are being retained, with reasons given for Picton and Wellington. The extended mockery of the previous plan's terminals is surplus, but the question itself is fully addressed first.
question: How have the terminal buildings been considered in the Minister’s thinking?
statement: We are retaining the existing terminal buildings. They are simple structures that can battle weather and earthquakes. Picton has a new concrete foundation, a steel structure, and we have been told it has a long future. Wellington’s building is in the right location beside the wharf, and so certain was KiwiRail and CentrePort about the terminal’s future that they started building a new baggage area months ago. The previous Government’s plan included—unbelievably—multi-storey new terminals with concrete so thick there was barely any room for the passengers and fixtures; so flash, even Louis XIV would have been embarrassed. While some may regret the absence of a Taj Mahal in Picton and the Sydney Opera House in Wellington, the people paying their taxes will not. And that’s why, over there, it hurts so much.

explanation: "Does he stand by all of his Government's statements and actions?" — "Yes." One word, and it is a complete answer to what was asked.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked what he is doing to address systemic police violence against Māori, citing three incidents. He declines to comment on the individual cases — a legitimate direct refusal on that limb — but the core of the question was what action he is taking, and on that he says nothing, substituting praise for the police. The refusal covers only the examples, not the question.
question: What is he doing to address systemic violence against Māori by the police, in light of three incidents in the past months alone where an 11-year-old autistic child was misidentified by police and forcibly medicated at the Henry Bennett Centre; a 15-year-old boy had his jaw broken by police in Napier; and Sam Matue, who was tasered, pepper sprayed by police, then died on the scene while being arrested at Ōrere Point?
statement: I won’t comment on individual cases, as that member will understand, given investigations that are ongoing, but I just say that I am very, very proud of the police, and I back our police.

explanation: Asked whether he will support mandatory body cameras, and if not why not. He gives a decision rule rather than a position: he will take advice from Police and back whatever tools they want. That engages the question conditionally without ever saying yes or no, then trails into unrelated beat-police talking points. Partial engagement.
question: Will he support the Māori Party policy requiring police officers to wear mandatory body cameras for their own safety and for the safety of the public, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, I’ll take my advice from the Police, and if that is a tool that they wish to have, I back them with any tools that they need to do their job. But I’m very proud that our police are out there on the beat. They’ve increased the beat police by 30 percent, and the public are feeling safer in their businesses, in their homes, and in their community, and that’s a good thing.

explanation: Asked whether the Government will implement the Understanding Policing Delivery recommendations, and if not why not. The answer never mentions the report, the recommendations, or any decision about them — it is entirely generic praise of police plus a gesture at complaints processes. The question is not engaged at any point.
question: Will his Government implement the recommendations of the Understanding Policing Delivery report, in which the New Zealand Police found that structural racism within the policies is the reason Māori are more likely to be stopped, tasered, and prosecuted than any other group; if not, why not?
statement: I back our police. Our police are out there making sure that they catch criminals and that they keep the community safe. They do a great job. There are obviously processes that people can have investigations or can make complaints around, but our police, each and every day, are out there protecting and serving this community, and I’m proud of them.

explanation: Asked whether her policies are working. She opens with "Yes" and then supports it. The question was squarely and completely answered on its own terms; the surrounding advocacy does not dilute the direct answer.
question: Are her policies working; if not, why not?
statement: Yes. We have been working hard to create a more proactive welfare system to support more job seekers into work. In the year to February 2025, there were 67,281 exits from the jobseeker benefit into work—an increase of 11 percent from the year before—despite the challenging economic conditions. We also know our policies are working because 98.1 percent are at green under the traffic light system, which means they are meeting their work obligations. Our Government is relentlessly focused on growing the economy, because when businesses have the confidence to grow and succeed, it’s good for jobs, it’s good for people, and it’s good for the incomes of New Zealand families.
