explanation: Asked if he stands by the Rail Minister's comments on delivering ferries and infrastructure. Answers 'Yes' and then substantiates with ferry specifications and procurement status. Directly on the question asked.
question: Does he stand by the comments of the Minister for Rail that the Government is delivering rail ferries and straightforward infrastructure?
statement: Yes, we are compelled to go with the truth. Two new ferries for the next 30 years—both will move 1,500 people and 2.4 kilometres of lanes for cars, trucks, and rail wagons each movement. That’s more than the current fleet. We are pleased to confirm to the House that the Ferry Holdings board has invited six commercial shipyards to compete on price and quality. We don’t, of course, talk about who they are so that we keep a commercial advantage as the buyer.

explanation: Asked if he stands by the Police Minister's comment that the Government will not defund police. He mocks the questioner's pronunciation, cites polling on public attitudes, and describes recruitment progress. Recruitment talk implies affirmation, but he never says whether he stands by the statement.
question: Does he stand by the comments of the Minister of Police that the Government will not defund the police?
statement: “Dun-ette”—what’s “dun-ette”? Your policy? Ladies and gentlemen, can I just say that people feel much happier with cops on the beat—even 48 percent of the Green vote felt that way. How many people felt that they’d be safer in a dark alley with a gang member? Well, less than 8 percent felt that way, and the Greens were all a part of them as well. Now, we’re going to get cops back on the beat. We are now well on track to be getting our extra 500 people. The intake is the largest it’s ever been, and so we’re flat out doing it—and do you know something? I think we had sometimes 7,000 applicants to be in the police at the very beginning. So the interest is starting to pick up big time.

explanation: Asked whether Māori-Crown relations have improved under this Government. He engages the subject seriously — says relations are not static, acknowledges challenges, lists successes — but declines to say improved or not, hedging around the yes/no core.
question: Te Arawhiti: Have Māori-Crown relations improved since the coalition Government took office?
statement: The honourable member will know that Crown-Māori relations are not static—they are tested, they have their ups and downs, and they evolve. There have been challenges over the last 18 months, and successes too, like Minister Jones’ Regional Infrastructure Fund supporting investments in Rātana, Waitangi, and Parihaka; like Treaty settlements led by Minister Goldsmith; the Ō-Rākau bill that transferred the ownership of Ō-Rākau back to Ngā Ahi e Toru, housing; and various fast-track projects—24 of which are either led by, or co-invested with, Māori organisations. We cannot break Crown-Māori relations. The Crown and iwi and Māori are inextricably tied through the Treaty and obligations and responsibilities that go with kāwanatanga, rangatiratanga, and, most importantly, kotahitanga.

explanation: Asked how undermining te reo, disestablishing the Māori Health Authority and dismissing tikanga achieves unification. He answers a different question — listing the Government's focus areas (economy, public services, law and order) — and never connects any of the three cited actions to the unification claim.
question: If his Government is focusing on unifying this country, as Christopher Luxon claimed, how does undermining te reo, destroying the Māori Health Authority, and dismissing tikanga achieve that?
statement: There are a number of steps that this Government is absolutely focused on—for example, getting the economy back on track, and that includes Māori and all New Zealanders delivering better public services, including folks who live in Hamilton that are Māori, Pasifika, Asian, or New Zealanders trying to get to the hospital and get proper patient health outcomes; and, of course, the law and order mahi that Minister Mark Mitchell is undertaking.

explanation: Asked which of three listed actions he is most proud of. He supplies something he is proud of — his 'respectful and dignified posture' — which fits the question's grammatical form but rejects all three options without engaging any of them, so the substance asked about is sidestepped.
question: What is the Minister most proud of: cutting Māori voices from councils, rolling back efforts to narrow the eight-year life expectancy gap between Māori and non-Māori, or allowing Te Tiriti to be used as a bargaining chip in coalition negotiations?
statement: I am very proud of maintaining a very respectful and dignified posture in this House and out in the electorate that I serve.

explanation: Asked how Māori can respect the legacy of a Minister who says he is too far down the food chain to protect Te Tiriti. Potaka never engages the 'food chain' claim or the question of respect for his legacy; he lists settlement and economic-development activity he is proud of and closes with an attack on the previous Government. It gestures at 'here is work worth respecting' but leaves the core premise untouched.
question: OK, Mr Speaker. Thank you very much. How can Māori respect the legacy of a Minister for Māori Crown Relations who claims he’s too far down the food chain to protect Te Tiriti?
statement: I’m actually very proud of the work that this Government has undertaken to progress a number of Treaty-related matters, including the mahi that Minister Goldsmith and I attended, one week ago, in Taumarunui with the Ngāti Hauā deed of settlement, including a number of matters that have advanced Māori economic development, including last week’s announcement around work that we are doing to assure that the Tōnui Māori framework—how Government can support Māori economic development—can move forward. I’m very proud of that focus on localism and devolution. What I would not be proud of, as the last Government showed, is monopolising Māori development and thinking that we know everything about Māori development. We don’t.

explanation: Asked what the point is of a Minister for Māori Crown Relations who only considers the Crown's interests. The answer states he is privileged and honoured and works in a team, then jabs at the Opposition ('handing out money like Al Bundy'). No engagement with the premise or the question.
question: Thank you very much. Can I ask the Minister: what is the point of having a Minister for Māori Crown Relations who only considers the interests of the Crown?
statement: Certainly, I’m very privileged and honoured to be the Minister responsible for Crown and Māori relations and someone who is working in a team, not just talking about things and handing out money like Al Bundy.

explanation: Asked what recent reports she has seen on fiscal policy response to economic shocks. Willis names the specific report (Treasury's draft long-term insights briefing released that morning), its subject and its motivation. Squarely answered.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the fiscal policy response to economic shocks?
statement: This morning, Treasury released a draft long-term insights briefing for public consultation. The paper is about the appropriate role of fiscal policy—that is, Government decisions about spending and revenue—through economic shocks and business cycles. Part of the motivation for the paper was a reflection on COVID times and how fiscal policy was used both during and after the pandemic. Looking ahead, it is relevant when thinking about the fiscal response to future shocks and significant global events such as the world is experiencing at present.

explanation: Asked what the briefing says about the relative roles of fiscal and monetary policy. The answer states exactly that: stabilisation left to monetary policy save in exceptional cases, a fiscal case at the effective lower bound, scepticism about infrastructure stimulus, medium-term focus otherwise. Direct and complete.
question: What does the draft long-term insights briefing say about the relative roles of fiscal and monetary policy?
statement: The paper confirms that in all but exceptional cases, macroeconomic stabilisation should be left to monetary policy run by the independent Reserve Bank. However, there is a case for using fiscal policy to stimulate the economy when the official cash rate is so low that reducing it further is not practical or effective. The paper is sceptical of using large-scale infrastructure investment as a form of stimulus, as it typically involves lengthy planning, design, and construction processes. Otherwise, discretionary fiscal policy should focus on the medium-term goals of debt sustainability and effective delivery of public services.

explanation: Asked how the findings are relevant to current global turmoil. She applies them: monetary policy first with OCR headroom at 3.5 percent, and fiscal repair to retain capacity to react. Answers the question as asked, with some campaign framing on debt at the end.
question: How are these findings relevant to the current global turmoil?
statement: Well, they confirm that in the first place, monetary policy is the way to deal with any immediate impact on the New Zealand economy. With the official cash rate at 3.5 percent, the Reserve Bank has plenty of room to reduce interest rates, if it needs to. In terms of fiscal policy, the current turmoil makes it even more important to get New Zealand’s fiscal position back on an even keel so that we retain market confidence and can react, if necessary. The operating balance has been in deficit for many years. We are now on a path back to surplus. Debt has risen very sharply since 2019. We are now on track to see that debt curve bend then start to decline—that is the crucial role fiscal policy is playing.

explanation: Asked what alternative approaches to fiscal policy she has seen. She describes one — a commentator arguing for more (investment) spending as stimulus — and contrasts it with Treasury's advice. This is a patsy question inviting an attack, but the attack is itself the responsive answer: an alternative approach is identified.
question: What alternative approaches to fiscal policy has she seen?
statement: I have seen one commentator saying that there may need to be more spending in the Budget to stimulate the economy and that “I think there’d certainly be a justified case for that”. The commentator also said, “if it’s investment spending, rather than short term spending, there is absolutely a case for that at the moment”. Since these statements suggest an entirely different approach from that which Treasury is advising in its draft long-term insights briefing, I would encourage Chris Hipkins to take up the Treasury’s invitation and make a submission.

explanation: Asked whether she is committed to the Act's Tiriti-honouring purpose, and if so how. Answer opens with 'Yes' and then gives the 'how' on her own terms (raising achievement, pāngarau resources in te reo Māori). Both limbs of the question are reached, though the 'how' redefines honouring the Treaty as achievement.
question: Is she committed to the purpose of the Education and Training Act 2020 that establishes and regulates an education system that “honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relationships”; if so, how?
statement: Yes. Honouring the Treaty in education means raising achievement and closing the equity gap by addressing the disproportionate representation of Māori students in the lower quartiles of educational achievement. That’s why, at the start of term 2, every kaiako teaching in Māori medium and kura kaupapa will have received their detailed pāngarau lesson plans, student workbooks, activities, and classroom-ready resources for their tamariki—the first roll-out of high-quality, curriculum-aligned math resources in te reo Māori, delivered by this Government.

explanation: Asked whether she has confidence in Elizabeth Rata's contribution to the curriculum given a specific quoted statement. Stanford defends the appointment process (one of 20 writers, hired for expertise, no trawling of histories) and turns to criticising the questioner's choice of topic, but never states whether she has confidence in the contribution. Adjacent to the question rather than on it.
question: Does she have confidence in Elizabeth Rata’s contribution to the curriculum, given she told the Justice Committee that New Zealand “is under serious threat from those who would replace liberal democracy with tribal sovereignty, and by doing so will create a racialised society—apartheid.”?
statement: Well, Elizabeth Rata was one of many writers of the English curriculum, one of 20, in fact. Actually, when the Ministry of Education are looking to contract writers for the curriculum, they look for experts in curriculum design and in English. What they don’t do is trawl back through people’s histories, because we are interested in the content of the curriculum. If the member was really interested in raising Māori achievement, she would be asking questions about the detail of the curriculum, but she’s not. She’s asking questions about what the people who wrote the curriculum believe. [Interruption]

explanation: Narrow follow-up: does she agree with Rata's remarks? The reply — she did not listen to that select committee contribution and it was not about education — implicitly declines to agree or disagree by disclaiming knowledge. That is a form of engagement, but the quoted words were put to her directly and she still gives no view on them.
question: My question was: does she agree with them?
statement: I didn’t listen to Elizabeth Rata’s contribution to that select committee—it was not to do with education.

explanation: Asked to reassure educators that Te Tiriti's place is safe, given alleged legislative downgrading. She disputes the premise squarely ('we're not downgrading it at all') and cites the relevant replacement section — engaging the question — but the section she cites is about achievement as the paramount objective, so the reassurance about Te Tiriti itself is only half delivered.
question: Can she reassure the thousands of educators associated with the 13 peak educational bodies that the place of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in education is safe, given that she is downgrading consideration of Te Tiriti o Waitangi through legislation?
statement: In answer to that question, we’re not downgrading it at all. The very first part of replacement section 127 in the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2), which is currently being introduced to the House, is about making sure that educational achievement is the paramount objective.

explanation: Terse supplementary asking where Te Tiriti sits in the provision she cited. The reply is a cut-off fragment referring back to her first answer; on its own it points at an earlier answer without delivering one here.
question: Where was Te Tiriti?
statement: And I said in my very first answer to the question—

explanation: Repeat of 'Where was Te Tiriti?'. She now completes the thought: honouring the Treaty means tamariki Māori achieving, which must be the paramount objective. That answers the question by asserting Te Tiriti is embodied in the achievement objective rather than named separately — responsive, though it substitutes her framing for the location the questioner sought.
question: Where was Te Tiriti?
statement: —that if we’re going to honour the Treaty, we need to make sure that our tamariki Māori are achieving in our education system—that has to be the paramount objective.

explanation: Prime's clipped challenge implies Te Tiriti is absent from the curriculum objectives. Stanford engages that implication head-on, asserting that honouring the Treaty is one of the essential qualifying objectives and citing section 127. Whether or not that is accurate is a veracity matter; as a response it meets the point put to her.
question: So not Te Tiriti as well.
statement: And one of the most essential qualifying objectives to that is making sure we all honour the Treaty, and it says that in section 127.

explanation: Asked how cutting Māori resource teachers squares with honouring Te Tiriti, Stanford argues the case directly: the delivery model is not working for tamariki Māori, RT distribution is inequitable (Northland example), and the funding will be redirected into Māori education. She engages the substance of 'how is this consistent', though she never returns to the Te Tiriti framing the question was built on, which leaves the core partly unreached.
question: How is proposing to cut Māori resource teachers (RTs), who work most closely with tamariki Māori needing the most learning support, being committed to honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: We’ve traversed this in question time many times. The model of delivery is not working for tamariki Māori. We’ve already said that there are numerous RTs of Māori based in areas where there are a very low proportion of kura kaupapa—where, in Northland, for example, we have many kura kaupapa and only two RTs of Māori. The way that we deliver the service is not equitable; it is not optimised. We are going to make sure we take that funding and put it back into Māori education so it is more equitable and it is more optimised so we see benefits in the classroom for tamariki Māori.

explanation: The question is narrow and two-pronged: why won't she meet the resource teachers of Māori, and why won't she accept the 6,000-signature letter. Stanford answers neither. She describes a consultation process that has closed and says responses will be considered — an adjacent procedural point that implies the meeting is unnecessary without ever saying why she declines it.
question: Why will she not meet with the resource teachers of Māori and accept their letter signed by over 6,000 supporters calling on her to retain funding for resource teachers of Māori?
statement: There has been a process of consultation—that has closed, and now we will look at those answers that are being given back and take those into consideration when we make our decisions.

explanation: Two parts: does he accept the 30/50 km/h survivability evidence, and will he listen to communities wanting 30 km/h. On the first he gives a qualified partial acceptance ('chance of survival is greatest at lower speeds') while disputing the simplicity — that engages rather than dodges. On the second he points to mandated variable 30 km/h limits outside schools and NZTA's reopened consultations. Both parts are reached, but neither is settled with a clean yes or no.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does he accept evidence that a person struck by a vehicle travelling at 30 km/h has a 90 percent chance of surviving, dropping to only 20 percent if hit at 50 km/h; if so, will he listen to the pleas from school principals, aged care residents, and communities who want to keep safer speeds of 30 km/h?
statement: I’m advised there’s a large body of research on the risk of a pedestrian being killed after being hit by a motor vehicle travelling at different speeds. While the chance of survival is greatest at lower speeds, I’m advised that crash outcomes are influenced by a range of factors. It’s not quite as simple as the member is indicating. The Government is committed to improving road safety, and we’re focused on targeting the highest contributing factors to fatal road crashes, such as alcohol and drugs, distracted drivers, and building and maintaining our road network to a higher standard. As to the second part of the question, the Government has taken steps to improve safety outside schools by requiring variable speed limits to be implemented outside schools by 1 July 2026. This includes variable limits of 30 km/h outside schools in predominantly urban areas. Furthermore, the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) has been listening to community concerns. Following strong local feedback to proposed speed changes in some parts of the country, such as Rākaia, in Canterbury, and Marybank, in Nelson, NZTA has announced new consultation on these speed changes to make sure they’re getting it right.

explanation: Bishop supplies the rationale asked for — the pragmatic view that limits should be low when children are present but not at midnight — and answers the second limb by saying councils can consult on lower limits after 1 July. He does not engage the 85 percent statistic that was the whole premise of the 'why claim this improves safety' challenge, so the central objection is left unanswered even though the question is otherwise addressed.
question: Why is he claiming that the variable speed limits around schools are an improvement to safety when 85 percent of deaths and serious injuries within 400 metres of a school gate happen outside school drop-off and pick-up times; and the rule, as drafted, is going to force councils to increase the speed limit around hundreds of schools in Auckland, and in Wellington, a primary school, an intermediate school, two aged-care facilities, a hospital, and two early childhood centres?
statement: Well, the Government has taken the pragmatic view that speed limits should be lower around school pick-up and drop-off times, because that’s when kids are there, but driving past a school at midnight should not require someone to drive at 30 km/h. As to the second part of the member’s supplementary, councils, as Road Controlling Authorities, have the ability to consult on lowering speed limits after 1 July, and some have already started doing that.

explanation: A 'what do you say to X' question, and he says it: all road deaths are tragedies, and the principal should raise the specific speed limit with the relevant road controlling authority. He also concedes unfamiliarity with the school rather than bluffing. The answer is thin comfort but it is squarely responsive to what was asked.
question: What does he say to the Point Chevalier School principal, who said, “I attended the funeral of a young man, about 10 years old. He was hit by a car … in a 50 km/h area. That could have been different if it was 30 km/h around that school.”?
statement: Well, I’d say to him that all deaths on our roads are tragedies, and I’d encourage him, if he feels strongly, as he clearly does, around the particular speed limit near that particular school, which I’m not familiar with, to talk to the relevant road controlling authority to express those concerns.

explanation: Asked what he says to a second principal recounting a crash outside drop-off times, Bishop answers by reference: exactly what he said to the previous one. It is terse and adds nothing to the new detail in the question, but it is a complete and direct response to the form of question put — he states his answer rather than evading it.
question: What does he say to Freemans Bay School principal Cindy Walsh, who, last year, was witness to a student being struck by a car outside of the school, outside of drop-off and pick-up times—“The car was travelling 30 km/h, as required. The student was taken to a hospital with moderate injuries and shock and was discharged the day after. If the car was travelling at 50 km/h, he would have received a serious injury or death.”?
statement: I’d say exactly the same thing I said to the person the member was referring to in the question before.

explanation: Asked whether he will amend the 2024 rule so authorities can retain 30 km/h limits, and if not why not, Bishop effectively answers no with a reason: no amendment is needed because the rule already permits it after 1 July, citing Hamilton City Council. The refusal is implicit rather than stated as 'no', which is the only thing holding this short of full marks; the redirect to Wellington City Council is a jab but comes after the answer, not instead of it.
question: Will he amend the 2024 speed limit rule to allow local authorities and NZTA to retain safer speed limits of 30 km/h where there is strong community support, especially around schools and aged-care facilities, where people are crossing the road all during the day; if not, why not?
statement: The rule allows for that. After 1 July, road controlling authorities can consult local communities on what the speed should be on the roads that they control. Hamilton City Council has already started it. I know that the member is particularly concerned about Wellington City Council. She should go and talk to the city council.

explanation: A closed clarifying question — is he saying councils don't have to reverse the limits before 1 July. Answer: 'No.' One word, unambiguous, complete.
question: Is he saying that councils don’t have to reverse the speed limits between now and 1 July?
statement: No.

explanation: The standard 'does she stand by' formulation with a confidence rider. Upston opens with 'Yes', which disposes of both limbs, then adds the funding boost, the strategy refresh and the working groups. The trailing material is padding, but the question was answered before it began, and padding after a direct answer is not a dodge.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “That is why we are prioritising disabled people, their families, and carers”; if so, is she confident that all Government agencies are acting in the best interests of disabled people?
statement: Yes. Prioritising disabled people, their families, and carers is a priority for this Government, and that is why we have provided a record $1.1 billion funding boost to Disability Support Services in last year’s Budget. The state of affairs left by the last Government needed immediate action to stabilise the disability support system. The disability strategy refresh is a key piece of work to improve the lives of disabled people, and I have recently announced the membership of key working groups. These groups will meet for the first time tomorrow and include the disabled community experts from across Government and business. Our Government is focused on improving the lives of disabled New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the immigration Minister's decision to exclude some disabled children of temporary migrants from visas, she says 'Yes, I'm very confident in the Minister of Immigration's decisions.' The plural 'decisions' generalises slightly away from the specific one put to her, but the leading 'Yes' answers the question asked.
question: Does she agree with the immigration Minister’s decision to exclude some disabled children of temporary migrants from being able to get a student or visitor visa?
statement: Yes, I’m very confident in the Minister of Immigration’s decisions.

explanation: Asked what assurances he can give that reforms won't diminish Māori customary gathering or public kai moana gathering. Jones gives exactly that: confirms mātaitai food-gathering rights of tangata whenua will not be diminished and that ordinary New Zealanders' interests won't be undermined. Both limbs of the question are engaged directly; only a small deduction because the assurance is asserted rather than conditioned.
question: What assurances can he provide, if any, that his proposed fisheries reforms will not diminish Māori customary gathering rights or the ability of New Zealanders to gather kai moana to feed their whānau?
statement: I can confirm to the House that the proposed changes that are currently going through the process of consultation will not diminish the mātaitai food-gathering rights of tangata whenua, a feature of the 1992 settlement. Similarly, nothing that is proposed is going to undermine the interests of garden-variety Kiwis, because sustainability will be uppermost in the officials’ minds as they develop proposals.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees taonga species are functionally extinct in many areas, rendering the 1992 settlement assets worthless, and if not why not. The response is not an answer at all — it is a procedural move asking the Speaker to rule the question out of order. The substance (agree/disagree, and the 'why not') is never touched. Small credit only because the response does at least engage with the question's admissibility rather than pivoting to unrelated talking points.
question: Does he agree that under the quota management system (QMS), many taonga species such as tipa—scallops—and koura—crayfish—have become functionally extinct in many areas, leading to the closure of their commercial fisheries and rendering the fisheries settlement assets granted to hapū and iwi in 1992 absolutely worthless; if not, why not?
statement: Point of order. Can I direct the Speaker of the House to educate the member that there are a plethora of Speakers’ rulings—196, 197—that rule that question out of order.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: will he propose compensation for loss of value of fisheries settlements to iwi? Jones recites the 1992 settlement history, stresses it was 'full and final' and that Māori quota is not legally distinctive — which implies no compensation — but he never says yes or no, and closes with a digression about who negotiated it. The implicature is there; the answer is not.
question: OK. Will he propose compensation for loss of value of fisheries settlements to iwi?
statement: The fisheries settlement, otherwise colloquially known as the “Sealord settlement”, was settled in 1992. The full and final settlement enabled Māori to receive quota and participate under a general set of rules governing the conduct of commercial fishing. There is nothing especially distinctive about the quota under the law that the member avers. All quota owners are bound by general legal decisions, a decision that was negotiated by others including Sir Tipene O’Regan; supported by the former All Black, a former member of Southern Māori, Tutekawa Wyllie, when they had a reputable representative.

explanation: Asked whether carrying over uncaught quota would improve sustainability, and if so how. He answers a different question — the state of the decision process ('not signed off permanently', 'still in consultation') — and then attacks the questioner. Declining on grounds of prematurity is partially responsive to why he won't say, but his belief about the sustainability effect, which was what was asked, is never given.
question: Does he believe that allowing fishing companies to carry over uncaught quota from one fishing year to the next fishing year will help improve the sustainability of local fish stocks; if so, how?
statement: Obviously, the member has galloped further than both experience and expertise—those decisions have not been signed off permanently. At this stage, we are still in consultation. So ko tāku ki te mema, tāria te wā. Makere mai koe i tō hōiho. E hoki ki te kōhanga. [I say to the member, wait. Get off your horse. Go back to kindergarten.]

explanation: Asked whether bulk-harvesting kahawai and exporting at under $2/kg is a good economic and social return. He does implicitly concede it is not — 'we need to enhance the value of this valuable stock' — which reaches the core of the question, but he immediately pivots to a rhetorical point about not dictating market prices rather than answering the value judgment squarely. Half engaged, half deflected.
question: Over 300,000 tonnes of fish is commercially harvested from Aotearoa’s oceans every year, and exported at rock-bottom prices—Minister, do you think the bulk harvesting of kahawai, the people’s fish, and exporting them for less than $2 a kilo qualifies as a good economic and social value return for New Zealand’s natural resources?
statement: I’m sure that I speak on behalf of a host of the members of the House who love fishing and realise that we need to enhance the value of this valuable stock. But we are not running a Soviet empire here, where politicians dictate what the market should pay.

explanation: Asked directly whether he is proposing to legalise dumping fish at sea and what the sustainability impact would be. He answers about the 1986 privatisation of commercial access and states the consultation does not contemplate dismembering the quota system — a different proposition entirely — then warns the member about the provenance of his questions. Dumping is never addressed.
question: Ka pai. Are you proposing legalising the dumping of fish at sea, and will this have a negative or positive impact on fish stock sustainability; if so, how?
statement: The access to the commercial fisheries in 1986 was largely privatised, and there are a host of views as to whether or not that system will hold well into the future. At the moment, the proposal that is out for consultation does not contemplate the dismemberment of the quota system—and consultation is still actually under way. But I have to say, as a warning to that member: please do not bring questions that bear a remarkable resemblance as to what LegaSea said to me last Friday.

explanation: Asked for a guarantee that cutting 673 roles won't affect front-line services. Bishop answers directly: no, no Minister can guarantee that, but he has stressed the expectation that front-line delivery not be affected. That is a clear no plus his actual position — the question is squarely met.
question: Can he guarantee that cutting a net 673 roles at Kāinga Ora will not impact any front-line services, including those working with the Ministry of Social Development to place people in public housing?
statement: No Minister can guarantee anything, particularly with regard to operational matters for the Chief Executive of Kāinga Ora, but I have stressed to Kāinga Ora that I expect front-line service delivery to not be affected by the change proposal they are undertaking.

explanation: Asked whether cuts will hit community-engagement and tenant-support staff. He says plainly he does not have the specific detail, offers to supply it in writing, and repeats his general expectation. Not knowing is a direct and complete response to what was asked; it loses a little because he substitutes the broader front-line expectation for the specific category queried.
question: Will his cuts impact staff who work on community engagement and provide support for tenants, including building trust with tenants?
statement: I don’t have the details as to the specific impact on community engagement. You’d need to put that down in writing; I can provide that. As I’ve said, I don’t expect there to be an impact on front-line service delivery for Kāinga Ora.

explanation: A 'why' question about a specific Cabinet decision to remove operating principles, including the fair-and-reasonable-landlord duty. He confirms amendments were agreed and offers one reason — the Act is complicated and confusing and can be simplified — which partly answers the why, but he never engages with the removal of that particular requirement and retreats to 'subject to further decisions'.
question: Why did Cabinet decide to remove the operating principles from the Kāinga Ora—Homes and Communities Act, including the requirement for Kāinga Ora to be a fair and reasonable landlord?
statement: Cabinet has agreed to make some amendments to the Kāinga Ora legislation, but the precise details of that will be worked through as part of our general reorganisation of the housing system. So it’s subject to further decisions. Generally, the Act is complicated and confusing, and our view is that the Act can be simplified.

explanation: Asked what his expectations of Kāinga Ora are on tenant dignity and sustaining tenancies. 'My expectation is that Kāinga Ora follows the law' is curt and minimal, but it states an expectation, which is precisely what was asked. Bluntness is not evasion; it scores high. Slight deduction as it does not touch the tenancy-sustaining limb.
question: What are his expectations of Kāinga Ora to ensure tenants are treated with dignity and supported to sustain their tenancies?
statement: My expectation is that Kāinga Ora follows the law.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his 'back-to-basics' statement and whether warm, dry housing and tenant dignity count as basics. The reply — that he is proud of Kāinga Ora's work — pivots to praise and is cut off before reaching either limb. Neither the stand-by question nor the 'are these basics' question is answered.
question: Does he stand by his statement that making changes to the way Kāinga Ora operates is “in line with a back-to-basics approach”; if so, does he not think that requirements for Kāinga Ora to provide warm, dry, and healthy housing and support tenants to lead lives with dignity are basics?
statement: I’m very proud of the work that Kāinga Ora has undertaken so far as part of the—

explanation: Two limbs: are staff responding positively, and will this hit service quality. He disowns the restructures as the chief executive's, concedes change is challenging for affected staff, and asserts better service delivery is compatible with efficiency — so the quality limb is addressed. Whether staff are responding positively, the actual first question, is never answered.
question: Are staff at Kāinga Ora responding positively to his continuous restructures and cuts, and, if so, does he think this will impact the quality of services provided to some of the most vulnerable people in our communities?
statement: They’re not my restructures; they’re the operational responsibility of the chief executive, and so they are undertaking that. Of course, there will be challenging situations for any staff affected by change proposals in any organisation but, as I’ve just pointed out to the House, it is possible to achieve better service delivery for vulnerable tenants—indeed, all tenants in Kāinga Ora properties—at the same time as focusing on efficiency, and the numbers I’ve just pointed out to the House demonstrate that point very neatly.

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on the housing market; he names a specific report (MBIE rental bond data) and reports its contents. Squarely answers.
question: What reports has he seen on the housing market?
statement: I’ve seen many reports, but yesterday I saw the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment’s rental bond data that shows the median rent for new tenancies is sitting at $600 per week; when this Government took office, the figure was $600 per week. For every month since, except for a minor blip in January, this has remained at $600. In both the Bay of Plenty and Canterbury, rents for new tenancies have actually fallen around 6 percent year on year to February. By way of comparison—just to pick two random dates—from October 2017 to December 2023, median rents for new tenancies across New Zealand rose by $200 per week.

explanation: Asked what reports on the social housing register and emergency housing; he gives register numbers and emergency housing numbers as at specific dates. Directly on point for both halves.
question: What reports has he seen on the social housing register and emergency housing?
statement: As of 31 March this year, there were around 19,000 households on the register; this is 6,000 fewer than when this Government took office, and 1,000 less than last quarter. Housing register numbers are continuing to drop because more applicants are being housed and because Ministry of Social Development front-line staff are more actively following up on whether or not people on the register are in housing need. As for emergency housing, households living in emergency housing motels have reduced by 85 percent under this Government, from over 3,000 in December 2023, to 459 at the end of March.

explanation: Asked what steps the Government has taken to support CHPs; he names two measures (the $150m lending facility and the bank loan guarantee scheme). Direct.
question: What steps has the Government taken to support community housing providers (CHPs)?
statement: It was a big day last month when we announced two measures to reduce the debt-financing barriers for community housing providers. This is something that the sector has long called for—it is complicated, but we have established lending facilities of up to $150 million for the Community Housing Funding Agency to unlock lower-cost finance for CHPs by pooling their financing requirements. This lays the foundation for the agency to borrow billions of dollars and lend at even lower rates for CHPs, supporting not just social housing but also broader affordable housing portfolios. We’re also engaging with banks on a loan guarantee scheme by way of the Minister of Finance. There is quite a lot of appetite for this. This will allow banks to pass on meaningfully reduced interest rates to community housing providers, creating neutrality between Kāinga Ora (KO) and the community housing sector. This Government backs both Kāinga Ora and the community housing sector to house vulnerable New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked what evidence supports removal of the RSE guidelines; she cites and quotes the ERO evaluation and its finding that optional guidelines left too much to chance. Evidence is actually produced, though the closing passage drifts to the replacement curriculum.
question: What evidence, if any, does the Minister have that supports the removal of the relationship and sexuality education guidelines from schools?
statement: The Education Review Office’s recent evaluation found that, and I quote, “While there was widespread support from students and parents for RSE being taught in schools, there is an inconsistency in the RSE teaching and learning that students experience throughout Aotearoa New Zealand. What students are taught, if they are taught it, and when they are taught it can depend on where they go to school.” The Education Review Office (ERO) found that schools find consulting difficult and divisive, and found the optional guidelines like those produced under the previous Government have left too much to chance. This Government is resourcing the sector with a knowledge-rich, year-by-year curriculum that clearly outlines what’s being taught and when, giving teachers certainty and parents clarity on what their children are learning so they can make informed choices about their education.

explanation: A yes/no question — did the ERO report recommend removal? She never says no, but does concede the ground by attributing the recommendation to herself and the coalition agreement. The core is engaged obliquely rather than stated.
question: Was there anything at all in the Education Review Office’s report that recommended the removal of the relationship and sexuality education guidelines from schools?
statement: I already outlined, in my previous answer, the findings of ERO that said that there was huge inconsistency around New Zealand and what students were learning and that many students were missing out on things. It was then my recommendation that we get rid of the RSE curriculum guidelines—also, can I say, in acknowledgment of our agreement with the New Zealand First Party in our coalition agreement to remove those RSE guidelines.

explanation: Asked to reconcile her recommendation with her own report's finding of 87 percent parental support. The 87 percent figure is never touched; she restates that the guidelines are not a curriculum. Gestures at justification without engaging the tension put to her.
question: How does she reconcile her recommendation to remove the relationship and sexuality education guidelines, given her own Education Review Office report found that those very guidelines were supported by 87 percents of parents and whānau?
statement: I’ve already made it very clear, in many answers in this House, including just the other night, that the RSE guidelines are not a curriculum. They are causing confusion. They are meaning that some students are learning some things and some are not. What we do need is a year-by-year, knowledge-rich curriculum document that is required to be taught by schools, which gives clarity to teachers and the ability for parents to pull their children out if they should wish to.

explanation: Two-part question. The first part is answered flatly — 'I always agree with the Deputy Prime Minister.' The second part (reconciling with the evidence) gets a partial answer via the ERO 'left too much to chance' point, though she never engages the 'woke'/'indoctrinate' characterisation itself.
question: Does she agree with the Deputy Prime Minister, who said the guidelines are “woke”, “out of touch”, and “indoctrinate our children”; if so, how does she reconcile these views with the actual evidence that she, as the Minister, was presented with?
statement: I always agree with the Deputy Prime Minister. In this case, it was very clear: the RSE guidelines are not a curriculum; they are a guideline. They are not year by year, they are not knowledge-rich, and they were leaving far too much to chance—as outlined in ERO’s report. We are now replacing those guidelines with a knowledge-rich curriculum that details every single year what will be taught and when to give teachers confidence and parents the knowledge of what their children will be learning if they choose to remove them from those lessons.

explanation: Asked whether that was her reason for not meeting Inside Out; she opens with an unambiguous 'No' and gives a reason. The reason is recycled boilerplate, but the question itself is answered.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Was the reason she chose not to meet with rainbow youth organisation Inside Out because she knows that the removal of the relationship and sexuality education guidelines will put rainbow youth at greater risk of harm?
statement: No, because we are creating, as I’ve already said so many times, a detailed year-by-year, knowledge-rich curriculum which covers all of those topics that parents will know what their children are being taught and when, leaving nothing to chance, unlike the RSE guidelines, which were vague and waffly, were not year by year, and were causing confusion, as outlined in ERO’s report.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made about the Ashburton Bridge; he states the announcement and its specific stages (business case approved, geotech, going to market). Direct.
question: Thank you. What recent announcements has he made about the Ashburton Bridge?
statement: Last week, the Government was very pleased to announce a major milestone that will be great news for locals and for freight in the South Island: the second Ashburton Bridge is ready to move ahead at pace. The business case has been approved, geotechnical investigations will begin soon, and next week, we go to market for technical and design support. This is a fantastic development for Cantabrians, a fantastic development for South Islanders, and for State Highway 1 resilience. As our Government focuses on “Going for Growth”, our work remains on getting essential infrastructure in place so that people can get where they want, when they want, safely and conveniently.

explanation: Asked what benefits the bridge will bring; he enumerates benefits (congestion, safety, delays, reliability, growth). Answers exactly what was asked.
question: What benefits will the second Ashburton Bridge bring?
statement: The benefits of the second Ashburton Bridge are numerous. The 24,000 vehicles using the bridge every day to commute, transport freight, and go about their lives will enjoy reduced congestion, improved road safety, reduced delays, improved reliability in the case of potential closures. It will also accommodate future growth.

explanation: Asked how the bridge supports future growth; he links South Island regional growth and export/tourism to the need for connecting infrastructure. Answers the question, though the growth-scoreboard material sits beside rather than on the link asked about.
question: How is the second Ashburton Bridge important for supporting future growth?
statement: I was pleased to see that in ASB’s recent Quarterly Regional Scoreboard, Otago, Canterbury, Tasman, and Southland were the four strongest-growing regions, all in the South Island. There is so much potential across the South Island, and infrastructure projects—like the second Ashburton Bridge—will be vital to connecting those regions together, and for transporting our goods to market. As we work to double our exports over the next 10 years in places like mining and coal, and see our tourism bounce back, projects like the second Ashburton Bridge are vital to ensuring that New Zealand continues to punch above its weight.

explanation: Asked how the bridge ties in with other Canterbury transport work; he names adjacent road upgrades and lists the other regional projects it sits alongside. Addresses the question asked.
question: How does the second Ashburton Bridge tie in with other transport work in Canterbury?
statement: Upgrades will also be made on the adjacent roads beside the bridge, but beyond that, we are focused on progressing delivery on our roads of national significance and our roads of regional significance. That includes State Highway 1 Belfast to Pegasus and the Woodend Bypass, Mr Doocey; State Highway 76 Brougham Street upgrades, for the members in Christchurch; State Highway 75 Halswell Road improvements, Megan Woods; and State Highway 1 Rolleston access improvements. We are also looking into further improvements for State highways south of Christchurch, including around capacity, resilience, and bridge replacements between the Lyttelton port and Timaru port, along with the role of rail and the potential four-laning of that corridor.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she made on a safety-first approach; she names the announcement (Tuesday, a full scoping review of appropriation measures) and its purpose. Directly and completely on point.
question: What recent announcements has she made regarding a safety-first approach for Oranga Tamariki?
statement: On Tuesday, I announced that I have asked Oranga Tamariki to undertake a full scoping review of all existing appropriation measures to ensure that they are focused on the things that matter most to our most vulnerable children and young people. I was concerned that Oranga Tamariki is currently required to report on and meet targets that take them away from their core purpose, which is the care and protection of children and young people. These children and young people deserve the best possible care and protection system we can provide, and I’m committed to removing any barriers or distractions that prevent them from achieving this.

explanation: Asked why a safety-first approach matters; she gives a reason — that measures/targets pull OT away from child safety, so reviewing them refocuses on what is most important. Somewhat circular ('safety matters because safety comes first') but it engages the 'why' rather than pivoting.
question: Why is it important that Oranga Tamariki takes a safety-first approach?
statement: Since becoming Minister, I’ve made it very clear to Oranga Tamariki that they must always put the safety and wellbeing of children at the forefront of their decision making. This is what I and this Government have consistently reinforced, including just last week, with the repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act. By reviewing all existing measures and targets, we can make sure that Oranga Tamariki is focused on what is most important, which is the safety of children.

explanation: Asked what measures and targets OT currently has; she names one concretely (58 percent of children in out-of-home placement over three months placed with family/whānau). Question squarely answered.
question: What are some of the measures and targets Oranga Tamariki currently have?
statement: Currently, Oranga Tamariki are assessed against a performance measure which states that the percentage of children in out-of-home placement for more than three months who are placed with family or whānau will be at least 58 percent. Of course, if a child or young person is not able to be safe at home, then wider whānau or family should be considered as a potential placement option. However, I’m concerned that having this sort of target as a performance measure for Oranga Tamariki sends a message that the safety of the child does not come first.

explanation: Asked whether there are other targets not focused on children's safety; answers 'Yes' and identifies one (the >23 percent iwi/Māori service contract funding measure). Direct yes plus the requested instance.
question: Are there any other current targets or measures which are not focused on children’s safety?
statement: Yes. Oranga Tamariki currently has a performance measure that the percentage of all service contract funding contracted with iwi and Māori organisations will be greater than 23 percent. These organisations should not just be seen as some sort of quota or tick-box exercise. What should determine the funding is the outcomes for our children. I want to make clear that there are a number of excellent iwi and Māori organisations doing great work within the community. I meet with them all the time in both my portfolios. This is a Government that believes in principles: principles, like focusing on outcomes, not outputs; principles, like safety, should always come first when it comes to our children and young people.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions; answers 'Yes'. One word, complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked why it is acceptable for his own pay to be set by cross-industry comparison when he removed that ability for low-paid women. He denies the premise ('we haven't') and describes what the law change did — engagement with half the question — but never addresses the comparison to his own pay-setting, which is the pivot of the question.
question: Why is it OK for the Prime Minister to have his pay set by an authority that compares his job to different jobs in different industries with different employers when he has removed that ability—under urgency—for low-paid women workers?
statement: Well, we haven’t. This is a Government that continues to support pay equity and eliminating sex-based discrimination. All that we have done is fix the labour law that was unworkable—and also unaffordable—and that compared librarians to fisheries officers.

explanation: A yes/no: is he saying he did not remove, under urgency, the ability to compare across industries? He describes the law as 'more workable, robust and sustainable' and confirms urgency, but never confirms or denies the removal of the comparison ability. The core is left unanswered.
question: Is the Prime Minister saying that he did not remove—under urgency—the ability for those low-paid women workers to compare their jobs to different jobs in different industries with different employers?
statement: Well, what we did was we passed a law to make sure that it was much more workable, robust, and sustainable; that’s what we did last week. We did it under urgency so that we actually have one system, not two systems, and it gives certainty and fairness to everybody.

explanation: Asked why the changes were rushed through on announcement day. He gives an actual reason — a choice between fast and slow, and a lengthy process would leave existing claimants in limbo. He does not address the 'preventing public and expert input' rider, but the 'why rush' core is answered.
question: If we are to believe the Prime Minster when he says that these pay equity changes were not about saving money, why did the Government rush them through on the same day that they were announced, preventing public and expert input and usual, good lawmaking practice?
statement: Well, look, I mean, there’s a couple of choices there: one is you can do it quickly, or you can do it slowly. We felt a lengthy process, for people who have had their claims in the system for a long period of time, was just going to put them into limbo. Importantly, they can now actually resubmit, under the new law, and advance their claims.

explanation: A narrow factual yes/no: did the Government request analysis on the emigration effect? He says he would not conflate the issues and rejects the characterisation — refusing the premise without ever saying whether such analysis was requested. A specific question wholly evaded.
question: Did the Government request any analysis on whether cutting off hundreds of thousands of our lowest-paid working women from pay equity claims would contribute to the record number of New Zealanders who are leaving this country under his administration?
statement: Well, I wouldn’t conflate those two issues, and I reject the characterisation of that question.

explanation: Asked whether he would take up an offer to spend a day working alongside affected women. He neither accepts nor declines, pivoting to a defence of the policy and an accusation of scaremongering. The invitation itself is never engaged.
question: Would the Prime Minister take up the offer of any of the many hard-working women that he has cut off from pay equity claims to spend a day in their shoes changing nappies, delivering babies, or educating young children, or does he plan to ignore them, as he has ignored good lawmaking practice?
statement: I’d just say to that member: we are not cutting off pay equity claims. We are committed to pay equity. Under the new law, individuals and unions can apply for pay equity claims. But it’s wrong to characterise it that way, and I think, in many ways, it’s been very disingenuous from the Opposition, with a lot of scaremongering, about what this is and what this isn’t. We are committed to pay equity, but we are fixing something that was unworkable and unaffordable, to make sure that we don’t have fisheries officers and librarians, and administration workers and civil engineers, all being compared.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions; answers 'Yes'. Complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-part question: did the Minister propose pay equity changes at the start of the term, and if so why were they never publicly mentioned. He effectively confirms the first ('focused on pay equity from day one') but the second, which is the substance, gets a fast-versus-slow rationale and an attack on Labour rather than an explanation of the absence from plans, speeches and announcements.
question: Did workplace relations Minister Brooke van Velden suggest changes to the laws around pay equity right at the start of the Government’s term; if so, why have they never been mentioned in any of his quarterly plans, in any Government Minister’s speeches, or in any public announcements until the law change was introduced last week?
statement: I’m well aware the Minister has been focused on pay equity from day one, and what I would say is that we made a decision. We had a choice: do you do it fast or do you do it slow? We watched Labour do it over three years—introduced the bill under urgency with massive amounts of flaws—and we decided to give people certainty.

explanation: Asked why the 7 April quarterly plan omitted the pay equity decision. Luxon offers a reason of sorts — not wanting to create uncertainty, hence urgency — which engages the 'why' but never addresses the omission from the plan document itself. Partial engagement with the core.
question: Why didn’t the quarterly plan he released on 7 April say anything about the fact that the Government had decided just one week earlier to scrap the existing pay equity process and extinguish all active claims?
statement: Well, we didn’t want to create a situation where there was uncertainty, and that’s why we moved under urgency.

explanation: Asked specifically HOW advance notice of a law change would create uncertainty. The answer restates the same assertion ('we didn't want to signal it, because we don't want uncertainty') without supplying the mechanism asked for. It stays on topic but circles the question rather than reaching it.
question: How would it have created uncertainty to tell people that you were going to change the law before you changed the law?
statement: Well, that’s the point; we didn’t want to signal that we were going to do that, because we don’t want to create uncertainty in the system.

explanation: Asked why Willis said the Government remained committed to pay equity when it had already agreed to explore reducing those obligations. He addresses the premise by asserting the statement was true and consistent, which is a partial response, but never answers the 'why' and pivots to disinformation/scaremongering talking points.
question: Why did Nicola Willis state, on behalf of the Government, in May last year, “The Government remains committed to pay equity and to meeting its obligations under the Equal Pay Act 1972” given the Government had already, at that point, agreed to explore changes to the law to reduce those obligations?
statement: Well, the statement is true, and it’s correct; this is a Government committed to pay equity. It’s a Government that is committed to equal pay and is committed to collective bargaining. I’ve seen a lot of disinformation, misinformation, and scaremongering out there, but we’re committed to pay equity and we’re committed to equal pay.

explanation: Asked why caucus was briefed on 4 May but the public was not told at the post-Cabinet press conference the next day. He answers a related but different question — why the Government moved with speed — and never addresses the disparity in disclosure.
question: Why were National MPs briefed on the changes to the Equal Pay Act on Sunday, 4 May, yet the following day, at his post-Cabinet press conference, he didn’t tell the New Zealand public, leaving them to find out the very same day the Government intended to push the law change through all stages under urgency in Parliament?
statement: Well, I’d just say to the member: there are two choices we had to make. One was that we could move with speed to give people certainty and clarity about the system. The alternative was to take a long time and put people into limbo. We wanted to move with speed.

explanation: Asked why the Government agreed to backdate settlements it had already decided to extinguish, and whether that was good faith. Neither part is engaged; the reply pivots entirely to prepared lines about Labour's unworkable law and librarians versus fisheries officers.
question: Why did the Government agree to backdate pay equity settlements as part of a range of collective employment agreement negotiations over the past year despite having already agreed to repeal the law and extinguish those very same pay equity claims they had agreed to backdate, and is that what his Government regards as good faith?
statement: Well, we have said to you from the beginning—day one—we have been concerned about the pay equity legislation being unworkable. The Minister has had that on her workplan from the beginning. We are making sure we are fixing Labour’s law, which was unworkable, increasingly unaffordable, and when it starts to compare librarians with fisheries officers, and admin workers with civil engineers, there’s a problem.

explanation: A yes/no on whether he was aware of the backdating agreement. He answers directly — 'I am aware of that' — before moving to justification. The core question is squarely answered.
question: Is he telling New Zealanders that, when the Government agreed to extinguish 33 existing pay equity claims, he was not aware that his Government had already agreed to backdate the payment of those claims through collective employment agreement settlements?
statement: I am aware of that, but what I am saying to the member is that we have decided to change and fix the pay equity legislation in this country. Labour rushed it through. Labour left a lot of flaws in it. We are fixing it, because it’s unworkable and unaffordable.

explanation: Asked to adjudicate between his own claim and Seymour's about the Budget motivation. He states the primary motivation was eliminating sex-based discrimination, which implies his own version, but never names who is correct and never addresses Seymour's statement at all.
question: Who is correct: Christopher Luxon when he said the decision to take billions of dollars from working Kiwi women had nothing to do with the Budget, or David Seymour, who said the decision to do so had saved the Budget?
statement: Our primary motivation for the legislation that we passed last week was to make sure that we have pay equity legislation in this country that is focused on the core intention of the legislation, which is to eliminate sex-based discrimination. I can also say that that legislation had a number of flaws, which, I think, if the member was honest about it, he would say that actually he admits there were flaws in that legislation. We are fixing it; that’s what we do in this Government. We fix Labour’s messes, we make sure that it’s workable and affordable, and we make sure that pay equity claims are there for people in the future.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements she made on the fiscal position. She states the announcement directly — the first forecast withdrawal from the Super Fund, its timing and size. Complete and on point.
question: What recent announcements has she made on the Government’s fiscal position?
statement: This morning, I announced that Budget forecasts will show, for the first time, a withdrawal from the New Zealand Superannuation Fund. In recent years, annual contributions to the super fund have been between $1.5 and $2.5 billion a year. We are now approaching the time when the super fund is big enough to ensure that withdrawals, rather than contributions, are the normal outcome each year. This is not a Government decision; it is driven by a formula in the relevant Act. It is something of a milestone event. The first withdrawal is forecast to be in the 2027-2028 fiscal year, a very modest withdrawal of $32 million. This is earlier than previously anticipated, mainly because the super fund’s investment returns have been better than expected.

explanation: Asked what is expected after 2027-28. She answers directly: bouncing between withdrawals and contributions short-term, withdrawals every year from 2031, fund still growing. Squarely answered.
question: What is expected after 2027-28?
statement: In the short term, there will be some bouncing around between withdrawals and contributions, but from 2031 onwards, projections show that withdrawals from the super fund are expected in every year. Withdrawals help cover the costs of New Zealand’s superannuation so taxpayers don’t face the full cost each year. This does not mean that the super fund will get smaller—far from it. The fund currently has $80 billion worth of investments, and on reasonable assumptions, super fund returns will outstrip withdrawals, and the fund will continue to get bigger every year. The Leader of the Opposition says, “Thank you, Labour.” I say, “Thank you, taxpayers.”

explanation: Asked what other announcements she made about the super fund. She names the specific further announcement — diversion of the contribution plus capital allowance into the Elevate NZ Venture Fund. Directly responsive.
question: What other announcements did she make about the super fund?
statement: I also announced that, next year, the $61 million contribution that would ordinarily have been made to the super fund, together with $39 million from the Budget 2025 capital allowance, will go into the Elevate NZ Venture Fund. Diverting super fund contributions to Elevate is not a new approach. The previous Government did the same in Budget 2019. Elevate invests in other venture capital funds alongside the private sector. These funds provide capital to potentially high-growth New Zealand businesses at an early stage in their development. Elevate was established in 2020 and is administered by the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation. It is the Government’s intention that realisations from Elevate’s investments will ultimately be used to fund superannuation.

explanation: Asked the benefits of investing in Elevate. She sets out the claimed benefits — closing the early-stage capital gap, commercialisation, developing a self-sustaining VC market. Answers the question asked.
question: What are the benefits of investing in Elevate?
statement: Innovative businesses begin as start-ups, and those start-ups require investment. That is usually risky, although it potentially has a high pay-off in the future. Few investors have the appetite to invest in firms at this stage of development, and New Zealand’s early-stage capital markets are typically short of funding. Elevate aims to close that funding gap by co-investing alongside private venture capital, resulting in more technologies being commercialised and exported. This is expected to stimulate the development of venture capital in New Zealand so the market eventually becomes self-sustaining, and to support many more start-ups and entrepreneurial ventures to flourish and help grow our economy.

explanation: Two parts: does she stand by the statement (answered 'Yes' outright) and which cancelled claims she thinks are not genuine. On the second she declines plainly, saying it is not hers to judge and identifying who does decide — a direct refusal rather than a dodge, though it leaves the named question unanswered.
question: Fạiȧkse’ea, Mr Speaker. Does she stand by her statement this morning that “we need to keep pay equity claims able to be lodged and able to be progressed where they are claims genuinely based on gender-based discrimination”; if so, which of the 33 cancelled pay equity claims does she not think are genuine, if any?
statement: Yes. In answer to the second part of the question, it is not for me to make a legal judgment to determine which claims are genuine. It is a legal question that will be considered by those negotiating the settlement or, ultimately, the Employment Relations Authority. Under the Act, claims with merit will be progressed.

explanation: Asked whether several billion less in contingency means women receive several billion less. Willis opens with a flat "No" and then explains why (contingency forecasting, not committed payments), and states future settlements are accepted. The core yes/no is squarely answered.
question: If the Government pays several billion dollars less in pay equity payments, does that mean women will receive several billion dollars less?
statement: No. I am grateful for the question because the member misunderstands the nature of contingencies. It is good budgeting practice for the Treasury to forecast potential costs that on the basis of probabilities may occur. Therefore, under the last Government, it was the practice that money was being put in the forecast, not revealed to New Zealanders, allowing for the fact that there could be significant future settlements. Whether or not those settlements would occur, and the size thereof, was still a matter to be determined through negotiations. I’d note that a number of the claims that were in progress had become bogged down due to the lack of clarity in the pay equity regime and the different approaches that employers and employees were taking to negotiating those claims. We now have a clear system, a transparent system, and we fully accept there will be future pay equity settlements.

explanation: Asked how 10 settlements were completed if the system was bogged down. She engages the premise by distinguishing the settled claims (Government as employer, at the table with public sector unions) but never reconciles that with her "bogged down" characterisation, and drifts into who benefited and funding retained. Partial engagement.
question: If the system was so bogged down, how were there 10 equity pay settlements done under the last term?
statement: It is the case that in the first instance, there were a number of claims where the Government was the employer and where the Government was therefore at the negotiating table with public sector unions. Those settlements stand. For the benefit of those opposite who seem to be ignorant of the fact, that has resulted in pay increases for nurses, for social workers, for teacher-aides, for librarians, for a number of women-dominated professions, and our Government has retained every single dollar of funding needed to honour those settlements.

explanation: Asked why she used the phrase "grievance industry". She addresses the remark by reframing what she says she was referring to (claims outside sex-based discrimination), which speaks to the phrase's intent, but never explains or defends the label as applied to advocates, and tails off into a growth-economy talking point.
question: Why did she call advocates for women being paid enough a “grievance industry”?
statement: What I referred to was the fact that the pay equity regime should be used and was intended to be used for settling claims that relate to sex-based discrimination. It is absolutely the case that significant groups of workers in the New Zealand economy—not just those dominated by women, but a number of groups—wish to see their pay increased. We have a number of mechanisms for achieving this. The principal one is through negotiation between employers and employees. It is appropriate that unions and others use those mechanisms to argue for further pay. But here’s the other thing: the best way to ensure that all New Zealanders can look forward to growing wages is to have a strong, growing economy in which employers—

explanation: A pointed yes/no: are Plunket or hospice nurses a grievance industry? No yes or no is given. She restates the test for a valid pay equity claim and lists factors affecting pay, then attacks the premise. Gestures at the topic without reaching the question.
question: Are underpaid Plunket nurses or underpaid hospice nurses a grievance industry?
statement: If groups of workers have had their work undervalued and underpaid as a consequence of gender-based discrimination, then it is appropriate that they make pay equity claims and that their claims be judged according to whether or not there has been sex-based discrimination. It is self-evident that there are a number of issues in an economy which can lead to pay levels. They relate to where people work, the industry in which they work, the qualifications required, the skills required. There are all number of factors that are brought to bear on the pay that people receive. To ignorantly claim it’s all down to pay equity is just wrong.

explanation: Asked why she is downplaying women's concerns to save her Budget. She implicitly rejects the premise and states what she says she is actually doing (correcting claims, upholding protections and settlements), which engages the accusation, but the second half turns on the questioner and onto fiscal-management talking points.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Why is she continuing to downplay the very real concerns of hundreds of thousands of women to save her Budget or, like always, everyone else is wrong but Nicola Willis is right?
statement: I am simply making it clear to those who have been misled by many claims, made in the past few days, that our Government is upholding protections for equal pay in law, that we are upholding pay equity settlements, and that we are both funding and putting in place a good system for resolving future pay equity claims. Beyond that, it is rich for the member opposite to talk about saving Budgets. I’ll tell you, the biggest constraint on this Government’s Budget is this: we believe in responsible fiscal management and don’t believe that simply spending more, taxing more, and borrowing more is the path to economic nirvana. That way lies terror.

explanation: Standard "does he stand by" question answered "Yes." One word, complete and direct.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Two-part: does he stand by three specific decisions, and how does he reconcile them with governing all New Zealanders. He explicitly answers only the first leg ("yes, and for very good reasons") and openly leaves the reconciliation — the substantive half — unanswered.
question: Does the Prime Minister stand by his Government’s decision to disestablish the Māori Health Authority, amend pay equity legislation, and remove Treaty clauses from legislation, and how does he reconcile these decisions with a commitment to governing all New Zealanders?
statement: Well, in part, to the first leg of that question: yes, and for very good reasons.

explanation: Two figures asked for. He gives a number for the first (at least 66,000 employees, with the caveat that records are incomplete) and explicitly declines the cost estimate on public-interest grounds — a stated refusal, which counts as answering. Only the closing lines drift to talking points.
question: How many health workers were part of the 17 funded health pay equity claims discontinued by his Government, and what was the total estimated cost of their outstanding claims?
statement: I’m advised that Health New Zealand does not hold all details about pay equity claims under the previous law. Based on the limited information it does have, Health New Zealand estimates there were at least 66,000 employees covered by claims under the previous law. It would not be in the public interest to disclose estimates relating to the cost of any claims as none of them had been settled. As the member will be aware, our Government is taking a more robust approach to pay equity, ensuring outcomes are fair, backed by evidence, and deliver lasting value for both workers and taxpayers. The right to equal pay remains as it ever was; it is protected in law and will always be, under this Government.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees the nursing settlement improved retention, and what he says to people waiting for community care. He neither agrees nor disagrees and offers nothing to those waiting; he recites the same equal-pay-in-law line and describes the claims process instead.
question: Does he agree that the hospital nursing pay equity settlement significantly improved nurse retention in hospitals, and if so, what does he say to New Zealanders who will wait for care in the community now that his Government abolished the general practice nurses’ pay equity claim?
statement: Well, as I said in my primary answer, the right to equal pay remains as it ever was. It is protected in law and will be under this Government. Those claims are able to be put forward for them to be negotiated and settled. It’s not for Ministers to make any determination as to whether those claims will be agreed. If there is a dispute, then the Employment Relations Authority can make those decisions.

explanation: A narrow factual question: what assurances did he seek about hospice sustainability. He never says what, if any, assurances were sought, repeating verbatim the boilerplate about rights protected in law and the negotiation/ERA pathway.
question: What assurances did he seek that extinguishing the pay equity claim for palliative care nurses would not affect the sustainability of free hospice services, given chief executive Wayne Naylor’s warning that “Dying New Zealanders and their families will fund the difference between the pay for a nurse in hospital and a nurse at a hospice,”?
