This is a Government that’s working incredibly hard and has prioritised economic growth so that we can actually help all families do well in New Zealand. We’re proud of what we’ve got going on here. We have got rid of the wasteful spending. We’ve got inflation down, lowering the cost of living. We have wages growing faster than inflation every quarter of this Government, unlike the previous one.

explanation: Asked to explain how cutting support for households with boarders is consistent with reducing child poverty. He does offer an explanation — fairness, counting all sources of revenue in assessments, fixing an anomaly — so the 'explain' is engaged, though he never connects it back to the child poverty consistency the question hinged on.
question: Can he explain how cutting financial support for around 13,000 low-income households who have boarders, often family, to make ends meet, is consistent with a commitment to reduce child poverty?
statement: Well, it’s all about fairness and making sure that when an assessment’s undertaken to get support from the taxpayers, all sources of revenue are considered in that. That’s an anomaly that we’re fixing.

explanation: Asked a binary choice: will he run the committee on the shortened timeframe Seymour requested, or the six months the House gave? Brewer never states which he will do. He mounts a justification for short submission periods (McGee, two comparator bills), which implies the shortened path, but the choice itself is never declared, and he opens by dismissing the questioner. Gestures at the question without reaching it.
question: Will he call meetings and manage the Finance and Expenditure Committee’s business in accordance with a shortened time frame, as requested by David Seymour; or in accordance with a six-month time frame accorded by this House, given the considerable interest in the Regulatory Standards Bill?
statement: The member can make as many claims as he wants, but he is dancing on the head of a pin. Can I quote that according to McGee’s Parliamentary Practice in New Zealand, “it is not uncommon for bills referred to select committee for four months to have a submissions period of four weeks”. In fact, the Public Works (Critical Infrastructure) Amendment Bill and the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill are both currently being considered by the Transport and Infrastructure Committee for four weeks.

explanation: "Does he stand by all of his Government's statements and actions?" — answered "Yes" in the first word, with elaboration following. Complete and direct.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, in particular our record investment into health services and infrastructure. This Government is investing an extra $7 billion in healthcare so that Kiwis can get better access to elective surgeries, GP appointments, and other critical services that they rely on. We’ve increased prescription repeats to 12 months, which means that people don’t need to go to the doctor with the frequency that they need to, reducing costs for households. We’ve also expanded access to urgent and advanced hours at GP clinics, as well as making cancer drugs freely available to New Zealanders. I’m very proud of the work that we’re doing to give better access to higher quality healthcare in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the housing-record statement; answered "Absolutely" and then defended the record. The yes/no is given squarely. (The counter-facts offered are a veracity/rigor matter, not forthrightness.)
question: Does he stand by his statement “This is a Government that’s incredibly proud of its housing record.” given that homelessness is rising, rough sleeping is increasing, new State house builds have ground to a halt, consents to build new houses are down, and his Government’s cutting support to first-home buyers?
statement: Absolutely. I’m incredibly proud of our record on housing, when I think about the abject failure of the previous Government. If you think about the four components of housing and the outcomes that are achieved, house prices are stable, rents for the first time are actually stable rather than having increased $180 per week. Importantly, the social housing wait-list is down from 27,000 to 19,000 people, and we have moved from over 5,000 households in motels and emergency accommodation down to 400, and that means 2,100 kids out of motels and into proper homes. I’m proud of that record. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked why he is proud given a coincident rise in homelessness. He does answer the "why proud" half — four dimensions, all improved — but never engages the homelessness figures that were the point of the question, and closes with a jab at the questioner. Half the question answered.
question: Why is he proud of the fact that taking people off the social housing register has coincided with a 58 percent rise in homelessness in Auckland and a 40 percent rise in homelessness in Wellington?
statement: Because either way you look at it, on all four dimensions of housing, this Government has done something about it in 18 months and improved outcomes. House prices are stable, rents are stable, the social housing wait-list is down, and we’ve got people out of emergency accommodation and into proper homes. The member should be thankful to the Government for fixing his mess. Just “Thank you.” would be enough.

explanation: A specific yes/no: does he agree with the Christchurch Methodist Mission's account of people turned away without reason? The reply never mentions the Mission or the claim, and pivots entirely to the previous Government's record. A clean dodge with an attack substituted.
question: Does he agree with the Christchurch Methodist Mission that most of the people the mission helps have been turned away from emergency housing without even being given a reason?
statement: I would just say to that member the record of his Government was abysmal on all aspects of housing—talked a big game; did not deliver. We—

explanation: "Does he accept that homelessness is increasing?" is a narrow yes/no. "What I accept is..." substitutes a different proposition and runs through emergency housing, the wait-list, rents and interest rates without ever addressing whether homelessness is rising.
question: Does he accept that homelessness in New Zealand is increasing?
statement: What I accept is that we have taken people out of emergency housing and motel life—which was the plan of the previous Government; just to consign people off to motels. We have got the social housing wait-list down, which is fantastic, we’ve got families in State houses finally, and we’ve got rents stable and we’ve got housing costs stable. Importantly, interest rates are down, and that means if you’ve got a home, you’ve actually got $300 a fortnight back in your pocket, because we’re managing the economy well on this side of the House.

explanation: The identical yes/no is put again and again answered with "What I accept is..." — a list of other housing statistics. The repetition makes the avoidance plainer: the question is never reached.
question: Does he accept that homelessness in New Zealand is increasing?
statement: What I accept is that we’ve got more people into housing, and I think that’s a really good thing. When I think about those people and families who have moved out of motel accommodation into proper homes, we know that 80 percent of those who have come out of emergency housing have actually found houses. The other 20 percent are available to access any of our accommodation support and services, as they wish and as they need to. But isn’t it fantastic: kids are out of motel rooms, the housing wait-list is down, rents are stable, and house prices are stable as well. That’s a good thing. And interest rates are coming down.

explanation: Asked why DV-fleeing women and children are no longer eligible. He rejects the premise outright — "That is not happening. Those services are available." Denying the factual basis is a direct engagement with the question rather than a pivot, though he spends the opening on the questioner and gives no detail. Whether the denial is true is a veracity matter.
question: Why are women and children fleeing domestic violence no longer eligible for emergency accommodation, on the basis that his Government has decided they contributed to their own homelessness, because they had a home and they left it?
statement: Well, again, that’s that member being a little—you know, that’s a mischaracterisation through that question. That is not happening. Those services are available, and that support is available.

explanation: A precise numerical question — how much of the wait-list fall is people housed versus people removed. No number of any kind is given; the reply is a general explanation of the four components of housing. The core is squarely avoided.
question: How many of that reduction in the wait-list is because people were housed, and how many of it was simply because they were taken off the wait-list?
statement: Well, for the benefit of the member, there are four components to housing: if you can’t buy a house, you rent one; if you can’t rent one, you actually go on a social housing wait-list; and if you can’t get one of those, you go into emergency housing. All four aspects are linked together, and that’s what this Government is doing exceptionally well—is dealing with all four components. As a result, we have more flexibility in the homeownership market, we have more flexibility in the rental market, we have more spaces being turned over and available through State housing and community housing providers, and we also have got people out of motels, because we prioritised families with kids from 1 April last year and we put them on to the social housing wait-list, which is fantastic.

explanation: "What recent reports has she seen on the economy?" — names the OECD economic outlook released yesterday and summarises it. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent reports has she seen on the economy?
statement: Yesterday, the OECD released its latest economic outlook publication. This notes that the global outlook is becoming increasingly challenging, with substantial increases in barriers to trade, tighter financial conditions, weaker business and consumer confidence, and heightened policy uncertainty all having adverse effects on growth prospects. It says that the key policy priorities for OECD countries are to ensure a lasting decline in trade tensions, policy uncertainty, and inflation; to establish a credible fiscal path to debt sustainability; and to implement ambitious reforms to strengthen growth prospects and improve competitiveness.

explanation: Asked what the OECD says about fiscal policy; she reports what it says, with quotations. Fully on the question asked.
question: What does the OECD say about fiscal policy?
statement: The OECD, in its latest report, says that restoring fiscal discipline is key for countries to avoid fiscal sustainability problems and build buffers for future shocks. It says that “Given high debt levels and … spending pressures, countries should ensure that public debt is … on a sustainable path”. It goes on to say that “Clear and credible medium-term fiscal plans are needed to show how countries intend to address pressures on public finances.” and specifically recommends countries undertake periodic spending reviews and target their policies. Members should note that these are all features of Budget 2025.

explanation: Asked what the OECD says about policies for investment; she gives the OECD's findings and its policy prescriptions. The Budget 2025 tag-on is self-promotion but comes after the question is answered.
question: What does the OECD say about policies for investment?
statement: The OECD’s report says that “Sluggish investment has lowered growth, productivity, and living standards.” It says that “Weak growth in the capital stock has been an important factor behind the slowdown in potential output per capita growth in many countries”. In its policy prescription, the OECD recommends minimising regulatory barriers to foreign direct investment. It also recommends adopting tax policies that promote stronger business investment, including expanding capital allowances—that is, allowing greater deductions for capital expenditure. Members should note, again, that this was a feature of Budget 2025 with the introduction of Investment Boost.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Eaqub's characterisation or considers it a mischaracterisation. He answers the binary squarely — 'I disagree completely' — then supports it on the housing limb. The ECE and benefit-cut limbs go unaddressed, so not complete, but the core question is engaged head-on.
question: Does he agree with economist Shamubeel Eaqub that this Budget is “anti - young people, anti - poor people and anti - brown people.”, or is this a mischaracterisation of cuts to early childhood education funding, cuts to young people’s benefits, or removing targeted funding for Māori housing?
statement: I disagree completely. As the member talked on housing, I think this is a Government that’s incredibly proud of its housing record. We have house prices stable, we have rents stable, we have taken 7,000 people off the social housing register, and, most importantly, we’ve taken 2,100 kids out of motel emergency accommodation and they’re in great homes with social housing providers and with Kāinga Ora. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her proposed WorkSafe changes and why. She says 'Absolutely' and gives her reason (businesses/workers wanted guidance WorkSafe wouldn't give). Both limbs answered.
question: Does she stand by her proposed changes to WorkSafe; if so, why?
statement: Absolutely—last year, I travelled New Zealand and heard from businesses, workers, and people who deal with health and safety every day who wished for more guidance and help from WorkSafe on how to comply with health and safety legislation, only to be told it’s not WorkSafe’s job. My reforms address this issue.

explanation: A narrow factual question: was she advised of that specific finding in her BIM? She neither confirms nor denies, says she'd have to cast her mind back, then substitutes a different report she prefers to talk about. The specific question is left unanswered.
question: Was she advised in her briefing to the incoming Minister that “organisations inspected by WorkSafe have lower rates of serious ACC claims compared to non-inspected organisations.”?
statement: I’d have to cast my mind back nearly 18 months to all of the briefings that I received when I first arrived, but if I look at one of the briefings that I know I did see, because I still have this one in front of me, this was the Business Leaders’ Health and Safety Forum report, which found that in comparison to another country that we quite often compare ourselves to—Australia—we have far more use of enforceable undertakings than Australia, we’ve had more legal proceedings yet fewer won than Australia, we’ve had far more fines imposed relative to our economic size than Australia, but we don’t have the same proactive relationship. That’s the report that I recall seeing and that’s what I’m focusing on.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her April 2024 statement. 'Of course I do' — direct and complete; the elaboration is additional, not a substitute.
question: Does she stand by her April 2024 statement, “If people know that there’s a possibility for a labour inspectorate agent to come into their place, or the WorkSafe agents to come into their place and inspect whether they are complying with the law, you’ve got both a carrot for compliance and the stick.”?
statement: Of course I do. That’s exactly what’s still happening. We have WorkSafe inspectors going into worksites every day. That’s not stopping; that’s continuing. We’re still having enforcement activity, prosecutions will still happen, and it’s important that we do have that stick. But what we’ve heard time and time again from business owners and workers is that when they’ve been asking for guidance and advice on what they need to do to comply with the law, they haven’t received it. It’s important we have the upfront guidance for people who are asking for it so that WorkSafe is there to help; it’s not just there to harm.

explanation: Asked whether the changes will decrease accident and fatality rates and by how much. She states her intention and the focus on critical risks but never says whether rates will fall, let alone by how much. Themes offered where a prediction and a number were asked for.
question: Will her changes refocusing WorkSafe from an enforcement agency to an advisory agency decrease workplace accident and fatality rates; if so, by how much?
statement: My intention with this policy is worker safety. We want businesses, we want workers, and we want WorkSafe focused on critical risks, the activities that will lead to death and serious injury. We have had far too much focus on tick-box exercises—making sure that people are complying and having a paper trail rather than identifying those critical and serious risks so we can focus on it, we can have guidance for it, and we can make sure that our workers are safe.

explanation: Asked what modelling she commissioned. She never names any modelling, but does effectively convey that none exists ('it's not possible to model every single interaction') and explains why, before pivoting to intention. It reaches the question obliquely rather than stating 'none' outright.
question: What modelling has she commissioned that shows refocusing WorkSafe from an enforcement agency to an advisory agency will decrease workplace injury and fatality rates?
statement: I think the member will be very aware that we are a Government, we are not a business. We set the rules that allow businesses to then follow them, and there are more things that happen in a business than just the rule that the Government sets. You’ve got the health and safety; you’ve got the Holidays Act; you’ve got so much red-tape regulation imposed by Government; you’ve got individual contributions; you’ve got managers, workers, individual workplace relationships. It’s not possible to model every single interaction that workers and businesses have on a shop floor. But what we can say with confidence is that our intention is that we will see a decrease in deaths and a decrease in serious injury because we are asking business owners, workers, and WorkSafe to focus on reductions of critical risks.

explanation: Asked a specific yes/no: does she still expect at least 2,200 interventions a year? She blames the previous Government for performance measures and describes refocusing WorkSafe, never engaging the 2,200 figure or the expectation.
question: Does she still expect WorkSafe to undertake at least 2,200 interventions a year to ensure minimum compliance with employment standards, as they were required to do under now removed performance measures?
statement: The previous Government removed and changed performance measures within WorkSafe. We have not seen good accountability of WorkSafe for years. We, as a Government, are refocusing WorkSafe’s efforts so we know where the money is going, we know that it’s being spent on guidance documents for businesses and workers who are struggling to know how to follow the rules. It needs to be easier, but we’re also asking them to enforce the law too. You can have both the carrot and stick.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on social housing tenancies. He identifies the direction to Kāinga Ora on the Sustaining Tenancies Framework and abusive tenants, with termination figures. Squarely responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made about social housing tenancies?
statement: Talofa lava e te Māngai o te Whare. In March 2024, the Government directed Kāinga Ora to remove the Sustaining Tenancies Framework and take firm action against abusive Kāinga Ora tenants. Over the past 12 months to April 2025, 63 tenancies have been terminated for disruptive and abusive behaviour—a significant increase on the previous 12 months, which saw 11 tenancies terminated; and two the year before, 2022-23. This is highlighting improvements in Kāinga Ora tenancy management as a result of firmer and faster action being taken.

explanation: Asked how the improvements were achieved. He gives the mechanism — a 600 percent increase in formal notices under the RTA and the three-notice pathway to the Tenancy Tribunal. Directly on the question.
question: How have these improvements been achieved?
statement: Under the previous Sustaining Tenancies Framework, disruptive and abusive behaviour in taxpayer-subsidised Kāinga Ora homes had little formal response from Kāinga Ora, resulting in some communities living in angst and in fear. Kāinga Ora has increased their use of formal notices under the Residential Tenancies Act by 600 percent on last year’s activity, with 1,463 being issued in this financial year. Where tenants receive three formal notices, Kāinga Ora can apply to the Tenancy Tribunal to end the tenancy. Only 2 percent of notices issued in the past 10 months have been third notices, signalling that the change of approach is working.

explanation: Asked what impact this is having on communities. He asserts the approach 'ultimately benefits everyone' and gestures at freed-up housing for those on the register, but much of the answer restates policy stance rather than describing community impact. Partially answers.
question: What impact is this having on communities?
statement: We believe in strong whānau and strong communities. The vast majority of the tenants across the 76,000 Kāinga Ora homes are neither disruptive nor abusive. The approach this Government is taking ultimately benefits everyone involved by recalibrating negative behaviour through formal warnings and following through with real consequences in the rare circumstances that tenants’ behaviour doesn’t improve. This Government will not tolerate disruptive or abusive behaviour in Kāinga Ora housing, and there are many, many whānau on the social housing register that are willing to move into such housing if vacated.

explanation: Asked what supports exist for tenants warned or evicted. He lists transitional housing, Housing First, rapid rehousing, housing support products, relocation and referral to alternative providers. Directly answers the question asked.
question: What supports are in place for tenants who receive formal warnings or have their tenancies terminated?
statement: There are many support services—transitional housing, Housing First, rapid rehousing, housing support products—that provide financial assistance and tautoko, including rent and bond support. Kāinga Ora uses relocation to another neighbourhood as a tool to incentivise tenants to change their behaviour, unless the behaviour is very severe. If the tenancy is terminated and another home is not offered, Kāinga Ora often seeks to help them move on by referring tenants to an alternative provider and support service. Where such whānau have significant vulnerabilities, Kāinga Ora will try to work with providers and support services to secure accommodation before ending the tenancy.

explanation: Asked why he set a four-week submission deadline against a six-month report-back. He gives the reason: the Minister's 23 May letter correcting his first-reading date to 23 September, on which the chair based his four-week decision. Squarely responsive.
question: Why did he respond to the referral by the House to the Finance and Expenditure Committee of the Regulatory Standards Bill with a six-month reporting deadline by issuing a call for submissions with a four-week deadline?
statement: I received a letter as Finance and Expenditure Committee chair from the Minister for Regulation on 23 May stating that he had misspoken on his intended report back during the first reading on 22 May, when he stated, “I intend to move that the bill be reported to the House by 23 December.”, when he in fact meant to say 23 September. Taking the Minister at his word, my decision, which I’m empowered to make as chair, was to open submissions for four weeks from 26 May. Submissions will close on 23 June.

explanation: Asked what school-property announcements were made in Budget 2025; she names the announcements directly ($460m, new schools/classrooms, 8,000 places, cost per classroom). Squarely answered.
question: What announcements has she made regarding school property as part of Budget 2025?
statement: Budget 2025 invests in delivering classrooms and schools that our students need to flourish. This Government has invested over $460 million to deliver new schools and classrooms, creating over 8,000 additional student places. We’ve also dramatically increased the efficiency with which we deliver the school property, so we get more bang for our buck. When you remove bespoke legacy projects from the most recent quarter, I’m delighted that we have nearly halved the cost of delivering a classroom from $1.2 million down to $626,000. Standardised and repeatable designs are efficient, effective, and mean more students get what they need to succeed.

explanation: Asked what was announced for Selwyn; she names the Selwyn growth plan items — Prebbleton primary, Lincoln land purchase, 52 classrooms. Directly on the question asked.
question: What announcements has she made for school property in Selwyn?
statement: Population data shows that Selwyn is one of the fastest growing areas in New Zealand with a 23 percent increase in student numbers between 2020 and 2024. In response, the Selwyn growth plan is delivering a new primary school in Prebbleton, purchase of land for a new primary school in Lincoln, and an additional 52 classrooms across five existing schools. As a Government we are delivering for the people of Selwyn and can I congratulate the member for her advocacy for the area.

explanation: Asked about the wider Canterbury region; she names Halswell primary, 51 additional classrooms, 2,500 student places. The closing rhetoric doesn't displace the answer.
question: What announcements has she made for school property in the wider Canterbury region?
statement: Well, to meet growing student population in the wider Christchurch region, we’ve also committed to delivering a new primary school in Halswell, an additional 51 classrooms to existing schools. This investment will deliver 2,500 student places in the region’s school network. Our children deserve a world-leading education that starts with a warm, safe, dry classroom. Through Budget 2025, we are delivering more classrooms more efficiently at a lower cost. This is a Government of delivery and we are delivering for the people of Christchurch.

explanation: Asked what else was announced; she supplies further distinct items ($90m learning-support classrooms, 300 property modifications, 50 Māori-medium classrooms). Directly responsive.
question: What else has she announced regarding school property?
statement: Budget 2025 ring-fences $90 million for around 25 satellite learning support classrooms and over 300 property modifications to ensure our schools are accessible and inclusive of students with additional needs. We’re also funding 50 new classrooms for Māori medium and kura kaupapa Māori education, increasing access to Māori immersion schooling for approximately 1,100 children. Budget 2025 delivers more classrooms at a far more affordable rate. This is what delivery looks like.

explanation: Asked if she stands by her statements and actions on pay equity; answers 'Yes' with the standard 'in the context in which they were made' qualifier. A direct yes, lightly hedged.
question: Does she stand by all her statements and actions in relation to pay equity in the education sector?
statement: Yes, in the context in which they were made.

explanation: Asked what advice she SOUGHT from the Ministry; she answers what advice she RECEIVED in May. Adjacent but a different question — as the questioner's immediate follow-up makes explicit. The 'seeking' side is never touched.
question: What advice, if any, did she seek from the Ministry of Education on the impact of the changes to the pay equity regime on the education workforce?
statement: I’ve answered this in a previous question time where I told the member that I received some advice in May around the effect that this would have on the teaching workforce.

explanation: Pressed again on what advice she sought; she says she doesn't have it in front of her without notice — a direct statement of inability, which is responsive — but then repeats the same 'I received information in May' non-answer rather than addressing what she requested.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. My question was what advice did she ask for, not what had the ministry given her. What advice did she seek from the ministry, was my question.
statement: Without putting the question on notice, I don’t have it in front of me, so all I can say is that I know that I received some information in May regarding the impact on teachers of the pay equity decision.

explanation: Asked what recent reports he has seen; he begins naming one (the Privacy Commission report released that morning) before being cut off by interruption. What exists is squarely on the question, but the answer is truncated mid-sentence.
question: What recent reports has he seen about tools to reduce retail crime?
statement: This morning, the Privacy Commission released its report into—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked why new tools are needed; he gives the rationale directly — 85% rise in retail crime, 91% theft victimisations, worker safety. Answers the 'why'.
question: Why do we need new tools to deal with retail crime?
statement: Between 2019 and 2023, retail crime increased by 85 percent, including a 91 percent increase in the victimisations relating to theft. The men and women working in retail need to feel safe in their workplace, and New Zealanders want to see law and order in our communities. We’re making good progress on that, such as seeing ram raids drop by more than 60 percent in 2024, but we need to go further. This Government is on the side of the retailers and their customers, not on the side of the criminals.

explanation: Asked what feedback he has seen from retailers on the report; he quotes Foodstuffs North Island's welcome of it. Directly answers the question asked.
question: What feedback has he seen from retailers on the Privacy Commission report?
statement: Foodstuffs North Island have welcomed the report, stating, “Our people continue to be assaulted, threatened, and verbally abused, and we’re committed to doing all we can to create safer retail environments.” Our Government supports the findings of the report and the use of facial recognition technology, but we still need to go further. I’ll be tasking the ministerial advisory group on retail crime to consider the report and see what else we can do in the area. We want to give the retailers the tools that they need to keep their customers and their workers safe.

explanation: Asked what other tools are under consideration; he names citizen's arrest rule changes and trespass legislation recommendations, though he also drifts into measures already taken (sentencing) and a vague 'exploring further measures'. Core largely reached.
question: What other tools is the Government considering to reduce retail crime?
statement: The Government is serious about reducing retail crime. The ministerial advisory group on retail crimes made recommendations to strengthen and clarify the rules in relation to the citizen’s arrest, with more recommendations to strengthen trespass legislation. We’ve tightened up the sentencing laws to make sure offenders face consequences for crimes, and we’re committed to exploring further measures to support retailers and victims.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions; answers 'Yes' and then elaborates. The elaboration is a talking point, but the question itself was answered outright.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes, and particularly our Budget 2025 investment into improving our justice system and keeping New Zealanders safe, because this Government understands that we can’t have a prosperous, functional society unless criminals face real consequences for wreaking havoc on communities. That’s why we’ve invested $472 million in corrections and $246 million into our court system to clear the backlog of cases. We’re cracking down on gangs, we’re tackling youth offending and retail crime, and we’re getting more officers out there on the beat.

explanation: Asked what the OECD says specifically about New Zealand; the answer quotes the NZ chapter directly (expenditure reduction programme, Investment Boost) before adding a self-congratulatory coda. The core question is squarely engaged.
question: What does the OECD say specifically about New Zealand?
statement: The New Zealand chapter of the report says that Budget 2025 “continues the programme of reducing expenditure as a share of GDP” and recommends the Government fully pursues this programme. It notes that the Government “took an important step to address the economy’s low capital intensity by introducing … ‘Investment Boost’, which allows firms to immediately deduct 20% of the value of a new asset from their taxable income on top of normal depreciation.” The Government’s fiscal strategy and the policies in the Budget to target assistance, review spending, restore fiscal discipline, and ensure public debt is on a sustainable path are good, sensible economic policies as recommended by external experts such as those in the OECD.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions; answered 'Yes' plus elaboration. Complete.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes, and especially our nearly $7 billion investment in infrastructure, which will go towards upgrading and building new hospitals, mental health facilities, classrooms, rail, and roads across the country. And our infrastructure investments will make it easier for Kiwis to get on with their daily lives, create jobs and opportunities, and ultimately contribute to a growing and productive economy.

explanation: Asked (a) whether he supports the 99.5% bots claim and (b) for evidence. He notes the Minister 'clarified' and meant form submissions — a glancing engagement that implies non-endorsement — then pivots to the bill's purpose. Neither support nor evidence is stated.
question: Does he support his Deputy Prime Minister’s claim that 99.5 percent of the submissions on the Regulatory Standards Bill were fake and driven by bots, and, if so, can he provide evidence for this?
statement: Well, I think the Minister has clarified his comments and said he also meant that that was about form submissions. But what I’d say is the purpose of this legislation is to make sure we make better quality rules and regulation so that it’s not a drag on productivity, so that we can grow the economy faster.

explanation: Asked whether he supports the 'meaningful consultation effectively requires you to be racist' statement. The answer talks about pre-consultation and the select committee process and never touches the statement at all.
question: Does he support his Deputy Prime Minister’s statement regarding the Crown’s failure to consult with Māori on the Regulatory Standards Bill that “meaningful consultation effectively requires you to be racist”?
statement: Well, what I’d say is that there has been good pre-consultation from the Ministry for Regulation around this bill over the summer period and there’s a four-week select committee process. I’d just say to all people who want to contribute to that bill to make it better legislation: feel free to contribute through the select committee process.

explanation: A sharp either/or — Ministry of Justice or the bill's author on the Treaty. The reply is a generic invitation to make select committee submissions; neither limb of the choice is addressed.
question: Does he agree with the Ministry of Justice that “the omission of the Treaty” from the Regulatory Standards Bill “does not recognise the constitutional significance of the Treaty … nor the Crown’s duty to acknowledge the rights and interests of Māori in the development of [policy]”, or does he agree with the man who wrote the bill that there is “absolutely no reason” to consider the Treaty when making law?
statement: As I’ve said before, I would encourage Māori, non-Māori, anybody who wants to strengthen this bill to contribute through the select committee process.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts the Waitangi Tribunal's finding. The answer recites process (pre-consultation, first reading, select committee) and never says accept or reject.
question: Does he accept the Waitangi Tribunal’s finding that excluding Te Tiriti from the Regulatory Standards Bill and its principles risks erasing pre-existing Māori rights in the same way the Treaty principles did?
statement: I’d just say to the member: we’ve had a pre-consultation period, we’ve had a first reading, we’ve got a select committee process before a bill comes back to this House. It’s important in that select committee process, given the devil will be in the detail of the implementation of this bill, that people have their say and make a contribution through the select committee process.

explanation: Asked to explain why he was 'comfortable' with the Minister's remark. He half-distances (Minister should have kept his opinions to himself) and then offers something that functions as an explanation — tastes in music differ, he gets grief for liking country. It reaches at the question obliquely but never explains his own stated comfort.
question: Can he explain why he said he was “comfortable” with a senior Cabinet Minister publicly calling a performance celebrating te ao Māori and Te Tiriti o Waitangi “a load of crap”, as Chris Bishop did during the Aotearoa Music Awards?
statement: Well, I think the Minister has said that he probably, in hindsight, should have kept his opinions to himself. But, as that member will know, there are lots of different tastes in music. As I’ve said publicly, I quite like country music, but a lot of people give me grief for that too and use similar language that Chris Bishop has used.

explanation: Asked whether she stands by all her statements and actions; 'In context, yes' is a direct yes with a qualifier. Answered.
question: Fa‘afetai lava lau afioga le Fofoga Fetalai. Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: In context, yes.

explanation: Asked how valuing care workers aligns with cancelling their pay equity claim. She does supply a reconciliation — the new regime lets meritorious claims be raised and settled — which addresses the alignment question, but never engages the specific cancellation and restart the question named.
question: How does her statement of valuing the work of care and support workers like Rosie Thompson align with her actions of cancelling their active pay equity claim and requiring care and support workers to start their claim again?
statement: Because we have ensured that there is a workable, sustainable pay equity regime in law that will allow claims with merit to be raised and, where appropriate, settled.

explanation: Asked for an assurance that collective bargaining will remedy gender pay inequity given some sectors are now excluded. The answer restates what the pay equity regime permits, says nothing about collective bargaining or the excluded sectors, and gives no assurance either way.
question: Can she assure working women that collective bargaining will remedy pay inequities based on gender, given some sectors such as secondary school teachers can no longer apply for a pay equity claim under the new legislation?
statement: As per the law, where claims are able to be made under the pay equity regime which demonstrate that workers have been undervalued and underpaid as a result of sex-based discrimination, they are able to raise and progress pay equity claims.

explanation: Asked what she says to a named worker; she says it — 'we value you and we value the work of all New Zealanders.' A direct response to the question posed, whatever its adequacy.
question: What does she say to Connie Buchanan, a care and support worker, who says, “We don’t have a chance trying to do it ourselves and negotiating with them. We’re women, we’re Māori and Pacific women, women from our migrant communities, Indians and Filipinas. And it’s like they don’t value us.”?
statement: I would say, quite simply: we value you and we value the work of all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked how her statements align with three specific actions (33 cancelled claims, the $12.8b contingency, teacher exclusion). She engages one item obliquely (the $12.8b is 'explained in Budget documents'), cites the nurses' settlement, then attacks the Opposition leader. The alignment question and two of the three items go unaddressed.
question: How do her statements of valuing the work of women care and support workers, midwives, nurses, and teachers align with her actions of cancelling 33 active claims, stripping $12.8 billion contingency for pay equity for her Budget, and making it impossible for some sectors like secondary school teachers to make a pay equity claim?
statement: Well, I point out that nurses have received a pay equity settlement, which we are upholding and continuing to fund. I’d also point out that the $12.8 billion figure that the member refers to is explained in Budget documents, and she might like to point that out to her leader, who today said that it’s an awfully big number that he doesn’t understand.

explanation: Asked to rule out a 'no additional warming' approach. He engages only the tail clause about the scientists' letter (dismissing it), then pivots entirely to farmer talking points. Never says whether he will or won't rule the approach out.
question: Will the Prime Minister rule out his Government pursuing a “no additional warming” approach to agricultural climate-changing gases, as 26 world-renowned scientists implored in an open letter to him just this week?
statement: Well, in answer to the last part of the question, I’d just say to the people that kindly wrote the letter to me that they should write it to 194 other countries before they send me a letter, and then I might read it. I just want that member to understand that New Zealand’s farmers are the very best in the world. They are the number one most carbon-efficient in the world. If you want to lower global greenhouse gas emissions, you would do more farming in New Zealand and less in other countries, and I think our farmers deserve tremendous praise because they are the bedrock of this economy. They’re doing an exceptionally good job of hauling us out of recession, and we ain’t going to shut down farming and send production overseas. We’re backing our farmers. They’re the best in the world. They’re the most carbon-efficient, and if they’d sent it to 194 other leaders before they’d sent it to me, then I might read it.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of the specific trade-off (other sectors carry more, or ambition drops and agreements are breached). The answer never touches the trade-off at all — it repeats the carbon-efficiency/production line. Different question answered.
question: Is the Prime Minister aware that adopting a “no additional warming” approach for agricultural gases would mean either requiring every other sector of the economy to carry a far higher burden to reduce emissions, or reducing our climate ambition and, therefore, breaching international trade and climate agreements?
statement: I would just say to the member—and I want everybody in this country to understand this—New Zealand farmers are the best in the world and they are the most carbon-efficient. So if you shut down farming in New Zealand and you move it to any other country on earth—any of the 194 other countries—global greenhouse gas emissions get worse. We have outstanding farmers. We have outstanding science and technology and innovation coming our way. We can be more productive. We can actually deliver our lower domestic and global emissions by embracing technology and actually increasing production.

explanation: Pressed on whether he would heed the international call. 'No—I said no.' is a complete, unambiguous answer to the clarified question. Blunt but squarely responsive.
question: Sorry, my first question was explicitly about whether he would heed the call from international—
statement: No—I said no.

explanation: Asked for a commitment to follow the Climate Change Commission's recommendation not to weaken the 2050 target. He notes advice has been received and defers ('more to say shortly'), then returns to farming talking points. No commitment given or refused.
question: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Will the Prime Minister commit, then, to following the recommendation of the independent, expert Climate Change Commission that—and I quote—there is “no evidence to support weakening the [2050] target, and enough to consider strengthening [it].”?
statement: Well, I’d just say to the member—and I think it’s well understood—we have had advice from the climate commission and we’ve had advice independently from our own independent work on methane targets. We’ll have more to say about that shortly, but I want to be very clear: we have the most carbon-efficient farmers in the world. You know, if you wanted to lower global greenhouse gas emissions, you would produce more in New Zealand and less in less carbon-efficient countries—it’s that simple. We ain’t shutting down farming in New Zealand. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he had sought assurances that the next emissions budget is on track, given two named risks. He answers the substantive core ('we remain on track') but not whether assurances were sought, and ignores the carbon-capture and waste-funding elements.
question: Has the Prime Minister sought any assurances from his climate or finance Ministers that we are still on track to meet our next emissions budget, given that a third of it relies on carbon-capture technology that the industry says is economically unfeasible, and another third on waste minimisation that his recent Budget cut funding to?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, we remain on track. We are back on track.

explanation: Asked what recent regional events funding announcement she had made; she states the announcement, the amount, the number of events and the fund it came from. Directly and completely answers.
question: What recent announcement has she made about regional events funding?
statement: This Government is driving economic growth in the regions by investing $2.6 million in over 150 regional events. I’m thrilled with the variety of exciting events on offer, encouraging more New Zealanders to enjoy and explore our beautiful country beyond the main centres. Events are excellent drawcards to get more visitors into our regions, particularly in quieter parts of the year, for the tourism and hospitality sector. This funding comes from the $5 million Regional Events Promotion Fund. Over the two rounds, the fund has invested in 284 regional events.

explanation: Asked how the funding supports tourism in Whanganui; she names the specific Whanganui events funded and the expected local economic effect. Squarely on the question asked.
question: How does this support regional tourism in the Whanganui region?
statement: This funding boost will support a wide range of events across Whanganui. The member will be particularly interested in the funding to the Whanganui Vintage Weekend, the Whanganui Suzuki Series, and the Cooks Classic athletic event. It’s great to continue to support this event and encourage many more visitors to that region. It will boost Whanganui’s local economy to create and support employment across the region.

explanation: Asked a binary — will the 13,200 affected households be better or worse off. She disputes the premise ('no change to the accommodation supplement', 'most people will not be impacted'), which engages the question obliquely, but never answers better or worse for those households.
question: Will the 13,200 low-income households who will have their housing assistance reduced due to the Government’s changes to the calculation of housing subsidies be better or worse off as a result?
statement: There has been no change to the accommodation supplement or public housing subsidy payments. The recent changes to boarders and income-related rent are based on common sense and fairness when accessing the appropriate accommodation support. Most people who receive housing subsidies will not be impacted by these changes. The system must be fair to taxpayers as well as those who are receiving housing assistance. The recent changes ensure that all housing income is taken into account when calculating housing assistance.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned by her ministry's warnings of increased hardship. 'No, because...' — an explicit answer to the yes/no put to her, with her reason. Responsive regardless of the reason's merit.
question: Is she concerned that her ministry warned her that the changes to the eligibility in the accommodation supplement will risk “increased hardship”, “further cost pressures for vulnerable households” and “increasing need for other hardship assistance”?
statement: No, because Budget 2024 was all about reducing the cost of living crisis, and what we do know is that those households who have the lowest incomes are the most harshly affected by the cost of living crisis, which is why we needed to make changes to this regime, to ensure that we alleviated pressure for low-income households.

explanation: Asked how leaving households worse off helps with the cost of living. She gives a rationale for the change (cutting spending, ending 'double-dipping') rather than explaining the cost-of-living benefit to those households; it circles the question without landing on it.
question: How does leaving 13,200 low-income households worse off as a result of the changes to the accommodation supplement eligibility by up to hundreds of dollars a week help with the cost of living?
statement: Because, as I said, Budget 2024 was about addressing the cost of living pressures. Job number one was to reduce Government spending, and this initiative addressed an area that most New Zealanders would have expected wasn’t happening. If you were a boarder paying board in a household, you could get the accommodation supplement. In the same household, if you were collecting board from multiple people, you would also get the accommodation supplement. That is double-dipping. That is exactly the kind of Government spending that we need to reduce.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees that losing $100 a week could mean someone cannot put food on the table. She neither agrees nor disagrees, restating the fairness-to-taxpayers line instead. The core proposition is left untouched.
question: Does she agree that, for someone living in poverty, losing $100 a week as a result of these changes could mean they can’t put food on the table?
statement: I’m not sure if I can say it any more plainly, but where we have accommodation assistance, it must take into account all housing income. That is fair and equitable to taxpayers as well as making common sense to those who are receiving housing assistance.

explanation: Asked what the Government is doing to improve mental health and wellbeing. The attributed response is not an answer at all — it is a further question ("How is the Government growing the mental health workforce?") from the same speaker, Leavasa, i.e. a pairing defect. Nothing in the response text engages the question, so on the pair as given the question is wholly unaddressed.
question: What is the Government doing to improve the mental health and wellbeing of New Zealanders?
statement: How is the Government growing the mental health workforce?

explanation: A narrow, quantitative question: the total investment value of Investor 1 and 2 applications with INZ and how it compares to unweighted Active Investor Plus value. The response supplies no figure and no comparison; it is another question from McDowall himself (about $1.5b withdrawn and follow-up work), again a same-speaker pairing artifact. A precise factual ask left entirely unanswered.
question: What is the total investment value of all Investor 1 and 2 applications that are currently with Immigration New Zealand, if any, and how does that figure compare to the total unweighted investment value of Active Investor Plus visa applications?
statement: Is he aware that under Labour, over $1.5 billion worth of investment has been withdrawn by people who gave up waiting for Immigration New Zealand to process their Investor 1 and 2 applications, and, if so, what work, if any, is being done to follow up on those people to try to get them back under the new regime?

explanation: A simple yes/no: does he stand by his statements and actions since the Auckland flooding and Cyclone Gabrielle. The response never says yes or no — it is Penk's own follow-up quoting the Canterbury earthquake timeline. Same-speaker artifact; the binary question is untouched.
question: Does he stand by all of his statements and actions in the six months since the Auckland Anniversary weekend flooding events and in the wake of Cyclone Gabrielle?
statement: Does he stand by his statement, then, “It’s worth noting that, after the Canterbury earthquakes, it was four months before decisions were taken on the future of affected areas. We want to move quicker than that.” given that it has now been six months since the initial flooding events?

explanation: Asked for two specific figures from the MBIE bond database: current nationwide median rent and the increase since October 2017. The response gives neither; it is Bishop's own follow-up about a "war on landlords". Same-speaker artifact, and the two requested numbers are never provided.
question: What is the current nationwide median rent according to the MBIE rental bond database, and what has been the increase in the nationwide median rent according to the MBIE rental bond database since October 2017?
statement: Does she accept that the Government’s war on landlords is hurting tenants by driving rents to record highs, and how can she defend a nationwide rent increase of $170 a week in the last six years?

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Twyford's "over-invested in roads" statement, and if not why not. No agreement or disagreement is expressed; the response is Brown's own follow-up about cancelled and re-announced road projects. Same-speaker artifact, question unengaged.
question: Does he agree with the former Minister of Transport Hon Phil Twyford’s statement that New Zealand has “over-invested in roads”; if not, why not?
statement: Did the Government cancel the Cambridge to Piarere motorway upgrade and the Woodend bypass projects because New Zealand had “over-invested in roads”, and what exactly has changed since then for the Government to suddenly re-announce these two cancelled roads?

explanation: Asked what reports he has seen on the New Zealand economy. Robertson's attributed response is only the fragment "Mr Speaker—" — an interrupted opening that names no report and conveys no substance. Whatever the cause (interjection or truncation), the question as paired receives no answer.
question: What reports has he seen on the New Zealand economy?
statement: Mr Speaker—

explanation: Asked whether she stands by her statement on dental care affordability and, if so, whether she has confidence people can access dental grants. Neither limb is addressed; the response is Menéndez March's own further question about unmet need and the 40/50 percent figures. Same-speaker artifact, so the standing-by question and the confidence question both go unanswered.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “Dental care is something that can be put off due to affordability difficulties, especially for low-income households. We know that issues with dental health have a negative impact on people’s general health, financial health, ability to work, and quality of life”; if so, does she have confidence people unable to afford dental care can access dental grants?
statement: Does she think Ministry of Social Development (MSD) dental grants are meeting the level of unmet need for dental care amongst low-income households; and if so, why are 40 percent of adults and 50 percent of Māori still unable to afford dental care?

explanation: A plain question: is she satisfied with Kāinga Ora's performance. No satisfaction or dissatisfaction is stated; the response is Bishop's own supplementary about the composition of the 15,000 figure. Same-speaker artifact; the question asked is not the question responded to.
question: Is she satisfied with the performance of Kāinga Ora?
statement: Is he aware that within the 15,000 figure he skites about, that includes 4,900 State homes sold or demolished under this Government and 4,000 redirects, which are the private rental market being leased by Kāinga Ora or other community housing providers to house people in need, and are not net new houses?

explanation: The 'question' is really an interjection — 'get used to it; you're the Minister of Energy.' Brown picks the interjection up verbatim and engages it head-on ('we are getting used to it, because...'), spelling out what he says getting used to it means (heaters off, EVs uncharged) and attributing it to the oil and gas exploration ban. Whatever one thinks of the reasoning or the blame-shifting, the challenge put to him is the thing he responds to, not a substitute topic. Marked down slightly because the barb was too unspecific to have a squarely-answerable core.
question: Well, get used to it; you’re the Minister of Energy.
statement: —shortage in energy—and the member over there says, “get used to it”. Well, we are getting used to it, because as Transpower show [Holds up graph] since 2018, when the last Government cancelled oil and gas exploration, the number of low residual notices has increased significantly from zero under the last National Government. So getting used to it means turning the heaters off, means not being able to charge your electric vehicles, which means that is the risk that they are facing because of that Government’s policies.

explanation: Woods interjects 'Two years' — a challenge on consenting timeframes. Bishop takes up that exact point ('that member neglects all of the preparatory work that goes into actually preparing a resource consent') and stays on the timeline question, quoting Contact Energy on consenting cost and duration. He engages the substance of the interjection rather than pivoting, though he declines to address the specific historical instance ('without litigating something that happened in the early 2000s'), which leaves part of the implied challenge untouched.
question: Two years.
statement: —that member neglects—yes, but the member neglects all of the preparatory work that goes into actually preparing a resource consent because of the strictures of the Resource Management Act. I just point the member, further—without litigating something that happened in the early 2000s, I would just point the member to the comments from almost every major electricity generator in the last couple of years when it comes to the Resource Management Act. I quote Contact Energy, for example: the single biggest barrier to the decarbonisation of the New Zealand economy is our planning system—which is the Resource Management Act. It costs too much and takes too long to get consent to build renewables.

explanation: A clear, narrow, yes/no question: does he believe the Government has a responsibility to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi? The attributed response never touches it — it is instead a fresh rhetorical question about how the Minister feels being 'wheeled out' to answer for the Prime Minister. The belief question is left entirely unanswered; the response substitutes a different question about process and motive.
question: Te Arawhiti: Does he believe that the Government has a responsibility to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
statement: How does the Minister for Māori Crown relations feel being wheeled out by this Government to answer a question that was directed to the Prime Minister, simply because he is Māori, and the Prime Minister wants to distance himself from the responsibilities of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?

explanation: The question asks whether the Minister believes ongoing colonisation is good for Te Tiriti partners — a direct yes/no proposition. The attributed response, 'Or blood quantum-ing,' is a four-word interjection that adds a rhetorical item to a list and engages none of the question's content. Nothing resembling an answer is offered.
question: Yes. Does the Minister for Crown relationships: Te Arawhiti believe that ongoing colonisation is good for Te Tiriti o Waitangi partners?
statement: Or blood quantum-ing.

explanation: The prompt is the interjected pun 'Back on track' rather than a formulated question, so there is little core to hit. Potaka repeats the phrase and then speaks squarely to the track and its funding — site risks, visitor management, revenue options, the DOC/Ngāti Hei work, and his decision. The response is on the subject that was put to him rather than a pivot elsewhere, though the prompt was too thin to demand anything specific, and the closing jab at the previous government's delay drifts off the point.
question: Back on track.
statement: Back on track. There will be ongoing challenges at this site, which is prone to storm damage, landslides, and rock falls. This funding package will help curate better visitor management, explore revenue generation opportunities, and start a more enduring access solution. Mautohe Cathedral Cove is the major drawcard to the Coromandel region. This investment is expected to increase regional GDP by around 7 percent once the track is fully operational again. DOC and Ngāti Hei have been working closely to ensure the experience of visiting Mautohe Cathedral Cove is safe, respects the cultural significance of the area, protects the fragile environment, and is sustainable. And I’m glad that I’ve made a decision rather than waiting another nine months to make a decision.

explanation: The question is precise and two-part: does he accept the ICJ ruling that Israel is acting illegally as an occupying force, and if so why has he not said so? What is attributed as the response is a point of order noting that the speaker could not tell whether a yes or a no was intended. Neither limb of the question is engaged; the record shows the question going unanswered on its face.
question: Does he accept the International Court of Justice ruling that Israel is acting illegally as an occupying force in Gaza; if so, why has he not said so?
statement: Point of order. I understand the quote and I know that I can’t expect a yes/no answer, but I wondered whether the person speaking was intending to say yes or no.

explanation: A sharply quantified question — how many of the 138 Whanaketia recommendations the Government will commit to adopting, 'if any'. The attributed response never returns a number, a range, or even a refusal to give one; it moves straight to a further question about whether she agrees with the report's findings on whakapapa deprivation. A different question is put where the count was asked for.
question: How many of the 138 recommendations from the Whanaketia report on historical abuse in State care and faith-based institutions will the Government commit to adopting, if any?
statement: Does she agree with the report’s findings that depriving tamariki Māori of their ’hakapapa was a significant source of harm and trauma, which has “led to much larger social problems such as declining health, higher rates of incarceration, family harm, unemployment, homelessness, mental distress, and substance harm, and reduced educational opportunities”? That’s a bunch; that’s a whole lot.

explanation: Hipkins interjects 'Yeah, but he didn't' — disputing a claim just made. Luxon meets it with a flat, unhedged assertion: 'As I said, there is no hiring freeze.' It is terse and adds nothing new, but terseness is not evasion: the contested proposition is the one he addresses, and he states his position on it without deflecting to another subject or to the questioner. Slightly short of full marks only because the specific 'he didn't' charge is answered by restatement rather than by direct rebuttal.
question: Yeah, but he didn’t.
statement: As I said, there is no hiring freeze.

explanation: Hipkins offers to repeat the question for the Prime Minister; Luxon replies "Yes, please." The offer is taken up directly and completely — no evasion, no pivot. Terseness is irrelevant to this attribute.
question: I’m happy to repeat it for the Prime Minister.
statement: Yes, please.

explanation: Sepuloni begins a supplementary directed at something Shane Jones did or said (the question is cut off mid-sentence in the record, but its subject is unambiguous). Peters responds with a quip that Prime Minister Luxon 'understands a bit of Latin' — a remark on an entirely different subject that engages nothing about Shane Jones. Whatever the truncated question's full content, the recorded response does not reach it. Scored low for non-engagement, not for brevity or tone; a blunt refusal to comment on Jones would have scored high.
question: Supplementary. Did Shane Jones—
statement: Well, I’m certain that Prime Minister Luxon understands a bit of Latin, as well.

explanation: Swarbrick's interjection asserts that a specific claim Luxon made is false. Luxon responds by restating his position and setting out the ERP2 plan (oil and gas ban repeal, agriculture out of the ETS, net zero by 2044). He engages the substantive disagreement rather than the questioner, but never identifies or defends the particular claim that was called untrue — he answers the general policy dispute instead of the specific challenge. Partial engagement.
question: It’s just not true.
statement: We’re not shutting down industries and driving farmers off the land. We’re not making life harder by forcing Kiwis out of their cars. Here’s the good news: on our plan, we repeal the broken oil and gas ban, we keep agriculture out of the emissions trading scheme, and we still hit net carbon zero six years earlier, in 2044. There’s a lot more to do, but our emissions reduction plan (ERP) 2 plan is a good one. It delivers emissions budget (EB) 1 and 2, and we’re on the right track.

explanation: The challenge is that the bill has already been sent to him. Luxon directly confirms it — 'It's in my inbox from an hour ago' — and states plainly that he has not seen it and will look at it. The dismissive framing ('it's big for you') is a Civility matter, not a dodge; the core factual point is conceded and answered squarely.
question: It’s in your inbox.
statement: It’s in my inbox from an hour ago. No disrespect; it’s big for you, but there’s a bit more going on as we run the country, so we will get to the bill. I’ll have a good look at the bill, but in fairness, I haven’t seen it.

explanation: Sepuloni's charge is that Peters/the project is directionless. Peters engages the metaphor and does eventually assert direction — 'We know where we're going' — plus a promised announcement in the new year. But the reply is largely a nautical aphorism and a pivot to Christmas sentiment; the claim of drift is rebutted only by assertion, with the substance mostly circled rather than met. Half credit.
question: You are adrift!
statement: Well, to use the shipping expression, an old saying: if you leave port with no port to go to for that boat, no wind’s a white wind. We know where we’re going. We’re going into Christmas and people will know that they can look forward to a bright new announcement in the new year whilst they’re worried about that more than anything else.

explanation: Paul asserts the form is not publicly available. Bishop's two-word reply, 'It's online,' contradicts exactly that claim. It is terse and offers no supporting detail, but brevity and lack of elaboration are Specificity concerns; as a matter of forthrightness this lands directly on the disputed point.
question: It’s not publicly available—
statement: It’s online.

explanation: Paul repeats and sharpens the claim that the form is neither online nor publicly available. Bishop responds to precisely that, offering a reason — she is holding up a photo of it, which he takes as evidence it is known and public — and concludes it is a publicly available document. Whether the inference is sound is a Rigor question; the question asked was engaged head-on.
question: It’s not online. It’s not publicly available, this form.
statement: Speaking to the point of order, the fact that she is holding up a copy of the photo of it indicates people know about it; it’s a publicly available document.

explanation: Asked how it is fair to leave thousands in hardship. Upston engages the fairness core directly — she argues the Budget 2024 change removed anomalies and that calculating housing assistance on all household income is fairer. She does not engage the 'thousands in hardship' premise identified by her own ministry, so the question is answered on one of its two limbs, but the central 'how is it fair' is squarely met with a reason.
question: How is it fair to leave thousands of people potentially in hardship, as identified by her own ministry?
statement: Because, as I said, the changes that have been made as a result of Budget 2024 reduced a couple of anomalies. Most New Zealanders would expect that housing assistance would be calculated based on all housing income. It wasn’t; we’ve changed it. It’s fairer, as it should be.

explanation: A narrow numeric question: how many people were wrongly told they had won. Stanford explains the ICT cause and then answers the number question head-on — she is advised it is not possible to track how many, and only three people have made contact. Saying the figure cannot be established, plus the one figure she has, is a direct engagement rather than a pivot; short of 1.0 only because the count itself is never resolved.
question: How many people were informed in error following Immigration New Zealand’s online ballot in May that they had won the right to apply for a parent residence visa?
statement: Immigration New Zealand’s parent resident visa expressions of interest online tool allows people to see if their expression of interest was successful in the ballot. The tool should show an exact match of the customer’s ballot number once they’ve inputted it. However, when the tool was recently rebuilt for the new website, an ICT error meant that in some instances it also showed ballot numbers that were close but not an exact match. I’m advised that it’s not possible to track how many people this happened to. However, Immigration New Zealand has only been contacted by three people.

explanation: Asked why she, as Minister, will not personally apologise. Stanford answers a neighbouring question — that officials have already apologised to Ms Renwick and will do so for others. The apology topic is engaged, and it implicitly conveys that no ministerial apology is coming, but the 'why won't you personally' core is never addressed.
question: Why won’t she, as Minister, personally apologise to Alison Renwick and any others who were wrongly told that they had won the right to sponsor for a parent residence visa?
statement: I understand that immigration officials have already spoken to the lady that the member mentions and have apologised. If they have details for other people, they will be doing the same.

explanation: Asked whether affected applicants will get a fee waiver. Stanford answers no, with a reason (the affected number is unknown, so a waiver would not be appropriate). A plain negative to a yes/no question — complete.
question: Will applicants who were wrongly told that they had won the right to sponsor for a parent residence visa be granted a fee waiver the next time they want to go into the ballot?
statement: Because we have no idea of how many people this has affected, it wouldn’t be appropriate for us to do that.

explanation: Asked how much revenue the $450 ballot fee generated over the last year. She states plainly that she does not have the figure and cannot answer, and directs the member to a written question. That is a direct response to the question asked rather than a pivot — no talking points, no attack — but the requested figure is not supplied, so it falls short of a complete answer.
question: How much revenue has been generated for the Government over the last year by the $450 fee that people pay to go into the ballot for only three months?
statement: I don’t have that information to hand so I can’t answer it. But if the member wants to put it in writing, then we’ll be able to answer it.

explanation: Asked whether she will admit that families are frustrated and still waiting 19 months on. She neither admits nor denies the frustration; instead she recounts a January social media video and says an announcement is imminent and earlier than intended. The delay is touched on obliquely, but the concession sought is sidestepped in favour of a forward-looking announcement.
question: Will she admit that many thousands of Kiwi families are frustrated and desperately waiting for the parent boost visa that she promised and 19 months later is still nowhere to be seen?
statement: Well, as I had indicated in January this year via social media video that went quite well, I indicated that we had started work on the visa. And we will be announcing the visa imminently with a date that people will be able to apply for it, which will be months earlier than we had originally intended.

explanation: Asked what announcements he has made about raising the SH1 speed limit. Bishop names the announcement directly — the start of public consultation on 110 km/h on Transmission Gully and the Raumati Straights. The question is fully answered; surrounding promotional material does not displace the answer.
question: What announcements has he made about increasing the speed limit on State Highway 1?
statement: Last week, I announced what many New Zealanders, I know, have been looking forward to: the start of public consultation on increasing the speed limits to 110 kilometres per hour on Transmission Gully and the Raumati Straights—22,000 vehicles using this relatively new road daily; important regional connector; safe, modern, reliable route for all road users. It’s the main gateway into Wellington and I’m very pleased that the Government is taking this important step to further enhance the road.

explanation: Asked why the Government is considering this change now. Bishop supplies reasons — growing the economy, cutting travel times, productivity, and Transmission Gully's high safety standard and low crash record. The 'why' is squarely engaged; the 'now' (why at this point in time rather than earlier or later) is not distinguished, so it is answered on the substance but not on the timing.
question: Why is the Government considering this change now?
statement: Delivering better quality infrastructure is part of the Government’s plan to grow the economy, reduce travel times, and increase the productivity of our transport network. We’re committed to providing State highways that get people where they need to go quickly and safely. Transmission Gully is designed and constructed to a very high safety standard, has very low crash numbers on the road since its opening in 2022, and safety features that greatly reduce the risk of death or serious injury in a crash.

explanation: Asked how New Zealanders can have their say. Answer states consultation opened last Friday, runs six weeks, and submissions go via the NZTA website — the mechanism asked for is given directly. The closing jab at the questioner's support is surplus, not a dodge.
question: How can New Zealanders have their say on this proposal?
statement: Consultation on raising the speed limits opened last Friday and will last for six weeks. People can submit on this consultation via the New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) website as well as find more information on this proposal. I’m looking forward to the strong support of the local MP for the area it connects to, Tim Costley.

explanation: Standard 'does she stand by all her statements' question, answered 'In context, yes.' A complete yes/no response to a yes/no question.
question: Malo le soifua manuia lau afioga Fetalai. Does she stand by all her statements and actions?
statement: In context, yes.

explanation: Asked what he would say to a named library worker. He supplies an actual message to her — the Government values the work, the legislated regime allows pay equity claims, and he encourages her to participate. It is boilerplate and cross-references previous answers, but the question ('what do you say to her') is squarely answered.
question: What does she say to a library worker, in relation to the pay equity changes, who says, “The end of our claim is devastating to myself and my colleagues. We were so close to a result, and to see that stripped away is incredibly painful. We will go on providing for our community. It’s just that now we will do it knowing that our Government does not value our work, and in the knowledge that we will have to start our long fight for fair wages all over again.”?
statement: On behalf of the Minister, I’d say to her the same thing that the Minister of Finance said in response to previous questions along similar lines yesterday and indeed the day before that, which is that the Government strongly values the work that these workers do, and that the pay equity regime that has been legislated by Parliament allows for pay equity claims. I would encourage her to participate in that process.

explanation: Two-part question: what he says to Marianne Bishop, and how he expects to retain essential care workers under those conditions. The first part is answered only by reference back to the previous answer (after a joke about surnames); the second, the retention question, is never touched.
question: What does she say to Marianne Bishop, a retired residential aged-care worker, who says, “Why would you want to work in aged care when you can get the same amount at a supermarket or McDonald’s?”; if so, how does he expect to maintain essential care workers under those kinds of conditions?
statement: Well, the first thing I’d say to Miss Bishop is probably to ask whether or not we’re related! And then the second thing I would say is exactly what I said in relation to the last answer.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the quoted library worker. 'No, I don't agree with that.' A blunt, complete answer to the question asked.
question: Does she agree with a tertiary library worker who says, “My colleagues are on extremely low pay and deserve better. They deserve to be able to afford their rent, groceries, and be able to top up their Snapper cards that enable them to get to work.”?
