There’s a significant uplift with hips, knees, and cataract operations, and a major step towards reducing the elective wait-list that has left too many New Zealanders waiting in pain for too long. These procedures will be delivered by unlocking capacity in both the public and private sectors. That’s why we’ve signed panel agreements with private hospitals whilst also increasing capacity at Health New Zealand’s dedicated elective facilities such as the Manukau Health Park, Tōtara Haumaru, and Burwood Hospital. We’re getting on with the job and putting patients first.

explanation: Asked how delivery will be ensured. He supplies a mechanism — unlocking capacity, longer-term panel contracts with private hospitals, expanded Health NZ elective facilities — which addresses the 'how'. Slight drift into phase-one results and a slogan, but the question is met.
question: How will the Government ensure that these procedures are delivered?
statement: By taking a smart, joined-up approach and working both with the public and private hospitals, we’ve already shown that Elective Boost can deliver results. We will continue to do this by unlocking capacity, partnering with private providers in a more strategic way with longer-term contracts, and—most importantly—getting Kiwis the care that they need. By 1 June, more than 12,764 additional procedures had already been delivered through phase one of the boost, far exceeding our target of 10,500 procedures by 30 June. New Zealanders don’t care who does the operation; they just want it done.

explanation: Asked what else is being done on planned care access. He names a distinct further measure — funding GP clinics to deliver minor procedures in the community — and lists the procedure types. Squarely responsive to 'what else'.
question: What else is the Government doing to improve New Zealanders’ access to planned care?
statement: Well, improving access to planned care is a top priority for this Government, and that’s why, as part of our record funding boost to general practice, we’re supporting GP clinics to deliver minor planned care procedures closer to patients in the community. This will reduce wait times for procedures such as minor gynaecological procedures, skin excisions, iron infusions, and oncology infusions, all whist delivering care closer to home and taking pressure directly off our hospitals. We’re turning the system around.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the 95 percent / four-month target. Opens with an unambiguous "Yes" and restates the target itself before adding supporting data. The core question is squarely answered.
question: Does he stand by his target that 95 percent of patients will be waiting less than four months for a first specialist appointment?
statement: Yes, our Government has brought back the health targets because patients deserve faster access to care. That includes our target for 95 percent of patients to receive their first specialist assessment within four months by 2030. The good news is that wait-lists are already improving. The latest data from the Health New Zealand national collections shows the total number of patients waiting has reduced by 2,955 between February and March, and those waiting over four months has also dropped by 2,940 during the same period. This shows that our focus on putting patients first is making a difference. There is still much work to do. Patients have been waiting for far too long, and we will continue to focus on reducing wait times to ensure that more New Zealanders get the care they need faster.

explanation: Asked whether he will take responsibility for phantom Nelson appointments. He never says yes or no on responsibility; he characterises the question as a union beat-up and asserts the 23 patients now have bookings. That contests the premise, which is minimal engagement, but the responsibility question itself is left untouched and the questioner's motives are attacked instead.
question: Will he take responsibility for Nelson patients being given appointments that don’t exist, with doctors that aren’t there, in order to say he’s meeting the target?
statement: That question is just repeating the beat-up from the unions in Nelson, who are trying to politicise an IT system rather than celebrate the fact that all 23 of those patients now have bookings over the next three months and will be seen.

explanation: Asked whether patients can expect a fake doctor's visit they don't even know is happening. He engages the operative element directly — they all received letters, sent 4 July, for appointments over three months — which is a denial of the specific charge, before trailing off into an attack on the Opposition. Addressed, though not framed as a yes/no.
question: Is this what patients can expect under a National Government: a fake doctor’s visit that they don’t even know is happening?
statement: Well, they all received letters. The letters were sent on 4 July for appointments over the coming three months. This is an Opposition which is politicising an IT system—

explanation: Asked what he expected would happen when setting a target without agreeing to adequate doctors at an understaffed hospital. He does not answer what he expected; he disputes the staffing premise (more doctors and nurses than 2023) and then redirects to the questioner's own record as Minister. Premise-contesting counts for something, but the question asked is not reached.
question: What did he expect would happen when he set a target to increase clinic visits but did not agree to this understaffed hospital having enough doctors?
statement: There are more doctors and more nurses at Nelson Hospital today than in 2023, when she was the Minister of Health. And, by the way, the people we are prioritising getting appointments for over the next three months were people put on the wait-list when she was the Minister.

explanation: A narrow yes/no: has he asked Health NZ to explain the statement to 1News? He never says whether he asked. He offers an account of the booking system's limitations — touching the subject matter of the alleged falsehood — then pivots to letters, his priorities, and the previous Minister. The specific question put is avoided.
question: Has he asked Health New Zealand to explain the obvious falsehood in their response to 1News on this matter: that Nelson’s booking system cannot make appointments more than six weeks in advance?
statement: Well, the system, which was put in place in 2018, when Labour was in Government, has limitations as to how long you can book patients in. What has happened is they have all received letters, with their bookings, over the next three months, and they will be seen. That’s my priority, and, as I said in answer to the earlier question, these are people who were put on the wait-list when she was the Minister. My focus is on getting these patients seen and off the wait-list so that we can deliver the timely, quality access to healthcare that New Zealanders need.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all the statements and actions of his Government. "Yes." Complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he is concerned about the reported upsurge in Christchurch homelessness and full emergency shelters. He does answer the concern element ("We're always concerned about people who are without housing"), but generically, and never engages the Christchurch report or the shelters; the rest is a rent/wait-list/motel record recital. Half-answered.
question: Is the Prime Minister concerned that the Christchurch City Mission has reported an upsurge in the number of homeless people in Christchurch, so much so that their emergency shelters are regularly full?
statement: We’re always concerned about people who are without housing, and that’s why this Government is doing an incredibly good job of trying to improve the situation that we inherited. It has been excellent to see that rents have come down $5 since we came into power, versus going up $180; it has been amazing and excellent to see that nearly 6,000 people have come off the social housing wait-list; and it’s been an outstanding achievement to ensure that we take several thousand people, including 2,100 kids, out of emergency hotel accommodation, and 85 percent of them are now in warm, safe, dry homes. I think all members of this House should celebrate that fact and that progress. That is something that we can all be very proud about because, actually, we are supporting vulnerable people when they need it most.

explanation: Asked why homeless pensioners are living in cars and tents in the red zone rather than housing. The reply implies an answer — support is available at MSD if they come — but does not explain why these people are not housed, and the bulk of the response is a comparison with the previous Government's record.
question: Then, why are homeless pensioners living in cars, vans, and tents in Christchurch’s red zone, instead of in emergency or social housing?
statement: Well, I just say to the member: anyone who needs any housing support can come to the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) and receive it. But if you think about what was, without doubt, an absolutely failed housing policy under Labour, under the Greens—where house prices went up; rents went up; the social housing wait-list went up from 6,000 to over 25,000, and is now back at 19,308, from memory—we are making progress. The fact that we have taken 2,100 children out of damp, squalid motel rooms—which the previous Government was very happy to throw people into—and we have prioritised them and got them into State houses or community housing providers, is an outstanding result. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Methodist Mission director's claim that housing support is not in fact available, and if not why not. He gives a plain no ("I disagree with the characterisation") and a reason (anybody who wants assistance can come to MSD and will receive it). Both limbs of the question are hit, before a lengthy pivot to Labour's legacy.
question: With what the Prime Minister was just saying about emergency support housing, does he agree, then, with the executive director of the Christchurch Methodist Mission that “Chris Bishop said in an interview that if people are homeless they could go to the Ministry of Social Development and housing support would be available for them … we know that’s not true.”, and, if not, why not?
statement: Well, I disagree with the characterisation of that question. Anybody who wants assistance can come to MSD and they will receive it. I will just ask the members to think about it: the legacy on housing of the previous Government was abysmal. We care about vulnerable people. That’s why we’re fixing the housing mess that we’ve inherited; rents are down; the social housing wait-list is down; and people are out of emergency housing in warm, dry homes. That’s a good outcome. Yes, there’s more to do. If people need assistance, that’s still available to them. But to have 85 percent of people—85 percent of households—out of emergency hotel accommodation, into warm, dry houses, that’s something we should be celebrating.

explanation: Asked why more people are being rejected for emergency housing support at MSD. The rise in rejections is never addressed or even acknowledged; he asserts support is available and moves to motel exits. Answers a different question than the one asked.
question: Then, why are there more people being rejected for emergency housing support at MSD?
statement: I’d just say to the member: if people are desperately needing support from MSD, it is available. But what I say is we’re not going to consign people to motel rooms and have kids raised in motel rooms. We want them in warm, dry homes, and we’re making great progress doing that: 86 percent of people taken out of emergency housing are now in proper homes. That’s a good thing for them, their families, and those kids.

explanation: Asked whether he denies specific rough-sleeping counts in three cities. He answers with "what I can confirm is" three times, none of which concerns rough sleeping — children out of motels, rents, the wait-list. The yes/no denial is never given and the figures are never touched.
question: Is the Prime Minister denying, then, that there are 300 people sleeping rough in Christchurch, 653 in Auckland, and 464 in Wellington, on most recent counts, all up since this Government restricted access to emergency housing?
statement: What I can confirm is there is 2,124 children that have been moved out of motels, into homes and houses; what I can confirm is that the average rents across New Zealand are down $5, not up $180 a week as they were under the previous administration; and what I can confirm is that there is now 19,308 people on the social housing wait-list, and that is down from 26,000 under a Labour-Greens Government that didn’t care about vulnerable people.

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he has made on councils getting back to basics. He names the specific announcement — the Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill introduced this week — and what it does. Directly responsive.
question: What recent announcements has he made on getting councils back to basics?
statement: This Government is getting councils back to basics, focusing on the core services Kiwis rely on. Too much ratepayer money is being spent on lower priorities instead of roads, water, waste, and infrastructure. The bill introduced this week—the Local Government (System Improvements) Amendment Bill—restores focus and tightens financial rules. When councils lose focus, rates go up, and that drives up the cost of living. We’re putting ratepayers first, and bringing back the discipline needed to deliver results for Kiwis. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked how refocusing councils on core services delivers better outcomes for ratepayers. Watts does state a mechanism (the bill forces focus on basics rather than 'pet projects') and names the outcome (better services, value for money), so the question is engaged, though the causal link is largely restated rather than explained.
question: How will refocusing councils on core services deliver better outcomes for ratepayers?
statement: Well, Kiwis expect their rates to go towards the basics: fixing roads, keeping water running, and collecting the rubbish. Kiwis are frustrated with rising rates, expanding bureaucracy, and poor value for money. This bill makes sure that councils focus on what matters most, not on pet projects or distractions. It’s about getting the basics right, delivering better services, and ensuring Kiwis get what they pay for.

explanation: Asked how new performance measures improve quality and consistency of services. He names the actual measure — mandatory public reporting on spending including contractors and consultants — and the route to improvement (transparency/accountability). Squarely on the question, though 'consistency' is not separately addressed.
question: How will the new performance measures improve the quality and consistency of services?
statement: For too long, ratepayers have not been able to see how their council is performing. This bill changes that. We’re setting new performance measures requiring councils to publicly report on spending, including what they pay contractors and consultants. This is about transparency, accountability, and giving ratepayers the tools to see where their money is going and whether they’re getting value for money.

explanation: Asked what other steps the Government is taking. He lists other steps: rates capping and cutting red tape. Directly responsive to what was asked.
question: What other steps is the Government taking to lift the performance of local councils and deliver better outcomes for communities?
statement: Well, this Government is tapping into the root causes of poor performance, not papering over the cracks. We’re looking at tools like rates capping to stop unnecessary increases, and cutting red tape so that councils focus on delivering the basics. This Government is focused on ensuring value for money and better results for local communities.

explanation: Two-part question: does she stand by the statement (answered 'Yes' outright), and how will New Zealanders judge job delivery given 47,000 departures. She answers the judgement part by nominating the yardstick — actual unemployment versus prior forecasts — so it is engaged, but the 47,000 emigration premise itself is never touched.
question: Does she stand by her statement, “I think New Zealanders will judge our government on what we do and what we deliver”; if so, how does she think New Zealanders will judge the Government’s ability to deliver jobs, when 47,000 people left New Zealand for Australia last year?
statement: Yes, I stand by that statement. In terms of how New Zealanders will judge the Government’s ability to deliver jobs, I would invite them to compare how the actual unemployment rate under this Government compares with what was being forecast would be the case under the previous Government. I can share with the member that the actual numbers of unemployed people have been consistently lower in every quarter under this Government than the previous Government was forecasting would be the case, prior to the election. It is certainly the case that the economy has been through a very tough period, and that is why our Government has been so focused on getting inflation and interest rates under control and encouraging growth and job creation. There is more to be done, but we are taking the right steps.

explanation: Asked how the Government can claim job creation when half of households say work is hard to find. She defends the claim by reference to forecast unemployment peaks and lower-than-forecast unemployment, which addresses the 'how can you claim it' core, but she never engages with the household finding that is the question's premise.
question: How can her Government claim it’s creating jobs when half of New Zealand households say that work is hard to find?
statement: Well, consistent with my answer to the previous question, it has been forecast by Treasury and other economic entities since the last Government was in power that unemployment would be peaking at around this point. What is good news—which the member is yet to reflect on—is that the rate of unemployment is lower than she was forecasting in her Cabinet.

explanation: Two parts: does she agree with Luxon (answered 'Yes' clearly), and how does she explain the 47,000 who left. The explanation is never given — she turns to attacking the questioner and restating her 'mission'. Half the question answered, the substantive half avoided.
question: Does she agree with Christopher Luxon, who said, “New Zealand is where the opportunities are—not Australia”; if so, how does she explain the 47,000 New Zealanders who saw no future for themselves here, under her Government?
statement: Yes, I absolutely support the patriotism of the Prime Minister, who has the good sense to say that New Zealanders should pursue their ambitions and aspirations here. If the member takes a different view, that she wants New Zealanders to leave for Australia, then she should ask herself what she’s doing in this House because when I come to work each day, I see it as my mission to make sure that this is an economy that does catch up with Australia, that doesn’t allow the wealth gap to persist, that actually removes some of the barriers that stop us digging wealth from the ground and that stop us making developments happen, and that doesn’t chase talent and capital out the door with new taxes. So, yes, we’re on a mission. This is a wonderful country. New Zealanders should stay here, because this Government is going to back them to succeed.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with Seymour that people leaving is always a bad sign, and if not why not. Her 'Yes' attaches to a different proposition (her aspiration that New Zealanders can pursue ambitions here), not to whether departures are always a bad sign, and she then moves to growth comparisons and a jab at the questioner. The specific agreement asked for is sidestepped.
question: Does she agree with the Deputy Prime Minister, David Seymour, in his view the numbers of New Zealanders leaving is always a bad sign; if not, why not?
statement: Yes, it is always my aspiration that New Zealanders feel they can pursue their ambitions here in New Zealand. What I always take note of is how we compare with Australia, and that’s why I was delighted that in the first three months of this year, New Zealand grew four times as fast as Australia. One quarter isn’t enough; we need that to occur again and again and again, which is why we are on the mission to ensure this is a better place to do business, a better place to employ people, and a better place to make resources into incomes and opportunities for New Zealanders. The member can be very critical, but I am yet to hear a single idea for how you would make this country better.

explanation: A pointed question about whether the Government's jobs approach amounts to 'everyone must go'. She does not address the jobs proposition at all, instead noting 2024 net migration to Australia matched 2023 and accusing the questioner of hypocrisy — a counter-attack on the previous government rather than a response to what was asked.
question: Did this Government confuse its “Everyone must go” tourism strategy with its approach to jobs—no work, low pay, and hard-working Kiwis lining up for Australia?
statement: I’m finding this occupation of the moral high ground rather curious when I note that Statistics New Zealand report that the net migration loss from New Zealand to Australia in 2024 was almost exactly the same as it was in 2023, and I do not recall the member at that time taking responsibility for every New Zealander who chose to pursue their fortunes elsewhere.

explanation: Asked what recent actions restore regional decision-making in vocational education. She names them precisely: breaking up the merged institution and re-establishing 10 regional polytechnics with their own governance from 1 January. Direct and complete.
question: What recent actions has the Government taken to restore regional decision-making in vocational education and training?
statement: It was clear to us from the start that Labour’s mega-merger of all regional polytechnics into one unwieldy national institution simply wouldn’t work—and it didn’t. So we are breaking it up: from 1 January next year, 10 regional polytechnics will be re-established with their own governance and decision making. We’re putting vocational education and training back into the hands of local communities where it belongs, delivering on what we campaigned for and what regional New Zealand has been asking for. This is a major milestone in building a system that is financially sustainable, responsible to employers, and focused on the future.

explanation: Asked what this means for Christchurch and Canterbury. She answers specifically about Ara returning to local control and what that means for the region's trades, health and engineering training. On point throughout.
question: What does this mean for the people of Christchurch and Canterbury?
statement: Canterbury’s polytechnic, Ara, plays a critical role in supporting Canterbury’s strong and diverse economy, particularly in trades, health, engineering, and technology. Restoring local governance puts decision making back in the hands of the region, where communities and industries know best what skills are needed. Returning Ara to local control will ensure it remains agile, practical, and deeply connected to the Canterbury economy and wider regional industries. It puts proud Cantabrians back in charge of shaping their workforce, and it sets Ara up for long-term success, supporting Canterbury as a regional powerhouse. This is great news for Canterbury.

explanation: A narrow factual question: has rough sleeping increased since he became Associate Minister. He engages — says the census showed an increase 2018–2023, that no current single data source exists, and that anecdotal reports suggest an increase — which is effectively 'I can't tell you definitively, but reports say yes'. That reaches the question, though it then drifts into praise for Going for Housing Growth.
question: Has the number of people sleeping rough, as defined by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development, increased since he became Associate Minister of Housing?
statement: Rough sleepers are a subset of those Kiwis unfortunately living without shelter in the census. Now, the number of rough sleepers increased between Census 2018 and 2023 and there’s no current single source of data for the number of rough sleepers as of today. Anecdotal reports and comments in this House and, actually, from some providers in some locations observe an increase in rough sleeping, but also acknowledge that there are various potential contributing causes for any changes: the cost of living, economy, mental health, and of course the lack of prudent spending by previous Governments. That’s why I’m supportive of the exemplary Going for Housing Growth mahi that is being led by Minister Bishop to ensure that more of the right houses in the right places are built for Kiwis in need.

explanation: Asked to explain a specific reported 150 percent rise over three months. He disputes recognition of the data point, which is a form of engagement with the premise, but offers no explanation and moves to general statements about homelessness and housing supply. The 'why' asked for is never approached.
question: Can he explain why homelessness in Tāmaki Makaurau rose almost 150 percent in just three months, as reported in the December 2024 insights report?
statement: I cannot recall that data point being referenced to me as a single source of truth data point. There may be some anecdotal reports in relation to that number, but what I can say is this: homelessness is something that continues to confront many, many Kiwis, and this Government is absolutely supportive of an intention to ensure more houses, the right type and the right place, are built for Kiwis in need.

explanation: Asked to justify emergency housing cuts given Māori over-representation in Tāmaki Makaurau. Potaka squarely rejects the premise ("I am unaware of any cuts"), which is a direct engagement, but then moves to children exiting emergency housing and an attack on the previous Government, never touching the Māori-specific element of the question. Partial.
question: How can he justify cuts to emergency housing when Māori in Tāmaki Makaurau make up 50 percent of those in need?
statement: I am unaware of any cuts to emergency housing. What I am aware of is there is absolute clarification of what is a genuine need for a short-term stay in temporary accommodation, and I’m very proud to say that in addition to the 2,125 children that have left emergency housing, expedited under priority 1, there’s an additional 1,000 children as well—so over 3,000 children have left emergency housing and the dank, dark, nefarious places that were, of course, supported by the previous Government.

explanation: Asked whether he supports all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: "Yes." Complete, unambiguous.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether growing emigration (191 leaving daily) and youth unemployment is the Government's growth strategy. The reply recites general aspirations about safe communities, education and healthcare, then pivots to attacking Labour and the Greens over oil, gas and mining. The emigration/jobs question is never engaged.
question: Is it the Government’s growth strategy to grow the number of New Zealanders leaving this country, with 191 New Zealanders leaving every single day and the number of young, qualified people desperately struggling to find a job?
statement: Our job in this Government is to make sure that we build a place where Kiwis can work hard and get ahead; that they can live in a community where they feel safe in their homes, their businesses, their communities; their kids get a world-class education, and their parents get looked after in healthcare. I just would say to members in the Labour Party and the Green Party that if you actually—it’s a bit ironic when you don’t support oil and gas and fast-track and construction and getting things done and built. And, actually, where do Kiwis go when they go to Australia? They go work in oil and gas and mining. Get on board: support mining, end the oil and gas ban—let’s get it done.

explanation: Asked whether cancelling 3,500 State homes and freezing the infrastructure pipeline was good for the economy. The answer stays in the housing domain (wait-list, rents, kids out of motels) but never addresses the cancellations, the infrastructure freeze, or the economic effect asked about. Gestures near the topic without reaching the question.
question: Is it good for the economy for his Government to have cancelled building of 3,500 State homes, shut down school and hospital and infrastructure rebuilds, effectively freezing the infrastructure pipeline and manufacturing sectors, leading BNZ’s senior economist to say, “The timeline for New Zealand’s long-awaited economic recovery just keeps getting pushed [out] further and further.”?
statement: What I’d say is absolutely fantastic is that we have lowered the social housing wait-list by about 5,000 or 6,000 people, which is great. What is fantastic is that average rents—which I know that member often takes a lot of interest in—that previously went up $180 a week under the Labour-Greens Government, is now down $5. And importantly, we’ve taken 2,100 kids out of damp motel rooms, and they’re now in lovely homes and houses.

explanation: Asked whether cutting $45m from innovation was good for the economy. He engages the subject-matter — defends the science sector reforms and argues R&D should convert into economic growth, implicitly claiming it is good for the economy — but never addresses the specific cut. Answers around the core rather than at it.
question: Was it good for the economy that his Government chose to slash $45 million from innovation in the Budget, while the co-president of the New Zealand Association of Scientists has said, “We lose something like $11 from the future New Zealand economy for every dollar [we] cut [in the science sector]”—a sector crucial for driving employment growth?
statement: I’m very proud of the reforms that we have going on in the science sector. What we are doing is making sure that our R & D efforts—and all our research and development that happens at universities and businesses and with our institutes—is actually converting and having impact. We want all research and development, and activity in the science sector, to convert into economic growth. We make no apologies about that. We’ve looked at good examples around the world where we see R & D being converted into economic growth—that’s very important to us; embrace more science, innovation, technology to grow the economy faster.

explanation: A narrow factual question: how many jobs have the tax cuts created? He supplies a forecast number (240,000 jobs expected over four years) rather than jobs created, and does not attribute it to the tax cuts. A number is offered, but not the one asked for.
question: How many jobs has this Government created with its tax cuts?
statement: Well, as that member will be well aware, after Budget 2025 we expect the economy to grow in the order of about 2.7 percent on average over the next four years. And excitingly, there’s 240,000 new jobs about to be created over that period of time too.

explanation: Asked whether it is good for the economy for young people to be unable to find work. Response is "Very odd question" — a dismissal of the questioner's framing rather than an answer or an explicit refusal. The question is not engaged at all.
question: Is it good for the economy for thousands of our young people to be forced to spend their days applying for hundreds of jobs, receiving only one to two interviews, leading them to see our country as a place with “No work. Shit pay. Why Stay?” [Holds up photo of protest sign]
statement: Very odd question.

explanation: Asked how global events are affecting the NZ economy. The answer directly enumerates the effects — export exposure, US tariffs, trade policy uncertainty, Middle East conflict — and states the net impact on growth. Squarely on the question.
question: How are global events affecting the New Zealand economy?
statement: Global events, of course, have a marked impact on the New Zealand economy. Around one in four New Zealanders derive their livelihoods from sectors that produce goods and services for export. Globally, the last few months have been particularly volatile. The United States announced new tariffs on imports from almost all countries, with rates being continually adjusted. Trade policy uncertainty is high, with little clarity on the final level of tariffs for particular counties when the current pause expires on 1 August. Conflict in the Middle East, particularly between Israel and Iran, has added to global instability and uncertainty. Uncertainty almost always has a negative impact on economic growth, and New Zealand is no exception.

explanation: Asked how tariffs are expected to impact the economy. The answer names the 10 percent US tariff, the affected exporters, and identifies the indirect trading-partner channel as the biggest impact. Directly responsive.
question: How are tariffs expected to impact the New Zealand economy?
statement: As announced in April, New Zealand would be subject to a 10 percent US tariff, although this has yet to confirmed. In terms of direct impacts, tariffs may affect New Zealand businesses that export to the US—such as beef and wine producers—but the biggest impact on the economy is expected to be indirect. Growth in our trading partners—some of whom face the prospects of much higher tariffs than us—is expected to slow, so they are likely, then, to purchase less from New Zealand than they otherwise would have. Trade policy uncertainty also has an impact on business confidence, with New Zealand firms less likely to invest. Unfortunately, those factors are negatively impacting growth, jobs, and wages in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked about the impact of other global factors. The answer covers exactly that — the ceasefire and oil prices, high commodity export prices, and Treasury's growth conditions. Direct and on point.
question: What is the impact of other global factors?
statement: Recently, some other sources of uncertainty have diminished. In particular, the ceasefire between Israel and Iran has reduced global volatility, with oil prices returning to pre-conflict levels—good news. Other global factors are, in fact, positive for New Zealand. Prices for New Zealand’s goods exports are high, for example, with the ANZ Commodity Price Index up 15.5 percent over the past year in New Zealand dollar terms. As a consequence, the export sector is supporting New Zealand’s economic recovery. As I said yesterday, Treasury’s conclusion in its latest economic update is that conditions for growth remain in place as mortgage rates continue to fall, and optimism for the future lifts.

explanation: Asked what the Government's response to global uncertainty is. The answer states it: sticking to the fiscal strategy of controlling spending and debt, plus the Investment Boost incentive. Addressed, with a brief swipe at others' stimulus position that does not displace the answer.
question: What is the Government’s response to this global economic uncertainty?
statement: This is not a time to panic, as others have done when saying there is “absolutely a case for more spending to stimulate the economy.” On the contrary, the Government is sticking to its fiscal strategy which aims to get spending and debt under control, and the Government can help by giving businesses a reason to keep on investing. That is precisely what we have done with the new Investment Boost incentive, which makes new investment more attractive for businesses.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: "Yes." One word, complete.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by the 'fewer lanyards, more hard hats' promise and why 15,000 construction jobs have gone. He never says whether he stands by the promise and never touches the 15,000 figure or the decline; he blames the questioner for interest rates and lists project pipeline values and a road opening. Gestures at sector activity but leaves both halves of the question unreached.
question: Does he still stand by Nicola Willis’ promise of fewer lanyards and more hard hats on Lambton Quay; if so, why does the Builder Sentiment report show a consistent decline in demand under his leadership, resulting in 15,000 fewer construction jobs?
statement: Well, I thank the member for his question and I acknowledge that he also has a responsibility there, given that he saw interest rates go to high levels that had a huge impact on the construction and building industry. But what I’m pleased to report is that there is $125 billion of projects under construction and there’s a pipeline worth $207 billion, and, right today, the good news is that if you’re from Christchurch, State Highway 76 and Brougham Street—we’ve just kicked that off this afternoon.

explanation: A narrow factual question — why was spending lower last year than the year before? The answer says nothing about spending levels at all, switching immediately to demanding the questioner support fast-track legislation. Pure pivot plus attack.
question: If the building and construction sector is doing so well under his Government, why did the Government spend less on the things that he just mentioned in the last year than it did in the year before?
statement: I’ll just say to that member that if he really cares about construction jobs, he would actually support fast-track legislation, wouldn’t he?—because that’s actually what you do. If you care about working people, you don’t just say it; you actually get rid of the regulations that are stopping them from getting into a house or stopping them from getting a road built, or stopping a hospital or a school getting built. So I’d just say to that member, I am looking forward to seeing if he wants to U-turn his repeal of the fast-track legislation or not.

explanation: Asked to choose between two named factors (faster consenting vs cancelled projects) as having the bigger impact. He answers a third thing entirely — spending control, inflation, interest rates — then diverts to Labour's PPP positions. The 'what will make a big difference is' framing brushes the question's shape without engaging either option.
question: Which does he think is going to have the bigger impact on the building and construction sector: the promise of projects coming to market faster, or the fact that his Government actually took projects off the market, like new State house builds, school upgrades, hospital rebuilds, roading projects, and public transport projects, to name a few?
statement: Well, what will make a big difference is—what we are doing is getting spending under control to lower inflation and to lower interest rates, get the economy growing, and to get people into jobs. That’s how it works—that’s called macroeconomics. But the second thing I’d say is that if that member, again, really cares about construction workers, why are there three different public-private partnership positions from the Labour Party—eh?

explanation: Asked whether the Engineering NZ chief executive is wrong that the Government's lack of infrastructure work devastated the profession. He concedes construction has been hit hard and implicitly contests the attributed cause (interest rates, not his Government), which partially engages, but he never says whether the CEO is right or wrong and spends most of the answer demanding the questioner back fast-track.
question: Well, is the chief executive of Engineering New Zealand wrong that his Government’s lack of infrastructure work has “devastated” the engineering profession?
statement: Well, construction has been hit hard, but it’s been hit hard because of high interest rates. High interest rates happened because Government spending was out of control, and you let inflation get out of control. If you really cared about all of these issues, instead of the crocodile tears, why don’t you back the fast-track legislation? Do it today—do it today. Do the U-turn—do it right now. If you really believe in it, back our roads of national significance. If you really believe in it, back our Investment Boost. Go do that.

explanation: A precise confirm-or-deny: were any of the 7,000 houses funded in Budget 2024 or 2025? He answers a different question — that houses are being built and the wait-list is falling — and never addresses the funding source at all. Textbook substitution.
question: Can he confirm that not one of the 7,000 houses just mentioned by the Minister of Finance was funded in Budget 2024 or Budget 2025?
statement: What I can honestly say is the houses are getting built and the State house wait-list is going down, and isn’t that a good thing? That’s a great thing that 6,000 people have a house now and they’re not on that wait-list that grew over four times under the previous administration.

explanation: Asked whether he will admit things are getting worse, particularly in construction. He neither admits nor denies; the reply is entirely a demand that the questioner reverse positions on fast track, Investment Boost and mining. The refusal to admit is left implicit rather than stated.
question: Is he so desperate to report progress that the only progress he can report is progress that was made under the previous Government, and why, a year and a half into his tenure as Prime Minister, will he not admit that things are getting worse for New Zealanders—particularly those in the building and construction sector—and not better?
statement: That’s why I would like that member to come on board and actually reverse his position on fast track, on Investment Boost, on actual mining, and on a bunch of things in order to get things built, because you can talk about stuff or you can do it. We do it, on this side of the House.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by all his Government's statements and actions. Answer: 'Yes.' One word, complete, unambiguous.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by calling the UN letter 'total bunkum'. He declines to revisit it and hands it to the Foreign Minister — a fairly plain refusal to engage further, which counts for something, but he never says whether he still stands by the words, which was the actual question.
question: Does he stand by his statement that the United Nations letter regarding the Regulatory Standards Bill and its impact on Te Tiriti o Waitangi is “total bunkum” and “a waste of time”?
statement: Well, I think I’ve actually said all I want to say about that yesterday, but we’ve got a Minister of Foreign Affairs who’s going to reply very eloquently on behalf of our Government to that letter, and I’m going to leave that to him.

explanation: Asked whether he also regards the 131,000 submitters as bunkum. 'I'll just reject the characterisation of that question outright' is a direct response amounting to no, so the core is engaged; but he then moves to a defence of the Bill's purpose rather than addressing the submitters themselves. Half-answered.
question: Does he also believe the more than 131,000 people who made submissions on the Regulatory Standards Bill are “bunkum” and a “waste of time”, given most of them raised the same issues as the UN special rapporteur did in their letter?
statement: Well, I’ll just reject the characterisation of that question outright. I mean, the Regulatory Standards Bill is designed to improve the quality of regulation that is passed in this Parliament by politicians, to make it transparent, to make sure that we have the rule of law upheld, and that we have property rights upheld. That has benefit, obviously, to Māori and to non-Māori.

explanation: Asked how he intends to repair the reputational damage from the Deputy PM's 'insane' remark. The only thing resembling an answer is that he trusts the Foreign Minister to respond on the Government's behalf; the rest praises that Minister and implicitly denies any damage. A sliver of the 'how' is there, but the question is largely sidestepped.
question: How does he intend to repair the international reputational damage caused by the Deputy Prime Minister on behalf of his Government, who described the UN special rapporteur as “insane” for raising concerns about indigenous rights?
statement: Well, I think New Zealand should be very grateful that we have an outstanding Minister of Foreign Affairs, someone that is hugely respected around the world, someone that actually has left New Zealand and built and deepened relationships around the world and, I’d just say, knows the UN incredibly well, and I trust him to respond on all of our behalf.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his earlier statement about article 2 of Te Tiriti. 'I fully respect article 2' is a short but squarely responsive affirmation, though it affirms the article rather than explicitly the prior answer, leaving a small gap.
question: Does he stand by his answer to the question on 31 July 2024 in which he agreed that “Article 2 of the Te Tiriti o Waitangi agrees Māori full and exclusive and undisturbed possession of their land, estates, forests, and other properties so long as they wish to retain them.”?
statement: Well, I fully respect article 2.

explanation: Asked how he reconciles agreeing with Treaty article 2 with fully agreeing with the DPM's letter to the UN. Luxon never touches the reconciliation — he describes the UN letter's contents, says a reply will be drafted, and vouches for the Foreign Minister. The tension put to him is left entirely unaddressed; only process is offered.
question: How does he reconcile his agreement with article 2 of the Treaty while also stating that he fully agrees with the content of the Deputy Prime Minister’s letter to the UN?
statement: Well, we get letters from the UN. In this case, it raised a number of issues on four or five points. We’re going to respond to those. We don’t agree with that position, but I trust the Minister of Foreign Affairs to actually draft a reply to the UN to actually articulate our position and our counterpoints as to why we don’t believe with the content of that letter or the substance of that letter, and I trust him completely to do that job for us.

explanation: Asked what accountability route indigenous people have when the Waitangi Tribunal, select committee submissions and the UN rapporteur are all disregarded. The reply pivots wholly to an 'outcomes for Māori' talking point (education, housing) and never engages with accountability mechanisms at all.
question: How are indigenous peoples in Aotearoa supposed to hold this Government to account for violations to our rights under Te Tiriti o Waitangi with a Prime Minister who completely disregards the Waitangi Tribunal, select committee submissions, and now the United Nations special rapporteur on the rights of indigenous people?
statement: Because this is a Government that’s about outcomes and results for Māori or non-Māori. We’re working incredibly hard to improve the education of Māori, whether it’s in maths or reading by providing our materials in te reo. We’re making sure that we take many Māori kids that have been, sadly, consigned to emergency housing so that they get into proper, warm, dry houses. We’re focused on outcomes—outcomes for Māori and non-Māori.

explanation: Asked what recent progress has been made on childhood immunisation rates. Answered directly with the specific figure (79.3 percent at 24 months, up 2.4 points year-on-year). Squarely on the question.
question: What recent progress has been made on childhood immunisation rates?
statement: Good news: new data released earlier this week shows that childhood immunisation rates at 24 months continue to rise across the country. This reflects our strong commitment to improving health outcomes for New Zealand kids. National coverage has climbed to 79.3 percent in the third quarter of 2024-25. That’s an increase of 2.4 percentage points compared to the same quarter last year. This result shows that our clear focus on health targets, combined with the efforts of our front-line health workforce, are delivering real improvements for children. When you focus on delivery, you get results.

explanation: Asked about progress across the regions. Answered with district-by-district gains (Auckland, Counties Manukau, Lakes, Capital and Coast, Whanganui, Nelson-Marlborough, South Canterbury). Exactly what was asked.
question: What progress has been made across the regions?
statement: The gains have been widespread and encouraging, with several districts showing strong improvements compared to the last quarter. Auckland’s lifted its coverage by 5.7 percentage points, Counties Manukau by 5.5, and Lakes by 5.2. Capital and Coast rose by 4.4 percentage points, while Whanganui achieved a 5.8 percentage point gain. In the South Island, Nelson-Marlborough saw a 5.2 percentage point increase, and South Canterbury delivered a remarkable 12.1 percentage point gain in that quarter. These results show that our investments in local services are working, and that our communities are stepping up to protect their children. However, there is still more work to do.

explanation: Asked why it is important to increase immunisation rates. Gives the reason: measles outbreak in Wairarapa, measles' infectiousness, immunisation as the most effective protection. Directly responsive, with a short slide into health-target framing at the end.
question: Why is it important to increase immunisation rates?
statement: Recently, we’ve seen cases of measles in the Wairarapa. This serves as a timely reminder of why immunisation matters. Measles is one of the most infectious diseases we face, and immunisation remains the most effective way to keep our children, families, and communities safe. We’re committed to giving every child the healthiest possible start to life, and that’s why we’ve brought back the health targets. These improvements are a vital step towards that goal.

explanation: Asked what other actions the Government has taken. Names them: performance payments for GP clinics tied to immunisation lifts, plus continued investment in outreach, local services and workforce. Answers the question asked.
question: What other actions has the Government taken to lift immunisation rates?
statement: We’re heading in the right direction, but there’s still more work to do, and that’s why, as part of our record funding boost for general practice, we’ve introduced performance payments for GP clinics that successfully lift childhood immunisation rates by up to 10 percent, or reach 95 percent of their enrolled population, with partial payments for partial achievement. We’re continuing to invest in community outreach, local services, and the workforce needed to lift immunisation coverage rates even further.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the PM's statement and, if so, why. Says 'Yes' and supplies the why (Australia is wealthier and pays higher wages). Both limbs of the question are engaged; the swipe at the opposition rides on top of a complete answer.
question: Does she agree with the Prime Minister’s statement that “the reason people leave a country is because they think they can earn higher incomes somewhere else”; if so, why?
statement: Yes, I think that is a key reason people migrate, amongst others. Australia, for example, is a wealthier country than New Zealand and can pay higher wages, including in industries—such as mining and oil and gas—that members opposite have tried to shut down.

explanation: Asked whether sub-inflation minimum wage rises are enough to retain workers who could earn more in Australia. She answers 'Yes' unambiguously, then adds a point about tax relief. The yes/no core is answered directly; the supporting material shifts to a different policy.
question: Are the minimum wage increases that are less than inflation enough to keep Kiwis working here when they can earn more pay in Australia?
statement: Yes, and minimum wage earners were among the 1.9 million New Zealanders who benefited from tax relief that that member would have denied them.

explanation: Asked why she believes 47,000 people left for Australia. She does give a causal answer — a tough economy, inflation, high interest rates and a contractionary effect — which is responsive, though it is wrapped in blame of the previous government and closes with a jab at the questioner.
question: Why does she believe 47,000 people moved to Australia last year?
statement: As I outlined extensively yesterday, for similar reasons that a similar number left the year before, which is that the New Zealand economy has gone through an extremely tough period. We had a Government that drove inflation to record levels for an extended period; interest rates soared to control that. That has had a contractionary effect on our economy, and this Government is working hard every day to rebuild and recover the economy. I’m yet to hear from that member a single idea about how to do that.

explanation: Asked why construction workers would stay given the Certified Builders survey. She does not give a reason to stay; instead she contests the premise with a competing sentiment survey showing improving confidence. Rebutting the premise is partial engagement — an answer is implied (conditions are improving) but never stated as the reason asked for.
question: Why would construction workers stay in New Zealand when, today, the Certified Builders Association said, “half of those surveyed expected conditions to get worse, [and] forward workloads declined”?
statement: Well, I’m also aware of the Builder Sentiment report that was released by EBOSS this morning. That report stated—and I quote—“The percentage of builders anticipating improving sector conditions has doubled on last year from 22 percent to 40 percent”, and it said, I quote: “This shift in sentiment reflects growing confidence and a more balanced outlook for the industry. … While a full recovery will take time, there’s a growing sense that the worst”—i.e., you guys—“is behind us.”

explanation: Two limbs: does she agree with her 2023 'voting with their feet' line, and does it apply now with higher outflows. The first is answered flatly ('Yes'). The second is only glanced at — she moves to her mission and the Going for Growth agenda rather than conceding or denying that the phrase applies to her own government's numbers.
question: Does she agree with Nicola Willis’ statement in 2023 that Kiwis are “voting with their feet”; if so, does that apply now when migration outflows are even higher?
statement: Yes. As I said yesterday, one of my driving missions and reasons for being in Parliament is that I want this to be a country where more young people feel they can pursue their ambitions and aspirations. The reality of how that is done is that we have to strengthen this economy so that businesses have the confidence to create not only more jobs but better paying jobs. That is why we have a Going for Growth agenda that is all about removing the barriers that have held New Zealand back from its growth potential for many, many years. We are making progress. There is much more work to do. We will keep doing it. As history has shown, as this economy recovers, more New Zealanders will choose to live their lives here.

explanation: Asked whether the Government is on track for the 2030 HIV elimination goal, and if not why not. She effectively answers yes — cases trending down since 2016, 'no reason to believe the goal will not be achieved'. Direct response to the on-track question.
question: Is the Government on track to achieve the National HIV Action Plan’s goal of effectively eliminating locally transmitted HIV in Aotearoa by 2030; if not, why not?
statement: I’m advised that the cases of locally acquired HIV continue to trend down from their peak in 2016. Based on the downward trend since 2016, there is no reason to believe the goal will not be achieved of effectively eliminating locally transmitted HIV in New Zealand by 2030.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned about the 31%-vs-90% shortfall and, if so, what action. She never says whether she is concerned; she offers her own figures (149 baseline, 59 in 2024), which at least engages the premise, and on action gives only 'full commitment to the HIV action plan ... solid progress'. Half-engaged: the premise is contested but the concern question is unanswered and the action is a restatement of commitment.
question: Is she concerned with the findings of the HIV epidemiology group’s most recent report that “locally-acquired infections overall have only decreased by 31 percent from the 2010 baseline set by the National HIV Action Plan … which is well short of the 90 percent reduction target by 2030.”, and, if so, what action is she taking to address it?
statement: The figures that I have had reported as the target is a 90 percent reduction on the 2010 total, which was 149. The 2024 figures are 59, and four cases unknown. In terms of the action that we are delivering as a Government, it is a full commitment to the HIV action plan, and we are making solid progress in that regard.

explanation: Asked whether she is concerned about perinatal transmission cases and what she will do. She addresses the cases directly by characterising them (two individuals who arrived pregnant), which engages the premise, but declines to say whether she is concerned and offers only continued commitment to the plan in place of any turnaround action.
question: Is she concerned by the Government’s failure to meet the National HIV Action Plan’s goal to maintain zero cases of transmission at birth, with new avoidable cases of perinatal transmission occurring for the first time in almost 20 years, and, if so, what will she do to turn it around?
statement: Unfortunately, as the member knows, the cases he refers to are about two individuals that travelled to New Zealand who were pregnant at the time. I don’t want to discuss further details of those individuals, but, as I have highlighted, we continue to be committed to the HIV action plan. There are a range of actions that have been committed, and the Ministry of Health and Health New Zealand are working well in that regard.

explanation: Asked what she will do about rising HIV inequity among trans, migrant and Māori populations. She answers the 'what will you do' squarely: eight contracts for expanded testing to priority populations, online and peer-led testing, contact tracers, prevalence modelling, antenatal screening audit, budget delivery. Slightly short of full marks only because the named populations are folded into 'priority populations' rather than addressed as such.
question: What, if anything, will she do to address the growing inequity in rates of HIV acquisition amongst trans, migrant, and Māori populations in Aotearoa, as highlighted in the HIV epidemiology group’s latest report as “highly concerning”?
statement: I can advise the member of the recent completion of a request for a proposal to expand innovative testing for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections to priority populations. Eight contracts are now in place, and two providers have commenced service delivery. Overall, these services will improve access and uptake of testing, and include a new national online service, community-based testing, and peer-led testing for priority populations. I can also advise that the other priorities include recruiting contact tracers to increase the capacity and capability of contact tracing for people newly diagnosed with HIV and other STIs, modelling HIV prevalence in New Zealand to better understand the burden of HIV and where further resources should be directed in order to better prevent transmission, and completing an audit on antenatal screening to identify gaps. The budget of $18 million, which was set in Budget 2022, is on track to be fully delivered.

explanation: Two-part question — why the drop in construction employment, and the impact on the infrastructure pipeline. Both legs are engaged: she gives a causal account (downturn, high interest rates, debt-dependent sector), disputes the size of the figure with an alternative series, and answers the pipeline leg with $6.4b of builds breaking ground. Contesting the number is engagement, not evasion.
question: Why are there more than 15,000 fewer people working in construction under this Government, and what impact does this have on the Government’s infrastructure pipeline?
statement: The construction sector has certainly been affected by the economic downturn and higher interest rates. The construction industry is very sensitive to changes in interest rates as construction projects are heavily reliant on debt funding. So no wonder construction has been affected; interest rates have been high in recent years to fight inflation, pumped up by reckless Government spending. But the member is overegging the impact on construction jobs by using a data series that Statistics New Zealand says has provisional status. Stats New Zealand notes that the household labour force survey (HLFS) is the data source for official statistics about our labour force, and since we came into Government, the HLFS shows a more moderate decrease in construction jobs of around 4,000. So I reject the extent of the member’s claim. In relation to the second leg of the question, the Government’s infrastructure pipeline is strong. Over the next six months, we will be breaking ground on at least $6.4 billion worth of publicly funded infrastructure builds across this country.

explanation: A narrow two-part numeric question — how many construction firms affected by the cancelled Kāinga Ora homes, and how many laid off workers. Neither number is given or even attempted; she pivots to a different statistic (7,056 homes delivered) and a jab about whose money it is. Squarely dodged.
question: How many construction companies have been impacted by the Government cancelling 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes, and what number of these companies have had to lay off workers?
statement: Well, this is a to and fro with that member that it seems will never be resolved because the fact is this, and I say it again: since November 2023, Kāinga Ora and community housing providers have delivered 7,056 newly constructed homes, funded not with Labour’s money, not with National’s money, but with taxpayer money. [Interruption]

explanation: Asked what the 750 firm failures and negative builder sentiment say about the Government's construction blueprint. She engages the sentiment claim head-on (citing a report showing sentiment rising) and points to fast-track as the blueprint action, but never addresses what the failures say about the Government's approach. Roughly half the question reached.
question: What does it say about this Government’s blueprint for the construction sector when 750 firms have gone under in the past year and half of those surveyed by the New Zealand Certified Builders Association say the conditions are expected to worsen?
statement: Well, I feel very strongly for any business that is unable to operate in a difficult economic environment, and it remains the focus of the Government’s activity to ensure that there are better business conditions and better settings in which businesses can thrive. In terms of the sentiment that is in the sector, I again quote the report I quoted earlier in question time, which has come out today, which shows that, in fact, sentiment amongst builders is increasing quite dramatically. I would also point to one very tangible action that the Government is taking that’s going to help a lot, and that is the fast-track legislation. There are up to 17 projects that have indicated they would commence this year if approved through that process, creating among them hundreds of construction jobs; jobs that the members opposite would cancel because they oppose fast track.

explanation: Asked when she will accept responsibility, premised on cancelling Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering. 'Well, I just reject that' is a direct answer to the accountability demand via rejection of the premise, and she explains her account of Apprenticeship Boost's funding. She never engages the apprentice-numbers claim, so it is not complete, but it is not a pivot either.
question: When will she accept responsibility for the fact the number of apprentices being trained is not enough to replace those who have left, given her Government cancelled the Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering?
statement: Well, I just reject that. What actually happened with Apprenticeship Boost was another of the fiscal cliffs left to us by the last Government, which is that they did the dirty; they said, “Oh, we’re funding this apprenticeship scheme, but oops, by the way, only for one year, not for the future.” Well, our Government came in, we rescued Apprenticeship Boost, and we found the funding for it. We continued that scheme. And, of course, we are now also bringing regional leadership back to training in our areas, rather than a nationalised Te Pūkenga that removes the ability of employers to have the influence that they want on things like apprentices.

explanation: Asked whether she agrees with the Infometrics economist that Australia is the better option for builders, and if not why not. She never says agree or disagree with that proposition; she agrees instead with an adjacent statement about interest rates and pivots to the Government's inflation record. It gestures at the underlying issue without answering the yes/no put to her.
question: Does she agree with the principal economist of Infometrics, who said, “If you’re a builder and want to keep being a builder, it may be Australia is the best option for you to continue being a builder for now”; if not, why not?
statement: Well, I agree that when New Zealand’s interest rates soared to extremely high levels, it made it very hard to be in our construction sector because it is very difficult to get finance for a project for which the interest costs are extraordinarily high. That is exactly why our Government has focused on doing everything we can to support inflation to come down and interest rates to come down. And the record speaks for itself. There have been more than two basis points of interest rate reduction since we came to office. Inflation is back on target. Those are the conditions that will allow for a healthy, sustainable construction industry.

explanation: Asked whether she will admit three things. 'No.' One word, unambiguous, complete — a refusal that fully answers the question asked.
question: Will the Minister admit that canning the Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering was a bad idea, her Government has no workforce plan, and her pipeline is a pipe dream?
statement: No.

explanation: Asked what recent results she has seen on NCEA co-requisite literacy and numeracy achievement. She gives exactly that — numeracy 57% (from 45.6%), reading 61.2% (from 58.7%), writing 55.3%, and the level 1 pass rate movement. Directly and completely responsive.
question: What recent results has she seen about literacy and numeracy achievement for the NCEA co-requisite?
statement: I was very pleased to see the latest results show a marked improvement in student achievement across all year levels. In numeracy, 57 percent of students achieved a significant increase, from 45.6 percent in May last year. In reading, this year, 61.2 percent, up from 58.7 percent last year. In writing, 55.3 percent of students achieved, holding steady from May last year. More than half of this year’s year 12 students who did not meet the co-requisite last year have now achieved it, moving the overall NCEA level 1 pass rate from 71.5 percent to 79.6 percent. More students are achieving in numeracy and literacy, meaning more young people are set up for success in the future.

explanation: Asked for results for high-equity index schools. She supplies the figures for those schools across numeracy, reading and writing. The question is answered squarely.
question: What results has she seen for high-equity index schools?
statement: The results for students in high-equity index schools are the ones that I am the most proud of. Whilst there is still some way to go, significant improvements have been made, with positive gains in reading, writing, and maths. There was an almost 15 percent jump in numeracy achievement, from under 20 percent last year in our low-decile schools to 34.1 percent in May this year. For reading, it was 41.2 percent compared to 34.7 percent. And, again, writing held steady. We can see that the persistent effort and focus on the basics from our students, and the incredible hard work and dedication of our teachers, is achieving meaningful results.

explanation: Asked what investment she has made to support schools with the co-requisite assessments. She names it: $2.2 million in 2024 across 141 schools, with targeted training and teacher-release funding. Directly on the question, with the closing talking-point line not displacing the answer.
question: What investment has she made to support schools with the co-requisite assessments?
statement: When we were made aware of last year’s results, we knew that we needed to provide additional targeted support for young people in literacy and numeracy. That’s why in 2024 we invested $2.2 million to support students in 141 lower-decile schools to get the foundational literacy and numeracy skills they needed to get across the line. Schools received targeted training and funding for teacher-release time to support teachers to directly work with groups of students in the greatest need. This is a Government of action that responds when there is a need, and we have a relentless focus on raising student achievement.

explanation: Asked how teaching the basics will enable continued success in the co-requisite. Stanford lists the reform package (curriculum, structured literacy/maths, teacher training, an hour a day) — responsive to the 'plans to teach the basics' half, but never makes the link to co-requisite achievement that the question turned on.
question: And how will the Government’s plans to teach the basics brilliantly enable students to continue to achieve success in the co-requisite?
statement: These early improvements are supported by a comprehensive reform package that is focused on lifting academic achievement. We’ve introduced a new year-by-year curriculum that’s internationally benchmarked in English and in maths. We’ve implemented structured literacy and structured maths and provided schools with hundreds of thousands of high-quality maths text books. We’ve trained tens of thousands of teachers in structured literacy and structured maths. We’ve implemented an hour a day of reading, writing, and maths. And, today, we called time on open-plan classrooms. While these results are positive, there’s still a lot of work to be done, and that’s why this Government is unapologetically reforming an education system, with a focus on academic achievement.

explanation: Asked what recent AML/CFT announcements she has made; she states directly what she announced (simplified CDD for low-risk situations, reduced compliance costs). Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcements has she made regarding New Zealand’s anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism regime?
statement: I recently announced a series of practical changes to the anti - money-laundering and countering financing of terrorism regime to reduce red tape and costs for everyday New Zealanders. The current system is overly risk-averse, making it unnecessarily difficult and expensive for people to access basic financial services. It shouldn’t take a mountain of paperwork to open a child’s bank account or to buy a home. That’s why we’re reforming the system, introducing simpler customer due diligence for low-risk situations, supporting common-sense compliance for families and small businesses, and minimising costs wherever possible.

explanation: Asked what changes reduce red tape for family trusts; she names the change — discretion for simplified checks on low-risk trusts — and its effect. Complete answer to exactly what was asked.
question: What changes is she making to reduce unnecessary red tape for Kiwis using family trusts?
statement: The current rules make selling property held in a trust a bureaucratic nightmare. Sellers are required to provide extensive documentation about trustees, beneficiaries, and sources of wealth. I’ve announced changes to give businesses the discretion to apply simplified checks for low-risk trusts such as family trusts. This will significantly reduce paperwork, lower service costs, and make it easier for Kiwis to buy and sell homes.

explanation: A yes/no question about banking access, answered 'Yes' immediately and then substantiated. Direct and complete.
question: Will the changes the Minister makes allow more Kiwis to access banking services?
statement: Yes. Current rules have made it too hard for New Zealanders, especially children, to open basic bank accounts. As a mother, I know how important it is to teach kids early how to save. That’s why I’m changing the law to reduce the documentation needed to open low-risk accounts. In many cases, only a birth certificate and proof of a parental relationship could be required to open a bank account for a child. This will make it easier for families to start saving and help set their child up for a stronger financial future.

explanation: Asked what changes provide relief to businesses; she describes the accountant-related simplification and the removal of enhanced due diligence on every transaction. Directly on point.
question: What changes is she making to provide relief to New Zealand businesses?
statement: Many small businesses are weighed down by rigid anti - moneylaundering regulations that slow their operations and increase their costs. For businesses that use accountants, the changes I’m introducing will simplify the compliance process. Accountants will only need to confirm that payments are consistent with the business’s usual activity, removing the requirement to apply the enhanced customer due diligence checks to every transaction. This reform will save time, reduce costs, and ease the compliance burden on small businesses and their clients.

explanation: Asked how many polytechnic jobs have been cut since she took office; she gives a figure — 620 FTE, including ~150 in head office — after a responsibility caveat. The number asked for is supplied; the trailing comparison with the previous Government is surplus, not a substitute.
question: How many jobs at polytechnics have been cut, or are proposed to be cut, since she took office?
statement: While I am not responsible for staffing numbers for the business division of Te Pūkenga—or polytechnics, as they will soon be referred to—I can confirm that since I took office, staffing numbers have reduced by 620 fulltime-equivalents, including approximately 150 less in Te Pūkenga head office. This has occurred as independent financial advisers have worked with individual polytechnics to develop their pathway to financial sustainability. I acknowledge how difficult that will be for those individuals, but this work should have been done more than five years ago. I will note, for context, in contrast, Te Pūkenga took almost 2½ years from when it was set up to produce their first long-term finance strategy and a short-term financial plan—and, even then, the Tertiary Education Commission noted that further work was needed before there was a credible plan to achieve financial sustainability.

explanation: Asked why she won't guarantee all polytechnics stay open; she does supply a reason — governance sits with community-appointed councils, not Wellington — which engages the 'why won't she' core, though much of the answer diverts into the previous entity's deficits.
question: Why won’t she assure the sector that all polytechnics will still be open in two years’ time under her watch?
statement: Because, unlike that member when his party was in Government, I don’t intend to run polytechs from Wellington. They will be run by communities. They will have councils that are appointed by communities that understand what is needed in their community, and so they will have accountability for ensuring they stay on the pathway to sustainability, which I’m very grateful for because, under the previous Te Pūkenga, they ran a deficit of $80 million in 2022, a deficit of $38 million in 2023, and budgeted a further deficit—had that previous Government still been in power—

explanation: A narrow factual question about job numbers at Otago Polytechnic. She restates that determining staffing is not her responsibility, which is a recognisable ground for not answering, but she never says whether she knows the number or will provide it, and the figure is not given.
question: How many jobs are proposed to be on the chopping block at Otago Polytechnic?
statement: As I said, I don’t have responsibility for determining the staffing level. What I will say, though, is that it seems—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked for proposed job losses at five named polytechnics. The reply is a repeat of the responsibility deflection ('I continue to remind the member...'), cut off before anything else; no number and no clear declination for these institutions.
question: How many more jobs are proposed to be put on the chopping block at Toi Ohomai, Western Institute, UCOL, Whitireia, and NorthTec?
statement: I continue to remind the member that I will not be responsible for determining—

explanation: Asked how many jobs are at risk at SIT and how that compares nationally. She says it is an operational matter for the council and management — a reason for not answering — then pivots to praise for SIT. Neither the number nor the comparison is addressed.
question: Thank you. How many jobs are at risk at the Southern Institute of Technology and how does that compare with other polytechnics across the country?
statement: That will be an operational matter for the council and the management of SIT. But can I just say, I would expect SIT to continue a long and distinguished history of running in a—

explanation: Asked why she won't share the financial information. She answers the 'why': it isn't appropriate to release until each polytechnic has worked it through with its own staff. The preamble about financial advisers is padding, but the core reason is stated.
question: Why won’t she share the financial information available to her to prove that her new model is in fact financially viable?
