question: Who is his Government here to serve: banks, supermarkets, and electricity companies making billions in profit, or regular, hard-working New Zealanders?
statement: Well, as the member will be well aware, we are here to support all New Zealanders, and we’re giving particular help to low and middle income working Kiwis. We’re doing that by offering tax relief for the first time in 14 years. It’s not a deeply ideological concept, but one that is the right thing to do, given the inflation that people have encountered. We are expanding the thresholds and the coverage of things like FamilyBoost for working families who have early childcare costs. Most importantly, we’re running the economy well, because if you care about low and middle income working New Zealanders, you run the economy well so that you don’t have high inflation and high interest rates.

explanation: Asked squarely whether he takes responsibility for the job losses. He never says yes or no; he explains the losses as a consequence of the previous government's spending. Blame-shifting engages the subject matter but not the question of his own responsibility.
question: Does the Prime Minister take responsibility for the 27,000 fewer jobs and 22,000 more people unemployed than at this time last year?
statement: Well, as I’ve explained before, what happens is that when you increase Government spending by 84 percent, it drives up domestic inflation. The only tool that you’re then left with is to drive up interest rates. When interest rates go up, businesses actually have got high interest rates and high inflation costs, and, as a result, they get squeezed, the economy goes into recession, and people lose their jobs. That is the unfortunate thing when you don’t run an economy well—that is the consequence. The people who suffer are low and middle income working people, who the other side of the House used to care about but don’t.

explanation: A yes/no question about guaranteeing a job for every person made unemployed. The answer is a list of growth policies (education, science reform, red tape, trade, infrastructure) and never reaches yes or no.
question: Will the Government guarantee a job for every person that it has made unemployed?
statement: Well, we are building an economy to create jobs. We are doing that by making sure we are getting kids taught the basics brilliantly so that they can access high-paying jobs. We’re doing that by making reforms to our science sector to make sure we create value-added products and services that we can sell to the world; we are getting rid of the barnacles that led to over-compliance and higher costs by getting rid of the red tape and the green tape that’s slowing New Zealand up; and we are making sure that we are expanding—doubling—trade and attracting investment to New Zealand, as well as building modern, reliable infrastructure. Those are the things that will lift the collective living standards of all New Zealanders.

explanation: Asked why the Government makes small businesses rather than banks bear interchange fees. He recites Commerce Commission fee reductions, then gestures at the premise with 'we expect it to be built into pricing' — a partial engagement with the incidence question, but the 'why small businesses rather than banks' core is left unaddressed.
question: Why is his Government forcing small businesses into paying bank interchange fees instead of the banks, which are making billions in profit absorbing it?
statement: Well, I’d just say to the member that the Commerce Commission came out last week and identified $90 million worth of reductions that merchants are charged by, say, Mastercard and Visa. We know there has been excessive charging going on. We’re proud of the fact that we’re removing fees and surcharges for New Zealand consumers, and, actually, if there are any other charges, we expect it to be built into pricing, just like it is for everything else.

explanation: A direct will-you question about banning interchange fees. No yes, no, or 'we won't' — he restates the $90m reduction and surcharge removal already announced, answering what has been done rather than what was asked.
question: Will the Government ban banks from charging interchange fees?
statement: Well, again, what you’ve seen is a Government that’s actually done something about it by lowering the interchange fees by $90 million—the fees that are charged by Mastercard and Visa—and making sure that $65 million of excessive charges that retailers often pass on to consumers that have no bearing to the cost of those transaction fees is taken away. We’re proud of the fact that we’re taking away fees and surcharges on debit cards, credit cards, and EFTPOS payments.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement; answer is 'Āna—yes.' Complete.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “This Government takes homelessness seriously”; if not, why not?
statement: Āna—yes.

explanation: Asked how he can claim to take homelessness seriously given a 90 percent rise. He offers the justification the question demands — a list of initiatives plus an admission of imperfection — so the 'how can you say that' core is engaged, though the 90 percent figure itself is never confronted.
question: How can he say that the Government is taking homelessness seriously when homelessness in Tāmaki-makau-rau has increased by 90 percent in just nine months under this Government?
statement: No one in this Government or, indeed, this House wants to see Kiwis living without shelter or on the streets, or living homeless. That’s why we have undertaken a number of initiatives—both existing and new initiatives—to ensure that we meet these challenges head on, whether or not that’s cost-proofing the transitional housing and Housing First costs that were not cost-proofed before this Government came into administration; the Going for Housing Growth initiatives that Minister Bishop is leading; Priority One and seeing over 2,000 children come out of emergency motels; or whether it is the 1,500 community housing provider houses that we are supporting, the $500 million of support that we continue to support with transitional housing, or other things. Yes, we are not perfect. However, we are confronting these issues head-on and making sure we remain agile to some of the key homelessness concerns that confront many Kiwis.

explanation: Asked how he is putting patients first given a cut to HDC funding. He engages the funding premise squarely — describes the previous one-off time-limited increase and the further $1 million his government added, plus HDC advice on wait-list progress. He never addresses the 'putting patients first' framing head-on, but the factual core of the charge (the cut) is met.
question: How is he putting patients first when he has cut funding to the Health and Disability Commissioner to investigate instances of poor treatment and breaches of the code of patients’ rights?
statement: There was a one-off increase in funding allocated in this year’s Budget to ensure that they could continue to address the wait-list—again, a significant wait-list—and complaints made to the Health and Disability Commissioner. There was a one-off funding increase that the previous Government had put forward, which was time-limited. We have put another $1 million in—a time-limited amount of money—to continue the work that the Health and Disability Commissioner is doing to get on top of the wait-list, and the advice that I have received from the Health and Disability Commissioner is that they’re making good progress on that.

explanation: Asked whether he accepts a list of failures and personal blame. The answer is a truncated fragment that begins to pick at one sub-element (the reporting) and never reaches an accept/reject of the proposition. Effectively unanswered, though a narrow thread was being taken up.
question: Does he accept that he has cut safety systems, suppressed reporting, ignored the warning signs, and closed off accountability, and that next time when tragedy strikes, he has no one to blame but himself?
statement: Well, when it comes to the reporting which the member talked about in her question, I—

explanation: Asked what recent announcements he had made on court fine recovery. He names the announcement directly — Friday's trial of vehicle-identification technology with clamping and seizure. Squarely on the question.
question: What recent announcements has he made on the recovery of court fines? [Interruption]
statement: Last Friday, I announced that the Government is trialling new technology to identify vehicles registered to those who have overdue court fines and reparations. If they do, the vehicle may be clamped and seized by bailiffs, and the message is simple: pay your court fine and reparations, and if you haven’t—if you’ve left somebody out of pocket—you might soon find yourself walking home. We promised to find new, effective ways to get people paying their court fines, and that’s exactly what we’re delivering.

explanation: Asked why recovery of overdue fines matters. He gives the reason directly: court credibility and re-victimisation of reparations victims, with the outstanding totals. Complete answer to the question asked.
question: Why is the recovery of overdue court fines important?
statement: Because when the courts impose fines or reparations, they need to be paid, or the system loses its credibility, and for reparations victims, the victims are victimised again. As of 30 June this year, there were $456 million in fines and $104 million in reparations outstanding, and that is not something that we’re prepared to tolerate.

explanation: Asked for insight on the clamping trial's success over the weekend. He supplies the trial results — vehicles scanned, offenders identified, payment outcomes, seizure, online payment uplift. Directly responsive.
question: What insight can he share on the success of the clamping trial over the weekend?
statement: Well, 4,859 vehicles were scanned by bailiffs positioned at breath-testing stations on the weekend. Of those, 208 people were identified as having outstanding fines. The majority of them had a payment plan in place, but there were 32 that didn’t. Of those 32, 31 paid their fines in full—without a surcharge, maybe; well, we’re going to change that—and one didn’t pay, and their vehicle was seized and towed. The Ministry of Justice noticed an 11 percent increase in the number of fine payments made online yesterday. The message can’t be clear enough: there are no more excuses—pay your fines.

explanation: Asked whether people will be left stranded. Answers 'No' outright and explains bailiff arrangements. A direct yes/no plus justification; the swipe at other parties does not displace the answer.
question: Will people be left stranded on the streets?
statement: No. I’ve seen some misinformed comments by other political parties scaremongering on this issue. Bailiffs will make sure that people who have had their cars seized or clamped have arrangements to get to where they need to go. But if you don’t want to use public transport and you don’t want your cars taken, take responsibility and call 0800 4 FINES to make a payment.

explanation: Two-part question: does he stand by the statement, and why 18,000 construction jobs lost. He answers 'Yes' to the first and gives a causal account (economic downturn/recession) for the second. Both parts reached, though the second slides into recovery messaging.
question: Does he stand by his statement, “This is a Government serious about investing in New Zealand’s future. Serious about infrastructure”; if so, why have 18,000 jobs been lost in the construction sector since this Government took office?
statement: Yes, and, in response to the second part of the question, the construction sector has undoubtedly been affected by the economic downturn. In answer to her question as to why the jobs have been lost, I would say that this Government came to office in November 2023 with record inflation, a cost of living crisis, high interest rates, and, ultimately, a recession, and in a recession, as the rest of the economy has discovered and as has the construction sector, unfortunately, jobs are lost. But we are doing what we need to do as a Government to get this economy growing again, and there are green shoots of confidence coming through, through the EBOSS report and others, and I would point the member to that.

explanation: Asked why 1,000 people lost construction jobs last month. He offers a literal, dismissive answer ('their employers decided not to employ them any more') which technically responds, then pivots to the government's construction pipeline rather than the cause. Half-engaged: the question is touched but the substantive core is skirted.
question: Why did 1,000 people lose their jobs in the construction sector last month?
statement: Well, ultimately, if you want the literal answer, the employers of those people decided not to employ them any more. This Government is doing what it can do across a range of initiatives in order to support the construction sector. As the member, I think, noticed—I hope she noticed—there is $6 billion of Government-funded construction due to start in the next six months across roading, across health, and across school property, where there’s $800 million alone of school property projects about to start in the next six months. There are significant roading projects about to start—and, of course, that’s just the Government-funded part of the construction sector. As interest rates come down, there will be increased economic confidence around the construction sector, particularly residential construction, and of course we want employers to have the confidence to employ more people as the economic recovery gets under way.

explanation: A narrow factual question — how many of the 47,000 emigrants were construction workers. He says plainly he does not have the number and invites a written question, which is a direct and complete response to what he can answer, before pivoting to an attack on the Opposition. Not a dodge, but the tail-end pivot dilutes it.
question: How many of the 47,000 Kiwis who left New Zealand last year were construction workers?
statement: I don’t have that number to hand, but if the member puts it down in writing, I’m happy to look at it. I would say—as the Prime Minister rightly pointed out as the member was asking that question—the Opposition is good at talk about construction sector losses, but very bad at offering—

explanation: Asked what the sector's low confidence says about the Government's commitment to infrastructure. He answers the 'what does it say' framing directly — it says we are in a recession caused by the last Government — and lists what he says is being done. He engages the question's form but redirects it to blame rather than addressing the commitment charge.
question: What does it say about this Government’s commitment to infrastructure when the building sector is the least confident sector surveyed by the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion for July 2025?
statement: What it says is that we are in a difficult situation economically caused by the recession induced by the last Government’s profligate spending and useless economic policies. The Government cannot magic up jobs overnight. The Government cannot magic up an economic recovery. What it actually takes is sound fiscal management, reducing red tape, sensible investments in infrastructure—which the Government is doing—across health, across education, across roads, and across rail, and that will generate the economic return to form that this country needs.

explanation: Asked how he can claim seriousness given re-announcements, stopped work and apprenticeship cuts. He contests one limb of the premise (no project can be named as stopped, Lake Onslow doesn't count) and is cut off before the rest. Partial engagement with one of three elements; re-announcements and apprenticeships untouched.
question: How can he claim to be serious about infrastructure when all his Government has done is re-announce infrastructure projects, stop construction work, and slash support for apprenticeships?
statement: Well, in relation to the second part of that member’s question, it’s interesting that she can’t name a single project that has been stopped, because stopping Lake Onslow in 2035 does not affect construction jobs today. Stopping—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked what TARGETED measures for rangatahi/wāhine Māori. He names some supports (rangatahi supported accommodation, transitional housing, granny flats, papa kāinga) but they are general programmes rather than targeted measures, and wāhine Māori are never addressed. Reaches part of the question.
question: What targeted measures will he implement to support rangatahi or wāhine Māori, who the Auckland Council has shown are overrepresented among the homeless in Tāmaki-makau-rau?
statement: Yes, and I’d acknowledge that there are some cohorts in our communities—our rangatahi included—that have been disproportionately represented in housing deprivation and homelessness stats for many, many years. We continue to provide a whole range of supports, whether or not that’s rangatahi supported accommodation, transitional housing, or other avenues for those cohorts in those communities that confront these serious housing and homelessness challenges. We are also very determined to ensure that more granny flats and papa kāinga are enabled through national environmental standards changes that can help accommodate some of these folks and whānau members who are in serious housing need.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether the strategy should be grounded in Te Tiriti principles. He says 'there are many views' and pivots to supply — never says whether it should or should not be so grounded.
question: Should the Government’s housing and homelessness strategy be grounded in Te Tiriti o Waitangi principles, as recommended by the Salvation Army and the Waitangi Tribunal?
statement: There are many views around how we can better confront the homelessness and serious housing deprivation challenges. On this side of the House, we are absolutely committed to ensure that we generate more supply so more Kiwis—Māori, rangatahi, wāhine, and otherwise—can be housed.

explanation: Loaded either/or about who the Government governs for. 'We govern for all New Zealanders' rejects the binary but does directly respond to the literal question asked; it does not, however, engage the tax-cut contrast embedded in it.
question: Who is the Government governing for: the tamariki and whānau who are homeless and freezing, or the landlords that received $3 billion worth of tax cuts?
statement: Can I riff off Minister Goldsmith—we govern for all New Zealanders.

explanation: Standard 'does he stand by his Government' question. Answered 'Yes' — complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Narrow factual 'why did Te Whatu Ora hire only 45 percent of the mid-year graduate cohort'. He moves to elective surgery backlogs and praise for nurses' remuneration; no reason for the hiring rate is offered at all.
question: Why did Te Whatu Ora only hire 45 percent of the mid-year cohort of nursing graduates last year when, at the same time, over half of all day shifts in surgical wards across 16 health districts were understaffed, putting patients at risk and increasing wait times?
statement: Well, I’d just say they are all understaffed today, and there’s 1,500 people that, sadly, aren’t getting their elective surgeries. That will cause a huge amount of pain and suffering for New Zealanders. What I’d just say on nurses is that we hugely value our nurses. They do an exceptionally, exceptionally good job. [Interruption] There has been good effort over improving remuneration over a number of years—

explanation: Asked why Te Whatu Ora cited financial constraints. He recites hiring numbers, attrition and total health spend — an implicit rejection of the premise, but he never addresses why the agency said what it said.
question: Why has Te Whatu Ora said that financial constraints are the reason it cannot afford to employ more nurses to achieve safe staffing levels?
statement: Well, I’ll just say to the member that, actually, Health New Zealand has hired 2,100 extra nurses since we came to Government. Importantly, retention of our nurses has improved, with attrition rates moving from 14 percent down to 8 percent over the last two years. We have made huge investments in health—the biggest investment in health of any Government in the history of New Zealand, up $17 billion last year, up another 7 percent this year, and a billion dollars extra going into infrastructure. We’ve been working on nurse remuneration, as I outlined in my answer to the first question, and we’re making good progress there. I’d just say to the union: get round the table, negotiate, and don’t put 1,500 people’s surgeries at risk.

explanation: Asked how minimum-wage workers, nurses and teachers cope with rising costs on ~1 percent pay rises. He engages the pay-versus-inflation core only for nurses (74 percent since 2011, 11 percent increase, inflation 2.5 percent), leaving minimum-wage workers and teachers untouched.
question: Then how are minimum-wage workers, nurses, and teachers meant to shoulder rising costs like household energy bills, which have gone up 8.4 percent in the last year, with pay increases of 1 percent per year or less?
statement: Well, I just said to the member, if I just take her through nurses’ pay, it’s gone up 74 percent since 2011. It’s double what it has been on average across the economy. Nurse pay, now—we should be proud about—is at $125,000, including allowances and including overtime, and that’s comparable to New South Wales despite them being much wealthier. As I said, starting nursing salary goes from, I think, $75,773 up another $8,400 between now and June next year, and that’s an 11 percent increase. Inflation’s at 2.5 percent.

explanation: Two parts: what he says to a named nurse about staffing, and how he justifies the tax cuts. He calls the member 'plain wrong' and lists health spending, which glances at the staffing claim; Tracy Black is never responded to and the tax-cut justification is dropped entirely.
question: What does he say to Tracy Black from Whakatāne, who says, “Every day we look after someone’s mum, dad, auntie, koro, pēpē, sibling, but without enough nurses, we’re forced to make impossible choices.”, and how does he justify his choices to dish out billions in tax cuts?
statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, the member is just plain wrong. We have spent more money on healthcare than any previous Government. We’ve spent $32 billion on healthcare. One out of every $5 of Government expenditure is going into our healthcare system. We have hired 2,100 more nurses and 600 more doctors, we have got clarity on the targets and what their outcomes are going to be for patients and made it a patient-focused endeavour, and we’re improving the efficiency of Health New Zealand to deliver those people and money, to deliver improved patient outcomes.

explanation: Asked 'when exactly' Palestinian statehood will be recognised. He confirms it is a matter of 'when, not if' — a sliver of engagement — but gives no timing and redirects to hostages, aid and a ceasefire.
question: When exactly will his Government recognise Palestinian Statehood?
statement: Well, we’ve had a longstanding position, as the member well understands, about a two-State solution. It’s a question, as you’ve heard the foreign Minister say, of when, not if. But, right here, right now, in the next 24 hours, what we need the world and everyone focused on is making sure that Hamas releases hostages. We need to make sure that Israel gives unfettered humanitarian assistance and actually respects territorial integrity so it doesn’t undermine the conditions for a two-State solution. We need to have diplomacy and dialogue and a ceasefire. That’s what we need to focus on right here, right now.

explanation: Asked what recent competition announcement she made; she states the Kiwibank capital-raise approval and its scale directly.
question: What recent announcements has she made about competition?
statement: This morning, I announced that Kiwibank’s parent company Kiwi Group Capital (KGC) has been given approval by the Government to raise up to $500 million from New Zealand professional investment groups to fund the bank’s growth. This is the first step towards giving the bank access to the capital it needs to truly compete with the big four Aussie banks while retaining its intrinsic New Zealand identity. Advice to the Government is that an additional $500 million of capital could support up to $4 billion of business lending or $10 billion of home lending. That is sufficient to add competitive pressure to the market and potentially benefit customers from other banks as well Kiwibank.

explanation: Asked why the Government is increasing Kiwibank's capital; answers squarely with the Commerce Commission finding and its recommendation to capitalise Kiwibank as a disruptor.
question: Why is the Government looking to increase Kiwibank’s capital?
statement: Last year, the Commerce Commission completed a market study into competition in the personal banking services sector. The study found that the four largest banks—ANZ, ASB, BNZ, and Westpac—did not face strong competition and that competition between them for customers was sporadic. This is to the detriment of bank customers in New Zealand. The commission recommended better capitalising Kiwibank to enable it to be a disruptive competitor. The Government agrees with the commission and is giving effect to its recommendations.

explanation: Closed question 'is this an asset sale?' answered 'No', with the reason and the ownership safeguards. Direct and complete.
question: Is this an asset sale?
statement: No, this is not an asset sale as all the funds raised will go to Kiwibank to support its future business growth. There is no return of capital to the Crown. A future Government may choose to publicly list Kiwibank to raise further capital, but that won’t occur without an electoral mandate. Irrespective of any future decisions, the Government has approved measures to safeguard the bank’s New Zealand identity. These measures include maintaining at least 51 percent Government ownership of KGC for the foreseeable future, and through a Kiwi share to be held by the Crown requiring, among other measures, a majority of the directors of KGC to be normally resident in New Zealand, and Kiwibank maintaining its principal place of business in New Zealand.

explanation: Asked when we will know whether the Kiwibank investment is happening. Willis gives a concrete outer bound (KGC has until 30 June next year to complete the capital raise) and says further announcements will come when appropriate given commercial sensitivity. That engages the 'when' squarely, though it stops short of a date for public confirmation — a timeframe plus a hedge on the announcement itself.
question: When will we know if an investment in Kiwibank is occurring?
statement: Kiwi Group Capital has until 30 June next year to complete a capital raise. Giving it this amount of time will allow KGC to take account of market conditions, investor feedback, and the timing of Kiwibank’s financial results release. The capital raise will be subject to final approval of terms and conditions from shareholding Ministers and Ministers will only approve the transaction if risks have been appropriately managed and the transaction is consistent with the Government’s interests. Further announcements will be made when it is appropriate to do so, bearing in mind the commercial sensitivity of negotiations between Kiwi Group Capital and potential investors.

explanation: Standard 'does he stand by' question, answered 'Yes.' One word, complete, no evasion.
question: Does he stand by all of his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: A 'why is X a higher priority than Y' question resting on a premise. 'They're not.' rejects the premise head-on, which is a direct and complete response to what was put to him — a denial rather than a pivot. Marked slightly below 1.0 only because the questioner's core (the ranking of priorities) is answered by rebuttal rather than explanation.
question: Why are pay rises for board directors a higher priority for him than paying teachers and nurses properly?
statement: They’re not.

explanation: A narrow factual question asking for a number of unemployed/jobless/underutilised New Zealanders. No number is given at any point; the answer pivots immediately to blaming the previous government's spending for the increase and to forecasts of unemployment trending down. The specific figure asked for is never reached.
question: How many New Zealanders are currently unemployed, jobless, or part-time, and looking for more work?
statement: Well, as the member will understand, there has been an increase in unemployment, and that is a function of reckless Government spending, leading to high inflation, high interest rates, putting an economy into recession. When you are a business and you are faced with high inflation and less demand, you get squeezed, and you end up having—sadly—to lay off workers. As we have said and discussed yesterday, that has peaked and is peaking about now. With the work that this Government’s doing to get our economy growing, we expect unemployment to continue to trend down as we go forward from here.

explanation: Asked whether he knows the number of unemployed, jobless, or part-time seeking more work. He responds with a figure (~206,000 jobseekers), which engages the question directly rather than deflecting, but it is a different measure than the one asked about. He answers a neighbouring question rather than the one put — partial engagement.
question: Does he know how many New Zealanders are unemployed, jobless, or part-time, and looking for more work?
statement: Jobseeker numbers are about 206,000, from memory.

explanation: Asked why he is unaware of the 400,000+ figure. He addresses the charge directly by disputing its basis — 'it's a different question. I gave you the jobseeker unemployment numbers' — which contests the premise of unawareness rather than changing the subject. He never confirms or engages with the 400,000 figure itself, so the core is only half met.
question: Why is he unaware, as Prime Minister, that over 400,000 New Zealanders are unemployed, jobless, or part-time, and looking for more work?
statement: Well, it’s a different question. I gave you the jobseeker unemployment numbers.

explanation: Asked why Kiwis should have confidence in the economic plan given the IMF joblessness forecast. The reply is a metaphor about the arsonist complaining about smoke, a complaint about the questions themselves, and a restatement that unemployment follows the previous government's mismanagement. No reason for confidence is offered and the IMF forecast is not touched — an attack on the questioner in place of an answer.
question: Why should Kiwis have confidence in doubling down on an economic plan that the International Monetary Fund predicts will see New Zealand have the highest rate of joblessness of all Asia-Pacific countries over the next two years?
statement: Well, I just would love the member to acknowledge—it’s sort of like, as I’ve said before, it’s being the guy that started the fire and then complaining about the smoke. It’s sort of like—honestly, it is quite a perverse set of questions I get daily from here, from the other side. The reality is, we have unemployment because it’s the last thing that happens when you recklessly run the economy with high spending, high inflation, high interest rates and put it into recession, which you did.

explanation: A yes/no question: is construction back on track, given 758 liquidations. He stays on the topic of construction but explains why the sector is struggling (interest-rate sensitivity, boom-bust exposure) rather than saying whether it is back on track, and the liquidation figure goes unaddressed before the answer is cut off. Adjacent to the question without reaching it.
question: Is the construction industry back on track, now that construction companies are collapsing at four times the rate they were before he became Prime Minister, with 758 construction firms going into liquidation in just the past year?
statement: Well, I’ll just say that the real reason that the construction sector has faced some big challenges—and let’s be clear, construction hits the booms and it hits the busts harder than any other sector in our economy—is because it’s very reliant upon something called interest rates. When interest rates go high, you actually have to borrow for development, and, as a result, that ends up squeezing and putting huge pressure on our construction firms. But I just want to say to the member: I appreciate the member’s—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked whether he will take responsibility for 18,000 construction jobs lost. Responsibility is neither accepted nor declined; the answer lists the $6 billion pipeline and construction activity, then turns on the questioner over crocodile tears and PPP positioning. The actual ask — will he take responsibility — is never answered either way.
question: So if everything the Government’s doing in construction is working so well, will he take responsibility for the fact that since he became Prime Minister, 18,000 jobs have disappeared from the construction sector, a number that continues to grow every month under his leadership?
statement: Well, this Government is doing everything it can. We have a $6 billion pipeline of Government projects between now and Christmas with shovels on the ground. We are building more schools and classrooms, we are building more houses, and we are doing more on hospital and health infrastructure. So we are doing everything we can to make sure that our construction sector is set up well, and I’d just say to the member: if you really cared about it—instead of the crocodile tears—get one position on PPPs.

explanation: Asked why 6,000 high-skilled jobs have been lost given cutbacks to spending projects. 'I disagree' plus the $6 billion commitment directly contests the premise of the question (that his Government has cut back), which is engagement rather than evasion. But the job losses themselves are not explained or accounted for, and the close is a demand that the member support roads of national significance — so only half the question is met.
question: If that’s so successful, why have we lost 6,000 high-skilled jobs, such as engineers, with civil contractors saying that they urgently need a lot more work to feed the industry because his Government has cut back on spending projects?
statement: I disagree. This Government is committed to $6 billion worth of Government spending between now and Christmas. It’s spending more on schools, hospitals, roads. If the member cares about it, support roads of national significance; support Investment Boost.

explanation: Asked, in a loaded metaphor, whether his 'cracking open the construction industry' claim amounted to wrecking it. He dismisses the framing as 'too cute by half' and asserts the opposite — picking up the mess, powering up the sector — which does reject the characterisation put to him. Much of the reply is directed at the questioner's record rather than his own claim, so the engagement is thin but present.
question: So when he claimed earlier this year that he was “cracking open the construction industry”, was he cracking it open in the way that a wrecking ball cracks open a building?
statement: Too cute by half, isn’t it? It’s a lovely metaphor. But, actually, son, let me just say: we’re getting the show on the road. We are picking up your mess. Unemployment’s the last thing, given your woeful economic mismanagement. And construction—we are doing everything we can to power up that sector, and we are going to do that.

asker: Te Pāti Māori—Te Tai Tokerau MARIAMENO KAPA-KINGI
explanation: Asked for a response to the Māori vs non-Māori suspected-suicide rate disparity (51.9 vs 16.4 per 100,000). The attributed reply contains no response at all — it is a further question about evidence-based initiatives in the next Suicide Prevention Action Plan. The question asked is never engaged. (Likely a pairing artifact: the 'answer' is another member's supplementary, not a minister's reply.)
question: What is his response to the rate of suspected suicide which, according to Te Whatu Ora’s data for 2022, is 51.9 per 100,000 for Māori males aged 25-44 years compared to 16.4 per 100,000 for non-Māori males?
statement: What evidence-based initiatives that specifically address suicide rates is the Minister considering in the next five-year Suicide Prevention Action Plan, and how will these address the disparities of suicide rates between Māori and non-Māori?

asker: Te Pāti Māori—Te Tai Tokerau MARIAMENO KAPA-KINGI
explanation: Asked whether the I Am Hope trust's free school counselling has made a difference to the youth suicide inequity (34.1 vs 16.9 per 100,000). The attributed reply asks a fresh question about what Māori-specific suicide-prevention initiatives are funded; it never addresses I Am Hope or any difference made. No engagement with the question.
question: Therefore, has the I Am Hope trust, who provide free counselling in schools, made a different to the inequity of youth suicide rates between Māori and non-Māori, which was 34.1 per 100,000 for rangatahi Māori compared to 16.9 for non-Māori youth?
statement: What Māori-specific initiatives is the Minister funding with regard to suicide prevention?

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with the Public Health Communication Centre report that Ka Ora, Ka Ako alleviates hunger and improves achievement, and if not why not. The attributed response is instead a request for a guarantee about quality, nutrition and student numbers — a different question. The agree/disagree core is untouched.
question: Does he agree with the Public Health Communication Centre Aotearoa report on Ka Ora, Ka Ako that “the evidence is clear: Ka Ora, Ka Ako alleviates hunger and less hunger improves school achievement”; if not, why not?
statement: Can he guarantee that the quality, nutritional value, and the number of students receiving free lunches will not decline because of these cost-cutting measures?

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with Sir Wayne Shelford's statement that NZ's veterans legislation is discriminatory and inadequate. The attributed response asks what the Minister will tell veterans removed from the VIP waiting list before Anzac Day — a separate question. The agreement question is never answered.
question: Does he agree with RSA National President Sir Wayne Shelford that “New Zealand has legislation that is discriminatory and inadequately provides for New Zealand’s veterans of military service”?
statement: What will the Minister, given that it is two weeks until Anzac Day, be telling those veterans who have been removed from the waiting list for Veterans’ Independence Programme (VIP) services?

explanation: Genter asks the Minister to address a specific technical point: whether a measure of housing affordability would include transport costs. Bishop replies only 'I'm happy to answer it.' He engages the request squarely at the level of willingness — he does not pivot, attack, or change subject — but the substantive core (does the measure include transport costs, yes or no) is never reached in the response as recorded. Partial engagement: acknowledges the question without delivering an answer to it.
question: Yeah, I appreciate the answer. However, I did ask a very specific, technical question, and I would love it if the Minister would address that part of the question, because the question was very specific about whether a measure of a housing affordability would include transport costs.
statement: I’m happy to answer it.

explanation: The captured question text is only the te reo preamble ("My question is to the Minister of Police"), so the substantive ask is not in the record, but Mitchell's response engages a specific line of questioning about firearms advice head-on: he names the particular briefings (info 23-02, info 24-35), states they cover the topics raised, and says they have already been released under the OIA with other titles proactively published monthly. That is a squarely responsive answer to an advice-related question rather than a pivot, so it scores high; the deduction reflects only that the truncated question makes complete alignment unverifiable. Other pairs in this batch were omitted as ineligible: 2024-08-07-b07-3 and -4, 2024-10-24-b03-5 and 2024-10-24-b08-5 are points of order; 2024-08-21-b09-3, -6, 2024-08-28-b02-4, 2024-09-11-b07-5 and 2024-09-17-b09-6 are heckles or rhetorical interjections, not questions; 2024-08-08-b07-0 and 2024-09-11-b12-0 have the 'answer' attributed to the questioner (a supplementary question, not a response), so there is no attributable answer to score.
question: Ko taku pātai ki te Minita o ngā Pirihimana o Aotearoa.
statement: Much of the advice that I’ve received regarding firearms includes advice specifically relating to those topics—briefings info 23-02 and info 24-35. Both provide specific advice on the topics. These have previously been released under the Official Information Act. The member is aware that the titles of other advice I’ve received are proactively released monthly on the Police website.

explanation: Jackson's challenge has a definite propositional core: the information has not been released publicly. Potaka never touches the release question at all — he rises on a point of order about a separate accusation (interference in Te Rōpū Whakahaere) and demands a withdrawal. This is a pivot away from the point put to him and, in part, a turn against the questioner. Whether or not raising the point of order was procedurally proper is irrelevant here; as a response to what was asked, the core was left entirely unaddressed.
question: It hasn’t been released publicly, this information.
statement: Point of order, Mr Speaker. The member has made an accusation that I have interfered with the whakahaeretanga or the operations of Te Rōpū Whakahaere. If that accusation is proved to be inaccurate, then I would expect the member to withdraw and apologise.

explanation: Verrall's interjection puts a jibe with a discernible core — that Seymour is inserting himself into a question that is not his. He opens with 'Yes, I most certainly can', which does engage the implied challenge about his standing to answer, so it is not a pure dodge. But the remainder leaves the challenge behind and becomes a general Pharmac achievement list (solid tumours, blood cancers, glucose monitors, 'access to medicines at a level never before seen'), which is a different subject from what was put to him. Partial engagement followed by a pivot.
question: Oh! He wants to be in this question now.
statement: Yes, I most certainly can, and that is an example of the decisions that Pharmac is making in order to ensure the money is put to the best possible use. It benefits people with solid tumours; it benefits people with blood cancers; but it also benefits people, for example, with type 1 diabetes, who now have continuous glucose monitors funded by the taxpayer through Pharmac. Right across the board, this Government is improving access to medicines at a level never before seen in this country.

explanation: Prime's interjection makes a specific charge about the curriculum containing 'too much Māori'. Stanford meets that charge on its own ground rather than sidestepping it: she names Māori content that should be taught (the Land Wars, Meri Te Tai), and then states her actual position — the problem as she sees it is that the history curriculum is too localised and inconsistent, and certain national content will be made universal. That is a response to the substance of the interjection, not a talking-point pivot. It falls short of full marks because she never squarely accepts or rejects the 'too much' framing itself, answering instead on consistency and localisation.
question: Too much Māori!
statement: That member should listen, because this is quite important. There are certain things like the Māori Land Wars, and people like Meri Te Tai, that we should all learn about. Unfortunately, the history curriculum is far too localised and it’s not consistent enough. We are going to make sure that there are certain things that every single child in New Zealand should learn about our national history and how it links to international events.

explanation: Swarbrick puts a narrow, numeric point to the Prime Minister: the NDCs, $24 billion. The figure is never engaged — not confirmed, not disputed, not reframed. Instead the reply turns immediately on the questioner's motives ('if you actually cared about the environment'). A specific quantitative challenge met with an attack on the person asking is the clearest form of non-answer; the number is still never given.
question: The NDCs, Christopher. It’s $24 billion.
statement: I’d just say to that member, if you actually cared about the environment—

explanation: Belich restates her question as being about the operations of the Crown entity (ACC), pressing that the Minister is obliged to monitor and review those operations. Simpson engages the substance rather than pivoting away: he states what the entity did (an operational decision), what it told him (the programme is merely paused for evaluation), and where he stands relative to it (arm's length). The core of the question — what is happening with that operation — is reached, but the responsibility half of her point (that he is meant to be involved in monitoring it) is deflected by the arm's-length framing rather than addressed. Partial engagement, so mid-range.
question: I seek your guidance. In anticipation of the Minister not answering that question, I did check the Cabinet Manual, and in relation to Ministers and Crown entities, it quite clearly states that he is to be involved and to monitor and review Crown entity operations and performance. My question was around the operations of that Crown entity.
statement: Thank you, Mr Speaker. ACC, as an independent Crown entity, have made an operational decision, and I stand at arm’s length from that operational decision. They have advised me that they are merely pausing the programme to evaluate it.

explanation: Asked what steps he has taken to reduce councils' use of road cones. The attributed response is only "Well—" before interruption; no step is named, so the question goes unanswered in this pair.
question: What steps has he taken to reduce councils’ use of road cones in New Zealand?
statement: Well—[Interruption]

explanation: Asked for evidence that a risk-based approach will reduce road cones. He supplies exactly that: State highway spend on temporary traffic management halved (15.8%→8.8% of maintenance, 6%→2.3% of capital), and explains the mechanism for extending it to councils via NZTA funding. Squarely on the question.
question: What evidence does the Minister have that a risk-based approach to temporary management will work to reduce the number of road cones?
statement: I’ve got good news. The amount of money spent on temporary traffic management has reduced on our State highways from 15.8 percent of maintenance cost, down to 8.8 percent—it’s about a halving—and from 6 percent of the cost of capital projects, down to just 2.3 percent. That’s on the State highway network. Now, what we’re doing is saying to councils, “You’ve got to adopt the guide, not the code, and if you don’t, no New Zealand Transport Agency (NZTA) Government money will flow, because we want the benefits we’re seeing on the State highway network from NZTA to also apply on the local road network.”

explanation: Asked why the Government is making the changes. He gives the reason directly — a quarter of 12,000 inspections found redundant traffic management, wasting time and ratepayer money. The 'why' is reached explicitly.
question: Why is the Government making these changes to temporary traffic management?
statement: I’ve got some figures from quarter 3 this year, which show that of 12,000 inspections of temporary traffic management on local roads, over 3,000—which is about a quarter—were found to be completely redundant. In other words, a quarter of the time, people were driving past road cones and temporary traffic management that had no merit or need for it at all. That, of course, drives people bananas and it slows people down and, of course, creates congestion, and, most of all, it’s a waste of taxpayers’ and ratepayers’ money. We are taking action.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement on recognising Palestinian statehood. Answers "Yes" and elaborates on the position. Direct and complete.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “It is a matter of when, not if, New Zealand will recognise Palestine Statehood”; if not, why not?
statement: Yes, we steadfastly support the establishment of a Palestinian State and the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination. We have done so for decades. As a strong proponent of the two-State solution, we wish to see an immediate end to the appalling humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza and for Israelis and Palestinians to be living side by side in peace and security. Very importantly, we have spoken to a range of countries all around the world, including speaking to the Palestinian Authority, who understand our position.

explanation: Asked whether now is the time to recognise Palestine and, if not, when. He effectively answers 'not now' by listing the preconditions required, engaging the substance, but supplies conditions rather than the 'when' the question expressly requested. Partial.
question: Is now the time for the New Zealand Government to recognise Palestine as a State, and, if not, when?
statement: New Zealand has consistently said that we are willing to recognise Palestine—and that it is a question of when, not if—but we do need to see progress on some of the fundamental issues relating to a Palestinian State’s legitimacy and viability, including representative governance, commitments to non-violence, regional support, and security guarantees for Israel. If we recognise the State of Palestine, New Zealand wants to know that what we are recognising is a legitimate, representative, viable political entity.

explanation: Asked how he will match the stance with tangible actions *now*, such as further sanctions or humanitarian support. He responds within the frame — sanctions and aid — but describes existing and continuing measures rather than the further/new action asked about. Half-answers.
question: How will he match his evolving stance on recognition of a Palestinian State with tangible actions now, such as further sanctions or desperately needed humanitarian support?
statement: The reality was that we have already had sanctions with respect to people both in Palestine and in Israel, and we’ve continued, to the best that we possibly can, through various agencies, our financial aid and support.

explanation: Asked whether New Zealand is ready to provide aid to Gaza immediately if the blockade lifts. Answers "Yes", which disposes of the question and makes the conditional second limb moot. One word, complete.
question: Is New Zealand ready to provide aid to Gaza immediately, in the case that Israel lifts its blockade, and, if not, what measures is he taking to make that happen?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked a narrow two-part question — would recognition carry further conditions on a ceasefire, and would it follow the UK model or be unconditional. The reply attacks the questioner's 'colonial mindset' and never touches either limb. A clear pivot away from a specific question.
question: Would New Zealand’s recognition of a Palestinian State have even further conditions on Israel agreeing to a ceasefire; and will it be in line with that of the United Kingdom, or would it be unconditional like other partners?
statement: We are not going to adopt the colonial mindset of some MPs. We remember the Statute of—

explanation: Asked whether he supports all the statements and actions of his Government. Answers "Yes" — direct and complete.
question: E tautoko ana ia i ngā kōrero me ngā mahi katoa a tōna Kāwanatanga?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked for the cause of a 90% rise in rough sleeping and whether it was the emergency housing policy change. Luxon never engages the causal question — he cites $550m of social service spending and the 2,100 kids out of motels, and attacks the previous Government's policy. The 'if not... policy changes' core is never confirmed or denied.
question: Why have Auckland Council outreach teams recorded a 90 percent increase in people sleeping rough if not, in the words of Auckland councillor Angela Dalton, recent Government policy changes have “made it harder to access emergency housing.”?
statement: Well, again, I’d say to the member: no Kiwi wants to see New Zealanders homeless. That’s why this Government spends $550 million a year in different social services organisations. We’re hoping to see whether there’s anything more that we can do to get more efficiency from that spend and more results, but, of course, the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) remains open to support people who need help and assistance in housing. But I am incredibly proud that we’ve moved 2,100 kids out of motel accommodation, which seemed to be the policy of the last Government.

explanation: A narrow question about what he expected when officials warned his changes would create rough sleeping. The answer is entirely rent, State house wait-list and motel-exit talking points; it never touches the official advice or what he anticipated. Concedes only 'work to do on homelessness'.
question: What exactly did the Prime Minister think would happen when his officials told him that his Government’s emergency housing changes would “create rough sleeping, people living in cars, and overcrowding.”?
statement: Well, I’m incredibly proud of the work that we’re doing to make housing more affordable for New Zealanders. We are in a situation where rent is stable; it’s probably come down about $5 a week versus being at $180 a week when we came to Government. We’ve taken 6,000 people out of the State house wait-list and got them into proper homes, and we’ve put 2,100 kids into homes by prioritising them if they’ve been in motels for longer than 12 weeks. We know that there’s still work to do on homelessness, but we have services available to support, and we’ll continue to look at that.

explanation: Asked how a person proves they did not contribute to their own homelessness. He gestures at the question once — 'MSD will have some criteria... and will work that through' — which acknowledges the mechanism exists but does not describe it, then pivots to supply, rents, wait-lists and motels. Barely reaches the question.
question: How exactly does someone prove that they did not “contribute to their own homelessness”, as his Government now requires people to do in order to get help to stop them being homeless?
statement: Well, again, MSD will have some criteria by which it engages with people who need assistance and help, and will work that through. But I’m just saying to the member, we know we have more work to do on housing, but it is actually about a supply of housing; it’s about making it more affordable. The good news is that, actually, rents are stable for people who are renting; people who are on a State house wait-list, that wait-list is coming down after having been driven up four times by the previous Minister of Housing; and, actually, we’ve taken 2,100 kids in 1,000 households out of dank, dark motel rooms because we want to make sure they’re in proper homes and houses. We continue to spend half a billion dollars with support organisations that can work with people with very complex needs—often in mental health, often in addiction—and will continue to do so.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether he has considered her invitations to visit Auckland Central. No yes, no no, no mention of his diary or the invitations; he says another Minister visited Auckland and pivots to homelessness under the previous Government.
question: Has the Prime Minister yet “considered in the context of my diary” the many invitations that I have made with him to visit Auckland Central and meet the people that he has made homeless?
statement: I can just say to the member that the Minister for infrastructure and housing was there last Friday, meeting with the commissioner in Auckland, and very open to looking at better ways to deliver better outcomes. But as the member would well know, under a previous Labour-Greens Government, homelessness went up 37 percent. It is a complex issue, and this Government is working its way through the myriad of housing issues that exist, because they’re often interrelated.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his statement on patient safety. He says 'In the context it was made, yes' — a direct and complete answer; the subsequent record recitation is padding but does not displace the answer.
question: Does he stand by his statement that “Patient safety is critical to ensure Kiwis have confidence in our healthcare system”?
statement: In the context it was made, yes. Patient safety is critical to ensuring Kiwis have confidence in our healthcare system, and that’s why we’re focusing the system on the needs of patients. Our Government inherited significant wait-lists, which meant that too many patients have been left waiting too long for the care they need, facing unacceptable delays. That’s why we’ve brought back health targets to drive accountability, invested a record $16.68 billion across three Budgets, and strengthened our front-line health workforce. These steps are delivering results, but we know there’s much more work to do. We’re putting patients first, and we won’t stop until New Zealanders get the timely, quality care they deserve.

explanation: Asked specifically why Health NZ's formulation is 'wherever we can' rather than 'always and in all hospitals'. He offers no account of that wording or the qualification behind it, substituting a commitment statement and staffing numbers.
question: Why is Health New Zealand’s answer to nurses’ call for safe staffing that they’re working towards safe staffing “wherever we can”, and not “always and in all hospitals”?
statement: Well, the answer to that question is that Health New Zealand is committed to ensuring the safety of its patients and making sure that we are focusing on reducing wait-lists. Under this Government, we’ve seen a significant increase in resource on the front line, with 2,100 more nurses working at Health New Zealand and over 600 more doctors, and that is about making sure that we are delivering the healthcare that New Zealanders need.

explanation: A yes/no question about whether he will listen to the picketing nurses' reports. He never says whether he will listen, nor addresses the bed-changing claim; he recites funding and workforce figures instead.
question: Will he listen to calls from picketing nurses who report that there aren’t enough staff to change beds after patients have soiled themselves?
statement: This Government is focused on delivering the increased resource to the front line. That’s why we’ve invested an additional $16.68 billion over three Budgets, that’s why we are focusing—there’s over 2,100 more nurses working at Health New Zealand today than in 2023 and over 600 more doctors, and our expectation of Health New Zealand is to make sure they’re delivering the timely, quality healthcare that all New Zealanders need and deserve.

explanation: Asked whether he understands the link between staffing shortages and in-hospital infections. He explicitly swaps the subject — 'what I understand is that when we have a nationwide strike...' — and answers about strike-cancelled operations, never engaging the staffing/infection link.
question: Does he understand that not having enough nurses to change beds and treat wounds is exactly what leads to the increase in in-hospital infections that I asked him about yesterday?
statement: Well, what I understand is that when we have a nationwide strike when the union walks off the job, we have thousands of patients not receiving the care that they need—patients who have been waiting far too long. Today, 1,500 patients are missing out on the hip, knee, and cataract operations that they deserve, thousands are missing out on the first specialist appointments they need, people needing diagnostic scans and screening are missing out on the care that they need, and I say to the union: get back to the negotiating table.

explanation: Two-part question: does 'fiscally constrained' mean underfunding, and can patient safety be guaranteed? The record-funding claim functions as an implicit 'no' to the underfunding half, so the question is glanced at, but the patient-safety half is untouched and he closes by turning the questioner's own letter back on her.
question: When Health New Zealand officials state that a fiscally constrained environment is stopping them from achieving safe staffing, do they actually mean that the Government has underfunded the health system and that patient safety can’t be guaranteed?
statement: Well, this Government is investing record funds into Health New Zealand—$16.68 billion in additional funding into Health New Zealand over three Budgets—but I would also note a quote that I’d like to read, which says, “Given the level of funding provided, it is imperative you remain in financial balance.” That was in a letter to Health New Zealand by none other than the Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall.

explanation: Asked what recent announcement was made on checkout transparency. He identifies it — surcharges at the checkout will be banned — and states its effect. Answers the question, with campaign flourish attached.
question: What recent announcement has the Government made about increasing transparency at the checkout?
statement: Well, those pesky surcharges at the checkout will soon be a thing of the past under this Government. This decision has struck a real chord with Kiwis, and I’ve received overwhelming positive feedback from fellow shoppers who are tired of being stung at the till. It’s a simple change that delivers greater transparency at the checkout, and it ensures that people know exactly what they’re going to be paying when they make a purchase. On this side of the House, we’ve heard their frustration and we’re doing something about it.

explanation: Asked how the surcharge announcement relates to the Commerce Commission's interchange fee decision. He states the relation squarely: the cap cuts retailer costs while the surcharge ban ensures those savings reach consumers — both sides of the same equation.
question: How does this relate to the Commerce Commission’s decision a fortnight ago on interchange fees?
statement: Well, that’s a good, insightful question, because two weeks ago, the Commerce Commission announced their decision to cap and reduce interchange fees from December of this year. Now, those are the behind-the-scene charges that are imposed on retailers when customers pay by card. These fees make up about 60 percent of total payment processing costs, and the cap is expected to save businesses around $90 million a year. Now, at the same time, we know that consumers are paying around $65 million a year more than they should in surcharges. Together, these reforms work to tackle both sides of the equation, to lower the cost for businesses and, at the same time, ensuring that those costs, that lower cost, is actually passed on to consumers at the point of sale.

explanation: Asked what he would say to small businesses concerned about the surcharging ban. He speaks directly to those concerns: fees reduced and capped, $90m saving, and overseas evidence that prices did not rise. Squarely on the question asked.
question: What would the Minister say to those concerned about the impact of this change on small businesses?
statement: As I said, it’s important to clarify that the surcharging ban is in conjunction with the Commerce Commission’s recent decision, and that’s a move that will mean a saving of $90 million a year for businesses. Businesses will, of course, still incur fees, but these have been greatly reduced by the Commerce Commission’s decision, and they’re capped at a rate that is deemed fair and reasonable by the Commission. Now, some businesses may be worried that they need to adjust their prices, but overseas experience—in the United Kingdom and in the European Union, when similar bans have been put in place—indicates that that is not likely to happen. Ultimately, a ban on surcharging is about making sure that the price of goods and services is transparent for everyone.

explanation: Asked why the ban is only being explored now. The answer never touches timing or prior inaction — it pivots entirely to praise of the Government for backing customers. The 'why now' core is untouched.
question: Why has a ban on surcharging only been explored now?
statement: On this side of the House, we’re proud to say that we back Kiwi customers. We know how frustrated they are when they get to the till and they get stung with a surprise—a surcharge on their purchases. In this Government, Kiwis have a pragmatic, reasonable, responsible Government prepared to make decisions of this sort to make people’s lives easier, and they’re loving it.

explanation: Two-part question. Part one (does she agree with the 2023 quote) is answered explicitly 'yes', with context. Part two (how 1% helps) is met with a plain, stated refusal to comment on active bargaining — a direct declination, not a dodge. Some drift into inflation figures, but both parts are engaged.
question: Does she agree with Erica Stanford, who said in 2023 that “we’re in a cost of living crisis and everyone is feeling the pinch really, really badly. Teachers are no different than anyone else”; if so, how will a proposed one percent pay increase help secondary teachers with the cost of living crisis?
statement: In answer to the first part of the question, that quote was from a breakfast TV political panel in March 2023—extraordinarily tough times that we’ve not seen in many decades. In this story, inflation was quoted to be running at 7.2 percent; food inflation for the March quarter was 12.1 percent. So, yes, I agree with Erica Stanford on that show, at that time, that we were in a terrible cost of living crisis, which we were subsequently voted in to resolve. Inflation is now within the target band, at 2.7 percent. Interest rates have fallen, and many families are refixing their mortgages and saving up to $740 a month. While there is more to do, our careful economic management has seen results. In response to the second part of the question, I’m not going to comment on an active bargaining process.

explanation: Asked why teachers get 1% while tobacco companies get hundreds of millions. She plainly refuses to comment on the bargaining process — a clear declination on the teacher-pay half, which counts as engaging. But the tobacco comparison is left entirely unaddressed and is not covered by the bargaining exemption.
question: Why were teachers offered 1 percent but tobacco companies get hundreds of millions?
statement: As I have already said, I am not at liberty to comment on the bargaining process that is actively under way.

explanation: Asked what the 80%-vs-1% gap says about priorities. She refers back to her prior refusal — an explicit, unambiguous declination to answer rather than a filibuster, so it engages the question by declining it; but the board-member pay element again falls outside the bargaining ground she invokes.
question: What does it say about the Government’s priorities when board members get an 80 percent pay increase but teachers only get 1 percent?
statement: My answer is the same as for the previous question.

explanation: Asked whether 1% is an effective pay cut given food and power price rises. She states plainly that she is not at liberty to comment while bargaining is under way. A blunt refusal, but a direct and complete response to the question put.
question: Is 1 percent an effective pay cut when the food prices are up 4.6 percent and electricity has increased 8.4 percent since last year?
statement: We are still in the middle of active bargaining, and I’m not at liberty to comment on that.

explanation: Two parts: does she stand by the statement, and does she think teachers deserve a pay cut. She declines the second on bargaining grounds and answers the first with an unambiguous 'yes, I stand by it', then substantiates. Both limbs are engaged — one answered, one plainly refused.
question: Does she stand by her statement that teachers deserve what this Government has been delivering them; if so, does she believe teachers deserve an effective pay cut?
statement: As I’ve already said, I’m not at liberty to talk about bargaining when we’re in the middle of it, but what I will do is stand by the statement I made in the House last question time: that, yes, teachers do deserve what this Government has been providing them outside of collective bargaining. I have made sure that we’ve pumped $750 million into learning support, because that’s what they asked us for. We created a new English and maths curriculum that we’ve fully funded and that we have all the professional learning and development for and all of the resources for. We’ve flooded 830,000 maths books into classes so that teachers wouldn’t have to keep photocopying resources every day of the week. We have been backing this teacher workforce, which is why more of them want to be teachers, because they want to be a part of this.

explanation: Asked why teachers should believe the Government is on their side. She disputes the question's admissibility and tells the member not to conflate pay equity with bargaining, but never offers any answer to why teachers should believe it — a rejection of the premise standing in place of a response.
question: Why should teachers believe this Government is on their side when it cancels pay equity and offers them an effective pay cut?
statement: I don’t think that question is at all in line with the primary question, and I said it in the last answer that I gave, at the last questioning, when I said that the member really needs to not conflate pay equity with collective bargaining.

explanation: Asked what recent health and safety announcements she has made. She enumerates them sector by sector — construction, agriculture, manufacturing. Exactly what was asked.
question: What recent announcements has she made on health and safety reform?
statement: This week, I have announced a range of sector-specific changes that my officials will be engaging industry on. I want to preserve the rural Kiwi way of life and ensure across all industries that the rules are simple, workable, and based on the on-the-ground reality. For construction, I announced that my officials will be consulting on changes to scaffolding rules, streamlining pre-qualifications, and providing better guidance on overlapping duties to improve productivity in the building sector. For agriculture, I’ve asked WorkSafe to engage farming communities to produce approved codes of practice to clarify the duties for different roles on the farm and for the safe use of farm vehicles. I have also asked my officials to ensure the existing regulations that stop kids working on farms do not prevent common-sense activities. We will be consulting rural communities on these. For manufacturing, I announced that we will be making long-overdue updates to machine guarding regulations—that my officials will be consulting on—so the rules are fit for purpose.

explanation: Asked who she heard from. She names the sources directly: submissions, the roadshow, Rural Women NZ, builders, SARNZ, Ports of Auckland, forestry, meat and wood processing. Fully responsive.
question: Who did you hear from to suggest these changes were needed?
statement: These changes are a result of feedback I’ve heard from submissions, my nationwide health and safety roadshow, and suggestions from colleagues. I heard from Rural Women New Zealand, who suggested the rules around kids on farms are uncertain. I want to ensure Kiwi kids can be involved in rural life. I’ve heard from builders, Scaffolding, Access and Rigging New Zealand (SARNZ), Ports of Auckland, and the forestry sector, that the current scaffolding rules are not fit for purpose. I’ve heard from a wide range of sectors that the machine guarding rules are out of date. From the meat industry to wood processors, there is widespread agreement that these rules need to reflect reality.

explanation: Asked why the announcements are being made now. She addresses timing — the earlier tranche of Act changes is done, she is now moving to WorkSafe and industry specifics, and signalling that reform continues after the roadshow. Reaches the 'why now' question, if somewhat loosely.
question: Why are you making these announcements now?
statement: There has been high interest in this Government’s health and safety changes. We have announced changes to the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 for landownership, small business carve-outs, directors, and the overall focus of the Act on critical risk. I am now announcing major changes to WorkSafe and digging deeper into specific industry concerns. I am letting Kiwis know that the roadshow might be over but the reforms continue, and we are continuing to listen and make these changes with Kiwis who have to work in these situations every day.

explanation: Asked what reports she has seen on her changes. She lists the specific bodies and their reactions. Directly and completely on point.
question: What recent reports has she seen on her changes?
statement: I have seen wide support for these announcements from Construction Health and Safety New Zealand, which represents the construction sector, welcoming improvements for pre-qualifications; SARNZ, which represents the scaffolding sector, welcoming a review of scaffolding; as well as the Wood Processors and Manufacturers Association, welcoming wood dust and welding fume improvements; as well as Business Canterbury, welcoming manufacturing settings and getting those right for machine guarding. I’ve heard from Federated Farmers, which represents the agricultural sector, who is welcoming proposals to make farm health and safety more practical and grounded in real-world farming.

explanation: Asked whether he stands by his Government's statements and actions; answered "Yes." One word, complete, squarely responsive.
question: Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked whether he agrees with his own quoted statement; answered "Yes." Direct and complete.
question: Does he agree with the statement he made during his speech on foreign affairs and trade on 10 April 2025 that “As Prime Minister, I have a responsibility to do everything I can to bolster the existing rules-based international order.”?
statement: Yes.

explanation: Asked how he is fulfilling the responsibility to uphold the international order given no sanctions on Israel. He disputes the framing but then answers the 'how': travel bans on two politicians, four tranches of bans on settlers, and consistent communication of concerns as the best available lever. The specific 'why not real sanctions' element is only implicitly addressed (limited influence/trade), so it stops short of complete.
question: How is he fulfilling his responsibility to uphold the rules-based international order by refusing to impose real sanctions on Israel as Palestinians are starved, slaughtered, and denied medical aid?
statement: Well, I disagree with the characterisation of that question. This is a Government that has recently placed travel bans on two extremist politicians who have been undermining the prospects of a two-State solution. It is a Government that has had four tranches now of travel bans on extremist Israeli settlers. Frankly, the best influencing that we can exert from this part of the world, with limited influence and limited trade, is to make sure that we are consistently and clearly communicating our concerns to Israel.

explanation: Asked what part of the rules-based order permits starvation and slaughter of civilians. The reply never engages that question — it recites what NZ has called for and the joint ministerial statements it has signed. It stays on the topic but answers a different question (what are you doing) than the one asked.
question: What part of the rules-based international order allows for the starvation and slaughter of innocent civilians?
statement: Well, I think, as you’ve heard, leaders all around the world, including our Minister of Foreign Affairs and myself, have talked to this issue over a number of months now. We want to see unfettered, free and flowing, humanitarian assistance into what is an absolutely appalling catastrophe, and that is what we have been calling for consistently. We are a small country, but we amplify our voice by joining with other countries to call for action in that regard. That’s why we have joined a series of ministerial statements over a number of months to make that case.

explanation: Asked whether upholding the order matters only when politically convenient; answered "No, and we're not doing that." Direct denial, complete.
question: Is it only important to uphold the rules-based international order when it is politically convenient?
statement: No, and we’re not doing that.

explanation: Asked why he is advancing reforms the Attorney-General warned breach NZBORA and disenfranchise voters. He does give a 'why': section 7 reports have accompanied other successful policies, and 13 days is ample enrolment time versus Australia's 26. The disenfranchisement and disproportionate-Māori-harm limbs are left untouched, so it engages the core but not the whole.
question: Why is the Prime Minister advancing electoral reforms that the Attorney-General has warned will breach the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act (NZBORA), disenfranchise over 100,000 people, and will disproportionately harm Māori and Pasifika voters?
statement: Well, the Attorney-General is fulfilling an independent role to review regulation. We would have received NZBORA section 7 reports, for example, for breath testing and for gang patches. Both those policies have been huge successes. Here, what we’re doing is making sure that people have 13 days to get enrolled. That is half the time that the Australians have, and it just represents the fact that New Zealanders are very smart people and will be able to get enrolled in 13 days before an election, rather than 26 like the Australians.

explanation: Asked whether he is aware of reports of Māori voters being removed from the roll; answered "I'm unaware of that" and referred it to the Minister of Justice. The awareness question is answered outright; the remainder is padding that does not detract.
